meaning: dishonest trickery used to gain money
example: The online charity turned out to be a fraud.
hook: A fraud is a trick to grab your money, like a fake prize email asking for your bank password.

traps.why: Honesty is the opposite of fraud, which is dishonest trickery.
A joke can trick people, but it is harmless fun, not stealing money.
Fraud is one kind of crime, but crime is far too general.

syn1.tip: Think of "credit card fraud," where someone tricks a bank to take money. Pick the word for a money trick.

sc1.stem: The "miracle" pill that supposedly turned water into gasoline was a _____, and the seller was caught keeping all the money from his buyers.

traps.why: A real breakthrough would be amazing, but the seller was caught cheating buyers.
A bargain is a good deal; buyers here lost all their money.
A donation gives money away; this seller took money by lying.

sc1.tip: The quote marks around "miracle" and "caught keeping all the money" tell you the pill was fake and the seller was a cheat.

decoys.why: A fake pill that cheated buyers is no impressive achievement, so feat does not fit.
Nobody agreed to give anything up; the seller simply tricked buyers out of their money.
The sentence describes a trick to take money, not a group reaching agreement.
The pill caused no change at all; it was a trick used to steal money.
Nothing was handed down from the past; the seller was cheating buyers out of money.
No competition is described, only a seller keeping money from a fake product.

traps.why: An honest deal is the opposite of fraud.
Fraud costs people money, but it is done on purpose, not by mistake.
A joke is playful; fraud is a harmful trick to take money.

syn2.tip: Fraud is always negative and done on purpose. Look for the choice that is both sneaky and deliberate.

sc2.stem: The website promised free tickets to the concert, but instead of sending tickets, it stole people's credit card numbers; the whole offer was a _____.

traps.why: A giveaway is what the site promised, but it stole instead of giving.
A treat is a pleasant surprise; stealing card numbers is nothing pleasant.
A mistake is accidental; stealing card numbers on purpose is much worse.

sc2.tip: "But" sets up a contrast: the promise of free tickets hid a plan that "stole" numbers. A deliberate money trick is the answer.

decoys.why: Stealing credit card numbers is cheating, not an achievement that takes skill or courage.
The offer was not a real future possibility; it was a trick to steal card numbers.
No one gave up anything to reach a deal; the website simply stole from people.
The sentence describes a theft scheme, not a group agreeing on something.
The offer did not speed up any change; it was a trick to steal card numbers.
Nothing was handed down from the past; the website was stealing from people.

meaning: something handed down from the past
example: The scientist's legacy lives on in her discoveries.
hook: A legacy is what you leave behind, like a grandparent's recipes or a school record that stands for years.

traps.why: A legacy comes from the past, so future points the wrong way.
Legend looks similar but means a famous story, not something handed down.
A will is the paper listing who gets things, not the things themselves.

syn1.tip: Think of "leaving a legacy": it is what someone leaves behind for the people who come later.

sc1.stem: The beloved teacher's greatest _____ was not a building or an award but the thousands of students who went on to share her love of learning.

traps.why: Regret is a sad feeling, but this sentence praises what she left behind.
A salary is pay while working, not what lasts after her career.
A failure is the opposite of something beloved and lasting.

sc1.tip: "Thousands of students who went on to share her love of learning" is what she left behind that keeps going. That is her legacy.

decoys.why: She was beloved and shared her love of learning, so a feeling of scorn does not fit.
The sentence is about what she left behind in her students, not wanting what others have.
Nothing here describes people arguing; the sentence praises what she passed on to students.
A beloved teacher who inspired thousands was not cheating anyone out of money.
She was the guide; the students were not her mentor but what she left behind.
No competition is described, only the students who carried on her love of learning.

traps.why: Something brand new is the opposite of something passed down from the past.
That is a legend, a word that only looks like legacy.
Legacies often follow a death, but legacy is what remains, not the farewell.

syn2.tip: A legacy lasts after the person is gone. Pick the choice about something passed from one generation to the next.

sc2.stem: Because the inventor's company kept making her safety helmets for decades after she retired, her _____ protected millions of bike riders she never met.

traps.why: Retirement is when she stopped working; what kept protecting riders is what she left.
A prediction looks ahead; the helmets are something left behind from her work.
Legend looks like legacy but means a story, and a story cannot protect riders.

sc2.tip: "Kept making her safety helmets for decades after she retired" shows something lasting that she left. Choose the word for what a person leaves behind.

decoys.why: Her helmets truly protected millions of riders, so nothing about them was trickery.
The sentence says nothing about arguments; it describes the lasting good her work did.
The helmets were real and protected real riders, so they were not something fake.
No competition is mentioned, only helmets that kept protecting people after she retired.
A feeling that others are worthless could not protect millions of bike riders.
The sentence is about the helmets she left behind, not a group's confidence.

meaning: traditions and culture passed down from ancestors
example: The festival celebrates the town's Irish heritage.
hook: Your heritage is what your family hands down: the foods, songs, and stories from where your ancestors came from.

sc1.stem: Proud of her Mexican _____, Lucia learned her grandmother's recipes, danced at the folk festival, and kept the family's old photographs safe.

traps.why: A vacation is a short trip, but recipes and dances come from family tradition.
Recipes might suggest a restaurant, but these are her grandmother's, passed down.
A passport is a travel document, not recipes and dances handed down.

sc1.tip: The examples "grandmother's recipes," "folk festival," and "old photographs" are all things handed down in a family. That points to heritage.

decoys.why: Lucia proudly keeps family traditions, so an unfair opinion is not what she is proud of.
Recipes, folk dances, and family photographs are traditions, not an unfair preference.
Nothing here involves public arguing; she is keeping her family's traditions alive.
Learning recipes and dancing at festivals shows tradition, not competition with others.
She is proudly preserving real family traditions, not taking part in trickery.
She treasures her family's culture, which is the opposite of looking down on it.

traps.why: Recent ideas are the opposite of customs kept for generations.
A will passes on money, but heritage means customs and culture.
A birthplace is one spot; heritage is the whole culture of your ancestors.

syn2.tip: Think of "Heritage Month," which honors the foods, music, and customs a group has kept for generations.

sc2.stem: Although Marco was born in Ohio and had never visited Italy, he treasured his Italian _____, from his great-grandfather's pasta recipe to the songs his family sang at holidays.

traps.why: Marco was born in Ohio, so Italy is not his birthplace.
He never visited Italy, so it cannot be an Italian vacation.
A fashion changes quickly; a great-grandfather's recipe has lasted generations.

sc2.tip: "Although... never visited Italy" tells you the Italian part of him comes from family. The "recipe" and "songs" are handed down.

decoys.why: Marco treasures recipes and family songs, which are traditions, not an unfair opinion.
Pasta recipes and holiday songs are family traditions, not a competition.
Nothing in the sentence involves an argument; it lists traditions he treasures.
His great-grandfather's recipe and family songs are real traditions, not a trick.
He treasures what his family passed down, not something someone else has.
No one is giving anything up in a deal; he is treasuring family traditions.

meaning: important and well known
example: A prominent scientist spoke at our graduation.
hook: Something prominent sticks out, like a famous face on a magazine cover or a tall tower everyone can see.

traps.why: Unknown is the opposite of prominent, which means well known.
Promising means likely to succeed later; prominent means already well known.
Famous people may be rich, but prominent is about importance, not money.

syn1.tip: Prominent people stand out and get noticed. Think of "a prominent leader" whom everyone recognizes.

sc1.stem: As a _____ scientist whose discoveries appeared in textbooks worldwide, Dr. Ito was often invited to speak at universities.

traps.why: Discoveries in textbooks worldwide mean she is the opposite of unknown.
An amateur does science as a hobby; worldwide textbook fame shows a top expert.
Careless is negative, but the sentence praises her worldwide discoveries.

sc1.tip: The clue "discoveries appeared in textbooks worldwide" tells you everyone knows her work. Choose the word for important and well known.

decoys.why: Her discoveries appear in textbooks and universities invite her, so she is famous for good things.
A scientist whose discoveries appear worldwide is important, not small and unimportant.
The sentence is about how well known she is, not whether she takes action.
Nothing suggests she feels hopeless; universities eagerly invite her to speak.
The clue is her well known discoveries, not pride in her looks or abilities.
Speaking invitations come from her famous discoveries, not from changing suddenly.

traps.why: Barely noticed is the opposite of standing out and being well known.
Prominent means widely known and important, much more than slightly popular.
Prominent people may feel proud, but the word means others know them.

syn2.tip: Prominent describes something that stands out so everyone sees it, like "a prominent nose." A prominent person stands out in public life.

sc2.stem: Because the mayor had led the town for twenty years and appeared on the news almost every week, she was one of the most _____ people in the state.

traps.why: Private people stay out of view; she was on the news every week.
Promising fits someone just starting; she has already led for twenty years.
Being on the news makes you known, not rich.

sc2.tip: "Appeared on the news almost every week" is the cause; the effect is that many people know her. Choose the word meaning well known.

decoys.why: Someone on the news every week is easy to notice, not hard to notice.
Nothing says the mayor did anything bad; she is simply well known.
Leading a town for twenty years makes her important, not small and unimportant.
The clue is how well known she is from the news, not whether she takes action.
The sentence explains why she is well known, not that she feels hopeless.
Appearing on the news makes her well known, not something you can see through.

meaning: to encourage the growth or development of
example: Reading at home fosters a love of books.
hook: To foster is to help something grow, the way a foster family cares for a child or a gardener tends seedlings.

traps.why: Discourage is the opposite: it holds growth back instead of helping it.
Foster children may be adopted, but here foster means help something grow.
Force pushes hard; foster gently helps something grow over time.

syn1.tip: Picture a foster parent caring for a child so the child can thrive. To foster anything is to nurture it and help it grow.

sc1.stem: To _____ a love of science in young children, the museum built a hands-on exhibit where kids could build volcanoes and handle real fossils.

traps.why: Prevent is the opposite of what a fun hands-on exhibit is built to do.
Measuring checks how much kids like science; the exhibit is built to grow it.
You cannot demand a love; the hands-on exhibit gently grows it.

sc1.tip: The museum "built a hands-on exhibit" so kids could enjoy science. That purpose shows they want the love of science to grow.

decoys.why: A fun hands-on exhibit is meant to grow a love of science, not hold it back.
The museum wants kids to love science, not to say that loving it is wrong.
Building volcanoes and handling fossils helps a love grow; it does not say the opposite.
The exhibit is built to help a love of science grow, not to measure it.
Nothing secret is being revealed; the exhibit is meant to help kids' interest grow.
The museum is trying to grow kids' love of science, not give reasons for it.

traps.why: Hold back is the opposite of helping something grow.
Foster sounds like faster, but it has nothing to do with speed.
A helper may watch closely, but foster means actively helping something grow.

syn2.tip: Foster is a gentle, positive word. In "foster a love of reading," it means help that love grow over time.

sc2.stem: Strict rules and constant tests can crush a child's curiosity, but a patient teacher who welcomes every question will _____ it instead.

traps.why: Squash means the same as crush, but "but" signals the teacher does the opposite.
Ignoring curiosity does nothing; welcoming questions actively helps it grow.
Punish is harsh; a patient, welcoming teacher helps curiosity grow.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts "crush" with what a "patient teacher who welcomes every question" does. You need the opposite of crush: help it grow.

decoys.why: The word instead shows the teacher does the opposite of crushing curiosity, so not hold it back.
A teacher who welcomes every question supports curiosity rather than calling it wrong.
The contrast is with crushing curiosity, so the teacher helps it grow, not says the opposite.
Tests already judge children; the patient teacher helps curiosity grow instead.
Curiosity is not a secret being revealed; the teacher helps it grow.
The curiosity was never lost; the teacher helps it grow instead of crushing it.

meaning: feeling hopeless and ready to try anything
example: The lost hikers were desperate for water.
hook: Desperate is how you feel when hope is nearly gone, like a goalie diving wildly to stop a last-second shot.

traps.why: Confident people feel sure of success, the opposite of desperate.
Separate sounds similar, but it means apart, not hopeless.
Annoyed is mild; desperate means nearly out of hope.

syn1.tip: Desperate is related to "despair," which means losing hope. Think of "desperate times," when people feel hopeless and will try anything.

sc1.stem: After three days stranded on the island with no food left, the sailors grew _____ and were willing to try any plan, no matter how risky, to be rescued.

traps.why: Cautious people avoid risk, but these sailors would try any risky plan.
Being stranded might be boring, but bored people don't risk anything to escape.
Cheerful is happy, but starving sailors willing to risk anything are not.

sc1.tip: "No food left" and "willing to try any plan, no matter how risky" show they had lost hope and would do anything.

decoys.why: The sailors were willing to try any risky plan, which is the opposite of passive.
Trying any plan no matter how risky shows they stopped thinking calmly, not that they grew rational.
Stranded with no food, the sailors felt hopeless, not excited and eager.
Nothing in the sentence shows the sailors acting better than others.
Starving sailors trying to be rescued are not focused on pride in their looks.
Being stranded with no food does not make the sailors famous or admired.

traps.why: Calm and patient is the opposite of a desperate, frantic person.
Slightly worried is far too weak; desperate people have nearly lost hope.
Eagerness is happy excitement; desperation comes from fear and hopelessness.

syn2.tip: A desperate person has run out of good options, so they grab at any chance. Think of "a desperate attempt."

sc2.stem: At first Jamal calmly searched his room for his lost phone, but after an hour with no luck he became _____, tearing apart drawers and digging through the trash.

traps.why: Patient describes how he started; "but" shows he changed.
Curious people explore for fun; tearing through the trash shows panic.
Playful is lighthearted, but tearing apart drawers shows panic.

sc2.tip: "At first... calmly" contrasts with "but after an hour." "Tearing apart drawers" shows he is frantic and ready to try anything.

decoys.why: Jamal tore apart drawers and dug through trash, which is the opposite of passive.
He started calmly, then became frantic, so he was becoming less rational, not more.
Tearing apart drawers is loud and obvious, not subtle.
After an hour with no luck, Jamal felt hopeless, not excited.
Searching for a lost phone has nothing to do with pride in his looks.
Nothing in the sentence shows Jamal being mean about little things.

meaning: full of energy and new ideas
example: Our dynamic new coach made practice exciting.
hook: Dynamic shares a Greek root with dynamite: picture a coach so full of energy she seems ready to burst with ideas.

traps.why: Dull is the opposite of dynamic, which means full of energy.
Dynamic shares a root with dynamite, but it doesn't mean likely to blow up.
Energetic people may be loud, but dynamic is about energy, not noise.

syn1.tip: Dynamic is a positive word for people full of energy and fresh ideas. Think of "a dynamic duo" who make exciting things happen.

sc1.stem: Unlike the dull speaker before her, the new principal was _____, striding across the stage, telling lively stories, and getting the whole audience to cheer.

traps.why: "Unlike the dull speaker" means she was the opposite of boring.
Nervous speakers don't stride confidently or get crowds cheering.
Strict suggests sternness, but she told lively stories that made people cheer.

sc1.tip: "Unlike the dull speaker" signals a contrast, and "striding," "lively stories," and "cheer" show she was full of energy.

decoys.why: She strode across the stage and got everyone cheering, which is the opposite of passive.
Striding, lively stories, and a cheering crowd are bold, not subtle.
The clue contrasts her with a dull speaker, so it is about energy, not importance.
Nothing says she acted superior; she won the audience over with lively stories.
Getting the whole audience to cheer has nothing to do with being mean about little things.
She seems confident and lively, not hopeless and ready to try anything.

traps.why: Tired is the opposite of dynamic and full of energy.
Hyper suggests jumpy, too much energy; dynamic is positive, focused energy.
Dynamic people bring new ideas, but modern just means recent.

syn2.tip: Imagine the opposite of a boring, sleepy speaker. Dynamic describes someone who brings action and excitement to a room.

sc2.stem: Because the new art teacher was so _____, always bursting with fresh project ideas and bouncing between tables, even students who hated drawing started looking forward to class.

traps.why: Gloomy is the opposite of a teacher bursting with ideas and bouncing around.
Art class can be messy, but the clue is about energy and ideas.
Dynamic shares dynamite's root, but an explosive temper would scare students away.

sc2.tip: "Bursting with fresh project ideas" and "bouncing between tables" describe someone full of energy. That energy is why students began looking forward to class.

decoys.why: A teacher bouncing between tables with fresh ideas is the opposite of passive.
Bursting with ideas and bouncing around is very noticeable, not subtle.
Students started looking forward to class, which would not happen with a teacher who acted superior.
Fresh project ideas and energy have nothing to do with being mean about small things.
The clue describes her energy and ideas, not her being famous.
The teacher sounds energetic and cheerful, not hopeless.

meaning: a public disagreement that many people argue about
example: The new homework rule caused controversy among students.
hook: Controversy starts with contra, meaning "against": picture a town split in two, each side arguing against the other.

traps.why: Agreement is the opposite of controversy, where people argue.
Conversation looks similar, but a chat is friendly, not a heated public argument.
A riot is violent disorder, much stronger than a public argument.

syn1.tip: Contro- comes from contra, meaning "against." A controversy is when people line up against each other on a question.

sc1.stem: The plan to replace the old oak tree with a parking lot created a heated _____ in town, with residents arguing loudly at every council meeting.

traps.why: Celebrations are happy; residents arguing loudly is not.
Residents arguing loudly shows the opposite of agreement.
Heated here means angry, not hot weather, and a drought involves no arguing.

sc1.tip: "Residents arguing loudly at every council meeting" shows many people publicly disagreeing. "Heated" here means angry, which fits a big argument.

decoys.why: Residents were arguing loudly, so there was no general agreement.
People arguing at every meeting have not reached an agreement where both sides give up something.
The old tree may be part of the town's past, but the clue is about arguing.
The sentence describes loud arguments, not something handed down from the past.
Residents arguing loudly does not describe respect earned through success.
A plan that causes loud arguments is not an achievement of skill or courage.

traps.why: Peaceful harmony is the opposite of people arguing in public.
Rumors spread around, but controversy means people argue over an issue.
A complaint is one person's gripe; a controversy divides many people.

syn2.tip: Think of a news story that "stirs up controversy." Many people take sides and argue openly.

sc2.stem: Most new school rules pass quietly, but the ban on phones at lunch sparked a _____ that filled the newspaper with angry letters for weeks.

traps.why: "But" contrasts with rules that pass quietly, so silence is the opposite.
Sparked here means started; angry letters show an argument, not a fire.
A celebration is happy, but the letters were angry.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with rules that "pass quietly," and "angry letters for weeks" shows many people arguing in public.

decoys.why: Weeks of angry letters show people disagreed, not that they agreed.
Angry letters for weeks mean the sides were fighting, not meeting in the middle.
A new phone ban is not something handed down from the past.
A rule that sparks angry letters is not an impressive achievement.
A ban cannot spark a person who guides someone.
The sentence is about a public argument, not the main character of a story.

meaning: showing great variety; made of different kinds
example: The coral reef is home to diverse kinds of fish.
hook: A diverse garden has roses, cacti, and sunflowers side by side: lots of different kinds in one place.

traps.why: Identical means all the same, the opposite of diverse.
Divided means split apart; diverse means made of many different kinds.
A crowd can be large without having different kinds in it.

syn1.tip: Think of "diversity" in a school: many backgrounds together. Diverse things differ from each other.

sc1.stem: The school's chess club was remarkably _____, with members ranging from sixth graders to teachers and from students born in Brazil to students born in Korea.

traps.why: Uniform means all alike, but the members range widely in age and birthplace.
Chess clubs can be competitive, but the examples show variety, not rivalry.
Chess players may be quiet, but the clue lists many different kinds of members.

sc1.tip: "Ranging from sixth graders to teachers" and "from Brazil to Korea" are examples of very different members. That variety is the clue.

decoys.why: Members ranging from sixth graders to teachers shows variety, not that the club is well known.
Elaborate means detailed and complicated, but the clue is about many different kinds of members.
Nothing says the club is famous; the clue lists members from different ages and countries.
Members from different ages and countries has nothing to do with being mean about little things.
The clue describes who the members are, not whether they take action.
A chess club with varied members is not something you can see through.

traps.why: All the same is the opposite of diverse.
Size isn't the point; even a small group can be diverse.
That is reverse, which only looks like diverse.

syn2.tip: Diverse is close to "different." A diverse menu offers many different dishes, not just one kind.

sc2.stem: Ten years ago every student in our small town had the same background, but today the school is far more _____, with families from twelve different countries.

traps.why: "But" contrasts with "the same background," so similar is backward.
Families from twelve countries show the school is connected to the world, not isolated.
Boring is negative; the sentence describes a school with many backgrounds.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts "the same background" with today. "Families from twelve different countries" shows the school now has great variety.

decoys.why: The contrast with everyone having the same background points to variety, not importance.
Families from twelve countries shows variety, not that the school is famous.
Nothing bad is described; the school simply has families from many countries.
The clue is about different backgrounds, not about having many detailed parts.
Families from twelve countries has nothing to do with being small or mean.
A school with families from many countries is not something you can see through.

meaning: honesty and strong moral principles
example: A person of integrity tells the truth even when it's hard.
hook: Integrity comes from the same root as integer, a whole number: a person of integrity is whole and honest everywhere.

traps.why: Deceit means lying and tricking, the opposite of integrity.
Intelligence looks similar but means being smart, not being honest.
Polite people have good manners, but integrity means honest and principled.

syn1.tip: Integrity is a positive word for character. Think of "a person of integrity" who does the right thing even when no one is watching.

sc1.stem: When the cashier gave her twenty dollars too much in change, Amina showed her _____ by returning the money right away, even though no one would have known.

traps.why: Greed would mean keeping the money; she gave it back.
Intelligence looks like integrity, but returning money shows honesty, not smarts.
"Right away" is about timing, but returning money no one would miss shows honesty.

sc1.tip: "Even though no one would have known" is the key. Doing the honest thing when you could get away with it shows integrity.

decoys.why: Returning extra money is honest, the opposite of dishonest trickery.
Giving money back shows she did not want what was not hers.
Returning the money politely shows honesty, not a feeling that someone is worthless.
Returning the money has nothing to do with an unfair preference.
Amina returned the money; she formed no unfair opinion about anyone.
The sentence is about her honest choice, not traditions from her ancestors.

traps.why: Sneaky habits are the opposite of honest, principled behavior.
Manners are about politeness; integrity is about honesty and doing right.
Stubbornness is negative; integrity is sticking to what is right.

syn2.tip: People with integrity stick to their principles. You can hear it in "she has too much integrity to cheat."

sc2.stem: Several players on the other team cheated to win, but our captain refused to bend the rules, and her _____ earned her respect from both teams.

traps.why: Trickery is what the cheaters used; the captain refused to bend rules.
Stubbornness is negative, but refusing to cheat earned her respect.
Jealousy might come from losing, but it wouldn't earn respect from both teams.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the cheaters with the captain who "refused to bend the rules." Sticking to what is right is integrity.

decoys.why: The captain refused to cheat, so fraud is what the other team did, not her.
She refused to bend the rules at all, so she did not give up anything.
Refusing to cheat is about honesty, not an unfair preference.
Prestige is the respect itself; the sentence asks what quality earned her that respect.
Rivalry is between the teams, but the blank names the captain's honest quality.
Refusing to bend the rules shows honesty, not wanting what others have.

meaning: an unfair preference for or against something
example: A good judge must decide without bias.
hook: Bias leans one way, like a scale that is tipped before anything has even been weighed.

traps.why: Fairness is the opposite of bias; it treats everyone the same.
Basis looks like bias but means the foundation of something.
Judges make decisions, but bias is the unfair leaning behind one.

syn1.tip: You hear bias in phrases like "without bias" about fair judges. It means an unfair leaning toward one side, so look for a negative word.

sc1.stem: Because the contest judge was the singer's aunt, the other performers worried that her _____ would keep her from scoring everyone fairly.

traps.why: Fairness would help her score everyone fairly, not stop her.
Judges need expertise, but skill would not keep her from being fair.
Basis looks like bias but means a foundation, which makes no sense here.

sc1.tip: The clue is "Because the contest judge was the singer's aunt." A family tie could create an unfair preference that keeps her from judging "fairly."

decoys.why: Integrity would help her score fairly, but the sentence says something would keep her from it.
The worry is about unfair favoritism toward her niece, not her family traditions.
Her high rank would not stop her from scoring fairly; favoring her niece would.
Morale is a group's spirit, which has nothing to do with judging her niece unfairly.
Consensus is a group's agreement, but the clue is one judge favoring her niece.
Something handed down from the past would not make her score her niece unfairly.

traps.why: Equal treatment is the opposite of bias, which favors one side.
Bias can cause unfair results, but it is a preference, not an accident.
Basic looks a bit like bias, but bias is not about facts.

syn2.tip: Picture a referee who always calls fouls on one team. That unfair tilt toward a side is bias.

sc2.stem: Coach Rivera claimed she picked the team captain fairly, but everyone noticed her _____ toward her own son, who got the job despite missing half the practices.

traps.why: The word "but" means the coach was not actually fair.
Being strict with her son would not explain him getting the job.
Generosity sounds kind, but giving a job unfairly is a negative thing.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts "fairly" with what everyone noticed, and "despite missing half the practices" shows an unfair preference for her son.

decoys.why: Her son got the job despite missing practices, so she showed unfairness, not honesty.
She gave her son the job, so she clearly did not think he was worthless.
She did not want what her son had; she unfairly favored him.

meaning: an agreement where each side gives up something
example: After a long debate, the twins reached a compromise about bedtime.
hook: In a compromise, both sides meet in the middle, each giving up a slice so everyone gets some pizza.

traps.why: A quarrel is a fight; a compromise ends one with an agreement.
Promise is hidden inside compromise, but compromise means both sides give something up.
A victory means one side wins; in a compromise both sides give a little.

syn1.tip: Think of "meeting in the middle." Two sides each give something up and agree, so look for a word meaning an agreement.

sc1.stem: Maya wanted pizza and Leo wanted tacos, so they reached a _____: they would have pizza tonight and tacos tomorrow.

traps.why: A deadlock means no agreement, but they did agree on a plan.
A verdict is a decision made by a judge, not by two friends.
A standstill means no progress, but they found a plan that worked.

sc1.tip: Look after the colon: "pizza tonight and tacos tomorrow" shows each person giving a little so both get part of what they want.

decoys.why: They settled the argument by each giving something up, which ends a disagreement.
They found a deal where each got a turn, not a competition.
Neither friend was favored; each one gave up something to agree.
Splitting dinner plans is a trade, not an act of great skill or courage.
The colon explains a deal where each side gives a little, not a cause of change.

traps.why: Refusing to budge is the opposite of giving up a little.
As a verb, compromise can mean endanger, but this noun means an agreement.
Winning outright means one side gets everything, which is not a compromise.

syn2.tip: Notice that each side moves a little toward the other. The phrase "meet in the middle" is a good way to remember compromise.

sc2.stem: Since neither the band nor the chorus would give up the gym, the principal proposed a _____ that let each group use it on alternate days, and the fighting finally stopped.

traps.why: Principals give punishments, but sharing the gym is not a punishment.
A contest picks one winner, but here each group gets the gym.
Promise is inside compromise, but here each side gives something up.

sc2.tip: "Neither... would give up the gym," so the fix was for "each group" to share on "alternate days." Both sides gave a little.

decoys.why: The plan made the fighting stop, so it ended the disagreement instead of starting one.
The principal's plan stopped the competition between the groups by letting each take turns.
Alternating days treats both groups equally, so nobody was unfairly favored.
Sharing the gym on alternate days is a fair deal, not dishonest trickery.

meaning: to give a good reason for
example: Mom asked me to justify spending so much on new shoes.
hook: To justify something is to show it is just, or fair, by giving good reasons for it.

traps.why: Criticize means to find fault, the opposite of giving reasons for something.
Adjust has "just" inside it but means to change slightly.
Judges deal with what is just, but judging is deciding, not defending.

syn1.tip: Justify contains "just," meaning fair, and -ify, meaning to make. You make something look fair by giving reasons for it.

sc1.stem: The teacher asked each student to _____ their answer by pointing to evidence in the text that supported their opinion.

traps.why: Pointing to evidence supports an answer; it does not abandon it.
Guessing means having no evidence, but these students use evidence.
Memorizing is about remembering, not supporting an answer with evidence.

sc1.tip: The words "by pointing to evidence... that supported their opinion" tell you the students were giving good reasons for their answers.

decoys.why: The evidence supported their opinion, so they backed up their answers instead of opposing them.
Pointing to supporting evidence defends an answer; it does not say the answer is wrong.
Pointing to evidence is a direct way to give reasons, not a hint.
Students were explaining why their answers were right, not getting something back.
Supporting evidence helps an answer; it does not hold it back.

traps.why: Finding fault attacks something; justifying supports it with reasons.
On a computer, justify can mean line up text, but not here.
Justify looks like justice, but it means explaining why something is right.

syn2.tip: When someone asks you to justify a choice, they want your reasons. Think "Why did you do that?"

sc2.stem: Jordan could not _____ staying up until two in the morning playing video games; he had no good reason, and he was exhausted for the test.

traps.why: He could easily criticize it, since he had no good reason.
The clue is about lacking a reason, not about forgetting.
Regret is a feeling afterward, but the clue says he had "no good reason."

sc2.tip: After the semicolon, "he had no good reason" restates the blank. You need a verb meaning to give a good reason for something.

decoys.why: The clue says he had no good reason, so the missing word means give a reason.
He surely noticed staying up late; the problem is he had no good reason for it.
You cannot bring back staying up late; the clue is about having no good reason.
The sentence is about lacking a good reason, not making a problem less severe.
Nothing is being protected from waste; the clue says he had no good reason.

meaning: the possibility of something happening in the future
example: The prospect of a snow day thrilled every student in class.
hook: Prospect means looking forward: pro means forward and spect means look, toward something that might happen.

traps.why: A memory is about the past; a prospect is about the future.
Respect looks like prospect but means admiration for someone.
Certainty is too strong; a prospect only might happen.

syn1.tip: Prospect has spect, meaning look, inside it. A prospect is something you look ahead to that might happen.

sc1.stem: The _____ of singing alone in front of the entire school made Nadia so nervous that she practiced her song every night for a month.

traps.why: She is still practicing, so the singing has not happened yet.
Joy is a happy feeling, but she is nervous about the singing.
Singing takes skill, but her nerves are about a future event.

sc1.tip: "Practiced her song every night for a month" shows the singing is in the future. She is nervous about a possibility coming up.

decoys.why: She had not sung yet and practiced for a month, so it was a future possibility.
The performance was real and coming up, which is why she practiced every night.
The thought made her nervous, not encouraged, and it was about something still to come.
Her solo was in the future, not something handed down from the past.
Nadia's nerves came from a future solo, not from a group agreement.

traps.why: A prospect is in the future, not something already over.
Spect means look, but a prospect is a future possibility, not a look.
A gold miner is a prospector, a related word, not a prospect.

syn2.tip: Think of "the prospect of a snow day." It is something that might happen soon, so look for a future possibility.

sc2.stem: Although rain had canceled the game twice, the _____ of finally playing on Saturday kept the whole team hopeful as they checked the forecast every morning.

traps.why: Saturday's game has not happened yet, so it cannot be a memory.
"Although" turns from the canceled games to something that kept them hopeful.
Respect looks like prospect but means admiration, which does not fit.

sc2.tip: "Finally playing on Saturday" is in the future, and it "kept the whole team hopeful." They were looking forward to a possibility.

decoys.why: The team felt hopeful about Saturday, not that the game was worthless.
Nobody argued about the game; the team hoped it would finally happen.
The game had not been played yet; they were still checking the forecast.
Saturday's game was a future possibility, not something handed down from the past.
No trickery is involved; the team was hoping the game could finally happen.

meaning: general agreement among a group
example: The class reached a consensus to visit the zoo.
hook: When the whole class nods yes to the same idea at once, the class has reached a consensus.

traps.why: A dispute is a disagreement, the opposite of consensus.
Census is inside consensus but means an official count of people.
Groups vote in elections, but voting can end without general agreement.

syn1.tip: Con means together. A consensus is when a group comes together on the same idea, as in "the group reached a consensus."

sc1.stem: After a long discussion, the student council reached a _____; every single member voted to hold the fundraiser in May.

traps.why: A deadlock means no agreement, but every member voted the same way.
Census looks like consensus but means counting people.
Fundraisers have deadlines, but the clue is about everyone agreeing.

sc1.tip: After the semicolon, "every single member voted to hold the fundraiser in May" shows that the whole group agreed.

decoys.why: Every member voted the same way, so there was agreement, not argument.
Everyone voting the same way shows agreement, not competition.
The clue is that every member agreed, not that someone was unfairly favored.
The vote already happened and everyone agreed, so this is not a future possibility.

traps.why: A split decision means the group was divided, not agreeing.
A head count is a census, which only looks like consensus.
Consensus is related to sense, but it means agreement, not a feeling.

syn2.tip: Picture everyone in a group nodding together. Consensus is what the whole group thinks, so look for something shared.

sc2.stem: Our family usually argues for an hour about which movie to watch, but last Friday we reached a quick _____ when everyone shouted for the same comedy.

traps.why: "But" shows Friday was different from the usual arguing.
Census looks like consensus but means an official count of people.
Movies can have intermissions, but the clue is about everyone agreeing.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the usual arguing, and "everyone shouted for the same comedy" shows the whole family agreed.

decoys.why: Everyone shouted for the same comedy, so this time there was no argument.
Everyone wanted the same movie, so the family agreed instead of competing.
The clue is that everyone picked the same comedy, which shows agreement.
The family already agreed on the comedy, so it was not just a future possibility.
Everyone shouting for the same movie shows agreement, not the group's confidence.

meaning: so slight it is hard to notice
example: There was a subtle hint of lemon in the cake.
hook: The b in subtle is silent, a subtle letter you barely notice when you say "SUT-ul."

traps.why: Obvious means easy to notice, the opposite of subtle.
Supple looks like subtle but means bending easily.
Secrets are hidden on purpose; subtle things are simply hard to notice.

syn1.tip: Think of "a subtle hint of lemon." You can barely taste it, so subtle means slight and hard to notice.

sc1.stem: The difference between the two shades of blue was so _____ that most people thought the walls were the same color until an artist pointed it out.

traps.why: An obvious difference would be noticed, but most people missed it.
Bright describes colors, but the clue is about how hard it was to notice.
Supple looks like subtle but means bending easily.

sc1.tip: "Most people thought the walls were the same color" until an artist pointed it out, so the difference was very slight.

decoys.why: People thought the walls matched, so the difference was hard to notice, not easy to see.
There were only two shades that looked the same, so there was no great variety.
A very deep difference would be easy to notice, but people missed this one.
The difference was tiny and hard to see, not made of many detailed parts.
Clear and obvious is the opposite of a difference nobody noticed until an artist pointed it out.
Nothing in the sentence says the colors kept changing; the difference was just hard to notice.

traps.why: Easy to spot is the opposite of subtle.
Too strong: subtle things can be noticed, just not easily.
Subtle starts like sub, under, but it means slight, not underneath.

syn2.tip: A subtle change is one you might miss unless you look closely, like a friend's new haircut that is just a little shorter.

sc2.stem: Instead of a loud, obvious joke, Ms. Park made a _____ joke that only a few students caught, quietly grinning in the back row.

traps.why: A blunt joke is direct and easy to get, not caught by few.
Jokes can be silly, but the clue is about how few students noticed.
Nothing suggests meanness; the students were grinning at it.

sc2.tip: "Instead of a loud, obvious joke" sets up a contrast, and "only a few students caught" it, so the joke was hard to notice.

decoys.why: The joke was the opposite of loud and obvious, so it did not stand out.
Only a few students even caught the joke, so it was not famous for anything.
A joke that only a few students caught was not famous or widely admired.
The sentence contrasts her joke with a loud one, so it was quiet, not full of energy.
Students grinned quietly; nothing suggests Ms. Park felt hopeless when she made the joke.

meaning: to judge the value, size, or quality of
example: The teacher will assess our science projects next week.
hook: A tax assessor sizes up a house to decide what it is worth; to assess is to size something up.

traps.why: Ignoring something means not looking at it, the opposite of assessing.
Assist looks like assess but means to help.
Praise is always positive; assessing is a neutral judgment of quality.

syn1.tip: Teachers assess your work when they grade it. Think of tests called assessments, which measure how well you know something.

sc1.stem: Before deciding whether the old bridge was safe for hikers, engineers had to _____ the damage by measuring cracks and testing the strength of each beam.

traps.why: They were measuring cracks carefully, not overlooking the damage.
Access looks like assess but means to reach or get into.
Repairs might come later; measuring and testing are about judging the damage.

sc1.tip: "Measuring cracks and testing the strength of each beam" are ways of judging how bad the damage is before "deciding whether" it is safe.

decoys.why: Measuring cracks and testing beams judges the damage; it does not make the damage less severe.
The engineers are measuring and testing to judge the damage, not revealing a secret.
Engineers checking safety would not give a good reason for the damage.
Measuring and testing is about judging how bad the damage is, not saying it is wrong.
You would not protect damage from loss; the engineers are measuring it to judge safety.
Measuring cracks does not hold back damage; it only helps the engineers judge it.

traps.why: Passing over something means skipping it, not judging it carefully.
You might fix something after assessing it, but assessing only judges.
Let in is what access means, a lookalike, not assess.

syn2.tip: An assessment is a test. To assess is to look something over and decide how good, big, or serious it is.

sc2.stem: Before choosing which puppy to adopt, the family wanted to _____ each one's energy level, so they watched how long every puppy ran around the yard.

traps.why: They watched closely, so they were not ignoring the energy levels.
Watching puppies run measures energy; it does not increase it.
Access looks like assess but means to reach or get into.

sc2.tip: "So they watched how long every puppy ran" shows the family measuring, which means judging each puppy's energy before "choosing."

decoys.why: The family only watched the puppies run, so they were judging energy, not encouraging it.
Watching the puppies run does not hold back their energy; it helps the family judge it.
The family is watching to judge each puppy's energy, not trying to make it stronger.
The family is not copying the puppies; they are watching to judge their energy.
The puppies use energy running, but the family is watching to judge it.
The family is measuring energy by watching, not giving a reason for it.

meaning: small and unimportant; mean about little things
example: They argued over a petty matter like who sat where.
hook: Petty comes from the French petit, meaning small, like petite; a petty fight is over something tiny.

traps.why: Important is the opposite of petty, which means small and unimportant.
Pretty looks like petty but means attractive.
Cruel is too strong; petty meanness is about little things.

syn1.tip: Think of "a petty argument" over who sits where. Petty things are small and not worth the fuss.

sc1.stem: The sisters stopped speaking for a week over something truly _____: who got to hold the remote during a single commercial break.

traps.why: A single commercial break is not important, so this misses the point.
Pretty looks like petty but means attractive, which makes no sense here.
The fight is about the remote, which everyone knows; nothing is hidden.

sc1.tip: After the colon, "who got to hold the remote during a single commercial break" is tiny, so the week-long fight was over something unimportant.

decoys.why: Fighting over the remote during one commercial is small and silly, not deep or meaningful.
Who holds the remote for one commercial is unimportant, not important and well known.
Holding the remote for one commercial break is simple, not complicated with many parts.
Not speaking for a week over a remote is not based on clear thinking.
A tiny fight over the remote is not famous or widely admired.

traps.why: Serious matters are important, the opposite of petty ones.
Petite looks like petty but describes a small body size.
Modest is a positive word for humble; petty is negative.

syn2.tip: Petty sounds like petite, meaning small. A petty matter is small and unimportant, and the word usually sounds disapproving.

sc2.stem: The mayor ignored the town's real problems, like broken streetlights, and instead spent the meeting on a _____ complaint about the color of the trash cans.

traps.why: "Instead" shows the complaint was less important than the real problems.
Pretty looks like petty but means attractive, not unimportant.
Mayors make official statements, but the clue is about how small it was.

sc2.tip: "Instead" contrasts the town's "real problems" with the trash can complaint, so the complaint was about something small and unimportant.

decoys.why: The mayor ignored real problems for trash can colors, which is small, not deep or meaningful.
Skipping broken streetlights to complain about trash can colors is not clear, sensible thinking.
The sentence is about how unimportant the complaint was, not whether it could be believed.
A complaint about trash can colors is small and unimportant, not hopeless or urgent.
The point is that the complaint was unimportant, not that it was careful about every detail.

meaning: having many detailed parts; complicated
example: They built an elaborate sandcastle with towers and tunnels.
hook: An elaborate cake has layers, swirls, and sugar flowers: elaborate means full of carefully worked details.

traps.why: Simple is the opposite of elaborate, which has many parts.
Elaborate contains labor, but it describes details, not tiredness.
Elaborate things may be colorful, but elaborate means many detailed parts.

syn1.tip: Picture "an elaborate sandcastle with towers and tunnels." Elaborate things have lots of parts, so look for a word about details.

sc1.stem: Instead of a simple birthday card, Nadia made an _____ pop-up model of a castle with moving drawbridges, tiny flags, and dozens of paper windows.

traps.why: "Instead of a simple birthday card" shows the model was not ordinary.
Elementary looks like elaborate but means basic and simple.
The verb elaborate means explain more, but this model is about details.

sc1.tip: "Instead of a simple birthday card" sets up a contrast, and "moving drawbridges, tiny flags, and dozens of paper windows" list many detailed parts.

decoys.why: A pop-up model of a castle is a copy, and the clues stress its many detailed parts.
Nadia may be excited, but the model itself is described by its many detailed parts.
A paper castle cannot act better than others; the clues list its many detailed parts.

traps.why: Plain means simple, the opposite of elaborate.
Enormous is about size; elaborate is about having many detailed parts.
As a verb, elaborate means explain more, but the adjective means detailed.

syn2.tip: An elaborate plan has many steps and pieces. Think of a costume with lots of layers and decorations.

sc2.stem: The directions for building the robot kit were so _____ that it took Marcus three whole afternoons and two phone calls to his uncle to finish it.

traps.why: Simple directions would not take three afternoons and phone calls.
Colorful directions would not make the robot take so long to build.
Exciting does not explain why Marcus needed so much time and help.

sc2.tip: "So... that it took... three whole afternoons and two phone calls" shows a cause and effect: the directions had many complicated parts.

decoys.why: Directions that took three afternoons and phone calls for help were not clear and easy.
Directions that took three whole afternoons were not small and unimportant.
The problem was that the directions were complicated, not whether you could trust them.
Being real and genuine would not make Marcus need three afternoons and two phone calls.
Famous directions would not explain why the kit took Marcus three afternoons to finish.

meaning: based on clear thinking and reason
example: Let's find a rational solution to the problem.
hook: Rational shares a root with reason: a rational person thinks things through instead of panicking.

traps.why: Foolish means lacking good sense, the opposite of rational.
National looks like rational but means about a whole country.
Rational is related to ratio, but it means thinking clearly, not math.

syn1.tip: Rational and reason come from the same root. A rational choice is one you can explain with clear thinking.

sc1.stem: Even though she was scared of flying, Sana tried to be _____ by reminding herself of the facts: airplanes are much safer than cars.

traps.why: "Even though she was scared" means she tried not to be frantic.
National looks like rational but means about a whole country.
Reminding herself of facts is calm, not dramatic.

sc1.tip: "Even though she was scared" sets up a contrast, and "reminding herself of the facts" shows she used clear thinking instead of fear.

decoys.why: Sana reminded herself of facts to stay steady, not to change suddenly in her feelings.
She was scared but calmed herself with facts, which is clear thinking, not hopelessness.
Sana actively reminded herself of facts, so she was not just accepting her fear.
Reminding herself that planes are safe is clear thinking, not acting better than others.
The sentence is about using facts to calm fear, not being proud of her looks.

traps.why: Emotional means led by feelings; rational means led by reason.
Rational looks like ration, a limited share, but it means reasonable.
Brilliant is too strong; rational just means thinking clearly.

syn2.tip: Think of "a rational solution," one that makes sense. Rational is a calm, thinking word, the opposite of panicking.

sc2.stem: When the fire alarm rang, Coach Diaz stayed _____, calmly counting students and choosing the safest exit while a few kids screamed and ran the wrong way.

traps.why: The kids were hysterical; the coach was calmly counting and choosing.
A fire alarm calls for clear thinking, not a happy mood.
Coaches are often athletic, but the clue is about clear thinking.

sc2.tip: "Calmly counting students and choosing the safest exit" contrasts with kids who "screamed and ran the wrong way," so the coach was thinking clearly.

decoys.why: Coach Diaz stayed calm and steady, while the kids who screamed were the ones changing suddenly.
He calmly counted students and picked an exit, so he was not hopeless or frantic.
Coach Diaz took action by counting students and choosing an exit, so he was not passive.
The sentence stresses that he stayed calm and clear thinking, not excited.
Calmly counting students and choosing a safe exit shows clear thinking, not acting superior.

meaning: real and genuine, not a copy
example: The museum confirmed that the old painting was authentic.
hook: An authentic autograph was truly signed by the star by hand, not printed onto a copy.

traps.why: Fake is the opposite of authentic.
Authorized looks similar but means given permission.
Old objects are often checked, but authentic means real, not old.

syn1.tip: Think of 'authentic Mexican food': the real thing made the true way, not an imitation.

sc1.stem: Experts examined the signature, the paper, and the ink before declaring that the letter was _____ and not a clever forgery made centuries later.

traps.why: Fake is the opposite; the letter is 'not a clever forgery.'
Experts check paper and ink, but damage has nothing to do with forgery.
The experts examined the signature, so the letter was signed.

sc1.tip: The words 'and not a clever forgery' tell you the blank means the opposite of fake: real.

decoys.why: A forgery might be elaborate, but the experts are deciding whether the letter is real.
The experts were checking whether the letter was genuine, not whether it was famous.
Being famous for something bad has nothing to do with whether the letter is a forgery.
The experts examined the ink and paper to prove it real, not to see through it.
The contrast is with a forgery, so the blank must mean real, not hard to notice.

traps.why: Copied is the opposite; an authentic thing is the original.
Real art may be expensive, but authentic is about being real.
Experts check famous works, but authentic means real, not well known.

syn2.tip: People say 'authentic' when something is the real deal. Pick the plain word for not fake.

sc2.stem: Grandma's tacos taste _____ because she makes them exactly the way her family has in Mexico for generations, using the same handmade tortillas.

traps.why: Artificial is the opposite of the real, traditional way she cooks.
Modern is about newness, but she cooks the way her family always has.
Cost isn't the point; the clue is about the traditional, true recipe.

sc2.tip: The clue 'exactly the way her family has in Mexico for generations' shows the tacos are the real, traditional thing.

decoys.why: The reason given is family tradition, which makes the tacos genuine, not complicated.
Making them exactly the same way for generations shows they are genuine, not varied.
Following an old family recipe makes food genuine, not full of new ideas.
The sentence stresses doing things exactly the same way, so sudden change is the opposite.
The sentence praises Grandma's tacos, and petty is an insult that does not fit.

meaning: accepting what happens without taking action
example: Don't be passive; speak up when you have an idea.
hook: A passive passenger just rides along while someone else does all the steering.

traps.why: Bold people act; that is the opposite of passive.
Passionate looks similar but means full of strong feeling.
Tired is about energy; passive is about not taking action.

syn1.tip: Passive sounds like 'pass': a passive person lets chances pass by without acting.

sc1.stem: Rather than sitting back and letting others make every decision, the coach wanted her players to stop being _____ and take charge on the field.

traps.why: Aggressive is the opposite of 'sitting back and letting others' decide.
Careless means making mistakes; the clue is about sitting back.
Passionate looks similar, but the coach wants players with energy.

sc1.tip: 'Sitting back and letting others make every decision' describes the blank. That is someone who does not act.

decoys.why: The coach wants players to take charge, so she would not ask them to stop being decisive.
Being full of energy is what the coach wants, not what she wants them to stop.
The coach wants players to stop sitting back, not stop being excited.
The clue is about sitting back and letting others decide, not about clear thinking.
Sitting back describes not acting, which has nothing to do with being careful.

traps.why: Taking charge is the opposite of being passive.
Passive looks like pass, but it isn't about moving past things.
Quiet people may seem passive, but passive means not acting.

syn2.tip: A 'passive fan' just watches and lets things happen. Choose the meaning about not acting.

sc2.stem: During the group project, Owen stayed _____, never offering ideas or volunteering for a task, so the other three members ended up doing all the work.

traps.why: A bossy person takes over; Owen never offered anything.
Cheerful is positive, but the sentence describes Owen doing nothing.
Busy means doing a lot, but the others did all the work.

sc2.tip: 'Never offering ideas or volunteering' restates the blank: Owen did not take any action.

decoys.why: Owen never offered ideas or volunteered, which is the opposite of excited.
Owen offered no ideas at all, so full of new ideas is the opposite.
Owen did nothing while others worked, which is not making firm choices.
Owen left all the work to others, so he was not careful about every detail.
Owen stayed in the background, so important and well known does not fit.

meaning: clear enough to see through
example: The jellyfish's body is almost transparent.
hook: Trans means through: something transparent lets you see right through it, like a clean window.

traps.why: Cloudy is the opposite; you can't see through it.
Glass is shiny, but transparent means you can see through it.
Trans is in transform, but here it means through, not change.

syn1.tip: Break it apart: trans means through. Light and sight pass right through something transparent.

sc1.stem: The glass frog's skin is so _____ that scientists can see its tiny heart beating right through its belly.

traps.why: Thick skin would hide the heart, not show it.
Color is about skin, but seeing through it needs see-through skin.
Frogs are slippery, but that wouldn't let anyone see its heart.

sc1.tip: The clue 'see its tiny heart beating right through its belly' tells you the skin lets you see through it.

decoys.why: Scientists can see right through the skin, so it must be clear, not just hard to notice.
Seeing the heart through the belly means the skin is clear, not detailed.
The sentence is about seeing through the skin, not about being important or well known.
Variety in the skin would not let scientists see the heart beating through it.
Seeing through the skin depends on it being clear, not on it changing suddenly.

traps.why: Murky is the opposite; murky water hides what is inside.
Glass breaks easily, but transparent is about seeing through it.
Transparent contains parent, but it has nothing to do with parents.

syn2.tip: Think of transparent tape or a transparent plastic bag: you can see what's on the other side.

sc2.stem: Unlike the frosted glass in the bathroom window, which blurs everything behind it, the kitchen window is _____, so you can easily spot the birds at the feeder.

traps.why: Blurry fits the bathroom glass, but 'unlike' signals the opposite.
Cracks are about damage, not about seeing birds easily.
Decorations would block the view, not make spotting birds easy.

sc2.tip: 'Unlike the frosted glass, which blurs everything' signals contrast, so the kitchen window must be easy to see through.

decoys.why: The window is contrasted with blurry glass, so it must be clear, not decorated.
You can easily spot birds through it, so the window must be clear to see through.
Both windows are real glass; the difference is that one is clear and one blurs.
Spotting birds easily depends on clear glass, not on variety.
A window full of energy makes no sense when the clue is about seeing through glass.

meaning: an achievement that takes great skill or courage
example: Climbing the mountain in winter was an amazing feat.
hook: Picture 'a feat of strength': a strongman pulling a bus with a rope. Don't confuse feat with feet.

traps.why: Failure is the opposite of a feat.
Feet sounds the same, but feet are what you stand on.
Feast looks similar but means a big meal.

syn1.tip: The phrase 'no small feat' means something hard to pull off. A feat is an achievement.

sc1.stem: Swimming across the cold, choppy English Channel is a remarkable _____ that only a small number of athletes have ever managed.

traps.why: A mistake isn't something athletes proudly 'managed.'
A hobby is too ordinary; this is rare and very difficult.
Feast looks like feat but means a big meal.

sc1.tip: 'Remarkable' and 'only a small number of athletes have ever managed' point to something rare and hard to accomplish.

decoys.why: Athletes have managed it, so it is a finished achievement, not a future possibility.
The sentence describes a hard achievement athletes managed, not something handed down.
Swimming the Channel is something athletes accomplish, not a competition between two groups.
Nothing in the sentence mentions people arguing; it describes a hard achievement.
Athletes have really managed the swim, so it is not something that only looks real.
Crossing cold, choppy water is an achievement, not an agreement where sides give something up.

traps.why: A mistake is the opposite of an impressive feat.
A chore is too easy; a feat takes great skill or courage.
A large meal is a feast, which only looks like feat.

syn2.tip: People brag about feats, like 'a feat of engineering.' Pick the choice about doing something hard and impressive.

sc2.stem: Most people thought the tiny robot built by our science club would fall apart in the first round, so winning the state championship was quite a _____.

traps.why: Winning a championship is the opposite of a letdown.
Feast looks like feat, but nobody ate anything.
Nuisance is negative, but winning is a proud success.

sc2.tip: 'Would fall apart in the first round' contrasted with 'winning the state championship' shows an impressive, hard-won success.

decoys.why: The club already won, so winning is an achievement, not a future possibility.
Winning a championship is an achievement, not an agreement between two sides.
The sentence is about a surprising win, not a group agreeing on something.
Winning against the odds is an achievement, not a competition between two groups.
The sentence celebrates an honest surprise win, and nothing suggests trickery.

meaning: something that encourages you to act
example: The prize was an incentive to read more books.
hook: A sticker chart is an incentive: each gold star gives you a reason to keep practicing.

traps.why: A penalty punishes; an incentive encourages.
Incident looks similar but means an event that happens.
A goal is what you aim for; an incentive pushes you toward it.

syn1.tip: Stores offer incentives like coupons to get you to buy. An incentive is something offered to get you moving.

sc1.stem: To give students an _____ to turn in homework on time, the teacher promised a pizza party to any class with perfect homework for a month.

traps.why: A pizza party helps students, so it isn't an obstacle.
An excuse explains not acting; the party encourages acting.
Incident looks like incentive but means an event.

sc1.tip: The teacher 'promised a pizza party' so students would turn in work. Something promised to get people to act is an incentive.

decoys.why: The pizza party is a real reward promised to encourage students, not a fake image.
The teacher offers a reward to encourage work, not to make students jealous.
A pizza party encourages students to act; it does not give them honesty.

traps.why: An obstacle holds you back; an incentive pushes you forward.
Instinct looks a bit similar but means a natural urge you're born with.
A result comes after an action; an incentive comes before it.

syn2.tip: You hear 'an incentive to save money.' It's whatever motivates you to act, like a prize or bonus.

sc2.stem: Dad usually has to beg my little brother to rake the leaves, but when he offered five dollars per bag as an _____, my brother finished the whole yard before lunch.

traps.why: Insult is negative, but the money made him happy to work.
The money helped him finish, so it wasn't an obstacle.
Instinct looks similar, but money can't be an inborn urge.

sc2.tip: 'Usually has to beg' contrasts with 'finished the whole yard before lunch.' The money changed his behavior, so it was an incentive.

decoys.why: Dad really offered five dollars, so it was a reward that encouraged work, not a trick.
The money encouraged your brother to rake; nothing in the sentence is about jealousy.
Five dollars per bag is a reward that encourages action, not honesty.

meaning: complete and careful about every detail
example: The mechanic gave the car a thorough inspection.
hook: Thorough grew from the old word 'through': a thorough cleaning goes through every single corner.

traps.why: Careless is the opposite of thorough.
Thorny looks similar but means full of thorns.
Thorough work can be tiring, but thorough means covering everything.

syn1.tip: Thorough comes from 'through.' Something thorough goes all the way through, leaving nothing out.

sc1.stem: The detective's search of the room was _____; she checked under the rug, inside every drawer, and even behind the paintings on the wall.

traps.why: A hasty search would skip places; she checked everywhere.
Nothing says the search was hidden; the examples show it was complete.
Pointless is negative, but the examples praise how complete it was.

sc1.tip: After the semicolon, 'under the rug, inside every drawer, and even behind the paintings' gives examples. She searched everywhere.

decoys.why: She checked under the rug and behind paintings, so her search was active, not passive.
The sentence lists every place she searched, which describes completeness, not something hard to notice.
Nothing here is mean or small; she searched everywhere, which shows care about every detail.
A search cannot be see-through; the clue is that she checked every possible spot.
Nothing shows she felt hopeless; the sentence stresses how carefully she checked everything.
Nothing changes suddenly here; the list of places shows a complete, careful search.

traps.why: Sloppy is the opposite of thorough.
Speed is about time; thorough is about covering every detail.
Fussy is negative, like picky; thorough is a good kind of careful.

syn2.tip: Think of 'a thorough checkup' at the doctor: nothing gets skipped. Choose the word for attention to every detail.

sc2.stem: Last year Mia skimmed her notes the night before the test, but this time her studying was _____, and she reviewed every chapter, quiz, and vocabulary list.

traps.why: Rushed fits last year, but 'but' signals a change.
Thoughtless looks a bit like thorough but means not thinking.
Hiding her studying has nothing to do with reviewing everything.

sc2.tip: 'But' contrasts with 'skimmed her notes,' and 'every chapter, quiz, and vocabulary list' shows she covered everything.

decoys.why: She actively reviewed every chapter and quiz, so her studying was the opposite of passive.
The sentence stresses that she covered everything, not that her studying was hard to notice.
Reviewing every chapter, quiz, and list is big, careful work, not small or unimportant.
Studying is not see-through; the contrast with skimming points to complete, careful review.
Nothing changes suddenly; the sentence shows she steadily reviewed every chapter, quiz, and list.
Nothing shows she acted superior; the clue is that she reviewed everything instead of skimming.

meaning: famous and widely admired
example: The renowned chef opened a small restaurant in our town.
hook: Renowned comes from the French word for name: a renowned chef's name is admired everywhere.

traps.why: Unknown is the opposite of renowned.
Renewed looks similar but means made new again.
Infamous means famous for something bad; renowned is praise.

syn1.tip: Renowned contains 'nown,' which can remind you of 'known.' Renowned people are well known and respected.

sc1.stem: Although the marine biologist was barely known when she began her research, her discoveries about coral reefs eventually made her _____ throughout the world.

traps.why: Unknown matches 'barely known,' but 'although' signals a change.
Infamous is for bad deeds; her coral discoveries were good.
Money isn't the opposite of 'barely known'; fame is.

sc1.tip: 'Although... barely known' sets up a contrast. By the end she must be the opposite: famous across the world.

decoys.why: Notorious means famous for something bad, but her coral reef discoveries are admirable.
The sentence contrasts barely known with world fame, so petty, meaning unimportant, is backward.
Her discoveries brought her fame worldwide; nothing suggests she accepted things without acting.
Discoveries do not make someone hopeless; the contrast with barely known points to fame.
The sentence is about how well known she became, not about her acting superior.
A person cannot become see-through worldwide; the contrast with barely known points to fame.

traps.why: Barely noticed is the opposite of renowned.
Re- often means again, but renowned doesn't mean new again.
Famous people may be rich, but renowned is about admiration.

syn2.tip: Picture 'a renowned scientist' giving speeches worldwide. The word carries praise, so pick the choice about admiration by many.

sc2.stem: The _____ violinist's concert sold out within minutes, and fans traveled from dozens of countries just to hear her play.

traps.why: An unknown player wouldn't draw fans from dozens of countries.
Nerves wouldn't make a concert sell out in minutes.
An amateur rarely draws fans from around the world.

sc2.tip: Sold out 'within minutes' and fans from 'dozens of countries' are effects of great fame. Pick the word for famous and admired.

decoys.why: Fans traveling from many countries to hear her shows admiration, not fame for something bad.
A sold-out concert with fans from dozens of countries shows she is important, not unimportant.
The clue is her huge worldwide fame, not whether she accepts things without acting.
Nothing suggests she is hopeless; the sold-out show and traveling fans point to fame.
The sentence is about how famous she is, shown by fans from dozens of countries.
A violinist is not see-through; the sold-out concert shows she is famous and admired.

meaning: very deep or meaningful
example: The book had a profound effect on my thinking.
hook: Profound comes from Latin for deep, toward the bottom: a profound idea sinks far below the surface.

traps.why: Shallow is the opposite of profound.
Profound contains found, but it doesn't mean discovered.
Noticeable is too weak; profound means very deep.

syn1.tip: Think of 'profound sadness' or 'a profound question': both go far beneath the surface. The word measures depth.

sc1.stem: The visit to the children's hospital had a _____ effect on Malik; he came home quiet and thoughtful and soon decided he wanted to become a doctor.

traps.why: A minor effect wouldn't change his whole future.
He came home 'quiet and thoughtful,' not laughing.
The effect lasted, since he decided on a career.

sc1.tip: He came home 'quiet and thoughtful' and 'decided he wanted to become a doctor.' That shows a deep, life-changing effect.

decoys.why: The visit changed his whole future, so the effect was deep, not slight and hard to notice.
Deciding to become a doctor shows the effect was big and meaningful, not small.
An effect that inspired a life decision is not one that accepts things without acting.
The sentence is about how deeply the visit moved him, not about something see-through.
An effect cannot act superior; the visit made him thoughtful and changed his plans.
The effect was personal to Malik, not famous and admired around the world.

traps.why: Unimportant is the opposite of profound.
Professional starts the same way but means about a job.
Deep ideas can be hard, but profound means full of meaning.

syn2.tip: In 'a profound effect,' something changes you deeply. Choose the word for important and full of meaning.

sc2.stem: Most of the speaker's jokes were silly and forgettable, but her closing words about kindness were so _____ that the whole gym fell silent to think about them.

traps.why: Shallow matches the silly jokes, but 'but' signals a contrast.
Hilarious words cause laughter, not silent thinking.
Shortness wouldn't make a whole gym stop to think.

sc2.tip: 'But' contrasts her closing words with 'silly and forgettable' jokes, and the crowd 'fell silent to think.' Her words were deep.

decoys.why: Her closing words contrast with the silly jokes, so they were deep, not small and unimportant.
Words that made everyone silently think about kindness were meaningful, not superior or rude.
Her words were about kindness and made people think, not about being proud of herself.
The gym fell silent to think, which shows her words were meaningful, not famous for something bad.
Words that made a whole gym stop and think were deep, not about accepting things.
Nothing about her words changed suddenly; they were deep enough to make everyone think.

meaning: something that looks real but is not
example: The magician created the illusion of a floating card.
hook: A shimmering puddle on a hot road is an illusion: your eyes see water that isn't there.

traps.why: Reality is what's truly there; an illusion only seems real.
Allusion sounds similar but means a hint or reference.
A magician makes illusions, but an illusion isn't a person.

syn1.tip: Magic shows and 'optical illusions' fool your eyes. An illusion is a trick: it looks real, but it isn't.

sc1.stem: The puddle shimmering on the hot desert road was only an _____; when the travelers drove closer, the "water" vanished completely.

traps.why: An oasis has real water; this water vanished.
Allusion sounds similar but means a reference, not a false sight.
Nothing blocked the road; the water simply wasn't real.

sc1.tip: The 'water' 'vanished completely' up close, and the quotation marks hint it was never real. That's an illusion.

decoys.why: The water vanished when they drove closer, so it was something fake, not a reason to act.
A shimmering puddle that vanished was something that only looked real, not honesty.
The sentence describes fake water that vanished, not a feeling of wanting what others have.

traps.why: Plain truth is the opposite of an illusion.
Light can cause illusions, but an illusion is what falsely seems real.
Illusion starts like illness, but it has nothing to do with sickness.

syn2.tip: Think of 'an optical illusion,' where lines seem to bend but don't. Choose the phrase for something that only seems real.

sc2.stem: The tiny room felt surprisingly large, but the extra space was just an _____ created by a wall of mirrors that made it look twice its real size.

traps.why: An addition is real space, but the room only looked bigger.
Illness looks like illusion but means being sick.
The clue says the space wasn't real, not that it helped.

sc2.tip: 'But' and 'made it look twice its real size' tell you the extra space wasn't really there. That's an illusion.

decoys.why: The mirrors only made the room look bigger, so the space was fake, not an encouragement.
The extra space only looked real because of mirrors, which has nothing to do with honesty.
Mirrors created space that was not really there, not a feeling of wanting what others have.

meaning: a reason for doing something
example: The detective searched for the thief's motive.
hook: Motive and move share a Latin root: a motive is what moves you to act.

traps.why: A result comes after an action; a motive comes before.
Motor looks similar but is an engine.
A method is how you do something; a motive is why.

syn1.tip: Detectives look for a motive: the why behind a crime. It's whatever moves someone to act.

sc1.stem: Lila's _____ for joining the cooking club was simple: she wanted to learn to bake her grandfather's favorite bread for his birthday.

traps.why: The sentence explains why she joined, not what happened after.
Recipes fit cooking, but the sentence gives her reason for joining.
Motion looks like motive but means movement.

sc1.tip: After the colon, 'she wanted to learn to bake' explains why she joined. A reason for doing something is a motive.
