decoys.why: The sentence gives her reason for joining, baking for her grandfather, not an unfair preference.
She joined to bake a gift for her grandfather, not because she wanted what someone else had.
Her loving plan to bake for her grandfather shows no feeling that anyone is worthless.
The colon introduces her reason for joining, not an unfair opinion formed without facts.
Nothing here involves competition; the sentence explains her reason for joining the club.
The sentence explains why she joined, her reason, not her honesty or moral principles.

traps.why: An outcome is what happens after, not the reason before.
Motion looks similar but means movement.
Detectives find motives for crimes, but a motive is the reason.

syn2.tip: Ask 'Why?' A motive answers why someone does something. Look for the choice that names the aim behind an action.

sc2.stem: Everyone assumed Theo's _____ for running for class president was to get out of class for meetings, but he truly wanted the cafeteria to serve healthier lunches.

traps.why: Candidates give speeches, but the sentence is about why he ran.
A consequence comes after; the sentence describes what he wanted beforehand.
Motor looks like motive but is an engine.

sc2.tip: 'Truly wanted' tells you the sentence is about why Theo ran. The blank names the reason behind his action.

decoys.why: The sentence compares two reasons for running, so it needs a reason, not an achievement.
Both getting out of class and healthier lunches are reasons for running, not feelings of wanting.
The sentence explains his reason for running, and nothing shows he thought anyone was worthless.
The sentence is about why he ran, not about competing against another candidate.
Getting out of class and healthier lunches are reasons for running, not unfair opinions.
Morale means group spirit; the sentence is about his reason for running for president.

meaning: an experienced person who guides someone
example: My mentor taught me how to write computer code.
hook: In Homer's Odyssey, Mentor was the wise friend trusted to guide young Telemachus while his father was away.

traps.why: A beginner is the one who needs a mentor, the opposite role.
Monitor looks similar but means someone who watches, not someone who guides.
A classmate learns beside you; a mentor has more experience and guides you.

syn1.tip: Think of a coach or an older student who shows you the ropes. That person guides you.

sc1.stem: During her first year of teaching, Ms. Chen relied on her _____, an experienced teacher down the hall who gave her advice and helped plan her lessons.

traps.why: Ms. Chen is the new one; the experienced teacher is helping her, not learning.
A rival competes against you; this teacher was helping her.
Monitor looks similar but means someone who watches, not someone who advises.

sc1.tip: The sentence explains the blank right after the comma: "an experienced teacher" who "gave her advice." That is a guide.

decoys.why: The sentence describes an experienced teacher giving advice, not the main character in a story.
A legacy is something handed down, but the sentence describes a person down the hall.
The sentence names a helpful experienced teacher, not something that speeds up change.
Integrity is honesty, but the sentence calls the blank an experienced teacher.
The blank is an experienced teacher who gave advice, not a reward that encourages action.
Prestige is respect, but the sentence says the blank is a teacher who planned lessons.

traps.why: A beginner is the learner, not the experienced person giving advice.
A critic judges harshly; a mentor helps kindly.
A fellow student is at your level; a mentor knows more than you.

syn2.tip: A mentor gives advice from experience. Look for the choice that means someone wise you can turn to.

sc2.stem: Because Jada had never played chess before, she asked an older club member to be her _____, and he spent every lunch teaching her new openings.

traps.why: An opponent plays against you; he spent lunches teaching her instead.
An apprentice is a learner; Jada is the learner here, not him.
A critic finds faults; he patiently taught her.

sc2.tip: Jada "had never played," so she needed help, and he spent lunches "teaching her." The blank is an experienced helper.

decoys.why: Jada wants someone to teach her chess, not the main character of a story.
He spent lunches teaching her, which describes a guide, not something that sparks change.
An incentive is a reward, but the sentence describes a person teaching her openings.
He helped and taught her, which is guidance, not competition.
A legacy is handed down from the past, not a club member who teaches you.
Prestige is respect from success, not a person who teaches a beginner.

meaning: showing great excitement and interest
example: The enthusiastic fans cheered for the entire game.
hook: Picture a fan leaping off the bleachers, face painted, screaming before the ball even lands.

traps.why: Indifferent means not caring at all, the opposite of excited.
Nervous is a worried feeling, not a happy, excited one.
Agreeable means willing to go along, much weaker than excited.

syn1.tip: Think of an "enthusiastic crowd" cheering. The word is full of energy and excitement.

sc1.stem: Unlike her brother, who groaned at the idea, Zoe was _____ about the museum trip and had already planned which exhibits to visit first.

traps.why: Reluctant describes the groaning brother, and Zoe is unlike him.
Sulky is a gloomy feeling; Zoe was busy planning happily.
A forgetful person would not have planned which exhibits to visit.

sc1.tip: "Unlike her brother, who groaned" signals Zoe felt the opposite. She "had already planned" exhibits, so she was excited.

decoys.why: Zoe already planned which exhibits to see, so she was not just going along.
Nothing in the sentence shows Zoe being mean about small things; she was excited.
Zoe is contrasted with a groaning brother, so the word must mean excited, not proud.
Zoe was eager and planning ahead, not hopeless.
The sentence is about her excitement for a trip, not pride in her looks.

traps.why: Bored and tired is the opposite of excited.
Excited people may be loud, but enthusiastic is a positive word.
Mildly curious is far too weak for great excitement.

syn2.tip: Enthusiastic fans cheer the whole game. Pick the choice with the most energy and good feeling.

sc2.stem: Marcus was so _____ about joining the robotics club that he showed up an hour early and asked a dozen questions before the first meeting began.

traps.why: A hesitant person holds back; Marcus rushed in an hour early.
Calm is too mild for someone arriving an hour early.
Upset is an unhappy feeling, but Marcus could not wait to start.

sc2.tip: "So ... that he showed up an hour early" shows cause and effect. Only great excitement explains arriving that early.

decoys.why: Marcus showed up early and asked many questions, which is the opposite of passive.
Arriving early with questions shows excitement, not meanness about little things.
The sentence shows Marcus eager to learn, not acting better than others.
Nothing in the sentence is about pride in his looks; he was excited to join.
Showing up an hour early shows excitement, not careful reasoning.
Arriving an hour early with a dozen questions is very easy to notice.

meaning: to make known information that was secret
example: The company refused to disclose its secret recipe.
hook: Dis-close means un-close: open up the box and let the secret out.

traps.why: Conceal means to hide, the opposite of making something known.
Enclose looks similar but means to shut something inside.
Dis-close is not "move away from close"; it means to open up.

syn1.tip: Dis- undoes close, the way dislike undoes like. To un-close a secret is to open it up.

sc1.stem: The magician refused to _____ how he performed the trick, saying that a secret once shared is no longer a secret.

traps.why: He refused, so the blank must be the thing he would not do: tell.
Magicians rehearse tricks, but the sentence is about sharing a secret.
He already did the trick; the question is whether he would share how.

sc1.tip: He said "a secret once shared is no longer a secret," so he refused to share it. The blank means make known.

decoys.why: The magician already knows his trick; the sentence is about refusing to share the secret.
The sentence is about not sharing a secret, not judging how good the trick was.
His reason is about keeping a secret, so the blank means reveal, not give reasons.
The sentence is about not sharing a secret, not saying the opposite of something.

traps.why: Keeping something hidden is the opposite of disclosing it.
Shut is the meaning of close, but dis- reverses it.
Guessing is about secrets too, but disclosing means telling them.

syn2.tip: Companies "disclose" information when they tell the public. Find the choice that means telling what was secret.

sc2.stem: Nina kept her diary locked for months, but tonight she finally decided to _____ its secrets, reading every page aloud to her best friend.

traps.why: Guarding is what she did before; "but" signals a change to sharing.
She read every page aloud, so she did not erase anything.
Enclose looks similar but means to shut in, not to share.

sc2.tip: "Locked for months, but" signals a change. "Reading every page aloud" shows she shared the secrets.

decoys.why: She read every page aloud, so she shared the secrets instead of protecting them.
She is reading her secrets aloud to a friend, not getting something back.
Reading the pages aloud means sharing secrets, not judging their value.
Nothing says she thought her secrets were wrong; she simply shared them.
You cannot copy secrets you admire; the sentence shows her revealing them.
She reads her diary aloud, which reveals secrets rather than disagreeing with them.

meaning: wanting what someone else has
example: Her shiny new bike filled me with envy.
hook: "Green with envy" pictures your face turning green as you stare at a friend's shiny new phone.

traps.why: Contentment means being happy with what you have, the opposite of envy.
Envoy looks similar but means a messenger sent by a government.
Admiration is a warm feeling; envy is wanting what others have.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "green with envy." It is the bad feeling of wanting someone else's things.

sc1.stem: When Kofi saw his friend's brand-new telescope, he felt a pang of _____ and wished he had one just like it.

traps.why: Pride is a feeling about your own things, not wishing for a friend's.
Gratitude is a thankful feeling, but Kofi wanted what his friend had.
Satisfied people do not wish they had something else.

sc1.tip: The clue is "wished he had one just like it." Wanting what a friend has is that feeling.

decoys.why: Kofi wished he had the telescope, so he admired it rather than looked down on it.
Prestige is respect you earn, not a feeling of wanting someone else's telescope.
The sentence describes wishing for his friend's telescope, not a competition between them.
Kofi wanted the telescope; nothing shows an unfair opinion formed without facts.
Integrity is honesty, not the feeling of wishing you had what a friend has.

traps.why: Being happy for someone is the opposite of envying them.
Respect is a positive feeling; envy is an unhappy one.
Envy is about wanting what someone has, not missing what you lost.

syn2.tip: When you envy someone, you want what they have. Pick the choice about wanting another person's things.

sc2.stem: Rosa tried to hide her _____, but everyone could tell how badly she wanted her cousin's new phone; she stared at it all through dinner.

traps.why: Someone bored would not stare at the phone all dinner.
Curiosity is wondering about something; Rosa badly wanted it for herself.
Generosity is a giving feeling, but Rosa wanted to have, not give.

sc2.tip: The sentence restates the blank: "how badly she wanted her cousin's new phone." That is the feeling.

decoys.why: Rosa badly wanted the phone, so she did not think it was worthless.
The sentence says she wanted her cousin's phone, not that she held an unfair opinion.
She was hiding how badly she wanted the phone, not her honesty.
Staring at the phone shows wanting it, not an unfair preference.
Rosa is hiding a feeling of wanting something, not respect she has earned.
The phone was real; Rosa was hiding her wish to have it.

meaning: famous for something bad
example: The bridge was notorious for its traffic jams.
hook: Al Capone was a notorious gangster: everyone knew his name, and none of the reasons were good.

traps.why: Unknown means nobody has heard of it, the opposite of notorious.
Celebrated means famous for good things; notorious is famous for bad things.
Nutritious looks similar but means healthy to eat.

syn1.tip: You hear of a "notorious criminal," never a notorious hero. It means well known for something bad.

sc1.stem: The old pirate ship was _____ along the coast; sailors everywhere knew its black sails and feared meeting it on the open sea.

traps.why: Sailors everywhere knew its sails, so it was not unknown.
Sailors feared meeting it, so it was not loved.
Old ships can be abandoned, but sailors feared meeting this one at sea.

sc1.tip: Two clues work together: "sailors everywhere knew" it, and they "feared meeting it." Known widely and feared means famous for bad things.

decoys.why: Sailors feared the ship, so it was famous for something bad, not admired.
The sentence is about the ship being feared and well known, not believable.
The ship had black sails sailors recognized; nothing is about seeing through it.
The sentence stresses fear and fame, not whether the ship was real or a copy.
A ship cannot feel excited, and the sentence says sailors feared meeting it.
A ship everyone feared on the open sea was hardly quiet and accepting.

traps.why: Being admired is good fame; notorious fame is bad.
Notorious things are talked about a lot.
The word starts like note, but it does not mean having notes.

syn2.tip: Notorious is a negative word: think of a "notorious villain." Look for the choice about being known for bad things.

sc2.stem: Though the diner was _____ for slow service and cold fries, people still lined up every weekend for its famous milkshakes.

traps.why: Nobody praises slow service and cold fries.
People do not recommend a place for its cold fries.
Nutritious looks similar but means healthy, which makes no sense here.

sc2.tip: "Though" and "still" set up a contrast: people come despite the diner's bad reputation. The blank is known for bad things.

decoys.why: Slow service and cold fries are bad things, so the diner was not admired for them.
The diner is known for bad service, not hopelessly wanting slow service.

meaning: to suggest something without saying it directly
example: Her smile implied that she liked the gift.
hook: When a friend says "Nice shoes" with a smirk, the smirk implies she doesn't mean it.

traps.why: To state is to say it directly; to imply is to hint.
The speaker implies; the listener infers, or figures it out.
Apply looks similar but means to put on or to request.

syn1.tip: Think of "Are you implying I'm wrong?" It means hinting at something without saying it outright.

sc1.stem: Ms. Lopez never said out loud that the essay was late, but her raised eyebrow seemed to _____ that she knew exactly when it had been turned in.

traps.why: Her eyebrow showed she knew, so it did not deny it.
Ms. Lopez gives the hint; the student would infer it.
Declaring is saying out loud, but she "never said" it.

sc1.tip: "Never said out loud ... but her raised eyebrow" shows she sent a message without words. That is hinting.

decoys.why: The eyebrow is sending a message, not noticing something, so perceive does not fit.
The eyebrow supports what she knew; nothing is being said the opposite of.

traps.why: Spelling something out means saying it clearly, the opposite of hinting.
Figuring out a hint is inferring; implying is giving the hint.
Apply looks like imply, but applying for something means requesting it.

syn2.tip: Imply means saying something without words, like a look or a tone. Choose the phrase about a quiet signal.

sc2.stem: Grandma's question, 'Did you finish your homework already?', was meant to _____ something; she was hinting that the video game should wait.

traps.why: Forbidding is a firm order, but Grandma was only hinting.
Grandma gives the hint; you would infer what she meant.
Announcing is saying it plainly, but she only asked a question.

sc2.tip: After the semicolon the sentence restates the blank: "she was hinting." A question that hints at something suggests it.

decoys.why: The sentence says Grandma was hinting, and confront means dealing with something directly.
Grandma was hinting at an idea, not saying the opposite of anything.
Her question was a hint, not a way of judging the value of something.
A question cannot bring something back; she was hinting the game should wait.
She was hinting at something, not protecting anything from waste.

meaning: able to make choices quickly and firmly
example: A decisive leader, she chose a plan within minutes.
hook: A decisive referee blows the whistle at once, makes the call, and never changes it.

traps.why: Hesitant people hold back from choosing, the opposite of decisive.
Divisive looks similar but means causing people to disagree.
Stubborn is the negative word for refusing to change your mind.

syn1.tip: Decisive is inside the word decide. A decisive person decides quickly and stands by it.

sc1.stem: While the other captains wasted time debating, Keisha was _____; she chose her team's strategy in seconds and never second-guessed it.

traps.why: She chose in seconds, so she did not hesitate.
Divisive looks similar but means causing arguments, not choosing quickly.
The other captains did the talking; Keisha chose fast.

sc1.tip: "While the other captains wasted time debating" sets up a contrast. She "chose ... in seconds and never second-guessed it."

decoys.why: Keisha chose quickly and acted, and passive means not taking action.
She never second-guessed her choice, so she did not change suddenly.
Choosing in seconds is quick and firm, not complicated with many parts.
Imminent describes events about to happen, not a person who makes quick choices.
The sentence is about choosing quickly, not about being see-through.

traps.why: Being unable to choose is the opposite of decisive.
That describes divisive, a lookalike word about causing disagreement.
That is a negative trait; decisive is a positive word.

syn2.tip: Look inside decisive for decide. The answer should describe someone who makes up their mind fast.

sc2.stem: Because Coach Ruiz was so _____, the team never wasted time in the huddle; she picked a play in seconds and everyone ran it with confidence.

traps.why: An uncertain coach would waste time, but this team never did.
Being liked does not explain picking plays in seconds.
Deceptive looks a bit similar but means tricky or misleading.

sc2.tip: "Because" signals cause and effect: the team "never wasted time" because she "picked a play in seconds."

decoys.why: The coach picked a play in seconds, and passive means not taking action.
Everyone ran the play with confidence, so she was steady, not likely to change suddenly.
Imminent describes something about to happen, not a coach who chooses quickly.
One coach cannot be made of different kinds; the clue is quick choices.
Being mean about little things would not make the team confident and quick.

meaning: to face a problem or person directly
example: She finally decided to confront her fear of heights.
hook: Con-front: you put your front toward someone and stand face to face.

traps.why: Avoiding means staying away, the opposite of facing something.
Comfort looks similar but means to make someone feel better.
Confronting means facing directly, not fighting or hurting.

syn1.tip: Look for front inside confront. You confront a fear by turning your front toward it.

sc1.stem: Instead of avoiding the classmate who had been spreading rumors, Tariq decided to _____ him and ask him to stop.

traps.why: "Instead of avoiding" means he did not ignore the classmate.
Comfort looks similar, but he wanted the rumors to stop.
He only asked him to stop, which is far milder than punishing.

sc1.tip: "Instead of avoiding" signals the opposite of avoiding. He went straight to the classmate to "ask him to stop."

decoys.why: Tariq wants the rumors to stop, so he would not copy the classmate.
Tariq wants to ask him to stop, not let him keep enjoying himself.
Tariq is against the rumors, so he would not publicly support this classmate.
Tariq wants the rumors to end, not to encourage the classmate's behavior.
Instead of avoiding him means facing him, not bringing him back.

traps.why: Steering clear means avoiding, the opposite of confronting.
Front is in the word, but confront does not mean leading the way.
Confronting someone is facing them, not fighting them.

syn2.tip: People "confront their fears." That means facing a problem directly instead of running from it.

sc2.stem: Mia's fear of the deep end kept her out of the pool all summer, so this year she has decided to _____ it by taking swimming lessons.

traps.why: Taking lessons is facing the fear, not running from it.
Confirm looks similar, but lessons would not prove her fear right.
Sharing a fear means telling others; lessons are how she tackles it.

sc2.tip: "So" shows cause and effect: the fear kept her out, so now she is "taking swimming lessons" to meet it directly.

decoys.why: Mia wants to get past her fear, not protect it from being lost.
Taking lessons is meant to face her fear, not help it grow.
Staying out of the pool indulged her fear; lessons do the opposite.
Swimming lessons do not give a good reason for her fear; they help her face it.
Mia does not want to support her fear; she wants to face it.

meaning: competition between two people or groups
example: The rivalry between the two schools is over fifty years old.
hook: Think Yankees versus Red Sox: two teams that have battled to beat each other for over a century.

traps.why: Cooperation means working together, the opposite of competing.
Revelry sounds similar but means noisy partying.
A rivalry is the contest itself, not winning it.

syn1.tip: A rival is someone you try to beat. A rivalry is the contest between rivals.

sc1.stem: Every year the two neighboring towns compete fiercely to grow the largest pumpkin, a friendly _____ that draws huge crowds to the autumn fair.

traps.why: The towns compete fiercely, so they are not partners.
The sentence calls it "friendly," so hatred is far too strong.
Pumpkins are harvested, but the sentence is about towns competing.

sc1.tip: "Compete fiercely" every year describes the blank. A friendly, ongoing competition between two sides is the answer.

decoys.why: The towns compete fiercely, which is the opposite of general agreement.
In a fierce competition neither town gives anything up to the other.
The towns are competing to grow pumpkins, not arguing about a public issue.
The blank names the competition between towns, not a person who guides someone.

traps.why: Teamwork means working together, the opposite of a rivalry.
One game is too narrow; a rivalry lasts over many contests.
Rivals compete, but a rivalry can be friendly, not hateful.

syn2.tip: Find rival inside rivalry. Rivals keep trying to beat each other, often for years.

sc2.stem: Although the twins share a room and finish each other's sentences, their _____ on the soccer field is intense; each one is desperate to score more goals than the other.

traps.why: "Although" signals a contrast with being close, so the blank is about competing.
Each twin wants to outscore the other, which is not teamwork.
Revelry sounds similar but means partying, not competing.

sc2.tip: "Although" contrasts their closeness at home with the field, where "each one is desperate to score more goals than the other."

decoys.why: Each twin wants to beat the other, so they are not in agreement.
Each twin is desperate to win, so neither is giving anything up.
The sentence describes twins competing against each other, not a group's team spirit.
Trying to outscore each other is competition, not traditions passed down from ancestors.
The clue is about scoring more goals than each other, not about honesty.

meaning: an unfair opinion formed without knowing the facts
example: The new student faced prejudice because of the way she dressed.
hook: Pre-judice means judging before: deciding what someone is like before you have even met them.

traps.why: Fairness means judging evenly, the opposite of prejudice.
Both start with pre-, but prediction is a guess about the future.
Judges give punishments, but prejudice is an unfair opinion.

syn1.tip: Split it: pre (before) plus judge. Judging people before you know them is an unfair, one-sided view.

sc1.stem: Before meeting any of the players, Kenji had already decided the rival team was lazy, a _____ that vanished once he saw how hard they practiced.

traps.why: Calling a team lazy is an insult, not a compliment.
He decided "before meeting any of the players," so he had observed nothing.
Judging people before meeting them is not fair.

sc1.tip: "Before meeting any of the players" he "had already decided." An opinion formed before the facts is the answer.

decoys.why: The blank names Kenji's unfair opinion about the team, not the competition between teams.
Only Kenji decided this, so it was not general agreement among a group.
Judging a team before meeting them is an unfair opinion, not a great achievement.
Kenji decided on his own; no two sides gave anything up.
Kenji's quick opinion about the team was not a tradition passed down from ancestors.

traps.why: An open mind waits for facts, the opposite of prejudice.
Courts make judgments, but prejudice is a personal unfair opinion.
Pre- means before, but prejudice is not a warning ahead of time.

syn2.tip: Look for pre- and judge in prejudice. It means judging too early, before the facts, which is unfair.

sc2.stem: Grandpa called video games silly without ever trying one, but after an hour of puzzle games with me, his _____ disappeared and he asked for a rematch.

traps.why: If his enthusiasm vanished, he would not ask for a rematch.
He had never tried one, so he had no experience to lose.
Asking for a rematch shows interest, so his curiosity did not disappear.

sc2.tip: "Without ever trying one" shows he judged too soon. "But" signals that the unfair opinion vanished once he played.

decoys.why: He asked for a rematch, so the competition did not disappear; his unfair opinion did.
Grandpa was enjoying himself, so his spirit and confidence would not disappear.
Grandpa did not lose his honesty; he dropped an opinion formed without trying games.
The sentence is about his opinion of games changing, not losing respect or rank.
What disappeared was his view of video games, not something handed down from the past.

meaning: believable; able to be trusted
example: The witness gave a credible account of the accident.
hook: Credible shares its Latin root cred, meaning believe, with words like credit and credentials.

traps.why: Doubtful is the opposite of credible; it means hard to believe.
Popular things are liked by many, but that doesn't make them believable.
Impressive is close to what incredible often means, but credible means believable.

syn1.tip: Look for cred, which means believe, plus -ible, which means able to be. Credible means able to be believed.

sc1.stem: Because the article cited no sources and was full of spelling errors, the students decided it was not a _____ source for their research report.

traps.why: The article was flawed, so saying it was not flawed contradicts the clue.
Popularity has nothing to do with missing sources and spelling errors.
Recent is about the date, but the clue is about whether it can be trusted.

sc1.tip: The words "cited no sources" and "full of spelling errors" show the article can't be trusted, so it is not a believable source.

decoys.why: The sentence is about whether the article can be trusted, not whether it is famous for something bad.
An article does not make quick choices; the clue is about missing sources and errors.
Passive describes not taking action, which has nothing to do with whether a source is trustworthy.
The problem is missing sources and spelling errors, not that the article changes suddenly.
Variety is not the issue; the students rejected the article because it could not be trusted.
The clue is about trust, and an article is not something hard to beat.

traps.why: Unreliable is the opposite; a credible source is one you can rely on.
Gullible describes someone who believes too easily, not something worth believing.
Edible means safe to eat; it only shares the -ible ending.

syn2.tip: Think of credit: a bank gives credit to people it trusts. Credible things deserve your trust.

sc2.stem: Although Marco's excuse about a dog eating his homework sounded silly at first, it became _____ when he showed the teacher the chewed, soggy pages.

traps.why: The excuse sounded silly at first; the chewed pages changed that, so ridiculous is backward.
Edible means safe to eat; it only looks like credible.
The pages made the story easier to believe, not more complicated.

sc2.tip: "Although" signals a change: the excuse "sounded silly at first," but the chewed pages proved it, so it became believable.

decoys.why: A transparent excuse is an obvious lie, but the chewed pages made his story believable.
Showing the pages made the excuse believable, not more complicated.
The sentence says the excuse turned out to be believable, not small or mean.
Nothing says the excuse became famous for something bad; the proof made it believable.
The soggy pages made the excuse believable, not hard to notice.
An excuse cannot be about to happen; the clue is that the proof made it believable.

meaning: something that causes or speeds up change
example: Her speech was the catalyst for the school's recycling program.
hook: In chemistry, a catalyst speeds up a reaction; in life, it is the spark that gets big changes going.

traps.why: An obstacle blocks change; a catalyst gets change started.
A catalog is a list of items for sale; it only looks like catalyst.
A result comes after a change; a catalyst comes first and causes it.

syn1.tip: Think of science class: a catalyst makes a reaction happen faster. Anything that sets off change is a catalyst.

sc1.stem: The discovery of gold in California was the _____ for rapid change, causing thousands of people to rush west and towns to spring up almost overnight.

traps.why: A setback slows things down, but the discovery made change happen fast.
Gold sounds like a reward, but the clue is about what started rapid change.
California was the place, but the discovery itself is what set off the change.

sc1.tip: "Causing thousands of people to rush west" shows the discovery started the change, so it was the spark.

decoys.why: Gold did not create agreement; the sentence says it caused rapid change.
No one gave anything up; the gold discovery set rapid change in motion.
Finding gold was not a shortage; it sparked a rush and new towns.
The gold was real and truly caused people to rush west.
Heritage is passed down from ancestors, but the sentence is about something that caused sudden change.
The sentence is about what caused rapid change, not competition between groups.

traps.why: A barrier stops things from moving forward; a catalyst pushes change ahead.
An outcome is what happens at the end, not what starts the change.
In science a catalyst can be a chemical, but the word means a trigger.

syn2.tip: A catalyst is the thing that starts something happening, like pulling a trigger. Picture a match lighting a fire.

sc2.stem: Mia's science fair win was the _____ that turned her quiet interest in robots into a real passion; in other words, it set everything in motion.

traps.why: An obstacle would block her passion, but the win set everything in motion.
A catalog is a list of products; it only looks like catalyst.
A reminder brings back the past; it doesn't set things in motion.

sc2.tip: "In other words, it set everything in motion" restates the blank: the win was what started the change.

decoys.why: A win is an event, not a person who guides her; it set everything in motion.
Her win was real and truly sparked her passion.
A win is not a shortage; the sentence says it set everything in motion.
No one gave anything up; the win sparked her passion for robots.
The sentence is about what started her passion, not an unfair opinion.
Nothing here seems self-contradictory; the win simply set everything in motion.

meaning: respect earned through success or high rank
example: Winning the national spelling bee brought great prestige to the school.
hook: Prestige once meant a magic trick; today it means the dazzling respect that comes with big success.

traps.why: Disgrace means loss of respect, the opposite of prestige.
Rich people may have prestige, but prestige is respect, not money.
Pride is a feeling inside you; prestige is respect others give you.

syn1.tip: Think of a prestigious school or award: it is admired because of its success and high rank.

sc1.stem: Being chosen to perform at the famous concert hall carried enormous _____ for the young orchestra, earning them invitations and admiration from musicians everywhere.

traps.why: Shame would not bring invitations and admiration from musicians.
Risk is a worried, negative idea; the clue shows only good results.
Concerts can cost money, but the clue is about admiration, not cost.

sc1.tip: "Earning them invitations and admiration from musicians everywhere" shows the honor brought respect, which is prestige.

decoys.why: The orchestra earned admiration from musicians, which is the opposite of being seen as worthless.
Others might feel envy, but the honor itself earned the orchestra respect and admiration.
Nothing in the sentence involves disagreement; it describes respect and admiration.
The performance gave the orchestra something, admiration, rather than a shortage.
The sentence describes earned respect, not an unfair opinion.
The admiration came from success, not an unfair preference.

traps.why: Public shame is the opposite of the respect that prestige brings.
A fortune is money, but prestige is respect, which money can't guarantee.
Hard work may earn prestige, but it isn't the respect itself.

syn2.tip: Prestige is how highly others rank you. Picture a trophy that makes everyone look up to the winner.

sc2.stem: Though the small art school had little money and few buildings, its famous graduates gave it more _____ than many larger colleges, and students competed hard to get in.

traps.why: Students would not compete to join a school that embarrasses them.
Graduates can't add buildings or room; the clue is about reputation.
Trouble is negative, but famous graduates and eager students show something good.

sc2.tip: "Though" sets up a contrast: little money, but "famous graduates" and students who "competed hard to get in" show the school was highly respected.

decoys.why: Students competed hard to get in, so the school was respected, not looked down on.
The school lacked money, but its graduates gave it respect, not a shortage.
Famous graduates bring a school respect and fame, not honesty.
Nothing here involves disagreement; famous graduates made the school respected.
The sentence is about the respect the school earned, not agreement among a group.
The graduates earned the school respect through success, not an unfair preference.

meaning: acting as if you are better than others
example: The arrogant player refused to listen to his coach.
hook: Picture someone with their nose in the air, strutting past everyone as if the whole world were their throne.

traps.why: Humble people don't think they are better than others; it's the opposite.
Confident is the positive version; arrogant means looking down on others.
Ignorant means lacking knowledge; it only looks like arrogant.

syn1.tip: Arrogant has a negative feeling. Picture a show-off who won't listen to anyone because he thinks he knows best.

sc1.stem: After winning one chess match, Derek became so _____ that he bragged to everyone and refused to take advice from players who had been competing for years.

traps.why: A shy person wouldn't brag to everyone.
Winning shows some skill, but bragging and refusing advice show an attitude.
Excited is a happy feeling; refusing expert advice shows something worse.

sc1.tip: "Bragged to everyone" and "refused to take advice" from experienced players show Derek thinks he is better than others.

decoys.why: Bragging to everyone is the opposite of quietly accepting things.
Excitement alone does not explain bragging and refusing advice from experienced players.
One win does not make him widely admired; the sentence describes him acting superior.
Refusing advice from experienced players after one win is not clear thinking.
A person cannot become outdated by winning; the clues are bragging and refusing advice.
The sentence is about bragging and acting superior, not being careful with details.

traps.why: Modest people play down their success, the opposite of arrogant.
Arrogant people may be rude, but arrogant specifically means acting superior.
Self-assured is a positive word; arrogant is negative.

syn2.tip: An arrogant person acts superior, like a snob who thinks others are beneath them.

sc2.stem: Unlike his _____ older brother, who sneered at anyone who could not keep up, Leo patiently helped the younger kids learn to skateboard at the park.

traps.why: Leo is the helpful one; "unlike" means his brother is different.
A clumsy brother would not sneer at people who can't keep up.
Quiet doesn't explain sneering; the clue is about looking down on others.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" contrasts the brother with patient Leo, and "sneered at anyone who could not keep up" shows the brother thinks he's better.

decoys.why: The brother sneered at others, which shows he thought he was better, not that he did nothing.
Sneering at people is not slight or hard to notice.
The brother sneered at slower kids, which is acting superior, not showing excitement.
The contrast is about attitude toward others, not about being famous and admired.
Nothing in the sentence is about whether the brother can be believed.
A brother is not outdated; the clue is that he sneered at others.

meaning: a feeling that someone is worthless
example: The champion looked at his rookie opponent with contempt.
hook: In "contempt of court," someone openly disrespects a judge; contempt means looking down on someone as worthless.

traps.why: Admiration means looking up to someone, the opposite of contempt.
Contentment means feeling satisfied; it only looks like contempt.
Anger can be hot and quick; contempt means thinking someone is worthless.

syn1.tip: You may know "contempt of court," when someone disrespects a judge. Contempt is a sneering, looking-down feeling.

sc1.stem: The champion treated his first-time opponent with _____, refusing to shake her hand and smirking as if she did not deserve to share the court with him.

traps.why: Refusing a handshake and smirking are not kind.
He acts as if she doesn't deserve to be there, not as if she scares him.
Smirking can look amused, but acting like she doesn't deserve the court is scornful.

sc1.tip: "Refusing to shake her hand" and "smirking as if she did not deserve" to be there show he thinks she is worthless.

decoys.why: The champion is not jealous of a beginner; he smirked as if she were beneath him.
Refusing a handshake and smirking show scorn, not a gut feeling.
He gave up nothing; he refused her hand and smirked at her.
The sentence describes how he treated her, with scorn, not something fake.
Nothing is self-contradictory; he simply acted like she was worthless.

traps.why: Honor shows high respect, the opposite of contempt.
Attempt rhymes with contempt, but it means a try.
Jealousy means wanting what someone has; contempt means thinking they're worthless.

syn2.tip: Picture a sneer or an eye roll. Contempt is the feeling that someone isn't worth your respect.

sc2.stem: Because the bully had laughed at her drawings for weeks, Nora felt nothing but _____ for him and would not even look at him when he apologized.

traps.why: Sympathy means caring about someone's feelings; Nora won't even look at him.
Gratitude is a thankful feeling, but the bully gave her nothing to thank.
Envy means wanting what he has; Nora wants nothing from the bully.

sc2.tip: "Because" the bully "laughed at her drawings for weeks," Nora "would not even look at him." She thinks he is worthless.

decoys.why: Nora does not want what the bully has; she refuses to even look at him.
The sentence describes a strong negative feeling toward the bully, not a gut feeling.
Morale is a group's spirit, but Nora feels scorn for one person.
Nora is not disagreeing with an opinion; she feels the bully is worthless.
Her feeling is real; she will not even look at him.
Nothing here seems self-contradictory; she plainly scorns the bully.

meaning: too proud of your looks or abilities
example: The vain prince stared at his reflection all day.
hook: Picture a peacock admiring its feathers in a mirror; that is vain. Don't confuse it with vein or weather vane.

sc1.stem: Ava was so _____ about her hair that she checked her reflection in every window she passed and spent an hour styling it each morning.

traps.why: A careless person wouldn't spend an hour styling her hair.
Checking every window and styling for an hour isn't relaxed.
Curious means wanting to learn; checking every reflection shows pride, not curiosity.

sc1.tip: "Checked her reflection in every window" and "an hour styling it each morning" show too much pride in her looks.

decoys.why: Ava spends an hour styling her hair each morning, so she is anything but passive about it.
Elaborate could describe a hairstyle, but not a person who keeps checking her reflection.
Petty means mean about small things, but the sentence shows pride in her looks.
Windows are transparent, but the sentence is about Ava admiring her own hair.
Checking every window and styling for an hour is not subtle at all.
Nothing about checking every window shows clear thinking; it shows pride in her looks.

sc2.stem: The famous actor was surprisingly modest in interviews, but his costar was so _____ that she demanded mirrors in every room and talked only about her own beauty.

traps.why: "But" shows the costar is unlike the modest actor, so humble is backward.
That fits "in vain," but the sentence is about her pride in her beauty.
Talent doesn't explain demanding mirrors and talking only about her beauty.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the costar with the "modest" actor, and "talked only about her own beauty" shows too much pride in her looks.

decoys.why: The sentence mentions fame, but the clue is talking only about her own beauty.
Someone who demands mirrors in every room is not passive.
The costar is contrasted with a modest actor, so a praising word like authentic does not fit.
Being believable has nothing to do with demanding mirrors and praising her own beauty.
Talking only about her own beauty is shallow, not deep or meaningful.
Demanding mirrors in every room is the opposite of subtle.

meaning: to say strongly that something is wrong
example: Many people condemned the littering at the beach.
hook: Picture a judge banging the gavel and declaring for all to hear that something is wrong; that is what condemn means.

traps.why: Praise means saying something is good, the opposite of condemn.
Condense means to make smaller or thicker; it only looks like condemn.
You can discuss something without saying it is wrong.

syn1.tip: Condemn has a strong negative feeling. Think of leaders who condemn cruelty: they say loudly that it is wrong.

sc1.stem: Scientists around the world were quick to _____ the company's illegal dumping of waste into the river, calling it harmful and irresponsible.

traps.why: Calling the dumping harmful is not defending it.
Condone means to allow or excuse; it looks like condemn but is nearly opposite.
Advertising promotes something; calling it harmful does the opposite.

sc1.tip: "Calling it harmful and irresponsible" is strong public disapproval, so the scientists said the dumping was wrong.

decoys.why: The scientists called the dumping harmful, so they would not publicly support it.
Calling the dumping irresponsible means they attacked it, not gave reasons for it.
The scientists called the dumping harmful, so they would not encourage it.
You do not make stronger something you are calling harmful and irresponsible.
Scientists calling the dumping harmful would never want to copy it.
Conserve fits the river topic, but you cannot protect dumping you are calling harmful.

traps.why: Warmly praise is the opposite of saying something is wrong.
Ignoring says nothing at all; condemning speaks out against something.
Mildly question is far too weak; condemning is strong disapproval.

syn2.tip: A building that is "condemned" is declared unsafe. To condemn is to declare strongly that something is bad or wrong.

sc2.stem: Unlike the many people who praised the new law, the mayor chose to _____ it in a fiery speech, calling it cruel and unfair to families.

traps.why: Applauding agrees with the people who praised it, but "unlike" means the mayor disagreed.
Mayors sign laws, but calling it cruel shows she spoke against it.
Doubting is much weaker than calling something cruel in a fiery speech.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" sets the mayor against people who "praised" the law, and "calling it cruel and unfair" shows strong disapproval.

decoys.why: Unlike those who praised the law, the mayor called it cruel, so she did not support it.
The mayor called the law cruel and unfair, so she was not defending it.
Calling a law cruel in a fiery speech does not make it stronger.
The mayor was against the law, so she would not encourage it.
The word unlike tells you the mayor disagreed, so she would not copy the law.
A fiery speech calling the law cruel is an attack, not a special pleasure.

meaning: likely to change suddenly
example: The weather in the mountains is volatile.
hook: Picture a volcano that might erupt any minute: volatile things, and people, can blow up or change suddenly.

traps.why: Steady means staying the same, the opposite of volatile.
Valuable means worth a lot; it only looks a little like volatile.
A volatile person might turn violent, but volatile means likely to change suddenly.

syn1.tip: You may hear about a volatile temper or volatile weather. Both can change in a flash.

sc1.stem: Mountain weather is so _____ that a sunny morning can turn into a hailstorm within an hour, so hikers must always pack rain gear.

traps.why: Stable weather wouldn't turn from sun to hail within an hour.
Mountains can be cold, but the clue is about sudden change.
A surprise hailstorm isn't pleasant; the clue warns hikers to be ready.

sc1.tip: "A sunny morning can turn into a hailstorm within an hour" shows the weather changes suddenly.

decoys.why: A storm can be imminent, but the clue is weather that changes suddenly within an hour.
Clear skies are not the point; the sentence describes sunshine turning into hail.
Weather does not choose to act, and the clue is about sudden change.
Weather cannot think, and the sentence is about quick, surprising change.
Being believable does not explain a sunny morning turning into a hailstorm.
Weather cannot be out of date; the sentence is about sudden change.

traps.why: Always the same is the opposite of volatile.
Volatile comes from a Latin word for fly, but it means likely to change.
That describes fragile things; volatile things change suddenly instead.

syn2.tip: Think of a volatile mood that flips from happy to furious. Volatile means it can change in a moment.

sc2.stem: Sam's older dog was calm around strangers, but his new puppy was so _____ that it could be licking someone's hand one moment and growling at them the next.

traps.why: "But" shows the puppy is unlike the calm dog, so gentle is backward.
Puppies are playful, but growling suddenly shows quick changes, not play.
Versatile means able to do many things well; it only looks like volatile.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the puppy with the "calm" dog, and licking "one moment" then growling "the next" shows sudden change.

decoys.why: A puppy that licks then growls is reacting quickly, not accepting things quietly.
Licking hands sounds eager, but growling the next moment shows sudden change, not excitement.
Growling is not merciless, and the puppy also licks hands; the clue is quick change.
Switching from licking to growling for no reason is not clear thinking.
A puppy cannot mock anyone; the sentence shows its mood changing suddenly.
The clue is the puppy switching moods, not making firm choices.

meaning: to notice or become aware of
example: Dogs can perceive sounds that humans cannot hear.
hook: Your eyes, ears, and nose help you perceive the world, like smelling smoke before you ever see the fire.

traps.why: Overlook means to miss something, the opposite of perceive.
Receive means to get something; it only looks and rhymes like perceive.
Believing means accepting something as true; perceiving means noticing it.

syn1.tip: Think of perception, how your senses take in the world. To perceive is to notice through seeing, hearing, or feeling.

sc1.stem: Bats use echoes to _____ insects flying in total darkness, finding their prey even when they cannot see it.

traps.why: Bats find their prey, so they don't ignore the insects.
Bats may scare insects, but the clue is about finding them without seeing.
Receive means to be given something; it only looks like perceive.

sc1.tip: "Finding their prey even when they cannot see it" shows bats become aware of insects by using echoes.

decoys.why: Bats are finding hidden prey, not revealing secret information.
The bats are detecting insects, not hinting at something.
Bats are finding their prey in the dark, not saying it is wrong.
Bats hunt insects; they are not copying them.
The sentence is about bats noticing prey, not publicly approving of it.
Bats are hunting the insects as prey, not protecting them.

traps.why: Fail to see is the opposite of perceive.
Thinking hard about something is different from first noticing it.
Deceive rhymes with perceive, but deceive means to trick.

syn2.tip: Perceive is about your senses picking something up. If you perceive a sound, you become aware of it.

sc2.stem: The change in the music was so tiny that most listeners missed it, but the trained conductor was able to _____ it right away and stopped the orchestra.

traps.why: Most listeners overlooked it; "but" shows the conductor did the opposite.
Conductors work with music, but he stopped the orchestra because he noticed something.
Deceive rhymes with perceive, but it means to trick.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the conductor with listeners who "missed it," and he "stopped the orchestra," so he noticed the change.

decoys.why: The clue is that most listeners missed the tiny change, so the point is noticing it.
The conductor noticed the change; he was not hinting at anything.
The conductor stopped the orchestra, so he was not copying the change.
He stopped the orchestra, so he was not approving of the change.
The sentence is about catching a tiny change most people missed, not easing pain.
You cannot bring back a change in music; the clue is that he noticed it.

meaning: get something back; bring back
example: The dog retrieved the tennis ball from the edge of the lake.
hook: Golden retrievers got their name because they retrieve, bringing back ducks and tennis balls their owners send flying.

traps.why: Abandon means to leave behind, the opposite of retrieve.
Relieve means to ease pain or worry; it only looks like retrieve.
You throw a ball for a dog, but the dog retrieves it by bringing it back.

syn1.tip: Think of a golden retriever bringing back a stick. The re- means back: retrieve means get it back.

sc1.stem: Realizing she had left her science project on the bus, Isabel raced to the depot to _____ it before the driver began his next route.

traps.why: She already forgot it; she races to the depot to get it back.
Nothing says the project is broken; she just left it on the bus.
Replacing means getting a new one; Isabel wants her own project back.

sc1.tip: "Left her science project on the bus" causes her to race to the depot, so she wants to get it back.

decoys.why: Isabel already knows where the project is; she raced to get it back.
Isabel left the project on the bus, so she needs to get it back, not reveal it.
Isabel raced to the depot to get her project back, not to judge its quality.
She left the project behind, so she needs to recover it, not approve it.
Racing before the bus leaves shows she wants her project back, not to give reasons.
You cannot copy a lost project; Isabel wants to get it back.

traps.why: Leave behind is the opposite of getting something back.
Re- can mean again, but here it means back, not trying again.
You may search first, but retrieve means actually getting it back.

syn2.tip: The re- in retrieve means back, as in return. A retriever dog gets the ball and brings it back.

sc2.stem: Instead of leaving his kite tangled in the tall oak tree, Jamal borrowed a long ladder from his neighbor to _____ it.

traps.why: "Instead of leaving" means Jamal does not abandon the kite.
Kites get launched, but a ladder in a tree is for getting it down.
Relieve means to ease pain or worry; it only looks like retrieve.

sc2.tip: "Instead of leaving his kite" signals a contrast: Jamal climbs a ladder so he can get the kite back.

decoys.why: Jamal can already see the kite; he needs the ladder to get it back.
A long ladder is for bringing the kite down, not judging its quality.
Jamal wants his kite back, not to hold it back or prevent it.
The ladder is for getting the kite out of the tree, not approving of it.
Jamal is not copying his kite; he climbs to bring it down.
The kite is not a secret; Jamal needs the ladder to get it back.

meaning: very strict, thorough, and demanding
example: The astronauts went through rigorous training.
hook: Rigorous has rigor inside it, an old word for stiffness: rigorous rules are strict and never bend.

traps.why: Easy is the opposite of rigorous.
Vigorous looks similar but means full of energy, not strict and thorough.
Hard training can be risky, but rigorous means strict and demanding.

syn1.tip: Think of rigorous training or a rigorous test: it asks a lot of you. The ending -ous means full of, so full of rigor, or strictness.

sc1.stem: The training program for future astronauts is extremely _____, requiring years of study, hours of daily exercise, and tests that only a few candidates pass.

traps.why: Relaxed is the opposite; tests only a few pass are not relaxed.
Lenient means going easy, the opposite of a program few can pass.
Brief is about length, and "years of study" shows it is long.

sc1.tip: The examples "years of study," "hours of daily exercise," and tests "only a few candidates pass" all describe a very hard, strict program.

decoys.why: Years of study and hard tests show a demanding program, and passive means doing nothing.
The program is still training future astronauts, so it is not out of date.
The details describe how hard the program is, not how famous it is.
Nothing in the sentence says the program changes suddenly; it describes steady, hard work.
Being see-through has nothing to do with years of study and tough tests.
A program cannot feel excitement, and the clues point to difficulty, not eagerness.

traps.why: Loose and careless is the opposite of rigorous.
Rigor once meant stiffness, but rigorous describes strict standards, not frozen things.
Rigorous work is hard, but it is not cruel or mean.

syn2.tip: A rigorous check leaves nothing out, and a rigorous coach accepts no shortcuts. Look for the choice that means strict and complete.

sc2.stem: Ms. Lee's art class was relaxed and easygoing, but her math class was far more _____, with daily quizzes, strict deadlines, and no excuses for late homework.

traps.why: Casual fits the art class; "but" signals the math class is the opposite.
Crowded is about class size; quizzes and deadlines show how demanding it is.
Enjoyable is a happy feeling word; strict deadlines point to a tough class.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets the math class against the "relaxed and easygoing" art class. Then "daily quizzes, strict deadlines" tells you it is tough.

decoys.why: Daily quizzes and strict deadlines show a demanding class, not one that does nothing.
The contrast is relaxed versus strict, so excitement does not fit the clues.
Daily quizzes and firm deadlines are steady rules, not sudden changes.
The sentence describes strict rules, not mocking remarks.
Quizzes and deadlines make a class demanding, not see-through.
Nothing suggests the math class is out of date; it is described as strict.

meaning: about to happen very soon
example: Dark clouds warned that a storm was imminent.
hook: Imminent sounds a bit like "in a minute": something imminent could happen any minute now.

traps.why: Eminent sounds similar but means famous and respected.
Distant means far off, the opposite of imminent.
An imminent storm may be dangerous, but imminent only means coming soon.

syn1.tip: Picture dark clouds just before rain: the storm is imminent. Ask yourself whether the choice means coming very soon.

sc1.stem: With the rocket's countdown clock showing only ten seconds left, the launch was _____, and the crowd held its breath.

traps.why: Postponed means pushed later, but the countdown shows only ten seconds left.
Eminent sounds similar but means famous, which makes no sense for a launch.
With "ten seconds left," the launch has not happened yet.

sc1.tip: The clue is "only ten seconds left" on the countdown and the crowd holding "its breath." The launch is about to happen.

decoys.why: Ten seconds left means the launch is about to happen, not outdated.
Astronaut training may be demanding, but the countdown clue is about timing.
The ten-second countdown tells you when the launch happens, not how famous it is.
The countdown clue is about how soon the launch comes, not how careful it is.
The crowd is waiting in suspense, and nothing about the launch seems evil.
Whether the launch is real is not the point; the countdown shows it is coming soon.

traps.why: Far in the future is the opposite of about to happen.
Finished means it already happened; imminent means it has not happened yet.
Someday is too weak; imminent means very soon.

syn2.tip: Imminent describes something right around the corner, like a launch at the end of a countdown. Pick the choice that means very soon.

sc2.stem: The weather forecasters said the hurricane was still a week away, but by Friday morning its arrival was _____, and families rushed to board up their windows before it hit.

traps.why: Distant fits "a week away," but "but" shows things changed.
If it were delayed, families would not rush to board up windows.
Harmless is the wrong feeling; families rushing to prepare shows worry.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with "still a week away," and families "rushed to board up their windows." The storm was about to hit.

decoys.why: The hurricane had not hit yet, so its arrival was coming, not outdated.
Families rushed because the storm was coming soon, not because anything was inactive.
An arrival cannot be strict or demanding; the clue is about how soon it hits.
The rush to board up windows shows timing, not careful attention to detail.
Being see-through makes no sense for a storm's arrival that was suddenly close.
An arrival cannot feel excitement, and the families were worried, not excited.

meaning: the main character in a story
example: The protagonist of the novel is a girl who trains dragons.
hook: Protagonist comes from Greek words meaning first actor: the character who takes center stage in the story.

traps.why: The villain usually works against the protagonist.
The author writes the story; the protagonist is a character in it.
Pro can mean for, but a protagonist is not a supporter or fan.

syn1.tip: In English class you hear protagonist and antagonist: the protagonist is the main character the story follows.

sc1.stem: Although the novel includes dozens of characters, the story is told through the eyes of its _____, a young inventor named Zara whose adventures drive every chapter.

traps.why: A sidekick helps the hero, but Zara's adventures "drive every chapter."
The reader reads the novel; Zara is a character inside it.
An illustrator draws pictures; Zara is a young inventor in the story.

sc1.tip: The clue is "whose adventures drive every chapter." The character at the center of every chapter is the main character.

decoys.why: Zara's adventures drive every chapter, so she is the main character, not a guide.
Zara is a person telling the story, not a reason for doing something.
The blank names Zara, a young inventor, and a person is not a contradiction.
Zara is a real character in the story, not something that only looks real.
The blank refers to Zara, a character, not a trick to fool people.
A rivalry is a competition, but the blank names one person, Zara.

traps.why: The chief enemy is the antagonist, who opposes the protagonist.
A minor character has a small part; the protagonist has the biggest one.
The setting is where the story happens, not who it follows.

syn2.tip: Proto means first, so the protagonist is the first, or most important, character in a story.

sc2.stem: Our teacher asked us to describe the story's _____, or main character, explaining what she wants most and how she changes by the final chapter.

traps.why: The villain opposes the hero; the sentence says "or main character."
A setting is a place, and a place cannot want things or change.
A theme is the story's message, not a character who wants something.

sc2.tip: The words "or main character" restate the blank right after it. Pick the word that means main character.

decoys.why: The sentence defines the blank as the main character, not what she wants.
The phrase "or main character" tells you the word means main character, not a guide.
The sentence says main character, not something that causes change.
A feat is an achievement, but the blank is defined as the main character.
The blank is defined as a character who wants things and changes, not a contradiction.
The blank means main character, one person, not a competition between groups.

meaning: the spirit and confidence of a group
example: Winning the game boosted the team's morale.
hook: Morale is a group's mood meter: a winning streak sends it soaring, while three losses in a row sink it.

traps.why: Moral looks similar but means a story's lesson or right and wrong.
Teamwork is working together; morale is how confident the group feels.
Gloom is a dark, hopeless mood, the opposite of good morale.

syn1.tip: You often hear "boost morale" or "team morale." Notice the extra e: morale is about a group's mood, not a lesson.

sc1.stem: After three straight losses, the team's _____ was so low that the coach brought in a former champion to give an encouraging pep talk.

traps.why: Moral looks similar but means a lesson; a pep talk lifts spirits.
A pep talk cannot fix a low budget; it lifts a group's spirit.
Encouraging words do not repair equipment; they lift a team's confidence.

sc1.tip: The clues are "three straight losses" and "an encouraging pep talk." Encouragement fixes low spirits, so the blank is the team's spirit.

decoys.why: A pep talk lifts a team's spirit, not its feeling that someone is worthless.
The coach wants to encourage the team, which fixes low spirit, not low jealousy.
An encouraging pep talk is meant to raise confidence, not agreement.
Losses and a pep talk point to the team's spirit, not its competition.
An encouraging talk boosts confidence, not gut feelings.
The champion is brought in to lift the team's spirit, not because their guide was low.

traps.why: A story's lesson is its moral, a different word without the final e.
Ranking is a team's place in the standings, not its spirit.
Shared gloom is the opposite of high morale.

syn2.tip: Think of "the team's morale was high": it describes how confident and hopeful a group feels.

sc2.stem: Although the hikers were cold, hungry, and soaked from the storm, their _____ stayed high because they sang silly songs and joked about the adventure all the way down.

traps.why: They were cold, and "although" shows something else stayed high.
They were hungry, so supplies were low, and songs do not add food.
Singing and joking show they felt cheerful, not afraid.

sc2.tip: "Although" signals a contrast with being "cold, hungry, and soaked," and "sang silly songs and joked" shows their spirits stayed up.

decoys.why: The hike was hard, but singing and joking kept their spirits high, not their ordeal.
Silly songs and jokes show good spirits, not a feeling that someone is worthless.
The hikers were singing together, so nothing shows disagreement staying high.
Jokes and songs keep up spirit and confidence, not respect from success.
Singing silly songs keeps spirits up; nothing in the sentence is about jealousy.
The hikers joked together, so the sentence is about shared spirit, not competition.

meaning: impressive and very hard to beat
example: The undefeated champion was a formidable opponent.
hook: Formidable comes from a Latin word for fear: a formidable opponent is one you would be nervous to face.

traps.why: Weak is the opposite of formidable.
Formal looks similar but means proper and dressed up.
A strong rival may be famous, but formidable means hard to beat.

syn1.tip: You hear "a formidable opponent" in sports. Ask which choice describes a rival that makes you nervous.

sc1.stem: The undefeated debate team from Lincoln High was a _____ opponent, so Amara's team spent weeks preparing for the match against them.

traps.why: Feeble means weak, but an undefeated team is strong.
Friendly is the wrong feeling; weeks of preparing shows they were worried.
Formal looks similar but means proper, which explains nothing about preparing.

sc1.tip: The clue is "undefeated" and "so Amara's team spent weeks preparing." You only prepare that long for a rival that is hard to beat.

decoys.why: An undefeated team that needs weeks of preparation is strong, not inactive.
Weeks of preparing shows the team was hard to beat, not proud of its looks.
An undefeated team is truly strong, not shallow or only good on the surface.
The clue is that they are undefeated and hard to beat, not see-through.
Nothing says the team mocks people; the clue is that they never lose.

traps.why: Easy to defeat is the opposite of formidable.
Formidable has nothing to do with forming things, despite its look.
Slightly tricky is too weak; formidable means very hard to beat.

syn2.tip: Picture an undefeated champion. Formidable describes someone or something so strong it seems frightening to take on.

sc2.stem: The tiny kitten looked harmless, but when the big dog wandered too close, she hissed and swatted so fiercely that she became a _____ enemy.

traps.why: Gentle fits "harmless," but "but" and "so fiercely" show the change.
Cuddly has a sweet feeling, but hissing and swatting are fierce.
Forgivable looks similar but means easy to forgive, not hard to beat.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with "looked harmless," and "hissed and swatted so fiercely" shows the kitten became a scary enemy.

decoys.why: The kitten hissed and swatted fiercely, which is the opposite of doing nothing.
The kitten only looked harmless, but her fierce fighting made her truly hard to beat.
The kitten fought fiercely; nothing shows she was proud of her looks.
Hissing and swatting is fierce fighting, not saying things you do not mean.
The kitten became hard to beat, not see-through.
The sentence shows the kitten was tough in one fight, not famous and admired.

meaning: showing no mercy or pity
example: The ruthless businessman fired workers without a second thought.
hook: Ruth is an old word for pity, so ruthless literally means without pity.

traps.why: Kind is the opposite of ruthless.
Restless looks similar but means unable to sit still.
Strict is too mild; ruthless means showing no mercy at all.

syn1.tip: The ending -less means without. Ruth is an old word for pity, so ruthless means without pity.

sc1.stem: The new owner was _____ in cutting costs, firing longtime workers without warning and showing no concern for how they would pay their bills.

traps.why: Firing workers without warning is not generous.
Hesitant means slow to act, but he fired workers "without warning."
Frugal is a positive word for saving money, but this owner was cruel.

sc1.tip: The clues are "without warning" and "showing no concern for how they would pay their bills." That describes someone with no mercy.

decoys.why: He fired workers without warning, so he was not open or clear about anything.
Eccentric means odd in a harmless way, but firing workers without concern is cruel, not harmless.
Firing longtime workers is a deep, serious cut, not something only on the surface.
The sentence describes cruel behavior, not someone widely admired.
Lucrative describes things that make money, not a person who shows no concern for workers.
The clue is about showing no concern for workers, which has nothing to do with being believable.

traps.why: Full of mercy is the opposite of ruthless.
Ruth here is not a name; it is an old word for pity.
A bit stern is too weak; ruthless means completely without mercy.

syn2.tip: Split it: ruth plus -less. Ruth meant pity, and -less means without, so the word means without pity.

sc2.stem: Unlike the forgiving referee from last week, today's referee was _____, handing out penalties for even the tiniest mistakes and ignoring every player's plea for a second chance.

traps.why: Lenient fits the forgiving referee, but "unlike" shows today's was different.
A distracted referee would miss mistakes, not punish the tiniest ones.
Cheerful is the wrong feeling for ignoring every plea.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the forgiving referee" signals the opposite of forgiving, and "ignoring every player's plea for a second chance" shows no mercy.

decoys.why: The referee punished every tiny mistake, which is harsh, not just odd and harmless.
The clue is ignoring every plea for a second chance, which shows no mercy, not excitement.
The sentence contrasts with a forgiving referee, so you need a word meaning merciless.
Being believable is not the opposite of the forgiving referee from last week.
Nothing in the sentence says the referee was famous; it says he showed no mercy.
Imminent describes events about to happen, not a referee who ignores every plea.

meaning: no longer used because something newer exists
example: Floppy disks became obsolete once people started using flash drives.
hook: Floppy disks and pay phones are obsolete: they still exist in museums, but newer things replaced them.

traps.why: Modern is the opposite of obsolete.
Absolute looks similar but means complete or total.
Obsolete things may still work; nobody uses them because newer ones exist.

syn1.tip: Think of floppy disks or VCRs. Something obsolete has been replaced by something newer, so people stopped using it.

sc1.stem: Once the library installed digital catalogs on every computer, the old wooden card drawers became _____, and the staff donated them to a local museum.

traps.why: Essential means necessary, but the digital catalogs replaced the drawers.
Absolute looks similar but means total, which makes no sense here.
New computers would not break the drawers; they just made them unneeded.

sc1.tip: The clue is "Once the library installed digital catalogs." The new system replaced the drawers, so they were no longer used.

decoys.why: The drawers were replaced and given away, not famous and widely admired.
The staff donated the drawers, so they were not making money from them.
The digital catalogs already replaced the drawers; nothing was about to happen.
The drawers stopped being used because something newer came, not because they changed suddenly.
Once replaced by digital catalogs, the drawers were no longer impressive or hard to beat.
The clue is that something newer replaced the drawers, not that they were deep or meaningful.

traps.why: Brand new is the opposite of obsolete.
A little old is too weak; obsolete means replaced and out of use.
Some old things are collected, but obsolete just means nobody uses them.

syn2.tip: Obsolete is about being replaced. Ask which choice describes something people have stopped using because something better came along.

sc2.stem: My grandfather's typewriter was once the best tool for writing letters, but now that everyone uses laptops and phones, it is _____ and sits unused in the attic.

traps.why: Useful fits "once the best tool," but "but now" shows that changed.
Popular things get used; this one "sits unused in the attic."
Price is not the point; laptops and phones replaced the typewriter.

sc2.tip: "But now that everyone uses laptops and phones" contrasts with "once the best tool," and it "sits unused." Newer things replaced it.

decoys.why: The typewriter sits unused in the attic, so it is not widely admired now.
It was once the best, but now laptops have replaced it, so it is not hard to beat.
A typewriter sitting unused in the attic is not producing any money.
The laptops already replaced it; nothing is about to happen soon.
A typewriter cannot feel excitement, and the sentence says it is no longer used.
The typewriter is not changing suddenly; it just sits unused because newer tools exist.

meaning: a lack or shortage of something needed
example: A deficiency of vitamin C can cause a disease called scurvy.
hook: Old sailors without fruit got scurvy from a vitamin C deficiency: their bodies were short on something needed.

traps.why: Surplus means more than enough, the opposite of deficiency.
Efficiency looks similar but means working without waste.
A deficiency can cause illness, but it means a shortage.

syn1.tip: You hear "vitamin deficiency" from doctors. It is related to deficit, which means being short, like a deficit in a budget.

sc1.stem: The doctor explained that Omar's constant tiredness came from an iron _____, so she told him to eat more spinach, beans, and red meat.

traps.why: With too much iron, the doctor would not say eat more iron.
With an allergy, she would tell him to avoid those foods, not eat more.
Efficiency looks similar but means working well, not a shortage.

sc1.tip: The doctor told him to "eat more spinach, beans, and red meat," foods full of iron. You add more when you have too little.

decoys.why: The doctor told him to eat more iron, so his problem was too little iron.
His tiredness was real and came from too little iron, not something fake.
Eating more iron foods fixes a shortage, not something that encourages you to act.
The tiredness may feel hard, but eating more iron points to a shortage of iron.
The doctor is explaining a missing nutrient, not a reason for doing something.
The doctor gave real advice about a real shortage, not a trick meant to fool him.

traps.why: Abundance means plenty, the opposite of deficiency.
Defiance looks similar but means refusing to obey.
You can have a vitamin deficiency, but a vitamin is not a shortage.

syn2.tip: A deficiency means you do not have enough of something you need. Look for the choice about not having enough.

sc2.stem: The new school library had plenty of computers and comfy chairs, but it had a serious _____ of books, since half the shelves sat completely empty.

traps.why: Abundance fits "plenty," but "but" and the empty shelves show the opposite.
A serious collection would fill shelves, but half sat empty.
Efficiency looks similar but means working without waste, not a shortage.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "plenty of computers," and "half the shelves sat completely empty" shows there were not enough books.

decoys.why: The shelves really were half empty, so the shortage of books was not fake.
Empty shelves show a lack of books, not something that causes change.
Half-empty shelves point to a shortage, not a group agreement.
Nothing is competing here; the empty shelves show the library needs more books.
Empty shelves simply mean too few books, which is not a statement that contradicts itself.
The empty shelves are real, so this is a true shortage, not a trick.

meaning: to publicly support or approve
example: The famous chef endorsed the new cookbook.
hook: When a star athlete appears in a sneaker ad, she endorses the shoes by publicly saying they are great.

traps.why: Oppose is the opposite of endorse.
Enforce looks similar but means to make people obey a rule.
People may buy endorsed products, but endorse means to publicly approve.

syn1.tip: Think of a celebrity endorsement in a commercial: the star publicly backs a product or idea.

sc1.stem: The doctor agreed to _____ the new sports drink only after studies proved it was safe, and she then appeared in ads recommending it to athletes.

traps.why: She later appeared in ads recommending it, so she did not criticize it.
A doctor recommending a drink in ads is not the company making it.
Enforce looks similar but means to make people obey rules.

sc1.tip: The clue is "appeared in ads recommending it to athletes." Recommending something in public means approving and supporting it.

decoys.why: She appeared in ads recommending the drink, which is the opposite of calling it wrong.
She agreed with the studies and recommended the drink, so she did not say the opposite.
Recommending the drink in ads helps it, while inhibit means to hold it back.
The ads show she publicly supported the drink, not that she brought it back.
You emulate a person you admire, but she was recommending a drink in ads.
The sentence is about recommending the drink, not protecting it from waste.

traps.why: Criticizing is the opposite of endorsing.
Quietly tolerate is too weak; endorsing is open, active approval.
Enforce looks like endorse but means making people follow rules.

syn2.tip: Candidates hope famous people will endorse them. To endorse is to put your name behind something in public.

sc2.stem: Mayor Diaz first opposed the plan for a new skate park, but after kids packed the meeting with petitions, she changed her mind and decided to _____ it.

traps.why: Reject matches her first view, but she "changed her mind."
Ignoring the plan is not changing her mind from opposing it.
Endure looks similar but means to put up with something hard.

sc2.tip: "First opposed" plus "but" and "changed her mind" tells you she flipped to the opposite of opposing: she supported it.

decoys.why: She first opposed the plan and then changed her mind, so now she supports it.
Changing her mind after opposing the park means she now backs it, not holds it back.
After changing her mind, she agrees with the kids instead of saying the opposite.
Facing the plan as a problem fits her first opinion, not her changed mind.
The petitions changed her mind, so she supports the plan; nothing was brought back.
You emulate a person you admire, not a plan for a skate park.

meaning: a true statement that seems self-contradictory
example: It is a paradox that the more you learn, the less you know.
hook: "Less is more" is a paradox: it sounds like nonsense, yet it often turns out to be true.

traps.why: Agreement is the opposite of a contradiction.
