Para looks like pair, but a paradox is not a pair of anything.
A paradox seems false but is true; a lie is simply false.

syn1.tip: Phrases like "less is more" seem to argue with themselves. A paradox is a statement that sounds self-contradictory but holds true.

sc1.stem: It sounds like a _____, but it is true: the harder you pull your fingers out of a woven finger trap, the more tightly it holds them.

traps.why: "Sounds like a fact, but it is true" makes no sense with "but."
Parade looks similar but means a march down a street.
A solution answers a problem; this statement seems impossible yet is true.

sc1.tip: "It sounds like a _____, but it is true" means the blank sounds false. Pulling harder makes the trap hold "more tightly," which seems backward.

decoys.why: The clue says it sounds impossible but is true, which describes a seeming contradiction.
Nothing is missing here; pulling harder making it tighter just sounds self-contradictory.
A finger trap is not a character in a story; it is a true fact that sounds impossible.
No one is competing; the sentence describes a fact that seems to contradict itself.
A mentor is a person, but the sentence describes a strange but true fact.
The sentence is about something that sounds false but is true, not a reason for acting.

traps.why: A paradox seems impossible, not obvious.
Despite the joke "pair of docs," paradox has nothing to do with doctors.
A paradox may seem wrong, but it is not a mistake.

syn2.tip: A paradox sounds impossible at first, yet it turns out to be true. Look for the choice that combines puzzling and true.

sc2.stem: Because the statement "I always lie" contradicts itself no matter how you read it, our class spent the whole period arguing about this puzzling _____.

traps.why: The statement "contradicts itself," which is the opposite of agreement.
Paragraph also starts with para, but this is one short statement.
Homework is schoolwork; the clue is a statement that contradicts itself.

sc2.tip: The cause is "contradicts itself no matter how you read it," and the effect is a class arguing about it. A self-contradicting puzzle is a paradox.

decoys.why: The class argued, but the puzzling thing was a statement that contradicts itself.
The arguing is not the puzzle; the self-contradicting statement "I always lie" is.
The clue is a statement that contradicts itself, not a competition between groups.
"I always lie" is not an unfair opinion; it is a statement that contradicts itself.
The class argued about a self-contradicting statement, not a main character in a story.
The puzzle is a statement that contradicts itself, not a gut feeling.

meaning: to reach or achieve a goal
example: She trained for years to attain a black belt in karate.
hook: When you attain a goal, you reach the spot you were aiming for, like finally earning that black belt.

traps.why: Abandon means give up, the opposite of reaching a goal.
Retain looks similar but means to keep something you already have.
Attempt only means try; attain means you actually got there.

syn1.tip: Attain goes with goals: you attain a dream or a black belt. Think of reaching the end you aimed for.

sc1.stem: After years of training at high altitude, the climber was finally able to _____ her lifelong goal of standing on the summit of Mount Everest.

traps.why: She stood on the summit, so she did not give up her goal.
Postpone means delay, but 'finally able' shows she succeeded at last.
Retain means keep; she reached a new goal rather than keeping an old one.

sc1.tip: The words 'finally able to' after 'years of training' signal success. She stood on the summit, so she achieved her goal.

decoys.why: The sentence says she finally reached her goal, and inhibit means to hold back.
Retrieve means getting back something you had, but she had never stood on the summit before.
Supporting a goal is not the same as reaching it, and she actually stood on the summit.
Years of training led her to reach the summit, not just judge her goal.
She did not just notice her goal; the training let her actually reach the summit.

traps.why: Lose is the opposite of reaching or gaining something.
Contain ends like attain but means to hold something inside.
Pursue means chase a goal; attain means you actually reached it.

syn2.tip: Attain is about arriving at a goal after effort, like reaching the top of a mountain you have been climbing.

sc2.stem: Because Priya studied her spelling words every night for three months, she was able to _____ her goal of making it to the final round of the state spelling bee.

traps.why: Months of hard study lead to success, not to giving up.
Retain means keep; her goal was something new she reached.
Delaying a goal would not be the result of studying every night.

sc2.tip: 'Because' links months of studying to a result. Hard work leads to success, so she attained her goal.

decoys.why: Her months of study helped her reach the final round, and inhibit means to prevent.
Retrieve means getting something back, but she was reaching the final round for the first time.
The studying helped her achieve the goal, not just publicly support it.
Studying every night let her reach the final round, not merely judge her goal.
Concede means admitting something unwillingly, but her studying paid off with success.

meaning: saying the opposite of what you mean to mock
example: "Great catch," he said in a sarcastic tone after I dropped the ball.
hook: A sarcastic 'Great job' after you drop your lunch tray means the opposite: it is a jab, not praise.

traps.why: Sincere means you truly mean what you say, the opposite of sarcastic.
Playful is friendly fun; sarcastic has a mean, mocking edge.
Loud is about volume, not about saying the opposite to mock.

syn1.tip: Sarcastic remarks say the opposite of what they mean to make fun of someone, like 'Nice going' after a mistake. That is mocking.

sc1.stem: When Jordan tripped over his own feet, his brother said "Nice moves, superstar" in a _____ tone that made it clear he meant the exact opposite.

traps.why: Sincere means meaning your words, but he meant 'the exact opposite.'
'Nice moves' sounds admiring, but he meant the opposite, so it mocked Jordan.
Quiet describes volume, not saying the opposite of what you mean.

sc1.tip: 'Meant the exact opposite' is the key clue. Saying the reverse of what you mean, to tease, is sarcastic.

decoys.why: The sentence says he meant the exact opposite, so his words were not believable.
A brother teasing about a trip is mocking, not evil or threatening.
Nice moves, superstar is a mocking joke, not a deep or meaningful remark.
Nothing in the sentence is about making quick choices; it is about meaning the opposite.
The tone showed he meant the opposite, which is mocking, not impressive or hard to beat.

traps.why: Respectful shows honor; sarcastic words show scorn.
Scholastic looks similar but means having to do with school.
Cheerful is a happy feeling; sarcasm is meant to sting.

syn2.tip: Picture a sneer and a rolled eye. Sarcastic words carry scorn, not kindness.

sc2.stem: Unlike her kind grandmother, who praised every drawing honestly, Mia's older sister made _____ comments like 'Wow, a masterpiece' while rolling her eyes.

traps.why: Rolling her eyes shows she did not mean the praise.
Encouraging is kind, but 'unlike her kind grandmother' shows the sister was not.
The topic is drawing, but artistic does not describe mocking comments.

sc2.tip: 'Unlike' her honest grandmother sets up a contrast, and 'rolling her eyes' shows the praise was fake. That is sarcastic.

decoys.why: She rolled her eyes, so her praise was mocking, not truly excited.
Rolling her eyes shows she did not mean it, so the comments were not believable.
Wow, a masterpiece with an eye roll is a mocking jab, not a deep thought.
The sentence contrasts honest praise with mocking praise, not quick decision making.
Comments cannot be outdated here; the clue is the eye roll showing mockery.
Nothing in the sentence is about money; it is about mocking praise.

meaning: seeming evil or threatening
example: A sinister laugh echoed from the dark hallway.
hook: Picture a cartoon villain rubbing his hands with a sinister grin: something evil is coming.

traps.why: Harmless means safe, the opposite of threatening.
Sincere starts like sinister but means honest.
Gloomy means dark and sad, not evil or threatening.

syn1.tip: Think of a movie villain's sinister laugh. The word warns of evil or danger, so menacing fits.

sc1.stem: In the mystery novel, the abandoned mansion had a _____ look, with broken windows like empty eyes and a gate that creaked as if warning visitors away.

traps.why: The gate seemed to be 'warning visitors away,' not inviting them in.
Majestic is grand and positive; broken windows and creaks feel creepy.
Modern is about the house's style, and an abandoned mansion is not new.

sc1.tip: Look at 'empty eyes' and 'as if warning visitors away.' Those creepy details make the house seem evil and threatening.

decoys.why: Windows like empty eyes and a warning gate make the mansion threatening, not harmless.
A house cannot mock anyone; the clues describe something creepy and threatening.
Nothing in the sentence is about money; the mansion seems to warn visitors away.
A mansion does not make choices; the details describe a frightening look.
The clues are about the mansion seeming scary, not believable or trustworthy.
Broken windows and a creaking gate suggest danger, not strictness or thoroughness.

traps.why: Kindness is the opposite of the evil that sinister suggests.
Sinister is much stronger than unusual; it suggests real danger.
A sad mood is not the same as a threatening one.

syn2.tip: Sinister things make you uneasy because they suggest harm is coming, like a sinister plot in a spy movie.

sc2.stem: The cartoon villain's _____ smile made the young viewers hide behind the couch cushions, because they knew he was plotting something terrible.

traps.why: A friendly smile would not make kids hide.
Goofy is silly and fun; the kids were scared.
Sincere looks a bit like sinister but means honest.

sc2.tip: Kids 'hide' because the villain is 'plotting something terrible.' That effect tells you the smile seemed evil.

decoys.why: The kids hid because he was plotting something terrible, so the smile was not harmless.
The viewers hid in fear, so the smile seemed evil, not just excited.
The sentence is about a smile that scared kids, not one that seemed trustworthy.
A smile is not outdated; the clue is that it frightened the young viewers.
The smile was not just average; it made kids hide behind cushions.
Nothing in the sentence is about money; the smile hinted at a terrible plot.

meaning: odd or unusual in a harmless way
example: My eccentric uncle wears a cape to the grocery store.
hook: Eccentric comes from Greek for 'out of the center': an eccentric person lives a little off-center from everyone else.

traps.why: Ordinary means normal, the opposite of eccentric.
Eccentric contains 'centr,' but it means off-center, not central.
Odd habits are not rude; eccentric people can be perfectly polite.

syn1.tip: Picture an uncle wearing a cape to the store. Eccentric people are harmlessly odd, a little off-center from normal.

sc1.stem: The _____ inventor kept forty clocks in his kitchen, all set to different times, and wore swim goggles whenever he read the newspaper.

traps.why: Forty clocks and goggles for reading are not sensible habits.
Clocks set to different times are the opposite of being on time.
His habits are strange but harmless, not threatening.

sc1.tip: The examples tell you: forty clocks at 'different times' and 'swim goggles' for reading are strange but harmless habits. That is eccentric.

decoys.why: Forty clocks and swim goggles for reading are strange habits, not dull ones.
His habits are odd but harmless, with nothing evil or threatening about them.
Clocks and goggles show quirky habits, not a lack of mercy.
The sentence describes his odd habits, not an inventor who is out of date.
Nothing in the sentence is about money; it lists his strange habits.
The details show odd behavior, not whether he is believable.

traps.why: Typical means usual, the opposite of eccentric.
Eccentric inventors may be clever, but eccentric means odd, not smart.
Eccentric is harmless; frightening has a scary, negative feeling.

syn2.tip: Eccentric is usually gentle and even fond, like an 'eccentric aunt.' Quirky captures that harmless strangeness.

sc2.stem: Most people in town dressed plainly, but Mrs. Ortiz was known for her _____ style, wearing a pineapple hat and mismatched rain boots even on sunny days.

traps.why: 'But' contrasts her with people who dressed plainly, so she is not ordinary.
Elegant is about style, but a pineapple hat is odd, not graceful.
Her outfits are harmless and funny, not creepy.

sc2.tip: 'Most people dressed plainly, but' signals a contrast. A pineapple hat and mismatched boots are odd, harmless choices, so eccentric fits.

decoys.why: The sentence says most people dressed plainly, but she did not, so her style was not dull.
A pineapple hat and mismatched boots are funny and odd, not threatening.
A clothing style cannot be merciless; her outfits were just unusual.
The sentence is about her odd outfits, not about making quick choices.
Nothing in the sentence is about money; it describes her strange clothes.
Mismatched boots and a pineapple hat are quirky, not strict or demanding.

meaning: disagreement with an official or popular opinion
example: There was dissent among club members about the new rules.
hook: Dissent joins dis- (apart) and sent (feel): your opinion feels apart from the group's.

traps.why: Consent means agreeing, the opposite of dissent.
Descent sounds almost the same but means going down.
Disagreement can cause anger, but dissent means differing in opinion.

syn1.tip: Dis- means apart. Dissent is when people's opinions go apart from the official or popular view.

sc1.stem: Although most of the committee approved the new dress code, there was strong _____ from two members, who voted against it and explained their objections.

traps.why: Most members gave support; the two members voted against it.
They explained their objections clearly, so they were not confused.
Descent sounds like dissent but means going down.

sc1.tip: 'Although most... approved' sets up a contrast. The two members 'voted against it,' so the blank means disagreement.

decoys.why: Two members voted against it, so the sentence needs disagreement, not group spirit.
They explained their objections, so this was disagreement, not an opinion formed without facts.
The members voted against the rule; nothing suggests they wanted what someone else had.
The sentence describes members voting against the rule, not a reward to act.
The two members objected and voted no, which is disagreement, not respect or rank.
They disagreed with a rule, which is not a competition between two groups.

traps.why: Approval is agreeing with a plan, the opposite of dissent.
Dessert looks similar but is a sweet treat after dinner.
Rebellion is a fight against rulers, much stronger than disagreeing.

syn2.tip: When you object to a rule out loud, you voice dissent. Think of a judge's 'dissenting opinion' against the majority.

sc2.stem: The principal's plan to cancel recess caused widespread _____ among students; in other words, almost nobody agreed with it, and many signed a petition opposing it.

traps.why: Consent means agreeing, but almost nobody agreed.
Excitement is a happy feeling, but students were opposing the plan.
Signing a petition is speaking up, not staying silent.

sc2.tip: 'In other words' restates the blank: 'almost nobody agreed with it.' Widespread disagreement is dissent.

decoys.why: The sentence says nobody agreed and students signed a petition, which shows disagreement, not group spirit.
Canceling recess made students oppose the plan, not respect it.
Students opposed the plan; nothing suggests they wanted what someone else had.
The sentence explains that almost nobody agreed, so it needs disagreement, not a reward.
The phrase in other words tells you the blank means disagreement, not a gut feeling.
The petition was real opposition, not something that only looked real.

meaning: only on the surface; not deep
example: Luckily, the scrape on her knee was only superficial.
hook: Superficial comes from Latin for 'surface': a superficial scratch barely breaks the skin.

traps.why: Deep is the opposite of staying on the surface.
Artificial ends the same way but means fake or human-made.
Super can mean great, but superficial means only on the surface.

syn1.tip: A superficial wound only scratches the surface. If something stays on top and never goes deep, it is shallow.

sc1.stem: Ethan's report was _____, listing a few facts about volcanoes without explaining how they form or why they erupt.

traps.why: A thorough report would explain how volcanoes form and erupt.
Volcanoes are explosive, but the blank describes the report.
Impressive is praise, but the sentence points out what the report lacks.

sc1.tip: 'Without explaining how they form or why they erupt' shows the report never went deeper than a few facts. It stayed on the surface.

decoys.why: The report skips explaining how volcanoes form, so it is not thorough or demanding at all.
A report listing only a few facts is not impressive or hard to beat.
Nothing in the sentence says the report was odd, only that it lacked depth.
The problem is missing explanation, not that the facts are outdated.
Listing facts is not mocking anyone, so sarcastic does not describe this report.

traps.why: Thorough and detailed means going deep, the opposite of superficial.
Super- can suggest 'above,' but superficial is not about being better.
A shallow thing can be big; superficial is about depth, not size.

syn2.tip: Superficial is built on 'surface.' Superficial things stay on the face, or top layer, of something and never go deeper.

sc2.stem: Unlike the coach's detailed feedback, which pointed out every mistake in our passing, the substitute's comments were _____, just a quick 'good job' and nothing more.

traps.why: A quick 'good job' and nothing more is not careful.
'Good job' is mild and positive, not harsh.
Superior means better, and these brief comments were not better.

sc2.tip: 'Unlike the coach's detailed feedback' signals a contrast, and 'nothing more' shows the comments stayed on the surface.

decoys.why: Rigorous describes the coach's detailed feedback, not the quick 'good job' it is contrasted with.
Pointing out every mistake is relentless, but the substitute said only one quick thing.
A friendly 'good job' shows no harshness, so ruthless does not fit.
Quick here means shallow comments, not making firm choices.
Nothing about 'good job' seems evil or threatening.

meaning: producing a lot of money or profit
example: Her lemonade stand became surprisingly lucrative during the summer heat wave.
hook: A lemonade stand on the hottest day of summer is lucrative: the coins keep piling up in the jar.

traps.why: Costly things take money; lucrative things bring money in.
Lucky starts the same way but is about chance, not money.
A business can be popular without making much money.

syn1.tip: Lucrative jobs and businesses bring in lots of money. Think of a 'lucrative deal' in a news story about big profits.

sc1.stem: Selling handmade bracelets at the craft fair turned out to be so _____ that Amara earned enough money to buy a new bicycle by August.

traps.why: A costly business would not earn enough for a bicycle.
Earning enough for a new bike is a happy result, not disappointing.
Bracelets may be colorful, but color does not explain earning money.

sc1.tip: 'So _____ that Amara earned enough money to buy a new bicycle' shows cause and effect. Earning that much means the business made a lot of money.

decoys.why: She earned enough for a bicycle, so the sales were far better than average.
If the bracelets were outdated, no one would buy enough to fund a bicycle.
The clue is about earning money, not about the work being strict or demanding.
The sentence shows steady success, not sales that kept changing suddenly.
The 'so... that' points to how much money she made, not nonstop effort.
Nothing suggests the selling was doubtful; it clearly paid off.

traps.why: Losing money is the opposite of lucrative.
Lucrative is not built on luck; it is about profit.
Spending wisely is about money going out, not coming in.

syn2.tip: Lucrative is all about money flowing in. A lucrative job pays very well.

sc2.stem: Dev's first business idea, washing cars, earned only a few dollars, but his second idea, walking neighborhood dogs, proved far more _____, paying for his entire summer camp.

traps.why: Dog walking paid for camp, so it brought money in.
Dog walking can be tiring, but the clue is about money earned.
Nothing suggests danger; the result was a good one.

sc2.tip: 'Only a few dollars, but' signals a contrast, and 'paying for his entire summer camp' shows the dog walking made much more money.

decoys.why: Mediocre fits the car washing, but dog walking paid for a whole summer camp.
The contrast is about how much money each idea earned, not how demanding it was.
Whether the dogs were harmless has nothing to do with paying for camp.
The sentence shows dog walking earning steadily, not changing suddenly.
An outdated business would not earn enough to pay for summer camp.

meaning: to win or succeed after a struggle
example: Our team prevailed in overtime after a tough game.
hook: In fairy tales, good prevails over evil: after a long struggle, the hero comes out on top.

traps.why: Lose is the opposite of prevail.
Prevent starts the same way but means to stop something happening.
Prevailing comes after a struggle, but it means winning, not struggling.

syn1.tip: You often hear 'justice will prevail' or 'good prevails over evil.' Both mean coming out on top after a fight.

sc1.stem: The underdog robotics team trailed for most of the competition, but thanks to a clever last-minute repair, they managed to _____ and take home the trophy.

traps.why: A team that surrenders does not take home the trophy.
They celebrated later, but first they had to win.
A tie is not enough to take home the trophy.

sc1.tip: 'Trailed for most of the competition, but' signals a turnaround, and 'take home the trophy' tells you they won in the end.

decoys.why: Giving up does not let a team take home the trophy.
Judging the trophy is not how the team came from behind to win.
Publicly approving something does not explain how the trailing team won.
The sentence is about winning after trailing, not saving something from waste.
Simply noticing something does not win a competition or a trophy.

traps.why: Giving up is the opposite of winning after a struggle.
Pre- can mean before, but prevail means winning, not coming first in line.
Trying hard is part of the struggle; prevail means you actually won.

syn2.tip: Prevail adds a struggle to winning. A team that prevails in overtime fought hard and still won.

sc2.stem: Because Lena refused to give up during the long, tiring chess match, she was able to _____ against the reigning champion and earn first place.

traps.why: She earned first place, so she did not lose.
Cheating is dishonest, but the sentence praises her for not giving up.
Complaining would not earn first place.

sc2.tip: 'Because Lena refused to give up' is the cause, and 'earn first place' is the effect. Winning after a long struggle means she prevailed.

meaning: to allow yourself or others a special pleasure
example: On her birthday, Grandma indulged us with extra dessert.
hook: When you indulge in a giant sundae after a hard week, you let yourself enjoy a special treat.

sc1.stem: After finishing her exams, Chloe decided to _____ in a lazy afternoon of comic books and a giant ice-cream sundae.

traps.why: Suffering is unpleasant, but comics and a sundae are a treat.
Investing is putting money in for later, not enjoying a pleasure now.
Struggle means hard effort, but this is a lazy afternoon.

sc1.tip: 'After finishing her exams' and 'a giant ice-cream sundae' show Chloe rewarding herself. Letting yourself enjoy a pleasure is to indulge.

decoys.why: A lazy afternoon of comics is a treat, not a struggle she won.

traps.why: Refusing a pleasure is the opposite of indulging.
That is what include means, a word that looks like indulge.
Indulging is enjoying a treat; it does not have to mean overeating.

syn2.tip: Think of grandparents who indulge kids with extra dessert. They allow a special pleasure the kids usually don't get.

sc2.stem: Dad usually limits us to one cookie after dinner, but on the last day of school he decided to _____ us and let everyone have three.

traps.why: He let everyone have three, so he did not restrict them.
Scolding is negative, but extra cookies are a happy treat.
Warning us does not fit with letting everyone have extra cookies.

sc2.tip: 'Usually limits us to one cookie, but' sets up a contrast. Letting everyone have three is allowing a special pleasure, so he chose to indulge us.

decoys.why: Dad let everyone have three cookies, so he was not holding them back.
Dad was giving a treat, not saying they did something wrong.
Nothing in the sentence shows Dad facing a problem with the kids.
Dad was allowing extra cookies, not judging his kids' quality.
No one said anything for Dad to argue against; he just gave a treat.

meaning: knowing something without proof; a gut feeling
example: My intuition told me the shortcut was a bad idea.
hook: That gut feeling that the shortcut is a bad idea, before you can explain why, is your intuition.

traps.why: Evidence is proof; intuition is knowing without proof.
Tuition is hiding inside intuition, but it means money paid for school.
Memory is knowing from the past; intuition is a feeling without proof.

syn1.tip: Intuition is the inner voice that tells you something before you have reasons. You might say 'my gut told me,' which is instinct.

sc1.stem: Though she had no proof, Grace trusted her _____ that something was wrong with the old ladder, and later the store found a crack in one rung.

traps.why: She 'had no proof,' so she was not trusting evidence.
Tuition looks like intuition but is money paid for school.
Balance matters on a ladder, but it cannot tell you about a crack.

sc1.tip: 'Though she had no proof' tells you Grace was not using facts. Sensing a problem without proof is intuition, a gut feeling.

decoys.why: The crack was real, so her feeling was not something false.
Prejudice is an unfair opinion about people, not a gut feeling about a ladder.
A reason for doing something is not a feeling that a ladder is broken.
Grace was not hiding anything; she sensed a danger without proof.

traps.why: Intuition is knowing without proof, so it is not a proven fact.
That is tuition, a word that looks like part of intuition.
Intuition is a kind of feeling, but it is about knowing, not emotion.

syn2.tip: People say 'trust your gut' to mean trust your intuition. It is knowing something without being able to prove it.

sc2.stem: Coach Rivera did not study any statistics before choosing Sam as goalie; she simply relied on _____, a hunch that he would stay calm under pressure.

traps.why: She 'did not study any statistics,' so she did no research.
Tradition looks similar but means customs passed down, not a hunch.
Luck is chance; the sentence says she had 'a hunch,' a feeling.

sc2.tip: The phrase after the comma restates the blank: 'a hunch that he would stay calm.' A hunch without facts is intuition.

decoys.why: The coach had a fair hunch about Sam, not an unfair opinion.
The sentence defines the word as a hunch, not the team's spirit.
She chose Sam on a hunch, not because of his rank or reputation.
A hunch is a real feeling she trusted, not something false that looked real.
She trusted Sam to stay calm, so she did not think he was worthless.

meaning: a trick meant to fool people
example: The photo of the giant squid was a hoax.
hook: Picture a toy submarine wearing a fake monster head and fooling the whole world: that famous Loch Ness photo was a hoax.

traps.why: Truth is the opposite of a hoax, which is meant to fool you.
Hoard looks like hoax, but it means a hidden pile of things.
Hoaxes can seem mysterious, but a hoax is a trick, not an unsolved puzzle.

syn1.tip: Think of headlines like "the moon landing hoax" or "a hoax phone call." Each one is about someone trying to fool people on purpose.

sc1.stem: The famous photo of the Loch Ness monster was later revealed to be a _____; the "monster" was actually a toy submarine with a fake head attached.

traps.why: A toy with a fake head is the opposite of a real discovery.
The photo showed a creature, but the clue says it was really a toy.
Once it was revealed as a toy, it was no longer a mystery.

sc1.tip: The clue is "actually a toy submarine with a fake head attached." Something faked to fool people is a hoax.

decoys.why: The photo was a fake meant to fool people, not a statement that seems to contradict itself.
A toy submarine with a fake head is a trick, not a painful experience.
The sentence reveals the photo was faked, not that it caused or sped up some change.
The photo itself was a trick; a motive would be the reason someone made it.
Nothing was lacking here; the sentence says the monster was a toy made to fool people.
A photo cannot be an experienced person who guides someone.

traps.why: A real discovery is true, the opposite of a fake meant to fool you.
Mistakes also spread wrong ideas, but a hoax is done on purpose.
Hoaxes often involve monsters, but the hoax is the trick itself.

syn2.tip: A hoax is never an accident. Look for the choice that shows someone fooling people on purpose.

sc2.stem: Everyone believed the news that school was canceled for a week, but the message turned out to be a _____ sent by an older student as an April Fools' prank.

traps.why: A fact is true, but this message was a prank.
A promise is a kind of message, but it is not meant to fool people.
Secrets are hidden, but this message was shared to trick everyone.

sc2.tip: The word "but" shows the news was not real, and "April Fools' prank" tells you it was a trick meant to fool people.

decoys.why: The message was a prank meant to fool everyone, not a statement that seems self-contradictory.
An April Fools' prank message is a trick, not a painful experience.
The sentence says the message was a prank, not something that caused change.
The message was the trick itself; a motive would be the reason for sending it.
A fake message about school closing is a trick, not a shortage of something.
Nobody was competing here; the student sent a fake message as a prank.

meaning: to make pain or a problem less severe
example: The nurse gave him ice to alleviate the swelling.
hook: Picture an ice pack on a twisted ankle: it does not cure the injury, but it alleviates the pain.

traps.why: Worsen is the opposite: it makes pain or a problem worse.
Elevate looks similar, but it means to lift something higher.
Cure is too strong; alleviate only makes a problem less severe.

syn1.tip: Think of medicine ads that "alleviate headache pain." The medicine makes the pain smaller, so alleviate means to ease.

sc1.stem: To _____ the crowding in the cafeteria, the principal added a second lunch period so fewer students would be eating at the same time.

traps.why: A second lunch period makes crowding smaller, not bigger.
The principal did more than watch; he took action to fix it.
Elevate looks like alleviate but means to raise up.

sc1.tip: Look at "so fewer students would be eating at the same time." The new lunch period makes the crowding problem less severe.

decoys.why: The principal wanted fewer students eating together, so he did not want the crowding to grow.
Adding a lunch period makes the crowding smaller, not stronger.
Adding a lunch period fixes the crowding; it does not measure it.
The principal was reducing the crowding, not giving a good reason for it.
You protect things from loss when you conserve them, but the principal wanted less crowding.
Adding a lunch period does not help anyone notice the crowding; it reduces it.

traps.why: Intensify means to make stronger, the opposite of alleviate.
Eliminate means to remove completely; alleviate just makes it lighter.
Doctors diagnose problems, but that means finding them, not easing them.

syn2.tip: Alleviate is about making a heavy problem lighter. Pick the word for taking some of the pain or weight away.

sc2.stem: The medicine did not cure Leo's cold, but it did _____ his stuffy nose and sore throat enough for him to sleep through the night.

traps.why: The sentence says the medicine did not cure the cold.
A worse sore throat would not help Leo sleep.
Trigger means to start symptoms, but the medicine helped him.

sc2.tip: The contrast "did not cure... but it did" points to something less than a cure. "Enough for him to sleep" shows it eased his symptoms.

decoys.why: Making his stuffy nose stronger would not help Leo sleep through the night.
The medicine helped him sleep, so it did not encourage his sore throat to grow.
Medicine eases symptoms; it does not judge how bad they are.
Noticing his sore throat would not let Leo sleep; the medicine made it less severe.
The medicine did not bring back his stuffy nose; it eased it.
Medicine cannot copy a sore throat; the sentence says it helped him sleep.

meaning: only ordinary or average; not very good
example: The restaurant's food was mediocre, so we never returned.
hook: A mediocre pizza is the one you eat and never mention again: not bad, not good, just plain okay.

traps.why: Excellent means very good, the opposite of mediocre.
Terrible is too strong; mediocre is ordinary, not awful.
Medical starts the same way but is about doctors and health.

syn1.tip: Mediocre is what you call something that is just okay. Its feeling is a little disappointed, like a C grade.

sc1.stem: The movie's trailer promised an amazing adventure, but the film itself was only _____: not terrible, but not good enough to recommend.

traps.why: The "but" shows the film did not live up to the amazing trailer.
The sentence says it was "not terrible," so dreadful is too strong.
Animated describes the kind of movie, not how good it was.

sc1.tip: The words after the colon restate the blank: "not terrible, but not good enough to recommend." That describes something merely average.

decoys.why: The sentence says the film was not good enough to recommend, so it was not impressive.
The sentence is about how good the film was, not how much money it made.
The clue after the colon is about quality, not whether the film seemed evil.
The film was just average, not out of use because something newer replaced it.
The sentence judges the film's quality, not when it will come out.
The colon explains the film was average, not that it was brief and clear.

traps.why: Truly outstanding is the opposite of mediocre.
That is too strong; mediocre things are only ordinary.
Medi- hints at middle, but mediocre describes quality, not location.

syn2.tip: People say "mediocre at best" about a show or meal that let them down. It means ordinary and nothing special.

sc2.stem: Everyone raved about the new pizza place, but Leah found its pizza _____, no better than the frozen kind her family buys at the grocery store.

traps.why: The "but" shows Leah disagreed with everyone who raved.
Too strong; it was just no better than ordinary frozen pizza.
Price is a different topic; the clue compares how good it tasted.

sc2.tip: "Everyone raved... but Leah" signals she did not agree, and "no better than the frozen kind" means only ordinary.

decoys.why: Leah thought it was no better than frozen pizza, so she did not find it impressive.
Leah is judging how the pizza tastes, not how much money it makes.
Pizza no better than frozen pizza is ordinary, not odd or unusual.
Leah found the pizza ordinary, not evil or threatening.
The sentence compares the pizza's quality, not whether it is out of use.
Pizza cannot be strict or demanding; Leah thought it was just ordinary.

meaning: never stopping or easing up
example: The relentless rain lasted for six days.
hook: To relent is to ease up, and -less means without, so relentless rain falls without ever easing up.

traps.why: Occasional means happening only now and then, the opposite of relentless.
Restless rhymes with relentless, but it means unable to sit still.
Relentless things can be powerful, but relentless is about never stopping.

syn1.tip: Split it: relent plus -less. To relent is to give up or ease off, so relentless means without ever easing off.

sc1.stem: The _____ wind blew for nine days without a single pause, wearing down the explorers who were trying to cross the frozen plain.

traps.why: Wind that lasts nine days is not brief.
The plain is frozen, and the clue is about never pausing.
Sudden is about how it starts, not lasting nine days.

sc1.tip: The clue is "blew for nine days without a single pause." Wind that never stops is relentless.

decoys.why: The wind blew without a single pause, so it did not change suddenly.
The wind wore down the explorers, so it was not harmless.
The wind was already blowing for nine days, not about to happen.
The sentence is about the wind never stopping, not about its quality.
Nothing says the wind was odd; it blew for nine days without pause.
A wind that wore down explorers for nine days was not dull or flavorless.

traps.why: Stopping now and then is the opposite of relentless.
That describes restless, a word that looks like relentless.
Relentless things may be loud, but the word means they never stop.

syn2.tip: Think of a relentless defender in basketball who guards you every second of the game. The word is about never stopping.

sc2.stem: Most players would have given up after falling behind by twenty points, but Mia was _____, chasing every loose ball until the final buzzer.

traps.why: The "but" shows Mia did not give up like most players.
Mia may be talented, but the clue is about never stopping.
A lazy player would not chase every ball until the end.

sc2.tip: "Most players would have given up... but Mia" sets up a contrast, and "until the final buzzer" shows she never let up.

decoys.why: Mia kept chasing every ball when others would quit, so she was far from ordinary.
The sentence is about Mia never giving up, not about pride in her looks.
Mia showed effort by chasing every ball, not by mocking anyone.
The sentence praises Mia for never quitting, not for being harmless.
A player chasing every ball is not out of date or replaced.
Mia chased every loose ball until the buzzer, which is anything but dull.

meaning: harmless; not dangerous
example: The doctor said the small bump was benign and nothing to worry about.
hook: Benign comes from Latin bene, meaning well, so a benign bump is one the doctor says will leave you well.

traps.why: Dangerous is the opposite of benign.
Bene- means good, but benign means harmless, not actively helpful.
Benign bumps are often small, but benign is about being safe.

syn1.tip: Doctors say a lump is "benign" when it is nothing to worry about. The bene- start has a good, safe feeling.

sc1.stem: Though the bright red beetle looked dangerous, the park ranger explained that it was completely _____ and would not hurt anyone who held it.

traps.why: The beetle "would not hurt anyone," so it is not poisonous.
The beetle is bright red, but the clue is about being safe.
Rare is about how often you see it, not whether it hurts.

sc1.tip: "Though... looked dangerous" sets up a contrast, and "would not hurt anyone" tells you the beetle is harmless.

decoys.why: The ranger said the beetle would not hurt anyone, so it was not threatening.
A beetle that would not hurt anyone is not merciless.
Though says it only looked dangerous; the ranger said it was harmless, not hard to beat.
The ranger was explaining the beetle was harmless, not that it changes suddenly.
Nothing in the sentence says the beetle never stops; it says it is harmless.
A beetle is not out of date; the ranger said it would not hurt anyone.

traps.why: Likely to cause harm is the opposite of benign.
Size is a different idea; benign things can be big but safe.
Pain is related to injuries, but benign means it will not harm you.

syn2.tip: A benign bump is the good news at the doctor. Look for the choice meaning safe, nothing to worry about.

sc2.stem: Because the snake in the garden turned out to be _____, Dad let it slither away instead of calling animal control to remove it.

traps.why: Dad would call for help if the snake were deadly.
Hunger has nothing to do with whether Dad needed help.
A huge snake would more likely make Dad call animal control.

sc2.tip: "Because" signals cause and effect. Dad let the snake go "instead of calling animal control," so it must be safe.

decoys.why: Dad let the snake go, so it must have been harmless, not threatening.
A merciless snake would be a reason to call animal control, not let it go.
A snake likely to act suddenly would worry Dad, but he let it slither away.
Dad did not call animal control, so the snake was not dangerous or hard to beat.
The sentence is about whether the snake was dangerous, not whether it never stops.
Dad let it go because it was harmless, not because it was eager.

meaning: lacking flavor or interest; dull
example: Without any salt, the soup tasted bland.
hook: Picture a bowl of plain white rice with no butter, no salt, and no sauce: that is bland.

traps.why: Spicy food is full of flavor, the opposite of bland.
Rotten food tastes bad, but bland food has little taste at all.
Blond looks like bland but describes light yellow hair.

syn1.tip: Think of a "bland diet" for an upset stomach: plain toast and rice with no spices. Bland means lacking flavor.

sc1.stem: The cook forgot to add any spices, so the stew was _____, and several campers reached for the hot sauce to give it some flavor.

traps.why: The cook forgot the spices, so the stew could not be spicy.
Burnt is a cooking problem, but the clue is about missing spices.
Hot sauce was added "to give it some flavor," not warmth.

sc1.tip: The cook "forgot to add any spices," so campers wanted "to give it some flavor." The stew had no flavor.

decoys.why: An odd, unusual flavor is the opposite of a stew with no spices at all.
Nothing threatening happened; the stew simply had no flavor, so campers added hot sauce.
The sentence is about taste, not about making money from the stew.
The stew was not replaced by something newer; it just lacked spices.
Nothing in the stew changed suddenly; the clue is that no spices were added.
Whether the stew was harmless does not explain why campers wanted more flavor.

traps.why: Exciting is the opposite of bland, which means dull.
Cold food can be unpleasant, but bland is about lacking flavor or interest.
Salt adds flavor, which bland food is missing.

syn2.tip: Bland works for food and for other things: a bland speech or bland colors. Either way, nothing about it stands out.

sc2.stem: The speaker's talk was so _____ that even the teachers struggled to stay awake; he never changed his tone or told a single joke.

traps.why: A lively talk would keep the teachers awake.
Loudness is about volume, and a loud talk would keep people awake.
Nothing shows anger; the clue says he never changed his tone.

sc2.tip: After the semicolon, "never changed his tone or told a single joke" explains the blank. A talk like that is dull.

decoys.why: The sentence says he never changed his tone, which is the opposite of volatile.
An odd, unusual talk would keep people awake, not put teachers to sleep.
He never told a single joke, so his talk was not mocking or sarcastic.
A brief, clear talk would not make teachers struggle to stay awake.
A threatening talk would not make people sleepy; the clue points to dullness.
Making money has nothing to do with listeners struggling to stay awake.

meaning: very eager and enthusiastic
example: My aunt is an avid gardener who grows forty kinds of tomatoes.
hook: An avid fan never misses a game, wears the jersey every Saturday, and knows every player's name by heart.

traps.why: Uninterested is the opposite of avid.
Vivid looks like avid but means bright and clear.
Avid people often get skilled, but avid means eager, not talented.

syn1.tip: You hear the phrase "avid reader" for someone who can't put books down. Avid has a happy, excited feeling.

sc1.stem: Jun reads at breakfast, on the bus, and under his blanket with a flashlight, so few readers in his class are as _____ as he is.

traps.why: A reluctant reader would not read everywhere he goes.
Reading late might make him sleepy, but the clue shows his eagerness.
Vivid looks like avid but means bright, which does not describe a reader.

sc1.tip: The examples "at breakfast, on the bus, and under his blanket with a flashlight" show Jun is very eager to read.

decoys.why: Jun reads everywhere, even under his blanket, so he is not uncertain about reading.
The sentence shows how eager Jun is to read, not how average he is.
A reader who reads at breakfast and on the bus is not dull about books.
Reading with a flashlight is not threatening; it shows enthusiasm.
Jun is not outdated; the clues show how eagerly he reads.
Jun does not earn money from reading; he just loves it.

traps.why: Unwilling is the opposite of avid, which means very eager.
Greedy is negative, but avid is a positive word for eagerness.
Experience comes from doing something a lot, but avid means eager.

syn2.tip: Think of an "avid fan" or "avid gardener." It describes someone who loves doing something and does it as often as possible.

sc2.stem: Lily used to complain about every family hike, but after one trip to the mountains she became so _____ about hiking that she now plans a new trail every weekend.

traps.why: The "but" shows Lily stopped complaining and started loving hikes.
Hiking can make people nervous, but she plans trails eagerly.
Nothing suggests confusion; planning hikes weekly shows excitement.

sc2.tip: "Used to complain... but" signals a change, and "plans a new trail every weekend" shows she is now very eager.

decoys.why: Lily used to doubt hiking, but now she plans a trail every weekend.
Planning a new trail every weekend shows she is eager, not uncertain.
Mocking hiking describes how she used to complain, not how she feels now.
Someone who plans hikes every weekend is excited, not quietly sad about hiking.

meaning: doubtful; not to be trusted
example: I was dubious about the ad's claim that the pill made you smarter.
hook: Dubious and doubt come from the same Latin family, so a dubious claim is one that fills you with doubt.

traps.why: Certain means sure, the opposite of doubtful.
Curious people ask questions, but dubious means you don't believe something.
Studious ends the same way but means hardworking at school.

syn1.tip: The -ous ending means full of, and dubious is full of doubt. Think of a "dubious excuse" that nobody believes.

sc1.stem: The salesman promised the cream would make hair grow back overnight, but Grandpa was _____ and decided to read reviews before spending any money.

traps.why: A convinced buyer would not stop to read reviews first.
Too strong; Grandpa is just unsure, so he checks the reviews.
Delighted is a happy feeling, but Grandpa does not trust the promise.

sc1.tip: "Promised... overnight, but Grandpa" signals a contrast. He "decided to read reviews before spending any money," so he doubts the claim.

decoys.why: Grandpa wanted to read reviews first, so he was not eager to buy the cream.
The salesman might seem threatening, but Grandpa was just doubtful about the promise.
Reading reviews before buying shows doubt, not quiet sadness.
Standing out has nothing to do with doubting the salesman's promise.
Grandpa was not being annoying; he simply did not trust the cream's claim.
Being harmless does not explain why Grandpa checked reviews before spending money.

traps.why: Completely convinced is the opposite of dubious.
An easily fooled person believes everything, the opposite of a dubious one.
Confused means not understanding; dubious means not believing.

syn2.tip: Say it slowly: dubious sounds a bit like doubt. Its feeling is suspicious, like when an ad seems too good to be true.

sc2.stem: Since the website had no contact address and dozens of spelling mistakes, Maria felt _____ about its promise of a free phone and closed the page.

traps.why: A confident person would not close the page right away.
Grateful is a warm feeling, but Maria does not trust the site.
Studious looks similar but means hardworking, which does not fit.

sc2.tip: "Since" signals a cause: "no contact address" and "spelling mistakes" are warning signs, so Maria doubted the offer and "closed the page."

decoys.why: Maria closed the page, so she was not eager about the free phone.
The spelling mistakes made Maria distrust the site, not feel sad.
The website might seem threatening, but Maria herself felt doubtful, not sinister.

meaning: to admit something is true, often unwillingly
example: After checking the map, Dad conceded that we were lost.
hook: On election night the losing candidate concedes, stepping to the microphone to admit that the other person won.

traps.why: Deny means to say something is not true, the opposite of concede.
Conceal looks like concede but means to hide.
People argue before they concede, but arguing is not admitting.

syn1.tip: Think of "conceding defeat" in a game or election. You admit the other side was right or won, even if you don't want to.

sc1.stem: Although she had argued for an hour that the answer was 12, Ana finally had to _____ that her classmate's answer of 15 was correct.

traps.why: "Finally" shows she stopped arguing, so she did not deny it.
Conceal looks like concede but means hide, which does not fit.
She doubted the answer before; "finally" shows she now accepts it.

sc1.tip: "Although she had argued for an hour" sets up a contrast, and "finally had to" shows she unwillingly admitted her classmate was right.

decoys.why: She finally stopped arguing, so she admitted the answer was right instead of denying it.
She had argued against 15, so she had to admit it, not give reasons for it.

traps.why: Insisting something is false is the opposite of conceding it.
That means conceal, a word that looks like concede.
Arguing comes before conceding; conceding means you finally accept the point.

syn2.tip: When you concede a point in an argument, you stop fighting it. Look for the choice that means agreeing something is true.

sc2.stem: When the scoreboard showed his team losing by thirty points with one minute left, the coach decided to _____ defeat, knowing a comeback was impossible.

traps.why: He knew "a comeback was impossible," so he would not deny losing.
Celebrate is a happy word, but losing by thirty is not cheerful.
He knew he could not prevent the loss, since a comeback was impossible.

sc2.tip: "Losing by thirty points" and "knowing a comeback was impossible" cause the coach to admit his team had lost.

decoys.why: The coach knew a comeback was impossible, so he could not prevent the defeat.
The coach was admitting the loss, not saying strongly that losing was wrong.
Losing by thirty points cannot be made less severe in one minute; he admitted it.
You copy someone you admire, but the coach was simply admitting his team lost.
The coach was not getting anything back; he was admitting defeat.

meaning: a very painful or difficult experience
example: Getting lost in the woods overnight was a frightening ordeal.
hook: Long ago an ordeal was a painful test, like walking on hot coals; now it means any terrible experience you must endure.

traps.why: A delight is a happy experience, the opposite of an ordeal.
Order looks like the start of ordeal but means a command or arrangement.
Journeys can be hard, but a journey is a trip, not a painful experience.

syn1.tip: Here trial means a hard test you must get through, as in "trials and troubles." An ordeal is a long, painful experience.

sc1.stem: Stuck for two days in an airport during a snowstorm, sleeping on hard chairs with almost no food, the travelers called their trip a true _____.

traps.why: Two days stuck on hard chairs with no food is not a success.
Too weak; two miserable days is much worse than an inconvenience.
Bargains are about cost, but the clue describes suffering.

sc1.tip: The details "stuck for two days," "sleeping on hard chairs," and "almost no food" describe a long, painful experience.

decoys.why: The snowstorm and hard chairs were real, so the trip was not a trick.
Being stuck with no food is just hard, not something that seems self-contradictory.
The travelers were not competing; they were suffering through a difficult experience.
Nothing about the trip was a false appearance; the hardship was real.
The sentence describes a painful experience, not something that causes change.
A trip cannot be a person who guides someone; the clues describe suffering.

traps.why: A pleasant adventure is the opposite of an ordeal.
Too weak; an ordeal is very painful or difficult, not a minor bother.
Some ordeals happen on trips, but a long trip isn't necessarily painful.

syn2.tip: People say "what an ordeal" after something miserable, like a long hospital stay. The word has a heavy, unhappy feeling.

sc2.stem: The dentist visit Max had dreaded for weeks turned out to be quick and painless, not the long _____ he had imagined.

traps.why: Max "dreaded" the visit, so he did not imagine a reward.
Celebration is happy, but Max expected something he dreaded.
Order looks like ordeal but means a command, which makes no sense here.

sc2.tip: "Quick and painless, not the long" sets up a contrast. The blank is the opposite of painless, something Max "dreaded."

decoys.why: Max imagined a painful experience, not a trick meant to fool him.
A dentist visit is not a competition; Max feared it would be painful.
The contrast is with quick and painless, so Max imagined something long and painful.
A dentist visit is not a main character; Max dreaded a painful experience.
A visit cannot be a guiding person; the clue is quick and painless.
Max imagined pain and difficulty, not a false outward appearance.

meaning: brief but clear and complete
example: Her concise answer covered everything in just two sentences.
hook: Concise comes from Latin for cut up: a concise answer has all the extra words cut away.

traps.why: Wordy is the opposite of concise; it means using too many words.
Precise looks and sounds like concise, but it means exact, not short.
Short answers are often simple, but concise is about length, not difficulty.

syn1.tip: A concise answer is short and to the point, with extra words cut out. Pick the choice that means short.

sc1.stem: The teacher asked for a _____ summary, so Ravi cut his ten-page draft down to a single paragraph that still included every important point.

traps.why: Ravi cut his draft down, so the summary was the opposite of lengthy.
A vague summary leaves things out, but Ravi kept every important point.
Nothing in the sentence is about being funny; it is about being short.

sc1.tip: The clue is "cut his ten-page draft down to a single paragraph" that "still included every important point." Short but complete means concise.

decoys.why: The summary still included every important point, so it was not shallow or surface level.
Ravi cut ten pages down to one paragraph, so his summary was short, not never ending.
A teacher would not ask for a dull summary; the clue is about being short and complete.
No teacher asks for an average summary; the clue is about cutting it short.
Nothing in the sentence is about mocking; it is about making the summary short.
The sentence is about cutting length, not about the summary standing out.

traps.why: Long and detailed is the opposite of concise.
Concise is short in a good way; rushed and careless is short in a bad way.
That describes precise, a word that looks like concise.

syn2.tip: Think of a teacher saying "Be concise": say it in fewer words without leaving anything out.

sc2.stem: Unlike his rambling speech last year that lasted twenty minutes, Marcus gave a _____ talk this time, making all his points in under two minutes.

traps.why: The word "unlike" means this talk was the opposite of last year's long one.
Speeches can be nervous, but the clue is about how short the talk was.
Boring is a negative word; the sentence praises the talk for being short.

sc2.tip: The signal word "Unlike" sets this talk against a "rambling" twenty-minute speech. "All his points in under two minutes" means short and complete.

decoys.why: His talk lasted under two minutes, so it did not go on and on.
He made all his points, so the talk was short but not shallow.
The contrast with his rambling speech is about length, not about being dull.
The sentence compares how long the talks were, not how good they were.
Nothing suggests mocking; the clue is that he made his points in under two minutes.

meaning: very obvious and done openly, without shame
example: Copying the answers word for word was a blatant act of cheating.
hook: A blatant lie is told right to your face, like cheating while the teacher is watching.

traps.why: Hidden is the opposite of blatant, which means done right out in the open.
Bland looks like blatant but means dull or without flavor.
Blatant acts are often rude, but blatant means easy to see.

syn1.tip: You hear blatant in phrases like "a blatant lie" or "blatant cheating": something wrong done in plain sight. Pick the choice that means easy to see.

sc1.stem: Sophie's copying was so _____ that she did not even bother to hide it; she simply turned her head and wrote down each of her neighbor's answers.

traps.why: Sophie did not bother to hide it, so she was the opposite of sneaky.
Careful copying would be hidden; Sophie simply turned her head and copied.
Copying answers is cheating, so a positive word like honest cannot fit.

sc1.tip: The clue is "did not even bother to hide it" and "simply turned her head." Cheating done openly is blatant.

decoys.why: She openly turned her head and copied, which is bold, not uncertain or hesitant.
Clever copying would be hidden, but she did not even bother to hide it.
The clue is that she did not hide it, which is about being obvious, not harmless.
Being brief has nothing to do with copying so openly she did not hide it.
The sentence is about how obvious her copying was, not how good it was.

traps.why: Done secretly is the opposite of blatant.
Blatant acts are on purpose and open, not accidents.
Too weak: blatant means very obvious, not just a little noticeable.

syn2.tip: Blatant describes bad behavior that does not even try to hide. Think "right out in the open."

sc2.stem: Most players try to hide a foul from the referee, but Dev made a _____ grab at his opponent's jersey right in front of her.

traps.why: The word "but" shows Dev did not hide it, so secret is the opposite.
Grabbing a jersey is a foul, so a positive word like polite does not fit.
Lucky is about chance; the clue is that he did it right in front of the referee.

sc2.tip: "Most players try to hide" a foul, "but" Dev did it "right in front of her." A foul done openly is blatant.

decoys.why: Grabbing a jersey right in front of the referee is bold, not hesitant.
The contrast is with hiding a foul, so the word must mean obvious, not harmless.
Brief and clear describes writing or speech, not a foul done openly in front of a referee.
The sentence contrasts hiding with doing it openly, not exciting with dull.
The point is that the foul was done openly, not that it was ordinary.

meaning: disagreement and lack of harmony
example: Discord among the band members led to their breakup.
hook: Discord comes from Latin dis (apart) and cor (heart): people whose hearts are pulling apart.

traps.why: Harmony means getting along, the opposite of discord.
Discovery starts like discord but means finding something new.
Discord can make people sad, but it means disagreement, not sadness.

syn1.tip: Dis- means apart. Discord is people pulling apart in disagreement, the opposite of accord, which means agreement.

sc1.stem: The once friendly book club fell into _____ when members could not agree on which novel to read next, and meetings soon became tense and unpleasant.

traps.why: Members could not agree and meetings turned tense, the opposite of harmony.
Tense meetings might get quiet, but the clue is that members could not agree.
Disuse looks similar and "fell into disuse" sounds right, but the club still met.

sc1.tip: The clue is "could not agree" and "meetings soon became tense and unpleasant." Disagreement that ruins friendliness is discord.

decoys.why: Meetings became tense and unpleasant, so the club did not gain respect.
Morale is group spirit, but the club fell into disagreement, which destroys it.
The sentence is about members not agreeing, not about gut feelings.
Nothing here seems self-contradictory; members simply could not agree.
Tense meetings over a book choice show disagreement, not severe pain or sorrow.

traps.why: Peace and quiet is the opposite of discord.
Discord can describe clashing notes, but it does not mean loud music.
Too weak: discord is real disagreement, not just being a little confused.

syn2.tip: Look inside the word: dis means apart. Discord is when people disagree and stop getting along.

sc2.stem: The twins usually get along perfectly, but when they had to share one bedroom, their constant arguments over space created _____ in the whole house.

traps.why: Constant arguments create the opposite of harmony.
Laughter is a happy word, but the twins were arguing.
Sharing a room might cause clutter, but the clue is their constant arguments.

sc2.tip: The signal word "but" contrasts getting along with "constant arguments." Arguing that spreads through a house is discord.

decoys.why: Constant arguments would not create good spirit; they create disagreement.
Arguing over bedroom space does not earn anyone respect or high rank.
The sentence is about arguments, not about gut feelings.
Arguments over space are not a statement that seems to contradict itself.
The arguments created disagreement, not a shortage of something.

meaning: uncertain; not yet final
example: We made tentative plans to meet on Saturday.
hook: Tentative plans are written in pencil, not ink, ready to be erased if things change.

traps.why: Definite means settled for sure, the opposite of tentative.
Attentive looks like tentative but means paying close attention.
Tentative plans are not hidden; they just are not final yet.

syn1.tip: Think of "tentative plans" or a "tentative date": penciled in but not decided. Pick the choice that means not settled.

sc1.stem: Our plans for the beach trip are only _____ because the weather might change, so we will decide for sure on Friday morning.

traps.why: They will decide for sure on Friday, so the plans are not final.
Beach trips are exciting, but the clue is that the weather might change.
Too strong: the trip is not canceled, just not decided yet.

sc1.tip: The clue is "because the weather might change" and "we will decide for sure on Friday." Plans that are not decided yet are tentative.

decoys.why: The weather might change, so the plans are uncertain, not brief.
The plans are not outdated; they just are not final until Friday.
The clue is that they will decide for sure later, which means uncertain, not obvious.
A beach trip plan does not make money; the clue is about not being final.
The sentence says they will decide for sure later, so the plans are uncertain, not dull.

traps.why: Fixed and settled is the opposite of tentative.
That is the meaning of attentive, a word that looks like tentative.
Too strong: tentative things might still happen; they are just not decided.

syn2.tip: A tentative answer or plan could still change. Think of the phrase "nothing is final yet."

sc2.stem: Mia gave a _____ answer at first, saying 'maybe' and 'I think so,' but after checking her notes she replied with total confidence.

traps.why: Her confidence came later, after the "but"; her first answer was unsure.
Saying "maybe" does not show cleverness; it shows she was not sure.
Nothing in 'maybe' or 'I think so' is rude; it just sounds unsure.

sc2.tip: The words "saying 'maybe' and 'I think so'" restate the blank. An unsure, hesitant answer is tentative, unlike her later "total confidence."

decoys.why: Saying maybe and I think so shows doubt, not brief and complete clarity.
Mia was unsure, not mocking anyone with her answer.
Her first answer was unsure, which is the opposite of bold and obvious.
Saying maybe shows uncertainty, not something that never stops.
The contrast with total confidence shows her first answer was uncertain, not eye catching.

meaning: ordinary and dull; everyday
example: Washing dishes is a mundane chore.
hook: Mundane comes from Latin mundus, world: the plain, worldly stuff of every day, like socks and dishes.

traps.why: Exciting is the opposite of mundane, which means plain and ordinary.
Humane looks like mundane but means kind and caring.
Mundane chores are dull, but they are still useful.

syn1.tip: Mundane tasks are ones you do every day without thinking, like laundry and dishes. Pick the choice that means ordinary.

sc1.stem: The astronaut said that even in space, life includes many _____ tasks, like brushing teeth and cleaning air filters, not just thrilling spacewalks.

traps.why: The tasks are set against "thrilling spacewalks," so they are the opposite of exciting.
Space can be dangerous, but brushing teeth is not.
Heroic is a grand, positive word; brushing teeth is plain and ordinary.

sc1.tip: The examples "brushing teeth and cleaning air filters" are contrasted with "not just thrilling spacewalks." Ordinary, everyday tasks are mundane.

decoys.why: Brushing teeth and cleaning filters are ordinary chores, not clever inventions.
Brushing teeth is completely normal, not odd or unusual.
Brushing teeth and cleaning filters are not threatening at all.
These tasks are contrasted with thrilling spacewalks, so they are calm and ordinary.
Brushing teeth does not make money; the examples show everyday chores.
Brushing teeth is not laughable; it is an ordinary everyday task.

traps.why: Rare and thrilling is the opposite of mundane.
Mundane comes from a word for world, but it means ordinary, not worldwide.
Too strong: mundane things are boring, not painful.

syn2.tip: Think of "mundane chores": the plain, ordinary jobs of daily life. The feeling is boring, not terrible.

sc2.stem: Leo found the fair's game booths so _____ after visiting them every summer for ten years that he barely glanced at them on his way to the new roller coaster.

traps.why: He barely glanced at the booths, so they were not thrilling to him.
Fairs are crowded, but the clue is that he had seen the booths for ten years.
He visited them every summer for ten years, so they were very familiar.

sc2.tip: Look at cause and effect: "every summer for ten years" made the booths so dull that "he barely glanced at them." Ordinary and boring means mundane.

decoys.why: He barely glanced at the booths, so they did not stand out to him.
Clever booths would catch his eye, but he barely glanced at them.
After ten years the booths felt familiar, not odd or unusual.
Nothing suggests the booths seemed evil; he was just bored with them.
The booths bored him after ten years, which has nothing to do with wild hurry.
The sentence is about Leo being bored, not about the booths making money.

meaning: a false outward appearance that hides feelings
example: Her cheerful facade hid how nervous she really felt.
hook: A facade is the fancy front of a building; a person's facade is the front they show to hide what is inside.

traps.why: A facade hides the reality; it is the opposite of what is truly there.
Decade ends like facade but means ten years.
A facade may hide a secret, but the facade is the outside, not the secret.

syn1.tip: Think of a building's facade, its front wall. A person's facade is the outside face they show, which may hide what is inside.

sc1.stem: Behind his calm, smiling _____, the new student was actually terrified, his hands shaking under the desk as the teacher called his name.

traps.why: Panic is what he felt inside; the blank is the calm outside covering it.
Nothing says a friend was there; "behind his" calm smile points to his own outside.
Decade looks like facade but means ten years, which makes no sense here.

sc1.tip: The clue is "Behind his calm, smiling" outside he "was actually terrified." A calm look hiding fear is a facade.

decoys.why: Anguish is the terror he was hiding, not the calm, smiling look on the outside.
Morale is a group's spirit, not a calm smiling look one boy shows.
He may be facing an ordeal, but an ordeal cannot be calm and smiling.
Intuition is a gut feeling, not an outward look hiding his fear.
Prestige is earned respect, and the sentence is about a look covering fear.

traps.why: A facade covers up true feelings; it is the opposite of them.
People may show a facade to friends, but a facade is not a group.
A building's facade is its front, not its back.

syn2.tip: You might hear "put up a brave facade." It is a show on the outside that does not match what someone really feels.

sc2.stem: The team captain kept up a cheerful _____ for the younger players, hiding her own disappointment about the loss until she got home and cried in her room.

traps.why: She was hiding her sadness, so the cheerful outside is the opposite of it.
Team captains wear uniforms, but a uniform cannot hide disappointment.
A complaint is negative, but she was acting cheerful.

sc2.tip: The phrase "hiding her own disappointment" restates the blank. A cheerful show that covers real feelings is a facade.

decoys.why: Her sadness is what she hid, so the cheerful thing she kept up cannot be anguish.
Discord means disagreement, but she was cheerfully hiding her feelings for the players.
Rivalry fits sports, but she was hiding disappointment, not competing with the younger players.
An ordeal is a painful experience, not a cheerful mask she keeps up.
A paradox is a contradictory statement, not a cheerful outward act hiding her feelings.

meaning: to copy someone you admire
example: Young players often emulate their favorite athletes.
hook: When you emulate your hero, you copy their moves because you hope to be just as good someday.

traps.why: Ignoring someone is the opposite of carefully copying them.
Emigrate looks like emulate but means to move to another country.
You admire the people you emulate, but emulate means to copy them.

syn1.tip: You emulate people you look up to, like copying a favorite athlete's moves. Pick the choice that means copy.

sc1.stem: Because he admired his older sister's skill on the violin, Theo tried to _____ her by practicing the same pieces and even holding his bow exactly as she did.

traps.why: He admired her and practiced the same pieces, the opposite of ignoring her.
She was the skilled one; Theo was learning by copying her, not teaching.
Mocking is copying to make fun, but Theo admired his sister.

sc1.tip: The clue is "Because he admired" her and he held his bow "exactly as she did." Copying someone you admire is emulating.

decoys.why: Theo did exactly what his sister did, which is copying her, not saying the opposite.
Theo admired his sister, so he was copying her, not facing her as a problem.
Holding his bow exactly as she did is copying, not publicly supporting her.
Theo practiced her pieces to be like her, not to make her feel less worried.
The sentence says Theo admired his sister, so he would not condemn her.

traps.why: Doing the opposite is the reverse of emulating someone.
Praising a hero is about words; emulating is copying what they do.
Emulating is a positive kind of copying, not stealing.

syn2.tip: Think "Young players emulate their favorite athletes." It means copying someone in a good way because you admire them.

sc2.stem: Instead of inventing his own style, the young painter chose to _____ Van Gogh, using the same swirling brushstrokes and bright yellows that his hero loved.

traps.why: He used the same brushstrokes and colors, the opposite of avoiding Van Gogh.
Van Gogh was his hero, so a negative word like criticize does not fit.
Outdo means to beat someone; he was copying Van Gogh, not trying to beat him.

sc2.tip: "Instead of inventing his own style" plus "the same swirling brushstrokes" and "his hero" tell you he copied someone he admired.

decoys.why: Van Gogh was his hero, so the painter copied him rather than condemning him.
He used the same brushstrokes and colors, which is copying, not doing the opposite.
Using the same brushstrokes is copying Van Gogh, not publicly supporting him.
The painter was copying his hero's style, not judging the quality of his work.
Van Gogh was his hero, and he copied him instead of facing him directly.

meaning: someone who does what they tell others not to
example: He called her a hypocrite for littering after her recycling speech.
hook: A hypocrite says "Don't litter" while dropping a wrapper: their words and actions point opposite ways.

traps.why: Hypocrites often criticize others, but a critic is simply someone who judges things.
Hypnotist starts like hypocrite but means someone who puts people in a trance.
A copycat copies others; a hypocrite does what they tell others not to do.

syn1.tip: A hypocrite does not practice what they preach. Picture someone giving a speech against junk food with chips in their pocket: a phony.

sc1.stem: Mr. Patel lectures us about eating healthy food, yet he eats candy bars every day at his desk, so many students think he is a bit of a _____.

traps.why: Students are criticizing Mr. Patel, so a positive word like hero does not fit.
He talks about healthy food, but eating candy daily is the point, not his knowledge.
Hypnotist looks like hypocrite but has nothing to do with saying one thing and doing another.

sc1.tip: The signal word "yet" shows he lectures about healthy food but "eats candy bars every day." Doing what you tell others not to do makes a hypocrite.

decoys.why: Nothing here is about talent; he tells students one thing and does another.
Mr. Patel is not a story character; he preaches healthy eating but eats candy.
He is not causing change; he does what he tells students not to do.
A misconception is a wrong idea, not a person who breaks his own rules.
Folly is a foolish act, and the sentence needs a word for a kind of person.

traps.why: An honest person lives by their own words, the opposite of a hypocrite.
A strict teacher may lecture, but that alone does not make someone a hypocrite.
Hypo can mean under, but a hypocrite is a fake, not someone lower.

syn2.tip: Think of the phrase "practice what you preach." A hypocrite preaches one thing and does another, showing two different faces.

sc2.stem: Ben is a true _____: he warns everyone that video games waste time, then secretly plays them until midnight every night.

traps.why: He plays games, but the clue is that he warns others against them.
Secretly breaking his own advice is the opposite of saintly behavior.
He criticizes games, but the clue is that he secretly plays them himself.

sc2.tip: The part after the colon explains the blank: he "warns everyone" about games, "then secretly plays them." Saying one thing and doing another is a hypocrite.

decoys.why: Ben shows no special talent; he warns others about games and then plays them.
Ben is not a story's main character; he does what he warns others against.
Ben causes no change; he just breaks the rule he gives everyone else.
A hoax is a trick, not a person who does what he tells others not to.

meaning: sad in a quiet, thoughtful, lasting way
example: The rainy afternoon put Grandpa in a melancholy mood.
hook: Melancholy comes from Greek words for black bile, which people once believed caused long, gloomy sadness.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of melancholy.
Melodious starts like melancholy but means sweet sounding, like a melody.
Grumpy is a bad mood, but it means cranky, not quietly sad.

syn1.tip: Melancholy is a soft, lasting sadness, like a rainy afternoon mood. Look for the choice that means sad and dark.

sc1.stem: Listening to the slow violin tune reminded Aunt June of summers long past, and she grew quiet and _____ as she stared out at the gray sea.

traps.why: Missing summers long past and a gray sea suggest sadness, not cheer.
She grew quiet, but the clue is her sad memories, not being tired.
Too strong: she grew quiet, not wildly upset.

sc1.tip: The clues "summers long past," "grew quiet," and "the gray sea" point to a gentle, thoughtful sadness. That is melancholy.

decoys.why: Aunt June grew quiet while staring at the sea, which is the opposite of frantic.
The slow tune and memories made her sad and quiet, not eager and enthusiastic.
She grew quiet and thoughtful, which is nothing like being annoying or unpleasant.
Remembering long-past summers by a gray sea is sad, not silly or laughable.
The sentence describes a quiet, sad mood, not someone odd or unusual.

traps.why: Full of joy is the opposite of melancholy.
Too strong: melancholy is a quiet sadness, not loud crying.
That describes melodious, a word that starts like melancholy.

syn2.tip: Picture someone staring out a rainy window, thinking of the past. That calm, heavy sadness is melancholy.

sc2.stem: Usually the life of the party, Omar seemed oddly _____ at the farewell picnic, sitting alone and gazing quietly at the friends he would soon leave behind.

traps.why: "Oddly" means he was not his usual lively self.
Picnics have food, but the clue is about leaving his friends.
Annoyed is a bad mood, but missing friends brings sadness, not irritation.

sc2.tip: "Usually the life of the party" but "oddly" different, "sitting alone" and about to "leave behind" friends: that contrast points to quiet sadness.

decoys.why: Omar was sitting alone and gazing quietly, which is the opposite of frantic.
Sitting quietly alone is not annoying; he was sad about leaving his friends.
Avid fits the life of the party, but here he was quietly sad, not eager.
Leaving his friends made Omar sad and quiet, not silly or laughable.
Gazing at friends he will miss is sad, not evil or threatening.

meaning: serious hardship or bad luck
example: The team showed great courage in the face of adversity.
hook: You often hear "in the face of adversity": hard times pushing against you while you keep going.

traps.why: Comfort is the opposite of adversity, which means hard times.
Adversary looks like adversity but means an enemy or opponent.
Diversity rhymes with adversity but means variety.

syn1.tip: You often hear "overcome adversity" or "in the face of adversity." It means the hard times people push through.

sc1.stem: Despite growing up in poverty and losing her hearing at age nine, the scientist overcame great _____ to earn a scholarship and later a doctorate.

traps.why: She grew up in poverty, the opposite of wealth.
Scientists may have talent, but nobody overcomes talent; poverty and hearing loss are hardships.
Too weak: poverty and losing her hearing are far more than an inconvenience.

sc1.tip: The examples "growing up in poverty" and "losing her hearing" are serious troubles she "overcame." Great hardship is adversity.

decoys.why: Poverty and hearing loss are hardships she overcame, not a natural ability.
She earned respect later; poverty and hearing loss were hardships, not prestige.
