Words on a board are seen, and the new glasses fix seeing, not memory.

meaning: silly and not serious or important
example: She spent her whole allowance on frivolous toys.
hook: Frivolous things are fluff: glitter, party hats, and silly jokes when it is time to be serious.

traps.why: Serious is the opposite of frivolous.
Furious looks a bit like frivolous but means very angry.
Frivolous purchases can cost a lot, but frivolous means silly, not costly.

syn1.tip: A frivolous lawsuit might be over a missing french fry. Look for the choice that means not serious.

sc1.stem: Mr. Kim urged the class to spend the fundraiser money on useful supplies like microscopes rather than _____ items such as glitter stickers and party hats.

traps.why: Practical means useful, which is what Mr. Kim wants instead of these items.
Microscopes are scientific; glitter stickers and party hats are not.
Stickers and hats aren't dangerous, just silly, so harmful is far too strong.

sc1.tip: The signal is "rather than." Useful microscopes are set against stickers and party hats, so the blank means silly and unimportant.

decoys.why: Glitter stickers and party hats are contrasted with useful supplies, so they are not clever.
Stickers and party hats are not heavy or hard to carry; they are simply unimportant.
Mr. Kim objects that the items are not useful, not that they are perfect.
The contrast is useful versus silly, and being clean has nothing to do with it.
Glitter stickers and party hats are not mysterious; the point is they are not useful.

traps.why: Deeply serious is the opposite of frivolous.
The -ous ending can mean full of, but frivolous isn't about energy.
Silly things may cost money, but frivolous is about mattering little.

syn2.tip: Picture someone asking about snack flavors during a fire drill. The question is frivolous because it has little importance right then.

sc2.stem: Grandpa called my plan to buy a light-up hat with my birthday money _____, saying it was a waste spent on something that didn't really matter.

traps.why: Sensible means wise, but Grandpa calls the plan a waste.
Spending on yourself isn't his point; he says the hat didn't matter.
Furious looks a bit like frivolous, but a plan can't be angry.

sc2.tip: After the comma, Grandpa restates his view: "a waste spent on something that didn't really matter." That describes something silly and unimportant.

decoys.why: Grandpa called the plan a waste, so he would not praise it as clever.
Grandpa thought the plan was a waste, not careful and responsible.
Grandpa complained the hat didn't matter, not that the plan was risky or unsafe.
Buying a hat is not hard work; Grandpa objected that it was unimportant.
The plan was easy to understand; Grandpa just thought it was a waste.
Calling something a waste is criticism, so Grandpa would not call it perfect.

meaning: a mistaken belief or idea
example: It is a misconception that bats are blind.
hook: Misconception splits into mis, meaning wrong, and conception, meaning idea: a wrong idea, like thinking bats are blind.

traps.why: A fact is true; a misconception is a belief that is wrong.
Deception ends the same way but means tricking someone on purpose.
People may argue about beliefs, but a misconception is simply a wrong one.

syn1.tip: Split it: mis means wrong, and a conception is an idea. A wrong idea is an error in thinking.

sc1.stem: Many people believe that goldfish have only a three-second memory, but this is a common _____; studies show they can remember things for months.

traps.why: Studies prove the belief wrong, so it can't be a fact.
The studies made a discovery, but the popular belief itself was wrong.
Experiments go with studies, but the blank names the wrong belief.

sc1.tip: Look at "but" and "studies show." The popular belief is proven wrong, so the blank names a wrong belief.

decoys.why: The belief is simply wrong, as studies show, not a true statement that seems contradictory.
The sentence says goldfish memory is actually good, so the issue is a wrong belief, not a shortage.
A facade hides feelings; this sentence is about people believing something untrue.
Nobody is complaining about unfairness; people simply believe something false about goldfish.
The sentence describes a belief that studies proved wrong, not a natural talent.
The goldfish idea is a mistaken belief, not a sign of something to come.

traps.why: A proven fact is true, the opposite of a mistaken belief.
Mis means wrong here, not missing.
A lie is told on purpose; a misconception is believed honestly.

syn2.tip: The prefix mis means wrong, as in misspell and misunderstand. A misconception is a belief that turns out to be wrong.

sc2.stem: Many people hold the _____ that the Great Wall of China can be seen from space, a mistaken idea that astronauts have shown to be false.

traps.why: Astronauts showed it is false, so it is not a fact.
Proof shows something is true; this idea was shown false.
A deception is a trick played on purpose; nobody is tricking anyone here.

sc2.tip: The sentence restates the blank right after the comma: "a mistaken idea that astronauts have shown to be false." That is a wrong belief.

decoys.why: The sentence calls it a mistaken idea shown false, not a true statement that seems contradictory.
Seeing the Great Wall from space is a false belief, not a complaint about unfairness.
People believe something about the Great Wall; they do not look down on anything here.
The sentence names a mistaken idea, not a natural ability.
The belief about the Great Wall is a false idea, not a sign of the future.

meaning: extremely fierce or intense
example: The ferocious wind tore shingles off the roof.
hook: Ferocious and fierce both come from a Latin word for wild: picture a lion roaring with its claws out.

traps.why: Gentle is the opposite of ferocious.
A ferocious animal may frighten you, but it isn't frightened itself.
Grumpy is only mildly cross, far too weak for ferocious.

syn1.tip: Ferocious sounds a bit like fierce, and they share a root. Think of a ferocious dog snarling behind a fence.

sc1.stem: The usually gentle river became _____ after a week of heavy rain, its roaring brown water tearing whole trees from the banks.

traps.why: Calm fits "usually gentle," but the river changed and began tearing out trees.
Heavy rain makes rivers deeper, and shallow water can't tear out trees.
Choppy water is a little rough; tearing out trees needs something much fiercer.

sc1.tip: "Usually gentle" sets up a change, and "roaring" water "tearing whole trees" shows how wild it became. You need a word for extremely fierce.

decoys.why: The water was roaring and tearing out trees, so it was moving wildly, not still.
The water was muddy brown and destructive, not clean and untouched.
Sedentary describes sitting people, and this river was roaring and tearing out trees.
A river tearing trees from its banks is fierce, not decorated with fancy detail.
Nothing about the river is mysterious; the clues show it became violent and powerful.

traps.why: Tame means gentle and calm, the opposite of ferocious.
Ferocious predators may be hungry, but ferocious means fierce and wild.
Precious rhymes with ferocious but means very valuable.

syn2.tip: The -ous ending means full of, and the start links to fierce. Something full of fierceness is savage.

sc2.stem: The storm was so _____ that its winds knocked down power lines across town and kept everyone indoors for two days.

traps.why: A mild storm wouldn't knock down power lines.
Brief is about time, and this storm kept people inside for days.
Breezy means gently windy, far too weak to knock down power lines.

sc2.tip: The words "so" and "that" show cause and effect. A storm that knocks down power lines must be extremely fierce.

decoys.why: Winds strong enough to knock down power lines are not still or motionless.
A storm that kept everyone indoors for days was serious, not silly.
The storm's damage shows it was fierce, not mysterious or hard to understand.
Knocked down power lines show a destructive storm, not a clean, untouched one.
The storm kept people indoors, but the storm itself was violent, not sitting still.

meaning: to make something last longer
example: The rain delay prolonged the game by an hour.
hook: Prolong has long right inside it: to prolong a visit is to make it last longer.

traps.why: Shorten is the opposite of prolong.
Belong rhymes with prolong but means to be part of something.
Postpone means move to a later time, not make something last longer.

syn1.tip: Look inside the word: prolong contains long. To prolong something is to make it longer, or extend it.

sc1.stem: Hoping to _____ their visit to the national park, the family called the lodge and asked whether they could stay three more nights.

traps.why: Staying three more nights makes the visit longer, not shorter.
They are already visiting; staying longer doesn't push the visit later.
Repeating means coming back another time; they want to stay longer now.

sc1.tip: The family asks to "stay three more nights." Staying more nights makes the visit last longer, so the blank means make longer.

decoys.why: The family wanted three more nights, so they wanted to extend the visit, not get in its way.
Asking to stay longer shows they wanted the visit to continue, not to block it.
The family asked for more nights, so they were not trying to hold back their visit.
National parks are conserved, but the family wanted their visit to last longer.
Staying three more nights makes a visit longer; it does not bring up a memory.

traps.why: Cutting something short is the opposite of prolonging it.
Putting something off delays its start; prolong makes it last longer.
Prolong contains long, but it has nothing to do with wishing.

syn2.tip: Think of a referee who prolongs a game with extra time. The game lasts longer than planned.

sc2.stem: Most of us wanted the boring assembly to end quickly, but the speaker seemed determined to _____ it with one long story after another.

traps.why: Long stories make the assembly longer, not shorter.
Telling one long story after another is the opposite of hurrying.
Speakers describe things, but the stories made the assembly last longer.

sc2.tip: "But" sets the speaker against students who wanted it "to end quickly." With "one long story after another," he makes it last longer.

decoys.why: The long stories made the boring assembly worse for the students, not less painful.
Telling one long story after another keeps the assembly going instead of wiping it out.
The speaker kept talking to stretch out the assembly, not to say the opposite of it.
The students found the assembly boring, so the stories made it longer, not attractive.
The clue is that students wanted it to end quickly, so the speaker made it last longer.

meaning: a natural ability to learn or do something
example: Mia has an aptitude for learning new languages.
hook: Aptitude starts with apt, as in apt to learn: an aptitude for drawing means it comes naturally to you.

traps.why: A weakness is something you're bad at, the opposite of aptitude.
Attitude looks like aptitude but means how you feel about something.
You can be interested in something without being naturally good at it.

syn1.tip: Aptitude tests measure what you're naturally good at. If you have an aptitude for math, you have a talent for it.

sc1.stem: Even as a toddler, Hiro had a remarkable _____ for music; he could pick out songs on the piano before anyone had taught him a single note.

traps.why: Playing songs on his own shows a gift for music, not a dislike.
Attitude looks like aptitude, but the clue is about natural ability.
Nobody had taught him, so he didn't have a teacher.

sc1.tip: He played songs "before anyone had taught him a single note." Doing something with no lessons shows a natural ability.

decoys.why: Hiro loved picking out songs on his own, so he did not look down on music.
Nothing in the sentence shows Hiro hated music; he played it eagerly before any lessons.

traps.why: Total inability is the opposite of aptitude.
Altitude looks like aptitude but means height above the ground.
Hard work is effort you put in; aptitude is ability you have naturally.

syn2.tip: Hear "apt" at the start, as in "apt to learn quickly." An aptitude is an ability that comes naturally.

sc2.stem: Although my brother practiced soccer every single day, he never showed much _____ for it, while his little sister scored three goals in her very first game.

traps.why: Practicing every day shows effort; what he lacked was natural ability.
The sentence says he lacked something good his sister had, not weakness.
Altitude looks like aptitude but means height, which makes no sense here.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets daily practice against the result, and his sister scores in "her very first game." The blank is the natural ability he lacked.

decoys.why: He practiced every day, so he did not scorn soccer; the contrast is about natural skill.
The sentence compares his skill with his sister's goals, not whether he hated soccer.

meaning: to take away or keep something needed from
example: Staying up late deprives your body of needed sleep.
hook: To deprive someone is to take away what they need, like a power outage depriving a whole town of light.

traps.why: Provide means to give, the opposite of deprive.
Derive looks like deprive but means to get something from a source.
Taking things away can be a punishment, but deprive just means withhold.

syn1.tip: You've heard of sleep deprivation, when people don't get the sleep they need. To deprive is to deny someone something.

sc1.stem: Building the parking lot would _____ the neighborhood's children of their only park, leaving them nowhere safe to play.

traps.why: Reminding brings something to mind; the lot would actually take the park away.
Relieve means freeing someone from a burden, but losing a park is bad.
Informing just tells them something; the children would lose their park.

sc1.tip: The lot leaves children with "nowhere safe to play." Something is taken from them, so the blank means take away.

decoys.why: Leaving children nowhere safe to play would worry them, not comfort them.

traps.why: Giving back is the opposite of taking away.
Deprive contains priv like private, but it doesn't mean keep secret.
Losing something can make you sad, but deprive means taking it away.

syn2.tip: Think of a phone being taken as punishment. Your parents deprive you of it, which means they take it away from you.

sc2.stem: The long drought would _____ the farm's thirsty crops of water, taking away the one thing they needed most to grow.

traps.why: Relieve sounds like freeing them of a burden, but water helps crops.
A drought can't remind crops of anything; it takes their water.
To assure crops of water would promise it, the reverse of taking it.

sc2.tip: The words after the comma restate the blank: "taking away the one thing they needed most." That is what the missing word means.

decoys.why: A drought takes water away from crops; it does not comfort them about anything.

meaning: decorated with lots of fancy detail
example: The ornate frame was carved with leaves and flowers.
hook: Ornate and ornament are related: picture a frame so covered in carved ornaments that hardly any plain wood shows.

traps.why: Plain is the opposite of ornate.
Old buildings are often ornate, but ornate is about decoration, not age.
Tasteless is an insult; ornate just describes lots of decoration.

syn1.tip: Ornate is related to ornament, like the decorations you hang on a tree. Something ornate is fancy and covered in decoration.

sc1.stem: Unlike the plain modern buildings around it, the old theater was _____, with carved angels, swirling patterns, and gold trim covering every wall.

traps.why: The theater is unlike the plain buildings, so it can't be simple.
The theater is old, but the clue lists decorations, not damage.
Theaters can be big, but angels and gold trim describe decoration, not size.

sc1.tip: "Unlike the plain modern buildings" signals a contrast, and the angels, swirls, and gold trim describe heavy decoration. The blank means fancy and detailed.

decoys.why: The clue lists carved angels and gold trim, which is about decoration, not cleanliness.
Nothing suggests the theater might fall; the sentence describes its fancy decoration.
Swirling patterns and gold trim show decoration, not something mysterious or hard to understand.
Stagnant describes still water or no growth, not a building covered in carvings.

traps.why: Simply designed is the opposite of ornate.
Fresh paint can look nice, but ornate means full of fancy detail.
Ornate things can cost a lot, but ornate is about decoration.

syn2.tip: Think of ornaments covering every branch of a holiday tree. Ornate describes something richly decorated with detail.

sc2.stem: The jewelry box was so _____ that it took the woodcarver three months to finish all the tiny flowers, vines, and birds on its lid.

traps.why: A plain box wouldn't have tiny flowers, vines, and birds.
Weight doesn't explain months of carving tiny details.
The woodcarver is still making it, so it can't be ancient.

sc2.tip: "So _____ that it took three months" shows cause and effect. Months of carving "tiny flowers, vines, and birds" means it was full of fancy detail.

decoys.why: Tiny flowers and vines took time because of detail, not because the box was heavy.
Three months of carving tiny flowers points to fancy detail, not clean and untouched.
Being unsafe or likely to fall would not make carving the lid take three months.
The carvings are flowers and birds, so nothing about the box is mysterious.

meaning: great skill and grace in handling something
example: She handled the tricky question with finesse.
hook: Finesse shares its start with fine: picture a cake decorator shaping sugar petals with a light, graceful, sure touch.

traps.why: Clumsiness is the opposite of finesse.
Fitness looks and sounds like finesse but means being physically healthy.
Skilled people may work fast, but finesse is about grace, not speed.

syn1.tip: Finesse comes from the French word for fine. Doing something with finesse means doing it with fine, graceful skill.

sc1.stem: The pastry chef decorated the cake with such _____ that each sugar flower looked delicate and real, as if it had just been picked from a garden.

traps.why: Clumsy work wouldn't make the flowers look delicate and real.
Working fast doesn't make sugar flowers look delicate and real.
Fitness looks like finesse but means physical health, which doesn't fit here.

sc1.tip: The result is the clue: each flower "looked delicate and real." Work that delicate takes graceful, refined skill.

decoys.why: Flowers that look delicate and real show careful skill, not looking down on the work.
The sentence praises the chef's delicate work and says nothing about pain or sorrow.
Sugar flowers that look real show great skill, the opposite of foolishness.
Decorating delicate sugar flowers shows graceful skill, not hostility toward anyone.

traps.why: Awkward fumbling is the opposite of finesse.
Finesse looks like finish, but it has nothing to do with ending.
Planning happens beforehand; finesse is the graceful skill shown while doing something.

syn2.tip: Picture a dancer or chef with a light, sure touch. Finesse is not just skill, but skill with grace and delicacy.

sc2.stem: While the younger players just kicked the ball as hard as they could, the team captain dribbled past defenders with _____, gently guiding the ball wherever she wanted.

traps.why: The younger players used force; the captain is gentle and controlled.
She guides the ball wherever she wants, so she isn't awkward.
Anger is the wrong feeling for someone gently guiding the ball.

sc2.tip: "While" contrasts kicking "as hard as they could" with the captain "gently guiding the ball." The blank means gentle, controlled skill.

decoys.why: She was gently guiding the ball, which shows graceful control, not hostility.
The captain is calmly controlling the ball, with no sign of pain or sorrow.
Camaraderie is friendship in a group, but the sentence is about her own ball skill.

meaning: requiring great effort; very difficult
example: The arduous climb up the mountain took the hikers nearly ten hours.
hook: Arduous comes from a Latin word meaning steep: picture an exhausting climb up a mountain that takes all day.

traps.why: Easy is the opposite of arduous.
Arduous tasks may be risky, but arduous means hard work, not danger.
Arduous jobs often take long, but arduous is about effort, not time.

syn1.tip: Arduous comes from a Latin word for steep. Think of an arduous climb up a steep hill: it is very difficult.

sc1.stem: For pioneer families, crossing the Rocky Mountains by wagon was truly _____; they pushed through deep snow, steep trails, and weeks of exhaustion.

traps.why: Deep snow and weeks of exhaustion show the trip was anything but effortless.
Thrilling is a happy, exciting word; the clues describe misery and exhaustion.
The trip lasted weeks, and the clue is about effort, not length.

sc1.tip: The semicolon leads to examples: "deep snow, steep trails, and weeks of exhaustion." All that shows the trip took huge effort.

decoys.why: Deep snow and weeks of exhaustion make the trip serious, not silly or unimportant.
Pushing through snow and steep trails is hard physical work, not sitting around.
Weeks of exhaustion are nothing playful or fanciful about the journey.
Ornate describes fancy decoration, but the sentence is about a hard, tiring journey.

traps.why: Needing no effort is the opposite of arduous.
Hard tasks can be dangerous, but arduous is about effort.
Arduous looks like ardor, which means passion, but arduous means hard work.

syn2.tip: Arduous tasks make you sweat, like carrying furniture up three flights of stairs. The word means needing great effort.

sc2.stem: My older sister said the science project would be quick and simple, but it turned out to be _____, keeping us up late gluing and measuring for five nights.

traps.why: Easy matches the sister's prediction, but "but" says the opposite happened.
A tiny project wouldn't keep you up late for five nights.
Relaxing is a pleasant word; five late nights of work is exhausting.

sc2.tip: "But" flips the sister's prediction of "quick and simple." Five late nights of gluing and measuring shows the project took great effort.

decoys.why: Five late nights of work show the project was hard, not silly or unimportant.
The clue is staying up late for five nights, which points to hard work, not playfulness.
The sentence contrasts quick and simple with long effort, not with how perfect it looked.
The contrast with quick and simple is about effort, not about fancy decoration.

meaning: strong dislike or hostility toward someone
example: The animosity between the two rival clubs lasted for years.
hook: Animosity is the glare two rivals shoot across the field, a dislike that can burn for years.

traps.why: Friendship is a warm feeling, the opposite of animosity.
Animation looks similar but means liveliness or cartoons, not dislike.
Annoyance is too weak; animosity is strong, lasting dislike.

syn1.tip: Think of the feeling between bitter rivals. Animosity is a strong, negative feeling aimed at someone.

sc1.stem: The two neighbors had argued about the fence for so long that their _____ was obvious; they glared at each other and refused to speak even at the block party.

traps.why: Glaring and refusing to speak show the opposite of friendship.
Shy people may stay quiet, but glaring shows dislike, not shyness.
Loneliness is about being alone, not about feelings toward a neighbor.

sc1.tip: The neighbors 'glared at each other and refused to speak.' That behavior shows strong dislike between them.

decoys.why: They glared and refused to speak, so they had no friendly relationship at all.
Neighbors who glare and won't speak share no friendship or trust.
A facade hides feelings, but these neighbors showed their dislike openly by glaring.
The sentence is about how the neighbors feel about each other, not skill or grace.
Glaring and refusing to speak show a feeling, not a natural ability.
Nothing in the sentence is about a gut feeling; it describes open hostility.

traps.why: Warm affection is the opposite of animosity.
Mild irritation is too weak; animosity is strong dislike.
Anim looks like animated, but animosity means hostility, not liveliness.

syn2.tip: Picture two rivals who refuse to shake hands. Animosity names that bitter, unfriendly feeling between people.

sc2.stem: Although the two soccer captains had been best friends in third grade, a bitter argument over the championship left nothing but _____ between them by eighth grade.

traps.why: A bitter argument destroys admiration; it leaves the opposite behind.
Loyalty fits their old friendship, but the bitter argument changed that.
Captains need teamwork, but a bitter argument leaves dislike instead.

sc2.tip: 'Although' they 'had been best friends,' a 'bitter argument' changed things. Look for a word that means the opposite of friendship.

decoys.why: They were friends once, but the bitter argument ended that friendship.
The word although tells you their friendly relationship was gone after the argument.
Soccer suggests plans, but a bitter argument leaves bad feelings, not a plan.
A bitter argument leaves bad feelings between people, not skill or grace.
The sentence describes feelings between former friends, not a natural ability.
A bitter argument leaves hostility, not a gut feeling, between the captains.

meaning: a friendly, understanding relationship
example: The new coach quickly built a rapport with her players.
hook: Rapport is that easy click you feel with someone who just gets you, like a favorite coach.

traps.why: Hostility is unfriendly, the opposite of a warm rapport.
Report looks similar but means an account of facts.
You talk with people you have rapport with, but rapport is the connection itself.

syn1.tip: Rapport is something you 'build' or 'have' with people, like a coach with players. Think of a friendly connection.

sc1.stem: Because Mr. Okafor learned every student's name and asked about their hobbies, he quickly developed a warm _____ with his new class.

traps.why: Learning names and hobbies brings people closer, not farther apart.
Classes have routines, but asking about hobbies builds a relationship.
Kind attention creates friendship, the opposite of a rivalry.

sc1.tip: He 'learned every student's name and asked about their hobbies.' Those kind actions build a friendly connection.

decoys.why: Learning names and asking about hobbies builds friendliness, not hostility.
The word warm and his caring questions show he did not look down on students.
A warm connection built by caring questions is harmony, not disagreement.
You develop a warm relationship with people, not a warm plan with them.
An aptitude is a personal ability; you cannot develop one with a class.
The sentence is about a warm connection with students, not skill or grace.

traps.why: Bitter conflict is the opposite of a friendly rapport.
Report only looks like rapport; it means a written account.
Meeting someone comes first, but rapport is the friendship that grows later.

syn2.tip: People say two friends 'have great rapport' when they understand each other easily. It names a warm, trusting relationship.

sc2.stem: On the first day the new lab partners barely spoke, but by October they shared jokes and finished each other's sentences, showing a strong _____.

traps.why: Sharing jokes shows friendship, the opposite of dislike.
Shyness fits the first day, but 'but by October' signals a change.
Lab partners might compete, but jokes and finished sentences show friendship.

sc2.tip: 'But by October' signals a change from barely speaking. Sharing jokes and finishing each other's sentences shows a close, friendly connection.

decoys.why: Partners who share jokes and finish each other's sentences like each other.
Sharing jokes shows the partners enjoy each other, not that they look down on each other.
Finishing each other's sentences shows harmony, not disagreement.
Jokes and finished sentences show a friendship, not a natural talent for lab work.
Sharing jokes is about friendship, not a careful plan for a goal.
The clues describe a growing friendship, not skill or grace in handling something.

meaning: to figure out from clues or evidence
example: From her smile, I inferred that she had passed the test.
hook: A detective spots muddy boots and infers you were outside; to infer is to read the clues.

traps.why: Ignoring evidence is the opposite of using it to infer.
Inform looks similar but means to tell someone facts.
A speaker implies a hint; the listener infers, or figures it out.

syn1.tip: Infer is what readers do with clues: you use evidence to figure something out, the way a detective infers who did it.

sc1.stem: Seeing muddy paw prints across the kitchen floor and an empty dog bed, Mom was able to _____ that Rex had escaped through the back door.

traps.why: The clues made Mom sure, not doubtful.
Mom wasn't pretending; real clues showed her what happened.
Mom read the clues herself; implying means hinting to someone else.

sc1.tip: Mom used 'muddy paw prints' and 'an empty dog bed' as evidence. Reaching a conclusion from clues is what the blank needs.

decoys.why: The paw prints and empty bed support the idea that Rex escaped; they do not disprove it.
Mom used the clues to reach a conclusion, not to say the opposite of one.

traps.why: Looking past clues is the opposite of using them to infer.
Hinting at means suggesting, which is implying, not inferring.
Making something up uses no clues; inferring depends on evidence.

syn2.tip: Teachers ask you to infer what a character feels from clues in the story. You figure it out instead of being told.

sc2.stem: Nobody told Priya about any surprise, but the whispering friends and the cake hidden in the closet let her _____ that a party was coming.

traps.why: The clues pointed to a party, so they would not make her doubt it.
Clues don't let you announce; they let you work something out.
Priya wasn't planning the party, so she couldn't promise it.

sc2.tip: 'Nobody told' her, 'but' whispers and a hidden cake gave it away. She worked it out herself from clues.

decoys.why: The whispering and hidden cake pointed to a party, so Priya had nothing to disprove.
Priya used the clues to figure out the surprise, not to deny it.

meaning: large, heavy, and hard to carry or use
example: The cumbersome suitcase would not fit in the car.
hook: Picture wrestling a giant mattress up narrow stairs; that heavy, awkward struggle is cumbersome.

traps.why: Light things are easy to carry, the opposite of cumbersome.
Awesome rhymes with the end of cumbersome but means amazing.
Big items can be valuable, but cumbersome means hard to carry.

syn1.tip: Cumbersome sounds clunky, and it means clunky: big, heavy, and awkward to carry, like an overstuffed suitcase.

sc1.stem: The old camping tent was so _____ that it took two people to carry it, so the family bought a lightweight one for their hiking trip.

traps.why: A light tent wouldn't need two people to carry it.
Cozy is a pleasant tent word, but the clue is about weight.
A flimsy tent is weak and thin, not heavy enough for two carriers.

sc1.tip: It 'took two people to carry it,' and the family replaced it with a 'lightweight one.' The blank must mean heavy and hard to carry.

decoys.why: Sedentary describes sitting a lot, not a tent so heavy it takes two people to carry.
Stagnant means not flowing, like still water; it does not mean heavy.
A perfect tent would not be replaced; the family wanted one that was lighter.
Needing two people to carry it is about weight, not about being silly.
The clue is that the tent was heavy, not playful or fanciful.
Nothing says the tent was confusing; the problem was that it was too heavy.

traps.why: Easy to handle is the opposite of cumbersome.
Price has nothing to do with being heavy and awkward.
Fragile things break easily; cumbersome things are heavy and clumsy to move.

syn2.tip: Think of a cumbersome suitcase that won't fit in the car. The word means big, heavy, and hard to move or use.

sc2.stem: Grandpa's old laptop was _____; it weighed nearly ten pounds and was so thick that it would not fit in my backpack.

traps.why: Portable means easy to carry, the opposite of a ten pound laptop.
Speed is about computers, but the clue describes weight and size.
Delicate means easily broken, not heavy and thick.

sc2.tip: The part after the semicolon explains the blank: it 'weighed nearly ten pounds' and wouldn't 'fit in my backpack.' That means heavy and awkward.

decoys.why: An old laptop might be confusing, but the clues are its weight and thickness.
Weighing ten pounds and not fitting in a backpack are flaws, not perfection.
Stagnant means not flowing or growing; the clues say the laptop was heavy and thick.
Ten pounds and too thick for a backpack describe bulk, not silliness.
The clues describe a heavy, bulky laptop, not a playful one.
Sedentary describes a person who sits a lot, not a heavy, bulky object.

meaning: to attract someone by offering something pleasant
example: The smell of cookies enticed us into the bakery.
hook: The smell of warm cookies drifting from a bakery door entices you inside before you even decide.

traps.why: Repel means to push away, the opposite of entice.
Entertain looks similar but means to amuse, not to attract.
Forcing makes people act; enticing makes them want to.

syn1.tip: Think of a store offering free samples to entice customers. Entice means drawing someone in with something they want.

sc1.stem: To _____ more shoppers into the new bookstore, the owner offered free hot chocolate and set out a table of colorful books by the door.

traps.why: Free hot chocolate invites people; it doesn't force them.
Treats and colorful books attract shoppers; they don't scare them.
Ordering is too pushy; free hot chocolate gently draws people in.

sc1.tip: The owner 'offered free hot chocolate' and set out 'colorful books by the door.' Offering pleasant things is how you draw people in.

decoys.why: Free hot chocolate draws shoppers in gently; it does not force anyone anywhere.
Incite means stirring people up to trouble, not attracting them with pleasant treats.

traps.why: Drive away is the opposite of entice.
Ordering people uses commands; enticing uses something pleasant.
Trapping holds someone against their will; enticing makes them want to come.

syn2.tip: Bait on a fishing hook entices a fish. To entice is to pull someone toward you with something appealing.

sc2.stem: The zookeeper tried shouting and clapping, but nothing worked until she held out a ripe banana to _____ the stubborn monkey down from the tree.

traps.why: A banana attracts a monkey; shouting was the frightening part that failed.
Holding out a banana isn't chasing; it invites the monkey to come.
Scolding is harsh; offering a treat is a pleasant way to attract.

sc2.tip: Shouting failed, 'but' a 'ripe banana' worked. Holding out a treat to draw an animal toward you is what the blank describes.

decoys.why: Shouting tried to force the monkey; the banana worked by tempting it instead.

meaning: a complaint about something unfair
example: The students listed their grievances for the principal.
hook: Grievance is in the same word family as grief: it's an unfair hurt you speak up about.

traps.why: A compliment is praise, the opposite of a complaint.
Grievance looks like grief, but it means a complaint, not sadness.
Grievances are about unfair treatment, but a punishment is not a complaint.

syn1.tip: People 'file a grievance' when something feels unfair. It sits close to 'grieve,' but it means a complaint you speak up about.

sc1.stem: The students brought their _____ to the principal, explaining that it was unfair that only seniors were allowed to use the new gym.

traps.why: Calling a rule unfair is complaining, the opposite of praise.
Students carry homework, but they were explaining an unfair rule.
Apologies admit your own fault; the students were pointing out an unfair rule.

sc1.tip: The students were 'explaining that it was unfair.' Telling someone in charge that a rule is unfair is making a complaint.

decoys.why: The students are calling something unfair, which is a complaint, not a show of respect.
They are explaining a problem to the principal, not showing hatred toward someone.
The students want something fixed, not to look down on it as beneath them.
The sentence is about something unfair, not friendship among the group.
You do not explain unfairness by bringing a friendly relationship to the principal.

traps.why: Praise is the opposite of a grievance.
Grievance sounds like grieving, but it means a complaint, not mourning.
Revenge strikes back; a grievance just states what is unfair.

syn2.tip: Workers bring grievances to their boss when they feel treated unfairly. Think 'complaint about something unfair.'

sc2.stem: Instead of grumbling in the hallway, the eighth graders wrote down their _____ about the short lunch period and politely asked the student council for a fix.

traps.why: Nobody asks for a fix to something they compliment.
Excuses explain your own mistakes, not a problem you want fixed.
Jokes are lighthearted; asking for a fix means they had a real complaint.

sc2.tip: They wrote about 'the short lunch period' and 'asked for a fix.' People only want a fix when they have a complaint.

decoys.why: They are unhappy about a short lunch, so they wrote a complaint, not praise.
The sentence says they asked politely, so they were not writing down hostility.
They politely asked for a fix, which does not match looking down on others.
They are complaining about lunch, not describing friendship within their group.
You cannot write down a friendly relationship about a short lunch period.
A short lunch is a fair complaint, not severe pain or great sorrow.

meaning: to slow or block progress
example: Bad weather impeded the building of the new bridge.
hook: Impede hides ped, meaning foot: imagine your feet tangled in rope, every step slowed and blocked.

traps.why: Assist means to help, the opposite of impede.
Impress looks similar but means to make people admire you.
Ped means foot, but impede means to block, not to walk.

syn1.tip: Think of things that impede traffic, like road work or snow. They get in the way and slow everything down.

sc1.stem: A lack of money continued to _____ progress on the new library, which sat half-built for more than a year.

traps.why: A lack of money hurts progress; it doesn't boost it.
Builders measure progress, but the clue shows progress being stopped.
A half-built library is nothing to celebrate; the tone is negative.

sc1.tip: A 'lack of money' left the library 'half-built for more than a year.' Something held up progress, so the blank means slow or block.

decoys.why: The library sat half-built, so lack of money blocked progress rather than strengthening it.
Lack of money stopped the work, so it did not stir up progress.
The library was still half-built, so progress was slowed, not completely wiped out.
Progress is not a person, and the sentence is about blocking, not easing worry.
Lack of money does not attract progress; the library stayed half-built.

traps.why: Speed up is the opposite of impede.
The ped part means foot, but impede isn't about stepping.
Impede means slow or block for now, not end forever.

syn2.tip: Imagine a fallen tree on a bike path; it impedes riders. Impede means to get in the way and slow progress.

sc2.stem: The new hallway rule was meant to speed up class changes, but instead the crowded single staircase seemed to _____ every student trying to reach class on time.

traps.why: Hurrying is what the rule wanted; 'but instead' signals the opposite happened.
A crowded staircase doesn't guide students; it blocks them.
Welcome is friendly, but a crowded staircase is a problem here.

sc2.tip: The rule was meant to 'speed up' class changes, 'but instead' things got worse. The blank must mean the opposite of speeding up.

decoys.why: The crowded staircase made students late, so it did not support or help them.
A crowded staircase slowing everyone down would worry students, not calm them.
Nothing pleasant is offered; the crowded staircase gets in students' way.
Students are trying to get to class, not being forced out of the school.
The sentence is about slowing students down, not stirring them up to act.

meaning: loyal and unwavering
example: The steadfast dog waited at the station every day.
hook: Steadfast is steady plus fast in its old sense of firmly fixed, as in 'hold fast.'

traps.why: Unreliable means you can't count on someone, the opposite of steadfast.
Fast here means firmly fixed, as in 'hold fast,' not quick.
Stubborn sounds negative; steadfast praises someone for staying true.

syn1.tip: Break it up: steady plus fast, as in 'hold fast.' Someone steadfast stays firmly fixed in their loyalty.

sc1.stem: Through every losing season, the team's _____ fans never stopped buying tickets, showing up in the rain to cheer as loudly as ever.

traps.why: Occasional fans come sometimes; these fans 'never stopped' coming.
Buying tickets takes money, but the clue is that they never stopped.
Fast in steadfast means firm, and speed has nothing to do with fans.

sc1.tip: The fans 'never stopped' coming 'through every losing season,' even 'in the rain.' Sticking with a team in bad times is loyalty.

decoys.why: Fans who show up in the rain every season are serious, not silly.
These fans never stopped coming, so they were loyal, not playful and fanciful.
The clue is that they never stopped coming, not that they sat a lot.
Nothing says the fans were unaware; the clue is their loyalty through losing seasons.
Cheering loudly in the rain shows loyalty, not shameless boldness.
Fans who never stopped showing up were steady, not likely to fall or fail.

traps.why: Wavering means going back and forth, the opposite of steadfast.
The fast in steadfast means firm, not quick.
Stationary means not moving physically; steadfast means firm in loyalty.

syn2.tip: Picture a dog waiting at the station every single day. Steadfast describes someone who stays true and never gives up.

sc2.stem: Most of the kids quit the robotics club after their robot broke twice, but Lena remained _____, staying late every Friday until it finally worked.

traps.why: The other kids were discouraged; 'but' shows Lena was different.
Skill helps with robots, but the clue is that she kept coming back.
Bored people quit; Lena stayed late every Friday.

sc2.tip: 'Most of the kids quit,' 'but' Lena kept 'staying late every Friday.' The blank describes someone who refuses to give up.

decoys.why: Lena kept working until the robot worked, so she was not stuck or unmoving.
Staying late every Friday shows she was serious, not silly.
The robot finally worked, and the clue is about her sticking with it, not clumsiness.
The sentence contrasts her with kids who quit, so it is about loyalty, not playfulness.
The clue is that she did not quit, not that she sat around a lot.

meaning: prove that a statement or idea is wrong
example: Jamal used library data to refute his friend's claim about sharks.
hook: When you refute a rumor, you bring the proof that knocks it flat: here's why that's wrong.

traps.why: Confirm means to show something is true, the opposite of refute.
Refuse looks similar but means to say no to something.
Re- often means again, but refute does not mean say again.

syn1.tip: You refute a claim by bringing evidence against it. Debaters refute arguments by showing they're false.

sc1.stem: Ava insisted that goldfish remember things for only three seconds, but Malik was able to _____ her claim with a study showing goldfish recalled a feeding signal for months.

traps.why: Malik's study goes against Ava's claim, so it doesn't support it.
Malik didn't ignore the claim; he answered it with a study.
Malik wasn't admiring Ava's claim; his study showed it was false.

sc1.tip: Malik had 'a study showing goldfish recalled a feeding signal for months,' which shows Ava was wrong. Using evidence to prove a claim false fits the blank.

decoys.why: Malik's study showed goldfish remember for months, so it weakened Ava's claim.
Malik did not figure out her claim; he used a study to prove it wrong.
The claim belongs to Ava, so Malik cannot give it up; he disproved it.
Malik was on one side of the argument, not settling it between two others.
Ava already made the claim, so Malik did not draw it out of her.
Malik's study ended the claim by disproving it rather than making it last longer.

traps.why: Prove right is the opposite of refute.
Turn down means refuse, a word that only looks like refute.
Disagreeing is weaker; refuting means showing with proof that it's false.

syn2.tip: Scientists refute old ideas with new evidence. Refute means you don't just disagree; you prove the idea wrong.

sc2.stem: Because the scientist's new photos clearly showed ice on the planet's surface, other researchers could no longer _____ her claim that water existed there.

traps.why: The photos made her claim stronger, so others could support it more, not less.
Re- suggests again, but the photos wouldn't stop anyone from repeating her claim.
The photos made the claim clearer, so understanding it got easier.

sc2.tip: 'Because' the photos 'clearly showed ice,' her claim was proven. Once proof is that strong, no one can show it is wrong.

decoys.why: The photos support her claim, so the point is that others could no longer disprove it.
She already stated the claim, and the clue is about others no longer arguing against it.
Her claim was not hard to notice; the photos made it impossible to disprove.
She already made the claim, so others were not drawing it out of her.
The claim is hers, so other researchers could not give it up.

meaning: involving much sitting and little physical activity
example: Doctors warn that a sedentary lifestyle can weaken the heart.
hook: Sedentary comes from the Latin word for 'to sit'; picture a whole Saturday spent on the couch.

traps.why: Energetic means full of activity, the opposite of sedentary.
Lazy is an insult; sedentary just describes a lot of sitting.
Sedimentary describes rock formed in layers, not a sitting lifestyle.

syn1.tip: Doctors warn about a 'sedentary lifestyle,' meaning lots of sitting. Picture desk jobs and long hours of screen time.

sc1.stem: After a summer spent mostly playing video games on the sofa, Theo decided to change his _____ habits by joining the cross-country team.

traps.why: Sofa gaming is the opposite of athletic habits.
Theo wants to change his habits, so they weren't healthy ones.
Cross-country is competitive, but he's changing habits of sitting on the sofa.

sc1.tip: Theo spent the summer 'mostly playing video games on the sofa' and wants to change that by running. The blank describes habits with little movement.

decoys.why: Playing video games on the sofa is easy, not habits that take great effort.
He wants to change his sofa habits, so they are not careful, good habits.
Habits of sitting on the sofa are not decorated with fancy detail.
Nothing about playing video games on the sofa is mysterious or hard to understand.
The clue is sitting on the sofa all summer, not being sharp at noticing things.

traps.why: Always moving is the opposite of sedentary.
Sedentary means sitting a lot, not unable to move at all.
Too much sitting can affect health, but sedentary means sitting, not illness.

syn2.tip: A sedentary job keeps you in a chair all day. If you picture someone seated for hours, you have the meaning.

sc2.stem: Because her new job kept her at a desk for eight hours each day, Aunt Rosa's routine became _____, so she started taking evening walks.

traps.why: Sitting at a desk all day is the opposite of athletic.
Sedimentary describes layered rock, not a daily routine.
Nothing about eight desk hours is adventurous; the clue is the sitting.

sc2.tip: 'Because' her job 'kept her at a desk for eight hours,' her days involved lots of sitting. That's why she started walking.

decoys.why: The clue is sitting at a desk all day, not her routine being silly.
Eight hours at a desk is dull and still, not playful and fanciful.
A routine of sitting at a desk is not decorated with fancy detail.
Sitting at a desk all day is calm and still, not fierce or intense.
Nothing is mysterious here; she sits all day, so she needs walks for activity.

meaning: to help two sides settle a disagreement
example: The counselor mediated the argument between the two friends.
hook: Mediate comes from a Latin word for middle: a mediator stands between two arguing sides and helps them meet halfway.

traps.why: Provoke means to stir up a fight, the opposite of settling one.
Meditate means to think quietly; it only looks like mediate.
Arguing is what the two sides do, not what the helper does.

syn1.tip: Think of the word middle hiding in mediate. A mediator stands in the middle and helps both sides settle things fairly.

sc1.stem: When the two lab partners could not agree on how to split the work, they asked their teacher to _____ and help them find a fair solution.

traps.why: Meditate means to think quietly, which would not settle the partners' disagreement.
The partners were already arguing; they wanted the teacher to help end it.
Punishing is harsh and would not help them find a fair solution.

sc1.tip: The words 'help them find a fair solution' show the teacher acts as a fair helper in the middle of two sides.

decoys.why: The partners wanted a fair solution, and striking back would only make the fight worse.
The teacher was asked to help find a fair solution, not to stir up more trouble.
The teacher was supposed to help them agree, not block their progress.
They wanted the disagreement settled, not made to last longer.

traps.why: Starting a quarrel creates a fight; mediating helps end one.
Medi hints at middle, but mediate is not about measuring anything.
A mediator stays fair to both sides instead of taking one.

syn2.tip: In the news, a mediator is someone called in to help two groups settle a dispute, like a strike between workers and owners.

sc2.stem: Instead of taking sides when her twin brothers fought over the video game controller, Mom sat between them and tried to _____ until they agreed to share turns.

traps.why: Quarreling is what the brothers were doing, not how Mom helped.
Retreating means pulling away, but Mom stayed between them to help.
Medicate means to give medicine, which would not end a fight.

sc2.tip: 'Instead of taking sides' and 'sat between them' show Mom acted as a fair go-between who helped both brothers agree.

decoys.why: Mom was not taking sides; striking back would not get the twins to share turns.

meaning: lacking skill; clumsy
example: The inept magician dropped his cards in front of the audience.
hook: Inept is in- plus apt: someone not apt for the job, like a juggler who drops every single ball.

traps.why: An expert is highly skilled, the opposite of inept.
Inert means not moving; it only looks like inept.
Nervous people may fumble, but inept means lacking skill.

syn1.tip: Break it apart: in- means not, and -ept is like apt, meaning able or fit. Inept means not able.

sc1.stem: Unlike his sister, who could fix any bike, Jonah was so _____ with tools that he once loosened the wrong bolt and the wheel fell off.

traps.why: Handy means good with tools, but the wheel falling off shows Jonah was not.
Adept looks like inept but means skilled, which is the opposite here.
Eagerness is about wanting to help, not about lacking skill.

sc1.tip: 'Unlike his sister, who could fix any bike' sets up a contrast, and the wheel falling off shows Jonah lacked skill.

decoys.why: Jonah loosened the wrong bolt, so he was clumsy, not skilled.
Unlike his handy sister, Jonah made a mistake, so he was not clever with tools.
A careful worker would not loosen the wrong bolt and make the wheel fall off.
Loosening the wrong bolt shows Jonah was not sharp with tools at all.
Cumbersome describes heavy tools, but the sentence describes Jonah's lack of skill.

traps.why: Graceful means smooth and skillful, the opposite of inept.
A lazy person avoids work; an inept one tries but lacks skill.
In- here means not, not inside, so inept has nothing to do with internal.

syn2.tip: Picture an inept waiter dropping trays of food. Clumsy fits that picture. Inept is the opposite of adept, which means skilled.

sc2.stem: Because the new goalie was so _____, the other team scored six easy goals before halftime, and the coach finally sent in a backup.

traps.why: A talented goalie would block shots, not let in six easy goals.
Being famous has nothing to do with letting in easy goals.
Lucky is a positive word, but six easy goals point to a bad performance.

sc2.tip: 'Because' links the blank to the result: six easy goals and a backup coming in. That points to a goalie who lacked skill.

decoys.why: Six easy goals got past him, so the goalie was not skilled.
A flawless goalie would not let in six easy goals and get replaced.
Being fierce does not explain six easy goals; the goalie simply lacked skill.
A sharp goalie would stop easy shots, but this one let six in.
Loyalty has nothing to do with letting in six easy goals.

meaning: firmly determined
example: She was resolute in her decision to finish the race.
hook: Resolute is related to resolution: a New Year's resolution is a firm promise, and only a resolute person keeps it.

traps.why: Hesitant means unsure, the opposite of firmly determined.
Absolute rhymes with resolute but means complete or total.
Stubborn is a negative word; resolute praises firm determination.

syn1.tip: Think of a resolution, a firm decision you resolve to keep. A resolute person sticks to the decision no matter what.

sc1.stem: Even after failing her driving test twice, Isabel remained _____, signing up for a third attempt the very next morning and practicing every day until she passed.

traps.why: A discouraged person gives up, but Isabel signed up again right away.
Reckless means careless, but practicing every day shows careful determination.
Resentful looks a bit like resolute but means bitter, which the sentence doesn't show.

sc1.tip: 'Even after failing' sets up a surprise, and 'signing up for a third attempt the very next morning' shows she stayed firmly determined.

decoys.why: She failed twice, but signing up again and practicing daily shows determination, not clumsiness.
Isabel kept practicing until she passed, so she was not stuck or standing still.
Practicing every day for a test shows she took it seriously, not lightly.
She signed up right away and practiced daily, which is the opposite of inactive.
Her steady daily practice shows firm determination, not playful fancy.

traps.why: Being easily discouraged is the opposite of staying firmly determined.
Re- and solve seem to suggest solving again, but that is not the meaning.
Slightly interested is far too weak; resolute means strongly determined.

syn2.tip: Resolute sounds like resolve. When you resolve to do something, you are firm in purpose and do not back down.

sc2.stem: Mia was _____ about learning the hard piano piece; no matter how many wrong notes she hit, she refused to quit and kept practicing every single night.

traps.why: Doubtful means unsure, but refusing to quit shows she was firm.
Musical fits the piano topic but not the clue 'refused to quit.'
Interested is too weak; practicing every night without quitting shows firm determination.

sc2.tip: The part after the semicolon restates the blank: 'refused to quit and kept practicing every single night' describes someone firmly determined.

decoys.why: The piece was difficult, but the blank describes Mia, who refused to quit.
She hit wrong notes, but the clue is that she refused to quit.
Practicing every single night shows she was serious, not silly.
She kept hitting wrong notes, so she was not yet skilled; she was determined.
Refusing to quit and practicing nightly shows firm determination, not playfulness.

meaning: to stir up or provoke
example: The false rumor incited panic in the crowd.
hook: Picture one angry shout in a quiet crowd that incites a riot, stirring everyone up at once.

traps.why: Calm means to settle people down, the opposite of stirring them up.
Invite means to ask someone to come; it only looks like incite.
Encourage is positive, but incite usually means stirring up something bad.

syn1.tip: Incite usually goes with trouble: you incite a riot, a fight, or panic. Think of stirring up bad feelings.

sc1.stem: The prankster's fake fire alarm did more than annoy people; it helped _____ panic, sending shoppers rushing for the exits.

traps.why: Preventing panic would not send shoppers rushing for the exits.
Explaining panic would not cause people to run for the doors.
Insert means to put something in; it looks like incite but doesn't fit.

sc1.tip: Look at the effect: 'sending shoppers rushing for the exits.' The fake alarm must have stirred up panic.

decoys.why: Shoppers rushed for the exits, so the alarm caused panic rather than making it disappear.
The alarm sent people rushing out, so it started panic instead of wiping it out.
The alarm did not slow panic; it set off a rush for the exits.
Shoppers rushing out shows the panic grew, not that it was held back.
The exits come up, but the alarm stirred up panic, not blocked anything.

traps.why: Settling down is the opposite of stirring people up.
Cite means to quote, but incite means to stir up, not to quote.
Push gently is too mild; incite means stirring up strong feelings.

syn2.tip: Picture a speaker who incites a crowd: the people get stirred up, angry, and ready to act.

sc2.stem: Instead of calming the angry fans after the referee's bad call, the team's mascot waved his arms and booed, which only seemed to _____ them further.

traps.why: Soothe means to calm, but the booing made the fans angrier.
Entertain is pleasant, but booing made the angry fans even angrier.
Invite looks like incite, but inviting fans further makes no sense here.

sc2.tip: 'Instead of calming' signals the opposite of calming, and 'only seemed to... them further' shows the mascot stirred the fans up more.

decoys.why: The sentence says he did not calm the fans, so he did not reassure them.
Booing angry fans stirs them up; it does not attract them with something pleasant.
Waving and booing made the fans angrier, not slowed them down.
The mascot's booing worked them up more, which is the opposite of holding them back.
The mascot was not proving anyone wrong; he was making the fans angrier.

meaning: a sign of something to come
example: The sailors saw the dark clouds as a bad omen.
hook: The word ominous comes from omen: dark storm clouds are an omen, a sign of what is coming.

traps.why: A memory looks back at the past; an omen points ahead.
Amen ends a prayer; it sounds like omen but means something else.
An omen may warn of a disaster, but it is not the disaster itself.

syn1.tip: The word ominous grows from omen. Ominous clouds are a sign that a storm is on the way.

sc1.stem: Ancient sailors believed that a seagull landing on the ship's mast was a lucky _____ that meant calm seas lay ahead.

traps.why: Storms are a sailing topic, but a storm does not predict calm seas.
An accident just happens; the seagull was read as predicting calm seas.
A rescue saves people; it does not tell what lies ahead.

sc1.tip: The phrase 'meant calm seas lay ahead' shows the seagull was read as a sign of what would happen next.

decoys.why: The sailors believed in the sign, so they would not call it a mistaken belief.
The seagull meant calm seas lay ahead, so it was a sign, not a show of respect.
The seagull did not give help; it was a sign of what was coming.
A seagull that predicts calm seas is a sign, not a talented young person.
A bird landing is not a plan; the sailors saw it as a sign of the future.

traps.why: An omen looks ahead, not back at the past.
A lucky charm is meant to bring luck; an omen only signals what's coming.
Any message is too general; an omen is a sign about the future.

syn2.tip: People read omens to guess what will happen next, so look for a choice about the future.

sc2.stem: Grandpa laughed when Lucy called the broken mirror a bad _____; he said shattered glass could not predict anything, so she should just sweep it up.

traps.why: A memory looks back, but Grandpa talks about predicting what comes next.
Amen sounds like omen but is a word that ends a prayer.
A lesson teaches from the past; the clue is about predicting the future.

sc2.tip: Grandpa answers that glass 'could not predict anything,' so Lucy must have called the mirror a sign of the future.

decoys.why: Grandpa thinks it is a mistaken belief, but Lucy called the mirror a sign of bad luck.
Grandpa says glass cannot predict anything, so Lucy called it a sign, not a foolish act.
Grandpa talks about predicting the future, not about a complaint.
The clue is that glass cannot predict anything, so Lucy saw it as a sign.
A broken mirror shows no respect; Lucy thought it predicted bad things.

meaning: give up or let go of something
example: The tired captain finally relinquished control of the ship to his first mate.
hook: To relinquish is to let go: picture a kid finally handing the TV remote over to a younger sibling.

traps.why: Holding onto something is the opposite of letting it go.
Re- often means again, but relinquish means give up, not repeat.
Taking turns shares something; relinquish means handing it over completely.

syn1.tip: When you relinquish a prize, a title, or control, you let it go and someone else takes it.

sc1.stem: After leading the debate club for three years, Hannah agreed to _____ her role as president so that a younger member could gain experience.

traps.why: Keeping the role would not let a younger member gain experience.
Performing her role would not open it up for a younger member.
Re- can mean again, but repeating her role would not help anyone else lead.

sc1.tip: 'So that a younger member could gain experience' gives the reason: Hannah had to let go of the job.

decoys.why: Hannah steps down so a younger member can lead, so she is not making her role last longer.
She is choosing to step aside, not putting her role at risk.
The president role still exists for the younger member, so it is not wiped out.

traps.why: Seize means to grab hold of, the opposite of giving up.
Relish means to enjoy; it looks like relinquish but means something else.
Losing happens by accident; relinquishing means choosing to give something up.

syn2.tip: Picture a king who must relinquish his crown: he surrenders it and lets someone else rule.

sc2.stem: Although the puppy whined and tugged, Leo refused to _____ his grip on the leash until they had safely crossed the busy street.

traps.why: Tightening is the opposite of letting go, and refusing to tighten makes no sense.
Relish looks like relinquish but means to enjoy, which doesn't fit.
Improving his grip is about the leash, but refusing to improve it makes no sense.

sc2.tip: 'Refused' plus 'until they had safely crossed' tells you Leo would not let go of the leash on the busy street.

decoys.why: Leo holds on until they cross, so refusing to make his grip last longer makes no sense.
The sentence is about letting go of the leash, not noticing his grip.
A grip on a leash is not a feeling or memory brought to mind.
A grip is not something you fill up again, and Leo is deciding whether to let go.

meaning: to make a doubt, fear, or belief disappear
example: The bright hallway light dispelled her fear of the dark.
hook: Dis- means apart or away: to dispel a fear is to drive it away, like sunlight burning off morning fog.

traps.why: Strengthen makes a fear bigger; dispel makes it disappear.
Dispel has spell inside, but it is not about spelling words.
Doubts are what get dispelled, not the act of dispelling them.

syn1.tip: You often hear 'dispel a myth' or 'dispel fears.' Both mean driving something away until it is gone.

sc1.stem: To _____ the rumor that the cafeteria served worm burgers, the cook invited students into the kitchen to watch her prepare lunch.

traps.why: Spreading the rumor is the opposite of what showing the kitchen would do.
Dispense means to hand out; it looks like dispel but doesn't fit.
Enjoying a rumor would not make the cook prove it false.

sc1.tip: The cook let students 'watch her prepare lunch' to prove the rumor false, so she wanted the rumor to go away.

decoys.why: Showing students the real cooking would calm the rumor, not stir it up.
The cook wants the rumor gone, not to make it last longer.
The cook is ending the rumor, not figuring it out from clues.
Inviting students in removes the rumor rather than bringing it to mind.

traps.why: Stir up makes feelings grow, the opposite of making them vanish.
Dispel is not about magic spells; it means to drive something away.
Dispel means making something vanish completely, not just moving it a bit.

syn2.tip: Dis- means apart or away. To dispel something is to drive it away so it no longer exists.

sc2.stem: Though Ava felt nervous about the new school, her friendly locker neighbor helped _____ her worries by inviting her to sit together at lunch.

traps.why: A friendly invitation would shrink her worries, not increase them.
Display means to show off, not to make something disappear.
Noticing her worries would not make them go away.

sc2.tip: 'Though' and 'nervous' set up a change, and a 'friendly' lunch invitation is a kind act that would make worries disappear.

decoys.why: A friendly invitation would make Ava's worries go away, not last longer.
The neighbor was kind, so she ended Ava's worries instead of bringing them up.
The neighbor's kindness made the worries disappear, not drew them out.
Inviting Ava to lunch would not fill her worries up again.

meaning: to draw out a response or reaction
example: The comedian's joke elicited loud laughter from the audience.
hook: Elicit starts with e-, meaning out: a good joke elicits laughter, drawing it right out of the audience.

traps.why: Holding back keeps a reaction in, the opposite of drawing it out.
Illicit, which sounds like elicit, means illegal; elicit means draw out.
Answering is the response itself; elicit means drawing that response out.

syn1.tip: The e- at the start means out. A question that elicits answers draws them out of people.

sc1.stem: The teacher asked open-ended questions to _____ thoughtful answers from even her quietest students, who rarely spoke in class.

traps.why: Silencing answers is the opposite of what open-ended questions are for.
Grading comes later; the questions were meant to get answers in the first place.
Punishing thoughtful answers is harsh and makes no sense here.

sc1.tip: Her students 'rarely spoke in class,' so the open-ended questions were meant to draw answers out of them.

decoys.why: The teacher wants quiet students to speak, so she is not crushing their answers.
Open-ended questions are meant to bring out answers, not block them.
The teacher wants to hear answers, not prove them wrong.
The teacher is trying to get answers from shy students, not block them.

traps.why: Keeping something in is the opposite of bringing a reaction out.
Rip out is far too forceful; elicit gently draws a response.
Saying something aloud is speaking, not drawing a reaction out of someone.

syn2.tip: You often hear 'elicit a response' or 'elicit a smile.' In each, something is brought out of a person.

sc2.stem: No matter how many silly faces Dad made, he could not _____ even a tiny smile from the grumpy baby, who kept frowning.

traps.why: Removing a smile is the opposite; Dad wanted to draw one out.
Elect means to choose by voting; it looks like elicit but doesn't fit.
Smiles are seen, not heard, and Dad wanted to bring one out.

sc2.tip: 'No matter how many silly faces' shows Dad tried hard, yet the baby 'kept frowning,' so he failed to draw out a smile.

decoys.why: Dad was trying to get a smile out of the baby, not figure one out from clues.
Dad made silly faces to draw out a smile, not to stop one.
Dad wanted a smile to appear, not to disappear.

meaning: to put at risk
example: Skipping practice could jeopardize your spot on the team.
hook: Jeopardy means danger, so to jeopardize something is to put it in danger, like texting while riding your bike.

traps.why: Protect means to keep safe, the opposite of putting at risk.
Destroy is too strong; jeopardize means put at risk, not ruin completely.
Jeopardy is also a quiz show, but jeopardize means put in danger.

syn1.tip: Inside jeopardize is jeopardy, which means danger. To jeopardize something is to put it in danger.

sc1.stem: Coach Rivera warned that missing too many practices could _____ Dante's chance of starting in the championship game.

traps.why: Missing practice would hurt his chance, not improve it.
Celebrating is positive, but the coach is giving a warning.
Discussing his chance would not be a result of missing practice.

sc1.tip: Coach 'warned,' and 'missing too many practices' is a bad habit, so the result must be putting Dante's chance at risk.

decoys.why: Missing practices is a warning sign, so it would not fill up Dante's chance.
The coach is warning about a danger, not something that makes Dante's chance last longer.
Missing practice does not reveal a secret, it puts Dante's spot at risk.
A chance is not a statement that can be proved wrong.

traps.why: Keeping something safe is the opposite of putting it at risk.
Ruin forever is too strong; jeopardize means something could be lost.
Warning about danger helps; jeopardizing causes the danger.

syn2.tip: You often hear 'jeopardize your chances.' It means doing something that could cost you, putting those chances at risk.

sc2.stem: Smart hikers stay on marked trails, but a few careless ones wander off and _____ their own safety by getting lost in the woods.

traps.why: Getting lost does not protect safety; it puts it at risk.
Enjoying safety sounds nice, but getting lost is a danger.
Exploring fits hiking, but you explore woods, not your own safety.

sc2.tip: 'Smart hikers' contrast with 'careless ones,' and 'getting lost in the woods' shows their safety is being put at risk.

decoys.why: Getting lost in the woods hurts their safety, so it does not fill it back up.
Careless hikers who get lost are risking their safety, not making it last longer.
The hikers are not revealing secrets, they are putting themselves at risk.
Getting lost does not mean noticing safety, it means endangering it.

meaning: playful and fanciful in an odd way
example: The whimsical garden had gnomes riding snails.
hook: A whim is a sudden silly idea; whimsical things feel like whims come to life, like a teapot dancing on legs.

traps.why: Serious is the opposite of playful and fanciful.
Wistful means sadly longing; it only looks a bit like whimsical.
Childish is negative; whimsical is a fond word for odd, playful fun.

syn1.tip: Whimsical comes from whim, a sudden silly idea. Whimsical things are playful and full of fancy.

sc1.stem: The children's book was full of _____ drawings, like pigs with butterfly wings and teapots that danced on tiny legs.

traps.why: Pigs with butterfly wings are the opposite of realistic.
Dancing teapots are fun, not frightening.
Wishful means hoping; it looks a bit like whimsical but doesn't fit.

sc1.tip: The examples after 'like' tell you: 'pigs with butterfly wings' and 'teapots that danced' are playful, fanciful ideas.

decoys.why: Pigs with butterfly wings are playful and odd, not covered in fancy detail.
Dancing teapots are silly and fanciful, not mysterious or hard to understand.
Pigs with butterfly wings and dancing teapots sound playful, not fierce.

traps.why: Practical means sensible and useful, the opposite of fanciful.
Spooky is odd in a scary way; whimsical is odd in a fun way.
A whim comes suddenly, but whimsical means playfully odd, not sudden.

syn2.tip: Picture a Dr. Seuss book: odd, imaginative, and fun. That fanciful feeling is what whimsical describes.

sc2.stem: Grandma's living room was plain and serious, but her backyard was totally _____, with flamingo statues wearing sunglasses and a birdbath shaped like a giant teacup.

traps.why: Formal matches the living room, but 'but' signals the backyard is different.
Messy is negative; flamingos in sunglasses show playful fun, not disorder.
Wistful means sadly longing; it looks like whimsical but fits nothing here.

sc2.tip: 'But' signals a contrast with 'plain and serious,' and flamingos in sunglasses show the backyard was playful and fanciful.

decoys.why: The backyard is the opposite of serious, and flamingos in sunglasses are playful, not loyal.
A teacup birdbath is fun and odd, not mysterious or hard to understand.
The sentence describes playful decorations, not a yard where people mostly sit.
The but contrasts the backyard with the serious room, so it should sound playful.

meaning: sharp at noticing and understanding things
example: The astute shopper noticed that the price was wrong.
hook: An astute detective spots the one crumb on the carpet that everyone else walked right past.

traps.why: Foolish is the opposite of astute.
Astonished starts like astute but means amazed, not sharp-minded.
Astute people may be admired, but famous means well known.

syn1.tip: Think of an "astute observer," someone who notices what others miss. Swap in "sharp" and the phrase still works.

sc1.stem: An _____ reader, Kwame noticed a tiny clue on page ten that revealed the mystery's ending long before any of his classmates figured it out.

traps.why: An inattentive reader would miss a tiny clue, not spot it.
Obedient is about following rules, not noticing clues.
An uninterested reader would not catch a clue before everyone else.

sc1.tip: The clue is "noticed a tiny clue" "long before any of his classmates." Only a sharp, observant reader catches that.

decoys.why: Kwame spotted a tiny clue before anyone else, so he was skilled, not clumsy.
The sentence is about noticing clues, not about being wild or hard to control.
Arduous describes a hard task, not a reader who notices a tiny clue.
Ornate describes fancy decoration, not a reader who catches clues early.

traps.why: Slow to notice is the opposite of astute.
Astute looks like astro, meaning star, but it has nothing to do with stars.
Hard workers may do well, but astute is about catching on fast.

syn2.tip: Astute describes the mind. If someone catches on fast and isn't easily fooled, they're astute.

sc2.stem: Most of the audience fell for the magician's fake move, but _____ Priya kept her eyes on his other hand and spotted where the coin really went.

traps.why: Gullible means easily fooled, but Priya was the one who wasn't fooled.
Astonished looks like astute but means amazed; Priya saw through the trick.
Timid means shy, which says nothing about spotting the coin.

sc2.tip: "Most... fell for" the trick, "but" Priya "spotted" the coin. The contrast calls for a word meaning sharp and not easily fooled.

decoys.why: Priya spotted where the coin went, so she was not confused at all.
Unlike the fooled audience, Priya was skilled at watching, not clumsy.
Nothing in the sentence says Priya was silly; it says she noticed the trick.
The clue is that she saw through the fake move, not that she was playful.
Sitting a lot has nothing to do with catching the magician's trick.
The sentence shows Priya noticing carefully, not showing off.

meaning: strike back after being harmed or insulted
example: When his brother hid his shoes, Leo retaliated by hiding his brother's phone.
hook: Re- means back: to retaliate is to pay someone back for a wrong, like a snowball for a snowball.

traps.why: Letting go of a wrong is the opposite of striking back.
That is retail, which looks like retaliate but means selling.
Running away is another reaction to harm, but it isn't hitting back.

syn1.tip: Re- often means back. When someone retaliates, they give back what they got, usually a hit or an insult.

sc1.stem: After the other team's fans booed during her free throws, Coach Kim urged her players not to _____ but to answer with good sportsmanship instead.

traps.why: Forgiving goes with good sportsmanship, so "not... but" wouldn't make sense.
Smiling is friendly, but the blank must be the opposite of sportsmanship.
Retreat starts like retaliate but means pull back, not pay back.

sc1.tip: Look at "not to _____ but to answer with good sportsmanship." The blank is the opposite of good sportsmanship: paying the booing fans back.

decoys.why: The coach wants players to avoid striking back, not to settle a disagreement.
Rising and falling unevenly makes no sense as a reaction to being booed.

traps.why: Making peace is the opposite of getting even.
Retaliating answers trouble; it doesn't start it.
Complaining is much weaker than actually paying someone back.

syn2.tip: Think of revenge and payback. Retaliate means answering a harm with a harm of your own.

sc2.stem: Because Maya had knocked over his sandcastle, Jonah wanted to _____ by kicking hers down, but their dad stepped in first.

traps.why: Kicking her castle down is not cooperating; it's paying her back.
Jonah was the one harmed, and kicking hers down is no apology.
Relate looks a bit like retaliate but means connect, not strike back.

sc2.tip: The cause is "Maya had knocked over his sandcastle," and the effect is "kicking hers down." That is paying her back.

decoys.why: Kicking her sandcastle down is striking back, the opposite of settling the fight.
You cannot rise and fall by kicking down a sandcastle; Jonah wanted revenge.

meaning: bold and shameless
example: The brazen squirrel snatched a sandwich right out of my hand.
hook: A brazen seagull doesn't sneak your fries; it marches up, stares you down, and takes them in plain sight.

traps.why: Bashful means shy, the opposite of brazen.
Brave is praise; brazen is bold in a bad, shameless way.
Blazing sounds a bit like brazen but means burning brightly.

syn1.tip: Brazen has a bad feeling: doing wrong openly, with no embarrassment. Think of "a brazen lie" told right to your face.

sc1.stem: In a _____ move that shocked the whole picnic, the seagull strutted across the table and grabbed a hot dog right out of Ethan's hand.

traps.why: A timid bird wouldn't strut across the table and grab food.
Graceful is a compliment, but the move shocked everyone.
Sneaky means hidden, but this seagull stole right in front of everyone.

sc1.tip: The seagull "strutted across the table" and took food "right out of Ethan's hand," in front of everyone. That is shamelessly bold.

decoys.why: The seagull strutted across the table, which is not sitting still at all.
Stealing a hot dog from a hand is shameless, not careful and correct.
Nothing here is about loyalty; the seagull boldly stole food.
Cumbersome means heavy and hard to carry, not a bold, shocking theft.
Ornate means fancy decoration, which does not describe grabbing a hot dog.

traps.why: Shy and polite is the opposite of brazen.
Brave and noble is praise; brazen boldness is something to be ashamed of.
Brazen is much stronger than a little rudeness.

syn2.tip: Picture a "brazen thief" robbing a shop in daylight. Brazen means bold in a way that should embarrass you but doesn't.

sc2.stem: Most kids slip notes when the teacher looks away, but Marcus was _____, passing his note across the room while she stared right at him.

traps.why: A cautious kid would wait for the teacher to look away.
