Polite is positive, but passing notes under her gaze is rude.
Sneaky kids hide; Marcus did it right in front of her.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts kids who wait with Marcus, who passes notes "while she stared right at him." That is bold and shameless.

decoys.why: The note is mentioned, but the clue is Marcus passing it while she watched.
Passing a note while the teacher stares is shameless, not careful about rules.
Breaking the rule right in front of the teacher is far from flawless.
The sentence is about how bold Marcus was, not how much he sat.
Cumbersome describes heavy objects, not a boy openly passing a note.

meaning: a person who gives money or help
example: A generous benefactor paid for the new town library.
hook: Bene means good and factor means doer, so a benefactor is a good doer who gives money or help.

traps.why: A borrower takes money; a benefactor gives it.
Bankers handle money, but they don't give it away to help.
A builder makes the library; a benefactor pays for it.

syn1.tip: Bene- means good, as in benefit. A benefactor does good for others, usually by giving money.

sc1.stem: Thanks to an unnamed _____ who gave a million dollars, the small town was able to build a new science center for its children.

traps.why: You wouldn't thank an enemy for giving the town a million dollars.
An applicant asks for money rather than giving it away.
Intruder is a negative word, but this person helped the town.

sc1.tip: The clue is "who gave a million dollars" so the town could build something for children. A person who gives money to help is a benefactor.

decoys.why: The person gave a million dollars; that is a giver, not a talented child.
The sentence praises a generous giver, not someone who breaks their own rules.
A tribute is a thing, but the blank is a person who gave money.
An omen is a sign, not a person who gave a million dollars.

traps.why: A greedy miser hoards money, the opposite of a benefactor.
Many rich people never give; a benefactor is one who does.
A fan cheers you on but doesn't give money or help.

syn2.tip: Think of benefit: a benefactor's help brings benefits to someone else. It's the giver, not the receiver.

sc2.stem: Our school had no money for the field trip, but a _____ from the neighborhood paid for every bus seat, so all forty kids could go.

traps.why: A thief takes money; this person paid for the trip.
A beggar asks for money instead of giving it.
A critic finds fault; this person generously helped.

sc2.tip: "Had no money... but" someone "paid for every bus seat." The contrast tells you the blank is a person who gives money to help.

decoys.why: Paying for every bus seat makes this person a giver, not a talented child.
The sentence thanks a generous helper, not someone who breaks their own rules.
A petition is a written request, and it cannot pay for bus seats.
A tribute cannot pay for buses; you need a person who gives money.
A complaint does not pay for a field trip; a generous giver does.

meaning: to block a path or view
example: A fallen tree obstructed the road.
hook: Obstruct contains struct, meaning build: picture someone building a wall right across your path.

traps.why: Clearing a path is the opposite of obstructing it.
Observe starts like obstruct but means watch.
Destroy is far stronger; obstructing just gets in the way.

syn1.tip: Think of an obstruction in a pipe or a player obstructing the goal. Something in the way blocks it.

sc1.stem: Fans were asked not to stand in the aisles, because they would _____ the path of anyone trying to reach the exits.

traps.why: Clearing the path would help people reach the exits.
Observe looks like obstruct but means watch, which wouldn't be a danger.
Following a path isn't a reason to ban standing in aisles.

sc1.tip: "Because" gives the reason fans can't stand in aisles. People in an aisle would block anyone heading for the exits.

decoys.why: People standing in aisles would block the path, not make it stronger.
The worry is blocking the way to exits, not noticing the path.
You cannot fill up a path again; the fans would block it.
Revealing a secret has nothing to do with standing in an aisle.
Fans standing in aisles get in the way; they do not give up the path.

traps.why: Clearing the path is the opposite of obstructing it.
Pointing the way helps people move; obstructing stops them.
Struct means build, but obstruct means block, not build something.

syn2.tip: An obstacle and an obstruction both sit in your path. To obstruct is to be the thing that stands in the way.

sc2.stem: Instead of helping the firefighters reach the house, the crowd of curious neighbors only managed to _____ their trucks on the narrow street.

traps.why: Guiding the trucks would be helping, but the sentence says instead of helping.
Repairing is helpful, but the crowd did the opposite of help.
Construct shares struct but means build, which makes no sense here.

sc2.tip: "Instead of helping" sets up a contrast. The neighbors did the opposite of helping the trucks reach the house: they blocked them.

decoys.why: The crowd failed to help, so they blocked the trucks rather than refilling them.
The sentence says they did not help, so they did not strengthen the trucks.
The narrow street clue shows the crowd blocked the trucks, not forced them out.
The crowd got in the way of the trucks; they did not attract them.
Revealing secrets makes no sense with trucks stuck on a narrow street.

meaning: good at finding clever ways to solve problems
example: The resourceful camper made a cup from birch bark.
hook: A resourceful kid is full of resources: hand them tape, string, and a cereal box, and they'll build whatever you need.

traps.why: Helpless is the opposite of resourceful.
Resources can mean money, but resourceful means clever, not rich.
Hard workers try hard; resourceful people find clever fixes.

syn1.tip: Think of a resourceful camper making a cup from bark. The word means full of clever ideas, not full of supplies.

sc1.stem: When the tent pole snapped during the storm, the _____ hikers used a sturdy branch and some shoelaces to build a replacement in minutes.

traps.why: Helpless hikers couldn't build a new pole in minutes.
A storm might frighten them, but fear doesn't explain the clever fix.
Resentful looks like resourceful but means bitter.

sc1.tip: The hikers "used a sturdy branch and some shoelaces" to fix things "in minutes." Making do with what's at hand shows a resourceful mind.

decoys.why: The hikers cleverly built a replacement in minutes, and inept means clumsy and unskilled.
Confused hikers would not quickly solve the problem with a branch and shoelaces.
These are hikers solving a problem, so being inactive and sitting a lot has nothing to do with it.
The hikers handled a real problem seriously, so silly and unserious does not fit.
Nothing here is about ignoring feelings; the sentence praises a clever fix.
Nobody is showing off; the sentence is about inventing a quick replacement.

traps.why: Being lost without help is the opposite of resourceful.
Resource can mean supplies, but resourceful is about cleverness.
Following rules is a different strength from inventing fixes.

syn2.tip: Ask what a resourceful person does when a plan breaks. They find a clever fix with whatever is around.

sc2.stem: Most of the team gave up when the robot's wheel fell off, but _____ Ana fixed it with a bottle cap and a rubber band.

traps.why: Discouraged fits the team that gave up, not Ana.
Respectful looks like resourceful but means polite.
Resources can mean money, but Ana used a bottle cap, not cash.

sc2.tip: "Most of the team gave up... but" Ana didn't. She made a clever fix from a bottle cap, so she was resourceful.

decoys.why: Ana fixed the robot with a bottle cap, so she was skilled, not clumsy.
Ana found a clever fix, so she was not confused or puzzled.
The sentence is about solving a problem, not about sitting around a lot.
Ana took the problem seriously and fixed it, so silly does not fit.
Nothing says Ana showed off; the clue is her clever use of a bottle cap.
The sentence is about a clever repair, not about ignoring others' feelings.

meaning: hard to control; wild
example: The unruly crowd pushed against the gates.
hook: Unruly breaks into un and ruly: not following rules, like a puppy tearing around ignoring every command.

traps.why: Orderly is the opposite of unruly.
Unlucky looks like unruly but means having bad luck.
Unruly crowds may be angry, but unruly means out of control.

syn1.tip: Split it: un- plus rule. An unruly crowd or class won't follow rules and is hard to control.

sc1.stem: The substitute could not calm the _____ class, whose students kept leaving their seats, throwing paper airplanes, and shouting over one another.

traps.why: Obedient students wouldn't throw paper airplanes and shout.
Tired students wouldn't be leaving seats and shouting.
Polite is positive, but this class behaved badly.

sc1.tip: The examples tell you: students "leaving their seats, throwing paper airplanes, and shouting." A class acting like that is out of control.

decoys.why: The students kept leaving their seats, which is the opposite of sitting still.
Throwing airplanes and shouting shows wild behavior, not sharp understanding.
The students were wild and loud, not confused.
Nothing shows the class was determined; they were simply out of control.
Ornate describes fancy decorations, not a class full of shouting students.
The students' behavior was not mysterious; it was openly wild.

traps.why: Easy to manage is the opposite of unruly.
Unruly isn't about lacking a king or measuring stick.
Unruly is much stronger than being a little loud.

syn2.tip: Think of "unruly hair" that won't lie flat. Whatever is unruly refuses to be controlled.

sc2.stem: At home, our puppy Biscuit sits calmly for treats, but at the dog park he becomes so _____ that he ignores every command and drags me across the grass.

traps.why: Gentle fits Biscuit at home, not the dog dragging you.
Unlucky looks like unruly but has nothing to do with ignoring commands.
A sleepy puppy wouldn't drag you across the grass.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Biscuit sitting "calmly" at home with the park, where he "ignores every command." Something that ignores commands is unruly.

decoys.why: Biscuit drags you across the grass, so he is not sitting around.
He ignores every command, so he is not loyal and steady at the park.
Biscuit is wild and ignoring commands, not confused.
Ornate means fancy decoration, which has nothing to do with a dog's behavior.
Nothing about Biscuit is mysterious; he is just hard to control.
The sentence is about ignoring commands, not cleverly solving problems.

meaning: not caring about others' feelings
example: His callous joke about her lost dog made her cry.
hook: A callus is hard skin; a callous person has a heart like that, too tough to feel others' pain.

traps.why: Caring is the opposite of callous.
Jealous rhymes with callous but means wanting what others have.
Grumpy is just a bad mood; callous means not caring about others' pain.

syn1.tip: Feel the hard callus on a hand: callous people have toughened feelings. A callous remark shows no care for someone's hurt.

sc1.stem: While everyone else rushed to help the boy who had tripped, Grant just laughed and kept walking, a _____ reaction that upset his classmates.

traps.why: Laughing and walking away is not sympathetic.
Cheerful sounds nice, but his laughing upset everyone.
Careful looks a bit like callous but means taking care to avoid mistakes.

sc1.tip: "While everyone else rushed to help," Grant "laughed and kept walking." That contrast shows he did not care about the boy's pain.

decoys.why: Grant laughed at the boy who fell, which shows no caring, not clever problem solving.
Grant walked away laughing, so he was not loyal or supportive.
Grant laughed and kept walking, so he was not confused.
Sedentary means sitting a lot, which does not describe a reaction to someone falling.
Grant laughed openly, so his reaction was uncaring, not sneaky.
Ornate describes fancy decorations, not how someone reacts to a classmate getting hurt.

traps.why: Sympathetic means feeling for others, the opposite of callous.
Cautious sounds a bit like callous but means careful.
Bossy people give orders; callous people ignore others' feelings.

syn2.tip: Someone callous isn't moved by others' pain. Think of "a callous shrug" when a friend is crying.

sc2.stem: Dylan made a _____ comment about Sam's broken arm; he plainly didn't care that Sam was in pain and missing the whole soccer season.

traps.why: A kind comment would come from someone who cared.
Careful looks a bit like callous but means taking care.
Polite is positive, but Dylan plainly didn't care about Sam.

sc2.tip: The part after the semicolon restates the blank: he "didn't care that Sam was in pain." A comment like that is callous.

decoys.why: Dylan plainly didn't care, and fervent means showing strong, sincere feeling.
The comment showed no caring about Sam's pain, not cleverness.
The clue is that Dylan didn't care, not that he was confused.
A loyal friend would care about Sam's pain, but Dylan did not.
Sedentary means inactive, which cannot describe a comment that ignores someone's pain.

meaning: showing off how important you think you are
example: The pompous mayor gave a speech mostly about himself.
hook: Pompous means full of pomp, like a peacock in a crown giving speeches about how great he is.

traps.why: Humble is the opposite of pompous.
Confident is praise; pompous is a put-down for showing off.
Popular starts like pompous but means well liked.

syn1.tip: The -ous ending means full of, and pomp is grand, showy display. A pompous person is full of showy importance.

sc1.stem: The _____ speaker used long, fancy words to impress the audience and spent most of his talk describing his own awards.

traps.why: A modest speaker wouldn't spend his talk on his own awards.
Gentle is a compliment, but this speaker was showing off.
A timid speaker wouldn't try to impress with fancy words and awards.

sc1.tip: Look at "to impress the audience" and "describing his own awards." Bragging and showing off point to self-importance.

decoys.why: Ornate describes fancy decorations; the speaker's bragging about his awards shows he is showing off.
He talked about himself to impress people, not to ask questions or learn.
Nothing says the speaker was confused; he was busy showing off.
The clue is bragging about his awards, not sitting around a lot.
Using fancy words to impress and describing awards is showing off, not clever problem solving.

traps.why: Modest and quiet is the opposite of pompous.
Being loud and happy isn't the same as showing off your importance.
Pompous is much stronger than feeling a little proud.

syn2.tip: Picture a speaker who loves the sound of his own voice and his own name. That showy self-praise is what pompous means.

sc2.stem: Although she had won three state championships, Coach Rivera was never _____; she praised her players and rarely mentioned her own trophies.

traps.why: She was modest, so "never modest" contradicts the rest of the sentence.
She won three championships, so "never successful" makes no sense.
Praising players is friendly, so "never friendly" contradicts the clue.

sc2.tip: "Although" she won so much, she was "never" this; she "rarely mentioned her own trophies." The blank means showing off your importance.

decoys.why: The clue is that she rarely mentioned her trophies, which is about not bragging.
Praising players and not mentioning trophies is about modesty, not sharpness.
A three-time champion coach being never determined makes no sense here.
Saying a champion never refused to give up does not match the clue about trophies.
Praising her players shows she is loyal, so saying never steadfast contradicts the sentence.
The sentence is about not bragging about trophies, not about bravery.

meaning: completely confused; puzzled
example: The perplexed tourist stared at the subway map.
hook: Picture someone staring at a maze map, turning it upside down, then sideways: that's a perplexed face.

traps.why: Certain is the opposite of perplexed.
Perplexed shares plex with complex, but it describes a confused person.
Confusion can be annoying, but annoyed means irritated, not puzzled.

syn1.tip: Think of a perplexed look: eyebrows scrunched, head tilted. Someone perplexed can't figure something out.

sc1.stem: The math problem seemed to have no solution, and even the teacher looked _____ as she scratched her head and reread the question three times.

traps.why: A confident teacher wouldn't reread the question three times.
Pleased is happy, but head-scratching shows she was stuck.
Bored people don't keep rereading a problem.

sc1.tip: The teacher "scratched her head and reread the question three times." Those actions show she was confused.

decoys.why: She scratched her head and reread the question, so she was puzzled, not sharp.
Scratching her head shows confusion, not showing off.
Nothing here is about ignoring feelings; the problem seemed to have no solution.
Rereading a hard problem three times shows confusion, not wanting revenge.
She was stuck on a hard problem, which is puzzled, not playful.
Ornate describes fancy decoration, not how a confused teacher looks.

traps.why: Confident is the opposite of perplexed.
Bored means uninterested, not unable to understand.
A mistaken person thinks they know; a perplexed person knows they don't.

syn2.tip: When a problem leaves you scratching your head with no idea what to do next, you're perplexed.

sc2.stem: Dad usually fixes anything in minutes, but the new TV remote, with its forty tiny buttons, left him _____ for the whole evening.

traps.why: Confident fits Dad's usual self, but "but" signals the remote stumped him.
Delighted is happy, but forty tiny buttons stumped him.
Proud fits fixing things fast, not being stuck all evening.

sc2.tip: "But" signals a change: Dad usually fixes things fast, yet "forty tiny buttons" stumped him. The blank means puzzled.

decoys.why: The forty tiny buttons left Dad puzzled, so he was not sharp at understanding them.
Dad is usually handy, but the word but tells you the remote stumped him.
Struggling with a remote all evening shows confusion, not showing off.
Nothing here is about ignoring others' feelings; Dad just couldn't figure out the remote.
A confusing remote leaves you puzzled, not wanting revenge.
Ornate describes fancy decoration, which does not describe how Dad felt.

meaning: fearless and adventurous
example: The intrepid explorer crossed the frozen sea alone.
hook: Intrepid holds trepid, as in trepidation, meaning fear; in- means not, so intrepid means not afraid.

traps.why: Timid means easily scared, the opposite of intrepid.
Reckless is careless risk taking; intrepid praises real courage.
Trepid does suggest trembling, but in- flips it to mean not afraid.

syn1.tip: Think of trepidation, which means fear. The in- at the front means not, so intrepid means without fear.

sc1.stem: Though most sailors refused to go near the icy, uncharted waters, the _____ captain steered her small ship straight toward them without hesitation.

traps.why: A timid captain would stay away like the other sailors.
The sentence says she steered toward danger without hesitation.
Sailors can get seasick, but nothing here is about feeling ill.

sc1.tip: "Though most sailors refused" sets up a contrast. She did the opposite of them, heading in "without hesitation," so she must be fearless.

decoys.why: She steered straight in without hesitation, so she was not confused or puzzled.
The clue is her courage near icy waters, not a lack of skill.
Sitting still has nothing to do with boldly sailing where others refused to go.
Nothing in the sentence shows her showing off; it shows she was fearless.
Cumbersome describes heavy objects, not a captain who boldly heads into danger.
A journey can be arduous, but a person cannot; the clue is her bravery.

traps.why: Cowardly means lacking courage, the opposite of intrepid.
Explorers may be fit, but intrepid is about courage, not muscles.
Tepid means lukewarm; it only looks like the end of intrepid.

syn2.tip: Picture the intrepid explorer crossing a frozen sea alone. What word describes someone who dares to do that?

sc2.stem: Nothing seemed to scare the _____ young diver; she leaped from the highest platform at the pool and swam into the deep end without a second thought.

traps.why: An anxious diver would be scared, but nothing scared her.
A cautious diver thinks twice; she acted without a second thought.
Divers can be graceful, but the clue is that nothing scared her.

sc2.tip: The first part, "Nothing seemed to scare," tells you the meaning, and the leaps "without a second thought" repeat it.

decoys.why: The sentence says nothing scared her, not that she was confused.
She leaped and swam, so she was active, not someone who sits a lot.
Cumbersome describes heavy, awkward things, not a fearless diver.
Nothing here is about ignoring others' feelings; the clue is that nothing scared her.
No one wronged her, so wanting revenge does not fit; she was simply fearless.
She did not show off; the sentence shows she had no fear.

meaning: holding on firmly; refusing to give up
example: The tenacious reporter kept asking questions.
hook: Tenacious comes from Latin tenere, to hold, like tenant: picture a terrier that holds on and never lets go.

traps.why: Wavering means unsure and ready to give in, the opposite of tenacious.
Tense means tight or nervous; it only looks like the start of tenacious.
Spacious means roomy; it just rhymes with tenacious.

syn1.tip: Tenacious shares a root with tenant, from a Latin word meaning to hold. A tenacious person holds on and keeps going.

sc1.stem: The _____ terrier refused to let go of the rope toy, hanging on with its teeth even when Javier lifted it completely off the ground.

traps.why: A fickle dog would drop the toy quickly; this one hung on.
A timid dog would let go, not dangle off the ground by its teeth.
A lazy dog would rest, not fight to keep the toy.

sc1.tip: Look at "refused to let go" and "hanging on with its teeth even when" lifted. The blank describes a dog with a grip that won't quit.

decoys.why: The clue is the dog hanging on, not sitting around doing nothing.
Javier lifted the terrier easily, so it was not heavy; the clue is gripping hard.
Fancy decoration has nothing to do with a dog refusing to let go.
The dog held on well even in the air, so it was not clumsy.
A task can be arduous, but the sentence describes a dog that would not let go.
A dog gripping a toy is not showing off how important it is.

traps.why: Discouraged people give up; tenacious people refuse to.
Pushy is a rude kind of insisting; tenacious praises someone who won't quit.
Talent helps people succeed, but tenacious is about refusing to give up.

syn2.tip: Think of a tenacious reporter who keeps asking questions. The word describes someone with a firm grip who will not give up.

sc2.stem: Most of the class quit the hard puzzle after ten minutes, but _____ Lena kept working on it all weekend until she finally solved it.

traps.why: Bored students quit; the word "but" says Lena was different.
Impatient people give up quickly, and Lena worked all weekend.
Luck didn't solve it; she kept working all weekend.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts Lena with classmates who "quit." She "kept working on it all weekend," so she refused to give up.

decoys.why: The puzzle was arduous, but the blank describes Lena, who refused to give up.
Lena finally solved the hard puzzle, so she was not lacking skill.
Nothing here is about hurting feelings; the clue is that she kept working all weekend.
No one wronged Lena, so revenge has nothing to do with her solving the puzzle.
Cumbersome describes heavy objects, not a girl who kept working until she succeeded.
Fancy decoration does not describe Lena; the sentence shows she never quit.

meaning: showing very strong and sincere feeling
example: She made a fervent plea to save the old oak tree.
hook: Fervent comes from Latin for boiling, so picture feelings bubbling over like a pot on high heat.

traps.why: Indifferent means not caring, the opposite of fervent.
Interested is too weak; fervent means very strong feeling.
Frequent means happening often; it only looks a bit like fervent.

syn1.tip: Hear it in the phrase "a fervent plea." Someone begging with all their heart is full of strong, sincere feeling.

sc1.stem: Despite her nervousness, Aisha gave a _____ speech about protecting the local wetlands, her voice trembling with emotion as she urged everyone to help.

traps.why: A dull speech has no feeling, but her voice trembled with emotion.
Despite her nervousness means her speech was strong, not shy.
Mild is too weak for a voice trembling with emotion.

sc1.tip: "Despite her nervousness" tells you the speech was not shy, and "trembling with emotion" shows how strongly she felt.

decoys.why: Her voice trembled with emotion as she urged everyone to help, so she cared deeply.
She was nervous and emotional, not showing off how important she was.
A speech trembling with emotion about saving wetlands is serious, not playful.
Nothing is sneaky here; she sincerely urged everyone to protect the wetlands.
Sitting still has nothing to do with a speech full of strong feeling.
She wanted people to help the wetlands, not to get revenge on anyone.

traps.why: Showing no emotion is the opposite of fervent.
Fervent comes from boiling, but it describes feelings, not temperature.
Anger is strong, but fervent means sincere, eager feeling, not a temper.

syn2.tip: Fervent comes from a word for boiling. Think of feelings so strong they bubble over, like a fervent fan or a fervent wish.

sc2.stem: Grandpa usually shows little interest in sports, but he is a _____ fan of the town's Little League team and never misses a single game.

traps.why: Casual fans care a little; never missing a game shows much stronger feeling.
A reluctant fan wouldn't come to every game; "but" signals a change.
A former fan stopped caring, yet he never misses a game.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts his "little interest" in most sports with this team. "Never misses a single game" shows very strong feeling.

decoys.why: The clue is that he never misses a game, which shows strong feeling, not unkindness.
Nothing suggests he is confused; he loves the team and never misses a game.
Going to every game shows deep enthusiasm, not showing off.
Nothing sneaky happens here; he is simply a devoted fan.
Being a loyal fan has nothing to do with wanting revenge.
The clue is his strong devotion to the team, not playful oddness.

meaning: fill up again after being used
example: Hikers replenished their water bottles at a cold mountain stream.
hook: Replenish is re- (again) plus a root meaning full, as in plenty: you make something full again.

traps.why: Drain means empty out, the opposite of replenish.
Relish means enjoy; it only looks like replenish.
Re- does mean again, but replenish means fill again, not do again.

syn1.tip: Find plen inside, as in plenty. Re- means again, so replenish means making something full again.

sc1.stem: After the bake sale emptied the cafeteria's supply cabinet, the student council had to _____ the flour, sugar, and paper plates before the next event.

traps.why: The bake sale already emptied the cabinet; it needs filling.
Bake sales sell things, but the cabinet is empty and needs supplies.
Re- can mean back, but there's nothing left to give back.

sc1.tip: The cabinet was "emptied," and the council needs supplies "before the next event." What do you do to an empty cabinet?

decoys.why: The cabinet was empty, so they needed to fill it again, not give supplies up.
They needed more supplies before the next event, not to take them away.
The supplies were used up, so the council needed to restock, not put them at risk.
You cannot block flour and plates; the empty cabinet needed filling again.
Making supplies last longer makes no sense when they are already gone.
Dispel is for fears or doubts, not for restocking flour and plates.

traps.why: Consume means use up, the opposite of filling back up.
You might buy supplies, but replenish means filling back up.
Punish means make someone suffer; it just sounds like the end of replenish.

syn2.tip: Picture hikers who replenish their water bottles at a stream. The bottles were used up, and now they are full again.

sc2.stem: The bird feeder in our yard was full on Monday, but by Friday the hungry squirrels had eaten everything, so Dad went out to _____ it with fresh seed.

traps.why: The squirrels already emptied it; Dad added fresh seed.
Nothing was broken, and you can't fix a feeder with seed.
Feeders need cleaning, but "with fresh seed" means filling it.

sc2.tip: The feeder went from "full" to eaten up, and Dad came "with fresh seed." He is making it full again.

decoys.why: Dad added fresh seed to an empty feeder, so he was filling it, not blocking it.
Adding fresh seed does not put the feeder at risk; it fills it up again.
Seed might entice birds, but the blank is about filling the empty feeder.
Nothing needed to be calmed or crushed; the feeder just needed more seed.
Dad was not slowing anything down; he was refilling the empty feeder.
The seed was already gone, so Dad needed to fill the feeder, not stretch anything out.

meaning: sneaky and dishonest
example: The devious fox tricked the crow into dropping its cheese.
hook: Devious comes from Latin for off the main road: a devious person takes a crooked, sneaky path.

traps.why: Honest means truthful, the opposite of devious.
Devoted means loyal; it only looks like devious.
Obvious means easy to see; it just rhymes with devious.

syn1.tip: Think of the devious fox that tricked the crow. Devious describes someone who gets what they want by secret tricks.

sc1.stem: The cartoon villain came up with a _____ plan, pretending to be the hero's friend while secretly stealing the map from his backpack.

traps.why: Pretending to be a friend while stealing is not truthful.
The hero is mentioned, but the villain's plan is not heroic.
Stealing the map is harmful, and the plan is meant to trick.

sc1.tip: "Pretending to be the hero's friend while secretly stealing" describes a plan full of lies and tricks.

decoys.why: The villain is sneaky, but nothing says he is getting revenge for something.
He only pretended to be friendly while secretly stealing, so the plan was not welcoming.
A plan cannot be confused; the clue is the pretending and secret stealing.
Sitting still has nothing to do with a plan built on lies and theft.
Pretending to be a friend in order to steal is sneaky, not playful.
The clue is the trickery and stealing, not strong sincere feeling.

traps.why: Sincere means honest and real, the opposite of devious.
Clever is praise; devious means tricky in a dishonest way.
Villains may be violent, but devious is about sneaky tricks.

syn2.tip: Devious has a negative feeling and comes from a word for off the road. A devious person goes around the honest path.

sc2.stem: Everyone thought the quiet new student was shy and sweet, but she was actually quite _____, secretly switching name tags so others would be blamed for her pranks.

traps.why: Letting others be blamed is the opposite of innocent.
Everyone thought she was shy, but "but" says the truth was different.
She acted "secretly," so she was not obvious.

sc2.tip: "But she was actually" sets up a contrast with "shy and sweet." Switching tags "secretly" so "others would be blamed" is sneaky and dishonest.

decoys.why: The word but tells you she was not sweet and friendly after all.
She framed others for pranks, but nothing says she was getting revenge.
The clue is her secret trickery, not bursting with energy and joy.
Getting others blamed for her pranks is not welcoming to anyone.
She was not confused; she cleverly and secretly framed other students.
Sitting still has nothing to do with sneakily switching name tags.

meaning: put an end to; calm or crush
example: The coach's steady voice quelled the team's rising panic.
hook: Firefighters quell a blaze and teachers quell giggles: picture a loud uproar being pressed down into silence.

traps.why: Worsen means make bigger or worse, the opposite of quell.
Dwell means live somewhere; it just rhymes with quell.
You notice trouble before you quell it; quell means stop it.

syn1.tip: Hear it in "quell the panic" or "quell a riot." You quell something that is getting out of hand.

sc1.stem: When rumors of a ghost in the gym spread through the school, the principal tried to _____ the panic by inviting everyone to tour the room in daylight.

traps.why: Fueling panic would make it grow, not end it.
Inviting a tour is taking action, not ignoring the panic.
Describing panic won't stop it; the tour is meant to end it.

sc1.tip: The principal acted "by inviting everyone to tour the room in daylight," which shows there is no ghost. That would end the panic.

decoys.why: The principal wants to calm the panic, and incite means to stir it up.
The daylight tour is meant to end the panic, not make it last longer.
Elicit means to draw out a reaction, but the principal wants the panic gone.
Fortify means to make stronger, but the tour is meant to weaken the panic.
Replenish means fill up again, and nobody wants to refill the school's panic.

traps.why: Stirring up trouble is the opposite of quelling it.
Putting up with panic means tolerating it; quell means stopping it.
Quell is stronger than a slight change; it means stopping completely.

syn2.tip: Picture a coach whose steady voice quelled the team's rising panic. The panic didn't just shrink; it ended.

sc2.stem: At first the crowd's anger only grew louder, but the referee managed to _____ it with a clear explanation, and the stadium soon fell quiet again.

traps.why: The stadium fell quiet, so the anger did not increase.
Applauding the anger would praise it; the referee wanted it gone.
Referees keep records, but recording anger wouldn't quiet a stadium.

sc2.tip: "At first" the anger "grew louder, but" then the stadium "fell quiet again." The blank is what the referee did to stop the anger.

decoys.why: The stadium fell quiet, so the referee calmed the anger instead of stirring it up.
The anger stopped and the stadium went quiet, so it did not last longer.
The crowd was already angry; the referee ended that reaction rather than drawing it out.
Fortify means to strengthen, but the anger faded and the stadium fell quiet.
Replenish means fill up again, which makes no sense for anger that ends in quiet.

meaning: friendship and trust among a group
example: The camaraderie on the team made every practice fun.
hook: Camaraderie comes from comrade, which first meant roommate: picture teammates bunking together at camp and becoming close.

traps.why: Rivalry means competing against each other, the opposite of camaraderie.
Camouflage means hiding by blending in; it only looks like camaraderie.
Popular kids have many fans, but camaraderie is trust within a group.

syn1.tip: Find comrade inside camaraderie. A comrade is a friend you stick with, so camaraderie is the friendly bond in a group.

sc1.stem: After months of early-morning rowing practices, the crew developed a warm _____, joking together and cheering for one another even off the water.

traps.why: Rivals compete; this crew cheered for one another.
Early practices are a routine, but joking and cheering show friendship.
Jealousy is a bitter feeling; the crew was warm and supportive.

sc1.tip: Look at "joking together and cheering for one another even off the water." That describes a warm friendship within the group.

decoys.why: The crew jokes and cheers for each other, which shows friendship, not hostility.
Cheering for one another shows respect and friendship, not looking down on others.
A grievance is a complaint, but the crew is joking and cheering happily.
Finesse is skill at rowing, but the clue describes friendship off the water.
A plan for winning races does not explain joking and cheering off the water.
Aptitude is natural ability, but the sentence describes how the crew feel about each other.

traps.why: Hostility means unfriendliness, the opposite of camaraderie.
Groups have leaders, but camaraderie is about friendship among members.
An acquaintance is someone you barely know; camaraderie is a close bond.

syn2.tip: Think of "the camaraderie on the team made every practice fun." It names the warm, trusting feeling teammates share.

sc2.stem: On the first day of camp the cabinmates barely spoke, but by the last night their _____ was so strong that they cried while hugging goodbye.

traps.why: They were shy at first, but "but" signals that changed.
Rivals wouldn't cry while hugging goodbye.
Barely knowing someone is too weak for crying while hugging goodbye.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts "barely spoke" with the last night. Crying "while hugging goodbye" shows they became close friends.

decoys.why: They hugged goodbye and cried, which shows friendship, not hostility.
Campers who hug and cry at parting care about each other rather than looking down.
A complaint would not make cabinmates cry while hugging goodbye.
Finesse is skill and grace, but the sentence is about a growing bond.
A natural ability does not explain why the cabinmates hugged and cried at parting.

meaning: to rise and fall in an irregular way
example: Gas prices fluctuated up and down all summer long.
hook: Fluctuate comes from Latin for wave: picture prices bobbing up and down like waves on the sea.

traps.why: Stabilize means stay steady, the opposite of fluctuate.
Flutter means flap quickly, like wings; it only looks like fluctuate.
Rise is only half of it; fluctuate means going up and down.

syn1.tip: Hear it in "prices fluctuate." Picture a line on a chart that keeps going up, then down, then up again.

sc1.stem: In the desert, temperatures can _____ wildly, soaring above 100 degrees during the day and then dropping close to freezing at night.

traps.why: Rise covers the soaring part but not the dropping at night.
Settle means become steady, but these temperatures change wildly.
Deserts are hot, but the temperatures also drop near freezing.

sc1.tip: The temperatures are "soaring" in the day and "dropping" at night. The blank must cover both going up and coming down.

decoys.why: The temperatures also soar during the day, so they do not only fall.
Temperatures cannot strike back; the sentence describes them going up and down.
Temperatures do not settle disagreements; they rise by day and drop at night.

traps.why: Staying the same is the opposite of fluctuating.
Flu looks like flow, but fluctuate means changing up and down.
That only goes up; fluctuate means moving both up and down.

syn2.tip: Fluctuate comes from a Latin word for wave. Waves go up and down over and over.

sc2.stem: Unlike the steady hum of the refrigerator, the noise from the old washing machine would _____ constantly, growing quiet for a moment and then suddenly roaring.

traps.why: Humming is what the steady fridge does; "unlike" says the washer differs.
Fade covers getting quiet but not the sudden roaring.
Flutter means flap quickly; it doesn't mean getting louder and softer.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the steady hum" tells you the washer's noise is not steady. "Growing quiet" then "roaring" means going up and down.

decoys.why: The noise gets quiet and then roars again, so it does not just fall.
A noise cannot strike back; the sentence describes it rising and falling.
A washing machine's noise does not settle arguments; it goes quiet and then roars.

meaning: eager to learn and full of questions
example: The inquisitive child asked why the sky was blue.
hook: Inquisitive shares a root with inquire and question: an inquisitive kid always has another question ready.

traps.why: Uninterested means not caring to know, the opposite of inquisitive.
Exquisite means very beautiful; it only looks like inquisitive.
Talkative people talk a lot; inquisitive people want to learn.

syn1.tip: Inquisitive is related to inquire, which means to ask. Picture the child asking why the sky is blue.

sc1.stem: Max was such an _____ boy that he took apart the toaster to see how it worked and asked the museum guide question after question.

traps.why: An idle boy wouldn't take apart a toaster or ask endless questions.
Taking things apart might look destructive, but asking questions shows curiosity.
Exquisite means very beautiful; it only looks like inquisitive.

sc1.tip: He took the toaster apart "to see how it worked" and asked "question after question." Both examples show a boy who wants to know things.

decoys.why: Max asks question after question to learn, which shows curiosity, not fearlessness.
He took the toaster apart to see how it worked, not to cause trouble.
Nothing says Max was clumsy; the clues show he wanted to learn how things work.
Asking the guide many questions shows eagerness, not annoyance.
Being friendly does not explain taking apart a toaster or asking endless questions.

traps.why: Lacking interest is the opposite of inquisitive.
Slightly is too weak; inquisitive means full of questions.
Arguers ask questions too, but inquisitive means wanting to learn.

syn2.tip: Look for inquire inside inquisitive. Someone who keeps asking questions really wants to find things out.

sc2.stem: While her older brother found bugs boring, Priya was _____ about them, and she spent hours peering through a magnifying glass and reading library books to learn more.

traps.why: Indifferent matches the bored brother, but "while" says Priya is different.
Some people fear bugs, but she studied them for hours.
Confused people ask questions too, but hours of eager study show curiosity.

sc2.tip: "While her older brother found bugs boring" sets up a contrast. She spent hours studying "to learn more," so she is eager to learn.

decoys.why: Priya happily spent hours studying bugs, so she was eager, not annoyed by them.
The sentence is about her wanting to learn, not about ignoring others' feelings.
Nothing says Priya showed off; she quietly read books to learn more.
Studying bugs with a magnifying glass shows curiosity, not sneakiness.

meaning: wanting to get revenge
example: The vindictive girl erased her rival's name from the sign-up sheet.
hook: Vindictive shares a root with vengeance: a vindictive person keeps score and waits to get even.

traps.why: Forgiving means letting go of hurt, the opposite of vindictive.
Victorious means winning; it only looks a bit like vindictive.
Angry is too general; vindictive means wanting payback.

syn1.tip: Vindictive sounds like vengeance, which means revenge. Think of someone who wants to get even.

sc1.stem: After losing the class election to Marcus, Kyle became _____ and spent weeks trying to get back at him by spreading silly rumors.

traps.why: A gracious loser congratulates the winner instead of spreading rumors.
Elections involve popularity, but Kyle lost and wanted payback.
Kyle lost the election, so he was not victorious.

sc1.tip: Kyle spent weeks "trying to get back at him." Getting back at someone is revenge, so the blank means wanting revenge.

decoys.why: Kyle spread rumors to get back at Marcus, which is the opposite of friendly.
Trying to get back at Marcus is not welcoming him at all.
Kyle just lost the election and wanted payback, so he was not joyful.
Kyle wanted revenge for losing, not answers to questions.

traps.why: Quick to forgive is the opposite of vindictive.
Slightly annoyed is too weak; vindictive people actively plan payback.
Winning and losing come up, but vindictive is about getting even.

syn2.tip: Picture the girl who erased her rival's name from the sign-up sheet. She was trying to hurt someone to get back at them.

sc2.stem: Ella is not the type to hold a grudge; even when her friends tease her, she laughs it off instead of being _____.

traps.why: Laughing it off is forgiving; "instead of" needs the opposite.
Victorious means winning, which has nothing to do with grudges.
She laughs, but the blank is what she avoids being.

sc2.tip: "Not the type to hold a grudge" and "instead of" tell you the blank is the grudge-holding, get-even attitude she avoids.

decoys.why: Laughing it off is friendly, so the blank needs what Ella avoids: revenge.
Laughing it off is cheerful, and the blank must name the grudge she avoids.
The clue says Ella does not hold a grudge, so the blank is about revenge.
The sentence is about holding a grudge, not about asking questions.
Ella laughs instead of being the blank word, so it must mean the opposite of friendly.

meaning: overflowing with energy, joy, and excitement
example: The exuberant puppy leaped and spun around the yard.
hook: Picture a puppy that leaps, spins, and barks with joy: that bursting, can't-sit-still happiness is exuberant.

traps.why: Gloomy means sad and dark, the opposite of exuberant.
Exhausted starts like exuberant but means worn out, not full of joy.
Exuberant people can be loud, but the word is about joy and energy.

syn1.tip: Think of an exuberant puppy leaping around the yard. The word is full of happy, bubbling energy.

sc1.stem: When the final buzzer sounded, the _____ players leaped into the air, hugged one another, and danced across the court while the crowd roared.

traps.why: Dejected players would slump, not leap, hug, and dance.
Players are often tired after a game, but these players are leaping and dancing.
Anxious is nervous energy; hugging and dancing show happy energy.

sc1.tip: Look at what the players do: "leaped into the air, hugged one another, and danced." Those actions show overflowing joy.

decoys.why: The players are leaping, hugging, and dancing, which shows joy, not annoyance and frustration.
Nothing in the sentence shows confusion; the players are celebrating happily.
Hugging one another is not uncaring; the sentence describes joyful celebration.
No one wants revenge here; the players are hugging and dancing with joy.
The players are celebrating together, not showing off how important they are.
Painstaking describes careful work, but the players are wildly celebrating a win.

traps.why: Calm and quiet is the opposite of bursting with energy.
Mildly pleased is far too weak; exuberant means overflowing with joy.
Exuberant is a positive word; rude and loud gives it a bad feeling.

syn2.tip: Exuberant feelings overflow. If a choice sounds small, still, or unkind, it is too far from the word's lively, happy feeling.

sc2.stem: My little brother is usually shy around strangers, but at his birthday party he was so _____ that he ran around shouting, laughing, and hugging every guest.

traps.why: Timid matches "usually shy," but the "but" signals a change to the opposite.
A sleepy child would not run around shouting and laughing.
Grumpy is negative; laughing and hugging show a happy mood.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with "usually shy," and "shouting, laughing, and hugging" shows joyful energy.

decoys.why: He is laughing and hugging guests, so he is joyful, not annoyed.
Hugging every guest shows happiness, not a wish for revenge.
A boy hugging every guest is not uncaring about others' feelings.
Nothing suggests he is confused; he is running around laughing with excitement.
He is not asking questions; the sentence shows him bursting with excited energy.
Painstaking means careful effort, but he is running and shouting with joy.

meaning: friendly and peaceful
example: The neighbors reached an amicable agreement about the fence.
hook: Amicable sounds like amigo, the Spanish word for friend; both come from the Latin amicus, meaning friend.

traps.why: Hostile means unfriendly and ready to fight, the opposite of amicable.
Friendly people may chat a lot, but amicable is about getting along.
An amicable deal may be fair, but amicable means friendly, not fair.

syn1.tip: Amicable sounds like amigo, Spanish for friend. You often hear about an amicable agreement, one made without fighting.

sc1.stem: Even though the two teams were fierce rivals on the field, their meeting after the game was _____, with players shaking hands and sharing snacks.

traps.why: Hostile fits "fierce rivals," but "even though" signals the meeting was the opposite.
Rivals are competitive on the field, but shaking hands and sharing snacks are friendly.
Awkward feels uncomfortable; handshakes and shared snacks show a warm meeting.

sc1.tip: "Even though" signals a contrast with "fierce rivals." Then "shaking hands and sharing snacks" shows the meeting was friendly.

decoys.why: The players shook hands and shared snacks, which is friendly, not revengeful.
Shaking hands and sharing snacks is calm and polite, not wild and out of control.
Sharing snacks shows kindness, not a lack of care for others.
Nothing sneaky happens; the players openly shake hands and share snacks.
The clue is about friendliness after a rivalry, not about how brief the meeting was.
The sentence describes a friendly meeting, not careful, effortful work.

traps.why: Bitterly opposed means fighting each other, the opposite of amicable.
Deeply in love is far too strong; amicable is simply friendly.
Obeying is about following orders, not about being friendly with someone.

syn2.tip: Think of an amicable agreement between neighbors: they settle things calmly and stay friends. Look for the choice that means getting along.

sc2.stem: Because the two sisters wanted to keep getting along, their talk about sharing the last slice of pizza was _____, ending in smiles and a fair split.

traps.why: A heated talk is an angry one, but this talk ended in smiles.
Applicable looks a bit like amicable but means fitting or relevant.
Nervous is an uneasy feeling; smiles and a fair split show warmth.

sc2.tip: "Because the two sisters wanted to keep getting along" causes the result: a talk "ending in smiles." That calls for a friendly, peaceful word.

decoys.why: The sisters wanted to keep getting along and ended smiling, so no revenge here.
The talk ended in a fair split, so it was honest, not sneaky.
Sisters who end in smiles are caring toward each other, not uncaring.
The talk ended calmly with smiles, not in wild, uncontrolled behavior.
The clue is that they wanted to get along, which points to friendliness, not shortness.
Nobody shows off here; the sisters smile and split the pizza fairly.

meaning: friendly and welcoming to guests
example: Our hospitable hosts served us tea and fresh bread.
hook: Hospitable shares a Latin root with host: a hospitable host throws open the door and makes every guest feel at home.

traps.why: Unfriendly is the opposite of welcoming guests warmly.
Hospitable looks like hospital, but it has nothing to do with being sick.
Hosts often clean up for guests, but hospitable means welcoming, not clean.

syn1.tip: Look for the word host inside hospitable. A good host makes guests feel welcome.

sc1.stem: The villagers were so _____ that they invited the tired travelers into their homes, served them warm meals, and offered them beds for the night.

traps.why: Suspicious people would not invite strangers in and offer them beds.
Villagers might be curious about travelers, but feeding and housing them shows welcome.
Hostile looks like host, but it means unfriendly, the opposite of this.

sc1.tip: The villagers "invited the tired travelers into their homes, served them warm meals, and offered them beds." Those actions describe welcoming guests.

decoys.why: Offering warm meals and beds shows care, the opposite of not caring.
The sentence is about welcoming guests, not about the villagers being rich and showy.
Inviting travelers in and feeding them is about welcoming, not asking questions.
The villagers kindly helped the travelers; nothing sneaky or dishonest happens.
Serving warm meals to tired travelers has nothing to do with revenge.
The villagers serve others kindly rather than showing off their own importance.

traps.why: Rude to visitors is the opposite of treating guests warmly.
Hospitable looks like hospital, but it describes welcoming people, not patients.
A fancy hotel may host guests, but hospitable means warm, not wealthy.

syn2.tip: Hospitable goes with hospitality, the warm treatment a host gives guests. Choose the meaning about welcoming visitors.

sc2.stem: Although the campground looked rough and wild, the rangers were _____, greeting each family with a smile and helping them set up their tents.

traps.why: Unwelcoming matches "rough and wild," but "although" signals the rangers were different.
Strict sounds stern, but smiling and helping show warmth.
Hospitable looks like hospital, but it is about welcoming, not being ill.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets the rangers against the "rough and wild" campground. "Greeting each family with a smile" shows they made visitors welcome.

decoys.why: The campground was wild, but the rangers greeted families politely, so they were not unruly.
Rough and wild suggests bravery, but the rangers' greeting and help show welcome.
Greeting families with smiles and helping them shows care, not coldness.
Helping families set up tents is humble and kind, not showing off.
Nothing sneaky happens; the rangers openly smile and help each family.

meaning: very annoyed and frustrated
example: The exasperated teacher repeated the directions for the fifth time.
hook: Exasperated is how you feel the tenth time your little brother asks, "Are we there yet?"

traps.why: Calm is the opposite of being very annoyed.
Exhausted looks similar but means very tired, not annoyed.
Puzzled means confused; exasperated means fed up and annoyed.

syn1.tip: Picture a teacher repeating the directions for the fifth time. That sigh of "not again" is exasperated.

sc1.stem: After the printer jammed for the sixth time in ten minutes, Mr. Chen threw up his hands, completely _____ with the stubborn machine.

traps.why: No one is satisfied when a printer jams six times.
Amused is a happy feeling; a stubborn machine makes people annoyed.
He might be confused, but six jams and thrown-up hands show annoyance.

sc1.tip: The printer "jammed for the sixth time in ten minutes," and he "threw up his hands." That cause leads to great annoyance.

decoys.why: Throwing up his hands after six jams shows frustration, not calm unconcern.
He threw up his hands at a stubborn machine, so he was not feeling friendly.
A printer jamming six times would not fill Mr. Chen with joy.
The machine is stubborn, but Mr. Chen throws up his hands, showing he is fed up.
Throwing up his hands means he gave up in frustration, not found a clever fix.
Fearlessness has nothing to do with being fed up by a jammed printer.

traps.why: At ease means relaxed, the opposite of fed up.
Mildly bothered is too weak; exasperated means very annoyed.
Sadness is an upset feeling too, but exasperated is about annoyance.

syn2.tip: Exasperated is what happens when something annoying keeps happening. Look for the choice that means you have had enough.

sc2.stem: At the start of the game Maya stayed patient with her little cousin, but after he changed the rules for the tenth time, she was _____.

traps.why: Content matches "stayed patient," but "but" signals her feeling changed.
Exhilarated looks a little like exasperated but means thrilled and excited.
Rule changes might confuse her, but ten changes would mostly annoy her.

sc2.tip: "Stayed patient" is contrasted by "but after he changed the rules for the tenth time." Her patience ran out, so she was very annoyed.

decoys.why: The word but shows she stopped being patient, so she was not calm and unbothered.
The sentence contrasts her early patience with how she felt later, so not friendly.
Rules changing ten times would wear her out, not fill her with joy.
The clue is that her patience ran out, which points to annoyance, not curiosity.
Her cousin kept changing the rules; nothing shows Maya acting sneaky.
The sentence is about losing patience, not about welcoming guests.

meaning: to reveal private or secret information
example: He refused to divulge the ending of the mystery novel.
hook: When you divulge a secret, it spills out; the word comes from Latin for spreading something among ordinary people.

traps.why: Conceal means to hide, the opposite of revealing.
Divide starts like divulge but means to split into parts.
Indulge rhymes with divulge but means to treat yourself.

syn1.tip: You often hear "refused to divulge" with secrets or names. Think of a secret spilling out.

sc1.stem: Even when her friends begged, Rosa would not _____ what surprise she had planned for the party, because she had promised to keep it secret.

traps.why: She promised to keep the secret, so she would happily hide it.
The promise was about keeping the surprise secret, not about changing it.
Divide looks like divulge but means to split, which makes no sense here.

sc1.tip: "She had promised to keep it secret" explains why she "would not" do it. The missing word means to tell the secret.

decoys.why: Her friends tried to draw out the secret; Rosa would not reveal it herself.
The sentence is about keeping a secret, not about making up something false.
There is no statement to prove wrong; she simply would not tell the secret.
She already planned the surprise; the issue is whether she would tell it.
The sentence is about revealing a secret, not making a fear or doubt disappear.

traps.why: Keep hidden is the opposite of making a secret known.
Divulge contains bulge, but it means telling, not swelling.
Asking about a secret is not the same as telling it.

syn2.tip: Divulge is used with secrets, names, and endings. Choose the meaning about letting information out.

sc2.stem: The magician kept most of his tricks a mystery, but at the end of the show he agreed to _____ how he made the coin disappear.

traps.why: Conceal matches "kept a mystery," but "but" signals he did the opposite.
Indulge sounds like divulge but means to give in to a wish.
The audience wonders about tricks; the magician knows and tells how.

sc2.tip: "Kept most of his tricks a mystery, but" signals a change. At the end, he agreed to tell his secret.

decoys.why: He agreed to explain the real trick, not to make up something false.
The magician is giving away his secret, not drawing a reaction out of someone.
Kept a mystery but agreed at the end means he revealed it, not proved it wrong.
The word but shows he finally shared the secret instead of blocking it.
The sentence is about explaining a trick, not starting something on purpose.

meaning: done with great care and effort
example: Restoring the old quilt was painstaking work.
hook: Painstaking means taking pains: putting in so much careful effort that the work almost hurts.

traps.why: Careless is the opposite of done with great care.
Painstaking contains pain, but it means careful, not hurting.
Careful work can be tiring, but painstaking describes the care itself.

syn1.tip: Split it: taking pains. When you take pains over something, you work at it very carefully.

sc1.stem: Repairing the ancient vase took months of _____ work, as the museum expert glued each of the three hundred tiny fragments back into place by hand.

traps.why: Hasty means rushed, but the expert spent months on it.
Pointless puts the work down; saving an ancient vase is worthwhile.
Painless looks like painstaking but means easy and without hurt.

sc1.tip: Look at "months," "three hundred tiny fragments," and "by hand." That much slow, careful effort fills the blank.

decoys.why: The repair took months and three hundred pieces, so the work was not brief.
Gluing tiny fragments by hand takes careful control, not wild and uncontrolled work.
The vase may be valuable, but the sentence describes careful effort, not showy richness.
Nothing in the sentence suggests joy or excitement, only slow, careful gluing.
The expert is carefully repairing the vase, with nothing sneaky or dishonest about it.

traps.why: Quick and sloppy is the opposite of slow, careful work.
Somewhat neat is too weak; painstaking means great care and effort.
Painstaking praises the effort; dull and boring puts the work down.

syn2.tip: Painstaking work, like restoring an old quilt, checks every detail. Look for the choice meaning extremely careful.

sc2.stem: Jake rushed through his science poster in ten minutes, but his sister spent a whole weekend on hers, measuring every line in a _____ effort to make it perfect.

traps.why: Hurried matches Jake, but "but" shows his sister was the opposite.
Painstaking has pain inside, but the sentence is about care, not hurt.
Playful means lighthearted; measuring every line shows serious care.

sc2.tip: "Rushed" is contrasted by "but his sister spent a whole weekend," "measuring every line" to make it perfect. That shows great care.

decoys.why: She spent a whole weekend on it, so her effort was not brief.
Measuring every line shows care, not showing off how important she is.
Nothing says she wanted revenge on Jake; she just wanted her poster perfect.
Measuring every line is careful and honest work, not sneaky behavior.
She knew exactly what she was doing; the sentence shows care, not confusion.

meaning: rich, expensive, and showy
example: The opulent hotel lobby had gold chandeliers.
hook: Picture an opulent palace dripping with gold, velvet, and crystal: wealth showing off in every room.

traps.why: Shabby means worn and run down, the opposite of opulent.
Opaque starts like opulent but means you cannot see through it.
Opulent places are often big, but opulent means rich and showy.

syn1.tip: Think of an opulent hotel lobby with gold chandeliers. The word is about showing off great wealth.

sc1.stem: The king's _____ palace was filled with marble floors, velvet curtains, and golden chandeliers, a sharp contrast to the simple huts of the villagers nearby.

traps.why: Humble describes the villagers' huts, not a palace of marble and gold.
Palaces can be old, but the clues are about wealth, not age.
Opaque looks like opulent but means not see-through.

sc1.tip: Look at "marble floors, velvet curtains, and golden chandeliers," and the "sharp contrast to the simple huts." The palace shows great wealth.

decoys.why: Marble, velvet, and gold describe richness, not how welcoming the king was.
The clues point to an expensive, showy palace, not careful effort.
Succinct describes short speech or writing, not a palace full of luxuries.
Nothing about the palace is sneaky; the details show wealth and luxury.
A building cannot seem calm and uncaring; the clues describe expensive decorations.

traps.why: Plain and simple is the opposite of rich and showy.
Opulent starts like open, but it has nothing to do with openness.
Cozy is too mild; opulent means grand, expensive, and showy.

syn2.tip: Opulent things show off money: gold, marble, velvet. Choose the meaning that is both wealthy and flashy.

sc2.stem: Because the movie star wanted everyone to see how rich she was, her birthday party was _____, with a gold cake, crystal glasses, and a live orchestra.

traps.why: Modest means simple and low-key, not a show of wealth.
Optional starts like opulent but means not required.
She wanted everyone to see, so the party was not about privacy.

sc2.tip: "Because the movie star wanted everyone to see how rich she was" causes a showy party. The gold cake and orchestra confirm it.

decoys.why: A gold cake and a live orchestra show a lavish party, not a brief one.
The sentence is about showing off wealth, not about friendly peacefulness.
She wanted everyone to see her riches, so the party was not casual.
The clues point to showy wealth, not careful effort.
A party cannot be full of questions; the clues describe expensive luxury.

meaning: to tell a secret to someone you trust
example: Lily confided her fears to her best friend.
hook: Confide shares a Latin root with confident and fidelity, words about trust: you confide only in someone you trust.

traps.why: Conceal means to hide, the opposite of sharing a secret.
Confuse starts like confide but means to mix someone up.
Boasting is talking about yourself to show off, not trusting someone.

syn1.tip: You confide in a best friend. Think of telling someone you trust something private.

sc1.stem: Jonah trusted his grandmother more than anyone, so he decided to _____ in her about the worries he had kept secret from everyone else.

traps.why: He trusts her, but the blank is about telling her his worries.
Confine looks like confide but means to keep something locked in.
Rejoice is a happy word, but he is sharing worries.

sc1.tip: "Trusted his grandmother more than anyone" leads to telling her "the worries he had kept secret." Telling a secret to someone you trust is the answer.

traps.why: Keep quiet is the opposite of telling someone your secret.
That is confine, which looks like confide but means to lock in.
Confident shares a root, but confide means telling, not feeling sure.

syn2.tip: The phrase "confide in a friend" means telling a trusted friend something secret. Look for the choice about telling.

sc2.stem: Mia usually keeps things to herself, but after a hard week she chose to _____ her secret to her older brother, who listened quietly and promised not to tell.

traps.why: Deny means to say something is not true, the opposite of telling it.
Confirm starts like confide but means to show something is true.
Selling a secret is sneaky; she trusts her brother, who promises not to tell.

sc2.tip: "Usually keeps things to herself, but" signals a change. Her brother "promised not to tell," so she shared her secret with him.

decoys.why: She shared a real secret with someone she trusted, not something she made up.

meaning: to make stronger, especially for protection
example: The settlers fortified the fort with thick log walls.
hook: Fortify has fort inside: to fortify something is to make it as strong as a fort.

traps.why: Weaken is the opposite of making stronger.
Foretell sounds a bit like fortify but means to predict.
You might improve a building by decorating, but that adds beauty, not strength.

syn1.tip: Find fort inside fortify, and the ending -ify means to make. To fortify is to make strong like a fort.

sc1.stem: Before the hurricane arrived, residents worked to _____ their homes, nailing boards over windows and piling sandbags against the doors.

traps.why: People may leave before storms, but nailing boards and piling sandbags means staying to protect.
Boards and sandbags make homes stronger, not weaker.
Forfeit starts like fortify but means to give something up.

sc1.tip: Look at the examples: "nailing boards over windows and piling sandbags against the doors." Those make homes stronger against the storm.

decoys.why: Boards and sandbags protect homes, so the residents were not putting them at risk.
They stayed and nailed boards to protect their homes instead of giving them up.
The boards block windows, but the goal was to make homes stronger, not block them.
They were protecting real homes, not making up something false.

traps.why: Tear down is the opposite of building up protection.
Making something larger does not make it stronger or safer.
A light patch is too weak; fortify means making something truly strong.

syn2.tip: Settlers fortified forts with thick walls. Fortified cereal has extra nutrients to make you stronger. Look for the choice about adding strength.

sc2.stem: On cold mornings, Dad likes to _____ himself with a big bowl of oatmeal so he has enough energy to shovel the whole driveway.

traps.why: Weakening himself would leave him without energy to shovel.
Oatmeal is about getting energy, not taking his mind off the work.
Burden sounds like a bad load; the oatmeal helps him.

sc2.tip: The words "so he has enough energy to shovel" show the result. The oatmeal makes him stronger for the job.

decoys.why: The oatmeal gives Dad energy, so it strengthens him instead of putting him at risk.
The oatmeal is for energy to shovel, not for calming him down.
Eating oatmeal for energy has nothing to do with scolding himself.

meaning: brief and clearly expressed
example: Her succinct summary covered the whole chapter in three sentences.
hook: Succinct comes from Latin for tucked up, like a robe belted tight so nothing extra flaps around.

traps.why: Wordy means using too many words, the opposite of succinct.
Successful starts like succinct but means getting what you wanted.
A short answer can sound rude, but succinct is a compliment.

syn1.tip: A succinct summary covers a whole chapter in three sentences. Think short, tight, and to the point.

sc1.stem: Unlike his rambling ten-minute speech last year, Omar's campaign speech this time was _____, making every point clearly in under a minute.

traps.why: Lengthy matches last year's speech, but "unlike" signals this one was different.
Nothing shows rudeness; making points clearly and quickly is a good thing.
Succulent looks like succinct but means juicy, like fruit.

sc1.tip: "Unlike his rambling ten-minute speech" signals a contrast, and "clearly in under a minute" tells you the speech was short and clear.

decoys.why: The sentence praises a short, clear speech, not one showing off importance.
A speech under a minute is plain and brief, not rich and showy.
Nothing says the speech was rude; the clue is that it was short and clear.
Making every point clearly is honest, not sneaky.
The sentence is about length and clarity, not anger about something unfair.

traps.why: Long and rambling is the opposite of short and clear.
Succinct praises short speech; short and rude gives it a bad feeling.
Silence goes too far; succinct still says something, just briefly.

syn2.tip: Succinct writing says exactly what it means with no extra words. It is a compliment, so look for a positive choice.

sc2.stem: Since the contest rules allowed only enough words to fit on one index card, Ana made her poem _____, saying everything she meant in just twelve words.

traps.why: A wordy poem would never fit on one index card.
Succulent looks like succinct but means juicy.
Vague means unclear, but she said "everything she meant."

sc2.tip: "Since the contest rules allowed only enough words to fit on one index card" causes a short poem, and "saying everything she meant" shows it was clear.

decoys.why: A twelve-word poem on an index card is short, not rich and showy.
The clue is the tiny word limit, so the poem was brief, not showing off.
A poem cannot have a huge appetite; the clue is about using few words.
Fitting her poem into twelve words is about brevity, not sneakiness.
Nothing says the poem was rude; the contest rules simply forced it to be short.

meaning: scold someone formally for doing wrong
example: The referee reprimanded the player for arguing about the call.
hook: A reprimand is the stern talking-to a referee or principal gives you right after you break the rules.

traps.why: Praise is the opposite of reprimand; it means saying someone did well.
Reminding is too gentle; a reprimand is a stern scolding.
Reprint starts like reprimand but means to print again.

syn1.tip: Think of a referee reprimanding a player for arguing. The word has a stern, negative feeling, like getting in trouble.

sc1.stem: When the lab partners left a gas burner on unattended, the science teacher had to _____ them sternly and remind the class about safety rules.

traps.why: Nobody gets praised sternly for leaving a burner on.
Comforting is kind; the teacher is stern because the students broke a safety rule.
Excusing them lets them off, but the teacher acts sternly about safety.

sc1.tip: The word "sternly" and the danger of leaving a gas burner on tell you the teacher is scolding the partners.

decoys.why: The teacher spoke sternly about danger, so she was scolding them, not soothing them.
The teacher wanted to stop unsafe behavior, not stir the students up.
Leaving the burner on put people at risk, but the teacher was scolding them.
The teacher was correcting the students sternly, not making them stronger.
Nothing in the sentence is about blocking them; the teacher was scolding.

traps.why: Cheering someone on encourages them, the opposite of a reprimand.
Telling on someone reports the wrongdoing; reprimanding is scolding them for it.
A gentle warning is too mild; a reprimand is a sharp scolding.

syn2.tip: A reprimand happens after someone does wrong, so look for the choice that means scolding them sharply.

sc2.stem: Instead of praising the team for winning, the coach chose to _____ them for their poor sportsmanship, listing every rude comment they had made.

traps.why: "Instead of praising" rules out congratulating; the coach is unhappy with them.
Nobody is rewarded for poor sportsmanship and rude comments.
Coaches train teams, but listing rude comments is scolding, not training.

sc2.tip: "Instead of praising" signals the opposite of praise, and "poor sportsmanship" and "rude comment" show the coach is scolding them.

decoys.why: The coach chose not to build them up and instead listed their rude comments.
Listing every rude comment is scolding, not calming the team down.
The coach was criticizing their behavior, not putting the team at risk.
Nothing is being blocked; the coach is scolding them for rudeness.

meaning: to make up something false
example: He fabricated an excuse for being late to class.
hook: Fabricate shares a Latin root with fabric; picture someone weaving a fake excuse out of nothing.

traps.why: Confessing means telling the truth; fabricating means making up something false.
Discovering finds something real; fabricating makes up something that isn't real.
Exaggerating stretches the truth; fabricating makes the whole thing up.

syn1.tip: Think of someone who fabricates an excuse for being late. The excuse did not happen; it was made up.

sc1.stem: Rather than admit she had forgotten her homework, Tessa tried to _____ a story about her dog getting sick, but her teacher saw through the lie.

traps.why: Confirming shows something is true, but her story was a lie.
The teacher would be the one believing; Tessa is creating the story.
Editing fixes a story; the clue is that she made up a lie.

sc1.tip: "Rather than admit" and "saw through the lie" show Tessa was making up a false story.

decoys.why: Tessa was making up a lie, not revealing a true secret.
Confiding means sharing a true secret, but her story was a lie.
Tessa was creating a false story, not making one disappear.
Tessa invented the story herself; she was not drawing it out of someone.
Tessa was inventing an excuse, not giving something up.

traps.why: Owning up means admitting the truth, the opposite of fabricating.
Finding out learns real facts; fabricating creates false ones.
Adding to a story is weaker; fabricating invents the whole thing.

syn2.tip: A fabricated story is a false one. Pick the phrase that means creating something untrue.

sc2.stem: The reporter was fired after editors learned she would _____ quotes, writing words that no real person had ever actually said to her.

traps.why: Recording quotes captures real words, but these words were never said.
Checking quotes is good reporting and would not get her fired.
Shortening real quotes is much weaker than writing words nobody said.

sc2.tip: The phrase "words that no real person had ever actually said" restates the blank: she made the quotes up.

decoys.why: Embellishing adds details to real quotes, but these words were never said at all.
Reporters do draw out quotes, but she was fired for inventing them.
Revealing quotes would not get her fired; she made up words no one said.
The sentence says she wrote fake words, not that she blocked anything.
She was inventing quotes, not using up a supply of them.

meaning: angry about something unfair
example: She was indignant when blamed for her brother's mess.
hook: You feel indignant when you get blamed for a mess your little brother made: angry because it's unfair.

traps.why: Pleased is the opposite of indignant, which means angry about unfairness.
Being blamed might embarrass you, but indignant means angry, not ashamed.
Indulgent looks similar but means giving in to wishes, not angry.

syn1.tip: Picture being blamed for something you didn't do. That hot, unfair feeling is being indignant.

sc1.stem: Ji-woo was _____ when the coach blamed her for the broken window, since she had been at the dentist when the ball was thrown.

traps.why: Nobody is grateful for being blamed for something they didn't do.
She was at the dentist, so she has nothing to feel guilty about.
Amused is too lighthearted; unfair blame makes people angry.

sc1.tip: "Since she had been at the dentist" shows she was blamed unfairly, and unfair blame makes someone angry.

decoys.why: Being blamed unfairly would upset her, not leave her calm and uncaring.
Nobody feels joyful when wrongly blamed for breaking a window.
The sentence is about how she felt about unfair blame, not about being rude.
Being blamed for something she did not do would not make her feel friendly.
She was angry about unfair blame, not sadly longing for something.
She was innocent, since she was at the dentist, so she was not sneaky.

traps.why: Calmly accepting things is the opposite of being indignant.
Guilt fits someone who did wrong; indignant people feel wrongly blamed.
Being puzzled is far too mild; indignant means truly angry.

syn2.tip: Indignant people feel they were treated unfairly, and it makes them angry.

sc2.stem: Although Marcus had cleaned the kitchen all by himself, his sister got the credit, so he felt _____ rather than proud of his hard work.

traps.why: Satisfied fits if you miss that his sister unfairly got the credit.
Thankful is a happy feeling; losing credit unfairly makes him angry.
Marcus did nothing wrong, so guilt doesn't fit.

sc2.tip: "His sister got the credit" for work he did alone is unfair, and "rather than proud" points to an angry feeling.

decoys.why: The sentence says he felt something other than proud, and pompous is a showy kind of pride.
His sister took his credit, so he would not feel joyful.
Losing credit for his hard work would bother him, not leave him uncaring.
Someone who loses credit unfairly feels angry, not friendly and peaceful.
The unfairness makes him angry, not sadly longing for something.

meaning: to fall straight down very fast
example: The temperature plummeted as soon as the sun set.
hook: Plummet comes from plumb, a lead weight on a string that drops straight down.

traps.why: Soar means rise high, the opposite of plummet.
Drifting down is slow and gentle; plummeting is a fast, steep fall.
Falling things may shatter, but plummet means the fall itself.

syn1.tip: Think of temperatures or a rock plummeting. The word always means a sudden, fast drop downward.

sc1.stem: As soon as the cold front arrived, temperatures began to _____, dropping forty degrees in just a few hours.

traps.why: Climbing means going up, but the temperatures dropped forty degrees.
Fluctuate means go up and down; these temperatures only fell.
Holding steady can't explain a forty-degree drop.

sc1.tip: "Dropping forty degrees in just a few hours" describes a fast, steep fall.

decoys.why: Temperatures dropped steadily by forty degrees, not up and down.
Temperatures cannot strike back; the sentence says they dropped fast.
Temperatures cannot mock anything; the sentence describes them falling quickly.

traps.why: Rising quickly is the opposite of plummeting.
A slow slide is too gentle; plummeting is fast and steep.
A fall can break things, but plummet means falling, not breaking.

syn2.tip: Plummet is about direction and speed: straight down, very fast.
