sc2.stem: The kite floated gently for an hour, but when the wind suddenly died, it began to _____ toward the lake and hit the water with a loud splash.

traps.why: Drift fits the gentle floating, but "but" and "loud splash" show a fast fall.
Soaring goes up, but the kite hit the water.
Hovering stays in one place, yet the kite crashed into the lake.

sc2.tip: "But when the wind suddenly died" signals a change, and "a loud splash" shows the kite fell fast.

decoys.why: The kite fell straight into the lake; it did not rise and fall.
A kite cannot strike back; it dropped fast when the wind died.

meaning: unable to believe something
example: She gave an incredulous stare when she heard her score.
hook: In- means not and cred means believe, so incredulous means not believing what you just heard.

traps.why: Convinced means fully believing, the opposite of incredulous.
Ridiculous has a similar ending but means silly.
Dishonest is about telling lies; incredulous is about not believing.

syn1.tip: Look inside the word: in- (not) and cred (believe), as in credit. Incredulous means not believing.

sc1.stem: When the announcer said the smallest runner had broken the state record, the crowd stared in _____ silence, sure they had misheard.

traps.why: The crowd was sure they misheard, so they weren't confident in the news.
Respectful silence is quiet, but the clue is that they couldn't believe it.
A record-breaking surprise wouldn't make a crowd bored.

sc1.tip: "Sure they had misheard" shows the crowd could not believe what the announcer said.

decoys.why: The crowd was sure they had misheard, which is disbelief, not anger at unfairness.
The clue says they thought they misheard, so they doubted it rather than felt annoyed.
The crowd could not believe the news; nobody was sadly longing for anything.
A shocking record left them staring, not calm and uncaring.
Friendly silence does not match a crowd sure they had misheard.

traps.why: Trusting quickly is the opposite of being incredulous.
Shocked people may go quiet, but incredulous is about believing, not speaking.
Slightly unsure is too weak; incredulous means you can't believe it at all.

syn2.tip: The cred inside incredulous is the same as in credible, meaning believable. Add in- for not.

sc2.stem: Everyone else believed Leo's story about meeting a famous singer, but his best friend just raised one eyebrow, looking completely _____.

traps.why: The "but" means the friend did not believe like everyone else.
Thrilled is excited; a raised eyebrow shows doubt, not excitement.
Starstruck fits the famous singer, but the friend doubts the story.

sc2.tip: "Everyone else believed" followed by "but" means the friend didn't, and a raised eyebrow shows doubt.

decoys.why: The friend did not believe the story, which is doubt, not curiosity.
Raising one eyebrow shows doubt, not overflowing excitement.
Nothing unfair happened to the friend; he simply did not believe Leo.
Being sociable has nothing to do with doubting Leo's story.
The contrast with everyone else believing shows doubt, not friendliness.

meaning: very angry
example: The irate customer demanded a full refund.
hook: Irate is related to ire, an old word for anger; picture a customer slamming a broken toaster on the counter.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite of irate, which means very angry.
Bothered is much too mild; irate means extremely angry.
Angry people may be loud, but irate means the anger itself.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "an irate customer" demanding a refund. The word is close to ire, which means anger.

sc1.stem: After waiting three hours for a flight that was then canceled, the _____ passengers crowded the desk, shouting and demanding answers.

traps.why: Shouting and demanding answers is not patient behavior.
A long wait can tire people, but sleepy people don't shout.
Polite people don't crowd a desk shouting.

sc1.tip: "Shouting and demanding answers" after a three-hour wait and a cancellation shows the passengers were very angry.

decoys.why: The passengers were shouting and demanding answers, so they were not calm or unbothered.
Shouting at the desk after a canceled flight is not friendly or peaceful.
A canceled flight after three hours of waiting would not make people joyful.
Hopeless people tend to slump quietly, but these passengers were shouting and demanding answers.
They crowded the desk to complain, not because they enjoyed being around people.
Nobody is welcoming guests here; the passengers are shouting about a canceled flight.

traps.why: Slightly upset is too weak; irate is very strong anger.
Being content is the opposite of being irate.
Confusing situations can annoy people, but irate means angry, not confused.

syn2.tip: Irate is a strong word. Pick the choice that shows anger at its highest level.

sc2.stem: Mr. Lee is usually calm when students forget their homework, but when someone spilled juice on his laptop, he became _____ and shouted for ten minutes.

traps.why: Relaxed fits "usually calm," but "but" signals a change to anger.
He might worry about his laptop, but shouting shows anger.
Someone else spilled the juice, so he has no reason to feel embarrassed.

sc2.tip: "Usually calm" plus "but" signals a change, and "shouted for ten minutes" shows extreme anger.

decoys.why: The sentence says he stopped being calm and shouted, so not caring is the opposite.
Shouting for ten minutes is not friendly or peaceful.
Juice on his laptop would not fill him with joy and excitement.
He shouted, which shows anger, not quiet hopeless sadness.
Sad longing does not fit someone shouting for ten minutes about a ruined laptop.
Being sociable has nothing to do with shouting about spilled juice.

meaning: laugh at or mock something as foolish
example: Critics scoffed at the idea of flying machines in 1900.
hook: When people scoff, they make a little "pfft" sound at your big idea, as if it could never work.

traps.why: Admiring is the opposite of scoffing at something.
Cough rhymes with scoff but just means clearing your throat.
Scolding is angry criticism; scoffing is laughing at something as foolish.

syn1.tip: Think of critics who scoffed at flying machines. They laughed at the idea as silly.

sc1.stem: When Aiden announced he would build a walking robot for the science fair, his older cousins began to _____, but they stopped laughing when it actually walked.

traps.why: "Stopped laughing" shows they had been mocking, not cheering.
Helping fits a project, but the cousins were laughing at it.
Gasping shows surprise, but the clue says they had been laughing.

sc1.tip: "They stopped laughing when it actually walked" tells you the cousins had been laughing at Aiden's plan.

decoys.why: The cousins were laughing at an idea, not striking back after being harmed.
The clue says they stopped laughing, so they were mocking him, not sharing secrets.
The cousins were laughing, not falling straight down.
Rising and falling irregularly does not describe cousins laughing at Aiden's plan.

traps.why: Cheering for an idea is the opposite of scoffing at it.
Laughing with someone is friendly; scoffing is laughing at them unkindly.
Frowning shows disapproval, but scoffing means mocking laughter.

syn2.tip: Scoffing has a mean, mocking feeling. Look for the choice that treats something as a joke.

sc2.stem: Because the idea of a fifth grader starting a lemonade empire sounded so silly, Maya's classmates would _____ whenever she talked about her business plans.

traps.why: People don't applaud an idea they think sounds silly.
Investing fits business plans, but the classmates thought the idea was silly.
Listening is neutral; the clue "so silly" points to mocking.

sc2.tip: "Because" the idea "sounded so silly," the classmates' reaction must be to make fun of it.

decoys.why: Maya did nothing to harm them; they thought her idea was silly and mocked it.
The sentence says her idea sounded silly, so they mocked it rather than shared secrets.
Classmates do not fall straight down whenever Maya talks about her plans.
Rising and falling irregularly does not describe reacting to an idea that sounds silly.

meaning: having a huge appetite; extremely eager
example: The voracious caterpillar ate every leaf on the plant.
hook: A voracious reader devours books the way a starving wolf devours dinner.

traps.why: Full means you've had enough to eat, the opposite of voracious.
Vicious sounds similar but means cruel or violent.
Picky is about what you eat; voracious means wanting huge amounts.

syn1.tip: Think of the voracious caterpillar eating every leaf. The word means a huge appetite.

sc1.stem: A _____ reader, Sofia finished three novels every week and always begged the librarian for more books before she left.

traps.why: A reluctant reader wouldn't beg for more books.
Careful describes how she reads, but the clue is how much she wants.
Three novels a week is far more than occasional reading.

sc1.tip: "Three novels every week" and "always begged the librarian for more" show a huge appetite for books.

decoys.why: Sofia begged for more books, so she cared a lot about reading.
Sofia was eagerly reading three novels a week, not sadly longing for something.
Nothing in the sentence shows Sofia was hopeless; she eagerly asked for more books.
The clue is about how much she reads, not about liking to be with people.
Begging the librarian for books is not sneaky or dishonest.
Succinct describes brief writing or speech, not someone who reads three novels a week.

traps.why: Barely interested is the opposite of a voracious appetite.
Slightly curious is too weak; voracious means extremely eager.
Voracious eaters may eat fast, but the word means eager, not quick.

syn2.tip: A voracious reader can never get enough books. The word means a huge, eager appetite for something.

sc2.stem: My little brother usually picks at his vegetables, but after soccer practice he is so _____ that he eats two full plates of pasta and asks for dessert.

traps.why: Picky fits his usual habit, but "but" signals the opposite.
Practice can make him tired, but eating two plates shows a huge appetite.
A satisfied eater wouldn't keep asking for dessert after two plates.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts his usual picking, and "two full plates" plus "asks for dessert" show a huge appetite.

decoys.why: He is eager for food, not eager to learn or ask questions.
Being full of joy does not explain eating two full plates of pasta.
Anger is not why he eats two plates; the clue is about appetite.
Asking for dessert after two plates shows hunger, not hopeless sadness.
Succinct describes brief speech or writing, not a big appetite.
Being rich and showy has nothing to do with eating two plates of pasta.

meaning: to deliberately cause something to start
example: The principal wanted to know who instigated the cafeteria food fight.
hook: The kid who instigates a food fight throws the first meatball and then watches the chaos spread.

traps.why: Stopping something is the opposite of instigating it.
Investigate looks similar but means look into something carefully.
Joining a fight means taking part after someone else instigated it.

syn1.tip: Think of the principal asking who instigated the food fight. She wants the person who got it going.

sc1.stem: Noah tried to _____ a snowball fight by tossing the first snowball at his cousin, and soon the whole playground had joined in.

traps.why: Throwing the first snowball begins a fight; it doesn't end one.
Noah threw a snowball on purpose, so he wasn't avoiding a fight.
Noah wasn't just watching; he threw the first snowball himself.

sc1.tip: "Tossing the first snowball" and "soon the whole playground had joined in" show Noah got the fight going.

decoys.why: He tossed the first snowball to get the fight going, not to stop it.
Tossing the first snowball starts a fight; you cannot keep going something not yet begun.
Throwing the first snowball got everyone to join, so he was not blocking the fight.
He was starting the snowball fight, not putting it at risk.
Tossing the first snowball begins a fight; it does not decorate or add details.
The fight really happened, so nothing was made up or false.

traps.why: Calming things down is the opposite of instigating trouble.
Taking part is joining in; instigating is causing it to begin.
Putting something off delays it; instigating makes it begin.

syn2.tip: Instigate usually goes with trouble, like fights or arguments. Pick the phrase that means deliberately causing it.

sc2.stem: The coach benched the two players who had tried to _____ an argument with the referee, since the coach blames whoever stirs up trouble, not those who get dragged in.

traps.why: Settling an argument is good, and the coach wouldn't bench them for it.
Joining is getting "dragged in," which the coach does not blame.
Players who avoid an argument wouldn't be benched for it.

sc2.tip: The coach "blames whoever stirs up trouble, not those who get dragged in," so these players began the argument.

decoys.why: The coach blames whoever stirs up trouble, so these players started the argument, not ended it.
The sentence says they stirred up trouble, not that they blocked the argument.
The coach punishes whoever stirs up trouble, which means starting the argument, not adding details.
Revealing secrets has nothing to do with stirring up an argument with the referee.
You cannot fill an argument back up; the clue is about stirring up trouble.
Using up a supply does not fit stirring up an argument with the referee.

meaning: calm and seeming not to care or worry
example: He gave a nonchalant shrug after losing the game.
hook: A nonchalant kid shrugs and yawns before a big test, as if nothing in the world could worry him.

traps.why: Anxious means worried, the opposite of nonchalant.
Seeming not to care isn't the same as being impolite.
Nonstop also starts with non but means without stopping.

syn1.tip: Picture a nonchalant shrug after losing a game. The word means calm and acting like it's no big deal.

sc1.stem: While the other contestants trembled backstage, Jada seemed completely _____, chatting and yawning as if the spelling bee final were no big deal.

traps.why: Terrified fits the trembling contestants, but "while" sets Jada apart.
She yawns, but "no big deal" shows calm, not tiredness.
She chats, but the clue "no big deal" is about being unworried.

sc1.tip: "While the other contestants trembled" sets up a contrast, and "as if the spelling bee final were no big deal" shows calm.

decoys.why: She acted like it was no big deal, so she was not frustrated.
Chatting and yawning shows she was relaxed, not very angry.
Treating the final as no big deal is calm, not hopeless and sad.
Nothing in the sentence shows Jada was unable to believe something.
Yawning shows calm, not overflowing energy and excitement.
Jada was relaxed about the contest, not sadly longing for something.

traps.why: Nervous and tense is the opposite of nonchalant.
Nonchalant people may yawn, but the word means unworried, not tired.
Cold and cruel is harsh; nonchalant is just relaxed and unbothered.

syn2.tip: A nonchalant person acts like nothing is a big deal. Look for calm plus not worried.

sc2.stem: Ben had practiced his piano piece so many times that he walked onstage looking _____, with his hands in his pockets and a relaxed grin.

traps.why: Jittery means nervous, but he had a relaxed grin.
Lots of practice can tire you, but a relaxed grin shows calm.
Embarrassed people don't stroll onstage with a relaxed grin.

sc2.tip: "Practiced so many times" causes confidence, and "hands in his pockets and a relaxed grin" shows he was calm.

decoys.why: A relaxed grin shows Ben was calm, not annoyed and frustrated.
Hands in his pockets and a relaxed grin do not look very angry.
A relaxed grin is not the look of someone sad and without hope.
Ben looked relaxed and grinning, not sadly longing for something.
Nothing in the sentence shows Ben couldn't believe something; he was just relaxed.
Rich and showy describes things, not a relaxed boy with his hands in his pockets.

meaning: rudely disrespectful, especially toward someone in charge
example: The insolent customer laughed at the manager's polite request.
hook: Picture a student smirking and talking back to the principal: that smirk is pure insolent attitude.

traps.why: Respectful is the opposite of insolent.
Indolent looks similar but means lazy, not rude.
Rude people can be loud, but insolent is about disrespect, not volume.

syn1.tip: Insolent has a negative feeling and is used for people who talk back to someone in charge. Look for the choice about bad manners.

sc1.stem: Marcus answered the substitute teacher with an eye roll and a sarcastic remark; his _____ reply earned him a trip to the principal's office.

traps.why: Courteous means polite, the opposite of an eye roll and sarcasm.
Witty is a compliment; this reply got him sent to the principal.
Indolent means lazy; Marcus's reply was rude, not lazy.

sc1.tip: The clues are "an eye roll and a sarcastic remark" and "a trip to the principal's office." That describes a rude, disrespectful reply.

decoys.why: An eye roll and a sarcastic remark are not friendly, so amicable is the opposite.
Hospitable means welcoming, but Marcus was mocking the teacher, not welcoming her.
Marcus was not asking questions; he was being rude with a sarcastic remark.
Wistful means sadly longing, but his eye roll shows rudeness, not sadness.
A quick sarcastic remark is not done with great care and effort.
Despondent means hopeless and sad, but the sentence describes a mocking, rude reply.

traps.why: Polite is the opposite of insolent.
Bold sounds brave and positive; insolent is a negative word for rudeness.
An insolent person may be angry, but the word means disrespectful.

syn2.tip: Think of an insolent remark to a teacher. It shows no respect for authority, so pick the word meaning without respect.

sc2.stem: Although the coach spoke calmly and kindly to him, Jamal stayed _____, talking back, rolling his eyes, and ignoring every instruction he was given.

traps.why: Respectful is the opposite of talking back and rolling his eyes.
The coach was calm; "although" tells you Jamal acted differently.
Confused players may miss instructions, but talking back shows rudeness.

sc2.tip: "Although" signals that Jamal acted unlike the kind coach. Then "talking back, rolling his eyes" spells out exactly what kind of behavior.

decoys.why: Talking back and rolling his eyes is not friendly, so amicable is the opposite.
Jamal was rude to the coach, not warm and welcoming.
Jamal ignored instructions instead of eagerly asking questions to learn.
Nothing in the sentence shows Jamal sadly longing for something; he is being disrespectful.
Ignoring every instruction is the opposite of working with great care.

meaning: to calm someone who is upset
example: The babysitter pacified the crying baby with a song.
hook: A baby's pacifier is named for this word: it pacifies the baby by calming its crying.

traps.why: Provoke means to stir up anger, the opposite of pacify.
Specify sounds like pacify but means to state exactly.
Feeding can quiet a baby, but pacify means to calm, not feed.

syn1.tip: Think of a pacifier, the thing that calms a crying baby. The Pacific Ocean was also named for seeming peaceful.

sc1.stem: To _____ the crying toddler, the flight attendant offered him a small stuffed bear and sang a soft lullaby until he fell asleep.

traps.why: Upset is the opposite of what a stuffed bear and lullaby do.
Scolding is harsh; a soft lullaby is gentle comfort.
The lullaby is about sleep, but it put him to sleep, not awake.

sc1.tip: The flight attendant offered "a small stuffed bear" and "a soft lullaby until he fell asleep." Those are ways to calm a crying child.

decoys.why: Giving a bear and singing a lullaby is soothing, not scolding.
The flight attendant was helping the toddler sleep, not putting him at risk.
Singing a lullaby is a kind act, not taking unfair advantage of the child.
The goal was to calm the crying toddler, not make him stronger for protection.

traps.why: Agitate means to upset or stir up, the opposite of pacify.
Punishing is one way to deal with someone upset, but it doesn't calm them.
Pacify comes from a word for peace, but it doesn't mean giving up.

syn2.tip: A pacifier soothes a fussy baby. Pacify means to make someone peaceful, so look for the word about comforting.

sc2.stem: The angry crowd shouted at the referee, but the stadium announcer managed to _____ the fans by promising a full replay review of the disputed call.

traps.why: Enrage means to make angrier; "but" shows the announcer did the reverse.
Crowds and announcers go together, but promising a review calms fans.
Punish is harsh; a promise is a friendly way to settle people down.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the "angry crowd" with what the announcer did. A promise that settles angry fans calms them down.

decoys.why: Promising a replay review calms fans; it does not scold them.
The announcer was settling the angry crowd, not taking unfair advantage of it.
A promise of a replay does not block the fans; it calms them down.
The announcer's promise made things better, so it did not put the fans at risk.

meaning: liking to be with other people; sociable
example: Gregarious Sam made five new friends on the first day of camp.
hook: Gregarious comes from Latin for flock: a gregarious person loves being in the middle of the flock.

traps.why: Shy is the opposite of gregarious.
Greedy starts like gregarious but means wanting too much.
Popular means liked by many; gregarious means liking to be with many.

syn1.tip: Picture the kid who chats with everyone at a party. Gregarious is a positive word for someone who loves company.

sc1.stem: Unlike her shy sister, who preferred reading alone, Bianca was _____, happiest when she was surrounded by friends at a crowded party.

traps.why: Timid describes her shy sister; "unlike" means Bianca is the opposite.
Studious fits the sister who reads alone, not party-loving Bianca.
Gracious means kind and polite; the clue is about loving crowds.

sc1.tip: "Unlike her shy sister" tells you Bianca is the opposite of shy, and "surrounded by friends at a crowded party" confirms she loves company.

decoys.why: Bianca loves crowded parties, so she is full of social energy, not lacking it.
Bianca is happiest with friends, so she is not sad and hopeless.
Bianca is happy at the party, not sadly longing for something.
The sentence is about loving company, not being rude to someone in charge.
Nothing in the sentence is about revenge; it contrasts shy and social sisters.
The contrast is shy versus sociable, not careless versus careful.

traps.why: Withdrawn means keeping to yourself, the opposite of gregarious.
Generous looks a bit like gregarious but means giving freely.
Crowds of friends can be noisy, but gregarious means enjoying company.

syn2.tip: Gregarious comes from the Latin word for a flock or herd. Someone gregarious likes to be with the group.

sc2.stem: Because my cousin Leo is so _____, he volunteered to greet every new student, and by lunch he had chatted with half the sixth grade.

traps.why: Reserved people keep to themselves, not chat with half the grade.
Greedy looks like gregarious but means wanting too much.
Grumpy is a sour mood; Leo happily greets and chats with everyone.

sc2.tip: "Because" links the blank to the result: he greeted every new student and "chatted with half the sixth grade." That shows someone who loves people.

decoys.why: Greeting every new student takes energy, so Leo is not listless.
Leo cheerfully chatted with half the grade, so he is not hopeless and sad.
Greeting new students is kind, not rudely disrespectful.
Leo wanted to meet people, not get revenge on anyone.
Nothing suggests Leo was very angry; he happily chatted with classmates.
Leo was busy meeting people, not sadly longing for something.

meaning: sadly longing for something
example: She gave a wistful look at the toy store window.
hook: Picture a kid pressing her nose to a toy store window, sighing for what she can't have: that's a wistful look.

traps.why: Content means satisfied, the opposite of wistfully wanting something.
Watchful looks like wistful but means alert and careful.
Jealous means resenting what others have; wistful is a soft, sad wish.

syn1.tip: Wistful sounds a bit like wishful. It describes a quiet, sad wish for something missing or past.

sc1.stem: Watching her old camp friends post photos from the lake, Rania felt _____, wishing she could be back there splashing in the water with them.

traps.why: Relieved means glad to be free of something, but Rania wants to be there.
Lake photos sound fun, but she is sadly wishing, not excited.
She looks at the photos, but she is wishing, not just wondering.

sc1.tip: The clue "wishing she could be back there" tells you her feeling is a sad longing for something she misses.

decoys.why: Rania wishes she were back at the lake, so she feels sad, not joyful.
Wishing she could be there shows Rania cares a lot, so nonchalant is wrong.
Rania misses her friends; the sentence shows longing, not anger.
Nothing in the photos is hard to believe; Rania simply misses being there.
Nothing unfair happened, so Rania has no reason to be indignant.

traps.why: Being fully satisfied is the opposite of wistfully wanting more.
Wistful is a gentle sadness, much softer than bitter anger.
That describes watchful, which looks like wistful but means alert.

syn2.tip: Think of a wistful smile when you remember a great summer. Wistful mixes sadness with wanting, a soft longing.

sc2.stem: Grandma usually laughs at old family photos, but when she found the one of her childhood farm, she grew quiet and _____, missing the home she left long ago.

traps.why: Cheerful fits her usual laughing, but "but" signals a change to sadness.
Furious is far too strong and angry for quietly missing a home.
Watchful looks like wistful but means alert, not longing.

sc2.tip: "But" shows a change from her usual laughing, and "missing the home she left long ago" restates the blank: a quiet, sad longing.

decoys.why: Grandma grew quiet and missed her old home, so she was not full of joy.
The sentence says Grandma grew quiet, which is not sociable and chatty.
Missing her childhood home makes Grandma sad, not very angry.
Grandma was not being rude to anyone; she was quietly remembering.
Missing the home she left shows Grandma cares deeply, so nonchalant is wrong.
The photo did not surprise Grandma; it made her miss her home.

meaning: very sad and without hope
example: He was despondent after missing the final shot.
hook: A despondent player sits alone after the loss, head in hands, sure nothing will ever go right again.

traps.why: Hopeful is the opposite of despondent.
Dependent looks similar but means relying on someone else.
Angry is a strong feeling too, but despondent means sad and hopeless.

syn1.tip: Despondent starts with "des," like despair. It is a heavy, negative word for someone who has lost hope.

sc1.stem: After learning that her science project had been ruined by the leaky roof the night before the fair, Mei was _____ and refused to leave her room.

traps.why: Elated means thrilled, the opposite of how a ruined project feels.
Refusing to leave sounds stubborn, but she stayed in from sadness.
Annoyed is too mild for losing her whole project the night before.

sc1.tip: Her project was "ruined" the night before the fair, and she "refused to leave her room." That points to deep, hopeless sadness.

decoys.why: Mei refused to leave her room, so she did not want company.
Hiding in her room shows Mei cared a lot about her ruined project.
Mei was shutting herself away, not welcoming guests.
The sentence is about her ruined project, not a huge appetite or eagerness.
Losing her project the night before the fair left Mei crushed, not friendly and peaceful.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of despondent.
Sad people may look tired, but despondent means without hope.
Defiant means refusing to obey; despondent means sunk in sadness.

syn2.tip: Despondent sounds close to despair, which means losing all hope. Pick the word for a sad person who has given up.

sc2.stem: Although the rest of the team cheered about reaching the playoffs, Jordan sat _____ on the bench, convinced that his injured ankle would keep him from ever playing again.

traps.why: Joyful fits the cheering team, but "although" says Jordan felt differently.
He was sure of something, but sure of bad news, not confident.
Relaxed is a pleasant feeling; Jordan expects never to play again.

sc2.tip: "Although" contrasts Jordan with his cheering team, and "never playing again" shows he has lost hope.

decoys.why: Jordan sat apart while the team cheered, so he was not being sociable.
Jordan feared he would never play again, so he clearly cared and worried.
Jordan was not rude to anyone; he was sad about his ankle.
Jordan was just sitting on the bench, not acting quickly without thinking.
The sentence is about Jordan losing hope, not having a huge appetite.

meaning: to use up the supply of
example: The long, hot hike depleted our water supply.
hook: When your phone battery is depleted, the charge has been used up and the screen goes dark.

traps.why: Fill up is the opposite of deplete.
Counting a supply tells how much is left; it doesn't use it.
De often means down, but deplete isn't about disappointing anyone.

syn1.tip: Deplete looks like the reverse of complete or replete, which mean full. To deplete something is to empty out its supply.

sc1.stem: If the town keeps pumping water from the well this quickly, it will _____ the underground supply within a few years, leaving nothing for future residents.

traps.why: Refilling would add water, but the sentence says nothing will be left.
Pollution harms water, but "leaving nothing" means the supply is used up.
Complete looks like deplete but means to finish or make whole.

sc1.tip: "Pumping water from the well this quickly" leads to "leaving nothing for future residents." The blank means to use up the supply.

decoys.why: Pumping water quickly and leaving nothing means using it up, and replenish means filling it back up.
The sentence says nothing would be left, so the supply would not be kept going.
Fast pumping weakens the supply until nothing is left; it does not make it stronger.
You cannot decorate an underground water supply, and the clue is about running out.

traps.why: Restock means to fill up again, the opposite of deplete.
Complete shares the ending but means to finish or make whole.
Collecting gathers a supply; depleting uses it up.

syn2.tip: You often hear "depleted supplies" or a "depleted battery." The de part means away, so the supply goes away.

sc2.stem: Lena wanted to save for the class trip, but buying snacks every day began to _____ her savings, and by Friday her piggy bank held only a few coins.

traps.why: Increase means to grow, but her piggy bank ended almost empty.
Depositing adds money to savings; snacks took money out.
Delete looks like deplete but means to erase, like a file.

sc2.tip: "Wanted to save, but" signals the plan failed, and "only a few coins" left shows her savings were being used up.

decoys.why: Her piggy bank ended with only a few coins, so her savings were not filled back up.
By Friday her savings were nearly gone, so snacks did not keep them going.
Buying snacks made her savings smaller, not stronger.
Snacks did not decorate her savings; the sentence says her money ran low.

meaning: acting quickly without thinking first
example: In an impetuous moment, Ben spent all his savings on a skateboard.
hook: An impetuous kid cannonballs into the pool before checking whether there's any water in it.

traps.why: Cautious means careful, the opposite of impetuous.
Brave praises someone; impetuous criticizes acting without thinking.
Impetuous is related to impetus, a push, but it means rash.

syn1.tip: Impetuous is related to impetus, a sudden push. An impetuous person is pushed into action before thinking.

sc1.stem: Rather than planning carefully, Sofia made the _____ decision to cut her own bangs five minutes before school photos, and she instantly regretted it.

traps.why: "Rather than planning carefully" tells you she was not careful.
Some choices are hard, but this one was made fast and regretted.
Wise is praise, but she "instantly regretted" the choice.

sc1.tip: "Rather than planning carefully" and "five minutes before school photos" show she acted on a sudden whim, then "instantly regretted it."

decoys.why: The sentence says she did not plan carefully, and painstaking means done with great care.
She instantly regretted it, so it was not a decision based on good reasons.
Nothing shows sad longing; the clue is that she acted fast without planning.
Cutting your own bangs is not rich or showy; the clue is about acting without thinking.
Being sociable has nothing to do with rushing into cutting her bangs.

traps.why: Thoughtful means thinking carefully, the opposite of impetuous.
Impolite starts like impetuous but means rude.
Impetuous people may act in anger, but the word means acting without thinking.

syn2.tip: Picture someone who leaps first and looks later. Impetuous is negative and describes jumping into action too fast.

sc2.stem: Max is so _____ that he jumped into the pool before checking how deep it was, and now he has a bruised knee to show for it.

traps.why: A cautious person would check the depth first.
Jumping is athletic, but the clue is that he didn't check first.
Impolite looks like impetuous but means rude, which isn't the clue.

sc2.tip: "So _____ that" sets up cause and effect: he jumped "before checking how deep it was." That is acting without thinking.

decoys.why: Max jumped in before checking the depth, which is the opposite of being very careful.
Jumping eagerly into a pool shows energy, not a lack of it.
Being sociable does not explain jumping in without checking how deep the pool was.
The sentence is about acting without thinking, not about using too many words.
Welcoming guests has nothing to do with jumping into a pool without checking.
Succinct describes brief speech or writing, not jumping into a pool carelessly.

meaning: to decorate or add details to
example: She embellished the plain cake with sugar flowers.
hook: Embellish holds the French word belle, beautiful: you embellish a plain cake by making it prettier with frosting flowers.

traps.why: Strip means to remove things, the opposite of embellish.
Embarrass starts like embellish but means to make someone ashamed.
You might embellish a cake, but baking it is a different step.

syn1.tip: Find belle, French for beautiful, inside embellish. To embellish is to make something prettier by adding to it.

sc1.stem: Every time Grandpa told his fishing story, he would _____ it a little more, until the fish had grown from ten pounds to a hundred.

traps.why: Shortening would cut the story, but the fish kept growing.
Old stories can be forgotten, but Grandpa kept adding to his.
He did retell it, but repeat doesn't explain the growing fish.

sc1.tip: "A little more" each time and the fish growing "from ten pounds to a hundred" show Grandpa adding extra details.

decoys.why: The fish grew bigger each time, so Grandpa was adding to the story, not using it up.
Revealing a secret does not make a fish grow from ten pounds to a hundred.
Telling a secret to someone you trust does not explain the fish getting bigger.
Speeding up the story would not make the fish grow; he was adding details.
You cannot scold a story, and the clue is that the fish kept growing.

traps.why: Removing details is the opposite of embellishing.
Editing changes a story, but embellishing adds extras, not corrections.
Embellishing adds to something real; it doesn't make up the whole thing.

syn2.tip: People embellish stories by adding extra flourishes, like a bigger fish. Think of adding decorations to something that already exists.

sc2.stem: Instead of leaving her plain white sneakers alone, Tasha decided to _____ them with glitter, colorful laces, and tiny painted stars before the school dance.

traps.why: Simplify means to make plainer, but she added glitter and stars.
You might clean sneakers before a dance, but glitter and stars decorate.
Embarrass looks like embellish but means to make someone ashamed.

sc2.tip: "Instead of leaving her plain white sneakers alone" signals a contrast, and "glitter, colorful laces, and tiny painted stars" are decorations.

decoys.why: Tasha was adding glitter and stars, not using up her sneakers.
Glitter and painted stars decorate sneakers; they do not make them stronger or protect them.
The sneakers were plain, so she was decorating them, not refilling them.
Adding glitter and colorful laces decorates the sneakers; it does not block anything.
Sneakers are not upset, so there is nothing to calm; she is decorating them.
Adding glitter and stars is decorating, not taking unfair advantage of her sneakers.

meaning: lacking energy or interest
example: After the long flu, Priya felt listless and stayed on the couch.
hook: Listless means without desire: picture a kid on a rainy day, flopped on the couch, too blah to do anything.

traps.why: Energetic is the opposite of listless.
Restless looks similar but means unable to sit still.
Listless isn't about having no list; it means lacking energy.

syn1.tip: The less ending means without, and the old word list meant desire. Listless means without the desire or energy to do anything.

sc1.stem: Usually the most energetic player on the team, Diego seemed _____ during practice, dragging his feet and barely bothering to chase the ball.

traps.why: Lively fits his usual self, but today he is dragging his feet.
An injury could slow him, but "barely bothering" shows lack of interest.
Restless means fidgety and unable to stay still, not slow.

sc1.tip: "Usually the most energetic" sets up a contrast, and "dragging his feet and barely bothering" shows he has no energy today.

decoys.why: Dragging his feet shows little energy or eagerness, the opposite of voracious.
He was barely moving, not rushing into things without thinking.
Nothing shows Diego was angry; the clue is that he was dragging his feet.
Being sociable does not explain dragging his feet and barely chasing the ball.
The sentence is about low energy, not about talking too much.

traps.why: Being full of pep is the opposite of listless.
Listless isn't about having no list or plan.
Illness can leave you listless, but the word means low energy.

syn2.tip: Picture a droopy, bored kid on a hot afternoon. Listless is negative and means having no energy or interest.

sc2.stem: The summer heat made everyone at camp _____; instead of racing to the lake as usual, the campers lay in the shade, too tired to even play cards.

traps.why: Eager campers would race to the lake, not lie in the shade.
Heat makes you sweaty, but the clue is that they were too tired.
Careless also ends in less but means not paying attention.

sc2.tip: The heat caused the blank, and the second half explains it: lying in the shade, "too tired to even play cards." That is lacking energy.

decoys.why: The campers were too tired to play cards, so they were not extremely eager.
Lying in the shade is not rushing into action; the campers were too tired to move.
They were too tired to even play cards together, so they were not acting sociable.
The sentence says the campers were too tired, not that the heat made them angry.
Nothing in the sentence shows the campers could not believe something.
Being qualified for something has nothing to do with campers too tired to move.

meaning: using more words than needed
example: The verbose instructions took two pages to explain one simple step.
hook: Verbose comes from verbum, Latin for word: a verbose writer uses a whole page to say "yes."

traps.why: Brief means short, the opposite of verbose.
Wordy writing can be hard to follow, but verbose means too many words.
Verbose is about how many words, not how loud they are.

syn1.tip: Look for verb inside verbose, from the Latin word for word. Verbose means full of too many words.

sc1.stem: Ms. Alvarez asked students to trim their _____ essays, since many had used three long paragraphs to make a point that needed only one sentence.

traps.why: Brief essays wouldn't need trimming.
Messy essays need fixing, but the problem here is too many paragraphs.
Excellent is praise, but the teacher wants these essays cut down.

sc1.tip: The clue "three long paragraphs to make a point that needed only one sentence" describes using far too many words.

decoys.why: The essays used three paragraphs for one sentence's point, so they were not brief.
The problem was too many words, not whether the essays were on topic.
The essays needed trimming because they were wordy, not because their reasons were good.
Nothing says the essays were the best; the clue is that they were too long.
Shared feelings have nothing to do with essays that used too many words.

traps.why: Using few words is the opposite of being verbose.
Verbose is about how many words, not how fancy they are.
Verb relates to words, but verbose doesn't mean talking aloud.

syn2.tip: Verbose comes from the Latin for word, and the ending means full of. Think of an essay stuffed with more words than it needs.

sc2.stem: Our class president gave a short, clear speech, but the visiting mayor was so _____ that half the audience fell asleep before she finished her opening remarks.

traps.why: Brief matches the class president; "but" says the mayor was different.
Inspiring speeches excite listeners; this audience fell asleep.
Speakers can be nervous, but that wouldn't make the speech go on and on.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the president's "short, clear speech" with the mayor's. The opposite of short is using too many words.

decoys.why: The mayor is contrasted with the short, clear speech, so she was not brief.
An angry speaker would not put the audience to sleep; the clue is a long speech.
Being sociable does not explain why half the audience fell asleep during her remarks.
Being qualified has nothing to do with a speech so long people fell asleep.
Disbelief does not explain the contrast with the short, clear speech.

meaning: a careful plan for reaching a goal
example: Our team's strategy was to tire out the other side early.
hook: A chess player thinking three moves ahead to trap the king is using a strategy.

traps.why: An accident is unplanned, the opposite of a careful strategy.
A strategy aims for victory, but it is the plan, not the win.
Tragedy ends like strategy but means a terrible event.

syn1.tip: Think of a coach drawing plays on a whiteboard before the big game. That drawing is the strategy.

sc1.stem: Before the chess tournament, Amina studied her opponent's past games and worked out a _____ for defending against his favorite opening moves.

traps.why: A trophy is the prize at a tournament, not a way to defend.
Careful study leads to a plan, the opposite of a mistake.
Studying past games gives her real knowledge, not gossip.

sc1.tip: "Studied her opponent's past games" and "worked out" a defense describe careful planning to win.

decoys.why: Amina studied carefully, so she worked out a plan, not a mistaken belief.
A complaint does not help you defend against chess moves; the sentence describes a plan.
A signed request has nothing to do with defending against opening moves in chess.
A show of respect is not something you use to defend against an opponent's moves.
She studied his past games carefully, so her plan was not a foolish act.
A doorway or starting point cannot be worked out for defending against chess moves.

traps.why: A sudden impulse is unplanned, the opposite of a careful strategy.
A strategy comes before the result; it is not the result itself.
Teams practice to carry out a strategy, but practice is not the plan.

syn2.tip: Generals and coaches make a strategy before acting. It is the thinking about how to win, not the winning.

sc2.stem: Instead of rushing the ball up the field as usual, our soccer coach drew a careful _____ on the whiteboard, showing exactly where each player should move.

traps.why: A guess is not careful, and it doesn't show exactly where players move.
Penalties happen in soccer, but a coach doesn't draw one to guide players.
A cheer pumps up a team but shows nobody where to move.

sc2.tip: "Instead of rushing" and "showing exactly where each player should move" tell you the coach made a careful plan.

decoys.why: The coach showed where each player should move, which is a plan, not a signed request.
A sign of the future does not show exactly where each player should move.
The drawing shows player movements, not something done to show respect.
A doorway is not what you draw to show where soccer players move.
The coach was planning player movements, not drawing a complaint about something unfair.
The sentence calls it careful, so it cannot be a foolish idea.

meaning: closely connected to the topic
example: Please include only relevant facts in your report.
hook: If your science fair talk drifts to your weekend at the beach, your teacher may ask, "Is that relevant?"

traps.why: Unconnected is the opposite of relevant.
Relaxed starts like relevant but means calm.
Interesting facts grab attention; relevant facts connect to the topic.

syn1.tip: Think of "relevant facts" in a report: they relate to your topic. Irrelevant ones wander off the subject.

sc1.stem: Ms. Okafor reminded us that our essays about ocean life should include only _____ details, so Jamal deleted his paragraph about his favorite pizza.

traps.why: Random details are just what Jamal cut, so this is backwards.
Length isn't the problem; the pizza paragraph was off topic.
The pizza part may be funny, but it was cut for being off topic.

sc1.tip: Jamal cut his paragraph "about his favorite pizza" from an essay "about ocean life." Only details connected to the topic belong.

decoys.why: The teacher wants details on the topic; Jamal cut the pizza part because it was off topic, not short.
Ocean life might make you think of pollution, but the clue is about staying on topic.
Details are not rich and showy; the pizza paragraph was cut for being off topic.
Nothing is being shared; Jamal deleted the pizza paragraph because it did not fit the topic.
A teacher would never ask for only clumsy details in an essay.
The teacher wants details connected to ocean life, not details full of sad longing.

traps.why: Off topic is the opposite of relevant.
Good writing can still wander from the topic.
Easy reading is about style, not about connecting to the topic.

syn2.tip: When a teacher says a detail is not relevant, she means it doesn't belong to the subject you're discussing.

sc2.stem: Because the debate topic was school uniforms, the judge stopped Mia when she started talking about her new puppy, saying the story was not _____.

traps.why: A short story wouldn't get her stopped; being off topic did.
A puppy story that's not boring wouldn't make a judge stop her.
Not irrelevant means on topic, so the judge would let her continue.

sc2.tip: "Because the debate topic was school uniforms" and the puppy story tell you the story did not connect to the topic.

decoys.why: A judge would not stop Mia for being too brief; the puppy story was off topic.
The story was not poisonous; it simply had nothing to do with school uniforms.
The problem was that the puppy story was off topic, not that it was not showy.
Nothing about sharing explains the judge's complaint; the puppy story did not match the uniforms topic.
A story is not sociable; the judge stopped her because it strayed from uniforms.
The judge would not stop a story for lacking dullness; it was off topic.

meaning: among the best of a group
example: Only elite gymnasts are invited to the national training camp.
hook: Olympic gymnasts and top orchestras are elite: the small, best group picked from many.

traps.why: Ordinary is the opposite of elite.
Polite rhymes with elite but means well-mannered.
Snobbish is a negative word; elite simply means the best.

syn1.tip: You hear "elite athletes" and "elite forces": the small group picked because they are the very best.

sc1.stem: Out of thousands of young swimmers who tried out, only the twenty fastest were chosen for the _____ training program in Colorado.

traps.why: A basic program wouldn't pick only the twenty fastest.
Cost isn't mentioned; the clue is about being the fastest.
Only twenty swimmers made it, so the program is small, not crowded.

sc1.tip: "Only the twenty fastest" out of "thousands" were chosen, so the program is for the very best.

decoys.why: Only the twenty fastest were chosen, so the program is the best, not lacking energy.
A program for the fastest swimmers would not be called clumsy.
Lasting a long time does not match the clue that only the fastest were chosen.
Nothing in the sentence suggests poison; the clue is that only the best were picked.
The clue is choosing the top twenty, not something shared between people.
Being picked as one of the fastest is exciting, and a program cannot be hopeless.

traps.why: Below average is the opposite of elite.
Rather good is too weak; elite means the very best.
Popular means well liked, not best at something.

syn2.tip: An elite team is chosen from many hopefuls, keeping only the strongest few.

sc2.stem: Although the chess club welcomes anyone who wants to play, its _____ team, which travels to national tournaments, accepts only the four strongest players.

traps.why: A casual team wouldn't accept only the four strongest players.
Being liked isn't the point; the team takes only the strongest.
The team travels to national tournaments, so local doesn't fit.

sc2.tip: "Although" signals a contrast with "welcomes anyone." Taking "only the four strongest players" means the team is for the best.

decoys.why: The club welcomes anyone, but this team takes only the four strongest, so sociable misses the contrast.
A team of the strongest players heading to nationals is not lacking energy.
The team accepts only the strongest players, so it is the best, not clumsy.
Nothing says the team is rude; the clue is that it takes only top players.
A team traveling to national tournaments is not described as hopeless.
Seeming not to care does not explain why it accepts only the four strongest players.

meaning: based on good reasons; acceptable
example: A doctor's note is a valid excuse for missing school.
hook: A ticket stamped valid gets you in; an excuse that is valid has solid reasons behind it.

traps.why: A flimsy reason is weak, the opposite of valid.
Valued looks similar but means treasured.
Valid shares an old root with valor, but it doesn't mean brave.

syn1.tip: Think of a "valid excuse" or a "valid ticket": something with good reasons behind it that is accepted.

sc1.stem: The teacher accepted Kai's excuse for the late assignment as _____, since he had a note from the hospital proving he had been sick.

traps.why: The teacher accepted it with proof, so it wasn't suspicious.
A hospital visit sounds dramatic, but the clue is about proof.
Kai was sick, but an excuse can't be contagious.

sc1.tip: "Accepted" plus "a note from the hospital proving he had been sick" shows the excuse had good reasons behind it.

decoys.why: Sickness might suggest chronic, but the teacher accepted the excuse because the note proved it.
The teacher accepted the excuse, so it was acceptable, not rude.
The hospital note proves the excuse was acceptable, not that it was wordy.
An excuse cannot be poisonous; the note shows it was based on good reasons.
The excuse came with proof from the hospital, so it was not hasty or thoughtless.
The teacher judged whether the excuse was acceptable, not whether it was sadly longing.

traps.why: Illogical means lacking good reasons, the opposite of valid.
Honest means truthful; valid means backed by good reasons.
An idea can be popular without good reasons behind it.

syn2.tip: Valid things pass a test: a valid ticket gets you in, a valid argument holds up. Invalid means not acceptable.

sc2.stem: Maya insisted her reason for skipping practice was _____, but the coach disagreed, saying a sleepover was not a good enough excuse to miss the big game.

traps.why: The coach thought it was weak; Maya insisted the opposite.
Timing isn't the argument; they disagree about whether it's good enough.
Maya told the coach her reason, so it wasn't secret.

sc2.tip: "But the coach disagreed" by saying it was "not a good enough excuse," so Maya believed her reason was acceptable.

decoys.why: Maya was defending her reason, so she would not insist it was rude.
Maya argued her reason was good enough, not that it was thoughtless.
The coach disagreed about whether the excuse was good enough, not whether it was clumsy.
The argument is about a good enough excuse, and a sleepover reason is not poisonous.
Missing one big game has nothing to do with something lasting a long time.
The coach said the excuse was not good enough, which is about acceptability, not wordiness.

meaning: a formal written request signed by many
example: Over two hundred students signed the petition for longer recess.
hook: Picture a clipboard passed around the cafeteria, collecting names to ask the principal for longer recess.

traps.why: A refusal says no; a petition asks for something.
Partition looks similar but means a wall that divides a space.
People sign a petition, but a signature is just one name.

syn1.tip: A petition asks for something. Think of signing a petition to ask the town for a new skate park.

sc1.stem: Hoping to convince the principal to add a vegetarian lunch option, Aisha circulated a _____ and collected signatures from three hundred students.

traps.why: Rumors spread around, but nobody collects signatures for one.
A menu lists lunch food; it doesn't gather signatures.
A recipe explains cooking; it can't convince a principal with signatures.

sc1.tip: She "circulated" it and "collected signatures" to "convince the principal." A paper signed by many to ask for change is a petition.

decoys.why: Aisha collected signatures, and a plan is not something people sign.
You cannot circulate a person who gives money and collect signatures on him.
Students signed something asking for a lunch option, not a mistaken belief.
An extra amount is not a document that three hundred students could sign.
A doorway cannot be circulated to collect signatures from students.
A talented young person is not a written request that students sign.

traps.why: A refusal turns something down; a petition asks for it.
A contract is an agreement, not a request for change.
A protest is louder; a petition politely asks in writing.

syn2.tip: A petition usually has a list of signatures at the bottom, all asking the same person for the same change.

sc2.stem: Neighbors who wanted a stop sign on our busy street wrote a _____, a formal letter asking the city council for one, and two hundred families signed it.

traps.why: A warning tells of danger; this letter asks for something.
Two hundred families don't sign a postcard to ask the council.
The letter asks for a sign, so it isn't a refusal.

sc2.tip: The words after the comma, "a formal letter asking the city council," plus "families signed it," restate the meaning of the blank.

decoys.why: The letter asked the council for a stop sign, so it was a request, not a show of respect.
The sentence calls it a formal letter families signed, not a plan.
Two hundred families signed a letter asking for something, not a mistaken belief.
A doorway is not a formal letter asking the city council for a stop sign.
An extra amount is not a letter that families could sign.
A benefactor is a person, but the sentence describes a signed letter.

meaning: uncomfortable or clumsy
example: There was an awkward silence after his joke fell flat.
hook: Think of a middle school dance: two kids standing apart, arms stiff, nobody knowing what to say.

traps.why: Graceful is the opposite of awkward.
Backward ends the same way but means toward the back.
Rude means impolite on purpose; awkward means clumsy or uncomfortable.

syn1.tip: Picture a newborn giraffe trying to stand on wobbly legs. Its awkward steps are clumsy and unsteady.

sc1.stem: When nobody laughed at the principal's joke, a long, _____ silence filled the room, and students shifted uncomfortably in their seats.

traps.why: Peaceful is too pleasant; the students were squirming.
Nobody laughed, so the silence was the opposite of joyful.
A welcome silence feels good, but the students felt uncomfortable.

sc1.tip: "Nobody laughed" and students "shifted uncomfortably in their seats," so the silence felt uneasy and embarrassing.

decoys.why: Students shifted uncomfortably, so the silence was not calm and carefree.
Verbose means using too many words, but the room was silent.
A sociable, friendly feeling does not match students squirming after a joke failed.
Voracious describes a huge appetite, not a silence after nobody laughed.
The sentence describes an uncomfortable silence, and relevant says nothing about that feeling.
Nothing came before a main event; the silence was simply uncomfortable.

traps.why: Relaxed is the opposite of an awkward, uneasy feeling.
Disastrous is far too strong; awkward moments are just uneasy.
An awkward silence is quiet, but quiet alone isn't the meaning.

syn2.tip: An "awkward silence" or an "awkward moment" makes everyone squirm. That uneasy feeling is the meaning here.

sc2.stem: The puppy ran smoothly across the grass, but on the slippery kitchen floor its steps became _____, and it slid into the table legs.

traps.why: Sliding into table legs is the opposite of graceful.
Sound isn't the point; the puppy lost its footing.
Speed isn't the contrast; the puppy became clumsy, not fast.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "ran smoothly," and the puppy "slid into the table legs," so its steps turned clumsy.

decoys.why: The puppy slid into the table, so its steps were not among the best.
Steps cannot be calm and uncaring; the clue is the slipping and crashing.
Valid means based on good reasons, which has nothing to do with slipping steps.
Verbose describes too many words, but the puppy's steps are not speech.
Nothing is being shared here; the puppy was sliding clumsily on the floor.
Being sociable does not explain why the puppy slid into the table legs.

meaning: allowed or qualified to do something
example: Students with a B average are eligible for the honor roll.
hook: Eligible means able to be chosen: if you meet the rules, your name can go on the list.

traps.why: Barred means kept out, the opposite of eligible.
Legible looks similar but means easy to read.
Wanting to join is different from being allowed to join.

syn1.tip: The ending "ible" means able to be. Eligible means able to be chosen because you meet the rules.

sc1.stem: Only students who have turned twelve by September are _____ to join the junior rowing team, so ten-year-old Pablo had to wait two more years.

traps.why: Pablo may be eager, but the age rule decides who may join.
Twelve-year-olds can join, so unable reverses the rule.
Fear isn't mentioned; the sentence is about an age rule.

sc1.tip: The rule "only students who have turned twelve" and Pablo having "to wait" show the blank means allowed by the rules.

traps.why: Not permitted is the opposite of eligible.
Being eligible lets you enter; it doesn't promise a win.
Skill isn't the point; eligible means you meet the rules.

syn2.tip: When a contest says who is "eligible to enter," it is listing who is allowed to take part.

sc2.stem: Although Rosa wrote a wonderful story, she was not _____ to enter the writing contest, because the rules allowed only eighth graders and she was in seventh.

traps.why: Courage isn't the issue; the rules kept her out.
Her wishes don't matter here; the grade rule decided it.
Not forbidden would mean allowed, but the rules kept her out.

sc2.tip: "Although" signals a contrast, and "the rules allowed only eighth graders" explains that seventh grader Rosa was not allowed to enter.

meaning: shared equally by two or more people
example: The two rivals had a mutual respect for each other.
hook: When you like your friend and your friend likes you right back, the feeling is mutual.

traps.why: One-sided is the opposite of mutual.
Mute starts like mutual but means silent.
Mutual feelings can be friendly, but mutual means shared by both.

syn1.tip: You've heard "the feeling is mutual," said when someone feels the same way back. Mutual means shared by both.

sc1.stem: Lena admired Omar's chess skill, and Omar admired Lena's just as much; their respect was _____, so they enjoyed practicing together.

traps.why: They admired each other "just as much," so it was even.
Nothing says they hid it; the clue is that both feel it.
Weak respect wouldn't make them enjoy practicing together.

sc1.tip: Each admired the other "just as much," so the respect went both ways equally.

decoys.why: They enjoyed practicing together, so their respect was not harmful.
Insolent means rudely disrespectful, but each admired the other.
They enjoyed practicing together, so their respect was not uncomfortable.
The clue is that both admired each other equally, not a lack of energy.
The sentence stresses that respect went both ways, not that it came first.
Immune is about protection from disease, not respect shared by two people.

traps.why: Felt by only one person is the opposite of mutual.
Mutual feelings can be private, but mutual means shared.
Growth over time isn't the point; mutual means both sides share it.

syn2.tip: A "mutual friend" is a friend of both people. Mutual always points two ways, to both sides at once.

sc2.stem: At first only Ben wanted to be friends, but by the end of camp the feeling was _____, and Carlos was asking to trade addresses too.

traps.why: "But" shows a change from one-sided to both boys.
Carlos wanting to trade addresses is warm, not awkward.
Privacy isn't the point; Carlos now feels the same way.

sc2.tip: "At first only Ben" changes with "but," and Carlos asking "too" shows both boys now felt the same.

decoys.why: Carlos was asking to trade addresses, so he clearly cared.
The boys became friends, so the feeling was not harmful.
Carlos eagerly asked to trade addresses, so nothing felt uncomfortable.
This happened by the end of camp, so the feeling was not coming first.
The clue is that Carlos now felt the same way, not that anyone qualified.
Verbose means wordy, but the sentence is about both boys sharing a feeling.

meaning: something done or given to show respect
example: The concert was a tribute to the town's firefighters.
hook: A band playing a famous singer's songs at a tribute concert is honoring that singer with music.

traps.why: An insult shows disrespect, the opposite of a tribute.
Tribe looks similar but means a group of related people.
An apology says sorry; a tribute shows respect.

syn1.tip: A "tribute concert" or "a tribute to our heroes" is held to show respect and thanks.

sc1.stem: To show their gratitude, the students planted a garden named for their beloved retired librarian, a fitting _____ to her forty years of service.

traps.why: Grateful students wouldn't punish their beloved librarian.
A garden named for her honors her; it doesn't challenge her.
The garden shows gratitude, not something to pull attention away.

sc1.tip: "To show their gratitude" for her "forty years of service" tells you the garden honors the librarian.

decoys.why: The students were grateful, so the garden was not a complaint.
Planting a garden honors her; it is not a signed request.
The garden honors her past service; it is not a sign of the future.
The garden is called fitting and shows gratitude, so it is not foolish.
A doorway or beginning does not honor someone's forty years of service.
The garden shows respect for her; it is not an extra amount of something.

traps.why: Disrespect is the opposite of a tribute.
A warning alerts people to danger; a tribute honors someone.
Rules tell people what to do; a tribute honors someone.

syn2.tip: People pay tribute to someone they admire, the way a team wears a coach's initials on their jerseys.

sc2.stem: The audience rose and clapped for five minutes as the old soldier walked onstage, for the whole assembly was a _____ to his bravery during the war.

traps.why: Long, standing applause shows respect, the opposite of an insult.
Nobody is competing; the assembly honors one man.
A complaint is negative, but the clapping shows admiration.

sc2.tip: The audience "rose and clapped for five minutes," a warm, respectful tone, so the assembly honored him.

decoys.why: The audience stood and clapped, so they were honoring him, not complaining.
Clapping for five minutes honors him; it is not a signed request.
A standing ovation for bravery is respectful, not foolish.
The assembly honored his bravery; it was not a plan to reach a goal.
The assembly honored his bravery, which has nothing to do with a doorway.
Nothing here is a mistaken idea; everyone was showing respect for his bravery.

meaning: poisonous
example: Some mushrooms are toxic and should never be eaten.
hook: A skull and crossbones on a bottle under the sink warns you the cleaner inside is toxic.

traps.why: Harmless is the opposite of toxic.
Some poisons smell bad, but many toxic things have no smell.
Toxic things are unpleasant, but unpleasant is far too general.

syn1.tip: Toxic waste and toxic chemicals come with warning labels because they can poison you.

sc1.stem: Pet owners should keep chocolate out of reach, because it contains a chemical that is _____ to dogs and can make them very sick.

traps.why: Dogs may like chocolate, but the clue says it makes them sick.
A harmless chemical wouldn't make dogs very sick.
Being familiar doesn't explain why it makes dogs sick.

sc1.tip: The chemical "can make them very sick," which is what poisons do, so the blank means poisonous.

decoys.why: The chemical can make dogs very sick, so they are not protected from it.
The sentence warns the chemical makes dogs sick, not that it loves them.
The clue says it can make dogs very sick, so you need a word meaning poisonous.

traps.why: Safe to eat is the opposite of toxic.
Taste isn't the point; toxic things can harm your body.
Dirt isn't poison; toxic means it can make you sick.

syn2.tip: Think of "toxic fumes" from paint or smoke. Breathing them can hurt your body, so toxic means harmful to health.

sc2.stem: The shiny berries looked as sweet as blueberries, but the park ranger warned that they were _____ and that eating even a few could send someone to the hospital.

traps.why: "But" turns away from sweet looks; they are dangerous, not delicious.
Ripeness doesn't send people to the hospital.
Being rare isn't dangerous; the warning is about getting sick.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with looking sweet, and "could send someone to the hospital" tells you the berries are poisonous.

decoys.why: The ranger warned they could send someone to the hospital, so they are not the best.
Berries are not protected from disease; the ranger warns they make people sick.
The ranger's warning is about danger from eating them, not about good reasons.
Even a few could hurt someone, so the problem is poison, not too many.
The ranger warns the berries are dangerous to eat, not that they come first.
Nothing is shared here; the warning is that eating the berries is dangerous.

meaning: publicly support or speak in favor of
example: Students advocated for more vegetarian options at lunch.
hook: Advocate holds the root voc, meaning voice or call: you use your voice for a cause you believe in.

traps.why: Oppose is the opposite: it means to fight against something.
Allocate looks similar but means to hand out or divide up.
You can discuss an idea without being for it at all.

syn1.tip: Inside advocate is voc, meaning voice. To advocate is to use your voice for something you support.

sc1.stem: Worried about plastic in the ocean, the eco club began to _____ a ban on plastic straws, writing letters and giving speeches to the school board.

traps.why: The club worries about plastic, so it would push for the ban, not against it.
Letters and speeches push for a ban; they are not just studying it.
Mention is too weak for writing letters and giving speeches.

sc1.tip: "Worried about plastic" plus "writing letters and giving speeches" shows the club is pushing hard for the ban.

decoys.why: The club wrote letters and gave speeches to push for the ban, not hold it back.
The club wanted the ban to happen, so they would not try to crush it.
The club had to write to the school board, so they could not force the ban themselves.
The club was sincerely asking for a real ban, not making up something false.

traps.why: Arguing against something is the opposite of advocating for it.
Voc means call, but advocate means supporting a cause, not calling someone.
Voting happens around causes, but advocating means speaking up for one.

syn2.tip: A lawyer is sometimes called an advocate because she speaks up for her client.

sc2.stem: Although Marco disliked giving speeches, he stood up at the town meeting to _____ for a new skate park, because he believed his friends needed a safe place to ride.

traps.why: Apologizing shows regret, but Marco believes in the park.
Waiting is too passive; he stood up and spoke.
Paying is about money, but the clue is about speaking up.

sc2.tip: "Stood up at the town meeting" and "because he believed his friends needed" show he is speaking in favor of the park.

decoys.why: Marco spoke up to support a skate park, not to pay anyone back for one.

meaning: lasting a long time or returning often
example: Her chronic allergies flared up every single spring.
hook: Chronic contains chron, meaning time, as in chronological: a chronic problem sticks around for a long time.

traps.why: Short-lived is the opposite: it means ending quickly.
Chron means time, but chronic is not about good timing.
Chronic problems can hurt, but chronic means lasting long.

syn1.tip: Chron means time, as in chronological. Chronic things take up lots of time because they keep going or coming back.

sc1.stem: Unlike a cold that goes away in a week, Ryan's _____ back pain has bothered him almost every day for over three years.

traps.why: Temporary means short, but this pain has lasted three years.
Sharp describes how pain feels, not how long it lasts.
Chron means time, but timely means well timed, which makes no sense here.

sc1.tip: "Unlike a cold that goes away in a week" and "for over three years" tell you the pain lasts a long time.

decoys.why: The pain has lasted over three years, so it is not something that comes before a main event.
Ryan has lived with the pain for years, so it is not deadly.
The sentence is about pain that lasts a long time, not something poisonous.
Immune means protected from illness, which does not describe pain that keeps bothering him.
Ryan's back pain is his alone, so it is not shared by two people.

traps.why: Brief and sudden is the opposite of something that keeps lasting.
A chronic problem can be mild; chronic is about how long.
Chron means time, but chronic does not mean well timed.

syn2.tip: Doctors call an illness chronic when it lasts for months or keeps returning, unlike a quick cold.

sc2.stem: Because Leo's cough was _____, returning every winter for five years, his doctor finally sent him to a specialist to find the cause.

traps.why: Brief is the opposite of returning every winter for five years.
Spreading to others is a different idea from coming back for years.
Loud describes sound, but the clue is about how long it lasts.

sc2.tip: "Returning every winter for five years" restates the blank, so you need a word for something that keeps coming back.

decoys.why: The cough came back for five years, so it clearly did not cause death.
The clue is that the cough kept returning every winter, not that it was poisonous.
A cough returning for five years is long lasting, not something that comes first.
Leo kept getting the cough, so nothing was protected from it.
Leo's cough was his own, not something shared equally between people.

meaning: very loving and loyal
example: The devoted fan attended every home game for twenty years.
hook: Picture a devoted dog greeting you at the door every single day, no matter what.

traps.why: Faithless is the opposite: it means not loyal.
Divided looks a bit like devoted but means split apart.
A devoted person may feel grateful, but devoted means loving and loyal.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "devote your time." A devoted person gives their heart and time to someone again and again.

sc1.stem: The _____ dog waited by the front door every afternoon until its owner came home from school, never missing a single day.

traps.why: A disloyal dog would not wait every single day.
A stray dog has no owner to wait for.
Devious looks similar but means sneaky.

sc1.tip: "Every afternoon" and "never missing a single day" show a dog that loves its owner and stays faithful.

decoys.why: A dog waiting faithfully every single day is not lacking energy or interest.
Waiting patiently every afternoon is the opposite of acting quickly without thinking.
The dog waits because it expects its owner, so it is not without hope.
The sentence shows the dog's loyalty, not that it is poisonous.
Nothing in the sentence is about the dog being qualified for something.

traps.why: Coldly distant is the opposite of warm, loyal love.
This turns loyalty into something negative, but devoted is a warm word.
Mildly interested is far too weak for devoted.

syn2.tip: Devoted carries a warm feeling of strong love and loyalty, so look for the choice that is both warm and strong.

sc2.stem: Although the team lost every game that season, its _____ fans still packed the bleachers each Saturday, cheering as loudly as ever.

traps.why: Unfaithful fans would stop coming, but these still packed the bleachers.
Former fans have stopped supporting the team, but these still show up.
Angry fans would boo, not cheer loudly every week.

sc2.tip: "Although the team lost every game" contrasts with "still packed the bleachers," so the fans stayed loyal.

decoys.why: The fans cheered as loudly as ever, so they were not lacking energy.
The team lost, but the fans kept cheering, so they were not hopeless.
The fans were cheering loudly, not sadly longing for something.
The sentence praises the fans for sticking with their team, not calling them harmful.

meaning: an idea or belief
example: Ella had a notion that the old house was haunted.
hook: Notion and notice both come from a Latin word meaning to know; a notion is something your mind believes.

traps.why: Motion looks like notion but means movement.
A notion is something believed, which may not be a fact.
A question asks something; a notion is something you think.

syn1.tip: You may have heard "I have no notion of what you mean." A notion is something in your mind.

sc1.stem: Many people hold the _____ that bats are blind, but in fact most bats can see quite well and also use echoes to find their way.

traps.why: "In fact" shows the idea is wrong, so it cannot be a fact.
Motion looks like notion but means movement.
Truth is too strong; the sentence says this belief is wrong.

sc1.tip: "But in fact" shows that what people believe is wrong, so the blank must be a belief, not something true.

decoys.why: Thinking bats are blind is a belief, not a complaint about something unfair.
People believe bats are blind; no ruler gave an official order about it.
Believing bats are blind is an idea, not a plan for reaching a goal.
The sentence is about a mistaken belief, not a sign of something to come.
You cannot hold a written request that bats are blind; this is about a belief.

traps.why: Doubt means not believing, the opposite of a notion.
Proof shows something is true; a notion is only believed.
Nation looks like notion but means a country.

syn2.tip: In "the notion that bats are blind," notion means something people believe, whether or not it is true.

sc2.stem: Jake gave up the silly _____ that he could finish his science project in one night after he stayed up until midnight and was only half done.

traps.why: A fact can't be silly or wrong, and Jake's idea was wrong.
Motion looks like notion but means movement.
Finishing quickly is something Jake hoped for, not feared.

sc2.tip: "Gave up the silly" plus "that he could finish" shows he dropped a mistaken belief once he was only half done.

decoys.why: Jake had a silly idea about finishing quickly, not an official order from a ruler.
Jake's belief that he could finish in one night is not a complaint.
Jake gave up an idea in his head, not a signed written request.
The sentence is about Jake's mistaken belief, not a sign of the future.
The word must be a belief that he could finish, not a natural talent.

meaning: coming before the main event
example: The preliminary round decided who would reach the finals.
hook: Pre means before, so preliminary rounds come before the big final, like tryouts before the real show.

traps.why: Final is the opposite: it means coming last.
Primary looks similar but means main or most important.
The middle looks like limit, but preliminary means coming first.

syn1.tip: Start with pre, meaning before. Preliminary things happen first, before the main event.

sc1.stem: Only swimmers who post fast times in the _____ heats on Friday morning will advance to the championship final on Saturday night.

traps.why: The final is on Saturday; these heats come before it.
Preliminary looks like limit, but limited heats makes no sense here.
Friday heats come earlier than Saturday's final, not later.

sc1.tip: "Friday morning" heats lead to the "championship final on Saturday night," so the blank describes rounds that come before.

decoys.why: Swimmers become eligible by racing; the heats themselves come before the final.
The heats happen once on Friday before the final, not over and over for a long time.
The sentence is about races held before the final, not anything poisonous.
The clue is that the heats come before Saturday's final, not that something is shared.
Heats cannot feel sad longing; the sentence describes races that come first.

traps.why: Coming last is the opposite of preliminary.
The main event matters most; preliminary steps only lead up to it.
Preliminary only looks like limit; it means coming before.

syn2.tip: You may have heard "preliminary results" on the news: early numbers that come before the final count.

sc2.stem: The architect showed us only a _____ sketch of the new library, a rough first drawing she would improve many times before building began.

traps.why: She will improve it many times, so it is not final.
Detailed doesn't fit a rough drawing that still needs work.
Primary means main, but this sketch is just a rough first try.

sc2.tip: The phrase "a rough first drawing" restates the blank, telling you the sketch comes before the real plans.

decoys.why: It was a rough first drawing she would improve, not the best version.
Verbose describes using too many words, but this is a rough drawing.
The sketch is a first draft before building, not something lasting a long time.
A rough first drawing of a library does not cause death or disaster.
A sketch cannot feel hopeless; the clue says it was a rough first drawing.

meaning: expressing opinions loudly and freely
example: Parents were vocal about wanting a crosswalk near the school.
hook: Vocal comes from voc, meaning voice: vocal people use their voices to say exactly what they think.
