traps.why: Silent is the opposite of speaking up freely.
Vocal music means singing, but here vocal means speaking your mind.
Local rhymes with vocal but means nearby.

syn1.tip: Voc means voice. A vocal person lets everyone hear their opinions.

sc1.stem: Most students quietly accepted the new lunch schedule, but a few were very _____ about their objections, complaining loudly at every assembly.

traps.why: "But" contrasts with the quiet students, so these ones were loud.
Calm doesn't match complaining loudly at every assembly.
Vocal can mean singing, but these students were complaining.

sc1.tip: "But" sets up a contrast with "quietly accepted," and "complaining loudly" tells you these students spoke up.

decoys.why: The few students complained loudly at every assembly, so they had plenty of energy, not none.
Loud complaining at every assembly shows fighting spirit, not hopeless sadness.
They complained loudly at every assembly, which is the opposite of being uncomfortable about speaking.

traps.why: Vocal people complain openly, so this is the opposite.
That's vocal as in singing, not speaking your opinions.
Vocal people speak openly, but not always in an angry shout.

syn2.tip: Picture parents who are vocal about a crosswalk: they speak up at every meeting until someone listens.

sc2.stem: Because Grandpa was so _____ about his dislike of loud music, everyone at the reunion knew exactly how he felt before the band even started playing.

traps.why: If he kept it secret, nobody would know how he felt.
Vocal can describe singing, but Grandpa was sharing an opinion.
Being confused would not make everyone know exactly how he felt.

sc2.tip: "Everyone knew exactly how he felt" is the effect, so Grandpa must have spoken his opinion openly.

decoys.why: Everyone knew how Grandpa felt, so he spoke up strongly rather than showing no interest.
An awkward person might hide his feelings, but everyone knew exactly how Grandpa felt.
The sentence is about Grandpa making his opinion known, not about him feeling hopeless.

meaning: protected from a disease or effect
example: After having chickenpox, she was immune to the disease.
hook: Your immune system is your body's guard, keeping germs from making you sick.

traps.why: Vulnerable is the opposite: it means easily harmed.
Healthy people can still catch a disease; immune means protected from it.
Immobile looks similar but means unable to move.

syn1.tip: Think of your "immune system," which fights off germs so they can't make you sick.

sc1.stem: Because she had received the measles vaccine as a baby, Fatima was _____ to the disease and did not get sick when it spread through the camp.

traps.why: Vulnerable means easily harmed, but she did not get sick.
Allergies are about the body too, but the vaccine kept her safe.
A vaccine doesn't make you exposed; it explains why she stayed well.

sc1.tip: "Because she had received the measles vaccine" is the cause, and "did not get sick" is the effect, so she was protected.

decoys.why: Fatima did not get sick because she was protected; she was not poisonous to the disease.
The vaccine protected Fatima; she was not deadly to the disease.
Nobody is loving and loyal to a disease; the vaccine kept her from catching it.
The sentence explains why she did not get sick, not how she was connected to the disease.

traps.why: Exposed means open to harm, the opposite of protected.
Contagious means able to spread a disease, not safe from it.
Immortal looks similar but means never dying.

syn2.tip: Immune things are shielded. When something can't affect you, like a virus after a vaccine, you are protected from it.

sc2.stem: Most of the class giggled at every joke in the play, but Oscar seemed _____ to the humor, sitting with a straight face the whole time.

traps.why: Sensitive means easily affected, but the jokes didn't affect Oscar.
Everyone heard the jokes; the point is they had no effect on him.
Being drawn to the humor would make him laugh, not keep a straight face.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Oscar with the giggling class, and "a straight face the whole time" shows the jokes had no effect on him.

decoys.why: Oscar kept a straight face, so he was not loving the humor at all.
The sentence says the jokes did not affect Oscar, not that he was connected to them.
Oscar was simply unaffected by the jokes; he was not poisonous to the humor.

meaning: more than is reasonable or needed
example: Excessive screen time can make it hard to fall asleep.
hook: Excessive is what you get when something goes past enough, like frosting piled three inches high on a cupcake.

traps.why: Moderate means a sensible amount, the opposite of excessive.
Expensive is about cost; excessive means too much of anything.
Exciting starts the same way but means thrilling.

syn1.tip: Inside excessive is "excess," meaning extra. Excessive amounts go beyond what is sensible.

sc1.stem: The coach warned that _____ training, such as running twenty miles every day, could cause injuries rather than make the players stronger.

traps.why: Twenty miles a day is not moderate, and moderate training rarely injures.
Useful training would make players stronger, not hurt them.
Cost isn't the problem here; the amount of running is.

sc1.tip: "Twenty miles every day" and "cause injuries rather than make the players stronger" show the training goes far past what is reasonable.

decoys.why: Running twenty miles every day is far too much effort, not a lack of energy.
The coach is warning about too much training, not training that comes first.
The example is about how much the players run, not whether they chose to.
The coach warns of injuries, not death, so this word is far too strong.
The problem is the huge amount of running, not whether the training is fair.

traps.why: Just enough is the opposite of going past the limit.
A bit extra is too weak; excessive means far too much.
Costly is about price, not about having too much.

syn2.tip: Think of "excess baggage," luggage over the limit. Excessive means more than the limit or more than needed.

sc2.stem: Mom said a little salt makes popcorn tasty, but the _____ amount Leo poured on made it so salty that nobody could eat a single bite.

traps.why: A tiny amount would not make the popcorn too salty to eat.
Perfect is positive, but nobody could eat the popcorn.
Salt's cost isn't the point; the amount ruined the popcorn.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts "a little salt" with Leo's amount, and "nobody could eat a single bite" shows he used way too much.

decoys.why: The popcorn was too salty to eat, so the amount was not reasonable.
The salt ruined the taste; nothing in the sentence says it could kill anyone.
The sentence is about how much salt Leo used, not when he added it.
The problem is that there was too much salt, not that it was easy to see.
Leo poured the salt himself, so nothing was shared between people here.

meaning: causing death or disaster
example: Some wild mushrooms contain poison that can be fatal if eaten.
hook: Fatal comes from the same Latin word as fate: a fatal mistake seals someone's fate, bringing death or disaster.

traps.why: Harmless is the opposite: it means causing no harm.
Final looks similar but means last.
Painful is too weak; fatal means causing death.

syn1.tip: You may know the phrase "a fatal accident," one in which someone died. Fatal means causing death.

sc1.stem: The hikers learned that eating certain wild berries could be _____, so the guide warned them never to taste anything they could not identify.

traps.why: Healthy berries wouldn't need such a strict warning.
Delicious is a happy word, but the guide is warning of danger.
Messy is far too mild for a warning never to taste anything.

sc1.tip: "So the guide warned them never to taste anything" is the effect, so the berries must be dangerous enough to kill.

decoys.why: The guide warned them because the berries are dangerous, not because eating them is fair.
A warning not to taste them means the berries are dangerous, not just a choice.
The guide gave a serious warning, so eating the berries clearly matters a lot.
The guide warns about danger from one taste, not about something that keeps returning.
The warning is about danger, not about eating berries being strange.

traps.why: Giving life is the opposite of causing death.
Minor harm is far too weak for fatal.
Fatal is related to fate, but it means deadly, not destined.

syn2.tip: Fatal goes with words like "fatal crash" or "fatal disease," all about something that kills or ruins.

sc2.stem: Most mistakes in a chess game can be fixed later, but leaving your queen unguarded is often a _____ error that ends the game within a few moves.

traps.why: A minor error could be fixed, but this one ends the game.
Clever is positive, but this error ruins the game.
Being common doesn't explain why the error ends the game.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts mistakes that "can be fixed later" with one that "ends the game," so the blank means disastrous.

decoys.why: The sentence stresses that this error ends the game, not that it comes early.
The error is one move that ends the game, not one that keeps happening.
An error that ends the game quickly is a terrible move, not a sensible one.
Leaving your queen unguarded is your own mistake, not one shared by both players.
The sentence contrasts fixable mistakes with ones that end the game, not connected ones.

meaning: full of life and excitement
example: The children had an animated discussion about their favorite dinosaurs.
hook: Animated cartoons are drawings brought to life; an animated person seems bursting with life too.

traps.why: Dull is the opposite: it means lacking life or energy.
Animated films are drawn, but an animated person is full of energy.
Animated people are excited, not angry.

syn1.tip: Animated cartoons make drawings move as if alive. An animated person is full of that same life and energy.

sc1.stem: Usually quiet in class, Priyanka became _____ when the topic turned to space travel, waving her hands and talking excitedly about Mars.

traps.why: She was talking excitedly, so she was not silent.
Bored is the wrong feeling; she was waving her hands with excitement.
Nervous people may fidget, but she was talking excitedly, not worrying.

sc1.tip: "Usually quiet" contrasts with "waving her hands and talking excitedly," so she suddenly became full of life.

decoys.why: Priyanka waved her hands and talked excitedly, so she was lively, not uncomfortable.
Getting excited about a favorite topic is normal, not very strange.
The sentence describes Priyanka's excitement, not whether she was off topic.
Waving her hands and talking excitedly shows liveliness, not being qualified for something.
The clue is her excited talking, which describes energy, not something being obvious.

traps.why: Low on energy is the opposite of animated.
That fits animated movies, not lively people.
Slightly interested is too weak; animated means excited and lively.

syn2.tip: Think of an animated conversation: people talking fast, waving their hands, and clearly excited.

sc2.stem: The tour guide was so _____ as she described the dinosaur bones, jumping and making roaring sounds, that even the sleepy kids sat up and paid attention.

traps.why: A dull guide would not make sleepy kids sit up.
Animated cartoons are drawn, but here the guide is full of energy.
Her roaring was for fun; frightened is the wrong feeling.

sc2.tip: "Jumping and making roaring sounds" made "even the sleepy kids" pay attention, so the guide must have been full of energy.

decoys.why: Jumping and roaring that woke up sleepy kids shows lively energy, not discomfort.
The clue is her jumping and roaring, which describes energy, not staying on topic.
Jumping and roaring show excitement, not whether she was being fair.
She was describing the dinosaur bones, so she was on topic and full of energy.
The sentence describes how lively the guide was, not how well things work together.

meaning: morally right and fair
example: Returning the lost wallet was the ethical thing to do.
hook: An ethical person does what is morally right, even when nobody is watching.

traps.why: Dishonest is the opposite of ethical.
Legal means allowed by law, and some legal things are still unfair.
Ethnic looks similar but describes a people or culture, not right behavior.

syn1.tip: Ethics are ideas about right and wrong, so an ethical choice is the morally right one.","x":""}

sc1.stem: Though copying answers from the leaked test would have been easy, Kwame made the _____ choice and told his teacher what he had found.

traps.why: Telling his teacher was honest, so dishonest is the opposite.
Copying was the convenient choice; Kwame chose the harder, right one.
Telling the teacher is the opposite of sneaky.

sc1.tip: "Though" sets up a contrast: copying was "easy," but Kwame did the right thing and "told his teacher."

decoys.why: Kwame did the honest thing by telling his teacher, so his choice was not harmful or poisonous.
Telling a teacher about a leaked test causes no death or disaster, so fatal makes no sense.
Nothing in the sentence says his choice went too far; it says he chose honesty over cheating.
His choice was directly connected to the leaked test, so irrelevant does not fit.
The sentence is about right versus wrong, not about something coming before a main event.
Kwame made this choice on his own, so it was not shared by two people.

traps.why: Wrong and unfair is the opposite of ethical.
Laws and ethics overlap, but legal does not always mean morally right.
That describes ethnic, a lookalike word, not ethical.

syn2.tip: If you have heard of a "code of ethics," it lists the right and fair ways to behave.

sc2.stem: Maya refused to share the embarrassing photo of her classmate, because she believed that spreading hurtful pictures for laughs was never the _____ thing to do.

traps.why: The photo was shared for laughs, but Maya cared about what was right.
Popularity is not the point; Maya refused because it was hurtful.
Cruel is the opposite; Maya avoided the photo because it was wrong.

sc2.tip: "Refused" and "because... hurtful" show Maya was choosing what is morally right.

decoys.why: The sentence is about whether spreading photos is right, not about speaking opinions loudly.
Maya refused because hurting people is wrong, not because the act would be clumsy.
Spreading photos for laughs might seem lively, but the sentence asks whether it is right.
Nothing here comes before a main event; the sentence is about doing the morally right thing.
The sentence judges whether an action is fair, not whether it lasts a long time.
Saying spreading photos is never the irrelevant thing to do makes no sense in this sentence.

meaning: a doorway; the point where something begins
example: The puppy paused at the threshold before entering the new house.
hook: A threshold is the strip under a doorway; step over it and something new begins.

traps.why: The center is the middle, the opposite of the edge where something starts.
A ceiling is part of a room, but a threshold is at the doorway's bottom.
Threshold seems to contain hold, but it has nothing to do with gripping.

syn1.tip: Picture a doorway: the threshold is the edge you step across to go inside.

sc1.stem: After years of careful experiments, the young researchers believed they stood at the _____ of a major discovery that would soon change medicine.

traps.why: The discovery would happen soon, so they were at its start, not its end.
Results come after a discovery, which had not happened yet.
Middle means partway in, but the discovery had not begun.

sc1.tip: "Would soon change medicine" tells you the discovery had not happened yet, so they were at its beginning.

decoys.why: A premise is an idea an argument rests on; you cannot stand at the premise of a discovery.
An omen is a sign, but the researchers stood at the starting point of a discovery.
A predecessor is a person who came before, not the point where a discovery begins.
The sentence describes being about to begin something, not having more than is needed.
Their careful work was leading to a real discovery, not a mistaken belief.
Nothing here shows respect; the sentence says they were right at the start of a discovery.

traps.why: A final stage is the end, the opposite of a starting point.
A porch is near the door, but a threshold is the doorway itself.
The hold in threshold does not mean holding on to something.

syn2.tip: "On the threshold of" something means just about to begin it.

sc2.stem: Nervous about her first day, Lena lingered at the _____ of the classroom, but once she spotted her best friend inside, she walked straight in.

traps.why: She had not gone in yet, so she could not be at the center.
A window is part of a room, but she walked in through the door.
The back is inside the room, and she had not entered yet.

sc2.tip: She "walked straight in" afterward, so before that she was standing at the doorway.

decoys.why: Her best friend appears later, but Lena lingered at a place, the doorway, not a friendship.
Lena then walked straight in, so she was standing at a doorway, not a relationship.
Lena was nervous, not hostile, and she lingered at a spot by the door.
Lena had no complaint; she paused at the entrance before walking in.
You cannot linger at an extra amount; she waited at the classroom's doorway.
An official order is not a place, and Lena lingered at the entrance.

meaning: a feeling or opinion
example: Her card expressed a sentiment of deep gratitude.
hook: Sentiment comes from the same Latin word as sense and sentimental: it is all about what you feel.

traps.why: A fact can be proved, while a sentiment is a feeling.
Sentence looks similar but means a group of words.
Cards hold greetings, but a sentiment is the feeling behind the words.

syn1.tip: Think of "sentimental," which describes someone full of feelings.

sc1.stem: When Dev said the field trip was the best day of the year, nearly everyone nodded, because his _____ was shared by the whole class.

traps.why: Calling the trip the best day is praise, not a complaint.
Dev said it out loud to everyone, so it was no secret.
Everyone nodded in agreement, the opposite of doubt.

sc1.tip: Dev "said" something and everyone "nodded," so the blank names the opinion they all shared.

decoys.why: Dev praised the field trip as the best day, so he was not complaining.
Calling the trip the best day shows happiness, not hostility toward anyone.
Everyone nodded at Dev's opinion, not at a natural talent he had.
Dev said what he felt about a past day, not a sign of something to come.
The class agreed with what Dev felt, not with any skill or grace he showed.
The class shared Dev's opinion, not a person who held a position before him.

traps.why: Proof shows something is true; a sentiment is just what someone feels or thinks.
A speech may share a sentiment, but it is the talk, not the feeling.
Scent sounds like the start of sentiment but means a smell.

syn2.tip: "I share your sentiment" means "I agree with what you think or feel."

sc2.stem: Although most of the town wanted the old library torn down, Mrs. Ortiz's _____ was the opposite: she believed the building should be saved and repaired.

traps.why: She believed something, which is an opinion, not proof.
A rumor is gossip passed around, but this is what she herself believed.
Repairs cost money, but the sentence is about what she believed.

sc2.tip: "Was the opposite: she believed" shows the blank is what she thought, an opinion against the town's.

decoys.why: The sentence says she believed the building should be saved, describing her opinion, not a signed request.
A benefactor is a person, but the blank is what Mrs. Ortiz believed.
The sentence describes what she believed, not a gift to show respect.
The building has doorways, but the blank describes her opinion about the library.
Her extra amount being the opposite makes no sense; the sentence is about her belief.
The sentence compares opinions about the library, not natural abilities.

meaning: very strange or unusual
example: Fans wore bizarre costumes to the comic book convention.
hook: Bizarre sounds like bazaar, a market, but means wildly strange, like a cat wearing a tuxedo.

traps.why: Ordinary is the opposite of bizarre.
Strange things can be scary, but bizarre only means very odd.
Costumes can be fancy, but bizarre means weird, not elegant.

syn1.tip: Bizarre things make you stare and say, "That is so weird."

sc1.stem: The deep-sea anglerfish looks truly _____, with a glowing lure dangling from its head and needle-like teeth that seem too long for its mouth.

traps.why: A glowing lure and huge teeth are not ordinary at all.
The details describe something strange and creepy, not lovely.
Needle teeth and a dangling lure describe an odd look, not a graceful one.

sc1.tip: The details after the comma, a "glowing lure dangling from its head" and teeth "too long for its mouth," describe something very strange.

decoys.why: The glowing lure and long teeth make the fish look strange, not full of excitement.
Nothing about the lure or teeth shows protection from disease; they show how strange it looks.
A fish cannot look morally right; the details describe how odd it looks.
Teeth that seem too long for its mouth suggest something strange, not things fitting well together.
The sentence describes the fish's weird features, not whether it qualifies for something.
How a fish looks cannot be done by choice; the details show it looks strange.

traps.why: Plain and normal is the opposite of bizarre.
Something bizarre can be loud, but bizarre means strange.
Bizarre is much stronger than slightly different.

syn2.tip: Bizarre is stronger than odd; it means so strange it is hard to believe.

sc2.stem: Most of the science fair projects were ordinary volcanoes and plant studies, but Jamal's was _____: a robot hamster that played the harmonica while reciting poems.

traps.why: The word but sets Jamal's project apart from the typical ones.
A singing robot hamster is the opposite of a simple project.
Nothing says it was unfinished; the clue is how strange it was.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Jamal's project with the "ordinary" ones, and a harmonica-playing robot hamster is wildly strange.

decoys.why: The hamster recites poems, but the sentence contrasts ordinary projects with a very strange one.
The sentence contrasts ordinary projects with Jamal's strange one, not something that came first.
Nothing here is about lasting a long time; his project was unusual compared to the ordinary ones.
The contrast is ordinary versus strange, not right versus wrong.
A harmonica-playing robot hamster is weird, not poisonous.
The project was Jamal's alone, and the sentence stresses how unusual it was.

meaning: done by choice, not required
example: Attending the weekend review session is voluntary.
hook: Volunteers do voluntary work: they choose to help, and no one makes them.

traps.why: Required is the opposite of voluntary.
Volunteers are helpful, but voluntary means done by choice.
Many people may join, but voluntary is about choosing, not popularity.

syn1.tip: Think of a "volunteer," someone who chooses to help; voluntary means done by choice.

sc1.stem: The Saturday study session is completely _____; no one is required to attend, but those who come usually do better on the exam.

traps.why: No one is required to come, so the session is not necessary.
The sentence says nothing about crowds, only about choosing to attend.
Those who come do better, and the clue is about choice, not dullness.

sc1.tip: The words after the semicolon, "no one is required to attend," explain the blank: going is your choice.

decoys.why: It happens before the exam, but the clue says no one is required to attend.
The clue is that attending is not required, not that students qualify to attend.
Nothing says the session is too much; the sentence says attending is your choice.
The clue is about whether attending is required, not how often the session happens.
Those who come do better on the exam, so the session clearly matters.
The sentence says no one is required to come, not that the session is widespread.

traps.why: Being forced is the opposite of choosing.
Volunteers often help others, but voluntary just means chosen.
Volunteers may work in groups, but voluntary means by choice.

syn2.tip: "Involuntary" describes a sneeze you cannot stop; take away "in" and voluntary means something you chose.

sc2.stem: Because the art club is _____, Priya only goes on weeks when she feels like painting, and nobody marks her absent when she skips.

traps.why: If it were required, someone would mark her absent.
Popularity would not explain why nobody marks her absent.
Painting is messy, but that does not explain skipping freely.

sc2.tip: "Only goes... when she feels like" and "nobody marks her absent" show attending is her choice.

decoys.why: Priya skips whenever she wants, so the club is not about loyal attendance.
The clue is that nobody marks her absent, meaning going is a choice, not that it is lively.
The sentence is about attending only when she feels like it, not something long lasting.
Nothing says the club is too much; she goes only when she chooses.
Being widespread would not explain why nobody marks her absent when she skips.
A poisonous club makes no sense; the sentence shows attending is up to her.

meaning: plain to see; obvious
example: Her joy was evident from her huge smile.
hook: Evident contains vid, meaning see, as in video: when something is evident, anyone can see it.

traps.why: Hidden is the opposite of evident.
Evil starts like evident but means very wicked.
Evident things are easy to see, not necessarily important.

syn1.tip: Inside evident is "vid," meaning see, as in "video." Evident things are easy to see.

sc1.stem: From the muddy paw prints across the kitchen floor and the empty food bowl, it was _____ that the dog had somehow gotten inside.

traps.why: The paw prints and empty bowl remove any doubt.
Muddy floors are not lucky; the clues just make the answer clear.
The clues were all over the floor, the opposite of secret.

sc1.tip: The "muddy paw prints" and "empty food bowl" are clues that make the answer plain to see.

decoys.why: The paw prints and empty bowl point right to the dog, so they are anything but unconnected.
The clues show what happened, not whether it was morally right.
The sentence is about what the clues prove, not about anyone choosing to do something.
Nothing in the sentence involves death or disaster, just a dog sneaking inside.

traps.why: Hard to notice is the opposite of evident.
Evidence is used in court, but evident just means clearly seen.
Vid means see, but evident means obvious, not pretty.

syn2.tip: Think of "self-evident": something so clear it needs no explaining.

sc2.stem: Leo tried to hide his disappointment about losing the spelling bee, but his slumped shoulders and quiet voice made his sadness _____ to everyone.

traps.why: The word but shows his attempt to hide his sadness failed.
Losing may embarrass him, but the clue is that others could see his sadness.
Slumped shoulders show sadness that others noticed, nothing funny.

sc2.tip: "Tried to hide... but" signals the opposite happened: his shoulders and voice let everyone see his sadness.

decoys.why: His slumped shoulders showed his sadness clearly, so it was not unimportant or unconnected.
Feeling sad after losing is normal, and the sentence is about everyone seeing it.
His sadness did not poison anyone; his body language simply made it easy to see.
Losing a spelling bee is not deadly; the sentence is about his sadness showing.

meaning: not connected to the topic
example: His comment about pizza was irrelevant to our science discussion.
hook: Ir- means not, so irrelevant means not relevant: off topic, like talking about pizza in math class.

traps.why: Connected is the opposite of irrelevant.
Irritating looks similar but means annoying.
An irrelevant point can be true; it is just off topic.

syn1.tip: Ir- means not, as in "irregular." Irrelevant means not relevant, not connected to the point.

sc1.stem: During the debate about recycling, Simone kept bringing up her favorite movies, points that were _____ to the topic and wasted everyone's time.

traps.why: Movies have nothing to do with recycling, so they were not related.
Her points wasted everyone's time, so they were not helpful.
Movies can entertain, but the clue is that they were off topic.

sc1.tip: "Favorite movies" in a debate "about recycling" that "wasted everyone's time" had nothing to do with the topic.

decoys.why: Her movie points had nothing to do with recycling, so they were not devoted to the topic.
Points cannot be protected from a topic; the sentence says they did not belong.
The sentence is about points being off topic, not about anything being easily harmed.
Her points wasted time because they were off topic, not because they were poisonous.

traps.why: Right on point is the opposite of irrelevant.
Irrelevant is about being off topic, not about being false.
Volume has nothing to do with whether a point fits the topic.

syn2.tip: Ask yourself, "Does it relate?" If not, it is irrelevant.

sc2.stem: Mr. Chen said our book reports should focus only on the story's plot and characters, so details about the author's pet cat were _____ and should be left out.

traps.why: Essential details would be kept, but these should be left out.
The cat may be cute, but the clue is that it is off topic.
True facts can still be left out if they do not fit the topic.

sc2.tip: "Focus only on... plot and characters, so" explains why cat details get left out: they do not connect to the report.

decoys.why: Details that fit the report would stay in, but these should be left out.
The cat details are cut for being off topic, not for being right or wrong morally.
Being obvious is no reason to cut details; they are cut for not matching the topic.
Nothing is being shared between people here; the cat details simply do not fit the topic.

meaning: able to work or exist well together
example: This charger is not compatible with my phone.
hook: Com- means together: compatible things go together, like a charger that actually fits your phone.

traps.why: Mismatched is the opposite of compatible.
Comfortable looks similar but means relaxed and at ease.
A charger can be portable, but compatible means it works with your device.

syn1.tip: Game boxes say "compatible with your console," meaning the two work together.

sc1.stem: The new video game would not run on Kofi's old console, because the two systems simply were not _____ with each other.

traps.why: Machines are not comfortable; the problem is they cannot work together.
Systems are not familiar with each other; the game simply would not run.
Competitive looks similar, but the issue is working together, not competing.

sc1.tip: The game "would not run" "because" of the blank, so the two systems could not work together.

decoys.why: Game systems do not speak their opinions; the problem is they cannot work together.
Machines are not morally right or wrong; the game just would not run on the console.
The systems failed because they could not work together, not because something went unstated.

traps.why: Unable to connect is the opposite of compatible.
That describes portable gadgets, not ones that work together.
That describes competitive, a lookalike word.

syn2.tip: Com means together, as in "combine"; compatible things can go together without problems.

sc2.stem: Mia and Jada argue about everything from music to pizza toppings, yet their friendship has lasted because their personalities are surprisingly _____ where it truly matters.

traps.why: The word yet shows their personalities fit despite the arguing.
Arguing might seem stubborn, but the friendship lasted because they fit together.
Competitive looks similar, but a lasting friendship needs people who get along.

sc2.tip: "Yet" and "has lasted" signal that despite the arguing, their personalities fit together well.

decoys.why: Their friendship has lasted, so their personalities must work well together, not poison each other.
Arguing loudly does not explain why the friendship lasted; the word yet signals the opposite.
Being strange would not explain why their friendship has lasted where it matters.
The sentence says their personalities are why the friendship lasted, so they clearly matter.

meaning: stated clearly and in detail
example: The recipe gave explicit instructions for every step.
hook: Explicit instructions spell out every single step, leaving nothing for you to guess.

traps.why: Vague is the opposite of explicit.
Explosive starts the same way but means likely to blow up.
Clear directions can be short; explicit is about clarity, not length.

syn1.tip: Explicit is the opposite of "implicit," which means hinted. Explicit means stated clearly.

sc1.stem: Unlike the vague hint she gave yesterday, Ms. Romero's directions today were _____: write exactly two pages, double-spaced, citing three library books.

traps.why: The word unlike shows today's directions were not vague.
Exact page counts and sources leave nothing mysterious.
The clue is about how clear the directions were, not whether they were required.

sc1.tip: "Unlike the vague hint" sets up a contrast, and "exactly two pages" shows the directions were clear and detailed.

decoys.why: The directions say write exactly two pages, so the assignment is required, not optional.
Directions about the assignment are on topic; the contrast is with yesterday's vague hint.
Two pages with three sources is ordinary; the sentence contrasts clear directions with a vague hint.

traps.why: Hinting is the opposite of stating something clearly.
Shouting is about volume; explicit is about being clear and detailed.
Explain looks like explicit, but explicit means already stated clearly.

syn2.tip: Being explicit means you "spell it out," leaving no doubt about what you mean.

sc2.stem: Because the sign at the pool was _____ about the rules, listing 'no running, no diving, and no food on the deck,' nobody could claim they didn't know.

traps.why: An unclear sign would let people claim they did not know.
A faded sign would be hard to read, but this one was clear.
Nothing suggests the sign was silly; it listed rules plainly.

sc2.tip: The sign was "listing" each rule, so "nobody could claim they didn't know": it stated the rules clearly.

decoys.why: A sign cannot speak loudly; it simply listed the rules clearly in writing.
The sign is not lively or excited; it just spelled out the rules in detail.

meaning: a good quality in a person's character
example: Patience is a virtue when you are waiting for bread to rise.
hook: "Patience is a virtue" means waiting calmly is one of the good qualities a person can have.

traps.why: Evil is the opposite of virtue.
Virus looks similar but is a germ that makes you sick.
A talent is a skill; a virtue is a good quality of character.

syn1.tip: You have heard "patience is a virtue": it means patience is a good quality to have.

sc1.stem: Grandpa always said that honesty was the greatest _____ a person could have, more valuable than talent, wealth, or good looks.

traps.why: Grandpa praised honesty, so it is not a fault.
The sentence says honesty is more valuable than talent, so it is something else.
Honesty is a quality a person has, not a prize they receive.

sc1.tip: Honesty is part of character, and "more valuable than talent, wealth, or good looks" tells you it is a good quality.

decoys.why: The sentence says honesty beats talent, and an aptitude is a kind of talent.
Honesty is a part of character, not a skill done with grace.
Honesty is not an extra amount of something; the sentence even puts it above wealth.
Grandpa praises honesty as valuable, and hostility is never a prized quality.
Honesty is not a complaint; Grandpa is describing a good part of someone's character.

traps.why: A bad habit is the opposite of a virtue.
Skills are abilities; virtues are good parts of your character.
Virtue is a lasting quality in a person, not a passing feeling.

syn2.tip: Kindness, honesty, and courage are all virtues: good qualities in someone's character.

sc2.stem: Marcus is not the fastest runner or the best shooter on the team, but his greatest _____ is loyalty: he never gives up on a teammate.

traps.why: Never giving up on a teammate is a strength, not a weakness.
Speed and shooting are skills; loyalty is a quality of character.
Loyalty is part of who Marcus is, not a prize he won.

sc2.tip: "Not the fastest... but" turns from sports skills to "loyalty," a good quality of his character.

decoys.why: The sentence says his strength is not skill, and loyalty is about character.
Never giving up on a teammate shows loyalty, the opposite of hostility.
Loyalty is not a complaint; the sentence praises a good quality in Marcus.
Loyalty is part of who Marcus is, not a sign of something coming.

meaning: to keep something going over time
example: It is hard to sustain a fast pace for a whole marathon.
hook: A singer sustains a long note by holding it, and a piano's sustain pedal keeps the sound ringing.

traps.why: Abandon means to give up, the opposite of keeping something going.
Obtain also ends in -tain, but it means to get something.
Starting something is different from keeping it going over time.

syn1.tip: Think of a singer who sustains a note: she keeps it going. Maintain also means to keep something going.

sc1.stem: The runner started the race at a blistering speed, but she could not _____ that pace, and by the third lap she had slowed to a jog.

traps.why: She did slow down, so reducing her pace is what she actually did.
Runners record their times, but slowing down shows she couldn't keep the pace.
Obtain looks similar but means to get, and she already had the speed.

sc1.tip: The word "but" signals a contrast: a "blistering speed" at first, then "slowed to a jog." She could not keep that pace going.

decoys.why: The sentence says she wanted to keep her fast pace going, not put an end to it.
She was trying to keep the pace up, not hold it back.
You use up energy, not a pace, and the clue is about keeping speed going.
She already started at that pace, so the problem was keeping it, not starting it.
Weakening her own pace makes no sense when the sentence is about failing to keep it.
Decorating or adding details has nothing to do with keeping a running speed.

traps.why: Bringing something to a halt stops it, the opposite of sustaining it.
Getting underway is beginning, not keeping something going.
The parts may suggest holding under, but sustain means keep going.

syn2.tip: Picture a runner who sustains her speed for the whole race. She keeps going at that pace.

sc2.stem: Our campfire kept dying out, so Dad added dry logs every few minutes to _____ the flames until the marshmallows were finally golden brown.

traps.why: Extinguish means to put out, but Dad was adding logs to feed the fire.
Contain looks similar, but adding logs keeps flames going rather than holding them in.
You might inspect a fire, but adding logs is about keeping it burning.

sc2.tip: The fire "kept dying out," so Dad "added dry logs every few minutes." That is the cause and effect of keeping something going.

decoys.why: Dad added logs to keep the fire alive, not to put it out.
The fire kept dying, so Dad wanted to keep the flames going, not hold them back.
Adding logs feeds the fire, so it does not use up the flames.
Dad was helping the flames by adding logs, not weakening them.
You calm an upset person, and Dad wanted the flames to keep burning.
Dry logs keep a fire going; they do not decorate the flames.

meaning: force a rule or burden on others
example: The library imposed a fine for every late book.
hook: Impose comes from Latin words for put on: you impose a rule by putting it on people who didn't ask.

traps.why: Lifting a rule takes it away, the opposite of imposing one.
Expose looks similar but means to uncover or reveal.
Suggesting is far too gentle; imposing forces something on people.

syn1.tip: Think of a library that imposes a fine. You have no choice; it is forced on you.

sc1.stem: To reduce noise in the cafeteria, the principal decided to _____ a new rule requiring silent lunches every Friday, which students did not welcome.

traps.why: The principal wanted less noise, so he was adding a rule, not canceling one.
Oppose looks similar, but the principal created the rule rather than fighting it.
Students "did not welcome" the rule, so nobody was celebrating it.

sc1.tip: The rule is "new" and students "did not welcome" it. The principal is forcing an unwanted rule on them.

decoys.why: The principal made the rule, so she would not secretly weaken it.
The principal put the rule in place, which is the opposite of holding it back.
Students might have to put up with the rule, but the principal is the one creating it.
Divulge means revealing a secret, but the principal is forcing a new rule on students.
Students did not welcome the rule, so nobody was being calmed here.
The principal is making a rule, not decorating or adding details to one.

traps.why: Doing away with a rule removes it, the opposite of imposing it.
Impose has pose inside, but it has nothing to do with posing.
A polite request is much too weak; imposing gives people no choice.

syn2.tip: People complain when someone imposes on them. It means pushing something on others that they did not want.

sc2.stem: Ms. Lee usually let us choose our own reading books, but this month she decided to _____ a strict list of required titles, giving us no choice at all.

traps.why: A suggestion leaves you a choice, but the sentence says "no choice at all."
Dropping the list would give students choice again, but they had none.
Expose looks similar but means to reveal, not to force on people.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts "let us choose" with "no choice at all." She forced a list on the class.

decoys.why: Ms. Lee gave students no choice, so she was enforcing the list, not weakening it.
The students had to put up with the list, but Ms. Lee is the one forcing it.
She made the list required, which is the opposite of holding it back.
The clue is giving us no choice at all, which is about forcing, not decorating.
A reading list is not a secret, and the clue says she forced it on the class.

meaning: an amount more than what is needed
example: The farm sold its surplus of apples at the market.
hook: Sur- means over, as in surface, so a surplus is the amount over what you need, plus some extra.

traps.why: A shortage is not enough, the opposite of a surplus.
Surprise starts the same way but means something unexpected.
Extra things may go into storage, but surplus means the extra amount itself.

syn1.tip: You can see "plus" inside surplus. A surplus is extra, more than what you need.

sc1.stem: Because the class ordered far more pizza than the students could possibly eat, the _____ was donated to the shelter down the street.

traps.why: They ordered "far more" than needed, so there was no shortage.
Ordering pizza gives a receipt, but you can't donate a receipt to feed people.
Surprise looks similar, but the clue is about leftover food.

sc1.tip: The class "ordered far more pizza than the students could possibly eat." What's left over is the extra amount.

decoys.why: A benefactor is a person who gives, but the blank is the leftover pizza that was given.
A complaint cannot be donated; the blank means the extra pizza.
The sentence describes extra pizza, not a plan, being sent to the shelter.
A feeling is not something you can carry down the street and donate.
The class ordered too much pizza, so the extra food was donated, not a request.
The blank is the extra pizza, not an earlier example that guides decisions.

traps.why: A missing amount means too little, the opposite of a surplus.
Plus is inside the word, but surplus means leftover, not a sum.
The full amount is all you need; a surplus goes beyond that.

syn2.tip: Think of a farm selling its surplus apples. Those are the ones left over after the farm has enough.

sc2.stem: Last winter our town ran out of road salt, but this year the crews bought so much that they now have a _____ piled high in the garage.

traps.why: A shortage was last winter; "but" shows this year they have too much.
A sample is a tiny amount, not something "piled high."
Surface looks similar but means the outside layer of something.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts "ran out" with "bought so much" and "piled high." They now have more than they need.

decoys.why: A person who gives help is not something piled high in a garage.
A plan cannot be piled in a garage; the clue is that they bought so much salt.
The sentence mentions last winter, but the blank is the extra salt, not an earlier example.
The blank is the extra road salt they bought, not a signed request.
Running out last year might cause complaints, but the blank is the pile of extra salt.
The garage has a doorway, but the thing piled high is the extra salt.

meaning: able to cause death
example: Some mushrooms contain a lethal poison.
hook: Think of the movie title Lethal Weapon: a lethal weapon is one that can kill.

traps.why: Harmless means causing no harm, the opposite of lethal.
Legal looks a bit like lethal but means allowed by law.
Painful is too weak; lethal means something can actually kill.

syn1.tip: You may have heard of a "lethal dose" of poison. That is enough to cause death.

sc1.stem: The box jellyfish is one of the most dangerous animals in the ocean, because its sting is _____ enough to kill a person within minutes.

traps.why: A gentle sting would not "kill a person within minutes."
Itchy is far too weak for a sting that can kill.
Jellyfish can be colorful, but color has nothing to do with killing.

sc1.tip: The sting is strong "enough to kill a person within minutes." A sting that can kill is deadly.

decoys.why: Immune means protected from harm, but this sting can kill a person.
The person stung is easily harmed, but the sting itself is the deadly thing.
Being well known for something bad cannot kill a person within minutes.
A sting is not morally right or wrong; the clue is that it can kill.
The sentence is about how deadly the sting is, not whether it is done by choice.
Working well together has nothing to do with a sting that kills within minutes.

traps.why: Something safe to handle is harmless, the opposite of lethal.
Mildly harmful is much too weak; lethal things can cause death.
Lethal things are scary, but lethal means they can kill.

syn2.tip: Lethal has a dark, serious feeling. Some mushrooms contain a lethal poison, meaning eating them could kill you.

sc2.stem: Most spiders in our backyard are harmless, but the black widow's bite can be _____, so Mom told us never to touch one.

traps.why: "But" contrasts with harmless, so the bite must be dangerous, not mild.
Itchy is too weak; Mom wouldn't ban touching a spider for an itch.
The bite may be tiny, but the contrast is about danger, not size.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets the black widow against spiders that are "harmless." Its bite must be the opposite: deadly.

decoys.why: Immune means protected, but Mom warned you because the bite is deadly.
People are easily harmed by the bite, but the bite itself is what can kill.
The sentence contrasts the black widow with harmless spiders, so its bite must be dangerous, not good.
The clue is that Mom said never touch one, which means the bite is deadly.
Whether a bite is by choice does not explain why Mom said never touch one.
Being common is not the danger; the contrast with harmless spiders points to deadly.

meaning: to take full or unfair advantage of
example: The team exploited the other side's weak defense to score.
hook: Gamers exploit a glitch when they use a bug in the game to get an unfair edge.

traps.why: Ignoring something means paying no attention, the opposite of using it.
Explore looks similar but means to travel through and discover.
Exploiting a weakness uses it; repairing a weakness fixes it.

syn1.tip: A team exploits the other side's weak defense by using it to score. Exploit means to use something to your advantage.

sc1.stem: Noticing that the opposing goalie always leaned left, Priya decided to _____ that weakness by aiming every penalty kick at the right corner.

traps.why: Priya aimed every kick at the weak side, so she didn't ignore it.
Fixing the goalie's weakness would help the other team, not Priya.
Explain looks similar, but Priya used the weakness instead of describing it.

sc1.tip: Priya spots a weakness and aims "every penalty kick at the right corner" because of it. She is taking advantage of it.

decoys.why: Priya wants to beat the goalie, so she would not make his weakness stronger.
Priya is not revealing a secret; she is using the weakness by aiming right.
The goalie's weakness is not a force Priya has to hold up against.
Priya is taking advantage of the weakness, not holding it back.
Nobody is upset here; Priya is using the goalie's habit to score.
Priya does not scold the goalie; she aims where he will not be.

sc2.stem: Instead of letting the rainy weekend go to waste, Jamal decided to _____ the free time by finally finishing the model rocket he had started months ago.

traps.why: "Instead of" letting it go to waste, he did the opposite of wasting it.
Dread is a gloomy feeling, but Jamal happily got something done.
You can measure time, but Jamal made full use of it.

sc2.tip: The words "instead of letting the rainy weekend go to waste" set up a contrast. Jamal made full use of his time.

decoys.why: Jamal did not want the weekend to go to waste, so he used the time well.
You might withstand the rain, but Jamal is making good use of the free time.
Jamal used the free time to finish his rocket, not to hold it back.
Fabricate here means making up something false, but Jamal was making real use of his time.
Jamal is not forcing anything on anyone; he is using the time well.
You cannot scold free time; the sentence is about putting it to good use.

meaning: someone who held a position before another
example: The new principal kept many rules from her predecessor.
hook: Pre- means before and the rest comes from a Latin word for going away: your predecessor held the job before you.

traps.why: A successor comes after you, the opposite of a predecessor.
Predator starts the same way but means an animal that hunts.
An assistant helps you in a job but didn't hold it before you.

syn1.tip: Pre- means before. Your predecessor is the person who had your role before you did.

sc1.stem: The new team captain promised to keep the traditions started by her _____, who had led the squad for three seasons before graduating.

traps.why: Her successor comes after her, but this person led the squad before.
An opponent is on another team and wouldn't start this squad's traditions.
Predator looks similar but means a hunting animal.

sc1.tip: The person "had led the squad for three seasons before graduating." That is the captain who came before her.

decoys.why: A precedent is an earlier example, not a person who led the squad before her.
The person led the squad for three seasons; nothing says they gave money or help.
A ranking system cannot be a person who led the squad and then graduated.
The blank is someone who led the squad and graduated, and a plan cannot graduate.

traps.why: Someone who comes after is a successor, the opposite of a predecessor.
Pre- means before, but a predecessor doesn't tell the future.
A coworker works with you; a predecessor held the job earlier.

syn2.tip: Think of a new principal who keeps rules from her predecessor. The predecessor was the principal before her.

sc2.stem: Our new mayor loves building bike lanes, unlike her _____, who spent eight years in office paving wider roads for cars instead.

traps.why: A new mayor's successor hasn't served yet, so couldn't have spent eight years.
Voters choose mayors but don't spend years in office.
A supporter backs a mayor but doesn't hold the office.

sc2.tip: The word "unlike" contrasts the "new mayor" with someone who already "spent eight years in office." That person came before her.

decoys.why: The blank is a person who spent eight years in office, not an earlier example.
The sentence describes the former mayor in office, not someone who gave money or help.
A plan cannot spend eight years in office; the blank is the mayor before her.

meaning: the basic idea a story or argument rests on
example: The movie's premise is that toys come alive at night.
hook: Every sitcom has a premise, like a family of aliens moving to the suburbs: the setup the whole show rests on.

sc1.stem: The novel's _____ is simple: a girl discovers that her grandmother's old radio picks up broadcasts from the future, and the whole plot grows from that idea.

traps.why: The idea comes first and "the whole plot grows from" it, so it's not the ending.
A novel has a cover, but a cover isn't an idea the plot grows from.
Promise looks similar, but the clue describes the story's starting idea.

sc1.tip: The sentence says "the whole plot grows from that idea." The missing word names the basic idea a story starts from.

decoys.why: The sentence describes the basic idea the plot grows from, not a feeling.
The radio hears the future, but the blank is the idea the whole plot grows from.
The blank is the novel's starting idea, not an earlier example that guides decisions.
The sentence describes the idea the plot grows from, not a plan for reaching a goal.
The sentence describes the story's basic idea, not a good quality of the novel.

traps.why: A final result comes at the end, not at the start.
A plot twist is a surprise later in a story, not its basic idea.
Pre- might suggest a preview, but a premise is the idea a story rests on.

syn2.tip: When a friend asks what a show's premise is, you tell them the basic setup the story starts from.

sc2.stem: Because the whole debate depended on the idea that homework helps students learn, Maya won by proving that _____ false.

traps.why: The idea everything depended on comes first, not at the end.
Debates have audiences, but you can't prove an audience false.
Promise looks similar, but the clue is the idea the debate depended on.

sc2.tip: The debate "depended on the idea that homework helps," so knocking down that idea made Maya win. That base idea is the missing word.

decoys.why: The debate depended on an idea, not an earlier example that guides decisions.
Maya proved an idea false, and a predecessor is a person, not an idea.
The debate rested on the idea that homework helps, not on a complaint.
Maya disproved the idea the debate depended on, not a signed written request.
The sentence is about an idea the debate rested on, not a sign of the future.

meaning: an official order from a ruler
example: The king issued a decree declaring a holiday.
hook: Picture a herald unrolling a scroll in the town square and shouting, "By royal decree."

traps.why: Degree looks and sounds similar but means a unit or a diploma.
A suggestion is too weak; a decree must be obeyed.
A rumor spreads among people, but a decree is an official command.

syn1.tip: Think of a king who issued a decree declaring a holiday. A decree is an order from someone in charge.

sc1.stem: The queen announced a royal _____ that every village must celebrate her birthday with a feast, and no one dared disobey the official command.

traps.why: A request can be refused, but "no one dared disobey" this command.
A rumor isn't official, but the sentence calls it "the official command."
Degree sounds like decree but means a unit or a diploma.

sc1.tip: The end of the sentence restates the blank: "the official command." A royal official command is a decree.

decoys.why: A petition is a request from many people, but the sentence calls this an official command.
The birthday feast honors her, but the blank is the official command she announced.
No one dared disobey it, so it is a command, not a record of events.
The queen gave an official command, not a sign of something to come.
The queen gave a command, and the sentence never mentions a complaint.
The sentence calls it an official command that must be obeyed, not a plan.

traps.why: A polite request is too weak; a decree is a command.
People may protest a decree, but a decree is the order itself.
Decree sounds like degree, which can mean a diploma.

syn2.tip: Kings, queens and emperors issue decrees. Picture a royal scroll: it carries a command everyone must follow.

sc2.stem: After the emperor issued a _____ banning swords in the city, guards began taking weapons from every traveler who passed through the gates.

traps.why: A warning doesn't ban anything, but guards began enforcing a real ban.
A complaint wouldn't make guards start taking weapons.
Decrease looks similar but means getting smaller.

sc2.tip: Because of what the emperor issued, "guards began taking weapons." Only an official order would cause guards to act like that.

decoys.why: An emperor gives orders; a petition is a request people send up to a ruler.
A record of events would not make guards start taking weapons; an order would.
The emperor banned swords, which is an order, not something given to show respect.
Guards enforced what the emperor issued, so it was an order, not a complaint.
The guards acted on an official order banning swords, not on a basic idea.

meaning: a fast spread of disease among many people
example: The flu epidemic closed several schools in February.
hook: Epi- means upon and dem means people, as in democracy: an epidemic is a disease falling upon many people.

traps.why: A cure ends a disease; an epidemic is the disease spreading.
Epic starts the same way but means a long heroic story.
An infection can hit one person; an epidemic spreads to many.

syn1.tip: You may have heard of a flu epidemic that closes schools. It is a disease breaking out among many people.

sc1.stem: When nearly half the students in the district caught the same stomach virus within one week, health officials called the rapid spread a local _____.

traps.why: Officials were describing the spread itself, not something that stops it.
Allergies don't spread from person to person like this virus did.
Epic looks similar but means a long heroic story.

sc1.tip: Look at "nearly half the students" and "rapid spread." A virus spreading that fast to so many people is an outbreak.

decoys.why: Officials named the rapid spread of the virus, not a mark of shame.
Many students got sick, but the sentence names a rapid spread of disease, not an extra amount.
A milestone is an important step forward, not a virus spreading through a district.
The sentence describes a disease spreading quickly, not a doorway or starting point.
Officials called the spread itself something, and a spread is not a record of events.

traps.why: A minor cold in one person is far too small for an epidemic.
A full recovery means people got well, the opposite of an epidemic.
Epidemic starts like epic, a heroic poem, but means spreading disease.

syn2.tip: The "dem" in epidemic is the same as in democracy, meaning people. An epidemic is a disease that spreads among many people.

sc2.stem: Doctors expected only a few flu cases this winter, but the virus spread so quickly that the city faced a true _____ within a month.

traps.why: A cure would stop the flu, but the virus was spreading quickly.
A sniffle fits "a few cases," but "but" signals something much bigger.
A vaccine prevents disease; the sentence describes the virus spreading.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts "only a few flu cases" with a virus that "spread so quickly." The city faced a widespread disease.

decoys.why: The virus spread quickly, so the city faced a disease outbreak, not an extra amount.
The sentence is about a virus spreading fast, not a mark of shame.
A milestone is a step of progress, not a fast-spreading flu.
The city faced a widespread disease within a month, not a doorway or starting point.
The flu actually spread, so this was the outbreak itself, not a sign of something coming.

meaning: an earlier example that guides later decisions
example: Her early success set a precedent for other girls in the club.
hook: Pre-cede means go before: a precedent is something that went before and shows what to do next time.

traps.why: President sounds similar but means a leader of a country or group.
An exception is a one-time break from the pattern; a precedent sets one.
Courts look at precedents, but a precedent is an earlier example.

syn1.tip: When something "sets a precedent," it becomes an example that people point to later. Pre- means before.

sc1.stem: When the principal allowed one class to have a pajama day, it set a _____, and soon every other class demanded the same privilege.

traps.why: You can set a record, but a record isn't a privilege others demand.
A limit holds things back, but here other classes wanted the same thing.
President sounds similar but means a leader, which makes no sense here.

sc1.tip: Because one class got pajama day, "soon every other class demanded the same privilege." The first event became an example others used.

decoys.why: Pajama day is an example others copied, not a person who held a position before.
Other classes demanded the same thing, so it was an example to follow, not progress.
The other classes wanted the same privilege because of an earlier example, not a starting point.
Every class wanted pajama day too, so it was not a mark of shame.
The classes copied the example, and the sentence says nothing about a split between friends.

traps.why: A later copy comes after; a precedent comes before.
Precedent sounds like president, a head of state, but means an earlier example.
The parts suggest going before, but precedent isn't about standing in line.

syn2.tip: Pre- means before. A precedent is something that happened before and guides what people decide later.

sc2.stem: Lena's request to bring her hamster was denied because there was no _____: no student had ever brought a pet to school before.

traps.why: President sounds similar but means a leader, not an earlier example.
Precaution looks similar but means a step taken to stay safe.
Punishment isn't the issue; the clue says no one had done it before.

sc2.tip: After the colon, the sentence restates the blank: "no student had ever brought a pet to school before." There was no earlier example.

decoys.why: The reason given is that no student had done it before, not that it was shameful.
The sentence explains that nobody had ever brought a pet, not that something was extra.
The request failed because no earlier example existed, not because of a missing stage of progress.
The colon explains no one had brought a pet before, so the blank is an earlier example.
The reason was that no student had ever done it, not a lack of anger.

meaning: a system ranking people or things by level
example: In a wolf pack, the hierarchy decides who eats first.
hook: Picture a ladder where everyone stands on a rung above or below someone else: that is a hierarchy.

traps.why: Equality means everyone is level, the opposite of a ranked system.
A monarchy is rule by a king or queen, not any system of ranks.
Hierarchy may look like it contains "higher," but it isn't about how tall something is.

syn1.tip: Think of a "pecking order" or "chain of command." A hierarchy lines people up from top to bottom.

sc1.stem: In a beehive's strict _____, the queen sits at the top, worker bees rank below her, and every insect knows its exact place.

traps.why: Chaos means no order at all, but every bee knows its exact place.
A honeycomb is part of a beehive, but it doesn't rank bees by level.
A routine is a daily habit; the sentence describes ranks from top to bottom.

sc1.tip: "Sits at the top," "rank below her," and "exact place" all describe levels from highest to lowest.

decoys.why: A queen might give orders, but the sentence describes ranks and places, not one official order.
The sentence stresses strict ranking from top to bottom, not friendship among equals.
The sentence describes who ranks above whom, not a plan for reaching a goal.
Nothing here is an earlier example; the sentence describes levels of rank.
A record of events in time order has nothing to do with the queen sitting at the top.
The sentence lists levels of rank, not a basic idea an argument rests on.

traps.why: Equal standing means no one outranks anyone, the opposite of a hierarchy.
A hierarchy involves a group, but this misses the ranking from top to bottom.
Kings may top some hierarchies, but hierarchy means any system of levels.

syn2.tip: Ask yourself who is on top and who is below. A hierarchy is about levels, like a boss, managers, and workers.

sc2.stem: Unlike the strict _____ at her old school, where seniors bossed everyone, the new art club treated every member as an equal, from beginners to experts.

traps.why: "Unlike" means the old school was the opposite of treating everyone equally.
Teamwork is working together; seniors bossing everyone shows ranks instead.
A tradition is a custom; the clue is about who outranks whom.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" contrasts the blank with "treated every member as an equal," so the blank is a system where some, like seniors, outrank others.

decoys.why: Camaraderie describes the friendly new club, but the blank is the bossy system it is unlike.
Seniors came first, but the blank names a ranking system, not one person who came before.
The sentence contrasts ranking with equality, not an earlier example guiding decisions.
A doorway or starting point does not describe seniors bossing everyone else.
The blank needs a system of ranks, not just a feeling or opinion.
Seniors bossing everyone is not presented as a good quality.

meaning: widespread; very common
example: Colds are especially prevalent in winter.
hook: Prevalent comes from the same Latin word as prevail: something prevalent has won out and shows up everywhere.

traps.why: Rare is the opposite of prevalent; rare things are hard to find.
Relevant looks similar but means connected to the topic at hand.
Diseases can be prevalent, but prevalent means common, not dangerous.

syn1.tip: Think of "prevail": something prevalent has spread and won out, so you see it everywhere.

sc1.stem: Smartphones are now so _____ among teenagers that it is hard to find a student in our school who does not carry one.

traps.why: If almost everyone carries one, smartphones are the opposite of rare.
Phones can cost a lot, but the clue is about how many students have one.
Relevant looks like prevalent but means connected to the topic.

sc1.tip: "Hard to find a student ... who does not carry one" means nearly everyone has one, so they are very common.

decoys.why: If almost every student carries one, smartphones are common, not strange.
The sentence is about how many students have phones, not how well things work together.
Phones that nearly everyone carries are hardly unconnected to teenagers' lives.
The clue is that nearly everyone has one, which points to common, not done by choice.
Nothing says phones are known for something bad; the clue is how many students carry them.
Smartphones are not deadly; the sentence says almost every student carries one.

traps.why: Scarce means there is very little, the opposite of prevalent.
Popular means liked; prevalent just means found often, liked or not.
Previous starts the same way but means coming before.

syn2.tip: You often hear "prevalent in winter" about colds. If something is prevalent, it is found almost everywhere.

sc2.stem: Although wild wolves were once _____ across the state, roaming nearly every forest, today only a few small packs survive in the northern mountains.

traps.why: Wolves roamed "nearly every forest," so they were once plentiful, not scarce.
Wolves can be dangerous, but the clue is about how widespread they were.
Protection is about wildlife, but the clue describes wolves being everywhere.

sc2.tip: "Although" contrasts the past with "only a few small packs" today, and "roaming nearly every forest" tells you wolves were once everywhere.

decoys.why: Wolves can be dangerous, but the clue is roaming nearly every forest, which means widespread.
The sentence contrasts wolves being everywhere with only a few surviving, not being easily harmed.
Wolves roaming nearly every forest were common, not strange or unusual.
Wolves howl, but the clue roaming nearly every forest is about how widespread they were.
The sentence is about where wolves lived, not protection from disease.
Morally right does not describe wolves roaming nearly every forest.

meaning: to pay back or make up for
example: The store compensated us for the broken television.
hook: Break a friend's pencil and hand them a new one, and you compensate them for their loss.

traps.why: To charge is to make someone pay you, the opposite of repaying them.
Compete starts the same way but means trying to win.
Spending is too general; compensate means paying someone back for a loss.

syn1.tip: Think of "compensate for a loss": you give something back to balance out what someone lost.

sc1.stem: Because the concert was canceled at the last minute, the theater promised to _____ ticket holders with full refunds and free passes to a future show.

traps.why: Charging takes money from people; refunds give money back.
A theater might warn people, but refunds are a way to pay them back.
Compliment looks a bit similar but means to praise someone.

sc1.tip: "Canceled at the last minute" is the cause; "full refunds and free passes" is the effect: the theater pays people back for their loss.

decoys.why: Giving refunds and free passes helps ticket holders; it does not take unfair advantage of them.
The theater is apologizing with refunds, not scolding the ticket holders.
Free passes to a future show would encourage fans, not make them less eager.
Refunds and free passes make up for a loss rather than weaken anyone.
The theater is paying people back for a canceled show, not making them stronger.

traps.why: Taking away makes a loss bigger; compensating makes up for it.
Apologizing is saying sorry; compensating means actually giving something back.
Compensate has nothing to do with pens; it means making up for a loss.

syn2.tip: Picture a scale: when one side loses weight, you compensate by adding something back to even it out.

sc2.stem: Lena's sister offered to _____ her for the broken headphones; in other words, she would save her allowance and buy Lena a brand-new pair.

traps.why: Blame fits the topic of broken things, but the sister is paying Lena back.
Charging would make Lena pay, but the sister is the one buying.
Forgiving lets a wrong go; buying a new pair makes up for it.

sc2.tip: "In other words" signals a restatement: saving up to "buy Lena a brand-new pair" means paying her back for her loss.

decoys.why: Her sister is buying Lena a new pair, which is making up for it, not scolding her.
Saving her allowance to replace the headphones helps Lena rather than taking advantage of her.
Buying a brand-new pair repays Lena; it does not weaken her.

meaning: well known for something bad
example: The infamous pirate Blackbeard frightened sailors along the coast.
hook: Infamous isn't "not famous": it means famous for the wrong reasons, like a villain everyone has heard of.

traps.why: The "in" seems to mean not famous, but infamous means badly famous.
Celebrated means famous for good things; infamous is famous for bad things.
Infinite looks similar but means endless.

syn1.tip: Infamous contains "famous," but the "in" doesn't mean "not." It describes someone well known for something bad, like an infamous pirate.

sc1.stem: The downtown intersection was _____ for its traffic jams; everyone knew it as the worst spot in the county, and drivers avoided it at rush hour.

traps.why: "Everyone knew it," so the intersection was famous, not unknown.
Praised is positive, but traffic jams and "worst spot" are negative.
Drivers avoided it because everyone knew about it, not because they ignored it.

sc1.tip: "Everyone knew it as the worst spot" tells you the intersection was well known for something bad.

decoys.why: The worst spot in the county with traffic jams is not kind or gentle.
The clue is that everyone knew it as the worst spot, a bad reputation, not moral fairness.
The sentence is about the intersection's bad reputation for jams, not causing death.

traps.why: Infamous people are known for bad deeds, the opposite of good ones.
Infamous people are very well known, just for bad reasons.
Slightly disliked is too weak; infamous means widely known for wrongdoing.

syn2.tip: Think of "the infamous Blackbeard." Everyone knew his name, and it made them shiver.

sc2.stem: Though the old pirate ship looks harmless now in the museum, it was once _____ for raiding villages, and sailors trembled at the mere sight of its black flag.

traps.why: Sailors trembled at the sight of it, so the ship was well known.
Trembling sailors show fear, the opposite of admiration.
Forgiven fits the topic of wrongdoing, but sailors still trembled at the ship.

sc2.tip: "Though" contrasts "harmless now" with the past, and "sailors trembled" shows the ship was widely known and feared.

decoys.why: A ship that raided villages and made sailors tremble was not kind or gentle.
Raiding villages is not morally right, and the sentence describes a feared reputation.

meaning: an important event or stage in progress
example: Learning to walk is a big milestone for a baby.
hook: Old roads had stones marking each mile; a milestone in your life marks how far you have come.

traps.why: A setback moves you backward; a milestone marks progress forward.
Milestone contains "stone," but it means an important stage, not a big rock.
Milestones once marked distance, but now the word means an important event.

syn1.tip: Think of a baby's first steps, a "big milestone." It is a key point that shows how far someone has come.

sc1.stem: Reading a whole chapter book by herself marked a major _____ for six-year-old Zoe, who had struggled with reading all year.

traps.why: Reading a whole book alone is progress, not a step backward.
She struggled before; reading the book herself is the achievement after it.
Milestone once meant a stone marking miles, but this isn't about distance.

sc1.tip: Reading "a whole chapter book by herself" after she "had struggled" is a big achievement, an important step in her progress.

decoys.why: Reading a whole book after struggling is an achievement, not a mark of shame.
The sentence celebrates Zoe's progress, not an earlier example that guides decisions.
Nothing broke or split; Zoe reached an important stage in her reading.
Zoe succeeded at reading; nobody deliberately ruined her plans.
Reading the book was an important step, not a record of events in time order.
The sentence is about Zoe's progress, not an extra amount of something.

traps.why: A setback is a step backward, the opposite of a milestone.
The "stone" in milestone doesn't make it an actual rock.
A milestone is one point along the journey, not the whole trip.

syn2.tip: Picture a mile marker on a road: each one shows you have reached a new point. Life milestones mark big steps forward.

sc2.stem: After months of falling off, Jamal finally rode his bike all the way around the block without help, a _____ his whole family celebrated with pizza that night.

traps.why: Riding without help is progress, not a step backward.
He fell off before, but this time he succeeded, which is no accident.
A chore is a dull task, not an exciting achievement worth celebrating.

sc2.tip: "Finally" after "months of falling off," plus a family celebration, signals a big step forward in his progress.

decoys.why: His family celebrated with pizza, so this was an achievement, not a mark of shame.
The family celebrated together, so nothing was split or broken.
Jamal finally succeeded; no one deliberately ruined his plans.
Riding around the block is an important step, not a signed formal request.
No ruler gave an order; Jamal reached an important stage in learning to ride.
The family celebrated a single achievement, not a record of events in time order.

meaning: extreme anger
example: The students feared the coach's wrath after losing the new uniforms.
hook: Wrath is anger so huge it feels like a storm, like "the wrath of the gods" in Greek myths.

traps.why: Calm is peaceful, the opposite of wrath.
Wreath looks similar but is a ring of leaves or flowers.
Annoyance is mild; wrath is extreme anger.

syn1.tip: You may know "the wrath of the gods" from myths: anger strong enough to bring down storms.

sc1.stem: Knowing how proud their mother was of her prize roses, the twins dreaded her _____ after their soccer ball flattened every bloom in the garden.

traps.why: Nobody dreads praise, and ruining her roses would not earn it.
She was proud of the roses, but the twins dreaded her anger, not pride.
Wreath looks like wrath but is a ring of flowers.

sc1.tip: "Dreaded" and "flattened every bloom" of her "prize roses" tell you the twins expected a very angry reaction.

decoys.why: The twins ruined her roses, so they feared anger, not a show of respect.
Nobody dreads being honored; the flattened roses point to her anger.
A good quality is nothing to dread, and the ruined garden calls for anger.
Flattened roses are not an important stage in progress; the twins fear her reaction.
The twins dread how their mother will feel, not a basic idea behind an argument.
An extra amount makes no sense as something the twins dread after ruining her roses.

traps.why: Patience means staying calm, the opposite of wrath.
Irritation is too weak; wrath is extreme anger.
Sorrow is a strong feeling too, but it is sadness, not anger.

syn2.tip: Wrath is a heavy, angry word. Picture a giant roaring after someone wrecked his castle.

sc2.stem: Usually the gentle librarian only whispered, but when someone spilled juice on a rare map, her _____ echoed through the building and sent kids scrambling for the exits.

traps.why: "But" shows she was not gentle this time; kids fled from her.
She usually whispered, but "but" signals something loud and angry instead.
Laughter wouldn't send kids scrambling after juice ruined a rare map.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts her usual "gentle" whispering with what came next, and kids "scrambling for the exits" shows huge anger.

decoys.why: Spilled juice on a rare map would bring anger, not a show of respect.
Kids scrambled for the exits, so she was furious, not honoring anyone.
The sentence contrasts her usual gentleness with something scary, so a good quality misses the point.
An idea cannot echo through a building and send kids running.
A record of events would not echo loudly and frighten kids away.

meaning: a record of events in time order
example: Her diary is a chronicle of her year in Japan.
hook: Chronicle holds "chron," meaning time, as in chronological: a chronicle tells events in the order they happened.

traps.why: A prediction is about the future; a chronicle records the past.
Chron means time, but a chronicle records events, not tells the time.
A novel is a made-up story; a chronicle records real events.

syn1.tip: Spot "chron," meaning time, as in "chronological order." A chronicle records events in the order they happened.

sc1.stem: Captain Lewis kept a detailed _____ of the expedition, writing down each day's weather, discoveries, and miles traveled in the order they happened.

traps.why: He wrote down what already happened, not what would happen.
Expeditions need budgets, but he was writing down daily events in order.
