A sketch is a drawing; he was writing down each day's events.

sc1.tip: "Writing down each day's" weather and discoveries "in the order they happened" describes a record kept in time order.

decoys.why: He wrote events in the order they happened, not ranked by level.
He wrote down every day, not just one important event.
He recorded each day as it happened, not an earlier example guiding decisions.
You cannot keep a detailed impressive sight; he kept a written record.
Daily weather and miles form a record, not one basic idea.
Weather and miles traveled are facts in time order, not a feeling.

traps.why: A forecast tells what will happen; a chronicle tells what did happen.
A fantasy is made up; a chronicle sticks to real events.
A calendar is about time too, but it plans days rather than recording events.

syn2.tip: Newspapers named "Chronicle" report what happened, day after day. A chronicle is a time-ordered account of events.

sc2.stem: Instead of jumping around in time like her last book, Maya's new graphic novel is a _____ of one summer, told day by day from June to August.

traps.why: "Instead of jumping around" means this book is orderly, not a jumble.
A souvenir is an object from a trip, not a day-by-day account.
The book tells about a summer day by day, not what will happen.

sc2.tip: "Instead of jumping around in time" sets up a contrast, and "told day by day from June to August" describes events in time order.

decoys.why: The book goes day by day in time, not ranked by level.
The clue is day by day from June to August, which describes a record, not a basic idea.
The book covers a whole summer day by day, not one important event.
The sentence is about telling events in order, not an impressive sight.
The book records a summer in order, not an earlier example guiding decisions.
A book told day by day is a record in time order, not just an idea.

meaning: a mark of shame or disgrace
example: There should be no stigma attached to asking for help.
hook: Long ago a stigma was a mark burned onto skin; today it is an invisible mark of shame.

traps.why: Honor is respect, the opposite of the shame a stigma brings.
Stamina looks a bit similar but means the energy to keep going.
Some illnesses carry a stigma, but stigma means the shame itself.

syn1.tip: You hear "the stigma of" something people unfairly look down on. It is a negative word for a mark of disgrace.

sc1.stem: The counselor hoped to remove the _____ around getting tutoring, reminding students that asking for help is nothing to be embarrassed about.

traps.why: The counselor wants to remove embarrassment, not pride.
Tutoring may cost money, but the clue is about feeling embarrassed.
Stamina looks a bit like stigma but means energy to keep going.

sc1.tip: "Nothing to be embarrassed about" tells you the counselor is fighting a feeling of shame attached to getting help.

decoys.why: The counselor wants to remove embarrassment, so the word must mean shame, not a good quality.
The clue is embarrassment, and honor is the opposite of what she wants to remove.
Nothing to be embarrassed about tells you the word is about shame, not progress.
An extra amount has nothing to do with feeling embarrassed about tutoring.
A desert water spot makes no sense around getting tutoring.

sc2.stem: Wearing glasses once carried a _____ at Ella's school, but now so many popular kids wear stylish frames that nobody thinks twice about it.

traps.why: A prize is positive, but "but now" shows glasses used to be looked down on.
Glasses have lenses, but the clue is about how people judged them.
Stamina looks a bit like stigma but means energy to keep going.

sc2.tip: "But now" signals a change: since popular kids wear glasses and "nobody thinks twice," glasses must once have brought shame.

decoys.why: Now nobody thinks twice, so glasses once carried shame, not a good quality.
The sentence is about how kids once judged glasses, not an important stage.
An extra amount does not explain why kids once thought twice about glasses.
Glasses did not carry a record of events; they carried shame.
The contrast with popular kids shows glasses once brought shame, not an earlier example.
A doorway or starting point makes no sense as something glasses carried.

meaning: easily affected or harmed
example: Young children are susceptible to colds.
hook: If you are susceptible to colds, every sneeze in the classroom seems to find you first.

traps.why: Immune means protected, the opposite of susceptible.
Suspicious looks similar but means not trusting someone.
Contagious means able to spread to others, not easily caught.

syn1.tip: You hear "susceptible to colds" or "susceptible to injury." It means easily affected, an easy target for germs or harm.

sc1.stem: Because their skin is so thin and delicate, babies are especially _____ to sunburn and should be kept in the shade.

traps.why: Thin, delicate skin makes babies less able to resist sunburn, not more.
Babies aren't used to sunburn; their delicate skin burns easily.
Suspicious looks like susceptible but means not trusting.

sc1.tip: "Thin and delicate" skin is the cause; the effect is that babies burn easily, so they "should be kept in the shade."

decoys.why: Thin, delicate skin means babies burn easily, and immune means protected, the opposite.
The sentence is about babies being easily harmed, not being unconnected to sunburn.
Babies are not deadly to sunburn; they are easily hurt by it.
The sentence says babies are easily harmed, not that they cause death.
Babies do not work well together with sunburn; their thin skin makes them easily burned.

traps.why: Fully protected is the opposite of easily affected.
Easily spread describes germs; susceptible describes who catches them.
Always sick is too strong; susceptible means likely to be harmed.

syn2.tip: Notice the "-ible" ending, like "able to be." Someone susceptible is able to be affected easily.

sc2.stem: Unlike the sturdy oak trees, which survived the ice storm without a scratch, the young maples were _____ to damage, and many lost branches overnight.

traps.why: "Unlike" the oaks, the maples were harmed, so they were not immune.
Young trees weren't used to damage; they were easily hurt by it.
Suspicious looks like susceptible but means not trusting.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" contrasts oaks that survived "without a scratch" with maples that "lost branches," so the maples were easily harmed.

decoys.why: The maples lost branches, unlike the oaks, so they were easily harmed, not protected.
The maples were badly damaged, so the word must mean easily harmed.
The maples lost branches, so they were easily harmed, not working well with damage.
The maples did not cause death; they were the ones damaged.
The trees were harmed by the storm, not causing disaster themselves.

meaning: speed up
example: The runner accelerated as she approached the finish line.
hook: A car's gas pedal is called the accelerator because pressing it makes the car accelerate, or speed up.

traps.why: Slowing down is the opposite of accelerating.
Moving along is too general; accelerate means going faster and faster.
Fast cars can crash, but accelerate only means gaining speed.

syn1.tip: Think of a car's "accelerator," the gas pedal: pressing it makes the car speed up.

sc1.stem: Seeing the finish line just ahead, the cyclist pedaled harder to _____, passing two other riders in the final hundred meters.

traps.why: Braking slows you down, but the cyclist passed other riders.
Cyclists steer, but pedaling harder and passing riders is about speed.
Celebrate sounds a bit like accelerate but means to have a party.

sc1.tip: "Pedaled harder" and "passing two other riders" show the cyclist gaining speed near the finish line.

decoys.why: The cyclist pedaled harder to pass riders, which means speeding up, not falling straight down.
Passing riders near the finish means going faster, not stepping in to stop something.
Pedaling harder to pass riders is about speed, not mocking anyone.
The cyclist pedaled harder to go faster, not to pay something back.

traps.why: Delaying makes things slower, the opposite of accelerating.
Accept starts the same way but means to take or agree to something.
Travel is too general; accelerate means picking up speed.

syn2.tip: Picture a runner near the finish line pushing to go faster. That burst of speed is accelerating.

sc2.stem: The roller coaster creeps slowly up the first hill, but once it tips over the top, the cars _____ so fast that everyone's stomach drops.

traps.why: "But" shows a change from creeping slowly, so the cars don't crawl.
The cars climb before the top; after the top they race downward.
Celebrate sounds a bit like accelerate but means to have a party.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the slow "creeps" up the hill with what happens after the top, and "so fast" tells you the cars speed up.

decoys.why: The cars go so fast that stomachs drop, which means speeding up, not stepping in.
Roller coaster cars cannot mock anything; the clue is how fast they go.
The cars speed up after the slow climb; they are not paying anything back.

meaning: to hold back or keep from showing
example: Kara suppressed a giggle during the quiet assembly.
hook: Suppress joins sub (under) and press: you press a feeling down under the surface so it cannot show.

traps.why: Release means let go, the opposite of holding something back.
Surpass looks similar but means to do better than someone.
Suppress contains press, but it means hold back, not squash flat.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase 'suppress a laugh.' You hold the laugh back so nobody sees it.

sc1.stem: During the silent moment at the ceremony, Luis tried hard to _____ a sneeze, pinching his nose so the sound would not escape.

traps.why: He pinched his nose so the sound would not escape, so he was not releasing it.
Support looks a bit like suppress but means hold up or help.
Faking a sneeze is about sneezes, but Luis wanted to stop a real one.

sc1.tip: The clue is 'pinching his nose so the sound would not escape.' He was trying to hold the sneeze back.

decoys.why: He pinched his nose so the sound would not escape, so he wanted to stop the sneeze.
Pinching his nose was meant to stop the sneeze, not make it come faster.
He wanted the sneeze kept quiet during the silent moment, not kept going.
Luis was not faking a sneeze; he was trying to keep a real one in.
Adding details to a sneeze makes no sense when he is trying to keep it silent.

traps.why: Letting loose means freeing something, the opposite of keeping it hidden.
The press in suppress fools you; it is about hiding feelings, not pushing.
Putting up with means tolerating something, not hiding it.

syn2.tip: Suppress a yawn, suppress a smile: in each phrase you stop something from showing on the outside.

sc2.stem: Although the movie's ending made Maya want to cry, she managed to _____ her tears because she did not want her little brother to tease her.

traps.why: Shedding tears means letting them fall, the opposite of holding them back.
Explaining her tears would not stop the teasing; hiding them would.
Compress looks similar but means squeeze into a smaller space.

sc2.tip: 'Although' signals she wanted to cry but did not. 'Did not want her little brother to tease her' shows she held the tears back.

decoys.why: She did not want to be teased, so she held back her tears instead of keeping them going.
Speeding up her tears would invite teasing, which is exactly what Maya wanted to avoid.
She already wanted to cry; the sentence says she managed to keep the tears from showing.
Her tears were real, and she was hiding them, not faking them.
Making her tears more dramatic is the opposite of hiding them from her brother.
Maya was not using her tears for advantage; she was keeping them hidden.

meaning: able to be touched; real
example: The trophy was a tangible reward for months of practice.
hook: Tangible comes from the Latin word for touch: if you can tap it with your hand, it is tangible.

traps.why: Imaginary things exist only in your mind, the opposite of tangible.
Tangled looks like tangible but means twisted into knots.
Tangible things can be useful, but tangible just means real and touchable.

syn1.tip: Think of 'tangible proof,' proof you can actually see and hold. The -ible ending means 'able to be.'

sc1.stem: After months of planning, the garden club finally saw _____ results: rows of real tomatoes and peppers that members could pick and hold.

traps.why: Members could pick and hold the tomatoes, so the results were real.
Rows of tomatoes and peppers after months of work is a happy result.
Tangled looks like tangible but means twisted, which the sentence never says.

sc1.tip: The colon explains the blank: 'real tomatoes and peppers that members could pick and hold.' Results you can hold are touchable.

decoys.why: The tomatoes were real enough to pick and hold, so the results were not imagined.
Tomatoes and peppers are exactly what a garden club wants, so they are not unconnected.
Nothing in the sentence suggests the vegetables could cause death.
Rows of tomatoes and peppers are a normal garden result, not strange ones.
The sentence describes a happy success, not results known for something bad.

traps.why: Things that exist only in thought cannot be touched at all.
That describes tangled, a word that only looks like tangible.
Tangible things may be valuable, but tangible is about being touchable.

syn2.tip: Its opposite, intangible, describes things like hope that you cannot touch. Drop the 'in' and you get touchable.

sc2.stem: Grandpa said that kind words are nice, but a thank-you card is more _____ because you can keep it in a drawer and read it again years later.

traps.why: A card you keep for years is lasting and real, not temporary.
Cost has nothing to do with keeping a card in a drawer.
Tactful means careful of feelings; it does not explain keeping something.

sc2.tip: 'But' contrasts spoken words with a card, and 'you can keep it in a drawer' shows the card is a real object.

decoys.why: You can keep the card in a drawer, so it is real, not imagined.
Grandpa's reason is that you can keep and hold the card, not that it is detailed.
Keeping a card in a drawer has nothing to do with being lively.
The clue is about keeping the card for years, not about choosing to send it.
Grandpa is praising the card, so he would not call it unconnected.
Grandpa's point is that you can hold the card, not that it is morally right.

meaning: weaken gradually or secretly
example: Constant teasing can undermine a child's confidence.
hook: Picture soldiers digging a tunnel under a castle wall to make it collapse: they undermine it from below.

traps.why: Strengthen means make stronger, the opposite of undermine.
Undermine contains mine, but it means weaken, not dig.
Underline looks similar but means draw a line under words.

syn1.tip: Picture digging under a wall to make it fall. 'Undermine someone's trust' means slowly weaken it.

sc1.stem: By whispering doubts to teammates before every game, Brody began to _____ the captain's authority until nobody listened to her instructions anymore.

traps.why: Whispering doubts hurts authority; it does not support it.
Underline looks like undermine but means draw a line or stress something.
Obeying is about authority, but nobody listened, so it was weakened.

sc1.tip: Look at the effect: 'until nobody listened to her instructions anymore.' The whispering slowly wore her authority down.

decoys.why: Nobody listened to the captain anymore, so Brody weakened her authority instead of supporting it.
Whispering doubts made the captain's authority fade, not keep going.
Brody whispered doubts, which is the opposite of speaking in favor of the captain.
Brody was not forcing the captain's authority on anyone; he was wearing it down.
Brody did not use the captain's authority for himself; he made people stop listening to her.
Spreading doubts does not decorate authority; it weakens it until nobody listens.

sc2.stem: Mia's coach praised her hard work, but staying up late every night before meets began to _____ her performance, leaving her slow and tired in every race.

traps.why: Being slow and tired shows her performance got worse, not better.
Coaches measure performance, but late nights left her slow, so it was weakened.
Undertake looks similar but means take on a job.

sc2.tip: 'But' signals the late nights worked against her hard work, and 'leaving her slow and tired' shows her performance was weakened.

decoys.why: She ended up slow and tired, so her performance was weakened, not kept up.
The sentence says she was slow in every race, so nothing sped her up.
Staying up late did not make up for anything; it left her slow and tired.
Being tired does not add details to a performance; it hurts it.
Late nights cannot speak in favor of anything, and they made her slower.

meaning: hold up against force and survive undamaged
example: The cabin was built to withstand heavy winter snow.
hook: In old English, with could mean against: to withstand a storm is to stand against it and stay standing.

traps.why: Collapsing means falling apart, the opposite of holding up against force.
Withdraw looks similar but means pull back or take out.
Withstand starts with with, but it does not mean stand together with someone.

syn1.tip: In this word, 'with' means against. To withstand a storm is to stand against it and stay unharmed.

sc1.stem: Engineers designed the new bridge to _____ hurricane winds of over 150 miles per hour without swaying or cracking.

traps.why: Engineers measure wind, but the clue is about surviving it without cracking.
Bridges do not make wind; the clue is about holding up against it.
Withhold looks similar but means keep something back from someone.

sc1.tip: 'Without swaying or cracking' tells you the bridge must survive the winds undamaged.

decoys.why: A bridge cannot speed up winds; it was built to hold up against them.
A bridge does not start hurricanes; it is built to survive them without cracking.
A bridge cannot calm a hurricane; it can only stand strong against it.
A bridge cannot hold back the wind; the clue says it stays standing without swaying.
The bridge is not using the winds for anything; it just has to survive them.

traps.why: Giving way means letting the force win, the opposite of withstanding.
The parts with and stand suggest standing beside, but that is wrong.
Pull back from is what withdraw means, a word that only looks similar.

syn2.tip: Things built to withstand weather, like roofs and bridges, hold up against strong force and survive without damage.

sc2.stem: The cheap umbrella flipped inside out at the first gust, but Dad's sturdy one could _____ even the strongest storm without bending a single spoke.

traps.why: Predicting a storm is about weather, but umbrellas hold up against storms.
Withdraw looks like withstand but means pull back.
Dread is a fearful feeling; the sturdy umbrella confidently held up instead.

sc2.tip: 'But' contrasts the umbrella that flipped with the 'sturdy' one, and 'without bending' shows it held up against the storm.

decoys.why: An umbrella cannot start a storm; Dad's sturdy one holds up against it.
An umbrella cannot speed up a storm; the clue is about not bending.
An umbrella cannot calm a storm; it just survives it without a bent spoke.
An umbrella cannot hold back a storm; it only stays strong while the storm blows.
The sentence compares which umbrella survives the wind, not which one uses it.

meaning: step in to change or stop something
example: The teacher intervened before the argument got worse.
hook: Inter means between and vene comes from a word for come: when you intervene, you come between two sides.

traps.why: Staying out means not getting involved, the opposite of intervening.
Joining in means taking part, not stepping in to stop or change things.
Vene relates to come, but intervene means come between, not return.

syn1.tip: Inter- means between, as in 'interstate.' To intervene is to come between people to change what is happening.

sc1.stem: When the two younger kids began arguing over the swing, the playground monitor decided to _____ and help them agree on taking turns.

traps.why: Pulling back would not help the kids agree on taking turns.
The kids were the ones arguing; the monitor came to settle it.
Complaining would not help the kids agree on taking turns.

sc1.tip: The phrase 'help them agree on taking turns' shows the monitor stepped into the argument to settle it.

decoys.why: The monitor helped the kids agree on turns, which is helping, not mocking.
The monitor took action to help them take turns instead of just guessing.
The monitor stepped into the argument, which is not about following group customs.

traps.why: Ignoring a problem means doing nothing, the opposite of stepping in.
Interview looks similar but means ask someone questions.
Conquering means taking total control, much stronger than stepping in.

syn2.tip: Teachers, referees, and parents intervene: they come between people when something needs to be stopped or changed.

sc2.stem: Most of the time Ms. Lopez lets her students solve problems on their own, but when the shoving started, she had to _____ before someone got hurt.

traps.why: Waiting is what she usually does; 'but' shows this time she acted.
Clapping for shoving has the wrong feeling; she wanted to stop it.
Just watching is not enough when someone might get hurt.

sc2.tip: 'But' contrasts letting students solve problems alone with this moment, and 'before someone got hurt' tells you she had to step in.

decoys.why: She acted to stop shoving before someone got hurt, which is not mocking anyone.
Guessing would not stop the shoving; she had to step in and act.
The sentence says she had to stop the shoving, not follow the group's customs.

meaning: a break in a friendship; a split
example: An argument created a rift between the two friends.
hook: Picture a crack splitting a glacier in two: that is a rift, and friendships can crack the same way.

traps.why: A bond holds people together, the opposite of a split.
Lift rhymes with rift but means raising something up.
A mistake might cause a rift, but a rift is the break itself.

syn1.tip: A rift in rock is a crack that splits it apart. A rift between friends splits them apart too.

sc1.stem: A silly argument over who would sit in the front seat caused a _____ between the cousins, and they refused to speak to each other for weeks.

traps.why: Refusing to speak for weeks shows a break, not a closer bond.
Gift sounds like rift, but nobody gives gifts after refusing to speak.
They argued over a seat, but the result was silence, not a contest.

sc1.tip: 'Refused to speak to each other for weeks' shows the argument broke their relationship apart.

decoys.why: A stigma is a mark of shame, not a split that stops cousins from speaking.
A milestone marks progress, but the cousins' argument broke their friendship apart.
A hierarchy ranks people, but the sentence describes cousins who stopped speaking.
A threshold is a doorway or beginning, not a break between people who stopped talking.
A precedent guides later decisions; the sentence describes a broken friendship.
A surplus is an extra amount, which has nothing to do with cousins refusing to speak.

traps.why: A close friendship is the opposite of a break between people.
A small disagreement is too mild; a rift is a real break.
Friends share secrets, but a rift is what pulls them apart.

syn2.tip: Rifts happen 'between' people. If two people stop talking after a fight, there is a rift between them.

sc2.stem: The twins had always been best friends, but after Sam told everyone Max's secret, a deep _____ grew between them that took months to heal.

traps.why: 'But' shows things changed from friendship, and 'took months to heal' means damage.
Shift looks like rift but means a change in position.
A secret started the trouble, but what grew between them needed healing.

sc2.tip: 'But' contrasts 'best friends' with what came after, and 'took months to heal' shows something broke between them.

decoys.why: A virtue is a good quality, but telling a secret hurt the friendship and needed healing.
Homage is honor shown to someone, not a hurt that took months to heal.
A milestone marks progress, but the sentence describes a friendship being damaged.
A stigma is a mark of shame, not a split growing between two friends.
A hierarchy ranks people by level, not a break between best friends.
A surplus is an extra amount, not something that grows between friends and must heal.

meaning: logical and clearly connected
example: Lia's essay was coherent, with each idea leading to the next.
hook: Coherent comes from cohere, meaning to stick together: in a coherent story, every idea sticks to the next one.

traps.why: Confused ideas do not connect, the opposite of coherent.
A talkative person says a lot, but coherent means it makes sense.
Co- can mean together, but coherent is about ideas, not people working together.

syn1.tip: A coherent answer hangs together and makes sense. When someone is too sleepy to talk sense, we say they are not coherent.

sc1.stem: Jake's first draft jumped randomly from topic to topic, but after he reorganized his notes, his second draft was _____ and easy to follow.

traps.why: The second draft was easy to follow, so it was not confusing.
Random describes the first draft; 'but' shows the second one changed.
Length is not the point; reorganizing made the ideas connect.

sc1.tip: 'But' contrasts the first draft that 'jumped randomly' with a second that is 'easy to follow.' The blank means clearly connected.

decoys.why: Jumping off topic describes the first draft; the reorganized draft was easy to follow.
A strange draft would not be easy to follow, and the second draft was.
Prolific means producing lots of work, not organized and easy to follow.
Hypothetical means imagined, but the clue is that the draft was easy to follow.
Drastic means extreme, which does not describe a draft that is easy to follow.
Restless describes a person who cannot sit still, not a well organized draft.

traps.why: Jumbled ideas are mixed up, the opposite of clearly connected.
Co- suggests teamwork, but coherent describes ideas that fit logically.
Writing can be beautiful yet confusing; coherent means it fits together logically.

syn2.tip: Inside coherent is cohere, meaning stick together. Coherent ideas stick together in a clear order.

sc2.stem: After staying up all night, Ben was so exhausted that his answers in class were barely _____, and the teacher could not understand what he was trying to say.

traps.why: Ben was tired, but answers cannot be tired; they can make sense or not.
Cheerful is a mood; the clue is that his answers made no sense.
Honesty is about truth, but the teacher could not understand him.

sc2.tip: 'The teacher could not understand what he was trying to say' tells you his answers barely made sense.

decoys.why: Ben was exhausted, and the teacher could not understand him, so lively is not the point.
Restless describes fidgeting, but the sentence says his answers could not be understood.
Prolific means producing a lot, but the clue is that his answers made no sense.
Ethical means morally right, which has nothing to do with the teacher not understanding.
Tangible means able to be touched, but the problem was that his answers made no sense.
Voluntary means done by choice, but the clue is that his answers were hard to understand.

meaning: extreme and having a strong effect
example: The drought forced drastic water limits across the state.
hook: A drastic haircut is not a little trim: it is shaving your whole head. Drastic means extreme.

traps.why: Minor means small and unimportant, the opposite of drastic.
Plastic rhymes with drastic but names a material.
Drastic steps are bold, but careless means not paying attention.

syn1.tip: Think of 'drastic measures' or 'a drastic change': not a little step, but a huge one with a strong effect.

sc1.stem: Instead of making small changes to the failing garden, Mr. Ito took _____ action, ripping out every plant and replacing all of the soil.

traps.why: 'Instead of making small changes' shows his action was not minor.
Plastic sounds like drastic but names a material, not a kind of action.
Ripping out every plant and all the soil is hard work, not lazy.

sc1.tip: 'Instead of making small changes' signals contrast, and 'ripping out every plant and replacing all of the soil' shows extreme action.

decoys.why: Mr. Ito really ripped out every plant, so the action was not just imagined.
Susceptible means easily harmed, which describes the garden, not his extreme action.
Compatible means working well together, but the clue is replacing everything instead of small changes.
Prolific means producing a lot, not extreme like ripping out every plant.
Replacing all the soil was connected to the garden problem, so it was not irrelevant.
Restless describes a person who cannot relax, not an action that changes everything.

traps.why: Gentle means mild and soft, the opposite of drastic.
Noticeable is too weak; drastic changes are huge, not just visible.
Fantastic ends like drastic but means wonderful.

syn2.tip: Drastic is about how big and strong a change is. A severe cut, like halving a budget, is a drastic one.

sc2.stem: When the river rose six feet overnight and flooded Main Street, the mayor ordered the _____ step of closing every school and road in town.

traps.why: Closing every school and road is a huge step, not a small one.
A flood emergency is serious, so cheerful has the wrong feeling.
Fantastic looks like drastic but means wonderful.

sc2.tip: A huge flood causes the mayor's response, and 'closing every school and road' is a big, extreme step.

decoys.why: The mayor ordered the closings, so they were required, not done by choice.
The mayor actually closed every school and road, so the step was real.
Closing roads during a flood is clearly connected to the problem, not irrelevant.
Compatible means working well together, but the clue is how extreme closing everything was.
Prolific means producing a lot of work, not an extreme step like closing everything.
The flooded town was susceptible, but the mayor's step itself was extreme.

meaning: kind and gentle, avoiding cruelty
example: The shelter uses humane traps that do not hurt the animals.
hook: Humane looks like human with an e: it means treating creatures the way a kind human should, without cruelty.

traps.why: Cruel means causing pain on purpose, the opposite of humane.
Humble looks similar but means modest, not kind and gentle.
A method can be efficient without being gentle; humane is about kindness.

syn1.tip: A 'humane society' is a group that protects animals from cruelty. Humane means treating others kindly.

sc1.stem: Rather than using poison, the school chose a _____ way to remove the raccoons, catching them gently in cages and releasing them in the forest.

traps.why: Catching raccoons gently and releasing them is the opposite of cruel.
Cost is not the clue; the clue is catching the raccoons gently.
Humble looks like humane but means modest.

sc1.tip: 'Rather than using poison' signals a contrast, and 'catching them gently' shows a kind way that avoids cruelty.

decoys.why: The school chose not to use poison and caught the raccoons gently, so nothing deadly.
The sentence stresses catching the raccoons gently, not doing something extreme.
Cynical describes distrust of people, not a gentle way to treat raccoons.
Rugged means rough and tough, but the raccoons were caught gently.
The school actually caught and released the raccoons, so the way was real.
Prolific means producing a lot, but the clue is the gentle way the raccoons were treated.

traps.why: Harsh means rough and severe, the opposite of humane.
Humid looks similar but describes damp, sticky air.
Tame describes animals that are not wild, not people who avoid cruelty.

syn2.tip: Humane looks like human. Think of the kindest, gentlest way a human could treat an animal.

sc2.stem: Because the farm's owners believed animals should never suffer, they gave their chickens room to roam and treated every injured hen in a _____ way.

traps.why: Owners who think animals should never suffer would not treat hens carelessly.
Farms want profit, but the clue is about preventing suffering.
Humorous looks similar but means funny.

sc2.tip: 'Because' shows the cause: owners who believed 'animals should never suffer' would treat hurt hens kindly.

decoys.why: The owners believed animals should never suffer, so they would not treat hens in a deadly way.
Cynical means distrusting people, but the owners were caring and kind to animals.
The clue is that animals should never suffer, which points to gentle care, not extreme care.
Rugged means rough, but owners who hate suffering would treat injured hens gently.
Restless means unable to relax, not the kind care the owners gave injured hens.
The owners really treated every injured hen, so their care was not imagined.

meaning: deliberate damage done to ruin plans
example: Investigators said the broken bridge model was an act of sabotage.
hook: Picture someone secretly cutting the wires on a rival's robot the night before a contest: that is sabotage.

traps.why: Repair means fixing something, the opposite of damaging it.
An accident causes damage by chance; sabotage is done on purpose.
Theft is taking things; sabotage is damaging them to ruin plans.

syn1.tip: Sabotage is damage done on purpose, often in secret, to make someone's plan fail.

sc1.stem: When the robotics team found their robot's wires had been deliberately cut the night before the contest, they suspected _____ by a jealous rival.

traps.why: Cut wires are not help; they were damage meant to ruin the robot.
Carelessness is accidental, but the wires were cut deliberately.
Teasing is too mild; cutting wires is serious damage.

sc1.tip: 'Deliberately cut' and 'jealous rival' show damage done on purpose to ruin the team's chances.

decoys.why: Homage is honor shown to someone, but cutting wires is done to ruin plans.
A jealous rival might feel anger, but the cut wires were deliberate damage.
Unrest is general disturbance, not one rival secretly cutting a robot's wires.
Virtue is a good quality, but deliberately cutting wires is a harmful act.

traps.why: Sabotage is never accidental; it is done deliberately.
Sabotage hurts plans rather than helping them.
A harmless prank is fun; sabotage aims to ruin plans.

syn2.tip: Spies and jealous rivals commit sabotage. The key idea is damage someone does deliberately to wreck a plan.

sc2.stem: At first the coach blamed bad luck for the bus's flat tires, but the security video showed it was _____: a rival fan had slashed them on purpose.

traps.why: Coincidence is chance, but the tires were slashed on purpose.
Weather can damage things, but the video showed a fan did it.
Fans give support, but slashing tires is harmful, not supportive.

sc2.tip: 'At first... but' shows the coach was wrong about bad luck, and 'slashed them on purpose' shows deliberate damage.

decoys.why: Homage shows respect, but slashing tires on purpose is meant to ruin the team's plans.
The rival may have been angry, but the slashed tires were deliberate damage.
Unrest is widespread disturbance, not one fan slashing tires on purpose.
Virtue is a good quality, but slashing tires on purpose is harmful.

meaning: imagined or supposed, not actually real
example: The teacher posed a hypothetical question about living on Mars.
hook: Hypothetical questions start with "what if": what if dogs could talk? They imagine things rather than report facts.

traps.why: Proven means shown to be true, the opposite of something only imagined.
Hypnotic starts like hypothetical but means putting someone into a trance.
Scientists use hypothetical cases, but scientific means based on science, not imagined.

syn1.tip: Think of "a hypothetical situation" that begins with "what if." It is supposed or pretend, not real.

sc1.stem: Since no one has ever visited a planet beyond our solar system, the science teacher asked a _____ question: what would you pack if you could travel to one?

traps.why: No one has visited such a planet, so the question cannot be about facts.
Historical means about the past, but this trip has never happened.
Hysterical looks similar but means wildly emotional, which makes no sense here.

sc1.tip: Look at "no one has ever visited" and "what would you pack if you could." The question is about something imagined.

decoys.why: No one has ever visited such a planet, so the question is imagined, not real.
The question asks something new, not something that repeats what was already said.
Asking what to pack has nothing to do with believing people are selfish.
A fun packing question cannot cause death.
The sentence describes an imagined question, not an extreme one with strong effects.

traps.why: Factual means based on facts, the opposite of imagined.
Hysterical looks similar but means wildly emotional or very funny.
Hypothetical questions can be hard, but hypothetical means imagined, not hard.

syn2.tip: Hypothetical goes with "what if." Anything you answer with "what if" is imagined, not something that really happened.

sc2.stem: Although the robot invasion in our debate was only _____, the class argued about it as seriously as if real robots were marching down Main Street.

traps.why: "As if real robots" shows the invasion was not actual.
The class was serious, but "although" says the invasion itself was not real.
Hypnotic looks similar but means causing a trance, not imagined.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets up a contrast with "as if real robots." The invasion must be the opposite of real: imagined.

decoys.why: The sentence contrasts the invasion with real robots, so it was not real or touchable.
An invasion in a class debate was only pretend, so it could not cause death.
The clue says it was not real, not that it was common.
Nothing in the sentence is about things working well together.
The contrast is about pretend versus real, not about kindness.

meaning: public honor or respect shown to someone
example: The mural pays homage to the town's first teachers.
hook: When a band plays a famous song to honor the person who wrote it, they pay homage: a public bow of respect.

traps.why: An insult shows disrespect, the opposite of homage.
Hostage ends like homage but means a captured person.
A monument can honor someone, but homage is the respect itself.

syn1.tip: You "pay homage" the way you "pay tribute": both mean showing public honor to someone.

sc1.stem: The young filmmaker paid _____ to her favorite director by recreating his most famous scene, shot for shot, in her own movie.

traps.why: You can pay money, but recreating his scene honors him rather than pays him.
Scorn is disrespect, but she copied the scene of her favorite director.
Postage ends like homage but is the cost of mailing something.

sc1.tip: She copied a scene by her "favorite director," "shot for shot." That is a way of honoring him.

decoys.why: Recreating a favorite director's scene honors him; it does not ruin his plans.
She admires her favorite director, so she is showing respect, not anger.
Copying a scene shows honor, not an extra amount of something.
Recreating a scene is a calm act of respect, not confusion or disorder.
You cannot pay a good character quality to someone; she is showing respect.

traps.why: Mockery makes fun of someone, the opposite of showing respect.
Homage starts with "hom" but has nothing to do with home.
People "pay" homage, but they pay it with respect, not money.

syn2.tip: Homage usually follows "pay," as in "pay homage to a hero." Think honor and respect shown openly.

sc2.stem: Instead of mocking the old cartoon, the animators paid _____ to it, hiding tiny drawings of its characters throughout their new movie as a respectful thank-you.

traps.why: "Instead of mocking" tells you they did the opposite of mockery.
Damages are money paid for harm, but this was a thank-you.
Mileage ends like homage but means distance traveled.

sc2.tip: "Instead of mocking" signals the opposite, and "respectful thank-you" restates it. They showed honor.

decoys.why: The animators gave a respectful thank-you, which is the opposite of ruining something.
The sentence says they were respectful instead of mocking, so anger does not fit.
Hiding drawings as a thank-you shows honor, not an extra amount.
A respectful thank-you is not a state of confusion or disorder.
The animators showed respect, not anger and disturbance.

meaning: an impressive or unusual sight
example: The fireworks display was a spectacle no one would forget.
hook: Spect means look: a spectacle is so dazzling everyone stares, like fireworks bursting over a dark lake.

traps.why: "Spectacles" can mean glasses, but one spectacle is an impressive sight.
Speck starts the same but means a tiny spot, nothing impressive.
An audience watches a spectacle, but the spectacle is the thing seen.

syn1.tip: Spect means look, as in spectator. A spectacle is something to look at, a remarkable sight.

sc1.stem: The northern lights were an amazing _____, painting the night sky with waves of green and purple that left the whole campground staring upward.

traps.why: Spectators are the people staring; the lights are what they stare at.
The lights were "amazing" and "painting the sky," not disappointing.
A forecast predicts the sky; the lights were actually filling it.

sc1.tip: "Amazing," "waves of green and purple," and "the whole campground staring upward" describe an impressive sight.

decoys.why: The lights were something amazing to look at, not a stage of progress.
The lights were in the night sky, not a green spot with water in a desert.
Colorful lights in the sky are a sight to admire, not a noisy fight.
Nobody was attacked; the campers were staring up at a beautiful sight.
The lights painted the sky; they were not a written record of events.
The sentence describes a beautiful sight, not a break in a friendship.

traps.why: A spectacle is impressive, the opposite of dull.
Spect means look, but a spectacle is what you see, not careful looking.
Crowds gather at a spectacle, but they are not the spectacle.

syn2.tip: Think of "quite a spectacle" at a parade or fireworks show. It names a big, eye-catching display.

sc2.stem: The tiny town's Fourth of July parade was usually just three tractors and a fire truck, but this year's hot air balloons made it a real _____.

traps.why: "But" contrasts the usual small parade, so this year was impressive, not a letdown.
A spectator watches; the parade itself cannot be one.
The parade was a tradition already; the balloons made it impressive, not traditional.

sc2.tip: "Usually just three tractors" plus "but" means this year was the opposite of plain. Look for an impressive sight.

decoys.why: Hot air balloons make a parade impressive to watch, not a noisy fight.
The balloons were a show for the town, not a surprise attack.
Balloons at a parade do not spread disease; they make an impressive sight.
The balloons made the parade exciting to see, not a record of events.
Nothing in the sentence describes a split between friends.
Balloons cannot turn a parade into an official order from a ruler.

meaning: a state of anger and disturbance
example: The sudden schedule change caused unrest among the campers.
hook: Un + rest: when a crowd cannot rest easy because it is angry and stirred up, there is unrest.

traps.why: Calm is peace and quiet, the opposite of unrest.
Un + rest might suggest tiredness, but unrest means angry disturbance.
A riot is a violent outburst; unrest is widespread anger, often milder.

syn1.tip: You often hear "political unrest" or "unrest in the streets." It means people are upset and things are stirred up.

sc1.stem: When the school canceled recess for the entire month, there was growing _____ among the students, who complained loudly and started petitions in every grade.

traps.why: Excitement is happy, but students were complaining about losing recess.
Contentment means satisfied, the opposite of complaining loudly.
No recess might be boring, but petitions show anger, not boredom.

sc1.tip: Recess was "canceled" and students "complained loudly and started petitions." That shows anger spreading.

decoys.why: Students complaining loudly are showing anger, not honor or respect.
Complaining and petitions show anger, not growing importance or reputation.
The students were upset about recess, not marked with shame.

traps.why: Peaceful order is the opposite of an angry, stirred-up situation.
Unrest is stronger than worry; people are angry and disturbed.
A celebration can be noisy, but it is happy, and unrest is angry.

syn2.tip: Split it: un + rest. A group that cannot settle down because people are angry is in unrest.

sc2.stem: Although the cafeteria had been peaceful all year, _____ broke out when the new menu replaced pizza Friday with boiled spinach, and students began chanting in protest.

traps.why: "Although" contrasts the peaceful past, and chanting in protest is not calm.
Applause is approval, but students were protesting the spinach.
The topic is food, but "chanting in protest" shows anger, not hunger.

sc2.tip: "Although... peaceful" signals a change to the opposite, and "chanting in protest" shows angry disturbance.

decoys.why: Chanting in protest shows anger, not honor or respect.
The students were protesting the menu, not gaining importance or reputation.
The students chanted in protest; nobody deliberately damaged anything.

meaning: greatest; highest possible
example: Handle the glass beakers with the utmost care.
hook: Utmost care means the most care you possibly can give, like carrying a full fishbowl across a crowded room.

traps.why: Least means the smallest amount, the opposite of utmost.
Average is ordinary; utmost is the highest possible.
Utmost often comes before "care," but it means greatest, not careful.

syn1.tip: Utmost has "most" inside it. Think of "the utmost care": the most care possible.

sc1.stem: The museum staff moved the fragile, two-thousand-year-old vase with the _____ care, wearing soft gloves and taking a full hour to cross a single room.

traps.why: Gloves and a full hour show huge care, not the least.
An hour to cross one room is far beyond usual care.
Quickest clashes with taking a full hour to cross a single room.

sc1.tip: "Fragile," "soft gloves," and "a full hour to cross a single room" show the greatest care possible.

decoys.why: Soft gloves and slow steps show gentle care, not rough or tough handling.
The staff was protecting the vase, so their care could not cause death.
Taking a full hour to cross a room shows calm patience, not restlessness.
The care was the greatest possible, not extreme in a harsh or forceful way.
Careful handling matters a great deal for a fragile vase.
Care for a vase does not spread from person to person like an illness.

traps.why: Lowest possible is the opposite of highest possible.
Fairly large is too weak; utmost means the very greatest.
Utmost has "most" in it but has nothing to do with time.

syn2.tip: Look for "most" at the end of utmost. It means the greatest amount there can be.

sc2.stem: Mateo usually rushed through chores, but when babysitting his baby sister, he showed the _____ patience, reading her the same picture book eleven times without complaining.

traps.why: "But" turns away from rushing; eleven readings show great patience.
His usual habit is rushing, so this patience was far beyond usual.
Eleven readings without complaining show long patience, not brief.

sc2.tip: "Usually rushed" plus "but" signals a change, and "eleven times without complaining" shows the greatest patience possible.

decoys.why: Reading one book eleven times without complaining shows calm, not restlessness.
Mateo was kind and patient with his sister, not believing everyone is selfish.
The book was repeated, but his patience was the greatest possible, not unnecessary.
His patience was the highest possible, not extreme in a harsh way.
Gentle patience with a baby sister cannot cause death.
The sentence is about how much patience Mateo had, not how it spreads.

meaning: producing a great amount of work
example: The prolific author wrote over a hundred books.
hook: A prolific apple tree drops more apples than you can pick; a prolific author fills whole shelves with books.

traps.why: Idle means doing nothing, the opposite of producing lots of work.
Professional also starts with "pro" but means doing something as a job.
Prolific people may become famous, but prolific means producing a lot.

syn1.tip: You often see "a prolific writer" or "a prolific scorer." Both produce a lot: many books or many goals.

sc1.stem: Agatha Christie was a remarkably _____ writer, publishing more than sixty mystery novels in addition to dozens of short stories and plays.

traps.why: Sixty novels plus stories and plays is the opposite of slow.
She wrote mysteries, but the clue counts how many works she produced.
An occasional writer writes now and then, not sixty novels.

sc1.tip: "More than sixty mystery novels in addition to dozens of short stories and plays" is a huge amount of work.

decoys.why: The sentence praises how much she published, not that she was known for something bad.
Her mysteries involve murder, but the sentence is about how many books she wrote.
Agatha Christie was a real writer who actually published those books, so she was not imagined.
Sixty novels shows she produced a lot, not that her work was unnecessary repetition.
Nothing in the sentence says she was easily harmed; it counts how much she wrote.
Drastic describes extreme actions, not a writer who publishes many books.

traps.why: Producing little is the opposite of prolific.
Prolific is about how much someone makes, not how good it is.
Fairly busy is too weak; prolific means a great amount of work.

syn2.tip: Prolific is about quantity. Think of a garden or author that keeps turning out more and more.

sc2.stem: Unlike his brother, who has finished only one painting in three years, Leo is so _____ that his bedroom walls are covered with dozens of new canvases.

traps.why: "Unlike" means Leo is the reverse of his slow brother.
Covered walls might look messy, but the clue is how much he paints.
Professional starts like prolific but means working as a job.

sc2.tip: "Unlike his brother" who finished "only one painting" signals the opposite: Leo produces "dozens."

decoys.why: The clue is dozens of canvases, which shows how much Leo paints, not how detailed.
The sentence contrasts how much each brother paints, not whether paintings repeat each other.
Nothing says Leo is known for something bad; he simply paints a great deal.
Being easily harmed would not cover his walls with dozens of new paintings.
The sentence is about how many paintings Leo finishes, not his distrust of people.
Leo and his canvases are real, and the sentence is about how much he produces.

meaning: unable to stay still or relax
example: The restless students kept glancing at the clock.
hook: Rest + less: without rest, a restless kid squirms, taps a pencil, and checks the clock every minute.

traps.why: Calm means still and relaxed, the opposite of restless.
Without rest sounds like tired, but restless means unable to stay still.
Careless also ends in -less but means not paying attention.

syn1.tip: Think of "restless legs" that keep bouncing. Restless means you cannot settle down or sit still.

sc1.stem: On the last afternoon before summer vacation, the students were so _____ that they tapped their pencils, bounced their knees, and stared out the windows.

traps.why: Tapping pencils and bouncing knees is the opposite of relaxed.
Without rest might sound sleepy, but bouncing knees shows too much energy.
Careless also ends in -less but means sloppy, not unable to sit still.

sc1.tip: "Tapped their pencils, bounced their knees, and stared out the windows" all show kids who cannot keep still.

decoys.why: Rampant describes things spreading out of control, not students fidgeting in their seats.
Excitement can spread, but tapping and bouncing show students who cannot sit still.
Tapping pencils and staring out windows show fidgeting, not logical, clear thinking.
The students are fidgety before vacation, not distrustful of other people's motives.
Bouncing knees and tapping pencils have nothing to do with being kind and gentle.
Drastic describes extreme actions or changes, not students who cannot stay still.

traps.why: Calm and peaceful is the opposite of restless.
Rest can mean a break, but restless means fidgety, not hardworking.
Restless people may be uneasy, but they are not necessarily angry.

syn2.tip: Rest + less means without rest. A restless person cannot relax, so they keep moving and fidgeting.

sc2.stem: After a long car ride, the puppy was anything but calm; she was so _____ that she ran circles around the yard and wouldn't stop jumping on everyone.

traps.why: "Anything but calm" rules out peaceful.
Long rides can make you sleepy, but she ran circles and kept jumping.
The car ride is the topic, but running and jumping show energy, not sickness.

sc2.tip: "Anything but calm" tells you the answer means the opposite of calm, and "ran circles" proves it.

decoys.why: The puppy is anything but calm, and humane means gentle and kind.
Rampant describes something spreading out of control, like weeds, not one jumpy puppy.
Nothing is spreading from one creature to another; the puppy just cannot settle down.
Running circles and jumping show she cannot stay still, not that she is tough.
A jumping, excited puppy is not deadly; she simply cannot relax.
Running in circles shows the puppy cannot settle, not that she is logical.

meaning: rough and uneven; tough
example: The jeep bounced over the rugged mountain trail.
hook: Picture a rugged mountain trail: jagged rocks and bumps that shake your jeep like a paint mixer.

traps.why: Smooth is even and flat, the opposite of rugged.
Rigid looks similar but means stiff and unbending.
Rugged mountains may be steep, but rugged means rough and uneven.

syn1.tip: Think of "rugged mountains" or "rugged terrain": land full of rocks and bumps, the rough kind.

sc1.stem: The hikers needed sturdy boots for the _____ trail, which climbed over jagged rocks, fallen logs, and steep, uneven ground.

traps.why: "Steep, uneven ground" is the opposite of flat.
Paved trails are smooth, but this one had jagged rocks and logs.
Rigid looks similar but means stiff, which does not describe a trail.

sc1.tip: "Jagged rocks, fallen logs, and steep, uneven ground" describe rough land. That is why they needed sturdy boots.

decoys.why: Jagged rocks and uneven ground make the trail rough, not neat and connected.
The hikers might be energetic, but the trail itself is described as rough and uneven.
A trail cannot be unable to relax; the clues describe rocky, uneven ground.
Kindness has nothing to do with a trail full of jagged rocks and logs.
The sentence describes how rough the trail is, not how common it is.
Every trail can be touched; the clue about jagged, uneven ground asks for roughness.

traps.why: Flat and even is the opposite of rugged.
Rugged contains "rug" but has nothing to do with rugs.
Rugged land is often in mountains, but rugged means rough, not tall.

syn2.tip: Rugged describes ground you stumble on: rocks, ridges, and bumps. Think of a jeep bouncing on a rough trail.

sc2.stem: Our old pickup truck is so _____ that it has survived twenty winters, three floods, and my sister learning to drive without a single breakdown.

traps.why: A fragile truck would break; this one never broke down.
Old trucks can be rusty, but rust does not explain surviving everything.
Ragged looks similar but means torn and worn out, not tough.

sc2.tip: "Survived twenty winters, three floods" and "without a single breakdown" show the truck is tough. Rugged can mean sturdy.

decoys.why: The truck survived floods without breaking down, so it is not easily harmed.
Surviving twenty winters shows the truck is tough, not full of energy and enthusiasm.
The sentence praises how sturdy the truck is, not that it cannot stay still.
The sentence admires the truck's toughness, not its reputation for something bad.
A truck does not produce work; the clues show it is tough and long lasting.
Drastic means extreme in effect, but the sentence shows the truck is durable.

meaning: believing people act only out of selfishness
example: The cynical reporter assumed every charity was secretly a scam.
hook: A cynical person hears "free gift" and immediately asks, "What's the catch?"

traps.why: Trusting means believing in people, the opposite of cynical.
Clinical sounds similar but means having to do with medical care.
A cynic doubts people's motives but is not necessarily mean to them.

syn1.tip: A cynical person always asks "What's the catch?" They distrust others and expect selfish reasons.

sc1.stem: When the new neighbor brought cookies, Raj's _____ uncle assumed she must want something in return, refusing to believe anyone would be kind for no reason.

traps.why: A grateful uncle would thank her, not suspect she wanted something.
Cookies are involved, but the clue is about refusing to believe in kindness.
A trusting person would believe she was simply being kind.

sc1.tip: He "assumed she must want something in return" and refused "to believe anyone would be kind for no reason."

decoys.why: The uncle assumes the neighbor has selfish motives, which is not kind or gentle thinking.
He refuses to believe in her kindness, so he is not easily influenced at all.
The sentence is about his distrust of people, not how well he speaks.
Suspecting the neighbor of wanting something shows distrust, not cheerful energy.
Being tough has nothing to do with doubting that anyone is kind for no reason.
The clue is that he doubts people's kindness, not that he cannot sit still.

traps.why: Believing the best of people is the opposite of cynical.
Cynics may be gloomy, but cynical is about distrusting people's reasons.
Cynical is a firm belief that people are selfish, not mild doubt.

syn2.tip: Picture someone who thinks every kind act hides a selfish reason. That suspicion of motives is being cynical.

sc2.stem: While her little brother still believes every toy commercial, Priya has grown _____ and assumes advertisers will say anything just to get her money.

traps.why: "While" contrasts her with her believing brother, so she is not trusting.
Money is mentioned, but Priya suspects advertisers; she is not greedy herself.
Clinical sounds similar but means medical or coldly scientific.

sc2.tip: "While" sets her against a brother who "still believes." She "assumes advertisers will say anything," so she distrusts them.

decoys.why: Her brother is the easily fooled one; Priya now doubts what advertisers say.
Assuming advertisers only want her money shows distrust, not kindness.
The sentence is about her suspicion of advertisers, not how well she speaks.
Doubting every commercial shows distrust, not energy and enthusiasm.
Being tough has nothing to do with doubting what advertisers tell her.
The sentence is about her distrust of commercials, not about producing lots of work.

meaning: unnecessary because it repeats something
example: Saying "free gift" is redundant because gifts are already free.
hook: "Free gift" and "tiny little" are redundant: the second word just repeats what the first already said.

traps.why: Essential means truly needed, the opposite of redundant.
Abundant rhymes with redundant but means plentiful.
Repeated words may sound clumsy, but redundant means needless, not confusing.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "free gift." Gifts are already free, so the word repeats itself. That is redundant.

sc1.stem: The editor crossed out the phrase "tiny little" in Ana's essay, explaining that using both words was _____ because they mean the same thing.

traps.why: The editor crossed it out, so the phrase was not necessary.
Contradictory words disagree, but these "mean the same thing."
Abundant sounds like redundant but means plentiful.

sc1.tip: The editor crossed it out "because they mean the same thing." Using both words repeats the idea for no reason.

decoys.why: The editor crossed the words out, so he found them a problem, not logical and clear.
The editor is cutting repeated words, not praising how well Ana expresses herself.
Two words meaning the same thing is repetition, not something complicated.
The words really appear in the essay; the issue is that they repeat each other.
The phrase tiny little repeats a meaning; it says nothing about selfish motives.

traps.why: Absolutely necessary is the opposite of something you do not need.
Redundant is a criticism of writing, not praise.
Redundant words are easy to follow; the problem is that they repeat.

syn2.tip: Redundant things could be removed without losing anything, because they just say or do the same thing again.

sc2.stem: Coach bought three more boxes of bandages, but they were _____, simply duplicating the full boxes already sitting in our team's first-aid kit.

traps.why: The kit was already full, so the extra boxes were not essential.
Cost is not the point; "simply duplicating" tells you they repeated supplies.
Coach bought the boxes, so they were not missing, just extra.

sc2.tip: "Simply duplicating the full boxes already sitting in" the kit restates the answer: the new boxes repeat what was there.

decoys.why: Bandages fit a first-aid topic, but they cannot spread from person to person.
Bandages are not deadly; the clue says they only duplicated what the team already had.
Any box can be touched; the clue simply duplicating means they were not needed.
The boxes were not hidden; the problem is that they repeated full boxes already there.
The sentence is about extra boxes that repeat what the kit already holds, not kindness.
Buying extra bandages is not extreme; it just duplicated supplies the team had.

meaning: able to spread from person to person
example: Her laughter was so contagious that soon everyone was giggling.
hook: One person yawns, then another, then the whole room: a contagious yawn jumps from person to person.

traps.why: Contained means kept in one place, the opposite of spreading.
Contiguous looks similar but means touching or next to something.
Illnesses can be curable, but contagious is about spreading, not healing.

syn1.tip: Think of a contagious yawn or laugh. It spreads from one person to the next, just like a cold you can catch.

sc1.stem: Jordan's excitement about the trip was so _____ that within minutes the entire bus was cheering and singing along with him.

traps.why: Hidden excitement could not spread to the whole bus.
Contiguous means touching or next to, which makes no sense for excitement.
Tiresome excitement would annoy people, not get them cheering.

sc1.tip: "So _____ that within minutes the entire bus was cheering" shows his excitement spread to everyone. You need a word meaning able to spread.

decoys.why: The whole bus caught his excitement, so it was not secret or hidden at all.
Cynical describes a distrustful attitude, but the sentence is about happy excitement spreading to others.
Susceptible describes people who catch things easily, not excitement that spreads to the whole bus.
His excitement was real enough to make the whole bus cheer, so it was not imagined.
Nothing in the sentence is repeated or unnecessary; the excitement spread from Jordan to everyone.
Lax means not strict, which has nothing to do with excitement spreading through the bus.

traps.why: Something contagious moves to others; this means it stays put.
Germs can be contagious, but so can laughter, which makes no one sick.
The tag inside contagious has nothing to do with tagging along.

syn2.tip: Germs, giggles, and moods can all be contagious. The key idea is spreading from one person to another.

sc2.stem: Unlike a broken arm, which stays with one patient, the flu is _____, so the nurse asked sick students to stay home.

traps.why: Broken arms hurt too, so painful gives no contrast with a broken arm.
Contained means kept in one place, but the flu spreads to others.
If the flu were harmless, the nurse would not send sick students home.

sc2.tip: "Unlike a broken arm, which stays with one patient" sets up a contrast. The flu must be the kind of illness that spreads to others.

decoys.why: Students can be susceptible to the flu, but the flu itself is what spreads between people.
The nurse is sending sick students home, so the flu here is very real, not imagined.
The contrast with a broken arm is about spreading to others, not about being touchable.
Humane means kind, and the sentence is about a sickness spreading, not about kindness.
Rugged means rough or tough, which does not explain why sick students should stay home.
Cynical describes a person's distrustful attitude, not an illness that passes between students.

meaning: make someone less eager or confident to try
example: The rain did not discourage fans from attending the game.
hook: Discourage takes the courage out of you: dis plus courage means losing the heart to try.

traps.why: Cheering someone on makes them more eager, the opposite of discourage.
Discouraging lowers eagerness; scaring to death is far too strong.
Disagree starts with dis too, but it means having a different opinion.

syn1.tip: Split it: dis plus courage. To discourage someone takes away their courage or eagerness, so they feel put off.

sc1.stem: Low scores on her first two tests did not _____ Ayana; instead, they motivated her to study harder, and she earned an A on the final.

traps.why: Inspiring her would match motivating, so "instead" would make no sense.
Discover looks similar but means find, and scores cannot find Ayana.
Dismiss means send away, which test scores cannot do to a student.

sc1.tip: "Did not _____ Ayana; instead, they motivated her" signals a contrast. The blank is the opposite of motivating, a word for making someone want to quit.

decoys.why: The word instead shows the scores could have pushed her down, not sped her up.
The sentence contrasts the blank with motivating her, so it needs something that lowers her eagerness.
Low scores do not pay Ayana back; the sentence asks what they failed to do to her confidence.
You cannot decorate a person, and the sentence is about Ayana losing or keeping her eagerness.
Test scores cannot take unfair advantage of her; the clue is about her motivation and confidence.

traps.why: Making someone more eager is encouraging, the opposite.
Discouraging lowers eagerness, but a ban stops something completely.
Embarrassment might discourage you, but it means shame, not losing eagerness.

syn2.tip: People say "don't get discouraged" when you want to give up. Discourage means lowering someone's eagerness to try.

sc2.stem: The coach worried that one bad loss might _____ the younger players, making them lose confidence and want to quit the team.

traps.why: Motivating players makes them want to keep going, not quit.
Reward is a happy word, but the players lose confidence here.
Dissolve starts with dis but means melt away, like sugar in water.

sc2.tip: The phrase "making them lose confidence and want to quit" explains the blank. You need a word meaning take away someone's eagerness.

decoys.why: Pacify means calm someone down, but the coach fears the loss will make players want to quit.
The coach worries players will lose confidence, so the loss would not keep them going.
The sentence is about players losing confidence, not about anything speeding up.
A loss cannot take advantage of players; the clue says it would make them lose confidence.
A bad loss does not pay players back; the sentence says it would make them want to quit.
Embellish means decorate, which has nothing to do with players losing confidence.

meaning: a green spot with water in a desert
example: The camels rested at an oasis shaded by palm trees.
hook: Picture a ring of palm trees around a cool blue pool in the middle of endless sand dunes.

traps.why: A wasteland is empty and barren, the opposite of a welcoming oasis.
A mirage is fake water you imagine; an oasis is real.
Basis looks similar but means the foundation of an idea.

syn1.tip: An oasis is a safe green spot in a harsh desert. People call any peaceful escape an oasis, like a quiet library on a noisy day.

sc1.stem: After hours of hiking across the hot, dusty canyon, the travelers finally reached a hidden _____ where cool spring water bubbled up beneath shady palm trees.

traps.why: Dunes are in deserts, but they are hills of dry sand, not water.
The travelers really reached the water, so it was not a mirage.
A wasteland is barren, not full of spring water and palm trees.

sc1.tip: "Cool spring water" and "shady palm trees" in a "hot, dusty" place describe one thing: a green, watered spot in dry land.

decoys.why: An ambush is a hidden attack, but this hidden spot has cool water and shady palms.
You can reach a milestone, but a milestone is not a place where spring water bubbles.
A pinnacle is a high point, but the sentence describes a shady spot with spring water.
The travelers found cool water and shade, a restful place, not confusion and disorder.
A brawl is a fight, but the sentence describes a peaceful spot with water and palm trees.
The spot is cool and shady after a hot hike, the opposite of wild excitement.

traps.why: An oasis is the wet, green break from dry sand.
That describes a mirage; an oasis has real water.
An oasis has water, but it is a small spot inside a desert.

syn2.tip: Think of desert travelers spotting palm trees in the distance. An oasis is real water and green plants surrounded by dry sand.

sc2.stem: Unlike the crowded, noisy cafeteria, the school library felt like a calm _____ where students could read in peace.

traps.why: A madhouse is wild and noisy, the reverse of calm and peaceful.
A mirage is not real, but students really read in the library.
Basis looks like oasis but means a foundation, not a place.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the crowded, noisy cafeteria" sets up a contrast. The library must be a peaceful escape, the way an oasis is an escape in a desert.

decoys.why: The library is unlike the noisy cafeteria and is called calm, so it is not turmoil.
Students read in peace there, so the library is not a place of wild excitement.
A brawl is noisy fighting, which matches the cafeteria, not the peaceful library.
The sentence calls the library calm and peaceful, which is the opposite of unrest.
A spectacle is an impressive sight, but the sentence describes a quiet place to read.
A hierarchy ranks people by level, which has nothing to do with a quiet place to read.

meaning: change something to improve or correct it
example: The class voted to amend the rules for recess games.
hook: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments: changes added to improve the U.S. Constitution.

traps.why: Amending makes something better; worsen means make it worse.
Amaze looks similar but means surprise someone greatly.
Lawmakers approve or amend rules, but approving accepts something as it is.

syn1.tip: Amendments to the Constitution are changes that fix or improve it. To amend something is to revise it.

sc1.stem: After students pointed out that the dress code was unfair to athletes, the principal agreed to _____ it by adding an exception for game days.

traps.why: Enforcing makes people follow a rule; adding an exception changes it.
Canceling gets rid of the rule, but she kept it and added an exception.
Defending keeps the rule unchanged, but she changed it.

sc1.tip: "Unfair" and "by adding an exception" tell you the principal changed the rule to fix it. You need a word meaning improve or correct.

decoys.why: The principal changed the rule by adding an exception, so he did not keep it as it was.
The dress code already existed; adding an exception changes it rather than forcing it on students.
The principal agreed with the students, so he was not holding out against their complaint.
Adding a game day exception corrects the rule; it does not combine anything into one whole.
The principal actually changed the dress code; he was not imitating it.
The sentence says the principal added an exception, so he changed the code instead of keeping it going.

traps.why: Damaging harms something; amending improves it.
Amending changes part of something; replacing swaps out the whole thing.
You obey rules as they are; amending changes them.

syn2.tip: Hidden inside amend is "mend," as in mending a torn shirt. Amending fixes or corrects something.

sc2.stem: Rather than throwing out her entire essay, Priya decided to _____ it, fixing a few weak sentences and adding a stronger conclusion.

traps.why: Discarding means throwing it out, which "rather than" rules out.
She might submit it later, but fixing sentences is improving it.
Amass looks similar but means collect a large amount.

sc2.tip: "Rather than throwing out her entire essay" means she kept it, and "fixing a few weak sentences" tells you she improved it.

decoys.why: Priya fixed weak sentences to make the essay stronger, not weaker.
She added a stronger conclusion, so she was not using up her essay.
Priya was really fixing her essay, not imitating how an essay looks.
The sentence describes Priya fixing and adding to her essay, not holding up against force.
Instead of hiding her essay, Priya kept it and improved it with fixes.
The clue says she was fixing and changing her essay, not just keeping it going.

meaning: having many small, complicated parts
example: The quilt had an intricate pattern of tiny stars.
hook: Picture a snowflake under a magnifying glass: so many tiny, detailed parts that it looks intricate.

traps.why: Simple means plain and easy, the opposite of intricate.
Intimate looks similar but means close and personal.
Intricate things are often delicate, but delicate means easily broken.

syn1.tip: Intricate things have lots of small parts woven together, like a detailed drawing or a maze. Think complicated, not plain.

sc1.stem: The ancient clock was so _____, with hundreds of tiny gears fitting together, that only one repairman in the city knew how to fix it.

traps.why: A basic clock would not need the one expert repairman.
Value does not explain why only one person could fix it.
Intimate means close and personal, which does not describe a clock.

sc1.tip: "Hundreds of tiny gears fitting together" and "only one repairman" who could fix it point to something with many complicated parts.

decoys.why: Rugged means rough and tough, but hundreds of tiny gears point to complicated, delicate work.
The gears all fit together, and nothing in the sentence suggests unnecessary repeated parts.
Every clock can be touched; the clue about tiny gears explains why it was hard to fix.
Coherent describes logical ideas, but the sentence is about a clock with many tiny parts.
Simultaneous means happening at once, which does not describe a clock full of tiny gears.
The clock was real enough to need a repairman, so it was not imagined.

traps.why: Plain means having few details, the opposite of intricate.
Intricate things may cost a lot, but intricate is about many parts.
Intricate things are complicated but still possible to make or understand.

syn2.tip: Picture an intricate quilt pattern of tiny stars carefully stitched. Intricate means full of fine details.

sc2.stem: Maya's first paper airplane was simple to fold, but the dragon in her origami book was far more _____, requiring forty-two careful folds and tiny tucks.

traps.why: Basic would fit only if you missed the contrast word "but."
Origami can be colorful, but the clue is about the number of folds.
Dragons can be scary, but the clue is about careful folds and tucks.

sc2.tip: "Simple to fold, but" signals a contrast, and "forty-two careful folds and tiny tucks" shows the dragon has many complicated steps.

decoys.why: The sentence contrasts simple with forty-two careful folds, which points to complicated, not repetitive or unnecessary.
Rugged means rough and tough, but forty-two careful folds and tiny tucks describe delicate detail.
Articulate describes people who speak clearly, not a paper dragon with many folds.
The contrast with a simple airplane is about the number of folds, not about logic.
Both paper models can be touched; the clue about forty-two folds points to complexity.
Prolific describes someone who produces a lot, not a single dragon with many folds.

meaning: spreading wildly and out of control
example: Weeds grew rampant in the abandoned garden.
hook: Picture weeds swallowing a garden and vines climbing everything while nobody stops them: that wild growth is rampant.

traps.why: Controlled means kept in check, the opposite of rampant.
Rampant things are often harmful, but rampant means spreading wildly.
Radiant looks a bit similar but means glowing or bright.

syn1.tip: You often hear "rampant" with bad things that spread, like "rampant cheating" or "rampant weeds." It means growing with nothing to stop it.

sc1.stem: Once the invasive vine arrived on the island, its growth was _____, smothering native plants faster than volunteers could pull it up.

traps.why: Limited growth would not smother plants faster than volunteers worked.
Beautiful is positive, but smothering native plants is a bad thing.
Plants grow in seasons, but the clue is about growth nobody can stop.

sc1.tip: "Smothering native plants faster than volunteers could pull it up" shows nothing could stop the vine. The blank needs a word for wild, uncontrolled growth.

decoys.why: The vine is smothering plants faster than anyone can stop it, which is wild, not finely detailed.
The vine actually arrived and is smothering real plants, so its growth is not imaginary.
Smothering native plants is harmful, so the growth is not kind or gentle.
The growth is out in the open, overpowering plants faster than volunteers can pull it.
Lax means not strict, which says nothing about growth spreading out of control.
The sentence describes fast, wild growth, not something unnecessary or repeated.

traps.why: Kept in check means controlled, the opposite of rampant.
Rampant spreading is fast and wild, not slow.
Rampage looks similar, but rampant is about spreading, not anger.

syn2.tip: Rampant describes something spreading wildly, like rumors racing around school. Ask yourself whether anything is stopping it. If not, it is rampant.

sc2.stem: Last month only a couple of students believed the rumor about a four-day school week, but by Friday it was _____, repeated in every hallway and classroom.

traps.why: Rare would fit only if you missed "but" and "every hallway."
Rumors are often false, but the clue is about how far it spread.
The clue is about the rumor spreading everywhere, not how fun it felt.

sc2.tip: "Only a couple of students... but by Friday" signals a big change, and "repeated in every hallway" shows the rumor spread wildly.

decoys.why: The rumor was repeated in every hallway, so it was anything but secret.
The rumor was repeated, but the sentence means it spread widely, not that it was unnecessary.
A rumor cannot be touched; the sentence is about how fast it spread.
The sentence is about the rumor spreading everywhere, not about having complicated parts.
Kindness has nothing to do with a rumor spreading through every classroom.
A rumor cannot believe anything; the sentence is about how widely it spread.

meaning: full of energy and enthusiasm
example: The class had a spirited debate about school uniforms.
hook: Think of school spirit: a spirited crowd jumps, chants, and cheers with energy that fills the whole gym.
