traps.why: Dull means lacking energy, the opposite of spirited.
Spiritual looks similar but is about religion or the soul.
Spirit can mean ghost, but spirited means full of energy.

syn1.tip: Think of "school spirit." Fans with school spirit cheer loudly. Spirited means full of that kind of energy.

sc1.stem: Although the team was losing badly, the fans remained _____, cheering, chanting, and waving banners until the final whistle.

traps.why: Gloomy fits only if you miss "although"; the fans kept cheering.
Spiritual is about religion or the soul, not cheering fans.
The team was losing, but cheering fans did not act defeated.

sc1.tip: "Although the team was losing badly" sets up a contrast, and "cheering, chanting, and waving banners" shows the fans stayed full of energy.

decoys.why: The fans kept cheering and chanting, which shows enthusiasm, not a gloomy, distrustful attitude.
Cheering, chanting, and waving banners is loud and visible, not secret or hidden.
The fans were really there cheering, so they were not imaginary.
The sentence describes the fans' energy, not something with many complicated parts.
The fans were full of energy, not unnecessary or repetitive.

traps.why: Sluggish means slow and tired, the opposite of spirited.
Frantic is wild and panicked, much stronger than spirited.
Rowdy is negative and unruly; spirited is a positive word.

syn2.tip: Spirited is a positive word for having lots of pep. A spirited team or debate is full of energy, not wild or out of control.

sc2.stem: After a long nap and a big snack, the puppy was suddenly _____, racing around the yard, chasing its tail, and pouncing on every leaf.

traps.why: Drowsy means sleepy, but the puppy is racing and pouncing.
It just had a big snack, and racing around shows energy.
Spirit can mean ghost, but the puppy is full of energy.

sc2.tip: "After a long nap and a big snack" explains the change, and "racing," "chasing," and "pouncing" describe a puppy full of energy.

decoys.why: A puppy racing and pouncing shows energy, not a belief that everyone is selfish.
A puppy cannot express ideas in words; it is racing and chasing its tail.
Racing around and pouncing on leaves is lively and obvious, not secret.
The sentence describes the puppy's energy, not something with many small parts.
The puppy is really racing around the yard, so it is not imaginary.
An energetic puppy is not unnecessary or repetitive; the clues point to energy.

meaning: a surprise attack from a hidden spot
example: The lion hid in the tall grass, waiting in ambush.
hook: Ambush comes from an old French word meaning to hide in the woods, exactly where attackers wait.

traps.why: A warning tells you danger is coming; an ambush gives no warning.
An ambush can start a battle, but it is specifically a hidden surprise.
Ambulance starts the same way but is a vehicle for sick people.

syn1.tip: Picture attackers crouched out of sight, waiting to spring on someone passing by. An ambush is a hidden trap.

sc1.stem: During the snowball fight, Mateo and his friends hid behind the hedge and set up a sneaky _____, leaping out to surprise their cousins with a barrage of snowballs.

traps.why: A truce stops a fight, but they leaped out throwing snowballs.
Snowmen fit the snowy scene, but you cannot leap out from one.
Ambulance looks similar but is a vehicle for sick people.

sc1.tip: "Hid behind the hedge" and "leaping out to surprise their cousins" describe a hidden attack. That sneak attack is the missing word.

decoys.why: They leaped out to surprise their cousins, an attack from hiding, not damage to ruin plans.
A brawl is an open, rough fight, but they hid and sprang out by surprise.
They were hiding behind a hedge, so they were not putting on an impressive show.
An oasis is a green spot in a desert, not a surprise attack in the snow.
You cannot set up a frenzy from a hiding spot; they planned a surprise attack.
An official order from a ruler has nothing to do with hiding behind a hedge.

traps.why: An ambush is a hostile surprise, not a friendly heads-up.
A retreat is moving away from a fight, not springing an attack.
A war is huge and long; an ambush is one sudden attack.

syn2.tip: An ambush depends on surprise. The attackers stay hidden, then strike suddenly, so ambush means a surprise attack.

sc2.stem: Instead of charging openly across the field, the soldiers hid quietly in the forest, planning their _____ for when the enemy troops marched down the road.

traps.why: A charge is an open attack, which "instead of" rules out.
Troops march in parades, but hiding soldiers are planning an attack.
Ambition starts like ambush but means a strong goal or dream.

sc2.tip: "Instead of charging openly" tells you the attack was not open, and "hid quietly in the forest" shows it was a hidden surprise.

decoys.why: The soldiers chose not to charge openly, and a brawl is a rough open fight.
The soldiers hid quietly in the forest, so they were avoiding any impressive show.
Soldiers hiding to attack marching troops are planning an attack, not an official order.
A record of events does not fit soldiers waiting in hiding for the enemy.
You plan an attack, not extreme anger; the clue is hiding quietly in the forest.
The soldiers want to attack the enemy, not show them honor or respect.

meaning: able to express ideas clearly in words
example: The articulate student explained the plan to the school board.
hook: Articulate comes from Latin for jointed: an articulate speaker joins words together smoothly, like well-fitted joints.

traps.why: Tongue-tied means unable to find words, the opposite of articulate.
Artistic starts with art too but means skilled at art.
Talkative people talk a lot, but not always clearly.

syn1.tip: Articulate people put their thoughts into clear words. If someone explains a hard idea so everyone gets it, they are articulate.

sc1.stem: Even at age ten, Nia was remarkably _____, explaining her recycling plan so clearly and persuasively that the adults at the town meeting applauded.

traps.why: A shy child would not win applause for a persuasive speech.
Artistic is about art, but the clue is about explaining clearly.
Stubborn is negative, but the adults applauded her clear explanation.

sc1.tip: "Explaining her recycling plan so clearly and persuasively" is the clue. The blank must describe someone who expresses ideas well in words.

decoys.why: Being loud enough to hear is not the same as explaining clearly and persuasively.
Nia shared a hopeful recycling plan and earned applause, which is not a selfish view of people.
The sentence praises how clearly she spoke, not that she repeated herself.
Nia was explaining a plan for the future, not longing for the past.
She explained her plan openly at a town meeting, so nothing was secret.
The clue is that she explained things clearly, not that she could not keep still.

traps.why: Articulate people explain things well, the reverse of this.
Articulate is a compliment; loud and pushy is negative.
Articulate begins with art, but it is about speaking, not painting.

syn2.tip: Think of the verb: you articulate ideas when you put them into words. An articulate person does that clearly and well.

sc2.stem: Usually Marcus mumbled and lost his place during reports, but at the science fair he was surprisingly _____, describing his volcano project in clear, confident sentences.

traps.why: Tongue-tied fits only if you miss "but"; he spoke clearly here.
Volcanoes are explosive, but the clue is about how Marcus spoke.
Boastful is negative; clear, confident sentences show skill, not bragging.

sc2.tip: "Usually Marcus mumbled... but" signals a contrast, and "clear, confident sentences" tells you he spoke well.

decoys.why: The sentence says he spoke in clear, confident sentences, not that he was fidgety.
He was describing his project out loud to people, so nothing was hidden.
The sentence praises his clear speaking, not that he repeated things needlessly.
The contrast is with mumbling, so the blank is about speaking clearly, not distrust.
He was describing his volcano project, not longing for the past.
Clear, confident sentences show care, not a careless, loose approach.

meaning: secret or hidden
example: The kids planned a covert operation to throw a surprise party.
hook: Covert comes from an old French word meaning covered: a covert plan is covered up so nobody sees it.

traps.why: Public means open for all to see, the opposite of covert.
Coveted looks similar but means strongly wanted, like a coveted trophy.
Spy missions can be dangerous, but covert means hidden.

syn1.tip: Covert looks like "covered." A covert plan is covered up so others cannot see it, like a spy mission.

sc1.stem: The students planned a _____ mission to decorate their teacher's classroom, whispering in hallways and meeting only after she had left the building.

traps.why: A public mission would not need whispering or waiting until she left.
Decorating might be hard, but the clue is about keeping it hidden.
Coveted means strongly wanted, which does not explain the whispering.

sc1.tip: "Whispering in hallways" and "meeting only after she had left the building" show the students kept their plan hidden from their teacher.

decoys.why: They whispered and met only after the teacher left, so the plan was kept quiet, not spreading wildly.
The clues about whispering point to secrecy, not to something unnecessary.
Decorating a teacher's room is a kind gesture, not a selfish, distrustful one.
Whispering and meeting after she left point to secrecy, not toughness.
Meeting only after she left shows they were very careful, not careless.
The sentence is about keeping the plan hidden, not about producing a lot of work.

traps.why: Overt means out in the open, the reverse of covert.
Covert actions can be harmless, like a surprise party; illegal is negative.
Secret plans may be clever, but covert means kept hidden.

syn2.tip: Think of "covert operations" in spy movies. Agents stay hidden so nobody knows what they are doing.

sc2.stem: Most of the soccer team's plays were obvious, but the coach also taught a _____ signal, a tiny tug on her ear that the other team never noticed.

traps.why: A loud signal would be noticed, but the other team never noticed.
A tiny ear tug is simple; the clue is about it being unnoticed.
Friendliness has nothing to do with the other team never noticing.

sc2.tip: "Most... were obvious, but" sets up a contrast, and "the other team never noticed" tells you the signal was hidden.

decoys.why: The signal was a tiny tug on her ear, not something extreme.
The signal was special because nobody noticed it, not because it repeated another one.
A tiny tug the other team never noticed is hidden, not spreading wildly.
The coach really taught and used the signal, so it was not imaginary.
The signal was a hidden ear tug, with no longing for the past.
A signal cannot believe anything; the clue is that no one noticed it.

meaning: not strict or careful enough
example: Security at the old museum was surprisingly lax.
hook: A lax rule is like a loose shoelace: it slips, and nobody bothers to tighten it.

traps.why: Strict is the opposite of lax.
Lax can sound relaxed, but it is about rules, not being tired.
Generous is a kind, positive word; lax means carelessly not enforcing rules.

syn1.tip: Lax hides inside "relax." Rules that are relaxed too much are lax, or loose.

sc1.stem: Unlike last year's strict babysitter, the new one was so _____ about rules that the kids stayed up past midnight eating ice cream.

traps.why: Strict is the opposite; the new babysitter is unlike the strict one.
A babysitter serious about rules would not allow midnight ice cream.
Worry about rules would not lead kids to stay up past midnight.

sc1.tip: "Unlike" sets her against a "strict" babysitter, and midnight ice cream shows she barely enforced any rules.

decoys.why: How well the babysitter speaks doesn't explain why the kids stayed up past midnight.
Being energetic has nothing to do with letting kids break rules, which is the clue here.
Missing the past doesn't explain why the babysitter let the kids ignore the rules.

traps.why: Far too harsh is the opposite of lax.
Lax is about rules not being enforced, not about moving slowly.
Kind and gentle is praise; lax is a complaint about carelessness.

syn2.tip: Think of "lax security": guards who never check bags are not strict enough.

sc2.stem: Coach Rivera was famously _____ about practice; players wandered in late, skipped drills, and never heard a single word of complaint from him.

traps.why: Strict is the opposite; a strict coach would complain about skipped drills.
Punctual is about being on time, and his players wandered in late.
Nothing shows he was nervous; the examples show he never enforced rules.

sc2.tip: The examples after the semicolon, late players, skipped drills, and "never heard a single word of complaint," show rules weren't enforced.

decoys.why: A spirited coach would care about practice, but he never complained about late players.
The players never heard a single word from him, so he was not expressing ideas clearly.
Longing for the past doesn't explain why players could skip drills without complaint.

meaning: happening at the same time
example: The twins gave simultaneous answers to the riddle.
hook: A simulcast is a show aired on TV and radio at the same moment: a simultaneous broadcast.

traps.why: Consecutive means one after another, not at the same time.
Similar looks close, but it means alike, not at the same time.
Sudden is about timing, but it means unexpected, not at the same time.

syn1.tip: Think of a "simulcast," one show aired on two channels at once. Concurrent also means running at the same time.

sc1.stem: Because the soccer final and the science fair were _____, both starting at exactly noon on Saturday, Rafael had to choose which one to attend.

traps.why: Separate events would not both start at exactly noon.
Similar looks close, but alike events wouldn't force Rafael to choose.
Big events can be crowded, but crowds wouldn't make him pick one.

sc1.tip: The phrase "both starting at exactly noon" means the events happen at the same time, which is why Rafael "had to choose."

decoys.why: The events weren't repeats of each other; the clue says both started at exactly noon.
Both events were real and Rafael had to pick one, so they weren't imagined.
The clue is about timing, both at noon, not about having complicated parts.
Events can't spread between people; the sentence is about both starting at the same time.

traps.why: Taking turns is the opposite of happening at the same time.
That is similar, a lookalike word, not simultaneous.
Speed is about timing too, but simultaneous means at the same moment.

syn2.tip: The ending sounds like "instantaneous." Simultaneous things share the same instant, so they happen at once.

sc2.stem: At most concerts the two drummers take turns soloing, but tonight they will play _____ solos, so the crowd should expect twice the noise at once.

traps.why: Separate solos are the usual plan; "but" says tonight is different.
Alternating means taking turns, which is what "but" says they won't do.
Similar looks close, but alike solos wouldn't make twice the noise at once.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with drummers who "take turns," and "twice the noise at once" tells you both solos happen together.

decoys.why: The clue says twice the noise at once, which means timing, not unnecessary repetition.
All solos can be heard; the clue is that they play at once instead of taking turns.
The crowd should expect real noise tonight, so the solos are not imaginary.
Secret, hidden solos would not give the crowd twice the noise.

meaning: a rough, noisy fight
example: The hockey game was stopped after a brawl broke out.
hook: Picture a cartoon brawl: a spinning dust cloud with fists, feet, and stars flying out of it.

traps.why: A truce is an agreement to stop fighting, the opposite of a brawl.
Crawl looks like brawl but means a slow creep.
Brawls can break out at games, but a game is not a fight.

syn1.tip: Think of a cowboy movie "barroom brawl": chairs flying, everyone swinging. That is a fight.

sc1.stem: The hockey game was stopped for twenty minutes after a shoving match between two players grew into a wild _____ involving both entire benches.

traps.why: A handshake is friendly, the opposite of a shoving match growing wild.
An argument is milder than shoving, but the fight "grew" bigger.
Benches clear for celebrations too, but a shoving match doesn't become a party.

sc1.tip: A "shoving match" that "grew into" something "wild" with "both entire benches" must be bigger and rougher than shoving.

decoys.why: It grew from a shoving match in plain view, not a surprise attack from hiding.
A rift is a split between people, but the clue describes a wild fight.
Showing honor and respect is the opposite of a shoving match that stopped the game.
A shoving match turning wild is not an important stage of progress.
Nobody caught a disease; the players were fighting each other.

traps.why: A peaceful meeting is the opposite of a brawl.
That is bawl, which sounds like brawl but means to cry.
An argument is only words; a brawl uses fists, so it's stronger.

syn2.tip: A brawl uses fists, not just words. If a choice is only shouting, it's too mild.

sc2.stem: The lunchroom argument began politely, but after someone shoved a tray, it became a messy _____, and three teachers had to pull the students apart.

traps.why: A debate is just talking; teachers pulling students apart means real fighting.
An apology ends trouble; this scene got worse after the shove.
Picnics involve food, but nobody pulls students apart at a picnic.

sc2.tip: "But" shows the talk stopped being polite, and teachers who "had to pull the students apart" means it turned physical.

decoys.why: Teachers had to pull students apart, so it was a physical fight, not just a split.
It started as a polite argument, not a surprise attack from a hidden spot.
Shoving a tray is not a way of showing respect.
A record of events wouldn't need three teachers to pull students apart.
An oasis is a peaceful spot, but this lunchroom scene was a messy fight.

meaning: to follow a group's rules or customs
example: Students must conform to the dress code.
hook: Conform is con (with) plus form: you shape yourself into the same form as everyone around you.

traps.why: To rebel is to fight the rules, the opposite of conform.
Confirm looks like conform but means to make sure something is true.
People may complain about rules, but conform means following them.

syn1.tip: Picture a cookie cutter: con- means "with," so you match the same form as everyone else. That means following, or complying.

sc1.stem: Rather than _____ to the trend of wearing the same brand of sneakers as everyone else, Jade proudly wore her hand-painted canvas shoes.

traps.why: Objecting is what Jade actually did; "rather than" needs the opposite.
Confess starts like conform, but admitting to a trend makes no sense here.
You hear about trends, but the clue is about copying everyone's style.

sc1.tip: "Rather than" tells you Jade did the opposite of the blank. She stood out, so the blank means going along "as everyone else" does.

traps.why: Breaking the rules is the opposite of conforming.
That means confirm, a lookalike word, not conform.
Conform holds "form," but it means following rules, not reshaping something.

syn2.tip: A "nonconformist" refuses to fit in, so conform means the reverse: to go along with the crowd.

sc2.stem: To look perfectly matched on stage, every band member must _____ to the uniform rules: white shirts, black pants, and absolutely no flashy jewelry.

traps.why: Objecting to the rules would ruin the goal of looking matched.
Bands play music for dancing, but the sentence is about following rules.
Confess starts like conform but means admitting something, which doesn't fit.

sc2.tip: The goal is to "look perfectly matched," and the colon lists rules everyone has to follow. So the blank means go along with them.

meaning: a state of great confusion or disorder
example: The kitchen was in turmoil before the big family dinner.
hook: Picture a kitchen in turmoil: pots boiling over, the smoke alarm beeping, and three cooks yelling at once.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite of turmoil.
Toil looks similar but means hard work, not wild confusion.
Turmoil can make people sad, but it means confusion and disorder.

syn1.tip: Turmoil ends with the same letters as "boil." Picture a boiling pot: everything churning and messy. That's chaos.

sc1.stem: When the fire alarm went off during the school play, the auditorium fell into _____, with parents shouting, children crying, and actors running offstage.

traps.why: Shouting and crying are the opposite of silence.
Plays get applause, but a fire alarm causes panic, not clapping.
Disappointment is too mild for shouting, crying, and running.

sc1.tip: The list after the comma, "shouting," "crying," and "running offstage," paints wild confusion, not one quiet feeling.

decoys.why: People shouting and running offstage shows disorder, not an orderly ranking system.
The people were frightened and confused by the alarm, not filled with extreme anger.
Nothing shameful happened; the alarm caused confusion and panic.

traps.why: Peace is the opposite of turmoil.
Turnover starts like turmoil but means a pastry or a change of people.
Worry is a mild feeling; turmoil is a whole scene of wild confusion.

syn2.tip: Things are "thrown into turmoil," like a room tossed upside down. Look for the choice meaning a big mess.

sc2.stem: The library was usually calm and orderly, but after a pipe burst overnight it was in total _____, with soggy books, buckets everywhere, and workers rushing around.

traps.why: Order describes the usual library; "but" says things changed.
Burst pipes can cut power, but the clues describe mess, not darkness.
Comfort is a pleasant feeling; soggy books and rushing workers are stressful.

sc2.tip: "But" flips the "calm and orderly" library, and "buckets everywhere" with "workers rushing around" describe wild disorder.

decoys.why: The sentence says the library was no longer orderly, so a ranking system doesn't fit.
A library can't feel anger; soggy books and rushing workers show confusion.

meaning: able to speak or write easily and smoothly
example: After a year in Spain, Elena became fluent in Spanish.
hook: Fluent shares a Latin root with "fluid" and "flow": a fluent speaker's words flow like water.

traps.why: Stumbling over words is the opposite of fluent.
Fluffy starts like fluent but means soft and puffy.
Loudness is about speaking too, but fluent means easy and smooth.

syn1.tip: Fluent shares a root with "fluid." Speech that flows like water is smooth.

sc1.stem: Having grown up speaking both Korean and English at home, Min-jun was _____ in both languages and switched between them without any hesitation.

traps.why: Confused speakers hesitate, but he switched "without any hesitation."
Shyness is about speaking too, but it doesn't explain easy switching.
Average is too weak for switching languages without hesitation.

sc1.tip: "Having grown up speaking both" explains why he switched "without any hesitation." Easy, smooth speaking is the answer.

decoys.why: He switched languages without hesitation, so he was skilled, not careless.
The sentence is about how easily he speaks, not about being unable to sit still.
Growing up with two languages made him skilled in them, not wistful about the past.
Nothing in the sentence is about distrusting people, only about speaking easily.
Nothing is secret here; the sentence describes how smoothly he speaks both languages.
Switching languages without hesitation shows ease, not care about keeping secrets.

traps.why: Stumbling over words is the opposite of being fluent.
The root means flow, but fluent describes speech, not actual liquid.
Fluent starts with "flu," but it has nothing to do with illness.

syn2.tip: You've heard "fluent in Spanish." It means you can speak the language easily, without stopping to search for words.

sc2.stem: My little brother is only learning French, so he pauses after every word, but my aunt is _____ and chats with the waiter in Paris at full speed.

traps.why: Hesitant describes the brother; "but" shows the aunt is different.
A waiter suggests food, but the clue is about how she speaks.
Quiet doesn't fit someone chatting "at full speed."

sc2.tip: "But" sets the aunt against a brother who "pauses after every word," and "at full speed" shows she speaks French easily.

decoys.why: She chats at full speed, the opposite of quietly avoiding attention.
The contrast is about speaking smoothly versus pausing, not about missing the past.
The sentence compares speaking skill, not how much she trusts people.
Talking at full speed in French shows skill, not carelessness.
Your aunt really chats with the waiter, so nothing about her is imagined.
The contrast is with pausing after every word, so she must speak smoothly, not repeat herself.

meaning: to support and keep a rule or tradition
example: Judges must uphold the law fairly.
hook: Uphold is up plus hold: picture judges holding a rule up high so nobody can knock it down.

traps.why: To overturn a rule is to throw it out, the opposite.
Upset also starts with "up" but means to disturb or knock over.
Up plus hold sounds like lifting, but uphold means keeping a rule strong.

syn1.tip: Up plus hold: you hold a rule up so it stays standing. "Uphold the law" means support it.

sc1.stem: The honor council's job is to _____ the school's code of honesty, making sure every student follows it rather than letting it be ignored.

traps.why: The council exists to stop the code from being ignored.
Rewriting changes a code; the council's job is making students follow it.
Up plus hold sounds like lifting, but you can't lift a code of honesty.

sc1.tip: "Making sure every student follows it rather than letting it be ignored" tells you the council keeps the code strong.

decoys.why: The council makes sure students follow the code, so it supports rather than weakens it.
The job is making sure the code is followed, not changing it.
The council protects the code; it does not take unfair advantage of it.
Holding back the code would let it be ignored, which is the opposite of the job.
The council keeps the whole code followed, not cutting parts of it out.
The sentence is about keeping the code followed, not decorating it.

traps.why: Abandon means give up on, the opposite of uphold.
The parts suggest raising up, but uphold means keeping a rule in place.
A holdup is a robbery, but uphold means keeping a rule standing.

syn2.tip: Courts "uphold a decision" when they keep it in place. Think of keeping something standing, not tossing it out.

sc2.stem: Grandma insists that every family member _____ our tradition of Sunday pancakes, so even my busy cousins rush home each weekend to flip them together.

traps.why: If they abandoned it, the cousins wouldn't rush home every weekend.
You can't invent a tradition that already exists.
Upset also starts with "up" but means to disturb, which doesn't fit.

sc2.tip: Because of Grandma, "even my busy cousins rush home" every weekend. That effect shows everyone keeps the tradition going.

decoys.why: Cousins rush home to keep the tradition going, so no one is weakening it.
Grandma wants the tradition kept as it is, not changed.
The cousins happily rush home, so they are not bitter about the tradition.
The point is keeping the pancake tradition alive, not decorating it.
Nothing is being cut; the family keeps the whole tradition going.
Grandma wants everyone to keep the tradition, not take unfair advantage of it.

meaning: to work together
example: The two classes collaborated on a giant mural.
hook: Collaborate is co (together) plus labor (work): two classes working together on one giant mural.

traps.why: Competing means working against each other, the opposite.
Elaborate looks similar but means to add more detail.
Teammates talk, but communicating isn't the same as working together.

syn1.tip: Spot "labor" (work) inside collaborate, plus co- for "together." Working together is cooperating.

sc1.stem: Instead of competing against each other, the two rival schools decided to _____ on a single robot, sharing ideas, parts, and practice time.

traps.why: "Instead of competing" rules this out; they did the opposite.
Rivals might argue, but sharing ideas and parts is teamwork.
Elaborate looks similar but means to explain in more detail.

sc1.tip: "Instead of competing" flips the meaning, and "sharing ideas, parts, and practice time" describes teamwork.

decoys.why: Sharing ideas, parts, and practice time is working together, not guessing.
The schools share everything as partners rather than forcing something on each other.
Both schools build the robot together; neither is stepping in to stop something.

traps.why: Working alone is the opposite of collaborating.
That is collapse, a lookalike word, not collaborate.
Collaborate contains the letters "lab," but it means teamwork, not science labs.

syn2.tip: Co- means "together" in "coworker" and "cooperate." A collaborator is a teammate.

sc2.stem: The science project was too big for one person, so Maya and Leo agreed to _____, with Maya building the volcano and Leo writing the report.

traps.why: Competing is the opposite of splitting the jobs on one project.
A huge project might tempt you to quit, but they each did a job.
Collapse looks similar but means to fall down.

sc2.tip: "Too big for one person" causes the plan, and splitting jobs, one "building" and one "writing," means they work together.

decoys.why: Maya and Leo split up real work, so they are not just guessing.
Nobody is stepping in to stop anything; the two are dividing up a project.
The sentence shows them sharing tasks, not following a group's customs.
Nobody is paying anyone back; they are dividing the project between them.
The sentence describes splitting up the work, not speeding something up.

meaning: guess without having all the facts
example: Fans speculated about who would win the cooking contest.
hook: Speculate comes from a Latin word for watching from a lookout: picture sailors squinting at a far ship, guessing what it is.

traps.why: To prove is to show for certain, the opposite of guessing.
Speak starts like speculate but just means to talk.
Calculating works things out exactly; speculating is guessing without facts.

syn1.tip: When sports reporters "speculate" about a game, they're guessing before the facts come in. Speculation is guesswork.

sc1.stem: Since the scientists had found only a single fossil tooth, they could only _____ about how large the ancient shark had grown.

traps.why: Bragging is boasting; one tooth gives nothing to boast about.
Sharks can be scary, but the clue is about missing facts.
Forgetting doesn't connect to having only one tooth to study.

sc1.tip: "Only a single fossil tooth" means they lacked the full facts, so they "could only" make guesses.

traps.why: Knowing for sure is the opposite of speculating.
The root spec means look, but speculate now means guessing.
Rumors involve guesses, but speculating doesn't mean spreading gossip.

syn2.tip: Detectives speculate when they form a theory before they have proof. Look for building an idea without all the facts.

sc2.stem: Since the coach has not announced the starting lineup yet, players can only _____ about who will start, trading hunches in the locker room.

traps.why: Nothing has been announced, so there is nothing to read yet.
Complaining is grumpy, but the players are just trading hunches.
Players trading hunches are clearly thinking about it, not forgetting.

sc2.tip: The lineup is "not announced yet," and "trading hunches" restates the blank. Hunches are guesses made without facts.

meaning: present from birth; natural
example: Spiders have an innate ability to spin webs.
hook: Innate shares a Latin root with "natal," as in prenatal: an innate trait is one you were born with.

traps.why: Learned means picked up later, the opposite of innate.
Inner looks similar but means inside, not present from birth.
Talent can be innate, but innate just means born with it.

syn1.tip: Innate sounds like "in-born": built into you from the start, like a spider's natural knack for webs.

sc1.stem: No one ever teaches baby sea turtles to crawl toward the ocean; this _____ instinct guides them from the moment they hatch.

traps.why: "No one ever teaches" them, so the instinct isn't learned.
Newly hatched turtles haven't had time to practice anything.
Ornate looks similar but means fancy and decorated.

sc1.tip: "No one ever teaches" them and it works "from the moment they hatch," so the instinct is something they're born with.

decoys.why: No one teaches the turtles, so the instinct is inborn, not spread between them.
Newborn turtles have no past to miss; the instinct is there from hatching.
The sentence is about an inborn instinct, not distrust of others.
The instinct is what guides them, so it is needed, not unnecessary.
The clue is that no one teaches them, so the instinct is inborn, not strict.
The instinct reliably guides them, and the clue points to it being inborn.

traps.why: Taught skills are learned, the opposite of innate.
In- here means "in," not "not"; innate means born with.
That is inmate, a lookalike word, not innate.

syn2.tip: Babies grab fingers without lessons; that is an innate behavior. Look for the choice about being born with it.

sc2.stem: Although Dad took years of lessons to play piano, my sister seems to have an _____ sense of rhythm; she tapped perfect beats before she could walk.

traps.why: Acquired means gained over time, like Dad's lessons; "although" signals a contrast.
Her perfect beats were real, so her rhythm isn't imaginary.
Ornate looks similar but means fancy and decorated.

sc2.tip: "Although" contrasts Dad's "years of lessons" with your sister, who had rhythm "before she could walk," so hers came naturally.

decoys.why: Rhythm is about beats, not explaining ideas in words, and she could not even walk yet.
The contrast with Dad's lessons shows her rhythm was natural, not just loud enough to hear.
The clue is that she had rhythm before walking, meaning natural, not unbeatable.

meaning: to combine into one stronger whole
example: The district consolidated two small schools into one.
hook: Consolidate has con (together) and solid inside: you press loose pieces together into one solid whole.

traps.why: Separate is the opposite of consolidate, which joins things together.
Console looks similar but means to comfort someone who is sad.
The solid inside might suggest freezing, but consolidate means joining things.

syn1.tip: Find solid inside and con- (together) at the front: consolidate means putting pieces together into one solid whole.

sc1.stem: To make studying easier, Ravi decided to _____ his scattered notes from three notebooks into a single, organized binder.

traps.why: Dividing splits notes apart, but he wants them in a single binder.
Console looks like consolidate but means to comfort, and notes need no comfort.
Throwing notes away would not put them into an organized binder.

sc1.tip: The words "from three notebooks into a single, organized binder" tell you he is joining scattered notes into one.

decoys.why: Ravi is combining notes into one binder, not correcting or improving them.
Nothing is being cut out as unacceptable; the notes are being gathered into one place.
Ravi wants studying easier, so he would not weaken his notes; he is making them stronger together.
He is not imitating his notes; he is putting three notebooks together into one binder.
Ravi is not hiding his notes; he is organizing them into a single binder.

traps.why: Divide is the opposite; consolidating turns many parts into one.
Arranging puts things in order but does not join them into one.
Consolidating makes something stronger, so weaken points the wrong way.

syn2.tip: Think of companies that consolidate: two businesses merge into one bigger, stronger company.

sc2.stem: Instead of keeping three separate lemonade stands on different corners, the cousins decided to _____ them into one big stand near the park entrance.

traps.why: Split means break apart, but they end up with one big stand.
Advertising helps a stand sell, but it doesn't turn three stands into one.
Consult looks similar but means ask for advice.

sc2.tip: The contrast "Instead of keeping three separate" stands and the phrase "into one big stand" show they joined them together.

decoys.why: The cousins want one big stand, so they are joining the stands, not weakening them.
They are not fixing the stands; they are merging three stands into one.
Nothing is being imitated; the sentence says three stands become one real stand.
The cousins are not holding the stands back; they are combining them near the park.

meaning: the highest point
example: Winning Olympic gold was the pinnacle of her career.
hook: Picture the thin, pointed top of a church tower reaching for the sky: that spire is a pinnacle, the highest point.

traps.why: Bottom is the lowest point, the opposite of a pinnacle.
Barnacle rhymes with pinnacle but is a shellfish stuck to rocks.
Mountains have peaks, but a pinnacle is only the very top point.

syn1.tip: Picture a pinnacle as the pointed tip of a tower or mountain. When you reach the pinnacle, nothing is higher.

sc1.stem: Performing a solo at the national music festival was the _____ of Andre's years as a young violinist; no later concert ever matched it.

traps.why: Bottom means worst, but nothing later matched this solo, so it was his best.
The clue is about how good the solo was, not when it happened.
Barnacle sounds like pinnacle but is a sea creature, not a high point.

sc1.tip: The phrase "no later concert ever matched it" tells you this solo was his best moment, the very top.

decoys.why: A national solo that nothing matched was an honor, not a mark of shame.
The sentence describes his best moment, not a time of confusion or disorder.
The solo was one event, not a written record of his years.
A performance is not an opponent; the clue says no later concert matched it.
The clue is about his highest moment, not the energy he had to keep going.

traps.why: The lowest point is the opposite of a pinnacle.
The pin inside is a coincidence; a pinnacle is a top, not a pin.
A turning point is when things change, not when they are at their best.

syn2.tip: People say someone reached the pinnacle of success, meaning the very top, the best they ever did.

sc2.stem: Reaching the state finals was the _____ of our soccer season; it was the farthest our team had ever gone, and every practice had led to it.

traps.why: A downfall is a collapse, but reaching the finals was their greatest success.
An opening is a start, but every practice led up to this, so it came at the top.
Pinwheel starts like pinnacle but is a spinning toy.

sc2.tip: The part after the semicolon restates the blank: "the farthest our team had ever gone" means the highest point.

decoys.why: Reaching the finals was the team's best achievement, not something shameful.
The sentence says it was the farthest they ever went, a high point, not chaos.
Nothing here describes a split in the team; it describes their greatest success.
Reaching the finals was an event, not a written record of the season.
The clue points to the season's highest point, not the team's energy level.

meaning: importance or reputation earned by achievement
example: Her stature as a scientist grew after the discovery.
hook: Stature can mean how tall you stand; a person of great stature stands tall in other people's respect.

traps.why: Disgrace is losing respect, the opposite of high stature.
Statue looks like stature but is a carved figure.
Posture is how your body stands; stature is how others respect you.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "a person of great stature": someone whose achievements earned them high standing and respect.

sc1.stem: After writing three award-winning novels, the author's _____ in the literary world grew so much that young writers traveled across the country to hear her speak.

traps.why: Statue looks like stature but is a sculpture, not a reputation.
Competing with other writers would not make fans travel to hear her.
Awards bring respect, so a negative word like embarrassment has the wrong feeling.

sc1.tip: The cause is "three award-winning novels" and the effect is writers traveling "across the country to hear her." Her reputation grew.

decoys.why: Award-winning novels bring respect, and writers traveled to hear her, so shame makes no sense.
Writers traveled to hear her because of her reputation, not her energy.
Special vocabulary does not grow from winning awards or draw crowds of young writers.
Nothing suggests anger; the sentence is about her growing importance and fame.
Her success brought admiration, not confusion or disorder.

traps.why: Shame means losing respect, the opposite of stature.
Statute looks like stature but means a written law.
Confidence is how you see yourself; stature is how others see you.

syn2.tip: Stature is earned by achievement. When a scientist's stature grows, her reputation grows.

sc2.stem: Although the coach was new to our town, her _____ as a former Olympic swimmer meant parents trusted her right away and signed their kids up for her lessons.

traps.why: Being new might suggest inexperience, but an Olympic past earns trust.
Posture is how she stands, which would not make parents trust her.
Shyness is a weakness here, but parents trusted her right away.

sc2.tip: The word "Although" sets up a contrast: she was new, yet "former Olympic swimmer" gave her respect that made parents trust her.

decoys.why: Parents trusted her right away, so her past brought respect, not shame.
Parents trusted her because of her Olympic reputation, not special words she used.
An opponent would not make parents trust her; her reputation did.
Extreme anger would not make parents sign up their kids right away.
Confusion and disorder would not earn the quick trust the sentence describes.

meaning: longing fondly for the past
example: Old photos make Grandma nostalgic for her childhood on the farm.
hook: Nostalgic is the warm ache you feel flipping through old photos and wishing you could visit those days again.

traps.why: Futuristic looks ahead; nostalgic looks fondly back at the past.
Historic means important in history; nostalgic is a personal feeling.
Bitter about the past is resentful; nostalgic is fond and warm.

syn1.tip: Think of a song that makes your parents say "that takes me back." Nostalgic is that warm, emotional longing for the past.

sc1.stem: Looking through his old kindergarten drawings, Jamal felt _____, wishing he could return to those carefree days of finger painting and naps.

traps.why: Ambitious people look ahead, but Jamal wishes to go back.
Relieved would mean glad those days are over, but he wants them back.
The drawings are art, but the clue is about longing for the past.

sc1.tip: The words "wishing he could return to those carefree days" show a fond longing for the past.

decoys.why: Jamal fondly wishes to return to carefree days, which is warm, not distrustful.
Wishing to go back to the past is about longing, not feeling unbeatable.
The sentence shows gentle longing for the past, not lively energy.
Nothing here is about keeping secrets; Jamal is longing for his kindergarten days.
Feelings are not repeated or unnecessary here; Jamal misses the past.

traps.why: Wanting change looks ahead, the opposite of longing for the past.
Studying history is facts; nostalgia is a fond personal feeling.
Nostalgia is fond, so anger has the wrong feeling.

syn2.tip: Nostalgic is the feeling of fondly looking back, like rewatching a show you loved when you were little.

sc2.stem: Most kids at the reunion couldn't wait to talk about high school plans, but Lena felt _____ and kept telling stories about their old second-grade classroom.

traps.why: Impatient fits the other kids looking ahead, but Lena looked back.
She did tell stories, but the blank names her feeling about the past.
Nothing shows anger; telling old stories shows fond memories.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts Lena with kids talking about the future. She told stories "about their old second-grade classroom," so she longed for the past.

decoys.why: The others were eager for the future, but Lena stayed happily talking about the past.
Lena tells fond stories about second grade, which is warm, not distrustful.
Lena kept telling stories openly, so she was not trying to stay quiet.
Telling old classroom stories shows longing for the past, not feeling unbeatable.
The sentence is about Lena's fond feelings, not something unnecessary or repeated.

meaning: loud enough to be heard
example: The whisper was barely audible from the back row.
hook: Audible splits into aud (hear, as in audio) and -ible (able to be): able to be heard.

traps.why: Silent means making no sound, the opposite of audible.
Visible means able to be seen; audible is about hearing.
Edible looks like audible but means safe to eat.

syn1.tip: The root aud means hear, as in audio and audience. Audible means a sound is able to be heard.

sc1.stem: The speaker's voice was barely _____ from the back of the noisy gym, so students in the last rows kept asking each other what she had said.

traps.why: Visible is about seeing, but the students were trying to hear her.
Edible looks like audible but means safe to eat.
The problem was hearing her at all, not whether her voice sounded nice.

sc1.tip: The effect "kept asking each other what she had said" shows the students could hardly hear her voice.

decoys.why: A voice is not large and heavy; the clue is about whether students could hear her.
Students asked what she said, so the issue is hearing her, not spreading something.
The noisy gym is about whether her voice could be heard, not defeated.
The problem is that students could not hear her, not that she kept secrets.
Her voice was faint in the back, not spreading wildly out of control.

traps.why: Too quiet to hear is the opposite of audible.
You can hear words without understanding them; audible is only about hearing.
Audible just means you can hear it, not that it hurts your ears.

syn2.tip: Find aud, the hearing root in audio and audience, plus -ible, meaning able to be. Audible sounds can just be heard.

sc2.stem: The tiny kitten's cry was so faint that it was hardly _____, yet Maya, with her sharp ears, noticed it from across the yard.

traps.why: Adorable looks a bit like audible but means cute.
Kittens cry when hungry, but the clue is about how faint the sound was.
Visible is about seeing, but the clue is "sharp ears."

sc2.tip: The words "so faint" and "sharp ears" point to hearing: the cry could hardly be heard.

decoys.why: Hardly covert would mean obvious, but the cry was so faint it was barely heard.
A cry is not large and heavy; the clue says it was faint and hard to hear.
The sentence is about how quiet the cry was, not about roughness or toughness.
Maya noticed the cry with sharp ears, so the point is hearing, not spreading.
A faint kitten cry is about being heard, not about being too strong to defeat.

meaning: too strong to be defeated
example: After twenty straight wins, the team seemed invincible.
hook: Invincible is in (not) plus vinc (conquer) plus ible (able): a hero no one is able to conquer.

traps.why: Vulnerable means easy to hurt, the opposite of invincible.
Invisible looks like invincible but means unable to be seen.
Victorious means you won once; invincible means you can't be beaten.

syn1.tip: Split it: in- (not) plus vinc (conquer) plus -ible (able to be). Invincible means not able to be conquered.

sc1.stem: The chess club had not lost a single match in four years, so other schools thought of them as _____ until a rookie team finally beat them.

traps.why: Four years without a loss is far from ordinary.
Invisible looks like invincible but means unable to be seen.
Talented is too weak; one loss does not prove they lacked talent.

sc1.tip: The clues "had not lost a single match in four years" and "until a rookie team finally beat them" show they seemed unbeatable.

decoys.why: Hefty means physically large and heavy, but the sentence is about a team that never lost.
A team that never lost in four years was not careless, so lax makes no sense.
Nothing about the chess club repeated something unnecessary; the clue is their unbeaten record.
The sentence is about never losing a match, not about longing for the past.
The club was not secret; schools saw them as unbeatable after four years without a loss.
Chess can be complicated, but the clue is that the team never lost a match.

traps.why: Easy to defeat is the exact opposite of invincible.
That describes invisible, a lookalike word.
Winning most games is too weak; invincible means never able to lose.

syn2.tip: Think of a video game power-up that makes you invincible: nothing can hurt or beat you while it lasts.

sc2.stem: Superheroes in movies often seem _____, but even the strongest ones have a secret weakness, like Superman losing his powers near kryptonite.

traps.why: Helpless is the opposite; the strongest heroes seem unbeatable.
Heroes are brave, but the contrast is about having a weakness.
Inventive starts like invincible but means good at creating things.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with "a secret weakness," so the blank means having no weakness at all, impossible to beat.

decoys.why: The word secret appears later, but the blank describes heroes who seem unbeatable despite a weakness.
The contrast is with having a weakness, so the blank must mean unbeatable, not careless.
The sentence contrasts seeming strong with having a weakness, not longing for the past.
Being loud enough to hear has nothing to do with having a secret weakness.
The sentence contrasts strength with weakness; nothing here is about repeating something.
Speaking clearly does not contrast with having a weakness like kryptonite.

meaning: a state of wild excitement
example: Shoppers rushed the store in a frenzy on the sale's first day.
hook: Think of sharks in a feeding frenzy, thrashing and snapping: frenzy is wild, out-of-control excitement.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite of a wild frenzy.
Interest is far too mild; a frenzy is wild, out-of-control excitement.
Frenzies often happen in crowds, but a frenzy is a state, not people.

syn1.tip: Picture shoppers rushing a store on sale day, pushing and grabbing. A frenzy is that wild madness.

sc1.stem: When the pop star's car pulled up, the waiting fans broke into a _____, screaming, jumping, and pushing toward the barriers to catch a glimpse.

traps.why: Screaming fans are not silent; that is the opposite.
A smile is too mild for screaming, jumping, and pushing.
A chorus is singing together, not pushing toward barriers.

sc1.tip: The examples "screaming, jumping, and pushing" show excitement so wild it's out of control.

decoys.why: The fans were pushing to see the star, not fighting each other.
The fans were waiting openly and excited, not hiding to launch a surprise attack.
A chronicle is a written record, but the fans were screaming and jumping.
An oasis is a green spot in a desert, not a burst of screaming excitement.
Nothing split apart; the fans all rushed toward the barriers together in excitement.

traps.why: Quiet peace is the opposite of a frenzy.
Mild curiosity is much too weak for a frenzy.
A gathering is a group of people, not their wild state of mind.

syn2.tip: The phrase "feeding frenzy" shows sharks going wild over food. A frenzy is excitement that goes out of control.

sc2.stem: The classroom was calm all morning, but when the principal announced an early dismissal for snow, the class erupted into a _____ of cheering and backpack-grabbing.

traps.why: Hush fits the calm morning, but the word "but" signals a change.
A murmur is too quiet for a class that erupted.
Lessons happen in class, but this blank describes wild cheering.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with "calm," and "erupted" signals an explosion of wild excitement.

decoys.why: The class was cheering about the snow day, not fighting each other.
A chronicle is a written record of events, not a burst of cheering.
A stigma is a mark of shame, but the students were happily cheering.
An early dismissal is not a stage of progress; the class erupted in wild excitement.
The class did not split apart; they all cheered and grabbed backpacks together.
An oasis is a desert water spot, not an outburst of cheering students.

meaning: to imitate how something looks or works
example: The ride simulates the feeling of flying through space.
hook: A flight simulator lets pilots practice in a fake cockpit; to simulate is to make something act like the real thing.

traps.why: Stimulate looks almost the same but means to excite or wake up.
Inventing creates something new; simulating copies something that already exists.
Simulate is related to similar, but it means copying, not comparing.

syn1.tip: Think of a flight simulator, a machine that copies the feel of flying a real plane. Simulate means to imitate.

sc1.stem: Astronauts train in giant swimming pools that _____ the weightlessness of space, letting them practice repairs while floating as they would in orbit.

traps.why: Stimulate looks like simulate but means to excite.
Astronauts explore space, but pools can't explore anything; they copy conditions.
The pools create a weightless feeling; they don't remove it.

sc1.tip: The phrase "floating as they would in orbit" shows the pools copy the feeling of space on Earth.

decoys.why: The pools let astronauts float as in orbit, so they imitate weightlessness rather than resist it.
The pools create the floating feeling of space; they do not hold it back.
The sentence is about copying the feeling of space, not speeding anything up.
The pools help astronauts practice floating, so they recreate weightlessness instead of weakening it.
Nothing is being removed for being unacceptable; the pools copy how space feels.
You cannot cancel weightlessness; the pools imitate it so astronauts can practice.

traps.why: Originate means to start something new, the opposite of copying.
Simplify starts like simulate but means to make easier.
Simulators help you practice, but simulate itself means to copy.

syn2.tip: Video games simulate real things like driving or flying. They copy how the real thing looks and works.

sc2.stem: Our science teacher used a fan and a tub of water to _____ a hurricane, creating a tiny version of its wind and waves right on her desk.

traps.why: Forecasters predict hurricanes, but she built a tiny model of one.
She created hurricane wind and waves; she did not stop them.
Stimulate looks like simulate but means to excite.

sc2.tip: The phrase after the comma restates the blank: "creating a tiny version" means copying how a hurricane looks and works.

decoys.why: She was creating a tiny version of a hurricane, not holding up against one.
The teacher made wind and waves on purpose, so she was not holding the storm back.
She was making a small copy of a hurricane, not speeding one up.
The sentence says she created a tiny version of the storm, not weakened it.
You cannot officially cancel a hurricane; she was making a model of one.

meaning: careful not to draw attention or reveal secrets
example: Please be discreet and don't tell anyone about the surprise party.
hook: Discreet sounds like discrete, but discreet is the quiet one: it keeps secrets and stays out of the spotlight.

traps.why: Gossipy people spread secrets, the opposite of discreet.
Discrete sounds the same but means separate.
Shy is feeling nervous; discreet is choosing to be careful.

syn1.tip: Discreet people choose their words carefully so they don't spill secrets or embarrass anyone.

sc1.stem: Because Olivia had promised to keep her friend's news private, she was _____ when others asked, politely changing the subject without revealing anything.

traps.why: Talkative fits someone who spills news, but she revealed nothing.
Honest means telling the truth, but she changed the subject instead.
She acted "politely," so a rude, negative word doesn't fit.

sc1.tip: The clues "keep her friend's news private" and "without revealing anything" show she was careful not to spill the secret.

decoys.why: Olivia was careful to keep the news private, so she was not careless.
The sentence is about keeping a secret, not about being loud enough to hear.
Olivia was keeping a promise politely, not resisting rules or authority.
The clue is that she revealed nothing, not that she expressed ideas clearly.
Olivia was guarding a secret, not longing for the past.
Nothing repeated; the sentence describes Olivia carefully keeping her friend's news private.

traps.why: Gossiping spreads secrets, the opposite of being discreet.
That defines discrete, which sounds the same but means something else.
Discreet people can talk freely; they just don't reveal private things.

syn2.tip: When someone says "please be discreet," they're asking you to keep something quiet and not draw attention.

sc2.stem: Unlike his brother, who announced every surprise before the party even started, Leo was _____ and never let a single hint slip about the gift.

traps.why: Careless fits his brother; Leo is the opposite and kept quiet.
He may be excited, but the clue is that he never gave a hint.
Discrete sounds the same but means separate, not secret-keeping.

sc2.tip: The word "Unlike" contrasts Leo with a brother who spoils surprises, and "never let a single hint slip" shows he kept secrets.

decoys.why: Leo never let a hint slip, so he was careful, not careless.
Leo stayed quiet about the gift, so being loud enough to hear does not fit.
The clue is that Leo kept the secret, not that he spoke clearly.
The contrast is about keeping secrets, not about having energy and enthusiasm.
Leo was keeping a surprise, not resisting rules or authority.
The sentence is about not revealing the gift, not about being impossible to defeat.

meaning: very strict and exact
example: The lab has stringent rules about wearing goggles.
hook: Picture rules pulled as tight as a guitar string, no slack at all: that's stringent, like stringent safety rules in labs.

traps.why: Relaxed rules are loose, the opposite of stringent.
String inside might suggest tangled, but stringent means very strict.
Stringent rules can be fair; they are just very strict.

syn1.tip: You often hear "stringent safety standards." Picture rules pulled tight with no wiggle room.

sc1.stem: The space agency has _____ cleanliness rules for its labs: workers must wear full-body suits, and even a single speck of dust can halt the work.

traps.why: Full-body suits and zero dust are not relaxed rules.
Basic is too weak for rules where one speck of dust stops work.
Space labs are modern, but the clue is about how strict the rules are.

sc1.tip: The examples "full-body suits" and "even a single speck of dust can halt the work" show extremely strict rules.

decoys.why: Full-body suits and stopping work over one speck of dust show the rules are strict, not loose.
The rules are described openly; the clue is how strict they are.
Rules cannot resist authority; the sentence shows how strict the lab rules are.
Cleanliness might make you think of germs, but rules do not spread from person to person.
The sentence is about strict cleanliness, not about whether rules can be heard.
Lab rules about dust have nothing to do with longing for the past.

traps.why: Loosely enforced is the opposite of stringent.
Slightly picky is too weak; stringent means very strict.
Clear rules aren't always strict; stringent is about how tight they are.

syn2.tip: Stringent rules leave no slack, like a rope pulled tight. Breaking even a small one is not allowed.

sc2.stem: At home, Nina's bedtime was flexible on weekends, but summer camp had _____ rules: lights out at nine sharp, and counselors checked every cabin.

traps.why: Loose fits her home bedtime, but "but" signals camp was different.
Lights out at nine sharp with cabin checks sounds strict, not fun.
The camp rules were clear; they were just very strict.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with "flexible," and "nine sharp" plus "checked every cabin" show very strict rules.

decoys.why: Lax describes Nina's flexible home bedtime, but camp had lights out at nine sharp.
The rules themselves are strict; rules cannot resist authority.
Counselors checked every cabin openly, so the rules were strict, not secret.
Rules cannot be nervous or upset; the clue is lights out at nine sharp.
Camp rules about bedtime do not long for the past; they are strict.
The sentence contrasts flexible and strict bedtimes, not things happening at the same time.

meaning: well thought of and trusted
example: Always get your news from a reputable source.
hook: Reputable is built on reputation: a reputable brand has spent years earning people's trust.

traps.why: Unreliable is the opposite of reputable.
Repeatable looks similar but means able to be done again.
Popular means liked by many people, not necessarily trusted.

syn1.tip: Think of "reputation." A reputable business has a good reputation, so people respect it.

sc1.stem: For her science report, Chloe used only _____ sources, such as university websites and well-known encyclopedias, instead of random blogs.

traps.why: Doubtful sources are the random blogs she avoided.
Long sources might help a report, but the clue is about trust.
Repeatable only looks like reputable and means able to be repeated.

sc1.tip: "Such as university websites and well-known encyclopedias" versus "instead of random blogs" shows she chose trusted sources.

decoys.why: The sources were well-known encyclopedias, not secret or hidden ones.
Chloe avoided random blogs, so her sources were carefully chosen, not careless.
Sources do not spread wildly out of control; the clue is about trust.
University websites do not long for the past; the sentence is about trusted information.
Nothing in the sentence is about timing, only about sources being trusted instead of random.
Websites and encyclopedias are read, not heard, so loudness has nothing to do with it.

traps.why: Shady means dishonest, the opposite of reputable.
Refundable looks similar but means you can get your money back.
Trusted brands may cost more, but reputable is about trust, not price.

syn2.tip: Inside reputable is "repute," the root of "reputation." Someone with a good reputation is someone people trust.

sc2.stem: Because the repair shop had fixed cars honestly for forty years and earned glowing reviews, Mom called it the most _____ garage in town.

traps.why: Dishonest is the opposite of fixing cars honestly.
Forty years is long, but the clue is honest work and good reviews.
Reportable looks similar but means worth reporting.

sc2.tip: "Fixed cars honestly" and "earned glowing reviews" are the cause. The effect is a garage people trust.

decoys.why: The shop worked honestly for forty years, so it was careful, not careless.
A shop with glowing reviews is well known, not secret or hidden.
Forty years is a long time, but a garage does not long for the past.
Honest work and glowing reviews show trust, not resisting rules.
A garage cannot be nervous or upset; the clue is about honesty and reviews.
The sentence praises the shop's honesty, not its size or weight.

meaning: an object made by people long ago
example: Archaeologists found an ancient artifact buried in the sand.
hook: Picture a museum glass case full of clay pots and arrowheads: every one is an artifact made by human hands.

traps.why: A fossil is natural remains, not an object people made.
Artist looks similar but means a person who makes art.
An invention is newly created; an artifact comes from long ago.

syn1.tip: Artifact contains "art," meaning skill in making things. Think of objects people made long ago that end up in museums.

sc1.stem: Among the most valuable items the archaeologists uncovered was a carved clay pot, an ancient _____ that revealed how early farmers stored their grain.

traps.why: Archaeologists dig up fossils too, but a carved pot was made by people.
Artist looks similar, but a pot is not a person.
Farmers grow crops, but the pot was something they made.

sc1.tip: "A carved clay pot" made by people and "the archaeologists uncovered" point to an old human-made object.

decoys.why: The pot revealed how farmers stored grain, so it explained things rather than being a mystery.
A carved clay pot is an object, not a surprise attack.
A clay pot is not a green spot with water in a desert.
The archaeologists found an object, not a state of anger and disturbance.

traps.why: Rocks form in nature; artifacts are made by people.
A modern machine is new, the opposite of an old artifact.
Artifact contains "fact," but it is an object, not information.

syn2.tip: Picture a museum display of old tools and pots. Artifacts are things people made and used long ago.

sc2.stem: Jayden thought the rusty spoon he dug up was just junk, but the museum guide explained it was a real _____ used by settlers three hundred years ago.

traps.why: A replica is a copy, the opposite of a real old object.
Fossils are dug up, but a spoon is made by people.
Minerals are found in the ground naturally; settlers made the spoon.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "just junk," and "used by settlers three hundred years ago" shows an old object people made.

decoys.why: A spoon is an object people used, not a written record of events.
Jayden thought the rusty spoon was junk, so it was not an impressive sight.
Settlers used the spoon as a tool, not as a mark of shame.
A spoon dug from the ground is an object, not the highest point of something.
Settlers used the spoon, and you cannot use a noisy fight like a tool.
The guide described an old object people used, not a plant disease.

meaning: the one responsible for a problem
example: The culprit who ate the cookies left crumbs everywhere.
hook: Every mystery ends by naming the culprit: the one whose sticky fingerprints are on the empty cookie jar.

traps.why: A victim is the one harmed, the opposite of the culprit.
A witness sees the wrongdoing but did not do it.
A detective finds the culprit; the detective is not to blame.

syn1.tip: Culprit shows up in mysteries: "Who is the culprit?" means who did the bad thing.

sc1.stem: When the garden's lettuce kept disappearing overnight, Ming set up a camera and discovered the _____: a chubby rabbit squeezing under the fence.

traps.why: The rabbit was taking lettuce, not being harmed.
Hero is too positive for a rabbit eating Ming's lettuce.
Rabbits can be pets, but this one was causing the problem.

sc1.tip: "Lettuce kept disappearing" and the rabbit "squeezing under the fence" show the rabbit caused the problem.

decoys.why: The lettuce vanished because of a rabbit, not a plant disease.
The camera solved the mystery, so Ming found the one responsible, not a mystery.
A chubby rabbit is not an object made by people long ago.
The garden may feel like one to the rabbit, but the rabbit itself is not an oasis.
The rabbit is the one causing the problem, not a terrible disaster itself.
A rabbit is not a mark of shame; Ming found who was eating lettuce.

traps.why: The one harmed is the victim, the opposite of the culprit.
That describes a detective, who catches the culprit.
A tattletale reports the problem but did not cause it.

syn2.tip: When something goes wrong and people ask who did it, the culprit is the answer: the one to blame.

sc2.stem: The muddy paw prints leading from the spilled trash can straight to the dog's bed made it obvious that Biscuit was the _____ behind the mess.

traps.why: Biscuit made the mess; he was not harmed by it.
A detective solves the mess; the paw prints point to the one who caused it.
A witness only sees the mess; the prints show Biscuit made it.

sc2.tip: The "muddy paw prints" lead "straight to the dog's bed," evidence pointing to the one who caused "the mess."

decoys.why: The paw prints made it obvious, so Biscuit was not a mystery.
The mess is a kind of disorder, but Biscuit is the one who caused it.
A spilled trash can is not a terrible disaster, and Biscuit is a dog.
Biscuit is a dog, not an object made by people long ago.
The sentence is about who made the mess, not a desert water spot.
Biscuit caused the mess; a dog is not a mark of shame.

meaning: the energy to keep going a long time
example: Swimming laps builds stamina for long races.
hook: Stamina is what keeps a marathon runner jogging at mile twenty-five when everyone else has stopped to walk.

traps.why: Fatigue means tiredness, the opposite of stamina.
Speed is about how fast, not how long you can keep going.
Stammer looks similar but means a stumble in speech.

syn1.tip: Coaches say runners need stamina to finish long races. Think of lasting a long time without tiring.

sc1.stem: Marathon runners need great _____, since they must keep moving for more than twenty-six miles without stopping to rest.

traps.why: Speed helps racing, but going far without rest takes lasting energy.
Fatigue is tiredness, which would make runners stop.
Balance is a sports skill, but the clue is about going a long way.

sc1.tip: "Keep moving for more than twenty-six miles without stopping" tells you runners need energy that lasts a long time.

decoys.why: The clue is running twenty-six miles without rest, which takes energy, not fame.
Wild excitement burns out fast, but the sentence is about keeping going for miles.
Special words will not keep you running for twenty-six miles.
Confusion and disorder do not help a runner keep moving without rest.
Anger and disturbance have nothing to do with running a long distance.
Showing respect to someone does not help you run twenty-six miles.

traps.why: A burst is quick and short; stamina lasts a long time.
Constant tiredness is the opposite of having stamina.
Big muscles mean strength, not the energy to keep going.

syn2.tip: Stamina is what keeps you going in the last lap. It is about lasting, not about being fast or big.

sc2.stem: Although Ava was the fastest sprinter on the team, she lacked _____ and was always gasping for air halfway through the long cross-country races.

traps.why: She is the fastest, so speed is the one thing she has.
Gasping for air shows she has plenty of tiredness.
Talent is too general; gasping halfway shows she runs out of energy.

sc2.tip: "Although" contrasts her speed with a weakness, and "gasping for air halfway through the long" races shows she lacks lasting energy.

decoys.why: Ava was gasping for air in long races, so she lacked energy, not reputation.
Gasping halfway through a long race shows she ran out of energy, not excitement.
Special words have nothing to do with gasping for air during a race.
The sentence is about getting tired in long races, not showing respect.
Lacking anger and disturbance would not make Ava gasp for air.
Lacking confusion would not explain why she tired out in long races.

meaning: to feel bitter about unfair treatment
example: Leo resented being blamed for his sister's mess.
hook: Resent is the verb behind resentment, the bitter feeling of getting blamed for your little sister's mess.

traps.why: Appreciate means value, the opposite of resent.
Resent is not "re" plus "sent"; it is about bitter feelings.
Ignoring means not paying attention; resenting means feeling bitter.

syn1.tip: Resent is the verb behind "resentment," the bitter feeling of being treated unfairly. Don't read it as "re-sent."

sc1.stem: Sofia began to _____ her older brother because their parents always gave him the front seat, even when it was clearly her turn.

traps.why: Unfair treatment would not make Sofia admire her brother.
Pity is feeling sorry for someone, but he got the better deal.
Thank is too positive for someone who keeps taking her turn.

sc1.tip: "Because their parents always gave him the front seat, even when it was clearly her turn" shows unfair treatment, which causes bitter feelings.

decoys.why: Sofia is upset about unfair treatment, not trying to teach her brother something.
She feels cheated out of her turn, so she would not pay her brother back.
Sofia is not imitating her brother; she feels bitter about the front seat.
Nothing is being cut out; the sentence is about her feelings of unfairness.

traps.why: Feeling thankful is the opposite of resenting.
Resent looks like "re" plus "sent," but it means feeling bitter.
Feeling sorry is pity; resenting is bitterness about unfairness.

syn2.tip: You resent something when it seems unfair, like being blamed for what someone else did. The feeling is bitterness.

sc2.stem: Instead of feeling grateful for the extra chores his coach assigned, Marcus started to _____ them, grumbling that the other players never had to stay late.

traps.why: "Instead of feeling grateful" rules out appreciating.
Finishing chores is an action; the clue is about his bitter grumbling.
He was grumbling about the chores, so he had not forgotten them.

sc2.tip: "Instead of feeling grateful" signals the opposite feeling, and "grumbling that the other players never had to" shows he felt unfairly treated.

decoys.why: Marcus was grumbling about the chores, so he was not supporting them.
The coach assigned the chores, so Marcus has no power to cancel them.
The sentence is about how Marcus felt, not combining chores into one.
Marcus was not imitating the chores; he was grumbling that they were unfair.
Grumbling shows bitter feelings, not changing the chores to improve them.

meaning: so good it is a model for others
example: Her exemplary behavior earned her the citizenship award.
hook: Exemplary sounds like example: exemplary work is the paper a teacher holds up and says, "Do it like this."

traps.why: Shameful is the opposite of exemplary.
Exempt looks similar but means free from a rule.
Average is too weak; exemplary means good enough to copy.

syn1.tip: Exemplary is related to "example." Something exemplary is so good it is an example for others to follow.

sc1.stem: Mr. Ito praised Fatima's _____ science notebook, holding it up so the class could see the neat diagrams and careful notes he hoped everyone would copy.

traps.why: The notebook has neat diagrams, the opposite of messy.
Ordinary is too weak; he wanted everyone to copy it.
The praise is about neat work, not what the notebook cost.

sc1.tip: Mr. Ito "praised" it and held it up as notes "he hoped everyone would copy," so the notebook is a model for others.

decoys.why: The notebook has neat diagrams and careful notes, so it is not careless at all.
Mr. Ito held it up for the class to see, so nothing about it was hidden.
He hoped everyone would copy it, so it is a model, not something breaking rules.
Rampant means spreading out of control, which does not describe a neat notebook.
Nothing in the sentence is about missing the past; it is about neat, careful work.
A notebook is not heard; the sentence praises its neat diagrams and notes.

traps.why: Work full of mistakes is the opposite of exemplary.
That means exempt, a different word that looks similar.
Barely good enough is much too weak for exemplary.

syn2.tip: Think of a teacher saying, "Do it like this." An exemplary piece of work is the model worth copying.

sc2.stem: Coach Rivera was frustrated by the team's sloppy passing, but she pointed to Dante's _____ footwork and told everyone to study exactly how he moved.

traps.why: Clumsy fits only if you miss the "but" after sloppy passing.
Decent is too weak for footwork everyone should study.
Exempt looks similar but means free from a rule.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Dante with the team's "sloppy passing," and "study exactly how he moved" shows his footwork is a model to copy.

decoys.why: The coach wants everyone to study Dante's moves, so his footwork is not careless.
Nervous, upset footwork would not be something the coach tells everyone to study.
The coach holds Dante up as a model, not as someone resisting her rules.
Footwork cannot long for the past; the sentence is about how well he moved.
She pointed to his footwork so everyone would watch it, so it was not hidden.
Footwork is not large and heavy; the clue is that others should copy it.

meaning: large and heavy
example: Dad lifted the hefty suitcase onto the airport scale.
hook: To heft a box is to lift it and feel its weight, so a hefty box makes you grunt.

traps.why: Light is the opposite of hefty.
Hearty looks similar but means warm and cheerful or filling.
A hefty price is large, but hefty itself does not mean costly.

syn1.tip: Heft means weight. If you heft a box, you lift it to feel how heavy it is.

sc1.stem: The movers groaned as they carried the _____ oak piano up three flights of stairs, stopping every few steps to catch their breath.

traps.why: A tiny piano would not make movers groan and rest.
Pianos can break, but the groaning shows the piano is heavy.
Shiny describes looks, but the clue is about how hard it was to carry.

sc1.tip: The movers "groaned" and stopped "every few steps to catch their breath," so the piano must be large and heavy.

decoys.why: Sleek describes a smooth look, but the movers groaning shows the clue is about weight.
Plentiful means many of something, but there is only one piano being carried.
A royal look would not make movers stop every few steps to catch their breath.
The movers groaned from the load, not because of how loud the piano is.
A piano cannot long for the past; the sentence is about how heavy it is.
Being a fine model piano would not make the movers groan on the stairs.

traps.why: Small and light is the opposite of hefty.
Tall and thin describes size, but not heaviness.
Soft and fluffy describes feel, not weight.

syn2.tip: Picture a hefty bag of dog food that needs two hands to lift. Hefty means it has a lot of size and weight.

sc2.stem: Grandpa's old dictionary was so _____ that it made Lily's backpack sag, while her new e-reader weighed less than a sandwich.

traps.why: A flimsy book would not make a backpack sag.
Old books get dusty, but dust does not make a backpack sag.
Hearty looks similar but means cheerful or filling.

sc2.tip: "Made Lily's backpack sag" is the effect of weight, and "while" contrasts it with something that "weighed less than a sandwich."

decoys.why: The dictionary made the backpack sag, unlike the light e-reader, so it was heavy, not streamlined.
Plentiful means many, but this is one dictionary that is heavy.
It is Grandpa's old book, but the sagging backpack shows the clue is about weight.
Looking royal would not make a backpack sag; the sentence compares weights.
Being trusted does not make a book weigh more than a sandwich.
Dictionaries hold words, but the sentence is about the backpack sagging from weight.

meaning: remove parts considered unacceptable
example: The TV station censored the rude words in the movie.
hook: When a TV show bleeps a rude word, someone has decided to censor it.

traps.why: Censor looks like census, a count, but it means remove unacceptable parts.
A sensor detects things; censor only sounds the same.
Printing shares words; censoring removes them first.

syn1.tip: Censored movies have bleeped or blacked-out words. To censor is to edit out what someone thinks is unacceptable.

sc1.stem: Before the school newspaper went to print, the advisor would _____ any article containing rude language, blacking out words she considered inappropriate.

traps.why: Approving would let the rude words stay, not black them out.
