Praise is too positive for articles she found inappropriate.
Sense sounds like censor but means notice or feel.

sc1.tip: "Blacking out words she considered inappropriate" tells you the advisor removes unacceptable content before printing.

decoys.why: She was blacking out words, so she was removing parts, not supporting the article.
The sentence says she blacked out words, which is an action, not just a bitter feeling.
Imitating an article would not explain blacking out words she found inappropriate.
Combining articles is not the same as blacking out rude words in them.
Speeding up an article makes no sense; she was removing words before printing.
You cannot give an article understanding; she was blacking out rude words.

traps.why: Sharing without changes is the opposite of censoring.
That is what a sensor does; censor only sounds the same.
That is a census, which looks similar but means counting.

syn2.tip: Think of a bleep over a rude word on TV. Someone censored it, taking out the part they judged unacceptable.

sc2.stem: The library's old policy let leaders _____ books they disliked, but now readers can see every page exactly as the author wrote it.

traps.why: Leaders would not recommend books they disliked.
Borrowing happens at libraries, but the contrast is about pages being changed.
Censor looks like census, a count, but counting does not hide pages.

sc2.tip: "But now readers can see every page exactly as the author wrote it" contrasts with the old way, when parts were removed.

decoys.why: Now readers can see every page, so the old policy removed parts, not just disliked them.
The contrast is about seeing every page, so leaders removed parts rather than spreading lies.
The old policy hid parts of books leaders disliked, so they were not supporting them.
Imitating books does not contrast with readers now seeing every page as written.
Combining books is not the opposite of seeing every page exactly as the author wrote it.
The contrast is about pages being changed or removed, not about holding books skillfully.

meaning: existing in large amounts
example: Apples are plentiful in the orchards every fall.
hook: Plentiful starts with plenty: picture an orchard in fall with more apples than you could ever pick.

traps.why: Scarce is the opposite of plentiful.
Pitiful looks similar but means sad or poor.
Plentiful food is about amount, not taste.

syn1.tip: Plentiful starts with "plenty." If something is plentiful, there is plenty of it.

sc1.stem: Unlike the dry desert, where food is scarce, the rainforest offers _____ fruit, so monkeys rarely have to travel far for a meal.

traps.why: Rare fits only if you miss "unlike" before the scarce desert.
Sour describes taste; the clue is about how much fruit there is.
Poisonous fruit would not give monkeys easy meals.

sc1.tip: "Unlike the dry desert, where food is scarce" signals a contrast, and "rarely have to travel far" means fruit comes in large amounts.

decoys.why: The contrast is with scarce food, so the clue is about amount, not heavy fruit.
Monkeys rarely travel far for food, so the fruit is easy to find, not hidden.
Smooth, shiny fruit does not explain why monkeys need not travel far.
Fruit fit for a king does not contrast with food being scarce.
Fruit cannot long for the past; the sentence contrasts scarce and abundant food.
Fruit happening at the same time does not contrast with food being scarce.

traps.why: Barely any is the opposite of plentiful.
The -ful means full, but plentiful is about amount, not taste.
Price is a different idea from how much there is.

syn2.tip: Hear "plenty" at the start. Plentiful things come in large amounts, like apples piled high at a fall orchard.

sc2.stem: After weeks of warm sun and steady rain, tomatoes were so _____ in our garden that we gave bags of them to every neighbor on the street.

traps.why: If tomatoes were scarce, there would be none to give away.
Rain can rot crops, but nobody gives neighbors bags of rotten tomatoes.
Pitiful looks similar but means sad or poor.

sc2.tip: "Warm sun and steady rain" caused a big harvest, and giving "bags of them to every neighbor" shows there were large amounts.

decoys.why: Giving bags to every neighbor shows there were many tomatoes, not that they were heavy.
Shiny tomatoes would not explain giving bags of them to every neighbor.
Tomatoes cannot resist rules; the sentence is about having too many to eat.
Being impossible to defeat does not explain giving tomatoes away to the whole street.
The tomatoes were so many you gave them away, not quiet and unnoticed.
Tomatoes are not heard; the clue is that there were too many to keep.

meaning: resisting authority or rules
example: The rebellious teenager refused to follow the curfew.
hook: Rebellious holds the word rebel: picture a kid crossing his arms and saying, "You can't make me."

traps.why: Obedient is the opposite of rebellious.
Rebels may be angry, but rebellious means resisting rules.
Skipping rules on purpose is different from not wanting to work.

syn1.tip: A rebel fights against those in charge. Rebellious means acting like a rebel, refusing to follow rules.

sc1.stem: Unlike his obedient sister, Theo was _____, ignoring the camp's lights-out rule and sneaking down to the dock to look at the stars.

traps.why: "Unlike his obedient sister" means Theo is the opposite of obedient.
Lights-out is about sleep, but Theo stayed up breaking the rule.
Helpful is too positive for sneaking out against camp rules.

sc1.tip: "Unlike his obedient sister" sets up a contrast, and "ignoring the camp's lights-out rule" shows Theo resists rules.

decoys.why: Theo is unlike his obedient sister, so he is not deeply loyal to the rules.
He ignored the lights-out rule, so he was not a model camper.
Mild describes weather, and the sentence is about Theo breaking a rule.
Nothing says he missed the past; he was ignoring the camp's rule.
He was sneaking down to the dock, so being loud does not fit.
Being kingly does not contrast with his obedient sister or explain breaking the rule.

traps.why: Following orders is the opposite of being rebellious.
That is too strong; rebellious usually means resisting rules, not fighting battles.
Rebels can be loud, but noise is not resisting authority.

syn2.tip: Rebellious holds "rebel." Picture someone saying, "You can't make me." That is resisting the rules.

sc2.stem: After the principal banned hats, a few _____ students wore them anyway, and some even started a petition arguing that the rule was unfair.

traps.why: Obedient students would not wear banned hats.
Starting a petition shows they knew the rule and resisted it.
Hats are about style, but the clue is about defying the ban.

sc2.tip: "Wore them anyway" after a ban, plus a petition calling "the rule" unfair, shows students resisting authority.

decoys.why: These students wore hats against the ban, so they were not model students.
They defied the principal's rule, so they were not loyal to it.
The rule might be strict, but the students were the ones resisting it.
Wearing banned hats and starting a petition is not mild behavior.
The students were fighting a rule they found unfair, not longing for the past.
The sentence is about breaking a hat rule, not about the students' size.

meaning: nervous, upset, and unable to stay calm
example: The agitated cat paced back and forth during the storm.
hook: A washing machine's agitator churns clothes back and forth; an agitated person feels that same churning inside.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite of agitated.
Agile looks similar but means quick and nimble.
Cheerful is lively but happy; agitated is lively in a nervous, upset way.

syn1.tip: Picture a washing machine churning clothes. An agitated person feels churned up inside, nervous and unable to settle.

sc1.stem: As thunder rumbled closer, the horses grew more and more _____, stamping their hooves and pacing nervously around the barn.

traps.why: Peaceful is the opposite; stamping and pacing show the horses were not peaceful.
Barn horses get hungry, but nervous pacing during thunder points to fear.
Agile looks similar but means nimble, not nervous.

sc1.tip: The clue is "stamping their hooves and pacing nervously." Those actions show animals that are upset and can't calm down.

decoys.why: The horses were stamping and pacing nervously, so they were not growing mild and calm.
Stamping hooves draws attention, so the horses were not being quiet and careful.
Horses can be sleek, but the sentence describes nervous pacing, not a smooth, shiny coat.
Horses can look regal, but pacing nervously in a storm shows fear, not royal dignity.
The thunder made the horses nervous, not fondly longing for the past.
The sentence is about nervous horses, not horses open to new ideas.

traps.why: Calm and steady is the opposite of agitated.
Busy people move a lot too, but happily, not nervously.
Quick and nimble describes agile, a lookalike word.

syn2.tip: Agitated people can't sit still because they are worried. Look for a choice showing both nerves and movement.

sc2.stem: Although my little brother usually sleeps calmly through the night, he was _____ before his first day of school, tossing, turning, and asking questions until midnight.

traps.why: Peaceful is the opposite; tossing and turning shows he couldn't settle.
Sleep is the topic, but he stayed up until midnight worrying.
Cheerful is too happy; tossing and turning shows nerves.

sc2.tip: "Although" signals a change from "calmly," and "tossing, turning" shows a nervous, restless boy.

decoys.why: Tossing and turning until midnight is the opposite of being mild and calm.
He was nervous about his first day ahead, not longing for the past.
The sentence shows he could not stay calm, not that he was open to new ideas.
Asking questions until midnight is not quiet or careful to avoid attention.
Tossing and turning all night is not a model of good behavior for others.
The sentence describes nervousness, not being careless or not strict enough.

meaning: openly and boldly stating opinions
example: Rosa is outspoken and always shares her honest opinion.
hook: Break it apart: an outspoken person speaks out, saying exactly what they think for everyone to hear.

traps.why: Shy is the opposite of outspoken.
Rude is negative; outspoken just means openly honest, not mean.
Talkative means talking a lot; outspoken means boldly sharing opinions.

syn1.tip: Think of "speaking out" about something you believe. An outspoken person says what they think openly.

sc1.stem: Unlike her shy brother, who rarely shares his views, Nadia is _____, never hesitating to tell the student council exactly what she thinks.

traps.why: Timid fits her shy brother, but "unlike" means Nadia is different.
Gloomy is about mood; the clue is about sharing opinions freely.
Outnumbered starts the same way but means having fewer people on your side.

sc1.tip: "Unlike her shy brother, who rarely shares his views" sets up a contrast. Nadia must boldly share hers.

decoys.why: Nadia never hesitates to say what she thinks, so she is not careful to keep quiet.
Being open to others' ideas is about listening, but Nadia is speaking her own views.
The sentence is about boldly sharing opinions, not simply being loud enough to hear.
Nothing says Nadia is nervous or upset; she just shares her views boldly.
The contrast is with her shy brother, so it is about speaking up, not being famous.

traps.why: Quiet and private is the opposite of outspoken.
Outspoken isn't about words already spoken; it describes a bold speaker.
Outspoken people are honest, not necessarily mean.

syn2.tip: Outspoken describes a person, not words. It means someone who boldly speaks out with their views.

sc2.stem: Because Marcus is so _____ about fairness, he stood up in the cafeteria and told the principal that the new lunch rules punished everyone for one person's mistake.

traps.why: Quiet is the opposite; he spoke up to the principal.
Rude is too negative; he spoke honestly about fairness, not to insult.
Unsure people hesitate; standing up to the principal shows boldness.

sc2.tip: "Because" links cause and effect. He "stood up" and "told the principal," so he speaks out boldly.

decoys.why: Marcus stood up in the cafeteria and told the principal, which is the opposite of keeping quiet.
Marcus is speaking up about new rules, not longing for the past.
Standing up to tell the principal is bold, not mild or moderate.

meaning: a long-time opponent who is hard to beat
example: The spelling champion finally faced her nemesis in the last round.
hook: In Greek myth, Nemesis was the goddess of payback; today your nemesis is the rival who always stands in your way.

traps.why: An ally is on your side, the opposite of a nemesis.
A coach is part of competition but helps you instead of opposing you.
A champion is a winner; a nemesis is the opponent you keep facing.

syn1.tip: Think of a superhero's nemesis, the villain who keeps coming back. It names the opponent you can't seem to beat.

sc1.stem: For three straight years, Claire had lost the state tennis final to the same player, so beating her _____ this year felt like the greatest victory of her life.

traps.why: A partner plays beside you; Claire kept losing to this player.
Coaches are in tennis, but Claire lost the final to another player.
Claire is a player, not a teacher; the clue describes a repeat opponent.

sc1.tip: "For three straight years" she "lost... to the same player." That repeated, tough opponent is her long-time rival.

decoys.why: The other player beat Claire fairly in finals; she did not cause a problem or do wrong.
Claire beat a player who had defeated her three years, not her own energy.
The sentence is about beating a long-time opponent, not beating the highest point.
Claire beat a person who kept defeating her, not the way someone behaves.
Nothing says the player is a mystery; she is a rival Claire lost to three times.

traps.why: A loyal partner helps you, the opposite of a nemesis.
A first-time challenger is new; a nemesis battles you again and again.
A minor annoyance is too weak; a nemesis is a serious, lasting foe.

syn2.tip: A nemesis keeps showing up to beat you, like Batman's Joker. Look for an opponent you face again and again.

sc2.stem: Although the two chess players smile and shake hands before every match, each considers the other a _____, since they have battled for the school title five years in a row.

traps.why: Teammates play together; these two battle against each other.
They have met for five years, so they are hardly strangers.
Players who've battled for the title five years are not beginners.

sc2.tip: "Although" tells you the smiles hide something. "Battled for the school title five years in a row" shows long-time rivals.

decoys.why: The players battle fairly for a title, so neither is to blame for a problem.
Each player sees the other as a long-time opponent, not an impressive sight.
A rival in chess is not a terrible disaster; they simply compete every year.
A brawl is a fight, but the blank names a person they battle against.
A blight is a plant disease, not a rival chess player.

meaning: cause something harmful or unpleasant
example: The hailstorm inflicted serious damage on the farmer's crops.
hook: Bullies inflict pain and storms inflict damage; the word always arrives carrying something harmful.

traps.why: Prevent means stop something from happening, the opposite of inflict.
Infect looks similar but means spread germs or disease.
The victim suffers harm; inflicting means doing the harm to someone.

syn1.tip: You "inflict pain" or "inflict damage." Something that inflicts harm makes it happen to someone else.

sc1.stem: The sudden hailstorm managed to _____ heavy damage on the orchard, denting parked cars and stripping nearly every apple from the trees.

traps.why: Repair is the opposite; the storm made the damage.
People measure damage, but dented cars show the storm caused it.
Prevent means stop; the dents and bare trees prove damage happened.

sc1.tip: Look at "denting parked cars and stripping nearly every apple." The storm did the harm, so the verb must mean cause.

decoys.why: The hail dented cars and stripped the apples, so it caused damage rather than survived it.
A storm does not skillfully hold and use damage like a tool; it causes it.
The damage was real, with dented cars and stripped trees, not imitated.
The hail damaged the orchard right away; it did not put the damage off until later.
The storm caused heavy damage instead of holding it back.

traps.why: Healing fixes harm, the opposite of inflicting it.
Spreading germs is infect, a lookalike word.
Feeling pain is what happens to the victim, not the one inflicting it.

syn2.tip: Inflict always comes with something bad: wounds, damage, punishment. Choose the phrase about making harm happen.

sc2.stem: The coach warned that a single careless tackle could _____ a serious injury on a teammate, so she made everyone practice safe blocking for a whole week.

traps.why: A careless tackle can't heal anyone; it causes harm.
The teammate would suffer the injury; the tackle causes it.
A careless tackle causes injuries rather than preventing them.

sc2.tip: "Careless tackle" and "serious injury" point to harm, and "so" shows the coach wants to stop the tackle from causing it.

decoys.why: The coach fears a tackle causing an injury to a teammate, not surviving one.
The coach worries about a real injury, not a pretend one.
A tackle does not skillfully hold and use an injury; it causes one.
A careless tackle would cause an injury, not hold one back.
The worry is about causing an injury, not putting one off until later.

meaning: say false things that damage someone's reputation
example: He slandered his neighbor by spreading lies about him.
hook: Slander throws mud: false words tossed at someone to stain their good name.

traps.why: Praise means say good things, the opposite of slander.
Slumber looks similar but means sleep.
Teasing is often playful; slander is lying to ruin someone's name.

syn1.tip: Slander means spreading lies to damage someone's good name. Picture mud smeared on a clean reputation.

sc1.stem: Jealous of her success, a rival baker tried to _____ Mrs. Okoye by spreading false rumors that her shop used spoiled ingredients.

traps.why: Praise is the opposite; a jealous rival spreading rumors wants to hurt her.
Copying recipes isn't spreading lies; "false rumors" points to damaging talk.
Defend means protect, but false rumors attack her.

sc1.tip: "Jealous" and "spreading false rumors" tell you the baker wanted to hurt her reputation with lies.

decoys.why: Spreading false rumors damages her name; it does not give her knowledge.
The baker spread false rumors about her, not cut parts out of something she said.
The rival already felt jealous; the blank is the action of spreading false rumors.
False rumors about spoiled ingredients tear her down rather than support her.
The rival was spreading lies about her, not imitating how she looks or works.

traps.why: Speaking well of someone is the opposite of slander.
Fair criticism is true; slander is false and hurtful.
Joking around is friendly; slander is meant to harm.

syn2.tip: The key to slander is that the words are false and hurtful. Pick the choice that includes lying.

sc2.stem: Instead of praising the new mayor for fixing the park, the angry letter tried to _____ her, claiming falsely that she had stolen money from the town budget.

traps.why: Thanking is kind; the letter made false claims to hurt her.
Electing is about mayors, but false claims of stealing attack her name.
Flattering means praising too much, the opposite of what the letter did.

sc2.tip: "Instead of praising" signals a contrast, and "claiming falsely" shows the letter spread lies to hurt her name.

decoys.why: The letter made false claims against her instead of praising or supporting her.
The letter spread a false claim about her, not knowledge for her.
The letter is angry, but the blank is the action of making false, damaging claims.
The letter accused her falsely; it did not remove parts of her words.
You revoke a rule or permit, but the letter was making false claims about her.

meaning: fit for a king or queen
example: The lion walked with a regal air across the plain.
hook: Regal comes from the Latin word for king, the same root found in "reign" and "royal."

traps.why: Humble means modest and plain, the opposite of regal.
Legal looks and sounds similar but means allowed by law.
Kings are often rich, but regal means fit for royalty, not rich.

syn1.tip: Regal shares a root with "reign" and "royal." Think of crowns and thrones.

sc1.stem: In her velvet cape and jeweled crown, the actress playing the queen looked truly _____ as she swept grandly across the stage.

traps.why: Shabby means worn out, the opposite of a jeweled crown.
Legal looks similar but means allowed by law.
Actors can be nervous, but she "swept grandly," showing royal dignity.

sc1.tip: "Velvet cape," "jeweled crown," and "swept grandly" all paint a picture of royalty, so the blank needs a royal word.

decoys.why: She swept grandly across the stage, which shows calm confidence, not nervous upset.
A jeweled crown and a grand sweep across the stage draw attention rather than avoid it.
She is playing the queen, the one in charge, not someone resisting authority.
The sentence describes how royal she looked, not how large or heavy she was.
Nothing in the sentence shows her longing for the past; it describes a royal appearance.
The clues are a cape and crown, which point to royalty, not religion.

traps.why: Poor and plain is the opposite of regal grandeur.
Allowed by law means legal, a lookalike word.
Boastful is negative; regal is a positive, dignified word.

syn2.tip: Picture a queen on her throne. Regal describes anything grand enough to belong to royalty.

sc2.stem: Our scruffy mutt usually looks silly, but after his bath and haircut he sat on the porch with his head held high, looking almost _____.

traps.why: Ridiculous matches "silly," but "but" signals a change.
Dogs on porches nap, but a head held high shows pride.
Legal looks like regal but means allowed by law.

sc2.tip: "But" flips "silly" around, and "head held high" shows a proud, dignified look, like a king.

decoys.why: He sat calmly with his head held high, so he was not nervous or upset.
Sitting proudly on the porch shows dignity, not resisting rules.
The sentence is about how proud he looked, not about missing the past.
A bath and haircut would not make a dog look large and heavy.
Head held high suggests royal pride, not deep religious feeling.
He was sitting quietly, and the sentence is about his proud look, not his opinions.

meaning: smooth, shiny, and streamlined
example: The sleek otter slid easily through the water.
hook: Picture a wet seal gliding through water, its fur smooth and shining: that is sleek.

traps.why: Rough is the opposite of sleek.
Sleepy looks similar but means tired.
Sleek things often look fast, but sleek describes a smooth shape.

syn1.tip: Picture a seal's wet, shiny fur or a race car's curves. Sleek means smooth and glossy.

sc1.stem: Engineers gave the new train a _____ design, with a glossy, rounded nose that lets it slice through the air at high speeds.

traps.why: Clunky means bulky and awkward, the opposite of a glossy, rounded nose.
Trains can be noisy, but the clue describes shape and shine.
Sleepy looks similar but means tired.

sc1.tip: A "glossy, rounded nose" that can "slice through the air" describes a smooth, streamlined shape.

decoys.why: A design that slices through the air at high speed is streamlined, not large and heavy.
The train is new and built for speed, not designed to recall the past.
The glossy, rounded nose is about smooth speed, not looking fit for a king.
Engineers may follow strict rules, but a glossy, rounded nose describes smoothness, not strictness.
The sentence is about a glossy, streamlined shape, not about keeping things hidden.
A train design cannot resist authority; the clues describe a smooth, shiny shape.

traps.why: Bumpy and dull is the opposite of sleek.
Sleek things may be fast, but sleek is about looks, not power.
Drowsy describes sleepy, a lookalike word.

syn2.tip: Sleek shapes have no bumps or rough edges, like a dolphin's body. Choose the phrase about a smooth, glossy look.

sc2.stem: My old bike was rusty and covered in scratches, but my new one is _____, with glossy black paint and curved lines that gleam in the sunlight.

traps.why: Battered fits the old bike, but "but" means the new one is different.
Weight is about bikes, but glossy, gleaming paint describes a shiny look.
Squeaky is a sound; the clue describes glossy, gleaming paint.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the new bike with the "rusty" old one, and "glossy black paint" points to a smooth, shiny look.

decoys.why: The clues are glossy paint and curved lines, which describe smoothness, not heaviness.
The sentence contrasts the old bike with the shiny new one, so longing for the past misses.
A bike cannot feel nervous; the clues describe gleaming paint and curved lines.
The sentence describes how the bike looks in the sunlight, not how it sounds.
Paint that gleams in the sunlight draws attention rather than avoiding it.
Glossy paint and curved lines describe appearance, not resisting rules.

meaning: deeply religious or loyal
example: Her devout grandmother attended services every morning.
hook: Devout sounds like devoted; a devout person stays loyal to their faith or cause, year after year.

traps.why: Disloyal is the opposite of devout.
Devious looks similar but means sneaky and tricky.
Fanatical is extreme and negative; devout is sincere, steady faith.

syn1.tip: Devout is close to "devoted." A devout person gives steady, sincere loyalty to a faith or a cause.

sc1.stem: A _____ fan of the team for fifty years, Mrs. Garza had never missed a home game, even during the coldest snowstorms.

traps.why: A casual fan wouldn't attend every game for fifty years.
Devious looks similar but means sneaky.
Famous is about being known; the clue shows loyalty.

sc1.tip: "For fifty years" and "never missed a home game, even during the coldest snowstorms" show deep, lasting loyalty.

decoys.why: Never missing a game for fifty years shows intense loyalty, not a mild interest.
Faithfully attending every game shows loyalty, not resistance.
The sentence is about her loyalty to the team, not her size.
Mrs. Garza is a loyal fan, and nothing suggests she is wild.
The clue is fifty years of never missing a game, which shows loyalty, not royalty.
Sleek describes a smooth, shiny surface, not how loyal a fan is.

traps.why: Barely interested is the opposite of devout.
Sneaky and sly describes devious, a lookalike word.
Fans can be loud, but devout means steady, deep loyalty.

syn2.tip: Picture someone who never misses a service or a game. Devout describes loyalty that runs deep and lasts.

sc2.stem: Grandpa is a _____ gardener; while the rest of us stay indoors on rainy mornings, he is outside at dawn caring for his roses, just as he has for forty years.

traps.why: A lazy gardener wouldn't work at dawn in the rain.
He has gardened for forty years, so he isn't new.
Part-time is too weak; he gardens every rainy dawn for forty years.

sc2.tip: The contrast "while the rest of us stay indoors" and "for forty years" show Grandpa's steady, deep devotion.

decoys.why: Gardening at dawn in the rain for forty years shows deep devotion, not mild interest.
Caring for roses faithfully for forty years shows loyalty, not resisting rules.
The sentence is about his dedication to gardening, not his size.
Grandpa carefully tends his roses, which is the opposite of wild.
Nothing describes Grandpa as ugly; the clues show his steady dedication.
Going out at dawn for forty years shows loyalty, not royalty.

meaning: mild in climate; not extreme
example: San Diego has a temperate climate all year.
hook: Temperate weather keeps the temperature in the comfortable middle, never blazing hot or freezing cold.

traps.why: Extreme is the opposite of temperate.
Temporary looks similar but means lasting a short time.
Tropical is a climate word, but it means hot and humid.

syn1.tip: Temperate starts like "temperature." A temperate climate keeps its temperature in a comfortable middle range.

sc1.stem: Unlike scorching deserts and freezing poles, the island has a _____ climate, with gentle summers and winters that are rarely cold.

traps.why: Harsh is the opposite; gentle summers show a mild climate.
Dry is about rain, but the clue is about heat and cold.
Temporary looks similar but means lasting a short time.

sc1.tip: "Unlike scorching deserts and freezing poles" rules out both extremes, and "gentle summers" confirms a mild climate.

decoys.why: Gentle summers and mild winters are the opposite of a harsh, strict climate.
The climate is gentle, not wild and extreme like deserts or poles.
The sentence is about mild temperatures, not having a large amount of something.
A climate cannot be large and heavy; the clue is gentle summers and winters.
Gentle summers and rarely cold winters describe mildness, not ugliness.
The sentence contrasts extreme and mild weather, not anything royal.

traps.why: Very harsh is the opposite of temperate.
Lasting a short time means temporary, a lookalike word.
Rain is weather, but temperate is about mild temperatures.

syn2.tip: Temperate places avoid both blazing heat and bitter cold. Look for the choice meaning balanced, in the middle.

sc2.stem: Grandma moved to the coast because its _____ weather, never too hot in July and never too cold in January, let her garden almost all year.

traps.why: Fierce weather is extreme; this weather is never too hot or cold.
Storms are weather, but the clue is about gentle temperatures.
Humid is about dampness; the clue describes mild temperatures.

sc2.tip: The phrase right after the blank, "never too hot... and never too cold," restates the missing word. It means mild.

decoys.why: Never too hot and never too cold means calm, steady weather, not stormy and restless.
Weather that is never too hot or too cold is gentle, not wild.
The weather is mild enough to garden all year, not harsh and strict.
The clue is about weather that is never extreme, not about large amounts of something.
Weather good for gardening all year is pleasant, not ugly or distorted.
The sentence is about mild temperatures, not something too strong to defeat.

meaning: to die or be destroyed
example: Many plants perish during a long, hard frost.
hook: Perishable food goes bad fast; to perish is to die or be destroyed.

traps.why: Survive is the opposite of perish.
Punish looks similar but means make someone pay for wrongdoing.
Sicken is too weak; perish means actually die.

syn1.tip: Food labeled "perishable" can spoil and go bad. To perish is to die or be destroyed.

sc1.stem: Without enough water during the long drought, the farmer feared his young tomato plants would _____ before the autumn rains finally arrived.

traps.why: Flourish means grow well, the opposite of what drought does.
Sprouting is about plants, but these are already growing and lack water.
Perch looks similar but means sit up high, like a bird.

sc1.tip: "Without enough water during the long drought" is the cause. What happens to plants with no water? They die.

decoys.why: Without water during a drought, the farmer fears his plants will die, not follow rules.
Tomato plants cannot work together; the drought means the farmer fears they will die.
The farmer fears the plants dying from lack of water, not stepping in to stop something.
Plants cannot guess; the drought clue tells you the farmer fears they will die.
Without water, plants weaken and die rather than combining into a stronger whole.

sc2.stem: While the sturdy oak survived the forest fire, the young pine trees nearby were not so lucky and began to _____ in the flames.

traps.why: Thrive matches the oak, but "not so lucky" shows the pines did worse.
Swaying is just moving; "not so lucky" and "flames" show destruction.
Sprouting is plant growth, which doesn't happen in flames.

sc2.tip: "While the sturdy oak survived" sets up a contrast, and "not so lucky" tells you the pines were destroyed.

decoys.why: The pines were not so lucky in the fire, which means they died, not followed rules.
Trees burning in flames are being destroyed, not working together.
The unlucky pines were caught in the fire, not stepping in to stop it.
Trees cannot guess; not so lucky in the flames tells you they were destroyed.
Unlike the surviving oak, the pines were destroyed, not made stronger.

meaning: open and willing to accept new ideas
example: The coach was receptive to the players' suggestions.
hook: A receptive mind works like a radio receiver: tuned in and ready to take in new signals.

traps.why: Stubborn is the opposite: a stubborn person refuses new ideas.
A polite person can still reject every idea. Receptive means willing to accept them.
Gullible means too easily fooled, a negative idea. Receptive is a good quality.

syn1.tip: Receptive belongs to the same family as receive. A receptive person is ready to receive ideas, like an open door.

sc1.stem: The new principal was _____ to student ideas, listening carefully to every suggestion and even adopting the plan for a school garden.

traps.why: Hostile is the opposite. A hostile principal would not adopt student plans.
Obedient means doing whatever you're told. The principal chose to adopt one plan.
Accustomed means used to something. Nothing says she was used to student ideas.

sc1.tip: Look at "listening carefully to every suggestion" and "adopting the plan." Those actions show a principal open to ideas.

decoys.why: The principal listened and adopted a student plan, so very strict is the opposite of the clue.
The sentence is about listening to ideas, not about boldly stating her own opinions.
Listening carefully and adopting a plan shows openness, not being nervous and upset.
The principal welcomed ideas, and resisting authority does not describe that at all.
Being fit for a king says nothing about listening to student suggestions.

traps.why: Unwilling to change is the opposite of being open to new ideas.
This is about talking. Receptive is about taking in what others say.
Receptive people consider ideas fairly. They don't automatically agree with everything.

syn2.tip: Think of a receptionist who greets and takes in visitors. Receptive people welcome and consider what others offer.

sc2.stem: My grandfather usually grumbles about new gadgets, but when I showed him how video calls work, he was surprisingly _____ and asked me to teach him more.

traps.why: Skeptical fits his usual grumbling, but "but" and "surprisingly" signal a change.
Learning new technology can be confusing, but he eagerly asked to learn more.
Forgetful has nothing to do with welcoming a new idea.

sc2.tip: "Usually grumbles" plus "but" signals a switch, and "asked me to teach him more" shows he welcomed the new idea.

decoys.why: He asked you to teach him more, so he was open, not nervous and upset.
The word surprisingly shows he did not resist the gadget this time, he welcomed it.
Asking to learn more shows openness, not being strict and exact.
His usual grumbling is the habit he broke, so boldly voicing opinions misses the clue.
The sentence is about accepting something new, not about keeping secrets quietly.
Being fit for a king has nothing to do with wanting to learn video calls.

meaning: famous and admired for great achievements
example: The illustrious scientist won two Nobel Prizes.
hook: Illustrious is related to luster: picture a famous name glowing brightly because of great deeds.

traps.why: Unknown is the opposite. Illustrious people are famous.
Illustrated looks similar but means having pictures.
Notorious means famous for something bad. Illustrious is famous for something great.

syn1.tip: Illustrious sounds like "luster," a bright shine. An illustrious person's name shines with fame earned through great work.

sc1.stem: Marie Curie's scientific career was truly _____: she became the first person ever to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

traps.why: Obscure means little known. Winning two Nobel Prizes made her famous.
Controversial adds argument and doubt. The sentence praises her achievement.
Lucky suggests chance, but Nobel Prizes come from hard-earned achievement.

sc1.tip: After the colon, "the first person ever to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences" describes a career of huge, admired achievement.

decoys.why: Science can be strict, but two Nobel Prizes point to fame and admiration.
The clue is her prizes and fame, not whether her career was clear to understand.
Being the first to win two Nobel Prizes is anything but mild or ordinary.
Plentiful describes large amounts of things, not a famous and admired career.
Record-setting Nobel Prizes made her famous, the opposite of staying unnoticed.

traps.why: Forgotten and ignored is the opposite of famous and admired.
It looks like illustration, but illustrious has nothing to do with pictures.
Famous people may be rich, but illustrious means admired for great achievements.

syn2.tip: Think of "an illustrious career," the kind full of awards and honors. The word carries strong praise.

sc2.stem: The violinist had played for presidents and kings for fifty years, so when she visited our small music school, every student lined up to meet the _____ performer.

traps.why: Amateur means not professional. She played for presidents and kings for decades.
Notorious means famous for bad things. Students lined up out of admiration.
Performers can be nervous, but that wouldn't make every student line up.

sc2.tip: Playing "for presidents and kings for fifty years" caused "every student" to line up, so she must be famous and admired.

decoys.why: Students lined up to meet her because she was famous, not because she avoided attention.
Nothing in the sentence says she was upset; it stresses her long, famous career.
Smooth and shiny describes objects, not a performer admired for fifty years of achievement.
Playing for presidents and kings shows fame, not resisting rules.
The clue is her great career, not whether she boldly states her opinions.

meaning: deeply religious
example: The pious monk prayed five times each day.
hook: Pious goes with piety: picture a pilgrim kneeling in prayer at every chapel along a long road.

traps.why: Sinful is the opposite of deeply religious.
Curious ends the same way but means eager to know things.
Ceremonies can be religious, but ceremonial means formal, not deeply faithful.

syn1.tip: Pious is the adjective for "piety," devotion to religion. Picture someone praying often and faithfully.

sc1.stem: The medieval pilgrims were so _____ that they walked hundreds of miles to visit a holy shrine, praying at every church along the way.

traps.why: Skeptical means doubting. Doubters would not pray at every church.
Long walks make people weary, but weariness didn't cause the journey.
Money has nothing to do with praying and visiting a holy shrine.

sc1.tip: Walking "hundreds of miles to visit a holy shrine" and "praying at every church" show faith strong enough to drive the journey.

decoys.why: Praying at every church shows deep faith, not resisting authority or rules.
The pilgrims prayed and visited a shrine, which shows religion, not fame.
Being made up would not explain why they walked hundreds of miles to pray.
Their long walk and prayers show devotion, not being nervous and upset.
Pilgrims praying at churches are being religious, not acting like kings or queens.
Being large and heavy does not explain walking far to visit a holy shrine.

traps.why: Doubting all religion is the opposite of a pious person's strong faith.
Mildly is too weak. Pious means deeply religious.
You can study religions without believing. Pious is about personal faith.

syn2.tip: Pious people pray, worship, and follow their faith closely. The word is about how strongly someone believes, not what they know.

sc2.stem: Though her older brother rarely thought about religion, Ana was _____, attending services every week and reading her prayer book each night before bed.

traps.why: Indifferent describes her brother. "Though" tells you Ana is different.
Studious is about schoolwork. Her activities are about faith.
Superstitious means believing in luck and omens, a less respectful idea than faith.

sc2.tip: "Though" sets Ana against a brother who "rarely thought about religion," and weekly services and nightly prayer show her deep faith.

decoys.why: Ana went to services every week, so she followed her faith rather than resisting it.
The sentence describes her quiet prayers and services, not boldly stating opinions.
Reading her prayer book each night shows faith, not nervousness.
Nothing says Ana was famous; the contrast with her brother is about religion.
Weekly services and nightly prayers show deep faith, not something mild.

meaning: carefully listening, watching, and noticing
example: The attentive waiter refilled our water glasses before we asked.
hook: An attentive student pays attention: eyes forward, ears open, pencil ready.

traps.why: Distracted is the opposite. An attentive person is focused.
Attractive looks similar but means good-looking.
Obsessed is far too strong. Attentive just means carefully noticing.

syn1.tip: Attentive is built like "attention." Someone attentive is paying attention, alert to what is going on around them.

sc1.stem: Unlike the students who doodled during the lecture, Marco was _____, taking careful notes and asking thoughtful questions at the end.

traps.why: Bored fits the doodlers, but "unlike" tells you Marco is different.
Doodling is drawing, but Marco was the one taking notes, not drawing.
Marco asked questions, so he wasn't silent. The clue is about focus.

sc1.tip: "Unlike the students who doodled" sets up a contrast, and "careful notes" plus "thoughtful questions" show Marco was paying close attention.

decoys.why: Taking careful notes shows focus, not being nervous and unable to stay calm.
Unlike the doodlers, Marco followed the lecture closely, so resisting rules is backward.
He asked questions, but the clue is careful listening and note taking, not bold opinions.
Expecting the worst has nothing to do with taking careful notes.
The sentence is about paying attention in a lecture, not about religion.
Being fit for a king does not contrast with doodling during a lecture.

traps.why: Careless is the opposite. Attentive people notice details.
Nosy is a negative kind of noticing. Attentive is a good quality.
Being awake is not enough. Attentive means actively watching and noticing.

syn2.tip: Hear "attention" inside attentive. Picture a waiter who notices your empty glass before you ask.

sc2.stem: The lifeguard stayed _____ all afternoon; she never looked at her phone and kept her eyes on every swimmer in the crowded pool.

traps.why: Careless is the opposite. She kept her eyes on every swimmer.
Lifeguards sit in the sun, but the clue is about watching swimmers.
Anxious adds worry. The clue shows calm, careful watching, not fear.

sc2.tip: After the semicolon, "never looked at her phone" and "kept her eyes on every swimmer" restate the blank: she was carefully watching.

decoys.why: She calmly kept her eyes on every swimmer, which is watchful, not nervous and upset.
Temperate describes mild weather, but the sentence is about her careful watching.
Smooth and shiny might describe a swimmer, but the clue is that she watched everyone.
The sentence never says she expected the worst; it says she kept watching closely.
She did her job carefully all afternoon, so resisting rules is the opposite.

meaning: wild, especially after once being tame
example: A colony of feral cats lives behind the grocery store.
hook: Feral cats come from tame pets but grow up outdoors, wild and wary of every human hand.

traps.why: Tame is the opposite. Feral animals avoid people.
Federal looks similar but means having to do with the national government.
Feral animals may be hungry, but feral means wild, not underfed.

syn1.tip: You often hear "feral cats," ones living outdoors away from people. Think wild, not tame.

sc1.stem: The kittens had been born in the woods and never handled by people, so they were completely _____, hissing and fleeing from anyone who approached.

traps.why: Friendly is the opposite. These kittens hissed and fled from people.
Kittens are cute, but the sentence describes hissing and fleeing, not charm.
Orphaned means without parents. The clue is about avoiding people.

sc1.tip: "Never handled by people" leads to "so," and "hissing and fleeing from anyone" shows the kittens are wild, not used to humans.

decoys.why: The kittens hissed and fled, so being too ready to obey is the opposite.
Fleeing from anyone who approached is the opposite of being open and welcoming.
Cats can be sleek, but the clue is that they were never handled by people.
Nothing says they looked ugly; the sentence describes how wild they acted.
Kittens born in the woods that hiss at people are wild, not royal.
Hissing and fleeing is not mild behavior, and the clue points to wildness.

traps.why: Domestic means living with people as pets. Feral is the opposite.
Vicious means cruel and violent. Feral animals are wild but usually avoid people.
A lost pet is missing, but feral means it has become wild.

syn2.tip: Feral describes animals that live like wild ones, even if their ancestors were pets. Picture a cat that hisses and runs from you.

sc2.stem: Our dog Biscuit sleeps on the couch and loves belly rubs, but the _____ dogs roaming the abandoned farm snarled and bolted whenever a person came near.

traps.why: Pampered describes Biscuit. "But" tells you the farm dogs are the opposite.
Playful is a happy word. These dogs snarled and ran from people.
Purebred is about a dog's family line, not whether it is wild.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the couch dog with these dogs, which "snarled and bolted whenever a person came near." They are wild, not tame.

decoys.why: The farm dogs snarled and bolted, which is the opposite of obeying people.
Dogs that snarl and run from people are not open or welcoming.
The sentence contrasts tame Biscuit with wild dogs, not smooth or shiny ones.
Size is not the contrast here; the difference is tame versus wild.
Dogs roaming an abandoned farm are wild, not famous for great achievements.

meaning: ugly or distorted in a strange way
example: Grotesque stone gargoyles stared down from the cathedral roof.
hook: Picture a grotesque gargoyle on a cathedral: bulging eyes, twisted snout, ugly in a strange way.

traps.why: Beautiful is the opposite of grotesque.
Picturesque has the same ending but means pretty as a picture.
Monsters are often gigantic, but grotesque is about ugliness, not size.

syn1.tip: Grotesque begins like "gross," and gargoyles on old buildings are a classic example: ugly in a twisted, strange way.

sc1.stem: The Halloween mask was truly _____, with a twisted nose, one bulging eye, and a mouth stretched crookedly across its face.

traps.why: Adorable is the opposite. A twisted nose and bulging eye aren't cute.
Masks can be colorful, but the details describe ugly shapes, not colors.
Picturesque looks similar but means pretty and charming.

sc1.tip: The examples after "with": "a twisted nose, one bulging eye, and a mouth stretched crookedly" all describe features that are ugly and bent out of shape.

decoys.why: The mask is twisted, bulging, and crooked, which is the opposite of smooth and streamlined.
A twisted nose and crooked mouth do not make a mask look fit for a king.
The sentence describes how ugly the mask looks, not whether it is famous for achievements.
Temperate describes mild weather, and nothing in the sentence is about climate.
Lucid means easy to understand, but the clues describe a strange, distorted face.

traps.why: Pleasant to look at is the opposite of grotesque.
Grotesque things can be big, but the word is about ugliness.
A bit untidy is far too mild. Grotesque is shockingly, weirdly ugly.

syn2.tip: Grotesque things are bent out of shape: twisted faces, odd bulges. Think of a gargoyle or a scary mask.

sc2.stem: In the fairy tale, the princess expected a handsome prince to arrive, but instead a _____ troll with warty skin and a lopsided jaw lumbered out of the forest.

traps.why: Charming fits the prince she expected, but "but instead" signals the opposite.
Royal fits a fairy tale, but warts and a lopsided jaw describe ugliness.
Tiny is about size, and "lumbered" suggests something big and heavy anyway.

sc2.tip: "But instead" contrasts the troll with a "handsome prince," and "warty skin and a lopsided jaw" show it was strangely ugly.

decoys.why: The word instead tells you the troll is the opposite of a handsome prince, not kingly.
Warty skin and a lopsided jaw are not smooth and shiny.
The clues describe the troll's ugly looks, not whether it is religious.
Lucid means clear and easy to understand, which does not describe warty skin.
Temperate describes mild weather, not a troll with a lopsided jaw.

meaning: strongest or most common
example: Blue is the predominant color in the painting.
hook: Predominant contains dominant: the color, sound, or idea that dominates by outnumbering all the others.

traps.why: Minor means small or less important, the opposite of predominant.
Predicted also starts with pred but means expected ahead of time.
Dominant can suggest bossy people, but predominant means most common.

syn1.tip: Find "dominant" inside predominant. The predominant thing dominates by being the strongest or most common, like the main color in a painting.

sc1.stem: Although the forest contains maples, birches, and oaks, pine is the _____ tree, making up nearly three-quarters of all the trunks.

traps.why: Rarest is the opposite. Pine makes up nearly three-quarters of the trees.
Tallest is about height, but the clue is about how many trees.
Greenest is about color, but the clue counts trunks.

sc1.tip: "Making up nearly three-quarters of all the trunks" tells you pine outnumbers the others, so it is the most common tree.

decoys.why: Pine makes up three-quarters of the trunks, so it is everywhere, not hidden away.
Forests can grow in temperate climates, but the clue is about pine being most common.
The sentence counts how many trunks are pine, not whether pine looks royal.
Making up most of the trunks means common, not famous for great achievements.
Feral means wild after being tame, but the clue is about how many trees are pine.
The sentence says nothing about pine looking ugly; it says pine is most common.

traps.why: Least common is the exact opposite.
Predominant is about how much there is, not about cost.
Pre can mean before, but predominant isn't about arriving first.

syn2.tip: If blue is "the predominant color," you see more blue than anything else. Predominant means there is more of it.

sc2.stem: Because nearly every student in our class speaks Spanish at home, Spanish is the _____ language you hear in the hallway during lunch and recess.

traps.why: Unusual is the opposite. Nearly every student speaks Spanish.
Only is too strong. "Nearly every" means some students speak other languages.
Official means chosen by a government or school, not most commonly heard.

sc2.tip: "Because nearly every student" speaks Spanish, it causes Spanish to be heard more than any other language: the most common one.

decoys.why: Nearly everyone speaks Spanish, so it is heard everywhere, not hidden away.
Outspoken describes bold people, but the clue is that most students speak Spanish.
The sentence is about how common Spanish is, not how easy it is to understand.
Nothing suggests Spanish sounds harsh; the clue is that nearly every student speaks it.
The clue is about how many students speak Spanish, not about kings or queens.
Students really speak Spanish at home, so it is not a made-up language.

meaning: clear and easy to understand
example: Her lucid explanation finally made fractions make sense to me.
hook: Lucid comes from the Latin word for light: a lucid explanation lets light into a confusing idea.

traps.why: Confusing is the opposite of lucid.
Lucky starts with luc but means having good fortune.
Clear explanations are often short, but lucid means easy to understand.

syn1.tip: Lucid shares a light root with "translucent." A lucid idea is clear, like light shining through glass.

sc1.stem: Even though the textbook's chapter on electricity confused everyone, Dr. Patel's _____ explanation using water pipes made the idea easy to grasp.

traps.why: Confusing describes the textbook. "Even though" tells you her explanation was different.
Technical explanations are often hard. Hers made the idea easy.
Lengthy is about length, but the clue says it was easy to grasp.

sc1.tip: "Even though" the textbook "confused everyone," the explanation "made the idea easy to grasp." The blank must mean clear and understandable.

decoys.why: The explanation made the idea easy to grasp, so it was good, not terribly bad.
Using water pipes as a comparison is not making things up; it made the idea clear.
The sentence praises how clear the explanation was, not how harsh it sounded.
The sentence is about the explanation being easy to grasp, not about anyone being upset.
An explanation that is easy to grasp is clear, not famous for great achievements.
The clue is that the idea became easy to grasp, not that the explanation was most common.

traps.why: Hard to follow is the opposite of lucid.
Detailed writing can still be confusing. Lucid means easy to understand.
Childish is an insult. Lucid is praise for clear thinking.

syn2.tip: Lucid is a compliment for explanations and writing. If the idea "finally makes sense," the explanation was lucid.

sc2.stem: Mr. Ortiz's directions for the science project were _____; every step was numbered, explained in plain words, and simple enough for a third grader to follow.

traps.why: Vague means unclear, the opposite of numbered steps in plain words.
Strict is about rules, not about how easy directions are to understand.
Optional means you don't have to do it. The clue is about clarity.

sc2.tip: After the semicolon, "numbered," "plain words," and "simple enough for a third grader to follow" restate the blank. The directions were clear.

decoys.why: Numbered steps in plain words are excellent directions, not very bad ones.
Plain words and simple steps describe clear directions, not harsh or rude ones.
The directions were real and easy to follow, not made up.
The clues show the directions were easy to follow, not the most common.
Nothing about the directions is ugly; the clues say they were simple and plain.
Temperate describes mild weather, but the clue is that a third grader could follow the steps.

meaning: officially cancel or take back
example: The library revoked his card after a year of unpaid fines.
hook: Revoke breaks into re (back) and voke (call): to revoke a permission is to call it back.

traps.why: Grant means to give permission, the opposite of revoke.
Provoke looks similar but means to make someone angry.
Re can mean again, but revoke means take back, not say again.

syn1.tip: Break it apart: re means back and voc means call. To revoke something is to call it back, cancelling it.

sc1.stem: After Liam was caught driving the golf cart recklessly around the campground, the manager decided to _____ his permission to use it for the rest of the summer.

traps.why: Extend is the opposite. Reckless driving wouldn't earn more permission.
Explaining the rules is related, but the effect lasts "for the rest of the summer."
Provoke looks similar but means to stir up anger.

sc1.tip: "Caught driving the golf cart recklessly" is the cause, and "for the rest of the summer" shows the effect: his permission was taken away.

decoys.why: Liam drove recklessly, so the manager took his permission away instead of keeping it.
Reckless driving would not earn Liam more permission; it got his permission taken back.
The manager is punishing Liam, not revealing his permission for the first time.
Censor means cutting out unacceptable parts of something like a book, not canceling permission.
The manager is not imitating Liam's permission; he is taking it away as punishment.
Combining things into one whole has nothing to do with punishing reckless driving.

traps.why: Give out is the opposite of taking back.
The parts suggest calling again, but revoke means officially taking something back.
Pausing is too weak. Revoking takes something away completely.

syn2.tip: You hear it in "revoke a license" or "revoke a card." Something that was given is officially taken back.

sc2.stem: Last year the city gave the food truck a permit to park downtown, but after dozens of complaints about litter, officials voted to _____ it.

traps.why: Renew means extend it. "But after dozens of complaints" signals taking it away.
Revive looks similar but means bring back to life.
Honor is positive. Complaints about litter lead to a negative action.

sc2.tip: "Gave the food truck a permit" followed by "but after dozens of complaints" signals a reversal. The officials took the permit back.

decoys.why: After dozens of complaints, officials would cancel the permit, not support and keep it.
Complaints about litter would not make officials enlarge the permit; they canceled it.
The permit was given last year, so it cannot be revealed for the first time now.
Censor means removing unacceptable parts of a text, not canceling a parking permit.
Officials responding to complaints would not imitate the permit; they would take it back.
There is only one permit, and the complaints point to canceling it, not combining it.

meaning: made up; not real
example: The author set her story in a fictitious town called Willow Bend.
hook: Fictitious is a cousin of fiction: a fictitious town, like a novel's characters, exists only on the page.

traps.why: Actual means real, the opposite of fictitious.
Suspicious rhymes with fictitious but means seeming dishonest.
Made-up things can seem mysterious, but fictitious just means not real.

syn1.tip: Fictitious is in the same family as "fiction," stories that are made up. Something fictitious is imaginary, not real.

sc1.stem: Although many readers believed Sherlock Holmes was a real detective and mailed letters to his London address, he is entirely _____, created by author Arthur Conan Doyle.

traps.why: Authentic means real, which is what readers wrongly believed.
Historical means really existed in the past. Holmes was created by an author.
Suspicious sounds like fictitious but means seeming dishonest.

sc1.tip: "Although many readers believed" he was real, he was "created by author Arthur Conan Doyle." That contrast tells you he is made up.

decoys.why: Sherlock Holmes is famous, but the clue says he was created by an author, so not real.
Detectives notice details, but the clue is that an author created him.
The sentence contrasts real with created by an author, not clear with confusing.
The sentence is about whether Holmes is real, not whether he lived hidden away.
Being created by an author makes Holmes made up, not royal.
The clue that an author created him points to made up, not most common.

traps.why: Based on fact is the opposite of fictitious.
Some true things are hard to believe. Fictitious means not real at all.
Slightly exaggerated is too weak. Fictitious means completely invented.

syn2.tip: Think of the fiction section of the library. A fictitious person or place was invented by someone's imagination.

sc2.stem: Because the reporter used a _____ name to protect the student's privacy, nobody at school could figure out who had given the interview.

traps.why: A genuine name would reveal who the student was.
A famous name wouldn't protect privacy. It would draw attention.
An official name is the real one, so everyone would know.

sc2.tip: The name was used "to protect the student's privacy," and as a result "nobody could figure out who" it was. So the name was made up.

decoys.why: Secluded describes a hidden place, not a fake name used to protect privacy.
A royal-sounding name would not explain why nobody could figure out who the student was.
A clear name would reveal the student, but the name was meant to hide who it was.
The reporter was protecting the student, so the name was fake, not terribly bad.
Using the most common name is not what kept the student's identity a secret.
Nothing in the sentence is about religion; the name was fake to protect privacy.

meaning: expecting the worst to happen
example: Ben was pessimistic about his chances of making the team.
hook: A pessimistic person sees the glass as half empty and packs an umbrella on a sunny day.

traps.why: Hopeful is the opposite of pessimistic.
Persistent starts like pessimistic but means not giving up.
Angry is a bad mood too, but pessimistic means expecting the worst.

syn1.tip: Think of the opposite, optimistic, which means hopeful. Pessimistic is the gloomy side: always expecting things to go wrong.

sc1.stem: Although the weather forecast predicted sunshine, Grandpa remained _____, packing three umbrellas because he was sure the picnic would be rained out.

traps.why: Optimistic is the opposite; he expects rain, not a nice day.
Cheerful has a happy feeling, but Grandpa is gloomily sure of rain.
Uncertain is too weak; the sentence says he "was sure" it would rain.

sc1.tip: "Although" signals a contrast: the forecast says sunshine, yet he packs three umbrellas and is "sure" of rain. He expects the worst.

decoys.why: Grandpa packed three umbrellas, so he was worried, not too satisfied to bother preparing.
Being open to ideas would mean trusting the sunny forecast, but Grandpa ignored it.
Temperate describes mild weather, not a person who expects the picnic to be rained out.
The sentence is about Grandpa expecting rain, not about him boldly stating opinions.
A submissive person would go along with the forecast, but Grandpa refused to believe it.

traps.why: Expecting the best describes an optimist, the opposite of a pessimist.
Planning is sensible; pessimistic is about gloomy expectations, not careful planning.
A little unsure is too weak; a pessimist is sure things will go badly.

syn2.tip: Picture the person who says "This will never work" before anything starts. That gloomy forecasting is being pessimistic.

sc2.stem: After losing the first five games of the season, Maya grew so _____ that she stopped practicing, convinced her soccer team would never win again.

traps.why: Hopeful is the opposite; she thinks her team will never win.
Determined is a positive reaction, but she quit practicing.
Losing can tire you out, but the clue is about expecting more losses.

sc2.tip: Look at the result: she stopped practicing, "convinced her soccer team would never win again." Expecting only bad results is the meaning you need.

decoys.why: Maya was sure her team would never win, so she was hopeless, not satisfied with herself.
Being attentive means paying close attention, which does not explain why she stopped practicing.
The sentence says she expected only losses, not that she was open to new ideas.
Temperate means mild, but Maya's feeling was strong enough to make her quit.
Nothing says Maya stated opinions boldly; the clue is that she expected to keep losing.

meaning: too ready to obey others
example: The submissive dog rolled over when the bigger dog approached.
hook: Sub means under: a submissive dog puts itself under the bigger dog, rolling over to show it gives in.

traps.why: Defiant means refusing to obey, the opposite of submissive.
Sub means under, but submissive isn't about being underwater.
Shy means nervous around people, not ready to obey them.

syn1.tip: Submissive comes from submit, as in "submit to the rules." Someone who submits goes along with what they're told.

sc1.stem: In a wolf pack, the younger wolves act _____ toward the leader, lowering their heads and tails to show that they accept its authority.

traps.why: Dominant describes the leader, the opposite of the wolves giving in.
Young wolves do play, but lowering heads shows accepting authority.
Protective means guarding others, not bowing to a leader.

sc1.tip: The clue is "lowering their heads and tails to show that they accept its authority." Accepting someone's power over you means giving in to them.

decoys.why: Wolves can be wild, but lowering heads to accept authority shows obedience, not wildness.
Regal fits the leader, but the younger wolves are lowering their heads to obey.
Lowering heads and tails is a gentle, obedient act, not a harsh one.
The leader is the strongest; the younger wolves are accepting its authority instead.
Wolves bowing to a leader are not famous for great achievements; they are obeying.

traps.why: Taking charge is the opposite of giving in to others.
Kind and helpful sounds positive; submissive means giving in too easily.
Shyness is about nerves, not about obeying whoever is in charge.

syn2.tip: Look inside the word for submit. A submissive person submits, giving in and following orders, often a bit too easily.

sc2.stem: Unlike her bold older sister, who argued with every rule, Lila was quiet and _____, doing exactly what the babysitter said without a word of complaint.

traps.why: Rebellious means fighting rules, the opposite of what Lila does.
Stubborn describes the arguing sister, not Lila.
Forgetful kids miss instructions, but Lila does exactly what she's told.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" sets up a contrast with the sister who "argued with every rule." Lila does "exactly what the babysitter said," so she obeys easily.

decoys.why: Lila did what she was told without complaint, so she was not harsh at all.
A wild child would not do exactly what the babysitter said.
Quiet does not mean hidden away; the clue is that she obeyed without complaint.
Acting like a queen does not match doing exactly what someone else tells you.
The sentence is about Lila obeying, not about her expecting bad things to happen.

meaning: special words used by a particular group
example: The doctor's medical jargon confused her patient.
hook: Doctors say "stat" and gamers say "noob": every group has its own jargon that outsiders can't follow.

traps.why: Gossip is talk about people, not a group's special words.
Language is too broad; jargon is one group's special vocabulary.
Jargon can be confusing like a riddle, but it means special words.

syn1.tip: Think of "computer jargon" or "legal jargon." It's the special set of words one group uses that outsiders don't understand.

sc1.stem: The computer technician's explanation was so full of _____ like "bandwidth throttling" and "DNS cache" that Grandma could not understand a single sentence.

traps.why: Jokes aren't technical terms like "bandwidth throttling."
The terms aren't mistakes; they're real technical words Grandma doesn't know.
Praise is positive, and it wouldn't confuse Grandma.

sc1.tip: The examples after "like" are "bandwidth throttling" and "DNS cache," special computer terms. Words only experts understand are what fills the blank.

decoys.why: Grandma was confused, but "bandwidth throttling" is an example of special words, not disorder.
Terms like "DNS cache" are technical words, not energy to keep going.
The examples given are computer terms, not anger and disturbance.
The explanation was full of technical terms, not wild excitement.

traps.why: Everyday words are the opposite of jargon, which outsiders can't follow.
This is too broad; jargon belongs to a particular group or job.
Jargon isn't rude; it's just technical words for insiders.

syn2.tip: Jargon usually comes with a field in front of it: "sports jargon," "science jargon." That tells you it's words special to one group.

sc2.stem: The science fair judges understood the student's _____ perfectly, but the younger visitors needed her to explain her project again using plain, everyday words.

traps.why: If she spoke simply, no one would need plain words explained again.
An accent is how words sound, but the fix was different words.
Handwriting isn't fixed by explaining with everyday words.

sc2.tip: "But" sets up a contrast with "plain, everyday words." The blank must be the opposite: special terms only experts like the judges understand.

decoys.why: The judges understood it perfectly, so it was not a mystery to them.
The visitors needed plain words, so the blank is about her words, not her behavior.
Her project was new, and the problem was her special words, not an ancient object.
Explaining again in plain words points to her vocabulary, not her energy.
The fix was using everyday words, so the blank must be about language, not a sight.

meaning: a mystery; something hard to understand
example: How the ancient stones were moved remains an enigma.
hook: Enigma was the name of a famous World War II code machine whose secret messages were a puzzle to crack.

traps.why: A solution answers a puzzle; an enigma is still unsolved.
Enemy starts with "en" too, but means a foe, not a mystery.
A detective solves mysteries but isn't a mystery itself.

syn1.tip: You may know the phrase "a riddle wrapped in a mystery inside an enigma." An enigma is something nobody can figure out.

sc1.stem: Scientists still cannot explain how monarch butterflies find the same Mexican forest each winter without ever having been there, so their navigation remains nature's most baffling _____.

traps.why: Scientists "cannot explain" it, so it isn't an explanation.
Nature teaches lessons, but the clue says the navigation is unexplained.
Proof settles a question, but this question is still open.

sc1.tip: The clue is "scientists still cannot explain" and "baffling." Something nobody can explain is a mystery.

decoys.why: Monarchs fly far, but the sentence says scientists cannot explain how they find the forest.
The forest is their destination, but the blank describes their unexplained navigation.
Nothing terrible happens; the butterflies' navigation is baffling, not a disaster.
Baffling and unexplained point to a mystery, not the highest point of something.
Butterfly navigation is not a set of special words used by a group.
The sentence describes something scientists cannot explain, not wild excitement.

traps.why: Easy to explain is the opposite of an enigma.
Lost things are hard to find; an enigma is hard to understand.
Enigmas can be spooky, but the word means puzzling, not frightening.

syn2.tip: People say a quiet, unusual person "is an enigma" when nobody can figure them out. Think puzzling, not lost or scary.

sc2.stem: Our new neighbor never speaks to anyone, leaves only at midnight, and has no name on his mailbox, so to the whole street he is a complete _____.

traps.why: Everyone knows a celebrity; nobody knows anything about this neighbor.
He never speaks to anyone, so he can't be everyone's friend.
Hero is strongly positive, and he has done nothing heroic.

sc2.tip: The clues come before "so": he never speaks, goes out at midnight, and has no name. Because nobody can figure him out, he's a puzzle.

decoys.why: The neighbor is not anyone's opponent; the street simply knows nothing about him.
He sounds suspicious, but the sentence never says he caused any problem.
He hides from everyone, so he is not an impressive sight; he is a mystery.
The neighbor is strange and unknown, not a terrible disaster.

meaning: hidden away from other people
example: We found a secluded beach with no one else around.
hook: A secluded spot is shut away from the crowd, like a hidden beach only you know about.

traps.why: Crowded is the opposite of secluded.
Excluded looks similar but means left out on purpose by others.
Secluded places are often peaceful, but secluded means hidden away.

syn1.tip: Think of "a secluded beach" or "a secluded corner." These are places tucked far away from other people.

sc1.stem: The family rented a _____ cabin deep in the woods, miles from the nearest neighbor and reachable only by a narrow dirt road.

traps.why: Miles from the nearest neighbor can't be crowded.
Spacious is about room inside, not being far from people.
Modern is about how new it is, not where it is.

sc1.tip: The clue is "deep in the woods, miles from the nearest neighbor and reachable only by a narrow dirt road." That describes a cabin hidden away.

decoys.why: The cabin is deep in the woods, but a building cannot be wild like an animal.
The family actually rented the cabin, so it was real, not made up.
Miles from neighbors describes a hidden place, and a cabin cannot accept new ideas.
A cabin cannot expect the worst; the clue is that it is far from everyone.
A cabin cannot listen or watch; the clues describe how far away it is.

traps.why: Out in the open is the opposite of hidden away.
Jail separates people too, but secluded means tucked away, not imprisoned.
Secluded is neutral; it says nothing about feeling sad.

syn2.tip: Secluded describes a place, like a cabin or a beach, that is tucked out of sight where few people go.

sc2.stem: Most of the lake's shore was packed with noisy swimmers, but we found a _____ cove behind the rocks where we could read in total quiet.

traps.why: Popular means many people come, but this cove was quiet.
A cove can be sandy, but the clue is about having no people.
Dangerous is negative, but the cove was a pleasant, quiet spot.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the shore "packed with noisy swimmers" with a spot "behind the rocks" in "total quiet." You want a word meaning tucked away.

decoys.why: Most of the shore was crowded, so the quiet cove was not the most common spot.
The cove was quiet and hidden behind rocks, not wild like an animal.
You actually found the cove and read there, so it was real.
A cove cannot be upset, and the sentence describes total quiet and calm.
Behind the rocks and away from swimmers describes a hidden spot, not openness to ideas.

meaning: a disease that destroys plants
example: A potato blight destroyed crops across Ireland.
hook: Picture healthy green leaves turning black and slimy overnight: that is a blight wiping out a crop.

traps.why: A cure ends a disease; a blight is the disease.
Flight rhymes with blight but means flying.
A blight ruins the harvest, but it isn't the harvest.

syn1.tip: You may have heard of the Irish potato blight. A blight is a sickness that kills plants and crops.

sc1.stem: In the 1840s, a terrible _____ swept through Ireland's potato fields, turning the leaves black and rotting the crops in the ground.

traps.why: A harvest gathers crops; it doesn't blacken and rot them.
Drought dries plants out, but this rotted crops in the ground.
A celebration is happy, but this was "terrible" and destroyed crops.

sc1.tip: The clue is "turning the leaves black and rotting the crops." Something that sweeps through fields and rots plants is a plant disease.

decoys.why: An oasis is a green, healthy spot, but the sentence describes leaves turning black and crops rotting.
A frenzy is wild excitement, not something that rots potato crops in the ground.
An ambush is a hidden surprise attack, not a disease that turns leaves black.
A brawl is a noisy fight between people, and it cannot rot crops.
An enigma is a mystery, but the sentence describes something that killed plants.

traps.why: A healthy crop is the opposite of one hit by blight.
Fertilizer helps plants grow; blight destroys them.
A drought also harms crops, but blight is a disease.

syn2.tip: Farmers fear "potato blight" and "tomato blight." Link the word with crops getting sick and rotting.

sc2.stem: Every elm tree on our street once stood tall and green, but after a _____ spread from tree to tree, workers had to cut down all the dying elms.

traps.why: A cure would save the trees, not leave them dying.
Fertilizer helps trees grow and doesn't spread from tree to tree.
A rainstorm doesn't spread from tree to tree and kill elms.

sc2.tip: Follow cause and effect: something "spread from tree to tree" and left them "dying." A sickness that spreads among plants fits.

decoys.why: A frenzy is wild excitement, and it would not leave elm trees dying.
A brawl is a fight between people, not something that spreads from tree to tree.
A vendetta is a bitter feud, and trees cannot catch one and die.
A proponent is a supporter of an idea, not a sickness that kills trees.

meaning: harsh and rough in manner or texture
example: Her abrasive comments made the new teammates uncomfortable.
hook: Sandpaper is abrasive, and so is a person whose words rub you the wrong way.

traps.why: Gentle is the opposite of abrasive.
Evasive ends the same way but means avoiding answers.
Firm is a positive word; abrasive means unpleasantly rough.

syn1.tip: Sandpaper and scouring powder are called abrasive because they scrape. An abrasive person scrapes at people's feelings.

sc1.stem: The new coach's _____ manner, with constant shouting and cutting insults, rubbed the players the wrong way until several considered leaving the team.

traps.why: Shouting and insults are the opposite of gentle.
Cheerful is positive, but players wanted to quit.
A shy coach wouldn't be constantly shouting.

sc1.tip: The clues are "constant shouting," "cutting insults," and "rubbed the players the wrong way." A manner that rubs people raw is harsh.

decoys.why: Shouting and cutting insults are not lovable, so endearing is the opposite here.
A coach who shouts and insults is not too ready to obey others.
Receptive means open and willing, but the coach's insults drove players away.
Temperate means mild, and constant shouting is far from mild.
Attentive is a kind, positive trait, but the players wanted to leave because of his manner.

traps.why: Kind and polite is the opposite of abrasive.
Honest and direct sounds positive; abrasive is rough in a hurtful way.
Abrasive people may be loud, but the word means harsh, not noisy.

syn2.tip: Think of scrubbing with something scratchy. Abrasive means rough like that, whether it's a surface or a person's manner.

sc2.stem: Unlike the soft cotton towels in the bathroom, the scrubbing pad in the kitchen is so _____ that it can scrape burned food right off a pan.

traps.why: Something smooth couldn't scrape burned food off a pan.
Absorbent looks similar but means soaking up water, like the towels.
Clean is about dirt, not the rough surface that scrapes.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the soft cotton towels" tells you the pad is the opposite of soft, and "scrape burned food" shows it's rough and scratchy.

decoys.why: Temperate means mild, but the pad is rough enough to scrape off burned food.
Being basic would not explain why the pad can scrape burned food off a pan.
The sentence contrasts the pad with soft towels, so it must be rough, not yielding.
Being lovable has nothing to do with scraping burned food off a pan.
Feral describes wild animals, not the rough texture of a scrubbing pad.
Lucid means clear and easy to understand, which does not describe a rough pad.

meaning: give someone knowledge or understanding
example: The museum guide enlightened us about ancient Egyptian writing.
hook: To enlighten is to switch on a light in someone's mind so they finally see and understand.

traps.why: Confuse is the opposite of enlighten.
Light is inside it, but enlighten means give understanding, not add light.
Entertaining amuses people; enlightening teaches them.

syn1.tip: Picture a light bulb over someone's head when they finally get it. To enlighten someone is to give them that understanding.

sc1.stem: Confused by the strange symbols on the old map, the travelers asked a local fisherman to _____ them about what each mark meant.
