Kwame is arguing against their evidence, not giving a person to blame.

traps.why: Approval supports an idea; a rebuttal argues against it.
An insult attacks a person; a rebuttal answers an argument with reasons.
A summary repeats points; a rebuttal pushes back against them.

syn2.tip: Think of the rebuttal round in a debate. You answer back, showing why the other side's points are wrong.

sc2.stem: Instead of simply agreeing with the article claiming video games rot your brain, Leah wrote a _____ for the school paper, citing studies that games improve problem solving.

traps.why: A summary would repeat the article; Leah argued against it.
"Instead of simply agreeing" rules out praising the article.
A headline is just a title; Leah wrote a whole argument with studies.

sc2.tip: "Instead of simply agreeing" signals disagreement, and "citing studies that games improve problem solving" shows she argued back.

decoys.why: Leah wrote an argument against the article, and a proponent is a person who supports something.
Answering one article with studies is an argument, not a long bitter feud.
Leah is disagreeing with the article's claim, not writing about someone unfairly blamed.
Citing studies makes her piece clear, not a mystery that is hard to understand.
Her piece answers the article's claim; it is not a terrible disaster.

meaning: barely enough; very little
example: The desert receives scant rainfall each year.
hook: A scant spoonful of sugar is barely any at all, just a few grains at the bottom.

traps.why: Plentiful means a lot, the opposite of scant.
Slanted means tilted; it only looks like scant.
Rare things can be precious, but scant is about the small amount.

syn1.tip: Scant sounds a bit like scanty and scarce. All three describe having very little of something.

sc1.stem: The team had only _____ time to prepare for the quiz bowl, just one short practice the night before, so they were nervous going in.

traps.why: Ample means plenty, but they had just one short practice.
Time can be valuable, but the clue shows how little they had.
Relaxed prep would not leave them nervous; they had too little time.

sc1.tip: "Only" and "just one short practice the night before" show the team had barely any time to get ready.

decoys.why: Just one short practice means very little time, not plenty of it.
The clue just one short practice is about how much time, not how hard it was.
The sentence is about the small amount of time, not whether it was important.
They really had one practice, so the time was real, just very short.
Emphatic describes forceful speech, and time cannot be said with force.

traps.why: More than enough is the opposite of scant.
Scant means very little, not nothing at all.
Timing is not the point; scant means a very small amount.

syn2.tip: Think of "scant rainfall" in a desert. There is a little, but hardly enough to get by.

sc2.stem: Last year the creek overflowed every spring, but after months without rain, only a _____ trickle of water now runs over the rocks.

traps.why: Roaring fits last year's flooding, but "but" points to less water now.
Frozen water would not run; the clue is about how little is left.
Months without rain leave only a small trickle, not a generous one.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "overflowed," and "months without rain" plus "only" show that very little water is left.

decoys.why: After months without rain, the trickle is tiny, not plentiful.
A dried-up creek's trickle is small and weak, not showy and bold.
Water trickling over rocks takes no great effort; the clue is about very little water.
The sentence contrasts overflowing with a trickle, so it is about amount, not importance.
Water cannot bite or sting; the clue months without rain points to very little.

meaning: said with force to show importance
example: Dad gave an emphatic no when I asked for a pet snake.
hook: An emphatic no comes with a fist on the table and no room to argue.

traps.why: Hesitant means unsure, the opposite of emphatic.
Empathetic means sharing feelings; it only looks like emphatic.
You can be emphatic without being angry; it means firm and strong.

syn1.tip: Emphatic is related to emphasis. When you put emphasis on words, you say them strongly so people know you mean it.

sc1.stem: When asked whether she would ever quit the swim team, Rosa's answer was _____: she slapped the table and declared, "Absolutely not, never!"

traps.why: "Absolutely not, never" is completely certain, not uncertain.
Slapping the table and declaring loudly is forceful, not polite.
"Absolutely not, never" is perfectly clear, not confusing.

sc1.tip: "She slapped the table and declared, 'Absolutely not, never!'" shows a strong, forceful answer.

decoys.why: Rosa slapped the table and shouted never, which is forceful, not too ready to obey.
Slapping the table is lively action, the opposite of not moving.
Secluded describes a hidden place, but Rosa's answer was loud and forceful.
The clue is the force of her answer, not whether it made people feel affection.
Rosa is firmly committed to swimming, not expecting the worst to happen.

traps.why: Doubtful words are the opposite of emphatic ones.
That describes empathetic, a lookalike; emphatic means firm and forceful.
Speed does not matter; emphatic means said with force and certainty.

syn2.tip: Look for emphasis inside emphatic. An emphatic answer stresses every word so no one doubts it.

sc2.stem: Usually my grandmother answers questions with a gentle maybe, but when I asked if I could skip my vegetables, her _____ reply left no room for argument.

traps.why: Vague fits her usual "maybe," but this reply left no room for argument.
Empathetic means understanding feelings; this reply was firm, not sympathetic.
A cheerful reply might still allow arguing; "no room" shows force.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with her usual "gentle maybe," and "left no room for argument" shows a firm, forceful reply.

decoys.why: Her reply left no room for argument, so it was firm, not too ready to obey.
The sentence contrasts her usual gentle maybe with a firm reply, not a lovable one.
A reply that ends all argument is forceful, not still or inactive.
Secluded describes a hidden place, and her reply was a firm answer to you.
The clue is how firm her reply was, not how long or plentiful it was.

meaning: easily annoyed
example: Without his morning coffee, Dad stays irritable until noon.
hook: Like skin that itches at the lightest touch, an irritable person gets annoyed by the smallest thing.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of irritable.
Furious is far too strong; irritable means easily annoyed, not raging.
Tired people can get cranky, but sleepy is about needing rest.

syn1.tip: Think of something that irritates your skin. An irritable person gets annoyed as easily as skin gets itchy.

sc1.stem: Whenever Tasha skipped lunch, she became _____ by the afternoon, snapping at her friends over the smallest things.

traps.why: Cheerful people don't snap at their friends; that's the opposite.
Irresistible looks similar but means too appealing to refuse.
She was talking to friends, but snapping shows annoyance, not chattiness.

sc1.tip: The clue is "snapping at her friends over the smallest things." Someone who snaps over tiny things is easily annoyed.

decoys.why: Snapping at friends over small things is not lovable, so endearing is the opposite.
She was snapping at her friends, not meekly obeying them.
The sentence is about snapping in annoyance, not feeling too satisfied to try hard.
Skipping lunch hints at hunger, but the clue is snapping at friends, which means annoyed.
Snapping at friends is active and angry, not lying still without moving.
She was with her friends snapping at them, not hidden away from people.

traps.why: Patient and calm is the opposite of irritable.
Both describe being easily upset, but irritable means annoyed, not scared.
Openly violent is much too strong; irritable people just snap or grumble.

syn2.tip: Look inside the word: irritable means able to be irritated. Someone irritable is quick to feel annoyed.

sc2.stem: Usually Marcus is relaxed and friendly, but after the long bus ride with no air conditioning he was so _____ that even his little sister's humming bothered him.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite; a calm person wouldn't be bothered by humming.
The hot bus might make him sweaty, but sweat doesn't explain being bothered.
Delighted is a happy feeling, but the sentence describes annoyance.

sc2.tip: "But" signals a change from "relaxed and friendly," and "even his little sister's humming bothered him" shows he was easily annoyed.

decoys.why: Being bothered by humming shows annoyance, not being lovable.
The clue is that humming bothered him, which means annoyed, not too satisfied.
The sentence is about being bothered easily, not about obeying others.
A hot ride might tire you, but the clue is that humming bothered him.
He was on a bus with his sister, not hidden away from people.

meaning: a person rejected by a group
example: In the story, the ugly duckling felt like an outcast.
hook: Break it apart: an outcast has been cast out, pushed outside the circle by the group.

traps.why: A favorite is loved by the group, the opposite of an outcast.
Outlaw looks similar but means a criminal on the run.
Outcasts may wander, but a traveler hasn't been rejected by anyone.

syn1.tip: Split it: out plus cast. An outcast has been cast, or thrown, out of a group.

sc1.stem: Because the other wolves drove him away from the pack, the old gray wolf lived as a lonely _____, hunting by himself at the forest's edge.

traps.why: A leader heads the pack; this wolf was driven away from it.
Outburst looks similar but means a sudden explosion of feeling.
Wolves may guard a pack, but he was driven out of it.

sc1.tip: "Because the other wolves drove him away from the pack" tells you he was rejected by the group.

decoys.why: The wolf was driven away from the pack, not supporting an idea.
Nothing says he was a hard-to-beat opponent; he was simply rejected by the pack.
A feud is not something a wolf can live as; he was a rejected wolf.
The wolf is a creature rejected by his pack, not a terrible disaster.
A wolf cannot live as a stuck situation; the clue is being driven away.

traps.why: A popular person is welcomed, the opposite of an outcast.
Cast can mean throwing a fishing line, but that's not this word.
A newcomer may feel left out, but hasn't been pushed away.

syn2.tip: Think of the ugly duckling, whom the other birds pushed away. An outcast is someone a group has rejected.

sc2.stem: Priya had been the most popular girl in class, but after everyone learned she was spreading rumors, she became a social _____ whom no one would sit with at lunch.

traps.why: A social butterfly is popular, the opposite of what Priya became.
A social worker helps people; it has nothing to do with rejection.
Outcome looks similar but means a result, not a person.

sc2.tip: "But" signals a change from "most popular," and "no one would sit with" her shows the group rejected her.

decoys.why: A scapegoat is blamed unfairly, but Priya really did spread the rumors.
No one would sit with her, so she was rejected, not a supporter of an idea.
The clue is that no one would sit with her, which means rejected, not a rival.

meaning: not moving or not chemically active
example: The lizard lay inert on the warm rock.
hook: Picture a lizard lying inert on a warm rock, so still it looks like part of the stone.

traps.why: Lively is the opposite of inert.
Inner looks similar but means on the inside.
Tired creatures may lie still, but inert means not moving, not worn out.

syn1.tip: In science, helium is an inert gas because it does nothing. Inert things just sit there, not moving or reacting.

sc1.stem: Helium is called a chemically _____ gas because it does not react with other substances, which is one reason it is safe to use in party balloons.

traps.why: Reactive is the opposite; the sentence says helium does not react.
Helium is invisible, but that isn't why it doesn't react.
The sentence says helium is safe, so dangerous is backward.

sc1.tip: The clue is "because it does not react with other substances." A gas that never reacts is chemically inactive.

decoys.why: The sentence says helium is safe in balloons, so it is not poisonous.
The clue is that helium does not react, which has nothing to do with being rough.
The sentence is about not reacting with other substances, not about being plentiful.
Not reacting with other substances means inactive, not strange or bizarre.
The clue is that helium does not react, not that it is basic or simple.
A gas that does not react is inactive, not showy and colorful.

traps.why: Explosive things react wildly, the opposite of inert.
Fragile means easily broken; inert is about not moving or reacting.
Alert rhymes with inert but means watchful and ready to act.

syn2.tip: Picture the lizard lying inert on a rock. It isn't moving at all.

sc2.stem: After the race, my brother collapsed on the couch and lay _____ for an hour, not even lifting a finger when his favorite show came on.

traps.why: Restless means unable to keep still, the opposite of what he did.
Inept looks similar but means clumsy or unskilled.
Busy means doing things, but he didn't even lift a finger.

sc2.tip: "Not even lifting a finger" restates the blank. Someone who doesn't move at all is lying still.

decoys.why: The race was strenuous, but lying on a couch without moving is not.
He was not even lifting a finger, so he was not eager to fight.
The clue is that he did not move at all, not that he was annoyed.
Lying still without lifting a finger is the opposite of showy and bold.
He was not doing anything at all, so he was not following a careful plan.

meaning: able to inject poison by biting or stinging
example: The venomous spider's bite can be very painful.
hook: Venom plus -ous, full of: a venomous snake is full of venom it injects with a bite.

traps.why: Harmless is the opposite of venomous.
Many venomous snakes are scaly, but scaly describes skin, not poison.
Ravenous sounds similar but means extremely hungry.

syn1.tip: Find "venom" inside the word, and -ous means full of. A venomous creature is full of poison.

sc1.stem: Hikers in the desert should watch where they step, because some snakes there are _____ and can deliver a dangerous bite.

traps.why: Harmless snakes couldn't deliver a dangerous bite.
Some desert snakes are active at night, but that doesn't make bites dangerous.
Timid means shy, which wouldn't make hikers need to watch their step.

sc1.tip: "Watch where they step" and "a dangerous bite" tell you these snakes can hurt you by biting, so they carry poison.

decoys.why: Snakes that deliver a dangerous bite are not lying motionless and harmless.
The sentence warns of a dangerous bite, so lovable does not fit.
A dangerous bite points to poison, not to looking rich and splendid.
Being colorful does not explain why a bite would be dangerous.
The clue is a dangerous bite, which means poisonous, not too satisfied.
The sentence is about a dangerous bite, not about being large in amount.

traps.why: Safe is the opposite of venomous.
Venomous animals may have fangs, but sharp teeth don't mean poison.
Contagious means a sickness spreads between people, not a poison bite.

syn2.tip: Think of venom, the poison a snake or spider injects. Venomous animals can poison you.

sc2.stem: Although the tiny blue-ringed octopus looks cute enough to pick up, it is actually _____, and a single bite can make a swimmer seriously ill.

traps.why: Gentle is the opposite; its bite makes swimmers seriously ill.
The octopus has blue rings, but color doesn't explain a harmful bite.
Adorable is a warm word, but the sentence warns of danger.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets up a contrast with "looks cute," and "a single bite can make a swimmer seriously ill" points to poison.

decoys.why: The word actually signals a contrast with looking cute, so lovable is backwards.
A creature whose bite makes swimmers ill is not harmless and inactive.
The octopus may be colorful, but the clue is a bite that makes people ill.
The bite makes swimmers ill, which means poisonous, not strange.
A harmful bite points to poison, not to looking rich and costly.
The sentence is about a bite that makes you ill, not about being too satisfied.

meaning: skill in using the hands
example: Knitting tiny doll sweaters requires great dexterity.
hook: Dexter is Latin for right hand, so dexterity means having handy, skillful hands.

traps.why: Clumsiness is the opposite of dexterity.
Hands can be strong, but dexterity is about skill, not power.
Sincerity ends the same way but means honesty.

syn1.tip: Picture someone doing quick magic tricks or knitting tiny sweaters. Dexterity is skill, especially with your hands.

sc1.stem: Building ship models inside glass bottles requires incredible _____, since every tiny mast and sail must be placed with tweezers through the narrow neck.

traps.why: Carelessness would ruin delicate work; it's the opposite of what's needed.
Tiny parts with tweezers need careful hands, not strong ones.
The sentence stresses delicate placement, not doing it quickly.

sc1.tip: "Every tiny mast and sail must be placed with tweezers" describes delicate handwork, which takes skillful hands.

decoys.why: Placing tiny pieces with tweezers needs careful skill, not a messy state.
The clue is placing pieces with tweezers, a hand skill, not special words.
Using tweezers through a narrow neck needs hand skill, not a certain way of behaving.
The task needs skillful hands right now, not future generations.
Placing tiny masts requires skill with your hands, not disapproval.

traps.why: Awkwardness is the opposite of dexterity.
Dexter once meant right hand, but dexterity means skill, not which hand.
Toughness is about being strong; dexterity is about being skillful.

syn2.tip: Think of a surgeon or a juggler. Dexterity is the clever, quick handling of things with your hands.

sc2.stem: My little brother usually drops everything he holds, but juggling lessons gave him such _____ that he can now keep four balls in the air.

traps.why: Clumsiness is the opposite; he can now keep four balls up.
Boredom is a negative feeling, but the sentence describes success.
Juggling takes skillful hands, not strong ones.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "drops everything," and keeping "four balls in the air" shows his hands became very skillful.

decoys.why: He can now keep four balls in the air, so he gained skill, not messiness.
Juggling four balls shows skill with the hands, not a way of behaving.
Lessons might teach terms, but keeping balls in the air needs hand skill.
The lessons helped him improve, so they did not give him suffering.
The clue is that he can now juggle well, which means skill, not disapproval.

meaning: very strange or bizarre
example: He wore an outlandish hat shaped like a giant fish.
hook: Something outlandish seems to come from an outland, a far foreign place, because it is so strange.

traps.why: Ordinary is the opposite of outlandish.
Outlandish isn't about being outside on land; it means very strange.
Outlandish outfits may be colorful, but colorful doesn't mean bizarre.

syn1.tip: Think of an outlandish hat shaped like a giant fish. It means so strange it seems from another land.

sc1.stem: At first scientists dismissed the idea that continents drift as _____, but evidence eventually showed that the bizarre-sounding theory was actually true.

traps.why: Scientists wouldn't dismiss an obvious idea; it was called bizarre-sounding.
Brilliant is praise, but dismissed shows scientists rejected the idea.
The topic is science, but dismissed as scientific makes no sense.

sc1.tip: "Dismissed" and "bizarre-sounding" tell you scientists thought the idea was too strange, even though "but" shows it proved true.

decoys.why: Scientists dismissed the idea, so they did not think it was important; they thought it was bizarre.
The theory is called bizarre-sounding, and methodical means careful and orderly, the opposite of strange.
The clue is bizarre-sounding, not wicked; deplorable means very bad, not strange.
People dismiss ideas they reject, not ideas they find lovable.
Emphatic describes forceful speech, but the clue says the theory sounded bizarre.

traps.why: Sensible is the opposite of outlandish.
Land might suggest countryside, but outlandish means weird, not rural.
Fashionable is approving; outlandish suggests something oddly strange.

syn2.tip: You may hear "an outlandish story" or "an outlandish costume." Both are wildly strange, hard to believe.

sc2.stem: Leo's outfit was so _____ that everyone in the cafeteria stared: he wore a purple cape, swim goggles, and a single rain boot.

traps.why: A plain outfit wouldn't make everyone stare; it's the opposite.
Clothes can be comfortable, but that wouldn't make people stare.
Outspoken looks similar but means saying your opinions boldly.

sc2.tip: The list after "stared" (a cape, swim goggles, one rain boot) shows the outfit was extremely strange.

decoys.why: Swim goggles and one rain boot are odd, not rich and costly-looking.
A cape, goggles, and a single boot are random, not careful and orderly.
Plain, basic clothes would not make everyone stare the way this odd outfit did.
An outfit does not have big, important effects; the clue shows it was just weird.
Belligerent describes a person eager to fight, not a strange-looking outfit.

meaning: bring under control; overcome
example: Firefighters worked all night to subdue the forest fire.
hook: Sub means under: to subdue a bucking horse is to bring it under your control.

traps.why: Release means let go, the opposite of subdue.
Subtract looks similar but means take away numbers.
Destroy is too strong; subdue means bring under control, not wipe out.

syn1.tip: Sub means under, as in submarine. When you subdue something, you bring it under your control.

sc1.stem: It took the zookeepers nearly an hour to _____ the frightened, thrashing alligator so the veterinarian could safely examine its injured foot.

traps.why: Releasing the alligator wouldn't let the vet examine it.
Zookeepers feed animals, but feeding doesn't stop thrashing for an exam.
Provoke means stir up, the opposite of calming a thrashing animal.

sc1.tip: The alligator was "frightened" and "thrashing," and the vet needed to examine it "safely." The keepers had to bring it under control.

decoys.why: The vet needs the alligator held still, not pushed forward.
The vet wants to examine the injured foot, not cut anything off.
You decipher hard writing; the thrashing alligator needed to be brought under control.
Nothing is being revealed; the thrashing alligator had to be calmed and controlled.
You wield a tool, not a thrashing alligator that needs to be calmed.
Teaching the alligator something would not stop its thrashing for the exam.

traps.why: Unleash means set free, the opposite of subdue.
Sub means under, but subdue isn't about guessing too low.
Animals may be examined after being subdued, but examine means inspect.

syn2.tip: Firefighters subdue a fire and police subdue a suspect. In both cases, they overpower it and get it under control.

sc2.stem: The rowdy crowd cheered louder and louder, but the principal managed to _____ them with just one stern look, and the gym fell silent.

traps.why: Exciting the crowd would make it louder, not silent.
Entertain is a fun word, but a stern look isn't entertaining.
Subtract looks similar but means take away numbers.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the loud crowd with the result, "the gym fell silent." The principal brought them under control.

decoys.why: The gym fell silent, so the principal calmed the crowd instead of driving it on.
The crowd got quiet, so the principal did not make their cheering larger.
A stern look silenced the crowd; it did not teach them anything.
The crowd was already gathered; the stern look brought it under control.
The principal was not figuring the crowd out; the look made them fall silent.

meaning: give in to a force or pressure
example: Eventually Noah succumbed to temptation and ate the last cookie.
hook: Picture a tired kid trying to stay up on New Year's Eve, then finally succumbing to sleep on the couch.

traps.why: Hold out means keep resisting, the opposite of succumb.
Give away looks close to give in but means hand something over.
Succumb comes from words meaning lie under, but it means give in.

syn1.tip: You often hear "succumb to temptation" or "succumb to sleep." Either way, the person stops resisting and gives in.

sc1.stem: Dalia had sworn to study all evening, yet she knew she might _____ to temptation once her friends started texting about the new episode.

traps.why: Objecting to temptation means fighting it, but yet signals she might fail.
Her friends were texting, but you reply to messages, not to temptation.
You rise to a challenge, but temptation is something you give in to.

sc1.tip: "Had sworn to study" followed by "yet" signals she might break her promise and give in to temptation.

decoys.why: Deviate goes with from, and the phrase to temptation needs a word meaning give in.
Convene means to meet formally, which has nothing to do with giving in to temptation.
Making something up on the spot does not fit giving in to temptation.

traps.why: Resist is the opposite of succumb.
Succeed looks similar but means do well, nearly the reverse.
People struggle before they succumb, but struggling means still fighting.

syn2.tip: Think of eating the last cookie after promising not to. When you succumb, you yield to a pressure you were fighting.

sc2.stem: After running the marathon in blazing heat, the exhausted runner began to _____ to dizziness and had to be helped off the course by medics.

traps.why: Adjusting means coping well, but the runner needed medics to help.
Runners may wave to medics, but you can't wave to dizziness.
Objecting means fighting back, but the runner could no longer resist.

sc2.tip: "Exhausted" and "had to be helped off the course" show cause and effect: the runner couldn't fight the dizziness and gave in.

decoys.why: An exhausted runner overcome by dizziness is not gathering for a formal meeting.
The runner was overcome by dizziness, not making something up without a plan.
The runner was giving in to dizziness, not entering someone's property.

meaning: stop someone from doing what they planned
example: A tall fence thwarted the raccoons' attempts to reach the trash.
hook: Picture a goalie diving to thwart a penalty kick, stopping the shooter's plan cold.

traps.why: Assist means help, the opposite of thwart.
Bad plans may get punished, but thwart means stop them happening.
Delay is too weak; thwart means stop the plan, not just slow it.

syn1.tip: Picture a goalie blocking a shot. To thwart someone is to stop their plan so it never succeeds.

sc1.stem: The squirrels kept stealing birdseed, so Grandma hung the feeder from a thin, slippery wire to _____ their plans to raid it.

traps.why: Supporting their plans would help the squirrels steal more seed.
Grandma already knew about the raids; the wire was meant to stop them.
Admire is a warm word, but Grandma was annoyed by the stealing.

sc1.tip: The squirrels "kept stealing," so Grandma used a "slippery wire." Her goal was to stop their plans.

decoys.why: Grandma wanted to stop the squirrels' plans, not make them bigger.
Grandma already knew their plan; the slippery wire was meant to stop it.
The slippery wire blocks the raid; it does not reveal the squirrels' plans.
A slippery wire works against the squirrels, so it would not push their plans forward.
A wire cannot say plans again; it was hung to stop the raid.

traps.why: Encourage means cheer someone on, the opposite of thwart.
A warning tells about danger, but thwart means actually stop the plan.
Thaw looks similar but means melt.

syn2.tip: A tall fence thwarted the raccoons. It blocked them from reaching the trash, so their plan failed.

sc2.stem: The robbers had planned the heist for months, but an alert security guard managed to _____ them before they even reached the vault.

traps.why: Help is the opposite; a guard stops robbers, not helps them.
Applaud means praise, but the guard was against the robbers.
Guards are hired, but hiring robbers wouldn't stop them.

sc2.tip: "Planned for months, but" signals the plan failed, and "before they even reached the vault" shows the guard stopped them.

decoys.why: The robbers never reached the vault, so the guard stopped them rather than pushing them on.
The guard stopped the robbers before the vault; he did not gather them for a meeting.
The heist failed, so the guard did not make the robbers' efforts larger.
The sentence says the guard stopped them before the vault, not that he revealed them.

meaning: turn away from the usual course or plan
example: The pilot deviated from the flight path to avoid a storm.
hook: De means away and via means road, so to deviate is to go off the road.

traps.why: Follow means stick to the path, the opposite of deviate.
Devote looks similar but means give your time or love to something.
Travelers may hurry, but deviate is about leaving the route, not speed.

syn1.tip: De means away and via means road, as in "via the highway." To deviate is to wander away from the planned route.

sc1.stem: The tour guide warned the hikers never to _____ from the marked trail, because the surrounding cliffs were unstable and visitors could easily get lost.

traps.why: Returning means coming back, but the warning is about wandering off.
Benefiting is good, but the guide is warning about something dangerous.
Hikers take photos, but photographing wouldn't get them lost.

sc1.tip: The guide warns about "unstable" cliffs and getting "lost," so the danger is leaving the "marked trail," or straying from it.

decoys.why: Trespass does not go with from the trail; the warning is about leaving the path.
The danger is wandering off the trail, not doing something without a plan.

traps.why: Stay on course is the opposite of deviate.
Speed is about how fast you go, not leaving the path.
De can mean down, but deviate means turn away, not go down.

syn2.tip: The pilot deviated from the flight path to avoid a storm. He turned aside from the usual route.

sc2.stem: Mom usually follows recipes exactly, but tonight she decided to _____ from the instructions and added cinnamon to the spaghetti sauce.

traps.why: Copying the instructions is what she usually does; but signals a change.
She was cooking, but cooking from instructions doesn't explain the surprise cinnamon.
Quoting means repeating words, not changing what she does.

sc2.tip: "Usually follows recipes exactly, but" signals she did something different, turning away from the instructions.

meaning: to ask for something, such as money or help
example: The animal shelter solicited donations of blankets and food.
hook: Those 'No Soliciting' signs on doors mean: do not knock here to ask for money or sell things.

traps.why: Decline means to say no, the opposite of asking for something.
Donating is giving what someone asks for, not doing the asking.
Solidify starts like solicit but means to make something solid.

syn1.tip: Think of 'No Soliciting' signs on doors. They tell people not to knock and ask for money.

sc1.stem: To pay for the class trip, the eighth graders went door to door to _____ donations from local businesses and neighbors.

traps.why: Refusing donations would not help pay for the class trip.
Money gets spent later, but going door to door is for asking.
Solidify looks like solicit but means to make solid.

sc1.tip: 'To pay for the class trip' and 'went door to door' tell you the students were asking people for money.

decoys.why: The students wanted to get donations, and renounce means to give something up.
You can't pay for a trip by taking back donations; they needed to ask for them.
Going door to door was meant to bring in money, not cut donations short.
The students wanted donations to happen, so they would not stop them.
Holding back donations would not help pay for the class trip.
Convene means people gather for a meeting; you can't convene donations.

traps.why: Giving away is the opposite of asking someone to give to you.
Paying back is about money too, but solicit means asking for it.
Speak with is too general; solicit means asking for something specific.

syn2.tip: Picture someone at your door asking for donations. That person is soliciting, asking for money or help.

sc2.stem: Rather than demand that classmates help clean the park, Jada decided to politely _____ volunteers by posting friendly sign-up sheets around school.

traps.why: Ordering is bossy, but 'rather than demand' and 'politely' rule that out.
Dismissing volunteers sends them away instead of asking them to come.
Volunteers might be rewarded later, but sign-up sheets ask for help.

sc2.tip: 'Rather than demand' and 'politely' show Jada asked people for help instead of ordering them to help.

decoys.why: The sentence says Jada was polite, but subdue means to overpower or control.
Jada wanted volunteers to help, so she would not stop them.
Jada posted sign-up sheets to get volunteers, not to give them up.
Friendly sign-up sheets encourage volunteers rather than hold them back.
Jada was trying to gather volunteers, not take them back.

meaning: showy, bold, and colorful
example: The singer wore a flamboyant suit covered in sequins.
hook: Flamboyant comes from a French word meaning flaming; picture an outfit so bright it seems to blaze.

traps.why: Plain is the opposite of flamboyant, which means bold and eye-catching.
Buoyant ends like flamboyant but means able to float or cheerful.
Flamboyant people may get noticed, but the word describes style, not fame.

syn1.tip: Flamboyant starts like flame. Something flamboyant blazes with color and grabs attention.

sc1.stem: While most guests wore plain dark clothing, Uncle Ray arrived in a _____ purple suit covered with sequins, feathers, and a glittering bow tie.

traps.why: Modest fits the plain guests, not a suit covered in sequins and feathers.
Buoyant looks similar but means able to float, which suits do not.
Drab means dull, but sequins and feathers are anything but dull.

sc1.tip: 'While most guests wore plain dark clothing' sets up a contrast, and 'sequins, feathers, and a glittering bow tie' show showy style.

decoys.why: A suit with sequins and feathers is fancy, not basic or simple.
Methodical describes careful planning, not a showy suit covered in glitter.
Momentous means important, but the sentence is about how flashy the suit looked.
A suit can't bite or sting; the clues describe bright, showy clothing.
Savory describes food flavor, not a glittering purple suit.
Complacent describes a lazy attitude, not sequins, feathers, and a bow tie.

traps.why: Quiet and modest is the opposite of flashy, bold style.
Flam looks like flame, but flamboyant means showy, not on fire.
Stars can be flamboyant, but the word is about showy style.

syn2.tip: Picture a parade costume full of feathers and sequins. That eye-catching style is flamboyant.

sc2.stem: Because the new mascot costume was so _____, with neon feathers and flashing lights, every fan in the stadium turned to stare at it.

traps.why: A dull costume would not make every fan turn and stare.
Costumes can be comfortable, but comfort does not make crowds stare.
Flammable looks similar but means easy to burn, not eye-catching.

sc2.tip: 'Neon feathers and flashing lights' caused 'every fan' to stare, so the costume was bold and showy.

decoys.why: A costume with flashing lights is the opposite of still and inactive.
Neon feathers and flashing lights make the costume fancy, not basic.
Methodical means orderly and planned, which would not make fans stare.
Complacent describes a person's attitude, not a bright, eye-catching costume.
Savory describes the taste of food, not a costume with neon feathers.
The clues describe how showy the costume looked, not how important it was.

meaning: a huge flood or overwhelming amount
example: After the announcement, a deluge of emails arrived.
hook: Picture a sudden deluge of rain turning your whole street into a rushing river.

traps.why: A drought is a long time with no rain, the opposite of a flood.
A puddle is far too small; a deluge is a huge flood.
Delay starts like deluge but means a wait, not a flood.

syn1.tip: Think of a storm so heavy the streets fill with water. A deluge is a flood of rain or of anything.

sc1.stem: After the city announced free pool passes, a _____ of applications poured into the office, so many that the staff needed a week to sort them.

traps.why: A trickle is a few, but sorting took the staff a whole week.
A handful is far too few to need a week of sorting.
A shortage means too few, but the applications 'poured' in.

sc1.tip: 'Poured into the office' and 'so many that the staff needed a week' tell you a huge flood arrived.

decoys.why: So many applications came that staff needed a week; that is no break.
Lots of applications for free passes is busy work, not a terrible disaster.
Demeanor is how a person behaves, not a huge pile of applications.
Applications for pool passes are not arguments answering someone else.
A proponent is one supporter, but the sentence describes a flood of applications.
Jargon is special vocabulary, not a large number of applications.

traps.why: A tiny trickle is a small amount, the opposite of a deluge.
A drizzle is too light; a deluge overwhelms everything.
De can mean down, but deluge means a flood, not a drop.

syn2.tip: Deluge can mean more than water. 'A deluge of emails' means so many arrive that you are buried in them.

sc2.stem: The school expected only a few complaints about the new lunch menu, but instead a _____ of angry notes filled the principal's mailbox by Friday.

traps.why: A handful matches 'a few,' but 'but instead' means many more came.
A trickle is small, but the notes filled the whole mailbox.
Someone might summarize complaints, but a summary would not fill a mailbox.

sc2.tip: 'Expected only a few' and 'but instead' signal the opposite happened: so many notes came that they 'filled' the mailbox.

decoys.why: A mailbox filled with angry notes is no break from something unpleasant.
Angry notes about lunch are a lot to handle, but not a terrible disaster.
A vendetta is a long feud, but the sentence describes a huge pile of notes.
The clue is that only a few were expected, so you need a word for many.
Blight is a plant disease, not a large amount of notes.
Posterity means future generations, which has nothing to do with angry notes.

meaning: eager to fight or argue
example: The belligerent goose chased everyone away from the pond.
hook: Belligerent comes from Latin bellum, war; a belligerent goose acts like it is going to war over its pond.

traps.why: Peaceful is the opposite of belligerent, which means eager to fight.
Belligerent people may be loud, but the word means ready to fight.
Intelligent ends with a similar sound but means smart.

syn1.tip: The Latin root bell means war, as in rebellion. A belligerent person is ready for battle.

sc1.stem: The normally friendly dog became _____ whenever the mail carrier approached, growling, barking, and lunging at the fence.

traps.why: Gentle fits 'normally friendly,' but growling and lunging are not gentle.
Obedience is about dog training, but lunging at the fence is not obeying.
Intelligent sounds similar but means smart, not ready to fight.

sc1.tip: 'Normally friendly' signals a change, and 'growling, barking, and lunging' show the dog became ready to fight.

decoys.why: Growling and lunging at the fence is not lovable behavior.
A dog that lunges and barks is very active, not motionless.
Barking and lunging show lots of energy, so lackluster does not fit.
Methodical means careful and orderly, not growling and lunging.
Flamboyant means showy and colorful, but the dog was acting ready to fight.
Momentous means very important, but the clues describe aggressive behavior.

traps.why: Eager to please is friendly, the opposite of looking for a fight.
Slightly grumpy is too weak; belligerent means ready to fight.
Belligerent starts with bell, but it has nothing to do with bells.

syn2.tip: Picture an angry goose charging at you. Belligerent describes someone looking for a fight or an argument.

sc2.stem: After losing the game, the _____ player shoved his opponent and shouted insults until the referee sent him off the field.

traps.why: A gracious player would shake hands, not shove and shout insults.
Players are often tired after games, but shoving shows a fight.
Intelligent sounds similar but means smart, not eager to fight.

sc2.tip: 'Shoved his opponent' and 'shouted insults' show the player was looking for a fight.

decoys.why: A player who shoves and shouts insults is not lovable.
Shoving and shouting show plenty of energy, not dullness.
The player shoved his opponent, so he was not motionless.
Methodical means calm and orderly, not shoving and shouting insults.
Flamboyant means showy, but the sentence describes a player eager to fight.

meaning: impossible to satisfy
example: Mateo has an insatiable curiosity about outer space.
hook: In- means not and sate means fill up; an insatiable hunger is a hunger that can never be filled.

traps.why: Easily satisfied is the exact opposite of never satisfied.
Very hungry is too weak; insatiable means no amount is ever enough.
Insanitary looks similar and means dirty, not impossible to satisfy.

syn1.tip: Break it up: in (not) + sati (as in satisfied) + able. Insatiable means not able to be satisfied.

sc1.stem: The growing teenager's appetite seemed _____; even after three bowls of cereal and two bananas, he raided the fridge for more.

traps.why: A tiny appetite would stop long before three bowls of cereal.
Picky eaters refuse food, but he kept eating everything.
Invisible looks similar but means unable to be seen.

sc1.tip: 'Even after three bowls of cereal and two bananas' he wanted 'more.' Nothing could fill him up.

decoys.why: He kept eating after three bowls, so his appetite was huge, not small.
Raiding the fridge after so much food shows a giant appetite, not a tiny one.
A weak appetite would not send him back to the fridge for more.
Savory describes food flavor, but the blank describes his appetite.
Sumptuous describes a rich meal, not an appetite that is never full.
The clue is that he always wanted more, not that he ate in an orderly way.

traps.why: Already full is the opposite of a want that never fills up.
Slightly eager is far too weak for a want that never ends.
Picky eaters want little, but insatiable means wanting more and more.

syn2.tip: The word satisfy hides inside insatiable, and in- means not. So it describes a want that never gets filled.

sc2.stem: Most kids lose interest in dinosaurs after a few years, but Leo's hunger for fossil facts stayed _____; he read every book the library had and begged for more.

traps.why: Faint fits kids who lose interest, but Leo begged for more.
Fossils are science, but the clue is that his hunger never ended.
Insincere looks similar but means fake, and Leo truly wanted more.

sc2.tip: 'Most kids lose interest ... but' sets up a contrast, and 'begged for more' shows his hunger was never filled.

decoys.why: Leo begged for more books, so his interest was strong, not dull.
Reading every book in the library shows huge interest, not very little.
Leo's hunger for facts was enormous, not extremely small.
Leo kept reading and asking for more, so his interest was not inactive.
Rudimentary means basic, but the clue is that Leo could never get enough.
Belligerent means eager to fight, which has nothing to do with loving fossil facts.

meaning: to come together for a formal meeting
example: The council will convene next Tuesday.
hook: Con- means together and ven means come, as in convention: when people convene, they come together to meet.

traps.why: Scatter means to spread apart, the opposite of coming together.
Convince starts like convene but means to persuade someone.
You might invite people to a meeting, but convene means actually gathering.

syn1.tip: Think of a convention, a big gathering of people. Convene means to gather for a meeting.

sc1.stem: The contest judges will _____ in the library at noon for an official meeting to review the entries and choose the winning paintings.

traps.why: Judges who scatter could not hold an official meeting together.
Convince looks similar but means to persuade, not to meet.
Artists compete in a contest, but judges meet to choose winners.

sc1.tip: 'For an official meeting' tells you the judges are coming together as a group.

decoys.why: The judges are gathering for an official meeting, not turning away from a plan.
Nothing pressures the judges; they are coming together to meet and review entries.
An official meeting in the library is planned, not entering somewhere without permission.
The meeting is official and set for noon, so nothing is unplanned.

traps.why: Split up means to go separate ways, the opposite of convene.
This is about meetings too, but convene means holding one, not canceling.
Con- can mean with, but convene is about meeting, not agreeing.

syn2.tip: Con- means together, as in connect. People who convene come together, usually for an official meeting.

sc2.stem: Every Monday the student council members _____ in Room 12, so the room fills with people arriving for the meeting right after lunch.

traps.why: If members scattered, the room would empty instead of filling up.
Intervene ends like convene but means to step in and interfere.
A room could be for relaxing, but 'arriving for the meeting' points to gathering.

sc2.tip: 'The room fills with people arriving for the meeting' shows the members come together.

decoys.why: Council members meeting in Room 12 every Monday are allowed there, not sneaking in.
A meeting every Monday in the same room is planned, not made up on the spot.
They meet every Monday in the same room, so they follow the usual plan.

meaning: to take back or pull back
example: A cat can retract its claws when it is calm.
hook: Re means back and tract means pull, as in tractor; a cat retracts its claws by pulling them back in.

traps.why: Extend means to stretch out, the opposite of pulling back.
React looks like retract but means to respond to something.
Re- can mean again, but retract means pull back, not do again.

syn1.tip: Re means back and tract means pull, as in tractor. To retract is to pull back.

sc1.stem: After learning that his facts were wrong, the reporter had to _____ his statement and print an apology in the next morning's newspaper.

traps.why: You would not defend a statement whose facts were wrong.
Newspapers publish, but the apology shows he took the statement back.
React looks similar but means respond, which does not fit 'his statement.'

sc1.tip: 'His facts were wrong' and 'print an apology' show he had to take back what he said.

decoys.why: His facts were wrong and he apologized, so he would not say the statement again.
A wrong statement needing an apology gets taken back, not formally confirmed.
He is apologizing for wrong facts, so he would not add more to his statement.
His own statement was not hard to read; it was wrong and needed taking back.
You cannot cut a statement apart; the apology shows he took it back.

traps.why: Stick out is the opposite of pulling or taking something back.
Retract looks like re plus track, but it means take back.
People often apologize after retracting words, but retract means taking them back.

syn2.tip: Think of a cat pulling its claws back in, or a person taking back something they said. Both retract.

sc2.stem: Our turtle happily stretches its neck out to munch lettuce, but whenever the dog barks, it will quickly _____ its head into its shell.

traps.why: Extend means stretch out, but 'but' and 'into its shell' mean pulling in.
Attract looks similar but means to draw something toward you.
Turtles can shake their heads, but 'into its shell' means pulling back.

sc2.tip: 'Stretches its neck out ... but' sets up a contrast, and 'into its shell' shows the head gets pulled back in.

decoys.why: The turtle is scared and pulls its head into its shell, not pushing it forward.
The turtle is not overpowering its own head; it pulls it back into the shell.
Nothing gets larger here; the turtle is hiding its head in its shell.

meaning: make or do something without planning
example: When the power went out, we improvised a lamp from a flashlight.
hook: Improvise means acting on the spot, like jazz players inventing a tune or actors making up a scene with no script.

traps.why: Rehearsing is practicing ahead, the opposite of making it up on the spot.
Improve starts like improvise but means to make something better.
Speeches are often memorized, but improvising means not working from memory.

syn1.tip: Think of improv comedy, where actors make up scenes on the spot. To improvise is to invent as you go.

sc1.stem: When Kai forgot the words to his speech halfway through, he had to _____, making up new lines on the spot that the audience never suspected.

traps.why: Rehearsing happens before a speech, not on the spot in the middle.
Improve looks similar but means make better, not make up.
Forgetting words might cause a pause, but he kept making up new lines.

sc1.tip: 'Forgot the words' and 'making up new lines on the spot' show Kai had to invent without planning.

decoys.why: Kai kept going by making up new lines, so he did not give in.
Kai made up new lines, which is adding words, not taking any back.
Kai was giving his speech, not entering someone's property without permission.

traps.why: Following a script is planned, the opposite of improvising.
That means improve, which looks similar but is a different word.
Vis means see, but im- means not, so improvise means not planned ahead.

syn2.tip: Im- means not, and the rest is related to provide, to see ahead. Improvising is acting without seeing ahead or planning.

sc2.stem: Usually Mom follows recipes exactly, but tonight we had no eggs or butter, so she had to _____ and toss in whatever she found in the pantry.

traps.why: Tossing in whatever she found is the opposite of careful planning.
Improve looks similar but means make better, not make up as you go.
Recipes involve measuring, but 'whatever she found' means no exact plan.

sc2.tip: 'Follows recipes exactly, but' signals a contrast, and 'toss in whatever she found' shows she cooked without a plan.

decoys.why: Mom kept cooking with whatever she found, so she did not give up.
Mom was using her own pantry, so she was not entering anywhere without permission.

meaning: careful and orderly, following a plan
example: The methodical detective checked every clue twice.
hook: Methodical holds the word method: a methodical person has a step-by-step method, like a detective checking every clue twice.

traps.why: Careless is the opposite of methodical, which means careful and orderly.

Methodical work can take time, but the word means orderly, not slow.

sc1.stem: Unlike her brother, who searched randomly, Aisha was _____ in looking for the lost key, checking each room one by one from top to bottom.

traps.why: Careless fits the random brother, but 'Unlike her brother' means Aisha was different.

Melodic looks similar but means tuneful, which has nothing to do with searching.

sc1.tip: 'Unlike her brother, who searched randomly' sets up a contrast, and 'one by one from top to bottom' shows careful order.

decoys.why: Checking each room from top to bottom shows care and effort, not dullness.
Checking rooms one by one is orderly, not showy or colorful.
The sentence describes how orderly her search was, not how upset she felt.
The clue is her room by room search, which shows order, not annoyance.
Her search is contrasted with random searching, so it was orderly, not bizarre.

traps.why: Here and there means randomly, the opposite of methodical.
Careful work may be slow, but methodical means in order.
Fussy and picky sound negative, but methodical is a compliment.

syn2.tip: Picture a detective checking each clue in order. Methodical describes careful work done step by step.

sc2.stem: Because Dev was so _____ about his science project, writing each step in a notebook and testing every sample three times, his results had no mistakes.

traps.why: Sloppy work would cause mistakes, not results with none.
Metallic starts like methodical but means made of metal.
Projects can feel boring, but testing three times shows great care.

sc2.tip: 'Writing each step' and 'testing every sample three times' led to 'no mistakes,' so Dev worked in a careful, orderly way.

decoys.why: Writing each step and testing three times shows great care, not a dull effort.
Nothing says Dev was upset; the sentence shows how careful and orderly he was.
Recording every step and retesting is orderly work, not showy or colorful.
Dev's careful steps led to no mistakes; nothing is about speaking with force.
The sentence is about his careful steps, not about being easily annoyed.

meaning: rich, splendid, and costly-looking
example: The hotel served a sumptuous breakfast buffet.
hook: Sumptuous comes from a Latin word for expense, so think of a sumptuous feast costing a huge sum.

traps.why: Shabby means worn and cheap, the opposite of sumptuous.
Scrumptious sounds similar but means delicious, not rich and splendid.
Huge is about size, but sumptuous means rich and costly-looking.

syn1.tip: Think of a palace feast with gold plates. Sumptuous describes rich, splendid things that look costly.

sc1.stem: The palace banquet was _____, with golden plates, silk tablecloths, and dozens of rich dishes that the guests could never finish.

traps.why: Humble means simple, but golden plates and silk are not simple.
Banquets can be crowded, but the clues describe rich splendor, not people.
Presumptuous looks similar but means too bold or rude.

sc1.tip: 'Golden plates, silk tablecloths, and dozens of rich dishes' are examples of rich splendor.

decoys.why: Dozens of dishes the guests could never finish is plenty, not barely enough.
Golden plates and silk tablecloths are splendid, not dull.
A banquet with dozens of rich dishes is grand, not extremely small.
Guests can be impossible to satisfy, but here they could not even finish the food.
The details describe richness and splendor, not a meal that takes great effort.

traps.why: Plain and simple is the opposite of rich and splendid.
A sumptuous meal may be tasty, but the word means splendid and costly.
This sounds negative, but sumptuous is an admiring word.

syn2.tip: Sumptuous comes from a Latin word for expense. It describes things so rich and splendid they look costly.

sc2.stem: Our campsite dinner was just beans from a can, but the wedding reception the next night was _____, with crystal glasses, silk napkins, and a towering cake.

traps.why: Modest fits the canned beans, but 'but' signals the reception was different.
Weddings can be noisy, but the clues describe costly, splendid things.
Suspicious looks a bit similar but means doubtful or untrustworthy.

sc2.tip: 'Just beans from a can, but' signals a contrast, and 'crystal glasses, silk napkins' show the reception was rich and splendid.

decoys.why: Scant describes the canned beans; the word
Crystal glasses and a towering cake are splendid, the opposite of dull.
A towering cake and crystal glasses describe something grand, not extremely small.
The sentence describes the fancy reception itself, not someone impossible to satisfy.
The clues are crystal and silk, which show richness, not something motionless.

meaning: shockingly obvious, usually of wrongdoing
example: Shoving the goalie was a flagrant foul.
hook: Flagrant comes from a Latin word meaning blazing: a flagrant foul blazes so brightly that everyone sees it.

traps.why: Hidden is the opposite of flagrant, which means out in the open.
Fragrant looks similar but means sweet smelling.
Flagrant acts are often illegal, but flagrant means shockingly obvious.

syn1.tip: Think of a "flagrant foul" in basketball: one so obvious and bad that everyone in the gym sees it.

sc1.stem: The referee had no choice but to eject the player after a _____ foul, a deliberate trip made right in front of the official for the whole stadium to see.

traps.why: A minor foul would not force the referee to eject anyone.
The sentence says the trip was deliberate, the opposite of accidental.
Sneaky fouls are hidden, but this one happened for the whole stadium to see.

sc1.tip: The clues "deliberate" and "for the whole stadium to see" tell you the foul was both bad and impossible to miss.

decoys.why: The foul was made for the whole stadium to see, so it was not tiny at all.

Sumptuous describes rich, splendid things like feasts, not a deliberate trip.
Savory describes salty food, which has nothing to do with a foul in a game.
The clue is how obvious the trip was, not how much effort it took.

traps.why: Barely noticeable is the opposite; flagrant things are impossible to miss.
Mildly impolite is far too weak for a shocking, obvious wrong.
That is fragrant, a lookalike word, not flagrant.

syn2.tip: Flagrant wrongdoing is out in the open for everyone to see. Look for the choice that means very obvious.

sc2.stem: Most kids who cheat on a test try to hide it, but Darnell's cheating was _____: he copied answers out loud while the teacher stood right beside his desk.

traps.why: Copying out loud next to the teacher is the opposite of secret.
Careful cheaters hide their tracks, but Darnell did it openly.
Harmless makes cheating sound okay; the sentence shows bold wrongdoing.

sc2.tip: "Try to hide it, but" signals a contrast. Darnell did the opposite of hiding, so his cheating was shockingly obvious.

decoys.why: He copied out loud beside the teacher, so his cheating was huge and obvious, not tiny.
The sentence stresses how obvious the cheating was, not that there was very little of it.
Inert means not moving, but Darnell was actively copying answers out loud.
Sumptuous means rich and splendid, which does not describe copying test answers.

meaning: hold back or stop from happening
example: Mia stifled a giggle during the silent assembly.
hook: Picture pressing a pillow over a giggle in class: you stifle it so no sound escapes.

traps.why: Let out is the opposite of hold back.
A stifling room makes breathing hard, but stifle means hold back.
Trifle, which looks like stifle, means to play with.

syn1.tip: You stifle a yawn or a laugh when you hold it in. Think of keeping something from coming out.

sc1.stem: During the long, silent exam, Lucas had to _____ a sneeze by pressing a finger under his nose so that he would not disturb anyone.

Stiffen looks like stifle but means make rigid.

Stiffen looks similar but means to become stiff.

syn2.tip: Stifled laughter is laughter you push down and keep inside. Pick the word that means keeping something from coming out.

sc2.stem: Ella wanted to scream with joy when she opened her test score, but the library was silent, so she tried to _____ her excitement and simply smiled.

traps.why: Expressing her joy is the opposite of keeping quiet in the library.
Explaining her excitement would still mean talking in a silent library.
Her joy was real, so she had nothing to fake.

sc2.tip: "Wanted to scream... but the library was silent" sets up a contrast. She kept her joy in, and "simply smiled" confirms it.

decoys.why: Repeating her excitement would be loud, but the library was silent so she held it in.
She only smiled, so she was holding her excitement back, not pushing it out.
She was not asking anyone for excitement; she was keeping her own in check.
Figuring out something hard to read fits a test score, but not her excitement.
Formally approving her excitement makes no sense when she is trying to keep quiet.
Teasing someone meanly has nothing to do with quietly holding back her joy.

meaning: salty or spicy rather than sweet
example: The savory soup was full of herbs and garlic.
hook: Savory foods, like garlic bread and salty pretzels, are ones you savor for their flavor, not their sugar.

traps.why: Sugary is the opposite of savory, which means salty or spicy.
Savvy looks similar but means smart and clever.
Spoiled food is bad; savory food is pleasantly salty.

syn1.tip: On a menu, "sweet or savory" splits desserts from salty, spicy foods. Savory sits on the salty side.

sc1.stem: Rather than sweet treats like cookies, Hana packed _____ snacks for the road trip, such as cheese crackers, salted nuts, and garlic pretzels.

traps.why: The sentence says "rather than sweet," so sugary is the opposite.
Salted nuts and garlic pretzels are full of flavor, not bland.
Savvy looks like savory but means smart, which snacks cannot be.

sc1.tip: The words "rather than sweet" and the examples "salted nuts" and "garlic pretzels" tell you the snacks are salty, not sugary.

decoys.why: The sentence contrasts sweet with salty snacks, and flagrant means obvious wrongdoing.
Garlic pretzels are tasty, not poisonous like a snake bite.
Snacks cannot be eager to fight; the clue is salty instead of sweet.
The clue is about flavor, salted nuts instead of cookies, not about being unharmed.
Snacks cannot be easily annoyed; the sentence describes their salty taste.
The snacks are described by flavor, not by being careful and orderly.

traps.why: Full of sugar describes sweet food, the opposite of savory.
Savory seems to contain save, but it has nothing to do with saving.
Baked foods can be savory, but savory is about flavor, not cooking.

syn2.tip: Savory foods are the salty, garlicky, or spicy ones. Cheese, soup, and pretzels are savory; cake is not.

sc2.stem: Grandpa can't eat much sugar, so for his birthday we skipped the cake and made him a _____ pie stuffed with chicken, mushrooms, and black pepper.

traps.why: Many pies are fruity, but this one is filled with chicken and pepper.
Grandpa can't eat much sugar, so a sugary pie is wrong.
Sour is a flavor, but chicken and pepper are not sour.

sc2.tip: "Can't eat much sugar" and "skipped the cake" rule out sweet, and "chicken, mushrooms, and black pepper" point to a salty, spicy dish.

decoys.why: Black pepper makes the pie spicy, not poisonous; it was a birthday treat.
A pie cannot be eager to fight; the clue is chicken instead of sugar.
Flagrant describes obvious wrongdoing, not a pie made with chicken and pepper.
A pie cannot feel bored; the sentence is about a salty, peppery flavor.
Brash describes a rude, bold person, not a pie stuffed with chicken.
The clue is that the pie had no sugar, so it describes taste, not orderliness.

meaning: dull, with no energy or sparkle
example: The team gave a lackluster performance and lost by twenty points.
hook: Lackluster splits into lack plus luster, which means shine: something lackluster has no shine or sparkle.

traps.why: Exciting is the opposite of lackluster.
Lackluster contains lack, but it means dull, not missing.
Terrible is too strong; lackluster means flat and dull, not awful.

syn1.tip: Break it apart: lack plus luster, a word for shine. Something with no shine or sparkle is dull.

sc1.stem: After weeks of exciting rehearsals, the band's actual concert was disappointingly _____; the players seemed bored, and the audience barely clapped.

traps.why: A bored band and barely clapping audience is the opposite of thrilling.
Concerts are loud, but the clue is about boredom, not volume.
Disastrous is too strong; the concert was boring, not a catastrophe.

sc1.tip: "Disappointingly," "seemed bored," and "barely clapped" show the concert had no energy, unlike the "exciting rehearsals."

decoys.why: Bored players and weak clapping mean the concert was dull, not showy and bold.
A disappointing concert with a bored audience was not rich and splendid.
The players seemed bored, not eager to fight or argue.
The sentence is about how dull the concert felt, not about a large amount.
Savory describes salty food, not a concert where the audience barely clapped.
The concert was disappointing because it lacked energy, not because anyone was unhurt.

traps.why: Full of energy is the opposite of lackluster.
Lack is inside the word, but it is about lacking sparkle, not supplies.
Quiet and calm sounds pleasant; lackluster is a disappointing dullness.

syn2.tip: Luster is the gleam on a polished car. A lackluster show is missing that gleam, so look for a choice meaning flat.

sc2.stem: Our class's science fair project was _____: we had no colorful poster, no working model, and no energy when the judges asked us questions.

traps.why: No poster, no model, and no energy is the opposite of impressive.
It was a science project, but the clue is about having no energy.
Cheerful is a positive feeling; the project had no energy at all.

sc2.tip: After the colon, the sentence restates the blank: "no colorful poster," "no working model," "no energy." That describes something dull and flat.

decoys.why: They had no colorful poster, so the project was not showy and colorful.
A project with no poster and no working model was not rich or splendid.
The sentence lists everything the project lacked, so it was not plentiful.
They had no energy with the judges, so they were not eager to argue.
Understanding others' feelings has nothing to do with a project lacking energy.
Savory describes salty food, not a science fair project.

meaning: extremely small
example: The ant carried a minuscule crumb back to its nest.
hook: Minuscule starts like minus and mini: something minuscule is so tiny you could easily miss it.

traps.why: Enormous is the opposite of minuscule.
Brief describes a short time; minuscule describes small size.
Muscular shares some letters but means strong and full of muscle.

syn1.tip: Minuscule begins like mini and minus, words linked to small or less. It means extremely small.

sc1.stem: The writing on the single grain of rice was so _____ that museum visitors needed a magnifying glass to read the words.

traps.why: Large writing would not need a magnifying glass.
Color does not explain why visitors needed a magnifying glass.
Foreign writing needs a translator, not a magnifying glass.

sc1.tip: The phrase "needed a magnifying glass to read" tells you the writing was extremely small, and "a single grain of rice" backs that up.

decoys.why: Visitors needed a magnifying glass, so the writing was tiny, not large in amount.
Bold, showy writing would be easy to see without a magnifying glass.
Forceful writing would not need a magnifying glass; the clue is about its size.
Rich and splendid does not explain why visitors needed a magnifying glass.
Strange writing is not hard to see; the magnifying glass shows it was tiny.

traps.why: Very large is the opposite of minuscule.
A bit smaller is too weak; minuscule means extremely small.
Minuscule looks like minus, but it is about size, not negative numbers.

syn2.tip: Minuscule is stronger than small. Think of "a minuscule crumb" an ant could carry: that is extremely small.

sc2.stem: Dad promised a big slice of birthday cake, but after my cousins grabbed seconds, the piece left for me was _____, barely a crumb on the plate.

traps.why: Barely a crumb is the opposite of huge.
Cake is delicious, but the clue is about size, not taste.
Decent means fair sized; barely a crumb is far smaller.

sc2.tip: "Promised a big slice, but" signals contrast, and "barely a crumb" restates the blank. The piece was extremely small.

decoys.why: The piece was barely a crumb, so it was tiny, not plentiful.
A slice that was barely a crumb was not rich and splendid.
The cousins may have been hungry, but the sentence describes the leftover piece's size.
Birthday cake is sweet, and the clue is about how small the piece was.
Barely a crumb is not showy or colorful; the clue is about size.

meaning: not hurt or harmed at all
example: The cat fell from the tree but walked away unscathed.
hook: Un means not, and scathed means hurt, so unscathed means you walked away without a scratch.

traps.why: Injured is the opposite of unscathed.
Unscathed looks a bit like unscared, but it means unhurt, not unafraid.
Unscathed people may be lucky, but the word means not hurt.

syn1.tip: The un- means not, and the rest comes from an old word for hurt. Walking away unscathed means without a scratch.

sc1.stem: Although the hailstorm dented every car in the lot, Grandma's little garden somehow came through _____, without a single broken stem.

traps.why: The garden had no broken stems, the opposite of damaged.
Even a little harm is wrong; the garden was not harmed at all.
Hail is frozen, but the clue says the garden was not harmed.

sc1.tip: "Although" sets up a contrast with every dented car, and "without a single broken stem" shows the garden was not harmed at all.

decoys.why: The garden is little, but the blank describes how it survived the storm, not its size.
The sentence stresses that not one stem broke, so it came through unharmed, not dull.
Gardens can be colorful, but the clue is about avoiding damage, not looking showy.
The sentence is about escaping harm from hail, not about the garden being motionless.
Nothing in the sentence says the garden looked rich or costly, only that nothing broke.

traps.why: Badly bruised is the opposite of unscathed.
Unscathed means not hurt at all, not even slightly.
Unscathed things often were in danger; they just weren't hurt.

syn2.tip: Picture the cat that falls from a tree and walks away fine. Unscathed means not harmed at all.

sc2.stem: Because Mateo's phone was wrapped in a thick rubber case, it survived the ten-foot fall onto concrete _____, with no cracks or scratches anywhere.

traps.why: A shattered phone would have cracks, the opposite of what happened.
Unplugged starts with un too, but it means not connected.
Even scuffs are harm, and the phone had no scratches anywhere.

sc2.tip: The cause is the "thick rubber case," and the effect is "no cracks or scratches anywhere." The phone was not harmed at all.

decoys.why: The sentence is about the phone having no cracks or scratches, not about how small it is.
The clue says there were no cracks or scratches, which means unharmed, not dull.
A showy case might be colorful, but the sentence is about the phone escaping damage.
A phone cannot be careful or orderly, and the clue is about having no damage.
Nothing strange happened; the sentence says the phone simply had no cracks anywhere.

meaning: to cut short or reduce
example: Rain curtailed our afternoon at the beach.
hook: Picture snipping a tail short: to curtail something is to cut it short, like rain ending your beach day early.

traps.why: Extend means make longer, the opposite of curtail.
Curtail contains tail, but it does not mean to follow.
Cancel is too strong; curtail means cut short, not stop completely.

syn1.tip: Rain that curtails a beach day cuts it short. Think of trimming something down, not adding to it.

sc1.stem: The town had to _____ its water use during the drought, banning lawn watering and limiting showers to five minutes.

traps.why: Bans and limits make water use go down, not up.
Measuring tracks water use, but banning and limiting cut it back.
Purifying water makes it clean, but bans and limits mean using less.

sc1.tip: Look at the examples: "banning lawn watering" and "limiting showers to five minutes." Both cut back how much water the town uses.

decoys.why: Banning lawn watering cuts water use, but propel would mean pushing it forward.
The town was limiting water use with bans, not formally approving it.
Showers were limited to five minutes, not cut off completely, so sever goes too far.
During a drought the town wanted less water use, not to ask for more.
The sentence describes cutting water use, not making something up without planning.

traps.why: Stretch out means make longer, the opposite of curtail.
Curtail looks like curtain, but it has nothing to do with windows.
The tail inside curtail does not mean following behind.

syn2.tip: Curtail means cutting something short or cutting it back, like a coach curtailing practice when lightning appears.

sc2.stem: Coach normally lets us scrimmage for an hour, but when thunder rumbled in the distance, she had to _____ practice and send everyone inside after ten minutes.

traps.why: Ending after ten minutes is the opposite of lengthening practice.
Practice was already happening; the thunder made it end early.
Organizing practice does not explain sending everyone inside early.

sc2.tip: "Normally... for an hour, but" sets up a contrast, and "after ten minutes" shows practice was cut short.

decoys.why: Coach sent everyone inside early, which is cutting practice short, not gathering for it.
Thunder made her end practice after ten minutes, not make up a new plan for it.
Practice ended early instead of lasting an hour, so it was cut short, not repeated.
Sending everyone inside after ten minutes cuts practice short rather than pushing it forward.
The sentence is about ending practice early because of thunder, not approving it.

meaning: all future generations of people
example: The town buried a time capsule for posterity to open.
hook: Post means after, so posterity is everyone who comes after us, like the kids who will open a time capsule.

traps.why: Ancestors came before us; posterity comes after us.
Prosperity looks similar but means wealth and success.
History is about the past; posterity is about future people.

syn1.tip: Post- means after, as in postgame. Posterity is the people who come after us, our descendants.

sc1.stem: The historians recorded interviews with the town's oldest residents to preserve their memories for _____, so that people living a century from now could hear them.

traps.why: Ancestors lived long ago, not a century from now.
Prosperity looks like posterity but means wealth.
Tourists visit now; the clue points to people a century from now.

sc1.tip: The phrase "people living a century from now" restates the blank. The memories are being saved for future generations.

decoys.why: It ends like posterity, but the sentence means people living a century from now, not hand skill.
The historians wanted memories preserved for future people, not left in a mess.
The interviews are kept so future people can hear them, not to show disapproval.
The clue points to people a century from now, not to pain or suffering.
The sentence is about future generations hearing the interviews, not a plant disease.

traps.why: Past generations are the opposite of posterity.
Post here means after, not the post office.
Photos may be saved for posterity, but posterity means future people.

syn2.tip: Things saved "for posterity" are kept for people not yet born. Think future generations, not the past.

sc2.stem: Grandpa says he doesn't need notes to remember his own childhood, but he still writes down his stories for _____, hoping his great-grandchildren will someday read them.

traps.why: He says he doesn't need notes, so the stories aren't for himself.
Writing may be fun, but the clue names great-grandchildren as readers.
Prosperity looks like posterity but means wealth.

sc2.tip: He "doesn't need notes" himself, so the stories are for others, and "great-grandchildren will someday read them" points to future generations.

decoys.why: It looks like posterity, but Grandpa writes for his great-grandchildren, not for hand skill.
Grandpa hopes his great-grandchildren will read his stories, which is loving, not disapproving.
The clue is about future readers like his great-grandchildren, not a messy state.
He writes so future family can read his stories, not for pain or suffering.

meaning: bored or unexcited from too much experience
example: After visiting fifty castles, the jaded tourist barely looked up.
hook: Picture a kid who has seen every movie twice and now just yawns at trailers: that kid is jaded.

traps.why: Eager is the opposite of jaded.
Jade is a green gem, but jaded has nothing to do with jewels.
Jaded people have too much experience, not too little.

syn1.tip: A jaded person is weary of something after too much of it, like a tourist bored by the fiftieth castle.

sc1.stem: Having ridden every roller coaster in the country, Victor had become so _____ that even the newest, fastest ride failed to excite him.

traps.why: The ride failed to excite him, so he was not thrilled.
Roller coasters can scare people, but the clue is about boredom.
Rides can make you dizzy, but the clue says nothing excites him.

sc1.tip: "Having ridden every roller coaster" is the cause, and "failed to excite him" is the effect. Too much experience left him bored.

decoys.why: Riding every coaster might leave him unhurt, but the clue is that nothing excites him anymore.
Monotonous describes a dull thing, but the sentence describes Victor feeling bored from experience.
The sentence says rides fail to excite him, which shows boredom, not rude boldness.
Victor is unexcited by everything, which is the opposite of showy and bold.
Grueling describes a tiring task, but the sentence is about Victor being bored by too many rides.

traps.why: Easily thrilled is the opposite of jaded.
Jade is green, but jaded has nothing to do with envy.
Deeply depressed is far too strong; jaded means bored.

syn2.tip: Jaded people have done something so often that it no longer excites them. Think of a "seen it all" feeling.

sc2.stem: My little sister squeals at every fireworks show, but my older cousin, who has watched hundreds of them, seems totally _____ and just scrolls on his phone.

traps.why: Scrolling on his phone is the opposite of being amazed.
Fireworks can be scary, but he is calmly scrolling, not afraid.
Nothing in the sentence suggests he doesn't understand the fireworks.

sc2.tip: "Squeals... but" sets up a contrast, and "hundreds of them" explains why. He has seen so many that he is no longer excited.

decoys.why: He ignores the show and scrolls his phone, so he is not sharing anyone's excitement.
Your cousin just scrolls on his phone, which is bored and quiet, not showy.
He is not picking a fight; he is bored after watching hundreds of shows.
The sentence is about him being bored from too many shows, not avoiding harm.
Insatiable means always wanting more, but he has seen hundreds and no longer cares.

meaning: to figure out by reasoning
example: From the muddy paw prints, Ana deduced that the dog had been outside.
hook: Detectives deduce: like Sherlock Holmes spotting mud on a boot and reasoning out exactly where someone has been.

traps.why: A guess needs no reasoning; deducing uses clues to reach an answer.
That is reduce, which rhymes with deduce, not deduce itself.
Deduct, which looks like deduce, means subtract.

syn1.tip: Detectives deduce: they look at clues and reason their way to an answer. To deduce is to conclude from evidence.

sc1.stem: From the wet umbrella by the door and the puddle on the floor, Detective Reyes was able to _____ that the visitor had just come in from the rain.

traps.why: The clues support the idea, so the detective would not doubt it.
Pretending ignores evidence; the detective used real clues.
Wishing has nothing to do with reasoning from the umbrella and puddle.

sc1.tip: The detective uses clues, "the wet umbrella" and "the puddle on the floor," to reason out an answer. That is what deduce means.

decoys.why: She figured this out from clues like the puddle; nobody said it before for her to repeat.
Reyes is reaching a new conclusion from the wet umbrella, not taking back something she said.

traps.why: Take away means deduct, a lookalike word, not deduce.
The word parts suggest leading away, but deduce means reason out.
