Guessing blindly is the opposite of carefully reasoning from clues.

syn2.tip: Think of the detective phrase "I deduce that..." It means figuring out an answer by putting clues together.

sc2.stem: Nobody told Priya who had eaten the last cookie, but she could easily _____ who the culprit was from the chocolate crumbs on her brother's shirt.

traps.why: She worked out the answer, the opposite of forgetting it.
Easily and the crumbs show she found the answer, not just wondered.
Nobody told her, so she could not have heard who did it.

sc2.tip: "Nobody told Priya, but" means she worked it out herself, using the "chocolate crumbs" as evidence. She reasoned her way to the answer.

decoys.why: Nobody told Priya, so she could not repeat it; she figured it out from the crumbs.

meaning: a situation where no progress is possible
example: Talks between the two clubs reached an impasse.
hook: An impasse is like a dead-end street: im- means not, so there is no way to pass through.

traps.why: A breakthrough is sudden progress, the opposite of being stuck.
Arguments can cause an impasse, but impasse means the stuck situation itself.
Impact looks similar but means a hit or a strong effect.

syn1.tip: The im- means not, so an impasse is a place you cannot pass. Picture a dead-end street where everything stops.

sc1.stem: Neither the art club nor the robotics team would give up the Friday room booking, so after an hour of arguing the two groups remained at a complete _____.

traps.why: Neither group gave in, so they never reached an agreement.
A compromise means each side gives a little; here neither side did.
Nobody won the room; both groups stayed stuck.

sc1.tip: "Neither... would give up" and "after an hour of arguing" show no side moved, so they were stuck with no progress.

decoys.why: Arguing is mentioned, but the blank names where they ended up: stuck, not an answering argument.
The groups argued, but the blank describes being stuck with no progress, not one angry speech.
After an hour of arguing, the groups got no break; they were stuck where they started.
A room booking argument is not a terrible disaster; the groups were simply stuck.
Skill with the hands has nothing to do with two groups refusing to give up a room.
Future generations have nothing to do with two clubs stuck arguing over Friday.

traps.why: A clear way forward means progress, the opposite of an impasse.
Quarrels may lead to an impasse, but impasse means being stuck.
A pause is short and ends easily; an impasse means no progress at all.

syn2.tip: Talks are said to "reach an impasse." Picture two cars nose to nose on a narrow road, neither able to move.

sc2.stem: The class could not agree on a field trip: half wanted the zoo, half wanted the science museum, and every new vote ended in the same tie, a frustrating _____.

traps.why: A decision would end the tie, but every vote stayed tied.
"Frustrating" shows bad feelings, not a happy celebration.
The trip is the topic, but the class never even chose one.

sc2.tip: "Every new vote ended in the same tie" tells you nothing moved forward. The blank renames that stuck situation.

decoys.why: The blank renames the tie, and a tie is not an argument answering another.
Every vote ending in the same tie is frustrating, not a welcome break.
A tied vote on a field trip is annoying, not a terrible disaster.
The blank renames the tie, not a person who supports the zoo or museum.
The blank describes the stuck vote, not the way someone looks or behaves.
Nothing ghostly happens; the class is just stuck in the same tie every vote.

meaning: to tease someone in a mean way
example: The older kids taunted him about his old sneakers.
hook: Taunt rhymes with haunt: a bully's taunts can haunt you long after the teasing stops.

traps.why: Praise means saying nice things, the opposite of mean teasing.
Haunt rhymes with taunt but means to visit like a ghost.
Bullies may dare people, but taunt means making fun of them.

syn1.tip: Taunting is something bullies do with mean words on the playground. Pick the choice that means making fun of someone.

sc1.stem: The older kids liked to _____ the new student about his accent, mimicking the way he spoke until the teacher stepped in.

traps.why: Mean mimicking is not a compliment; it is the reverse.
Asking questions isn't mean, and a teacher wouldn't need to stop it.
The kids weren't teaching about accents; they were copying him to be mean.

sc1.tip: "Mimicking the way he spoke until the teacher stepped in" shows mean behavior a teacher must stop, so the blank means tease cruelly.

decoys.why: They were mimicking his speech to be mean, not questioning him closely.

traps.why: Cheering someone on is kind support, the opposite of taunting.
Joking with friends is friendly; taunting is mean.
Bullies may scare people, but taunting means mocking them.

syn2.tip: Taunting is teasing with a sting. Friendly teasing doesn't count, so look for the choice that is both teasing and mean.

sc2.stem: Most fans clapped kindly for Leo even after he missed the final shot, but a few rude ones in the stands began to _____ him about his clumsy throw.

traps.why: Encouraging is what the kind fans did; "but" points to the opposite.
Coaching helps a player improve; rude fans were not trying to help.
Consoling is kind comfort, the wrong feeling for rude fans.

sc2.tip: "But a few rude ones" contrasts with the kind fans, so the blank is something mean, like making fun of him.

decoys.why: Rude fans in the stands were mocking Leo, not questioning him closely about the throw.

meaning: a deep crack in the earth
example: A rope bridge stretched across the deep chasm.
hook: The ch in chasm sounds like k: picture a canyon so deep and wide you would need a bridge to cross.

traps.why: A summit is the top of a mountain, not a deep crack.
Bridges cross chasms, but a bridge is not the gap itself.
Charm starts like chasm but means pleasing appeal.

syn1.tip: Chasm usually comes with "deep" or "wide." Picture a huge crack in the ground, like a canyon you cannot jump across.

sc1.stem: The explorers stopped at the edge of a deep _____ that split the mountain in two, its bottom so far below that they could barely see the river.

traps.why: A summit is the top, but this place had a bottom far below.
A tunnel goes through a mountain; it doesn't split it open to the sky.
A ditch is shallow, but this bottom was almost too far to see.

sc1.tip: "Split the mountain in two" and a bottom "so far below that they could barely see the river" describe a huge, deep gap.

decoys.why: The blank is a physical crack splitting the mountain, with a bottom far below.
The river is far below; the blank is a deep crack, not a flood.
The explorers stand at the edge of something with a bottom, a crack, not a sudden change.
The sentence describes a deep split in the mountain, not a disaster happening to someone.
Nothing ghostly appears; the explorers see a deep crack with a river far below.

traps.why: A high peak rises up; a chasm drops far down.
A rope bridge may cross a chasm, but it isn't the gap.
A dent is tiny; a chasm is huge and deep.

syn2.tip: Chasms are big. Think of the Grand Canyon: a deep, wide opening in the earth, much bigger than a hole or a ditch.

sc2.stem: Most of the hiking trail was an easy stroll, but near the end it stopped at a rocky _____ so wide that only a swaying rope bridge could carry hikers across.

traps.why: A hilltop is high ground; you don't need a bridge to cross it.
A ledge is a narrow shelf on a cliff, not a gap to cross.
A pothole is far too small to need a rope bridge.

sc2.tip: Only "a swaying rope bridge" could carry hikers "across," so the blank must be a wide, deep gap in the land.

decoys.why: Hikers cross on a rope bridge over a wide rocky gap, not a flood.
A rope bridge crosses a wide gap in the rock, not a sudden change.
The easy part was the stroll; the blank is the hard gap at the end.
The blank is a wide rocky gap needing a bridge, not a terrible disaster.
A bridge carries hikers across a wide gap, not across a messy state.

meaning: a messy, disorganized state
example: After the party, the living room was in disarray.
hook: An array is a neat arrangement; add dis- and the neat rows fall apart into a jumble.

traps.why: Order means everything is neat, the opposite of disarray.
Dismay looks similar but means a feeling of alarm or worry.
Messy places can be noisy, but disarray is about things being jumbled.

syn1.tip: Spot the parts: dis- means not, and an array is a neat arrangement. Disarray is the state of not being neat.

sc1.stem: After the toddlers' playdate, the living room was in complete _____: toys covered the floor, cushions were scattered, and crayons were everywhere.

traps.why: Scattered toys and cushions show the room was not in order.
The room may be quiet after the kids leave, but the details describe mess.
Dismay is a feeling, and a living room can't feel anything.

sc1.tip: The colon brings examples: toys "covered the floor," cushions "scattered," crayons "everywhere." Those details describe a very messy state.

decoys.why: Scattered toys and crayons make a mess, not a terrible disaster.
The room is messy with toys everywhere, not stuck where no progress is possible.
The details describe a messy room, not a short break from something unpleasant.
Toys and crayons everywhere describe a mess, not skill with the hands.

traps.why: Tidiness means neat and in place, the opposite of disarray.
Display also starts with dis but means a show or exhibit.
Messy things aren't necessarily broken; disarray means mixed up.

syn2.tip: You often hear "in disarray" about a messy room or a team that lost its plan. Pick the choice meaning things are mixed up.

sc2.stem: Our coach expected the team to be ready for the big game, but when the bus broke down and three players got lost, the whole morning fell into _____.

traps.why: "Fell into place" means things worked out, the opposite of this morning.
A routine is normal and expected; this morning was anything but.
"Fall into line" means to obey, but this morning became chaotic.

sc2.tip: "But" signals things went against the coach's plan, and a broken bus plus lost players means everything got chaotic.

decoys.why: A broken bus and lost players bring confusion, not a welcome break.
The morning fell apart into confusion; skill with the hands does not fit.
Future generations have nothing to do with a disorganized morning before a game.
The sentence describes a confused, messy morning, not fake showy boldness.

meaning: overly bold and self-confident, often rude
example: The brash rookie bragged that he would beat the champion easily.
hook: Picture a brash rookie strutting into the locker room, bragging loudly before he has played a single game.

traps.why: Modest people don't brag, the opposite of brash.
Brave is boldness praised; brash is boldness that is rude.
Brisk looks similar but means quick and lively.

syn1.tip: Brash people brag and push themselves forward, often rudely. It has a negative feeling, so look for a word for annoying overconfidence.

sc1.stem: On his very first day, the _____ new player announced that he was the best on the team and that the captain should hand him the ball.

traps.why: A humble player would never announce he was the best.
He claimed skill, but the clue is his rude bragging, not ability.
First days can be nerve-racking, but he was boasting, not worried.

sc1.tip: He "announced that he was the best" and told the captain to "hand him the ball" on his "very first day." That's rude overconfidence.

decoys.why: On his very first day, he is eager and boastful, not bored from experience.
Announcing he is the best shows too much boldness, not a lack of energy.
Demanding the captain's ball shows no care for others' feelings.
Boasting and demanding the ball is rude boldness, not careful orderly planning.
The sentence shows him boasting, not having bad luck.
Nothing hurt him; the clue is his rude, boastful announcement.

sc2.stem: Unlike her quiet, polite older sister, Mia was so _____ that she told the principal his new lunch rules were silly and that she could do his job better.

traps.why: Timid people are fearful and wouldn't talk to the principal that way.
Honest is a kind word, but bragging she could do his job is rude.
Lunch is the topic, but hunger doesn't explain bragging about his job.

sc2.tip: "Unlike her quiet, polite older sister" tells you Mia is loud and rude, bragging she could do the principal's job better.

decoys.why: Telling the principal she could do his job better is bold, not dull.
Calling his rules silly shows no care for the principal's feelings.
Her blunt remark to the principal is rude boldness, not careful planning.
Mia is not bored; she boldly criticizes the principal to his face.
The clue is her rude confidence, not bad luck.
Her size is not the point; she speaks to the principal with rude confidence.

meaning: dull because it never changes
example: The speaker's monotonous voice put half the audience to sleep.
hook: Mono means one and tone is sound: a monotonous voice stays on one note until everyone dozes off.

traps.why: Exciting is full of thrills, the opposite of monotonous.
Monstrous looks similar but means huge or horrible.
Mono means one, but monotonous is about sameness, not being alone.

syn1.tip: Mono means one, as in monorail. Monotonous means one tone over and over, so it gets boring.

sc1.stem: The drive across the plains was _____: mile after mile of flat wheat fields looked exactly the same, and Marco fell asleep before noon.

traps.why: Thrilling things keep you awake, but Marco fell asleep.
Long drives can be risky, but the clue is fields that look the same.
Colorful means full of variety, but every mile looked exactly the same.

sc1.tip: "Mile after mile" of fields that "looked exactly the same" and Marco falling asleep point to something boring because it never changes.

decoys.why: The fields looked exactly the same, so nothing about the drive was strange or bizarre.
Flat wheat fields that never change are the opposite of showy and colorful.
Jaded describes a bored person like Marco, not the drive itself.
The drive went on mile after mile, so it was not extremely small.
Plain wheat fields are not rich or splendid, and nothing here looks costly.
Shrill describes a high sound, but the clue is about sameness that put Marco to sleep.

traps.why: Varied means full of changes, the opposite of monotonous.
A monotonous voice can be loud; the problem is sameness, not volume.
Tone suggests music, but monotonous means boringly the same.

syn2.tip: Something monotonous keeps doing the same thing again and again. Look for the choice about repeating, not about volume or music.

sc2.stem: Jaden loved the first few levels of the video game, but after the hundredth round of jumping over the same barrels, it became _____ and he switched it off.

traps.why: Exciting fits the first levels, but "but" shows his feelings changed.
Games can cost money, but the clue is jumping the same barrels.
Monstrous looks similar but means huge or horrible.

sc2.tip: "But" shows his feelings changed, and "the same barrels" after a "hundredth round" shows the game got boring from repeating.

decoys.why: Jaden could feel jaded, but the blank describes the game, which cannot feel bored.
Jumping over the same barrels again and again is ordinary, not bizarre.
The game turned dull from repeating, not showy and colorful.
He switched the game off, so it did not leave him impossible to satisfy.
A video game cannot be poisonous to breathe; the clue is about endless repetition.
Unscathed means unharmed, which says nothing about the game becoming boring.

meaning: able to understand and share others' feelings
example: The empathetic counselor listened patiently to each worried student.
hook: Path means feeling, as in sympathy: an empathetic friend feels your worries right along with you.

traps.why: Uncaring means not caring about others, the opposite of empathetic.
Energetic looks similar but means full of energy.
Polite is about good manners, not sharing someone's feelings.

syn1.tip: Look for path, meaning feeling, inside the word. An empathetic person can feel what someone else feels.

sc1.stem: Having moved schools three times herself, Gabriela was especially _____ toward new students, because she knew exactly how lonely the first week could feel.

traps.why: Knowing how lonely it feels would make her warm, not cold.
Being interested in new kids isn't the same as feeling their loneliness.
Suspicious is a distrustful feeling, the wrong tone for her kindness.

sc1.tip: "Because she knew exactly how lonely the first week could feel" shows she shares new students' feelings from her own moves.

decoys.why: Gabriela understood how lonely new students feel, so she was kind, not rude.
Knowing how lonely the first week feels makes her caring, not eager to fight.
The sentence is about sharing feelings, not bossing new students around.
Her own moves made her understanding, not bored or unexcited about new students.
Being stiffly proper has nothing to do with knowing how lonely someone feels.

traps.why: Ignoring pain is the opposite of feeling it with someone.
That describes energetic, a word that only looks like empathetic.
Advice is helpful, but empathy means feeling what others feel.

syn2.tip: Empathy means putting yourself in someone else's shoes. Empathetic people feel along with others, so pick the choice about sharing feelings.

sc2.stem: My brother usually laughs when I trip, but when I lost my dog, he was surprisingly _____, sitting with me quietly and saying he felt sad too.

traps.why: Amused fits his usual laughing, but "but" shows he changed.
Energetic looks similar, but he was sitting quietly.
Nosy is a negative word, but he was kind and shared your sadness.

sc2.tip: "But" shows a change from his usual laughing, and "saying he felt sad too" tells you he shared your feelings.

decoys.why: He sat quietly and shared your sadness, which is the opposite of rude boldness.
He sat with you and felt sad too, so he was not looking for a fight.
Sitting quietly beside you is gentle, not bossy and controlling.
The sentence says he sat with you quietly, not in a high, piercing voice.
He said he felt sad too, so he was not bored or unmoved.
Quietly sitting with someone is the opposite of showy and bold.

meaning: to formally approve or confirm
example: The club members voted to ratify the new rules.
hook: The U.S. Constitution became law only after enough states voted to ratify it, giving their official yes.

traps.why: Reject means to say no, the opposite of ratify.
Ration looks similar but means to hand out in small amounts.
Groups debate before voting, but ratify means the final yes.

syn1.tip: You may have heard that states had to ratify the Constitution. Ratify is what a group does when it votes yes to make something official.

sc1.stem: The student council wrote a new dress code, but it could not take effect until a majority of the class voted to _____ it officially.

traps.why: Rejecting it would stop the code, not let it take effect.
Discussing doesn't make a rule official; only approval does.
The council already wrote and proposed it; the vote makes it official.

sc1.tip: "Could not take effect until" the vote shows the vote is what makes it official, so the blank means formally approve.

decoys.why: The vote lets the dress code take effect, so it approves it rather than taking it back.
The vote is what lets the code take effect, not what stops it.
Voting here makes the dress code official instead of blocking it.
The vote lets the code take effect, so it is approving it, not cutting it short.
Students convene to meet, but you cannot convene a dress code to make it official.
Saying the dress code again would not make it official; the vote has to approve it.

traps.why: Formally rejecting is saying an official no, the opposite of ratify.
Discussion comes before ratifying; ratify is the final approval.
Suggesting is much weaker than giving official approval.

syn2.tip: Ratify sounds official: votes, treaties, signed rules. Pick the choice meaning a group gives its final, formal yes.

sc2.stem: The team captains agreed on the new practice schedule in the hallway, but it was not final until the coach signed the form to _____ it.

traps.why: Canceling would end the schedule, not make it final.
Ration looks similar but means to hand out in small amounts.
Questioning a plan doesn't make it final; signing gives approval.

sc2.tip: "Not final until the coach signed the form" shows the signature makes the schedule official, so the blank means approve formally.

decoys.why: Signing the form made the schedule final, not taken back.
The coach's signature makes the plan final instead of stopping it.
The schedule was already planned; the coach signed to approve it, not make it up.
The signature makes the schedule final; it does not cut the schedule short.
Signing the form lets the schedule go ahead instead of holding it back.
The captains met in the hallway, but you cannot convene a schedule by signing a form.

meaning: a look or word showing disapproval
example: Her mother's look of reproach made Tia apologize at once.
hook: A look of reproach is the raised eyebrow a teacher gives that silently says, "I expected better from you."

traps.why: Praise shows approval, the opposite of reproach.
Approach looks similar but means coming closer.
Punishment is a penalty; reproach is only a look or word of disapproval.

syn1.tip: Reproach often comes as "a look of reproach," the disappointed glance that makes you feel guilty. Pick the choice about disapproval.

sc1.stem: Mr. Castillo never raised his voice; a single look of _____ over his glasses was enough to make a chattering student fall silent and apologize.

traps.why: Approval wouldn't make a student apologize.
A bored look wouldn't make someone fall silent and apologize.
Amusement is a happy feeling, the wrong tone for a look causing apology.

sc1.tip: The look made the student "fall silent and apologize," so it must show disapproval. People apologize when they feel blamed.

decoys.why: He never raised his voice, so he gave no long angry speech, only a look.
The look made the student apologize, so it showed disapproval, not a break.
His look was disapproving, not a show of fake boldness.
Nothing tricky happened; his look simply showed the student he disapproved.
A rebuttal is an argument, but he said nothing at all, only gave a look.
A single look over his glasses is not a long, bitter feud.

traps.why: Admiration is approval and respect, the opposite of reproach.
Confusion can show on a face too, but reproach shows disapproval.
Fury is wild anger, much stronger than quiet reproach.

syn2.tip: A look of reproach says "you let me down." It is quiet disappointment, not rage, so choose the calm word for disapproval.

sc2.stem: Grandpa did not need to scold me for breaking the window; the quiet _____ in his eyes told me how disappointed he was.

traps.why: Pride shows he is pleased, but he was disappointed.
A sparkle is a happy look, the wrong feeling for disappointment.
Approach looks similar but means coming closer.

sc2.tip: "Told me how disappointed he was" restates the blank: the look in his eyes showed disapproval instead of scolding.

decoys.why: The sentence says it was quiet and he did not scold, so no angry speech.
His eyes showed disappointment, not a break from something unpleasant.
Grandpa was disappointed, not showing fake boldness.
His eyes showed disappointment, not clever trickery.
One broken window and a quiet look are not a long, bitter feud.
A rebuttal is a spoken argument, but Grandpa said nothing at all.

meaning: weaken or damage
example: Loud music can impair your hearing over time.
hook: You've seen signs for the hearing impaired: impair means to weaken something so it works less well.

traps.why: Improve means make better, the opposite of impair.
Repair rhymes with impair but means to fix.
Destroy is too strong; impair means weaken, not wreck completely.

syn1.tip: You've probably seen "hearing impaired" or "vision impaired." To impair something is to weaken it or make it work less well.

sc1.stem: Staying up until three in the morning before the test was a mistake, since lack of sleep can _____ a person's memory and ability to concentrate.

traps.why: Sharpening memory would be good, but staying up "was a mistake."
Repair rhymes with impair but means to fix.
Tests measure memory, but lack of sleep damages it.

sc1.tip: "Was a mistake" and "lack of sleep" tell you the effect is bad, so the blank must mean weaken or damage.

decoys.why: Staying up was a mistake, so lack of sleep hurts your memory rather than approving it.
Deduce is about reasoning, but the sentence says lack of sleep damages memory.
Lack of sleep cannot question your memory; it weakens it.
Lack of sleep does not tease anyone; the sentence is about weakening concentration.
Lack of sleep does not ask for your memory; it harms it.
Lack of sleep does not threaten anyone; it weakens memory and focus.

traps.why: Strengthen is the opposite of weakening something.
Impair seems to mean "not a pair," but it means to weaken.
Doctors test hearing, but impair means damage it.

syn2.tip: Impair is not about pairs. Think of "impaired vision": eyes that work, just not fully. Look for the choice meaning make weaker.

sc2.stem: A cracked helmet may look fine, but even a small break can _____ its ability to absorb a hard fall, leaving your head less protected.

traps.why: Boosting would make it safer, but your head ends up less protected.
Repair rhymes with impair, but a break doesn't fix anything.
A break doesn't prove safety; it leaves your head less protected.

sc2.tip: "But" warns that looking fine isn't the whole story, and "leaving your head less protected" shows the break weakens the helmet.

decoys.why: The break leaves your head less protected, so it weakens the helmet rather than approving it.
A crack cannot figure anything out; it damages the helmet's ability to protect you.
A break does not make anything up; it weakens the helmet.
The crack does not pull back the helmet's ability; it damages it.
A small break does not ask for anything; it leaves your head less protected.
A crack cannot question the helmet; the sentence says it weakens protection.

meaning: extremely tiring and demanding
example: The grueling marathon left runners collapsing at the finish.
hook: Picture a grueling boot camp: hours of push-ups that leave you too tired to lift your arms.

traps.why: Relaxing is the opposite of grueling.
Gruesome looks similar but means horrible or gory, not tiring.
Grueling things are often long, but grueling means draining, not long.

syn1.tip: Think of a grueling workout or a grueling race. The word always describes something that wears you out.

sc1.stem: After the _____ six-hour hike through desert heat, the scouts collapsed in their tents and slept until noon the next day.

traps.why: A leisurely hike would not make the scouts collapse.
Hikes can be scenic, but pretty views don't explain the collapsing.
Gruesome looks similar but means horrible or gory, not tiring.

sc1.tip: The scouts "collapsed in their tents" and "slept until noon." That result tells you the hike wore them out.

decoys.why: The hike lasted six hours in desert heat, so it was hardly extremely small.
Lackluster means dull, but the scouts collapsed from exhaustion, not boredom.
Sumptuous describes rich, fancy things, not a hot hike that wore the scouts out.
Savory describes food flavor, and the sentence is about a tiring hike.
Supple means flexible, which says nothing about why the scouts slept until noon.
Prim means stiffly proper, which does not explain why the scouts collapsed.

traps.why: Easy and pleasant is the opposite of grueling.
Slightly difficult is far too weak; grueling means extremely demanding.
The word contains gruel, but grueling describes hard, tiring effort.

syn2.tip: Grueling describes something that takes all your energy, like a long race. Look for the choice about being worn out.

sc2.stem: Coach Ramirez promised an easy warm-up, but practice turned out to be _____, with two hours of sprints that left the whole team gasping on the grass.

traps.why: Relaxing fits the easy warm-up, but "but" signals the opposite happened.
Mild is too weak for two hours of sprints that left players gasping.
Optional is about practice rules, not how tiring it was.

sc2.tip: The word "but" flips "an easy warm-up" around, and "gasping on the grass" shows practice was extremely tiring.

decoys.why: Two hours of sprints was a big workout, not an extremely small one.
Lackluster means lacking energy, but the team was gasping from hard work.
Sumptuous describes rich, costly things, not a practice that left everyone gasping.
Empathetic describes caring people, not a hard practice full of sprints.
Flamboyant means showy, but the sentence is about how exhausting practice was.
Prim means stiffly proper, which does not explain the team gasping on the grass.

meaning: to gather together in a crowd
example: Students congregate in the courtyard before school.
hook: Con means together and greg comes from the Latin for flock, so people congregate like a flock of sheep.

traps.why: Scatter is the opposite of congregate.
Congratulate looks similar but means to praise someone's success.
A church congregation worships, but congregate just means to gather.

syn1.tip: Con means together, as in connect. People who congregate come together in one spot.

sc1.stem: Every morning before the bell rings, students _____ in the courtyard, standing in noisy clusters to trade news and finish homework.

traps.why: Students who scatter would not stand in clusters together.
Whisper is about talking, and the clusters are described as noisy.
Wandering means moving around, not standing together in clusters.

sc1.tip: The students are "standing in noisy clusters" in one place. Forming clusters means they gather together.

decoys.why: The students belong at their school, so standing in its courtyard is not trespassing.
Trading news is friendly chatting, not interfering in other people's business.
The students form noisy clusters, so they are gathering, not shrinking or weakening.
They do this every morning as a routine, so they are not turning from the usual plan.
Nothing is forcing the students to give in; they are simply gathering together.
The sentence describes students crowding together, not making something up without a plan.

traps.why: Spread apart is the opposite of congregate.
Congregations pray, but congregate means gathering anywhere for any reason.
Crowds may talk loudly, but congregate is about gathering, not noise.

syn2.tip: Think of a congregation, a group that has gathered. The verb congregate means forming that group.

sc2.stem: During class the students sit quietly at separate desks, but at lunch they _____ around the same table, crowding together to share snacks and stories.

traps.why: Scattering is the opposite of crowding together around one table.
Study fits class, but lunch is about sharing snacks and stories.
Nothing in the sentence is about a contest; they are crowding together.

sc2.tip: "But" sets "separate desks" against lunch, and "crowding together" tells you they gather around one table.

decoys.why: The students are crowding together at the table, not pulling back from it.
They all come to the same table, so they are joining up, not turning away.
The students crowd together, so they are gathering, not becoming smaller or weaker.
Sharing snacks and stories is friendly, not interfering in someone else's business.
The lunch table is theirs to use, so sitting there is not trespassing.
No force is pushing them; the students simply choose to crowd together at lunch.

meaning: harmful or poisonous, especially to breathe
example: The factory released noxious fumes into the air.
hook: Noxious shares a Latin root meaning harm with obnoxious, so noxious fumes are the kind that hurt you.

traps.why: Healthy is the opposite of noxious.
Anxious rhymes with noxious but means worried.
Noxious gases may be cloudy, but noxious means harmful.

syn1.tip: You often hear about noxious fumes or noxious weeds. Both are things that can hurt you.

sc1.stem: Chemistry students must work under the vent hood because some experiments give off _____ gases that can make people dizzy or sick.

traps.why: Harmless gases would not make people dizzy or sick.
Fragrant means pleasant smelling, the wrong feeling for gases that make people sick.
Color doesn't explain why the gases make people sick.

sc1.tip: The gases "can make people dizzy or sick," which is why students need a vent hood. That points to harmful gases.

decoys.why: Savory describes tasty food, but these gases make people dizzy or sick.
Shrill describes a sound, and the sentence is about gases that make people sick.
Sumptuous means rich and splendid, but these gases are dangerous to breathe.
Lackluster means dull, which would not require a vent hood to stay safe.
Supple means flexible, which does not explain why the gases make people sick.
Tiny size is not the point; the vent hood is needed because the gases are harmful.

traps.why: Harmless is the opposite of noxious.
Obnoxious looks similar but means annoying, not poisonous.
Many gases are invisible, but noxious is about harm.

syn2.tip: Noxious fumes from a factory make people sick. Pick the choice that means something can poison you.

sc2.stem: Grandpa used to spray _____ chemicals on his garden, but now he uses only safe, natural sprays that will not hurt the bees or the neighbor's dog.

traps.why: Gentle chemicals would be safe, but "but" shows the old ones weren't.
Cost isn't the contrast; the sentence contrasts harmful with safe.
Organic matches the new natural sprays, not the old ones Grandpa stopped using.

sc2.tip: "But now he uses only safe" sprays that "will not hurt" animals. The old chemicals must be the opposite: harmful.

decoys.why: Savory describes food flavor, but the sentence contrasts these chemicals with safe sprays.
Sumptuous means splendid, but Grandpa switched because the old chemicals were harmful.
Supple means flexible, which has nothing to do with hurting bees or the dog.
The contrast is with safe sprays, so the old chemicals were harmful, not dull.
Paltry means meager, but the sentence contrasts the old chemicals with safe ones.
Shrill describes a piercing sound, not chemicals that could hurt bees.

meaning: bossy and controlling
example: The overbearing coach decided every detail for the players.
hook: Picture someone looming over you, bearing down and telling you exactly how to do everything: that's overbearing.

traps.why: Meek means quiet and easily led, the opposite of overbearing.
Over and bearing suggest carrying too much, but the word means bossy.
Confident is a positive word; overbearing is negative and means controlling.

syn1.tip: Imagine someone standing over you, pressing their will on you. An overbearing person bosses everyone around.

sc1.stem: Our group project went badly because one member was so _____ that she insisted on making every decision and never let the rest of us speak.

traps.why: An easygoing person would let others speak and decide.
A timid person would not insist on making every decision.
Organized is positive, but the project went badly because of her.

sc1.tip: She "insisted on making every decision" and "never let the rest of us speak." That describes someone bossy.

decoys.why: She never let anyone else speak, which is the opposite of understanding others.
A bored, unexcited person would not insist on making every decision.
Someone with no energy would not push to control every decision.
Being unlucky does not explain why she never let the rest of the group speak.
Precocious means advanced for her age, but the sentence describes her being bossy.
Prim means stiffly proper and neat, not controlling every decision.

traps.why: Very relaxed is the opposite of overbearing.
Over and bear hint at a heavy load, but the word means controlling.
Slightly firm is too weak; overbearing people control everything.

syn2.tip: An overbearing parent or coach decides every detail for others. Look for the choice about controlling people.

sc2.stem: Unlike his _____ older brother, who orders everyone around and controls the TV remote, Leo lets his friends choose the games and listens to their ideas.

traps.why: A patient brother wouldn't order everyone around.
A shy person doesn't order everyone around.
Being athletic has nothing to do with ordering people around.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" sets the brother against Leo, who "listens." The brother "orders everyone around," so he is bossy.

decoys.why: The brother orders everyone around; it is Leo, who listens, who is more like that.
The brother is described as bossy and controlling, not bored or unexcited.
Being unlucky has nothing to do with ordering everyone around.
The sentence is about the brother being bossy, not about him avoiding harm.
Precocious means advanced for one's age, but the clue is that he controls everyone.
Someone with no energy would not bother taking control of the TV remote.

meaning: to question someone closely and thoroughly
example: The detective interrogated the witness for an hour.
hook: Picture a detective in a small room firing question after question at a nervous suspect.

traps.why: Answering is the opposite of asking questions.
Interrupt looks similar but means to cut in while someone talks.
Police may accuse suspects, but interrogate means to ask questions.

syn1.tip: You hear interrogate in detective stories: police interrogate a suspect. Notice the word interrogation contains the idea of asking.

sc1.stem: Before letting her go on the overnight trip, Mia's parents would _____ her for twenty minutes: where exactly she was going, who would be there, and when she would return.

traps.why: Ignoring her is the opposite of asking her many questions.
Interrupt looks similar but means cutting in, not questioning.
The list after the colon is questions, not compliments.

sc1.tip: After the colon comes a list: "where exactly," "who would be there," "when she would return." Those are pointed questions.

decoys.why: The parents ask detailed questions, which is questioning her, not covering her up.
The parents are letting her go, so they are not stopping her plans.
They are asking her questions, not asking her for money or help.
The parents are carefully checking on her plans, not teasing her meanly.
They ask where and when, which is questioning, not forcing her with threats.
The parents want her to answer, so they are not holding her back from speaking.

traps.why: Ask casually is too weak; interrogating is close, pointed questioning.
Answering is the opposite of interrogating.
Punishment may come later, but interrogate only means questioning.

syn2.tip: Think of an interrogation room on a TV show, where detectives ask question after question. That is the meaning.

sc2.stem: Because Dad wanted to know every detail about the broken window, he began to _____ my little brother, asking what time it happened and who threw the ball.

traps.why: Comfort is kind, but Dad is demanding details, not soothing him.
Punishment might follow, but asking questions is what Dad does here.
Ignoring him is the opposite of asking him questions.

sc2.tip: "Because Dad wanted to know every detail," he starts "asking what time" and "who threw." That is close questioning.

decoys.why: Dad is asking for details about the window, not teasing your brother meanly.
Dad asks what happened, which is questioning, not asking for money or help.
The sentence shows Dad asking questions, not forcing your brother with threats.
Dad wants answers about the window, so he is questioning, not covering your brother.
Dad wants your brother to talk, so he is not holding him back from speaking.
Dad is asking questions to learn details, not weakening or damaging your brother.

meaning: unlucky
example: The hapless tourist lost his luggage twice in one week.
hook: Hap is an old word for luck, found in happen and perhaps, so hapless means without luck.

traps.why: Fortunate means lucky, the opposite of hapless.
Hap looks like happy, but hapless means without luck.
Hapless people may trip, but hapless is about bad luck, not skill.

syn1.tip: Split it: hap plus less. Hap is an old word for luck, as in happen, so hapless is without luck.

sc1.stem: The _____ goalie slipped in the mud, lost his glove, and then watched a ball bounce off his own teammate into the net, all in one minute.

traps.why: Slipping and losing a glove in one minute is not lucky.
Talent is about skill, and the sentence lists only mishaps.
Hap looks like happy, but nothing in this minute is happy.

sc1.tip: Look at the list: he "slipped in the mud, lost his glove," and gave up a goal "all in one minute." That's bad luck.

decoys.why: Slipping, losing a glove, and an own goal is chaos and bad luck, not careful planning.
Nothing shows the goalie acting bold or rude; the sentence lists a string of bad luck.
The sentence is about one unlucky minute, not about understanding anyone's feelings.
Nothing says the goalie is young or advanced; every detail shows misfortune.
The goalie never bosses anyone around; things just keep going wrong for him.
Savory describes food flavors, not a goalie having terrible luck.

traps.why: Blessed with luck is the opposite of hapless.
Hap is not short for happy; it is an old word for luck.
Hapless people suffer bad luck; it isn't their carelessness.

syn2.tip: The ending less means without, as in hopeless. Hap meant luck, so the word means without luck.

sc2.stem: Everyone expected the _____ team to lose again after a season of injuries and bad bounces, but this time the ball finally rolled their way and they won.

traps.why: A season of injuries and bad bounces is not fortunate.
An undefeated team wouldn't be expected to lose again.
Popularity has nothing to do with injuries and bad bounces.

sc2.tip: "Lose again" and "injuries and bad bounces" show bad luck, and "finally rolled their way" confirms luck had been against them.

decoys.why: The team had a season of injuries, so it was hurt, not unharmed.
The clue is injuries and bad bounces, which point to bad luck, not careful planning.
Nothing describes the team as bold or rude; the sentence is about their bad luck.
The sentence is about bad bounces and losing, not about sharing feelings.
Sumptuous means rich and splendid, which has nothing to do with an unlucky team.
No one is being bossy here; the team simply kept having bad luck.

meaning: a short break from something unpleasant
example: A snow day gave us a reprieve from the big test.
hook: In old movies, a prisoner gets a last-minute reprieve, a call that delays the punishment just in time.

traps.why: A burden weighs you down; a reprieve lifts the weight for a while.
Reprimand looks similar but means a scolding.
A reprieve feels good, but it's a break, not a prize you earned.

syn1.tip: Think of a snow day giving you a reprieve from a test. A reprieve is a welcome pause from something bad.

sc1.stem: The week of scorching heat was finally interrupted by a cool, rainy afternoon, a brief _____ before temperatures climbed again the next day.

traps.why: A cool, rainy afternoon is a drop in heat, not an increase.
A forecast predicts weather; the rain actually interrupted the heat.
A rainy afternoon is the opposite of a drought.

sc1.tip: The heat was "interrupted" for "a brief" time "before temperatures climbed again." That is a short break from something unpleasant.

decoys.why: The heat was the suffering; the cool afternoon was a break from it, not more suffering.
Reproach looks like reprieve but means disapproval, and no one is scolding anyone here.
The rain gave a short break from the heat, not a situation where progress stopped.
A chasm is a crack in the earth, not a cool pause in hot weather.
No one gives an angry speech; the sentence describes weather giving relief.
There is no argument being answered, just a brief break from the heat.

traps.why: A new punishment is the opposite of a reprieve.
A reprieve is usually temporary; the unpleasant thing often comes back.
Re can mean again, but reprieve doesn't mean another attempt.

syn2.tip: A prisoner's reprieve delays the punishment. Picture a pause before something unpleasant returns.

sc2.stem: The coach had planned laps all afternoon, but a sudden thunderstorm gave the tired team a _____, so they rested inside until the sky cleared and practice resumed.

traps.why: The storm stopped the workout; the team rested instead.
Resting inside is a relief, not a punishment.
Trophies come from winning; the storm only paused practice.

sc2.tip: The storm caused the team to rest, "so they rested inside," and then "practice resumed." That is a short break.

decoys.why: Reproach looks like reprieve, but the team got to rest, not a scolding.
The storm let the tired team rest, which is the opposite of an angry speech.
No one argued back; the storm simply gave the team a break from laps.
No one is being blamed; the team just gets to rest until the sky clears.
There is no bitter feud here, only a welcome pause from running laps.

meaning: high-pitched and piercing
example: The shrill whistle made everyone cover their ears.
hook: Think of a teakettle screaming on the stove or a referee's whistle: that thin, ear-stabbing sound is shrill.

traps.why: Muffled means soft and dull, the opposite of shrill.
Thrilling looks like shrill but means exciting.
Booming is a loud sound too, but it's deep, not high.

syn1.tip: Say shrill out loud with a sharp, thin voice. It names a high sound that stabs your ears, like a whistle.

sc1.stem: The smoke alarm let out a _____ beep so high and sharp that the dog howled and ran under the bed.

traps.why: A gentle beep wouldn't make the dog howl and hide.
The beep is "so high," so it can't be deep.
Faint is far too weak for a sound that sends the dog running.

sc1.tip: The beep was "so high and sharp" that the dog "howled and ran under the bed." That describes a piercing sound.

decoys.why: Noxious fits smoke, but the sentence describes the beep as high and sharp, a sound.
A sound so sharp it made the dog howl was not tiny.
The beep was so sharp the dog ran away, so it was not dull.
Savory describes the taste of food, not a high, sharp beep.
An alarm cannot be bad-tempered; the clue is that the beep was high and sharp.
Supple means flexible, which does not describe a high, piercing sound.

traps.why: Low-pitched is the opposite of shrill.
A sound can be shrill and perfectly in tune.
Shrill is about how high a sound is, not how long it lasts.

syn2.tip: A shrill whistle makes you cover your ears. Look for the choice about how high the sound is.

sc2.stem: Mom's singing voice is usually warm and low, but when she spotted a spider in the bathtub, she let out a _____ scream that rattled the windows.

traps.why: Deep matches her usual voice, but "but" signals a change.
A silent scream could not rattle the windows.
Spotting a spider brings fright, not cheer.

sc2.tip: "Usually warm and low, but" tells you the scream was the opposite of low: a high, sharp sound.

decoys.why: A scream that rattled the windows was huge, not extremely small.
The scream rattled windows, so it was anything but small or meager.
A window-rattling scream at a spider had plenty of energy, not a dull one.
The clue is a sudden, piercing scream, not a dull sound that never changes.
She was frightened by a spider, not making a dry, gently mocking joke.
She screamed from fright at the spider, not from being rude and grumpy.

meaning: stiffly proper and neat
example: The prim librarian frowned at every noisy giggle.
hook: Prim is short and tight, like pursed lips and a buttoned collar on someone who never relaxes the rules.

traps.why: Sloppy is the opposite of prim.
Prime looks similar but means first or best.
Prim people are often pictured as old, but prim is about stiff neatness.

syn1.tip: You may have heard "prim and proper." The two words go together because they mean nearly the same thing.

sc1.stem: The _____ governess sat perfectly straight, her hair pinned in a tight bun, and she frowned whenever the children forgot to say please.

traps.why: A carefree person wouldn't frown at children forgetting please.
A tight bun and straight posture are not sloppy.
She frowns at the children, so cheerful has the wrong feeling.

sc1.tip: She "sat perfectly straight," wore "a tight bun," and "frowned" at forgotten manners. All of that shows stiff properness.

decoys.why: She insists on please and sits perfectly straight, the opposite of rude and pushy.
She frowns when children forget manners, so she clearly cares a great deal.
She sits perfectly straight with a tight bun, stiff rather than bending easily.
A governess is an adult, and the clues describe neat, proper manners, not early talent.
Nothing unlucky happens to her; the details show how stiff and proper she is.
Savory describes food, not a neat, proper woman who demands good manners.

traps.why: Very easygoing is the opposite of prim.
That is what prime means; prim is a different word.
Slightly tidy is too weak; prim means stiffly proper.

syn2.tip: Picture someone sitting straight with hands folded, frowning at giggles. Prim means stiff and overly proper.

sc2.stem: At the messy pizza party, my _____ cousin refused to eat with her fingers, using a fork and napkin while everyone else licked sauce off their hands.

traps.why: Sloppy fits the party, but she is the neat one using a fork.
Hunger doesn't explain why she refused to eat with her fingers.
Rowdy means wild; she is the calm, careful one.

sc2.tip: "While everyone else" sets her apart from the messy crowd. A fork and napkin at a pizza party show she is fussily proper.

decoys.why: Savory fits pizza, but the blank describes the cousin, who acts neat and proper.
Using a fork and napkin at a messy party shows careful manners, not rudeness.
She cares enough about manners to avoid using her fingers, so she is not indifferent.
Nothing unlucky happens to her; she simply chooses to eat neatly and properly.
Supple means flexible, but the clue is her stiff, proper manners at the party.

meaning: a long, angry speech
example: The coach launched into a tirade about sloppy passing.
hook: Picture a coach pacing the locker room, yelling for ten straight minutes about dropped passes: that's a tirade.

traps.why: Praise is kind words, the opposite of an angry tirade.
Parade rhymes with tirade but means a procession.
An argument has two sides; a tirade is one person's angry speech.

syn1.tip: People "launch into a tirade" or "go on a tirade." Both phrases describe someone ranting angrily for a long time.

sc1.stem: When he discovered muddy footprints on his clean carpet, Mr. Patel went on a ten-minute _____, angrily listing every rule the children had broken.

traps.why: He is angry at the children, not saying sorry.
Parade rhymes with tirade, but he is angrily listing rules.
He might clean later, but here he is "angrily listing" rules.

sc1.tip: He went on for "ten minutes," "angrily listing every rule." A long, angry speech is the answer.

decoys.why: He was angrily listing broken rules, which is the opposite of laughter.
The children got no break; he spent ten minutes angrily scolding them.
He knew exactly what he thought and said it angrily, so he was not unsure.
He was angry about the carpet, not showing off fake boldness.
An apparition is a ghost, not an angry speech about muddy footprints.

traps.why: A gentle reminder is the opposite of a tirade.
Too weak; a tirade is long and furious.
That's a parade, which only rhymes with tirade.

syn2.tip: A tirade goes on and on, full of anger, like a coach yelling about sloppy passing. Look for long and angry.

sc2.stem: Instead of calmly explaining why we were late, Coach Lee launched into a _____, shouting about responsibility until his face turned red and the whole team stared at their shoes.

traps.why: "Instead of calmly explaining" rules out a calm explanation.
A joke is lighthearted, but he is shouting and red-faced.
He is shouting angrily, the opposite of a compliment.

sc2.tip: "Instead of calmly" signals the opposite, and "shouting" until "his face turned red" shows a long, angry speech.

decoys.why: The team got no break; the coach shouted at them until his face turned red.
He was shouting with certainty about responsibility, not stuck on what to do.
You launch into a speech, not into a person; he was shouting angrily.
A chasm is a crack in the earth, but the coach launched into angry shouting.

meaning: bending easily; flexible
example: Gymnasts stretch daily to keep their muscles supple.
hook: A supple gymnast bends like a willow branch in the wind, curving easily without ever snapping.

traps.why: Rigid means stiff and unbending, the opposite of supple.
Subtle sounds a bit like supple but means slight or hard to notice.
Gymnasts are strong, but supple is about bending, not power.

syn1.tip: Picture a gymnast's supple muscles stretching into a split. The word describes something that bends easily.

sc1.stem: Fresh leather is _____ and easy to fold, but leather left out in the hot sun turns stiff and cracks.

traps.why: Brittle describes the sun-baked leather that cracks, not the fresh leather.
Leather can be shiny, but the clue is about folding and bending.
Subtle sounds like supple but means slight, which does not fit folding.

sc1.tip: The word "but" sets fresh leather against leather that "turns stiff and cracks," so the blank means soft and easy to bend.

decoys.why: Prim means stiffly proper, but the sentence says fresh leather is easy to fold, not stiff.
Lackluster means dull, but the clue is about leather folding easily, not about shine.
Noxious means poisonous to breathe, which has nothing to do with leather being easy to fold.
Minuscule means tiny, but the sentence contrasts folding easily with turning stiff, not size.
Savory describes salty food, and leather that folds easily has nothing to do with taste.

traps.why: Hard to bend is the exact opposite of supple.
Supple looks like supply, but it has nothing to do with having plenty.
Quick movement is speed; supple is about bending without breaking.

syn2.tip: Think of fresh leather or a stretched muscle. Supple things bend and fold easily.

sc2.stem: Because the yoga teacher had practiced stretching every morning for twenty years, her body was still _____ enough to touch her toes without bending her knees.

traps.why: A rigid body could not reach the toes; years of stretching cause bendiness.
Simple looks a little like supple but means plain or easy to understand.
Stretching can make you sore, but soreness does not help you touch your toes.

sc2.tip: "Stretching every morning for twenty years" is the cause; touching her toes easily is the effect, so the blank means able to bend.

decoys.why: Prim means stiffly proper, but touching her toes needs a body that bends easily.
Twenty years might make someone jaded, but being bored does not help you touch your toes.
Her routine might be monotonous, but the blank describes her body being able to bend.
Apathetic means uninterested, yet she stretched every morning, and the blank is about bending.
The stretching might be grueling, but a body cannot be grueling enough to touch its toes.

meaning: pitifully small or meager
example: He earned a paltry two dollars for an hour of hard work.
hook: A paltry tip is so small it feels almost like an insult, like one penny for an hour of work.

traps.why: Huge is the opposite of paltry, which means pitifully small.
Salty rhymes with paltry but describes taste, not amount.
Paltry pay may feel unfair, but the word is about how little there is.

syn1.tip: You often hear "a paltry sum" for a disappointing amount of money. The word carries a feeling of being let down by smallness.

sc1.stem: After weeks of washing cars every weekend, the club raised a _____ fifteen dollars, hardly enough to buy even one new soccer ball.

traps.why: Whopping means huge, but "hardly enough" for one ball shows the amount was tiny.
Fifteen dollars is exact, but the clue is about the amount being too small.
Respectable sounds pleased; the club is disappointed it was "hardly enough."

sc1.tip: "Hardly enough to buy even one new soccer ball" after "weeks of washing cars" tells you the amount was disappointingly small.

decoys.why: The weeks of work were grueling, but the blank describes fifteen dollars, which was hardly enough.
Washing cars may be monotonous, but the blank describes a tiny amount of money.
Gaudy means showy, but the sentence says fifteen dollars was hardly enough for one ball.
Savory describes salty food, not an amount of money that was hardly enough.
Supple means flexible, which makes no sense for fifteen dollars that was hardly enough.

traps.why: More than enough is plenty, the opposite of paltry.
Poultry means chickens and turkeys; it only sounds like paltry.
Paltry money may be hard earned, but paltry describes its tiny size.

syn2.tip: Paltry amounts leave you wishing for more. Think of a paltry two dollars for a whole day of chores.

sc2.stem: Although the movie star earned millions for every film, she left the waiter a _____ tip of only a few coins, which surprised everyone at the table.

traps.why: Lavish means very generous, but "only a few coins" is tiny.
Polite sounds kind, but the tip surprised everyone by being so small.
Tips are customary, but a usual tip would not surprise everyone.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets her millions against the tip, and "only a few coins" tells you the tip was pitifully small.

decoys.why: A movie star might be gaudy, but the tip was only a few coins, not showy.
Savory describes restaurant food, but the blank describes a tip of only a few coins.
Supple means flexible, and a tip of a few coins is small, not bendy.
Noxious means poisonous to breathe, but the sentence is about how tiny the tip was.
Shrill describes a sound, but the clue is that the tip was only a few coins.

meaning: showing adult abilities very early in life
example: The precocious four-year-old could already read chapter books.
hook: Precocious comes from Latin for ripened early, like one fruit turning ripe long before the rest of the tree.

traps.why: Slow means behind others, the opposite of a precocious child's early talent.
Precious looks similar but means dear or valuable, not advanced early.
Pre- means before, but precocious means skilled early, not ready ahead of time.

syn1.tip: Pre- means before. A precocious child shows grown-up skills before most kids that age, like reading chapter books at four.

sc1.stem: Mozart was a _____ child, composing his first pieces of music at age five, when most children are just learning their letters.

traps.why: Composing at five "when most children are just learning their letters" is not typical.
Precious looks like precocious but means dear, not early talented.
Music can be noisy, but the clue is about talent arriving early.

sc1.tip: "Composing his first pieces of music at age five, when most children are just learning their letters" shows talent far ahead of his age.

decoys.why: Shrill is about high sounds, but the clue is that Mozart composed music at age five.
Monotonous music never changes, but the sentence praises him for composing so early.
Hapless means unlucky, but the sentence is about his early talent, not bad luck.
Surly means rude, but the sentence is about composing music years before other children could.
A five-year-old is small, but the clue is about his amazing early abilities, not his size.
Prim means stiffly proper, but the sentence is about talent showing up very early.

traps.why: Behind for age is the opposite of a precocious child's early skill.
Precocious kids have adult abilities, but they are young, not old.
Precious, which looks like precocious, can mean cute; precocious means advanced early.

syn2.tip: The pre- at the start means before. A precocious kid is ahead of schedule, doing things before others their age.

sc2.stem: My little cousin is so _____ that at just six years old she beats adults at chess and reads her dad's science magazines for fun.

traps.why: Childish means immature, but she beats adults and reads grown-up magazines.
Precious looks similar but means dear, which would not explain beating adults.
She reads for fun, but being playful would not let her beat adults at chess.

sc2.tip: "So ... that" links the blank to its result: a six-year-old beating adults at chess is far ahead of her age.

decoys.why: Hapless means unlucky, but she beats adults at chess, which shows skill, not bad luck.
A six-year-old is small, but the clue is that she has adult-level abilities.
Jaded means bored from experience, but she reads science magazines for fun.
Apathetic means uninterested, but she reads science magazines for fun.
Shrill describes a sound, but the sentence is about her early skill at chess and reading.

meaning: a ghostly figure
example: The campers claimed they saw an apparition near the lake.
hook: An apparition suddenly appears, pale and floating, then vanishes; the word is related to appear.

traps.why: Ghost costumes exist, but an apparition is the ghostly figure itself.
Partition looks similar but means a dividing wall.
Ghosts may haunt graveyards, but an apparition is the figure, not the place.

syn1.tip: Apparition is related to appear. It is something that suddenly appears, like a pale figure floating near a lake at night.

sc1.stem: Through the fog on the old castle stairs, the tourists thought they glimpsed a pale, floating _____, but it turned out to be a curtain blowing in the draft.

traps.why: Castles have statues, but statues do not float.
Partition looks like apparition but means a dividing wall.
Castles have dungeons, but a dungeon cannot be pale and floating.

sc1.tip: "Pale, floating," "fog," and "old castle" set a spooky scene, and "turned out to be a curtain" means they mistook it for a ghost.

decoys.why: A vagabond is a homeless wanderer, but the tourists thought they saw a pale, floating ghost.
A chasm is a crack in the earth, and it cannot float or turn out to be a curtain.
A deluge is a flood, but the tourists thought they glimpsed a pale, floating figure.
A malady is an illness, which you cannot glimpse floating on castle stairs.
Mirth is laughter, but the tourists thought they saw something ghostly in the fog.

traps.why: Apparel looks similar but means clothing.
Monsters are scary too, but they have solid bodies; an apparition is ghostly.
Skeletons are spooky bones, but an apparition is a floating ghostly figure.

syn2.tip: Look for appear inside apparition. It names a ghostly figure that seems to appear out of nowhere.

sc2.stem: The shape drifting through the graveyard vanished straight through a stone wall, so the frightened campers decided it must have been an _____ rather than a person.

traps.why: Owls fly at night, but no owl can pass through a stone wall.
Apparatus looks similar but means a piece of equipment.
An intruder is a living person, and the campers decided it was not.

sc2.tip: "Vanished straight through a stone wall" causes their decision, and "rather than a person" tells you it was ghostly, not alive.

decoys.why: An outcast is a person, but the campers decided it was not a person at all.
An affliction is suffering, but the shape drifted through a wall like a ghost.
An upheaval is a big change, not a shape that drifts through a stone wall.
An impasse is being stuck, but the clue is a shape passing straight through a wall.

meaning: to force someone by using threats
example: You cannot coerce someone into being your friend.
hook: To coerce is to squeeze someone with threats until they give in, like a bully demanding your lunch money.

traps.why: Allow means letting someone choose, the opposite of forcing them.
Persuade is the gentle, friendly version; coerce uses threats.
Curse sounds a bit like coerce but means to swear or cast a spell.

syn1.tip: You may hear that a confession was "coerced," meaning pressured out by threats. The word feels harsh and bullying.

sc1.stem: The cartoon villain tried to _____ the whole town into obeying him by threatening to switch off its electricity.

traps.why: Coaxing is gentle sweet talk, but the villain uses threats.
Bribing offers rewards, but the villain threatens to switch off electricity.
Curse sounds like coerce, but threats force obedience; they do not cast spells.

sc1.tip: "By threatening to switch off its electricity" shows the villain using threats, so the blank means force, not gentle persuasion.

decoys.why: Villains thwart plans, but the sentence says he threatened the town into obeying him.
Contaminate means to pollute, but he used threats to make the town obey.
Interrogate means to question closely, but he threatened the town to force obedience.
Solicit means to ask politely, but he used threats to force the town to obey.
Tarnish means to dull or damage, but the sentence is about forcing obedience with threats.

traps.why: Letting someone choose is the opposite of forcing them.
Gently talking someone into something is friendly; coercing uses threats.
Co- often means together, but coerce means to force, not cooperate.

syn2.tip: Think of the phrase "coerced into it," said when someone had no real choice because they were threatened.

sc2.stem: Instead of kindly asking the younger kids to share the swings, the bully tried to _____ them into leaving by warning that he would break their bikes.

traps.why: Encourage is kind and supportive, but he is threatening to break bikes.
Charming wins people over nicely, which is the opposite of "instead of kindly asking."
A bribe offers a reward, but the bully only gives a threat.

sc2.tip: "Instead of kindly asking" signals a contrast, and "warning that he would break their bikes" is a threat, so the bully forces them.

decoys.why: Solicit means to ask, but the sentence says he did not kindly ask; he threatened.
Interrogate means to question, but the bully warned he would break their bikes.
Thwart means to block plans, but he used threats to make the kids leave.
Tarnish means to dull or damage, but the bully threatened to make them leave.
Smother means to cover so no air gets in, but the bully used threats, not covering.

meaning: dryly funny, with gentle mockery
example: Dad gave a wry smile when the "waterproof" tent leaked.
hook: A wry smile is crooked and knowing, the face you make when your umbrella breaks the moment it starts raining.

traps.why: Wiry looks like wry but means thin and tough.
Wry mockery is gentle; cruel is far too harsh.
Goofy humor is loud and silly; wry humor is quiet and dry.

syn1.tip: Think of "dry humor": a joke told with a straight face. A wry smile is a small, knowing grin at bad luck.

sc1.stem: When the forecast's "sunny day" turned into a downpour, Coach Henley gave a _____ grin and said, "Well, at least the field won't need watering."

traps.why: The coach is not truly happy about the rain; he is joking dryly.
His joke is gentle and harmless, so cruel is far too strong.
Wiry looks like wry but describes a thin, tough body, not a grin.

sc1.tip: After a downpour, the coach jokes "at least the field won't need watering," a dry, ironic joke about bad luck.

decoys.why: The coach is making a joke about the rain, so his grin is not rude or bad-tempered.
He jokes that the field won't need watering, which is playful, not sad and lonely.
His grin goes with a dry joke, not with being stiffly proper and neat.
A grin makes no sound, so it cannot be high-pitched and piercing.
A quick grin at a joke is not extremely tiring or demanding.

traps.why: Wry always has a bit of humor, so it is never completely serious.
Wry teasing is gentle, not cruel.
Rye bread is made from grain; wry only sounds like rye.

syn2.tip: Picture Dad's "wry smile" when the waterproof tent leaked. He is quietly amused at the irony, not angry or silly.

sc2.stem: Instead of complaining when the power went out during her birthday party, Mom made a _____ joke about finally getting a candlelit dinner, and everyone laughed.

traps.why: A nasty joke would be mean, but everyone laughed at her gentle humor.
Wiry looks like wry but means thin and tough, not dryly funny.
Tearful is sad, but "instead of complaining" Mom made everyone laugh.

sc2.tip: "Instead of complaining" tells you Mom chose humor, and joking about a "candlelit dinner" in a blackout is dry and ironic.

decoys.why: Mom chose not to complain, and everyone laughed, so her joke was not rude or bad-tempered.
Her joke made everyone laugh, so it was not sad and lonely.
Mom is an adult, so her joke cannot show adult abilities unusually early.
The sentence is about the joke's humor, not about a high-pitched, piercing sound.
Gaudy describes showy colors or decorations, not a clever joke about candlelight.

meaning: dull the shine of; damage a reputation
example: Salt water tarnished the silver bracelet.
hook: Silver left in damp air tarnishes, turning dark and dull, just as one lie can darken a good name.

traps.why: Polishing makes something shine, the opposite of tarnishing it.
Varnish looks and rhymes with tarnish but means coating wood with shiny finish.
Tarnish dulls or damages; destroy is far too strong.

syn1.tip: You hear of a "tarnished reputation" or tarnished silver. Both mean something once shiny or clean is now marked and dulled.

sc1.stem: The team had won every award for good sportsmanship, so the players worried that one teammate's angry outburst would _____ their spotless reputation.

traps.why: An angry outburst would hurt the reputation, not make it shine.
Varnish looks like tarnish but means coating wood, which makes no sense here.
They already earned the reputation; they fear the outburst would damage it.

sc1.tip: The reputation is "spotless" and they "worried" about an "angry outburst," so the blank means damage or stain it.

decoys.why: An angry outburst would hurt their reputation, not formally approve or confirm it.
You aggravate a problem or injury, but a spotless reputation is not a problem.
The teammate might taunt players, but you cannot tease a reputation in a mean way.
The worry is about damaging the reputation, not taking it back.
Nobody is asking for money or help; the worry is about harming their good name.

traps.why: Making something sparkle is the opposite of tarnishing it.
Tarnish only dulls a surface; smashing is much too strong.
Paint covers a surface, but tarnish is darkening that comes from damage.

syn2.tip: Picture an old silver spoon gone dark and spotty. That dark film is tarnish, and it dulls the shine.

sc2.stem: After a year in Grandma's damp basement, the silver trophy had begun to _____, its once gleaming surface now dull and covered in dark spots.

traps.why: Sparkle is the opposite of "dull and covered in dark spots."
Vanish rhymes with tarnish, but the trophy is still there with dark spots.
Cracking is damage, but the clue describes dullness and spots, not breaks.

sc2.tip: "Once gleaming" but "now dull and covered in dark spots" restates what the blank means: losing its shine.

decoys.why: One trophy cannot gather into a crowd; the sentence describes its shine growing dull.
A trophy does not come together for a meeting; it is turning dull and spotted.
The trophy is not changing course; the sentence says its surface turned dull and dark.
A trophy cannot make something up without planning; it is losing its shine.
A trophy cannot interfere in anyone's business; the sentence is about its dull surface.

meaning: interfere in other people's business
example: Please don't meddle in your sister's argument with her friend.
hook: Meddle sounds like medal, but nobody wins a prize for meddling in a fight that is not theirs.

traps.why: Ignoring means staying out, the opposite of meddling.
Pedal rhymes with meddle but means pushing bike pedals.
Assist is welcome help; meddling is unwanted butting in.

syn1.tip: People say "stop meddling" or "don't meddle in my business." The word has a negative feeling of unwanted interference.

sc1.stem: Whenever his older sisters argued, Max could not resist the urge to _____, offering unwanted advice that only made both of them angrier.

traps.why: His advice was "unwanted" and made them angrier, so it was not help.
Listening quietly would not involve offering advice that made them angrier.
Tattling is telling an adult; Max is giving unwanted advice to his sisters.

sc1.tip: "Offering unwanted advice" in an argument that isn't his, which "only made both of them angrier," shows Max butting in.

decoys.why: Max was offering advice, not asking for it.
Max was giving unwanted advice, not teasing his sisters in a mean way.
Max is one person butting in, not a crowd gathering together.
Max kept offering advice instead of taking anything back.
Max was not calling a formal meeting; he was butting into his sisters' argument.
Nothing is growing smaller or weaker; Max keeps jumping into the arguments.

traps.why: Staying out of things is the opposite of meddling.
Medal sounds like meddle but is a prize, not interfering.
Lending a hand is welcome help; meddling is unwelcome.

syn2.tip: Think of a "meddling" neighbor who pokes into everyone's affairs. Meddling means getting involved where you aren't wanted.

sc2.stem: Our neighbor means well, but she loves to _____ in everyone's business, rearranging our garden gnomes and telling my parents how to raise us.

traps.why: Investing in a business means putting in money, not rearranging gnomes.
"Means well, but" warns her actions are unwelcome, not real help.
Pedal rhymes with meddle but means pushing bike pedals.

sc2.tip: "Means well, but" signals something annoying, and moving our gnomes and telling parents how to raise us is interfering.

decoys.why: The neighbor is one person, so she cannot gather into a crowd in anyone's business.
She is not holding formal meetings; she is moving gnomes and giving parenting advice.

meaning: to cover something so it gets no air
example: Grandma smothered the pan fire with a heavy lid.
hook: Smother has mother hidden inside: picture a mother bear hugging her cub so tightly it can hardly breathe.

traps.why: Smolder looks similar but means to burn slowly with smoke.
Igniting starts a fire; smothering puts it out by blocking air.
Smother contains mother, but it means cutting off air, not caring for.

syn1.tip: Think of smothering a fire with a blanket or lid. Covering it blocks the air, so it can't breathe.

sc1.stem: When grease in the pan caught fire, Dad grabbed a metal lid to _____ the flames, cutting off their air until they went out.

traps.why: Fanning adds air, but the lid is "cutting off their air."
Spraying water can fight fire, but a lid works by blocking air.
Feeding flames makes them grow, but these flames "went out."

sc1.tip: "Grabbed a metal lid" and "cutting off their air until they went out" tell you the blank means covering the fire so it can't breathe.

decoys.why: Dad wanted the fire to go out, not to make it worse.
The lid cut off the air to put out the fire, not to make it impure.
You cannot threaten flames; the lid works by cutting off their air.
Dad was putting out a fire, not teasing the flames in a mean way.
Flames have no shine or reputation to damage; Dad was cutting off their air.
Dad was not formally approving the fire; he was putting it out.

traps.why: Fanning gives a fire more air, the opposite of smothering.
That is smolder, which only looks like smother.
Mother is inside smother, but the word means blocking air.

syn2.tip: Picture Grandma putting a heavy lid on a pan fire. Smother means covering something so no air gets in.

sc2.stem: Instead of letting the campfire burn all night, the ranger piled thick dirt over it to _____ the last glowing coals.

traps.why: Relighting would keep the fire going, but the ranger is stopping it.
Campfires roast marshmallows, but dirt piled on coals is meant to put them out.
People poke campfire coals, but piled dirt covers them instead.

sc2.tip: "Instead of letting the campfire burn," the ranger "piled thick dirt over it," burying the coals and cutting off their air.

decoys.why: The ranger did not want the fire burning all night, so she would not make it worse.
The dirt was meant to put out the coals, not to make them impure.
The ranger was putting out the glowing coals, not dulling their shine.
You cannot formally approve coals; the ranger was covering them to put them out.
The ranger was not handing out coals; she was burying them under dirt.
Coals cannot be questioned; the ranger covered them so the fire would stop.

meaning: rude and bad-tempered
example: The surly clerk barely looked up from his phone.
hook: A surly person answers with a grunt and a scowl, like a bear woken too early from its nap.

traps.why: Polite is the opposite of surly.
Early looks like surly but is about time, not mood.
Surly is grumpy and rude; furious is much stronger anger.

syn1.tip: Picture a "surly clerk" who grunts and won't look up. Surly is a grumpy, unfriendly rudeness.

sc1.stem: The usually friendly bus driver was _____ that morning, grunting instead of saying hello and snapping at anyone who asked a question.

traps.why: That fits a usually friendly driver, but he was grunting and snapping.
Early looks like surly, but grunting and snapping describe a mood, not time.
Being late is about time, but the clue describes rude behavior.

sc1.tip: "Usually friendly" signals a change, and "grunting instead of saying hello" and "snapping" describe a rude, grumpy mood.

decoys.why: He grunted and snapped at people, which is the opposite of understanding their feelings.
Grunting and snapping are not dryly funny; they show he was in a bad mood.
Snapping at riders is rude, not stiffly proper and neat.
The sentence is about his bad temper, not about being easy to shape or change.
Gaudy describes showy looks, but the sentence describes his grunting and snapping.
The sentence is about his rude behavior, not about bending easily.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of surly.
Curly looks like surly but describes hair.
Tired people can be grumpy, but surly is about rudeness, not tiredness.

syn2.tip: Surly has a sour feeling. Think of someone grunting and snapping at you instead of saying hello.

sc2.stem: Because the waiter was so _____ with every table, sighing loudly and rolling his eyes at questions, the restaurant manager finally asked him to work in the kitchen.

traps.why: A patient waiter would not sigh and roll his eyes at questions.
Clumsy waiters spill things, but sighing and eye rolling show rudeness.
Sighing and eye rolling are grumpy, not raging, so furious is too strong.

sc2.tip: "Sighing loudly and rolling his eyes at questions" shows rudeness, and that behavior causes the manager to move him away from customers.

decoys.why: Sighing and rolling his eyes at customers is the opposite of sharing their feelings.
Loud sighs and eye rolling are rude, not stiffly proper and neat.
The sentence is about his rude manners, not about bending easily.
Nothing says he was easy to change; he was moved because he was rude.
Paltry means meager, but the sentence describes a rude attitude toward customers.
Gaudy describes showy things, not a waiter who sighs and rolls his eyes.

meaning: showing no interest or concern
example: The apathetic audience barely clapped after the show ended.
hook: Inside apathetic is 'path,' meaning feeling, and 'a' means without, so an apathetic person feels nothing about it.

traps.why: Eager is the opposite of apathetic; eager people care a lot.
