Demonstrations are not described by how few words they use; the example is about silliness.

traps.why: Solemn means grave and serious, the opposite of zany.
Brainy rhymes with zany but means very smart.
Witty humor is clever wordplay; zany humor is wild silliness.

syn2.tip: Zany and wacky even sound alike in feeling. Both describe goofy, over-the-top fun.

sc2.stem: My older cousin acts calm and serious at work, but at family parties he turns _____, juggling dinner rolls and dancing like a chicken.

traps.why: Quiet matches "calm and serious," but "but" signals a change.
Grumpy is a bad mood; juggling rolls and chicken dancing are playful fun.
Dinner rolls are food, but he is juggling them, not eating them.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "calm and serious," and "juggling dinner rolls and dancing like a chicken" shows wild silliness.

decoys.why: Juggling rolls and dancing like a chicken is not quiet, shy, or modest.
The sentence says he stops being calm and serious, so sensible judgment is backwards.
The clue is silly juggling and dancing, not speaking in very few words.
He is performing for everyone at the party, not avoiding people.
Juggling and dancing show silliness, not being old and in poor condition.

meaning: to avoid a duty or task
example: Leah never shirks her chores, even on weekends.
hook: To shirk is to sneak away from a job, like a cat slipping out the door at bath time.

traps.why: To tackle a job is to face it, the opposite of shirking.
Shriek looks like shirk but means scream.
You might complain about a chore, but shirking means avoiding it.

syn1.tip: You often hear "shirk your duties" or "shirk responsibility." It means slipping out of work you should do.

sc1.stem: Whenever it was his turn to clean the hamster cage, Owen tried to _____ the job by suddenly claiming he had a stomachache.

traps.why: Faking a stomachache is a way to escape the job, not finish it.
Sharing means doing part of it; Owen wanted to skip it entirely.
Scheduling plans a chore; a fake stomachache is a way to get out of it.

sc1.tip: "Suddenly claiming he had a stomachache" is a fake excuse. Excuses are used to avoid a duty.

decoys.why: Faking a stomachache is a way to avoid the job, not to hand out shares of it.
Owen is trying to get out of the job, not judge its quality.
Claiming a stomachache does not dig up or discover the job; it dodges it.
A fake stomachache is an excuse to escape the chore, not to make it fresh.
The sentence is about avoiding a chore, not proving someone right or innocent.

traps.why: Carrying out a duty is the opposite of shirking it.
Assigning gives a job to someone; shirking is escaping your own job.
That is what shrink means, and shrink only looks like shirk.

syn2.tip: Shirk is always about duties and chores. Someone who shirks finds a way out of the work.

sc2.stem: Unlike her twin, who always finds an excuse to _____ his chores, Mia finishes hers right after school without being asked.

traps.why: Mia completes chores; "unlike" tells you her twin does the opposite.
People don't need excuses to enjoy something; excuses help you escape it.
Organizing chores is still doing them; the twin is avoiding them.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" sets the twin against Mia, who "finishes hers." And "finds an excuse" means he gets out of his chores.

decoys.why: The twin finds excuses to avoid his chores, unlike Mia, not to hand them out.
Mia does her chores while her twin avoids his; judging their value is not the contrast.
Someone making excuses wants fewer chores, not to gather a large pile of them.
Excuses are for getting out of chores, not for making them fresh and lively.
The contrast with Mia shows he avoids chores, not that he digs them up.

meaning: hate strongly
example: My cat abhors baths and hides when she hears running water.
hook: Abhor shares a Latin root with horror: you abhor the things that make you shudder.

traps.why: Adore means love deeply, the opposite of abhor.
Dislike is too weak; abhor means hate strongly.
Absorb looks like abhor but means soak up.

syn1.tip: Hear the "hor" in abhor and think of horror. You abhor something that fills you with disgust.

sc1.stem: Nora happily eats broccoli and spinach, but she has always seemed to _____ Brussels sprouts, gagging at even the smell of them cooking.

traps.why: She loves broccoli, but "but" and gagging show she hates sprouts.
Tolerating means putting up with it; gagging at the smell is much stronger.
Cooking is mentioned, but gagging shows how she feels about sprouts.

sc1.tip: "Happily eats broccoli... but" sets up a contrast, and "gagging at even the smell" shows strong hatred.

decoys.why: She gags at the smell, so she would not gather a large amount of them.
Gagging at the smell shows strong hate, not judging their quality.
The clue is her gagging, which shows hatred, not digging up sprouts.
The sentence is about how much she hates sprouts, not making them fresh again.
Gagging at the smell shows hate; it has nothing to do with proving something right.

traps.why: Admiring something is the opposite of abhorring it.
Abhor is strong hatred, not a slight dislike.
You might avoid what you fear, but abhor is about hating, not fearing.

syn2.tip: Abhor is related to abhorrent, meaning disgusting. It is one of the strongest ways to say you hate something.

sc2.stem: Because my parents _____ loud alarm clocks, they wake up to soft music instead of the harsh beeping that used to make them jump.

traps.why: If they adored loud alarms, they wouldn't switch to soft music.
Owning alarm clocks would not explain switching away from the beeping.
Designing clocks has nothing to do with why they chose soft music.

sc2.tip: "Because" signals a reason. They dropped the "harsh beeping that used to make them jump," so they must hate it.

decoys.why: They switched to soft music, so they would not collect loud alarm clocks.
They replaced the clocks because the beeping made them jump, not because they judged their value.
The harsh beeping made them jump, which explains hating the clocks, not digging them up.
Switching to soft music shows they hate the beeping, not that they proved the clocks right.
The clue is that the beeping bothered them, not that they handed out alarm clocks.

meaning: messy and not cared for
example: His unkempt hair stuck out in every direction.
hook: Kempt is an old word for combed, so unkempt hair has never met a comb.

traps.why: Neat is the opposite of unkempt.
Unkind looks like unkempt but means mean.
Tired people may look unkempt, but unkempt is about a messy appearance.

syn1.tip: Un- means not, and kempt is an old word for combed. Unkempt hair or clothes look uncombed and messy.

sc1.stem: After a week of camping without showers or a mirror, Noah came home looking _____, with tangled hair, a scruffy face, and wrinkled clothes.

traps.why: Tangled hair and wrinkled clothes are the opposite of polished.
Camping can be relaxing, but the clue describes how messy he looked.
Unkind looks like unkempt, but the clue describes hair and clothes.

sc1.tip: The examples after "with" settle it: "tangled hair, a scruffy face, and wrinkled clothes" all describe a messy look.

decoys.why: Camping might sound brave, but the clue describes his messy hair and clothes.
The sentence describes his tangled hair and scruffy face, not a friendly mood.
Nothing about tangled hair and wrinkled clothes means easily shaped or changed.
The clue is his messy appearance, not whether he showed good judgment.

traps.why: Groomed means neat and cared for, the opposite of unkempt.
Unkempt is not "un-kept" meaning thrown away; it means uncombed and messy.
Smell is a different problem; unkempt describes how something looks.

syn2.tip: You often hear "unkempt hair" or "an unkempt lawn." Both look scraggly and not cared for.

sc2.stem: Grandma's garden was always neatly trimmed, but after she moved away, the yard grew _____, with weeds and overgrown bushes everywhere.

traps.why: Tidy matches "neatly trimmed," but "but" signals the yard changed.
Colorful sounds pleasant, but weeds and overgrown bushes show neglect.
An empty house may be quiet, but the clue describes weeds and bushes.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "neatly trimmed," and "weeds and overgrown bushes everywhere" shows a yard nobody cared for.

decoys.why: The yard is full of weeds because no one cares for it, not easily shaped.
An overgrown, weedy yard shows nobody is taking care of it, not good judgment.
A yard cannot be friendly; the clue is the weeds and overgrown bushes.
The sentence contrasts neatly trimmed with weedy, so the blank is about messiness, not modesty.

meaning: easily bent or shaped
example: Warm clay is pliable and easy to shape.
hook: Pliable things bend like a pipe cleaner: twist them, fold them, shape them however you like.

traps.why: Rigid means stiff and unbending, the opposite of pliable.
Reliable looks like pliable but means trustworthy.
Clay can be sticky, but pliable is about bending easily.

syn1.tip: The ending -able means able to be. Pliable is related to pliers and ply: able to be bent or folded.

sc1.stem: The craft wire is _____ enough to twist into animal shapes with bare hands, yet it holds its form once you finish bending it.

traps.why: Stiff wire couldn't be twisted into shapes with bare hands.
Wire may be shiny, but the clue is about twisting it by hand.
Fragile wire would snap, yet this wire holds its form.

sc1.tip: "Twist into animal shapes with bare hands" tells you the wire bends easily.

decoys.why: Languid describes a slow, tired person, not wire you can twist into shapes.
Unkempt means messy, but the sentence is about wire bending easily in your hands.
Haphazard means random, which says nothing about wire being easy to bend.
Animal shapes sound silly, but the wire itself must bend easily, not be funny.
Terse describes speech with few words, not wire you twist with bare hands.
Genial means friendly, but the sentence needs a word for wire that bends easily.

traps.why: Hard to bend is the opposite of pliable.
That means reliable, which only looks like pliable.
That means fragile; pliable things bend without breaking.

syn2.tip: Think of warm clay or a pipe cleaner. If you can shape it with your hands, it is pliable.

sc2.stem: Dry modeling clay cracks when you press it, but after a few minutes in your warm hands it becomes soft and _____ enough to shape into a dragon.

traps.why: Brittle fits dry clay that cracks, but "but" signals the clay changes.
Clay can be colorful, but warming it doesn't change its color.
Reliable looks like pliable but means trustworthy, not easy to shape.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "cracks," and "soft and... enough to shape into a dragon" means easy to bend and mold.

decoys.why: Languid fits a tired person, not clay that has softened enough to shape.
Warm hands sound friendly, but the clay must become easy to shape, not cheerful.
Decrepit means falling apart, like the dry clay that cracked, not the softened clay.
A dragon can be fun, but the clay must become easy to mold, not silly.
Soft might suggest quiet and shy, but the clay needs to be easy to shape.
Unkempt means messy and uncared for, which does not explain clay you can shape.

meaning: amusement shown through laughter
example: The clown's silly tricks filled the room with mirth.
hook: Mirth and merry come from the same old English word, so mirth is merry laughter.

traps.why: Gloom is sadness, the opposite of mirth.
Myth looks like mirth but means an old legend.
Audiences clap and laugh, but mirth is the laughing, not clapping.

syn1.tip: Mirth is related to merry. Picture a room full of merry people laughing together.

sc1.stem: The class had been gloomy all week, but the comedian's assembly show filled the auditorium with _____, and students were still giggling at lunch.

traps.why: Sadness matches "gloomy," but "but" and giggling show the mood changed.
Assemblies may have music, but the clue is giggling at a comedian.
Tension is a nervous feeling; giggling students are having fun.

sc1.tip: "Gloomy all week, but" signals a change, and "still giggling at lunch" shows the room filled with laughter.

decoys.why: Students were giggling all through lunch, so the show brought laughter, not disapproval.
A comedian may act bold, but giggling students show the room was full of laughter.
Guile is trickery, but the giggling students point to amusement and laughter.
Dexterity is hand skill, but the sentence is about students laughing at a funny show.

traps.why: Deep sorrow is the opposite of mirth.
A quiet smile is too weak; mirth means laughing fun.
Cheering supports a team; mirth is laughter at something funny.

syn2.tip: You may hear "filled with mirth" in stories about holidays or parties. It means joyful laughter and fun.

sc2.stem: When my baby sister sneezed so hard that spaghetti flew onto Dad's glasses, the whole table was full of _____, and we laughed until our stomachs hurt.

traps.why: Laughing until your stomach hurts is the opposite of sorrow.
Spaghetti on glasses could annoy Dad, but everyone laughed.
Manners belong at dinner, but the clue is the laughter.

sc2.tip: The funny sneeze causes the reaction: "we laughed until our stomachs hurt." The table was full of laughter.

decoys.why: Spaghetti on Dad's glasses might seem rude, but we laughed, so there was no disapproval.
Bravado is fake boldness, but the table was laughing until stomachs hurt.
Nobody was tricking anyone; the sneeze made everyone laugh.
Flying spaghetti shows no hand skill; the sentence says everyone laughed.

meaning: to brag about your success or others' failure
example: Good winners do not gloat after beating their opponents.
hook: Picture a winner doing a victory dance right in the loser's face: that's gloating.

traps.why: Sulking is what a sad loser does, not a bragging winner.
Float looks like gloat but means rest on water.
Celebrating can be kind; gloating is mean bragging that rubs it in.

syn1.tip: Gloating has a mean feeling. You gloat over a win when you brag about it to make others feel bad.

sc1.stem: Coach reminded the team that after a victory they should shake hands politely rather than _____ about the score in front of the disappointed players.

traps.why: Winners have no reason to worry about a score they won.
Float looks like gloat but makes no sense with the score.
Think is too general; the coach means bragging in front of the losers.

sc1.tip: "Rather than" sets up a contrast with shaking hands "politely." The opposite of polite winning is bragging about the score.

decoys.why: The team won, so the worry is bragging, not crying softly about the score.
The team already won, so there is nothing to struggle with in front of the losers.

traps.why: Acting humble is the opposite of gloating.
That is what float means, and float only looks like gloat.
Winning comes before gloating; gloating is bragging about it afterward.

syn2.tip: Think of "no gloating" after a game. It means don't rub your win in the losers' faces.

sc2.stem: Max began to _____ about his spelling bee win, so by Friday none of his classmates wanted to sit with him at lunch.

traps.why: A smile is too mild to make classmates avoid him.
Studying fits a spelling bee but wouldn't drive classmates away.
Float looks like gloat but means drift on water.

sc2.tip: "So" shows a result: nobody wanted to sit with him. Something about how he talked about "his win" annoyed everyone.

decoys.why: Max won the spelling bee, so he was bragging, not crying about it.
Max won, so he was not struggling; his bragging drove classmates away.

meaning: showing strong, forceful feeling
example: She gave a vehement no when asked to quit the team.
hook: A vehement speaker pounds the table and leans in, so every word comes out with full force.

traps.why: Mild means gentle and weak, the opposite of vehement.
Violent is too strong; vehement means forceful feeling, not hurting anyone.
Talkative is about how much you speak; vehement is how strongly.

syn1.tip: You often hear "vehement protest" or "vehement denial." Both are said with strong, forceful feeling.

sc1.stem: Liam was _____ in his opposition to cutting the music program, pounding the podium and speaking with fiery passion at the school board meeting.

traps.why: Pounding the podium with fiery passion is the opposite of halfhearted.
The topic is music, but the clue describes how he spoke.
Speaking at a meeting can be scary, but "fiery passion" shows force.

sc1.tip: "Pounding the podium and speaking with fiery passion" describes very strong, forceful feeling.

decoys.why: Pounding the podium with fiery passion is the opposite of quiet and shy.
Fiery passion and pounding the podium show energy, not slow relaxation.
Liam was fiercely opposing the cut, not acting friendly and cheerful.
The clues stress fiery passion and pounding, not calm good judgment.
Liam was not sorry for anything; he was passionately arguing against the cut.
Speaking loudly at a public meeting is the opposite of secretive.

traps.why: Calm and quiet is the opposite of vehement.
Vehement is strong feeling, not physical violence.
Length is about how much is said; vehement is about how strongly.

syn2.tip: Picture someone shouting "Absolutely not" and pounding a fist. That strong, forceful feeling is vehement.

sc2.stem: Most students only shrugged when the cafeteria removed pizza from the menu, but Aria was _____ in her complaints, writing three angry letters to the principal.

traps.why: Indifferent matches the shrugging students, but "but" sets Aria apart.
Pizza is food, but the clue is about how strongly she complained.
Three angry letters are not polite; they show fierce feeling.

sc2.tip: "Only shrugged... but" sets up a contrast, and "three angry letters" shows Aria's feelings were very strong.

decoys.why: Writing three angry letters is the opposite of quiet and modest.
Unlike the shrugging students, Aria put lots of energy into her complaints.
Her letters were angry, so she was not friendly and cheerful.
Aria was not sorry; she was angry about the pizza being removed.
Three angry letters about pizza show strong feeling, not careful good judgment.

meaning: a state of not knowing what to do
example: Choosing between two great summer camps left Maya in a quandary.
hook: Stuck at a fork in the road with two good paths and no idea which to take? That's a quandary.

traps.why: A solution ends confusion; a quandary is being stuck.
Quarry looks like quandary but means a pit where stone is dug.
An argument is a fight between people; a quandary is inner uncertainty.

syn1.tip: You are usually "in a quandary," stuck between choices and unsure what to do, just like a dilemma.

sc1.stem: Invited to her best friend's birthday party and the regional chess final on the same afternoon, Keiko was in a real _____ about which to attend.

traps.why: Busy afternoons can be rushed, but the clue is not knowing which to pick.
Quarry looks like quandary but is a stone pit.
Rage is anger; Keiko feels torn, not furious.

sc1.tip: "On the same afternoon" and "which to attend" show two good choices at once, leaving her unsure what to do.

decoys.why: Keiko was unsure which event to choose, not giving a long angry speech.
Two events at once gave Keiko a hard choice, not a break from trouble.
Being stuck between two choices is not a literal crack in the earth.

traps.why: A clear answer is the opposite of a quandary.
That is a quarry, which only looks like quandary.
A quandary comes before you choose; a mistake is choosing wrong.

syn2.tip: Picture standing between two doors, unable to pick one. That puzzled, stuck feeling is a quandary.

sc2.stem: The math problem put Devon in a _____: he could not decide whether to start over or keep checking his messy work, and the clock kept ticking.

traps.why: The ticking clock suggests time, but the clue is that he couldn't decide.
A huff is an angry mood; Devon is unsure, not angry.
Quarry looks like quandary but means a pit for digging stone.

sc2.tip: The colon explains the blank: "he could not decide whether to start over or keep checking." Being stuck between choices is the meaning.

decoys.why: Devon could not decide what to do; nothing says he gave an angry speech.
With the clock ticking, Devon got no break; he was stuck deciding.
Devon's problem was not knowing what to do, not a deep crack in the ground.

meaning: quiet, shy, and modest
example: The demure girl smiled politely but rarely spoke in class.
hook: Picture a demure kitten tucked in a corner, eyes lowered, hoping nobody makes a fuss over her.

traps.why: Bold is the opposite of demure; bold people push forward.
Secure ends like demure but means safe, not shy.
Grumpy people may be quiet, but demure means modest, not bad-tempered.

syn1.tip: Think of a demure smile: small, quiet, and modest. Demure people avoid attention, just like shy people do.

sc1.stem: On stage the singer was loud and flashy, but at home she was quiet and _____, preferring to read alone rather than attract attention.

traps.why: Outgoing matches the loud stage singer, not the quiet one at home.
Dramatic fits the stage, but the blank describes her quiet home life.
She may be famous, but the sentence describes how she acts at home.

sc1.tip: The word "but" sets up a contrast with "loud and flashy." The blank must match "quiet" and "rather than attract attention."

decoys.why: The sentence contrasts her loud stage self with a quiet home self, and zany means wildly silly.
She is quiet and avoids attention at home, so strong, forceful feeling does not fit.
Nothing in the sentence suggests rudeness; it describes her as quiet and avoiding attention.
Being fearless has nothing to do with preferring to read alone instead of attracting attention.
The sentence is about her quiet behavior, not about her being messy.
The clue is about quietness and avoiding attention, not about being random or unplanned.

traps.why: Boastful people brag; demure people do the opposite.
Mature looks a bit like demure but means grown-up.
Fearful is too strong; demure people are quiet, not afraid.

syn2.tip: Demure describes someone who keeps a low profile and doesn't show off. Ask which choice means not showing off.

sc2.stem: The new student was so _____ that she kept her eyes down, spoke softly, and blushed whenever the teacher praised her work in front of everyone.

traps.why: Confident people don't hide their eyes or blush at praise.
A boastful student would enjoy praise, not blush at it.
Gloomy is quiet but sad; nothing here says she is unhappy.

sc2.tip: The details after "so ... that" explain the blank: "eyes down," "spoke softly," "blushed" at praise. Those all describe a quiet, modest person.

decoys.why: She keeps her eyes down and speaks softly, which is the opposite of wildly silly.
Blushing at praise and speaking softly show shyness, not rudeness.
A fearless student would not keep her eyes down and blush when praised.
She speaks softly, so strong, forceful feeling is the wrong description.
Friendly and cheerful does not explain why she keeps her eyes down and blushes.
She speaks softly out of shyness, and nothing suggests she is short or rude.

meaning: capable of making mistakes
example: Even the best referees are fallible and sometimes miss a call.
hook: Fallible sounds like "fail-able": anyone who is fallible is able to fail or make a mistake.

traps.why: Flawless means without mistakes, the opposite of fallible.
Fallible isn't about falling down; it's about making mistakes.
Making mistakes is different from lying on purpose.

syn1.tip: The ending -ible means able to. Fallible people are able to fail, so they are not perfect.

sc1.stem: Although many people trust calculators completely, the math teacher reminded the class that machines are _____ too, since one mistyped number produces a wrong answer.

traps.why: The teacher says machines give wrong answers, so they aren't always accurate.
Useful is too positive; the teacher is warning about mistakes.
Calculators may be complicated, but the point is that they can be wrong.

sc1.tip: "Although" signals a contrast with "trust calculators completely." Then "wrong answer" tells you the blank means able to make mistakes.

decoys.why: The teacher says machines give wrong answers, so showing good judgment is the opposite point.
The sentence is about machines making mistakes, not about them being old and broken.
A calculator being easily bent has nothing to do with producing a wrong answer.
Machines being fearless does not explain why one mistyped number gives a wrong answer.
The problem described is wrong answers, not machines arriving late.
The sentence is about mistakes, not about machines using few words.

traps.why: Never wrong is the opposite; fallible means you can be wrong.
Fall in fallible is misleading; it's about errors, not tripping.
Easy to break means fragile; fallible is about making errors.

syn2.tip: Its opposite, infallible, means never wrong. Take away the in- and you get someone who can be wrong.

sc2.stem: Since even expert weather forecasters are _____, Coach always keeps a backup plan ready in case the predicted sunny day turns into a sudden thunderstorm.

traps.why: If forecasters were certain, Coach wouldn't need a backup plan.
Cheerful fits sunny forecasts, but it doesn't explain the backup plan.
Being skilled wouldn't make Coach need a backup plan.

sc2.tip: "Since" gives the reason for the backup plan. Coach plans for a surprise storm because forecasters can be wrong.

decoys.why: Coach needs a backup plan because forecasts can be wrong, not because forecasters show good sense.
Forecasters being fearless would not make Coach need a backup plan.
Friendly forecasters give no reason to worry that a sunny prediction might be wrong.
The sentence is about wrong predictions, not about forecasters being old and worn out.
The worry is a wrong forecast turning into a storm, not forecasters being late.
Strong feeling has nothing to do with a predicted sunny day turning stormy.

meaning: a disease or illness
example: Scurvy was a common malady among sailors long ago.
hook: Mal means bad, so a malady is something bad happening to your body: an illness.

traps.why: Health is the opposite of a malady.
Melody sounds like malady but means a tune.
Medicine treats a malady; it isn't the malady itself.

syn1.tip: Look for mal, meaning bad, as in malfunction. A malady is something bad wrong with your body.

sc1.stem: Centuries ago, sailors on long voyages often suffered from scurvy, a _____ caused by a lack of vitamin C that made their gums bleed.

traps.why: A remedy cures illness; scurvy made gums bleed.
Vitamin C prevents scurvy; scurvy itself is a sickness.
Sailors suffered from it, but scurvy came from missing vitamins, not punishment.

sc1.tip: Scurvy was "caused by a lack of vitamin C" and "made their gums bleed." Something with a cause and symptoms like that is a disease.

decoys.why: Scurvy made gums bleed, so it is an illness, not a state of not knowing what to do.
Sailors suffered from scurvy, so it was not a break from something unpleasant.
Scurvy is caused by missing vitamin C, not a huge flood at sea.
A ghostly figure cannot be caused by a lack of vitamin C or make gums bleed.
Scurvy is a physical sickness with bleeding gums, not a feeling of doubt.
An angry speech cannot be caused by missing vitamin C.

traps.why: A cure ends a malady; it is the opposite.
Mal means bad, but malady is a bad illness, not evil behavior.
A symptom is a sign of a malady, not the malady itself.

syn2.tip: Mal means bad, and a malady is a bad condition of the body. Which choice names a sickness?

sc2.stem: The mysterious _____ spread quickly through the chicken coop, and within a week half the hens had stopped laying eggs and were too weak to stand.

traps.why: A remedy would make hens stronger, not weaker.
Melody sounds like malady, but a tune can't weaken hens.
A vaccine prevents sickness; it wouldn't make hens too weak to stand.

sc2.tip: Look at the effect: hens "stopped laying eggs" and were "too weak to stand." Something that spreads and causes that is a sickness.

decoys.why: Mysterious sounds ghostly, but the hens grew weak and stopped laying, which points to sickness.
Not knowing what to do cannot spread through hens and make them too weak to stand.
The hens became too weak to stand, which is the opposite of a lively celebration.
Laughter would not make hens stop laying eggs and grow too weak to stand.
The hens got worse, so this was no short break from trouble.
A situation with no progress does not spread through a coop and weaken hens.

meaning: rude and disrespectful
example: It was impertinent of him to roll his eyes at the coach.
hook: An impertinent kid talks back to the principal, rolls his eyes, and asks rude questions he shouldn't.

traps.why: Courteous means polite, the opposite of impertinent.
Impatient starts like impertinent but means unable to wait.
Violent is far too strong; impertinent is about rude words or manners.

syn1.tip: Think of a kid who talks back to a teacher. That cheeky, rude behavior is impertinent.

sc1.stem: When the substitute asked the class to settle down, Brady gave a truly _____ reply, asking whether she even knew how to teach, and was sent straight to the office.

traps.why: A polite reply wouldn't get Brady sent to the office.
Clever is too positive; his reply got him in trouble.
Important looks like impertinent but doesn't explain the punishment.

sc1.tip: Brady questioned whether the teacher "knew how to teach" and "was sent straight to the office." That effect shows his reply was rude.

decoys.why: Brady mocked the teacher and was sent to the office, so he was not sorry.
Asking if she even knew how to teach is bold and rude, not shy and modest.
A friendly reply would not get Brady sent straight to the office.
Insulting the substitute showed poor judgment, which is why he was sent to the office.
His reply was mocking and disrespectful, not sad and mournful.
The reply got him in trouble for rudeness, not for being slow or lacking energy.

traps.why: Respectful is the opposite of impertinent.
Important looks like impertinent but means mattering a lot.
Playful teasing is friendly; impertinent remarks are rude.

syn2.tip: Impertinent has a negative feeling and is used for someone who talks back. Pick the choice that means bad manners.

sc2.stem: Unlike her younger brother, who often made _____ remarks to their grandparents, Lila always said please and thank you and listened politely at dinner.

traps.why: Grateful remarks would be like Lila's, not unlike them.
Gentle remarks don't contrast with Lila's polite manners.
Pertinent means on topic, which doesn't contrast with being polite.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" signals a contrast. Lila is polite, so her brother's remarks must be the opposite of polite.

decoys.why: The brother is contrasted with polite Lila, so his remarks were not friendly and cheerful.
Unlike polite Lila, the brother's remarks were rude, not wise and sensible.
The word unlike tells you he was the opposite of polite, not shy and modest.
The contrast is with Lila's politeness, so sorry remarks would not make sense.
The sentence contrasts politeness with rudeness, not with sadness.

meaning: slow, relaxed, and lacking energy
example: The cat stretched in a languid way across the sunny windowsill.
hook: Picture a languid cat melting across a sunny windowsill, too relaxed to chase anything.

traps.why: Energetic is the opposite of languid.
Liquid looks like languid but means a runny substance.
Asleep goes too far; languid people move, just slowly.

syn1.tip: Picture someone lying around on a hot afternoon. Languid has a slow, droopy feel, like lacking the energy to do much.

sc1.stem: On the hottest afternoon of the summer, the lions lay _____ in the shade, barely lifting their heads even when the zookeeper brought their food.

traps.why: Alert lions would lift their heads at food.
Hungry lions would jump up for food, but these barely moved.
Lions can be fierce, but these were barely moving.

sc1.tip: "Hottest afternoon" and "barely lifting their heads even when" fed show the lions had almost no energy.

decoys.why: The lions barely lifted their heads, which is the opposite of wild and full of energy.
Lions may seem fearless, but the clue is that they barely moved in the heat.
Lying in the shade barely lifting their heads shows no strong, forceful feeling.
Wildly silly does not match lions too hot and tired to lift their heads.
They were not hiding; they were too tired in the heat to move.
The clue is that they barely lifted their heads, which is about low energy, not friendliness.

traps.why: Full of energy is the opposite of languid.
Languid looks like language, but it isn't about speech.
Languid is relaxed and slow, not sorrowful.

syn2.tip: Languid sounds like languish, to droop or weaken. Think of a droopy, slow-moving body with little energy.

sc2.stem: At recess the twins raced around the playground nonstop, but by the end of the long, sticky afternoon they moved in a _____ way, dragging their feet to the bus.

traps.why: Lively describes recess, not the tired end of the day.
Dragging their feet is slow, not hurried.
Graceful is about movement, but dragging feet isn't graceful.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts racing "nonstop" with later. "Dragging their feet" confirms they moved slowly, without energy.

decoys.why: That fits recess, but the word but tells you they later dragged their feet.
Dragging their feet to the bus shows tiredness, not wild silliness.
Kids dragging their feet show no strong, forceful feeling.
Being fearless has nothing to do with being worn out after a long, sticky afternoon.
The clue is dragging their feet, which means slow and tired, not random.
Good judgment does not describe kids too tired to lift their feet.

meaning: to prove someone right or innocent
example: The video replay vindicated the player who was wrongly penalized.
hook: When the instant replay shows you were right all along, it vindicates you and clears your name.

traps.why: Accuse means to blame, the opposite of vindicate.
Indicate is inside vindicate but means point out.
Forgiving assumes someone did wrong; vindicating shows they didn't.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "clear your name." When evidence vindicates you, it proves you were innocent or right.

sc1.stem: Everyone laughed at Aiden's claim that the old map showed a hidden creek, but the surveyors' discovery of the stream would later _____ him completely.

traps.why: The discovery proved Aiden right, so it wouldn't embarrass him.
Finding the creek made things clear, not confusing.
Everyone mocked him at first; the "but" shows that changed.

sc1.tip: "Everyone laughed," "but" the stream was found. The contrast shows the discovery proved Aiden right.

decoys.why: Finding the stream proved Aiden right, so it would not scold him.
Everyone laughed at him first; the discovery shows he was right, not rejected.
Being proven right would please Aiden, not make him furious.
The surveyors uncovered the stream, but they did not dig up Aiden himself.
Finding the creek supports Aiden's claim; it does not destroy him.

traps.why: Prove wrong is the opposite of vindicate.
That's vindictive, a lookalike; vindicate means prove someone right.
Arguing tries to win; vindicating comes from proof.

syn2.tip: People say they feel vindicated when they were doubted but turn out to be right. Pick the choice about being proven right.

sc2.stem: When the security camera footage showed a raccoon tipping over the trash cans, it helped _____ our dog, who had been blamed for the mess all week.

traps.why: The footage showed a raccoon did it, so it cleared the dog.
The video proved the dog innocent, so punishing it makes no sense.
Training is about dogs, but the footage proved the dog innocent.

sc2.tip: The footage "showed a raccoon" did it, and the dog "had been blamed." So the video proved the dog innocent.

decoys.why: The footage showed a raccoon did it, so it cleared the dog instead of scolding him.
The video proved the dog innocent, so it would not lead anyone to reject him.
The sentence is about clearing the dog's name, not making him angry.
The footage cleared the dog of blame; it did not make him feel young again.
Showing the raccoon did it helped the dog, so it did not make things worse.

meaning: to judge the value or quality of
example: An expert appraised the old painting at five thousand dollars.
hook: On TV antique shows, experts appraise old treasures by telling owners what they're worth.

traps.why: Ignoring means paying no attention, the opposite of carefully judging.
Approve looks like appraise but means say yes to.
You might appraise before buying, but appraise isn't buying.

syn1.tip: Think of a home appraisal or a jewelry appraisal: an expert decides how much something is worth.

sc1.stem: Before selling Grandpa's coin collection, the family hired an expert to _____ it so they would know how much each coin was really worth.

traps.why: Polishing cleans coins but doesn't tell what they're worth.
Ignoring the coins wouldn't tell the family their worth.
Praise sounds like appraise but doesn't tell how much coins are worth.

sc1.tip: The goal is "so they would know how much each coin was really worth." The expert's job is to judge their value.

decoys.why: Grandpa already gathered the coins; the expert was hired to judge their worth.
The coins were not hidden; the family wanted to know how much each was worth.
Giving out shares does not tell the family how much each coin is worth.
The expert was hired to find the coins' value, not to make them look new.
Nobody hires an expert to wear coins away before selling them.

traps.why: Overlooking means not examining at all.
That's praise, which sounds like appraise but isn't judging value.
Appraising may come before selling, but it isn't selling.

syn2.tip: An appraiser studies an item and puts a price on it. Look for the choice about deciding value.

sc2.stem: Rather than simply guessing which used bike was the better deal, Dad asked the mechanic to _____ both, carefully judging their brakes, tires, and gears before he decided.

traps.why: The mechanic carefully judged the bikes, so he didn't ignore them.
Repairing fixes bikes; the sentence says the mechanic was judging them.
Praise sounds like appraise but means say nice things.

sc2.tip: The phrase "carefully judging their brakes, tires, and gears" restates the blank. Dad wanted the bikes' quality judged.

decoys.why: The mechanic was judging the brakes and tires, not fixing the bikes up.
Dad wanted the bikes carefully judged before deciding, not rejected right away.
The sentence says the mechanic was judging the bikes, not handing them out.
Dad wanted to compare the bikes, so destroying them makes no sense.
The mechanic was carefully judging the bikes, not feeling hatred for them.

meaning: lively, noisy celebration
example: The revelry after the championship lasted until midnight.
hook: Revelry is the noise of a party that goes all night: music, cheering, dancing, and fireworks.

traps.why: Mourning is sad grieving, the opposite of joyful revelry.
Revelation looks like revelry but means a surprising discovery.
A ceremony can be quiet and serious; revelry is wild and noisy.

syn1.tip: Revelry comes from revel, as in revelers at a party. It means lively partying.

sc1.stem: The sounds of _____ drifted from the town square all night, as people danced, sang, and set off fireworks to celebrate the harvest festival.

traps.why: People were dancing and celebrating, not grieving.
Fireworks boom like thunder, but the sounds came from people celebrating.
Traffic is noisy, but the noise came from dancing and singing.

sc1.tip: The examples "danced, sang, and set off fireworks to celebrate" tell you the sounds were lively partying.

decoys.why: People were dancing and singing to celebrate, so the sounds were of celebration, not messiness.
Dancing and fireworks at a festival show joy, not disapproval.
The crowd was celebrating the harvest, not putting on fake boldness.

traps.why: Sorrow is sadness, the opposite of revelry.
Rivalry sounds like revelry but means competition.
Parties have decorations, but revelry is the noisy fun itself.

syn2.tip: Revelers are people having a loud, happy time at a party. Pick the choice that means having fun together.

sc2.stem: The library was usually hushed, but after our team won the state spelling bee, the _____ in the study room grew so loud that the librarian asked us to quiet down.

traps.why: Silence can't grow loud.
Studying happens in libraries, but it isn't loud.
Grumbling is unhappy; the team had just won.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts "hushed" with what happened after the team "won." Winners make loud, happy noise.

decoys.why: The team had just won, so the noise was happy celebrating, not an angry speech.
The sentence is about loud noise after a win, not a messy room.
The team really won, so their loud joy was not fake boldness.
After winning the spelling bee, the team was cheering, not showing disapproval.

meaning: secretive; trying not to be noticed
example: He cast a furtive glance at the cookie jar.
hook: A furtive glance is the quick, secret peek a kid sneaks at the cookie jar when Mom isn't looking.

traps.why: Open means done in plain view, the opposite of furtive.
Fertile looks like furtive but means able to grow things.
Guilty people may act furtive, but guilty means having done wrong.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "a furtive glance": a quick look you hope nobody catches. That's sneaky.

sc1.stem: Hoping no one would notice, Bella stole a _____ look at her phone under the desk while the teacher's back was turned.

traps.why: Bella hoped no one would notice, so her look wasn't bold.
Proud is too positive; she was hiding her phone.
Festive looks like furtive but means cheerful and party-like.

sc1.tip: "Hoping no one would notice," "under the desk," and "the teacher's back was turned" all show Bella was being secretive.

decoys.why: Bella hoped no one would notice, so her look was sneaky, not forceful.
She looked while the teacher's back was turned, so it was secretive, not lazy.
The sentence is about hiding the look, not about sounding sad.
Bella was being sneaky, not rude, while she checked her phone.
The clue is that she hoped no one would notice, not that she was friendly.

traps.why: Obvious means easy to notice, the opposite of furtive.
Festive looks like furtive but means cheerful and party-like.
Criminal is too strong; furtive means trying not to be noticed.

syn2.tip: Furtive actions are done quietly so nobody sees. Look for the choice about hiding what you do.

sc2.stem: Unlike his brother, who grabbed snacks openly, Marcus made _____ trips to the kitchen at night, tiptoeing past his parents' door so the floor would not creak.

traps.why: Marcus tiptoed so the floor wouldn't creak, so he wasn't noisy.
Public means seen by all, which is like his brother, not Marcus.
Cheerful doesn't explain tiptoeing to avoid being heard.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" contrasts Marcus with his brother who acted "openly." Tiptoeing so the floor "would not creak" shows he was secretive.

decoys.why: Marcus tiptoed so the floor would not creak, the opposite of wild and noisy.
His trips were quiet and secret, not wildly silly.
The sentence contrasts him with his open brother, so the point is secrecy, not slowness.
Tiptoeing past his parents' door is careful and quiet, not forceful.
The trips happened at night, but the clue is about hiding, not being late.

meaning: feeling sorry for doing wrong
example: The contrite boy apologized for breaking the window.
hook: A contrite puppy with drooping ears after chewing your shoe looks truly sorry for what it did.

traps.why: Proud is the opposite of feeling sorry for doing wrong.
Contrary looks like contrite but means stubbornly opposing.
Devastated is far too strong; contrite means sorry, not crushed.

syn1.tip: Contrite people regret what they did and want to apologize. Think of a kid saying "I'm sorry" and meaning it.

sc1.stem: After accidentally breaking his neighbor's window with a baseball, Sam felt so _____ that he apologized at once and offered to pay for the glass.

traps.why: Pride wouldn't make Sam apologize and offer to pay.
Anger wouldn't lead to an apology.
Breaking the window was careless, but the feeling causing an apology is regret.

sc1.tip: Sam "apologized at once and offered to pay." People do that when they feel sorry for what they did.

decoys.why: Sam apologized at once, so he felt sorry, not that he looked down on anyone.
Apologizing and offering to pay is respectful, not rude.
The clue is his quick apology, which shows he felt sorry, not just gloomy.
Apologizing and paying for the glass show regret, not fearlessness.
He broke a window and apologized, so he felt sorry, not cheerful.

traps.why: Defiant people refuse to admit wrong, the opposite of contrite.
Contrite contains trite, but it doesn't mean dull.
Polite people apologize, but contrite means feeling guilty, not good manners.

syn2.tip: Contrite is how you feel after doing something wrong: full of regret and ready to apologize.

sc2.stem: Instead of making excuses for forgetting her best friend's birthday, Nora was genuinely _____, admitting her mistake and baking a cake to make up for it.

traps.why: Defensive people make excuses, which Nora didn't do.
Baking a cake can be fun, but she baked it to make up for a mistake.
Contrary looks like contrite but means stubborn, which doesn't fit admitting mistakes.

sc2.tip: "Instead of making excuses" sets up a contrast. "Admitting her mistake" and trying "to make up for it" show she felt sorry.

decoys.why: Nora admitted her mistake and baked a cake, which is the opposite of rude.
Making up for a mistake shows she felt sorry, not that she looked down on anyone.
Nora openly admitted her mistake instead of hiding it.
She forgot a birthday, but the clue is that she felt sorry, not that she was late.
Admitting a mistake and baking a cake is warm, not short and rude.

meaning: sounding sad and mournful
example: We heard the plaintive cry of a lost kitten.
hook: Plaintive shares its origin with complaint, so picture a sad, mournful complaint set to a voice.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of plaintive, which sounds sad.
Plain means simple; it only looks like the start of plaintive.
A plaintive cry may be loud, but plaintive is about sadness, not volume.

syn1.tip: Think of complaint, which shares its origin with plaintive. A plaintive sound is like a sad complaint.

sc1.stem: Late at night, the lonely puppy let out a _____ whimper from its crate, a sound so sorrowful that Ella got up to comfort it.

traps.why: Joyful is the opposite of the sorrowful sound described.
Puppies can sound playful, but this whimper is called sorrowful.
Plain looks like plaintive but means simple, not sad.

sc1.tip: The phrase "so sorrowful" tells you the whimper sounded sad and mournful.

decoys.why: The whimper is described as sorrowful, and zany means wildly silly and funny.
A lonely puppy's sorrowful whimper is not wild, noisy, and full of energy.
A whimper is soft and weak, so it cannot be strong and forceful.
The sound is sorrowful and lonely, not one that looks down on something.
The puppy sounds sad, not short and rude, which is why Ella comforts it.

traps.why: Joyful is the opposite of plaintive.
Angry cries complain too, but plaintive sounds sad, not mad.
A plaintive sound can be faint or loud; plaintive is about sadness.

syn2.tip: Picture a lost kitten crying for its mother. That sad, mournful sound is plaintive.

sc2.stem: Unlike the happy barking at the park, the old dog's _____ howl at the empty doorway showed how much he missed his owner, who had left for college.

traps.why: Excited fits happy barking, but the sentence contrasts that with missing someone.
Playful is a happy feeling; missing his owner makes the howl sad.
Howls can be fierce, but missing someone sounds sad, not threatening.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the happy barking" signals a contrast, and "missed his owner" tells you the howl sounded sad.

decoys.why: The howl shows how much he misses his owner, so it is sad, not silly.
The sentence contrasts the howl with happy barking, so it is not wild and energetic.
The dog misses his owner, so his howl is sad, not looking down on anything.
A howl showing he misses his owner is sad, not rude or disrespectful.
The howl expresses missing someone, which is sad, not short and rude.

meaning: gloomy and sullen
example: After losing the final game, Kenji sat morose and silent.
hook: Picture a kid slumped at the dinner table after a loss, scowling and refusing to speak. That is morose.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of morose.
Moral means good and right; it only looks like morose.
Both are bad moods, but furious is hot anger, not sulky gloom.

syn1.tip: Morose describes a sulky, gloomy mood. Picture someone who won't smile or talk after bad news.

sc1.stem: Usually cheerful, Ava became _____ after her best friend moved away, sulking in her room and refusing to talk at dinner.

traps.why: Bubbly fits "usually cheerful," but she changed after her friend left.
Relieved is a good feeling; sulking and refusing to talk are not.
Moral means good and honest; it doesn't describe a sulky mood.

sc1.tip: "Usually cheerful" signals a change, and "sulking" and "refusing to talk" describe a gloomy mood.

decoys.why: Ava is sulking and refusing to talk, which is the opposite of wildly silly.
Sulking quietly in her room is not wild, noisy, and full of energy.
The sentence is about Ava being gloomy after a loss, not about being fearless.
Nothing in the sentence is about believing things too easily; Ava is sulking.
Sulking and refusing to talk shows gloom, not good judgment.

traps.why: Bright and lively is the opposite of morose.
Calm is a pleasant quiet; morose is an unhappy, sullen quiet.
A morose person may be quiet, but from gloom, not shyness.

syn2.tip: Morose people sulk. If you can picture someone slumped and silent after losing, that is morose.

sc2.stem: Because the rain canceled the beach trip he had looked forward to all month, Theo stayed _____ all afternoon, staring out the window and barely speaking.

traps.why: Thrilled is the opposite of how a canceled trip would make him feel.
Relaxed is a pleasant calm; a canceled trip and silence suggest gloom.
Staring out a window might look curious, but the canceled trip points to gloom.

sc2.tip: "Because the rain canceled" a trip he had waited for, and "barely speaking" shows a sulky, gloomy mood.

decoys.why: Theo is staring out the window and barely speaking, so he is not wildly silly.
Barely speaking all afternoon is the opposite of being wild and noisy.
Theo barely speaks, so he is not showing strong, forceful feeling.
The sentence is about Theo's disappointment over rain, not about bravery.
Theo is gloomy and quiet, and nobody in the sentence is treated rudely.

meaning: wild, noisy, and full of energy
example: The rambunctious puppies tumbled over each other in the yard.
hook: Picture rambunctious puppies tumbling, yapping, and knocking over the water bowl all at once.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite of rambunctious.
Rambling means wandering or talking on and on, not wild and noisy.
Rambunctious kids are wild, but violent is far too strong.

syn1.tip: Say it out loud: rambunctious bounces and bumps like the noisy, wild energy it describes.

sc1.stem: The kindergartners were so _____ after the sugary party snacks that they raced around the classroom, shrieking and knocking over chairs.

traps.why: Sleepy kids don't race around shrieking; that's the opposite.
Rambling means wandering in talk; it doesn't explain racing and shrieking.
Sugar might make kids queasy, but queasy kids don't race around shrieking.

sc1.tip: "Raced around," "shrieking," and "knocking over chairs" all describe wild, noisy energy.

decoys.why: The kids raced around shrieking, so they were full of energy, not lacking it.
Shrieking and knocking over chairs is the opposite of quiet and shy.
Kids racing around after a party are excited, not gloomy and sullen.
Shrieking kids are trying to be noticed, not secretive.
The snacks made them wild, and the sentence describes behavior, not being round and plump.
Nothing shows the kids felt sorry; they were busy racing and shrieking.

traps.why: Quiet and still is the opposite of rambunctious.
Rambunctious kids may knock things over, but from energy, not slowness.
Rambunctious describes lively energy, not meanness.

syn2.tip: Think of a playground after a sugary snack: running, shouting, bumping. That wild, noisy energy is rambunctious.

sc2.stem: The twins sat silently through the long wedding ceremony, but once the music started at the party, they turned _____, sliding across the dance floor and shouting with glee.

traps.why: Bashful fits the silent ceremony, but "but" signals they changed.
Dancing can be graceful, but sliding and shouting show wild energy.
Shouting can be angry, but "with glee" shows happy energy.

sc2.tip: "But once the music started" signals a change from silence, and "sliding" and "shouting with glee" show wild energy.

decoys.why: Demure fits the silent ceremony, but the blank describes sliding and shouting at the party.
Sliding across the floor and shouting shows lots of energy, not slow relaxation.
The twins were shouting with glee, which is the opposite of gloomy.
Shouting with glee is happy, not sad and mournful.
Shouting on the dance floor is not trying to avoid being noticed.
The twins are gleeful, and nothing suggests they feel sorry for doing wrong.

meaning: to wear away slowly by chemical action
example: Salt water corroded the metal railing.
hook: Corrode shares a Latin root with rodent, meaning gnaw: picture rust slowly gnawing an old car's fender.

traps.why: Polishing makes metal shine, the opposite of corroding it.
Correct means fix a mistake; it only looks like corrode.
Heat melts metal quickly; corroding is a slow chemical wearing away.

syn1.tip: Corrode is what happens to a bike chain left out in the rain: it rusts and slowly wears away.

sc1.stem: Salty ocean air can slowly _____ the metal on seaside bicycles, eating away at the chains until they turn orange and crumble.

traps.why: Protecting the metal is the opposite of eating away at the chains.
Correct looks like corrode but means fix, which makes no sense here.
Ocean air feels cool, but cooling doesn't make chains crumble.

sc1.tip: "Eating away at the chains" and "turn orange and crumble" describe slow chemical damage to metal.

decoys.why: The air eats away the chains until they crumble, the opposite of making them fresh.
Salty air cannot judge the value of metal; it eats away at it.
The sentence is about metal crumbling away, not digging anything up.
The metal is being eaten away, not gathered in a large amount.
Air cannot prove metal innocent; the sentence describes chains crumbling.

traps.why: Build up is the opposite of wearing something away.
Smashing breaks things fast by force; corroding wears them away slowly.
Heat can change metal, but corroding is a slow chemical wearing away.

syn2.tip: Corrode shares a root with rodent, meaning gnaw. Rust slowly eats away metal the way a mouse gnaws.

sc2.stem: Dad wiped the old grill clean and gave it a fresh coat of paint, so rain would not _____ the metal and leave it full of crumbly orange holes.

traps.why: Strengthening is the opposite of leaving metal full of holes.
Rain does dampen things, but dampness alone doesn't leave crumbly holes.
Decorating is pleasant; crumbly orange holes are damage.

sc2.tip: Paint protects metal, "so" shows the reason, and "crumbly orange holes" describes rust damage.

decoys.why: Dad fears rain will leave crumbly holes, which is the opposite of making it fresh.
Rain leaving orange holes in metal has nothing to do with digging up something.
Rain cannot judge the grill's value; the worry is about crumbly holes.
The sentence is about metal wearing away into holes, not gathering things.
Rain cannot scold metal; Dad is worried about it rusting into holes.

meaning: short and rude in speech or manner
example: The busy clerk gave a brusque reply and turned away.
hook: A brusque reply is short and sharp, like a door shut in your face: "Not now."

traps.why: Polite is the opposite of brusque.
A brusque person isn't necessarily giving orders; brusque means short and curt.
Cruel means wanting to hurt; brusque is only short and rude.

syn1.tip: Brusque sounds like a quick brush-off. A brusque answer is cut short and rude.

sc1.stem: When Lily asked the librarian for help, he gave a _____ two-word answer and turned back to his computer without even looking up.

traps.why: A patient helper would look up and explain, the opposite of this.
A clever answer is smart, but turning away without looking shows rudeness.
He seemed rude, not enraged; furious is much too strong.

sc1.tip: "Two-word answer" and "without even looking up" show a short, rude manner.

decoys.why: A two-word answer without looking up is short and cold, not wild and noisy.
Turning away without looking up is rude, not a sign of good judgment.
The librarian barely answered and turned away, which is not silly or funny.
He ignored Lily without looking up, so he was not feeling sorry.
The answer was short and dismissive, not sad and mournful.

traps.why: Warm and friendly is the opposite of brusque.
Brusque is curt, not raging; loud and furious is much too strong.
Brusque people say little, but from rudeness, not shyness.

syn2.tip: Picture a busy clerk who says "Next" without looking up. That clipped, rude manner is brusque.

sc2.stem: Coach Patel is usually _____ with new players, barking orders without a smile; in other words, she is curt and impatient until they earn her trust.

traps.why: Gentle is the opposite of barking orders without a smile.
Generous is a kind word, but curt and impatient are not kind.
No smile could seem shy, but barking orders is rude, not shy.

sc2.tip: "In other words, she is curt and impatient" restates the blank, so it means short and rude.

decoys.why: The coach barks orders, which is not quiet, shy, and modest.
The sentence says she is curt and impatient, not easily bent or gentle.
She barks orders without a smile, so she is not wildly silly.
The sentence calls her impatient, the opposite of slow and relaxed.
Nothing suggests she feels sorry; the sentence says she is curt and impatient.

meaning: make extremely angry
example: The unfair call enraged the home crowd.
hook: Enrage puts you in a rage: picture a bad call turning a calm crowd into a roaring mob.

traps.why: To calm someone is the opposite of enraging them.
Engage means involve or hold attention; one letter separates it from enrage.
Annoy is too weak; enrage means make extremely angry.

syn1.tip: Find rage inside enrage. To enrage someone is to fill them with rage.

sc1.stem: Seeing litter dumped all over the freshly cleaned park was enough to _____ the volunteers, who had spent the whole weekend picking up trash there.

traps.why: Litter on their clean park would not please them; that's the opposite.
Amuse is a happy feeling; ruined hard work brings anger.
The weekend's work might tire them, but seeing litter would make them furious.

sc1.tip: "Who had spent the whole weekend picking up trash" explains why fresh litter would make them furious.

decoys.why: Seeing their hard work ruined would upset the volunteers, not make them feel fresh and lively.
Litter cannot hate anyone. The sentence needs a word for what the litter does to the volunteers.
Litter cannot scold the volunteers. The sentence is about how the litter makes them feel.
Litter cannot scold anyone. The sentence describes how the mess makes the volunteers feel.
Dumped litter does not prove the volunteers right. It ruins their weekend of work.

traps.why: Making someone peaceful is the opposite of enraging them.
Jealousy is a strong feeling too, but enrage means make furious.
Grumpy is too mild; enraged people are extremely angry.

syn2.tip: En- can mean put into, as in endanger. Enrage puts someone into a rage.

sc2.stem: Losing a board game usually just makes Marco shrug, but cheating will _____ him so much that he storms out of the room shouting.

traps.why: Relaxing is the opposite of storming out shouting.
Engage looks like enrage but means hold interest, not make furious.
Cheating might puzzle someone, but storming out shouting shows fury.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts a calm shrug with "storms out of the room shouting," so cheating makes him furious.

decoys.why: He storms out shouting, so cheating does not make him feel fresh and lively.
Cheating cannot hate Marco. You need a word for how cheating makes him feel.
Cheating cannot scold Marco, and mild scolding does not match storming out shouting.
Cheating cannot warn or scold Marco. The sentence is about his shouting anger.
Cheating does not prove Marco right. It makes him storm out shouting.

meaning: reject with scorn
example: The cat spurned the cheap food and waited for tuna.
hook: Picture a cat sniffing cheap food, lifting its nose, and stalking away: it spurns the meal.

traps.why: Accept is the opposite of spurn.
To spur is to urge on, like a rider and horse; spurn means reject.
Postponing puts off a decision; spurning firmly turns it down.

syn1.tip: Spurn means turning something down with a sniff. Picture a proud person waving away a gift.

sc1.stem: The proud chef would always _____ offers to sell his secret recipe, laughing at even the largest sums that food companies proposed.

traps.why: He laughs at the offers, so he certainly doesn't accept them.
Considering means thinking offers over; laughing at them shows scorn.
Requesting means asking for offers; he laughs at them instead.

sc1.tip: "Laughing at even the largest sums" shows he rejects the offers with scorn.

decoys.why: He laughs at the offers, so he is turning them down, not gathering them.
A proud chef laughing at offers is not begging for them.
You cannot prove an offer innocent. The chef laughs the offers away.
The companies bring the offers to him, so there is nothing hidden to dig up.

traps.why: Gladly welcome is the opposite of spurn.
Politely declining is gentle; spurning is rude and scornful.
Urge forward is what spur means; spurn is a different word.

syn2.tip: Spurn carries scorn. It is not a polite no but a proud, insulting refusal.

sc2.stem: Because Jordan had teased her all year, Mia decided to _____ his invitation to the party, tossing the card in the trash with a roll of her eyes.

traps.why: Tossing the card in the trash is the opposite of accepting.
Forgetting is accidental; tossing it with an eye roll is a deliberate rejection.
Answer is too general; the eye roll shows a scornful rejection.

sc2.tip: "Because Jordan had teased her" gives the reason, and "tossing the card" with an eye roll shows a scornful no.

decoys.why: Mia tosses the card in the trash, so she is not begging Jordan for anything.
Mia throws the invitation away with an eye roll instead of judging its value.
Mia throws the card into the trash. She does not dig it up.
Rolling her eyes and tossing the card does not prove the invitation right.

meaning: too ready to believe things
example: The credulous boy believed his brother's story about a dragon in the basement.
hook: Credulous holds cred, meaning believe, as in credit: a credulous person believes almost anything.

traps.why: Suspicious is the opposite of credulous.
Credible means believable; a credulous person believes too easily.
Cred means believe, but credulous describes believing others, not being worth believing.

syn1.tip: Cred means believe, as in credit. A credulous person believes things too easily, even silly stories.

sc1.stem: Only the most _____ students believed the rumor that the school would replace all homework with video games starting Monday.

traps.why: Doubtful students would not believe such an unlikely rumor.
Credible means believable; it describes the rumor, not trusting students.
Studious students work hard; believing a silly rumor shows being too trusting.

sc1.tip: "Only the most" and a rumor about video games replacing homework point to students who believe too easily.

decoys.why: Scornful students would mock the silly rumor, but these students believed it.
Wild energy might fit kids excited about video games, but the sentence is about believing the rumor.
The rumor is silly, but the sentence asks what kind of student would believe it.
Being gloomy does not explain why someone would believe an unlikely rumor.
Being messy has nothing to do with believing a rumor.
Feeling sorry for doing wrong does not make someone believe a rumor.

traps.why: Hard to fool is the opposite of credulous.
Credulous people may believe scary tales, but credulous is about believing, not fear.
Cred means believe, but credulous describes the believer, not the story.

syn2.tip: Credulous people fall for tricks. Picture someone believing a friend who says there's a dragon in the basement.

sc2.stem: While her older sister instantly saw through the prank, _____ little Rosa really believed the cat had learned to talk.

traps.why: Suspicious fits the sister, but "while" sets Rosa against her.
Clever is praise, but believing a cat can talk is not clever.
Curious kids ask questions; believing the cat talks shows trusting too easily.

sc2.tip: "While" contrasts Rosa with a sister who "saw through the prank," so Rosa believes too easily.

decoys.why: Rosa really believed the cat could talk, so she was not looking down on the prank.
A talking cat is silly, but the contrast is that Rosa believed it.
Being wild and noisy does not contrast with her sister seeing through the prank.
Being quiet and shy does not explain why Rosa believed the prank.
Being round and plump has nothing to do with believing a prank.
Nothing in the sentence shows Rosa was gloomy. The point is that she believed the trick.

meaning: showing that you look down on something
example: She gave a scornful laugh at his silly excuse.
hook: Scornful means full of scorn: picture a nose in the air and an eye roll at someone's cheap sneakers.

traps.why: Admiring is the opposite of scornful.
Scolding means telling someone off; scornful means looking down on them.
Disappointment is sadness at a letdown; scornful means looking down on someone.

syn1.tip: Split it: scorn plus -ful, full of. Scornful means full of scorn, sneering at what seems beneath you.

sc1.stem: The famous chef gave a _____ sniff at the frozen pizza, as if the very idea of eating something so cheap were beneath her.

traps.why: She thinks the pizza is beneath her, so she is not delighted.
Pizza is about eating, but the clue is her looking down on it.
A polite sniff makes no sense when she thinks the pizza is beneath her.

sc1.tip: "As if the very idea of eating something so cheap were beneath her" shows she looks down on the pizza.

decoys.why: Sniffing can mean crying, but here the chef thinks the pizza is beneath her.
The chef feels above the pizza, not sorry for doing something wrong.
A modest, shy sniff would not show that she thinks the pizza is beneath her.
Believing things too easily has nothing to do with sniffing at cheap food.
She is openly showing that the pizza is beneath her, not hiding her sniff.

traps.why: Respectful is the opposite of scornful.
Scornful people may be calm; scorn is looking down on, not rage.
Playful teasing is friendly; scornful is cold and superior.

syn2.tip: Picture a curled lip and a sniff. That sneering, superior look is what a scornful person wears.

sc2.stem: Since Jake thought he was the best skater in town, he gave a _____ laugh whenever younger kids fell, which made many of them quit coming to the park.

traps.why: A kindly laugh wouldn't drive kids away; that's the opposite.
A nervous laugh shows worry, but Jake thought he was the best.
A cheerful laugh wouldn't make kids quit; his laugh was mean.

sc2.tip: "Since Jake thought he was the best" explains why he looked down on others, and kids quitting shows the laugh mocked them.

decoys.why: Jake thought he was the best, so his laugh did not show he felt sorry.
A boy who thinks he is the best does not give a shy, modest laugh.
Jake was laughing at kids who fell, so his laugh was not sad.
Believing things too easily has nothing to do with laughing at kids who fall.
A slow, lazy laugh would not show Jake thought he was better than the younger kids.

meaning: to warn or scold firmly
example: The librarian admonished us for talking too loudly.
hook: Picture a lifeguard blowing her whistle and wagging a finger at a running kid: she admonishes him.

sc1.stem: Before the field trip, Ms. Ruiz had to _____ the class sternly, reminding them that anyone who wandered off would spend the day on the bus.

traps.why: Praise doesn't fit "sternly" or a threat of sitting on the bus.
Entertaining is fun; a stern reminder of consequences is not.
Teachers count students on trips, but a stern reminder is a warning.

sc1.tip: "Sternly" and "anyone who wandered off would spend the day on the bus" point to a firm warning.

decoys.why: Ms. Ruiz speaks sternly and threatens a day on the bus, so she is not begging.
A stern warning about staying on the bus would not make the class happy and excited.
She is warning the class, not judging their value or quality.
Ms. Ruiz is warning the class, not proving them right or innocent.
A stern reminder about wandering off is a warning, not something that refreshes the class.

traps.why: Compliment is the opposite of admonish.
Admit means confess; it only shares a start with admonish.
Explain is too general; admonish means a stern correction.

syn2.tip: Admonish has a stern feeling. Think of a librarian's sharp "Shh" after you talk too loudly.

sc2.stem: Although the puppy looked adorable chewing his new sneakers, Mateo had to _____ it with a firm 'No' and take the shoe away.

traps.why: A firm 'No' and taking the shoe away is the opposite of rewarding.
Cuddling fits adorable, but a firm 'No' is a scolding.
Admire looks like admonish, and fits adorable, but not a firm 'No'.

sc2.tip: "Although" warns that cuteness won't win, and "a firm 'No'" shows Mateo scolds the puppy.

decoys.why: A firm No is a scolding, not begging the puppy.
Saying a firm No and taking the shoe would not make the puppy happy and excited.
Mateo is scolding the puppy with a firm No, not judging its value.
The puppy was chewing his sneakers, so Mateo is not proving it innocent.
Nothing is hidden. Mateo stops the puppy with a firm No.

meaning: round and plump
example: The rotund pumpkin won first prize at the county fair.
hook: Rotund and round both come from Latin rotundus; picture a rotund snowman built from three big snowballs.

traps.why: Skinny is the opposite of rotund, which means round and plump.
Rotund looks like rotate, but it describes a round body, not spinning.
Muscular describes strong bodies; rotund is about being round and plump.

syn1.tip: Rotund sounds like round. Think of a rotund pumpkin: round and plump.

sc1.stem: The _____ walrus, shaped like a giant barrel and weighing nearly two tons, flopped heavily onto the ice.

traps.why: Slim is the opposite; a barrel shape is round, not thin.
Nimble means quick and light, but this walrus flopped heavily.
Frozen fits the ice, but the barrel shape describes a round, plump body.

sc1.tip: Look at "shaped like a giant barrel" and "nearly two tons." You need a word for a round, heavy body.

decoys.why: The clue is shape, but a barrel shape means round and plump, not easily bent.
The walrus flopped heavily, which is the opposite of wild and full of energy.
A two-ton walrus flopping heavily is not trying to go unnoticed.
The sentence describes the walrus's barrel shape and weight, not a shy personality.
Nothing shows the walrus looking down on anything; the clues describe its round body.
The sentence is about body shape and weight, not about believing things.

traps.why: Slender means thin, the opposite of rotund.
Rotten looks a bit like rotund, but it means spoiled.
Huge is about size; rotund is about a round, plump shape.

syn2.tip: Hear the word round inside rotund. A rotund body is round and chubby.

sc2.stem: Unlike his skinny brother, who could slip through any gap in the fence, Marco was so _____ that his round belly got stuck halfway.

traps.why: Lanky means tall and thin, like the brother, not Marco.
Clumsy is about movement; a round belly is about body shape.
Rotten looks like rotund but means spoiled, which makes no sense here.

sc2.tip: "Unlike his skinny brother" sets up a contrast, and "round belly" confirms Marco is round and plump.

decoys.why: Being easily bent would help him slip through, but his round belly got stuck.
Sneaking through a fence fits secrecy, but the clue is his round belly getting stuck.
Being wild and noisy would not make his round belly get stuck.
The contrast with his skinny brother is about body size, not shyness.
Getting stuck might annoy him, but the blank describes why he got stuck: his round belly.
Believing things too easily has nothing to do with a belly stuck in a fence.

meaning: to twist and squirm
example: The worm writhed on the wet sidewalk.
hook: Writhe is related to wreath, a ring of twisted branches; picture a worm twisting itself into a little wreath.

traps.why: Freezing means holding still, the opposite of twisting and squirming.
Write sounds a bit like writhe, but it means putting words on paper.
Someone in pain might scream, but writhe means twisting the body.

syn1.tip: Picture a worm on a hot sidewalk. The way it twists and wiggles is how things writhe.

sc1.stem: When Tara placed the earthworm on the dry paper, it began to _____, twisting and curling its body as it searched for damp soil.

traps.why: Relaxing is the opposite of twisting and curling.
Stretching makes a worm long and straight, not twisting and curling.
The worm wants soil, but on dry paper it can only twist.

sc1.tip: The words "twisting and curling its body" describe the missing action, so pick the word that means squirming.

decoys.why: The sentence describes twisting and curling movements, not crying sounds, and worms make no sounds.
The worm is twisting and curling in place, not rushing along out of control.
A worm has no hands or feet, and the sentence describes twisting, not climbing.
A slow, relaxed walk does not match a worm twisting and curling on dry paper.
The worm is struggling on dry paper, not recovering from illness.
A worm searching for damp soil has nothing to brag about.

traps.why: Straighten is the opposite of twist.
Wither looks like writhe, but it means to dry up and shrink.
Worms crawl, but writhe means twisting and squirming in place.

syn2.tip: Writhe is related to wreath, a ring of twisted branches. Writhing is twisting your body.

sc2.stem: Because the scratchy wool sweater itched so badly, Leo began to _____ in his seat during the long concert, unable to keep his body still for even a minute.

traps.why: Relaxing means staying calm, but Leo could not keep still.
A long concert might make you sleepy, but Leo could not keep still.
People clap at concerts, but itching makes you squirm, not clap.

sc2.tip: "Because the scratchy wool sweater itched" is the cause, and "unable to keep his body still" is the effect: squirming.

decoys.why: Leo stays in his seat, so he cannot be walking in a relaxed way.
Leo is stuck in his seat, not rushing along and swerving.
Leo is not climbing; he cannot keep his body still in his seat.
The itchy sweater makes him uncomfortable, so he is not recovering from anything.
An itchy sweater gives Leo nothing to brag about.
Leo is a person squirming in his seat, not metal wearing away.

meaning: to walk in a slow, relaxed way
example: We sauntered along the boardwalk eating ice cream.
hook: Picture a cowboy sauntering into town, thumbs in his belt, in no hurry at all.

traps.why: Dash means to run fast, the opposite of a slow, relaxed walk.
Marching is walking too, but stiff and purposeful, not relaxed.
Saunter is a kind of moving, but it means a slow, relaxed walk.

syn1.tip: Picture someone sauntering along a boardwalk eating ice cream, slow and in no hurry.

sc1.stem: While the other runners sprinted to the finish line, Felix chose to _____ across it, smiling lazily and waving to the crowd as if on a holiday walk.

traps.why: Racing is what the others did; Felix did the opposite.
Stumbling is clumsy, but smiling lazily shows a relaxed walk.
Leaping takes a burst of energy; lazily shows he walked slowly.

sc1.tip: "While the other runners sprinted" sets up a contrast, and "smiling lazily" and "holiday walk" show a slow, casual walk.

decoys.why: Felix smiled lazily as if on a holiday walk, not rushing and swerving.
Crossing a finish line on a flat course needs no climbing with hands and feet.
Felix is smiling and waving calmly, not twisting and squirming.

traps.why: Rushing is the opposite of a slow, easy walk.
Pacing nervously is walking with worry; sauntering is calm and carefree.
Marching is stiff and firm; sauntering is loose and lazy.

syn2.tip: Sauntering has a lazy, happy feeling, like a slow walk on vacation.

sc2.stem: With no homework due and the whole summer afternoon ahead, Maya would _____ down to the corner store, stopping to pet every dog and admire every flower she passed.

traps.why: Sprinting is fast, but stopping at every dog shows a slow walk.
You can drive to a store, but not while petting every dog.
Trudging is slow but tired and gloomy; Maya's afternoon is carefree.

sc2.tip: "No homework due" and "the whole summer afternoon ahead" make Maya relaxed, and stopping for every dog shows a slow, easy walk.

decoys.why: Maya stops to pet dogs and admire flowers, so she is not rushing out of control.
Walking down to the corner store needs no climbing with hands and feet.
Maya is strolling and relaxed, not twisting and squirming.

meaning: to climb awkwardly using hands and feet
example: The kids clambered over the rocks at low tide.
hook: Clamber sounds like climb plus clumsy; picture kids clambering up a snow pile on hands and knees.

traps.why: Gliding is smooth and easy, the opposite of a clumsy climb.
Clamor looks like clamber, but it means to shout noisily.
Hikers may climb, but clamber means climbing awkwardly with hands and feet.

syn1.tip: Clamber sounds like climb. Picture kids clambering over rocks at low tide, using hands and feet.

sc1.stem: The children had to _____ up the steep, rocky slope on their hands and knees, grabbing at roots and stones to pull themselves higher.

traps.why: Gliding is smooth, but they crawled on hands and knees.
Tumbling means falling down, but they were pulling themselves higher.
Strolling is easy walking; hands and knees shows a hard climb.

sc1.tip: "On their hands and knees" and "grabbing at roots and stones" show a clumsy climb using hands and feet.

decoys.why: The children are on their hands and knees on a steep slope, not walking relaxed.
Grabbing roots to pull themselves higher is slow work, not rushing out of control.
They are climbing upward with hands and knees, not twisting in place.

traps.why: Going down gracefully is the opposite of climbing up clumsily.
That is clamor, which looks like clamber but means shouting.
Clumsy climbers might fall, but clamber means climbing up.

syn2.tip: Hear climb inside clamber, then add clumsy: hands, knees and feet all working hard.

sc2.stem: The cat leapt gracefully onto the top bunk in one jump, but my little brother had to _____ up the wobbly ladder, gripping each rung and kicking his legs.

traps.why: Leaping is what the cat did; but shows your brother moved differently.
