Gliding is smooth; gripping and kicking show a clumsy climb.
Clamor looks like clamber but means to shout noisily.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the cat's graceful jump with your brother "gripping each rung and kicking his legs," a clumsy climb.

decoys.why: Gripping each rung and kicking his legs is awkward climbing, not a relaxed walk.
Your brother moves slowly up the ladder rung by rung, not rushing out of control.
The sentence shows him climbing a ladder, not twisting and squirming in place.

meaning: to scold mildly
example: Mom chided me for leaving my shoes on the stairs.
hook: Chide rhymes with side; picture Mom calling you to her side to chide you for muddy shoes.

traps.why: Praise means to say good things, the opposite of scolding.
Hide rhymes with chide, but it means to keep out of sight.
Punishing goes further than chiding, which is only a mild scolding.

syn1.tip: Picture Mom chiding you for leaving shoes on the stairs: a mild scolding, not a big punishment.

sc1.stem: Grandpa would gently _____ us for forgetting to close the gate, shaking his head and sighing, "How many times must I remind you?"

traps.why: You don't praise someone for forgetting; Grandpa is disappointed.
Teasing is playful, but his sigh shows real disapproval.
Punishing is too harsh; a head shake and sigh are mild.

sc1.tip: "Shaking his head and sighing" and "How many times must I remind you?" show gentle disapproval, a mild scolding.

decoys.why: Grandpa acts gently and just reminds them, which is far milder than rejecting with scorn.
Grandpa only sighs gently over a forgotten gate; he does not hate them.

traps.why: Praising is the opposite of criticizing.
Threatening is far too harsh; chiding is a mild scolding.
Teasing is for fun; chiding shows real disapproval.

syn2.tip: Chide has a disapproving but mild feeling, like a sigh and a head shake.

sc2.stem: Instead of yelling when I spilled juice on the new rug, Aunt Rosa would only _____ me softly, saying I should be more careful next time.

traps.why: No one thanks you for a spill; she wanted you to be careful.
Blasting someone is like yelling, and "instead of yelling" rules it out.
Teasing is joking, but she gave a serious warning.

sc2.tip: "Instead of yelling" means she did something milder, and "I should be more careful" shows she still scolded a little.

decoys.why: Aunt Rosa speaks softly instead of yelling, so she is not rejecting you with scorn.
Aunt Rosa only reminds you softly to be careful; she does not hate you.
The sentence is about Aunt Rosa's mild words, not about making you angry.
Aunt Rosa is speaking gently to you, not shocking and disgusting you.
Telling you to be more careful is a mild scolding, not making you excited.
Aunt Rosa is correcting your spill, not judging your value.

meaning: easily annoyed and whiny
example: The tired toddler became peevish and whined at everything.
hook: A pet peeve is something that bugs you; a peevish person acts like everything is a pet peeve.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of peevish, which means grumpy and whiny.
Tired kids often get cranky, but sleepy is not the same thing.
Furious is far too strong; peevish is small, whiny annoyance.

syn1.tip: Think of a pet peeve, something that annoys you. A peevish person is easily annoyed.

sc1.stem: Having skipped his nap, the little boy grew _____ by dinnertime, complaining that his milk was too cold and his peas were touching his potatoes.

traps.why: Cheerful kids don't complain about cold milk and touching peas.
Missing a nap might make him sleepy, but the complaints show crankiness.
It was dinnertime, but complaining about food shows irritation, not hunger.

sc1.tip: The petty complaints, milk "too cold" and peas "touching his potatoes," show a boy who is easily annoyed and whiny.

decoys.why: Skipping a nap sounds sleepy, but his complaining shows irritation, not slow relaxed calm.
Tired kids can be wild, but the sentence describes whining complaints, not noisy energy.
He is complaining about his food, not feeling sorry for anything he did.
A boy loudly complaining about his peas is not quiet, shy, or modest.
Nothing in the sentence is about believing things; he is complaining about everything.
He did not get round and plump by dinner; the clue is his grumpy complaining.

traps.why: Always calm is the opposite of easily annoyed.
Sadness is a different bad mood; peevish means grumpy and irritable.
Rage is much too strong for small, whiny grumpiness.

syn2.tip: Peeve is inside peevish. Something that peeves you annoys you.

sc2.stem: My sister is usually sweet and patient, but after a long day at summer camp she turns _____, snapping at anyone who asks her a simple question.

traps.why: Gentle matches "usually sweet," but "but" signals a change.
A long day can tire you, but snapping shows irritation.
Quiet people don't snap at others; snapping shows she is irritable.

sc2.tip: "Usually sweet and patient, but" signals a change, and "snapping at anyone" shows she becomes easily annoyed.

decoys.why: Snapping at people is the opposite of being quiet, shy, and modest.
She snaps at people; nothing shows she feels sorry for doing wrong.
She is tired after camp, but snapping at people shows irritation, not relaxed slowness.
The sentence is about snapping at questions, not about believing things too easily.
She snaps openly at everyone, so she is not secretive or trying to hide.
Making mistakes has nothing to do with snapping at people who ask questions.

meaning: to rush along while swerving out of control
example: The sled careened down the icy hill.
hook: Picture a runaway shopping cart careening down a hill, swerving wildly with nobody steering.

traps.why: Creeping is slow and careful, the opposite of careening.
Careening may end in a crash, but careen means swerving along.
Careening is a kind of moving, but wild and out of control.

syn1.tip: Picture a sled careening down an icy hill, rushing and swerving with no one steering.

sc1.stem: Hitting a patch of ice, the runaway shopping cart began to _____ wildly across the parking lot, lurching left and right before crashing into a snowbank.

traps.why: Gliding is smooth, but the cart was lurching wildly.
It crashes at the end, but first it swerves across the lot.
Freezing fits the ice, but the cart was moving wildly.

sc1.tip: "Runaway" and "lurching left and right" show the cart was rushing along out of control, swerving wildly.

decoys.why: The cart moved wildly and crashed, which is the opposite of a slow, relaxed walk.
The cart slid across flat ice; it did not climb using hands and feet.
The cart rushed across the lot; twisting and squirming in place does not fit.
Rusting away slowly cannot make a cart lurch wildly across a parking lot.
A shopping cart cannot brag; the sentence describes it swerving out of control.

traps.why: Gliding smoothly is controlled, the opposite of careening.
Careening can lead to a crash, but it means swerving wildly.
Speed is part of it, but careening means swerving, not going straight.

syn2.tip: Careen has a wild, scary feeling, like a cart lurching left and right with no driver.

sc2.stem: Grandma drives her car slowly and steadily, but my cousin let his go-kart _____ around the track, bumping walls and sliding on every sharp turn.

traps.why: Creeping is slow, like Grandma, but "but" signals the opposite.
Parked karts don't bump walls or slide around turns.
An idling kart sits still, but this one was sliding around turns.

sc2.tip: "Slowly and steadily, but" sets up a contrast, and "bumping walls and sliding on every sharp turn" shows wild swerving.

decoys.why: The sentence contrasts the cousin with slow, steady Grandma, so a relaxed stroll is backwards.
The go-kart slid around a flat track; it did not climb with hands and feet.
The go-kart sped around the track bumping walls, not twisting and squirming in place.
Wearing away slowly does not explain bumping walls and sliding on sharp turns.
A go-kart cannot brag; the sentence describes it sliding out of control.

meaning: an uneasy feeling of doubt or guilt
example: She had no qualm about speaking in front of the whole school.
hook: Having qualms means a queasy, uneasy feeling about a choice; no qualms means you feel completely fine doing it.

traps.why: Confidence is feeling sure, the opposite of a qualm.
Calm sounds like qualm, but it means peaceful and relaxed.
Terror is far too strong; a qualm is a small uneasy feeling.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "no qualms about it," which means having no doubts at all.

sc1.stem: Hiro felt a slight _____ about copying his friend's homework, an uneasy twinge of guilt that made him close the notebook and do the work himself.

traps.why: A thrill is excitement, but Hiro felt an uneasy twinge of guilt.
Calm sounds like qualm, but Hiro was uneasy, not peaceful.
Confidence is the opposite of the guilt and doubt Hiro felt.

sc1.tip: "An uneasy twinge of guilt" restates the blank, so you need a word for a nagging feeling of doubt or guilt.

decoys.why: The sentence calls it an uneasy twinge of guilt, not laughter and amusement.
He felt uneasy and guilty, which is the opposite of showy boldness.
Copying is trickery, but the blank is his uneasy feeling of guilt about it.
He felt guilt, not an illness; the sentence calls it an uneasy twinge.
He chose to do the work himself, so he got no break from anything.

traps.why: Being certain is the opposite of having a qualm.
That describes calm, which sounds like qualm but means something else.
Sadness is a bad feeling, but a qualm is doubt or guilt.

syn2.tip: A qualm is a small nagging feeling that something might be wrong, like a twinge of guilt.

sc2.stem: Although everyone else jumped off the high dive without a second thought, Priya had a _____ about the height and stood at the edge for ten minutes.

traps.why: A thrill would make her jump; she stood frozen with doubt.
Calm sounds like qualm, but a calm diver would just jump.
A dream about heights doesn't explain standing at the edge so long.

sc2.tip: "Although everyone else jumped without a second thought" contrasts with Priya waiting "for ten minutes," so she had an uneasy doubt.

decoys.why: The high dive is tall, but Priya had a doubt about it, not a crack in the earth.
She hesitated at the edge from doubt, not because she had an illness.
Standing nervously at the edge is not a break from something unpleasant.
She stood silently at the edge; nothing says she gave a long, angry speech.
She felt uneasy about the height, not disapproval aimed at someone.

meaning: shock and disgust greatly
example: The litter on the beach appalled the visiting students.
hook: Appall comes from an old French word meaning to grow pale; something appalling can drain the color from your face.

traps.why: Delight means to please greatly, the opposite of appall.
Appeal looks like appall, but it means to attract or ask.
Annoy is too weak; appall means to shock and disgust greatly.

syn1.tip: Think of the word appalling, used for something so bad it shocks and disgusts you.

sc1.stem: Photographs of beaches buried under plastic trash are enough to _____ anyone who cares about sea turtles and other ocean life.

traps.why: No one who loves sea turtles is delighted by trashy beaches.
Amuse is a happy feeling, but buried beaches are upsetting.
Annoy is too mild for beaches buried under plastic trash.

sc1.tip: Beaches "buried under plastic trash" would horrify "anyone who cares about sea turtles," so pick a word for strong shock and disgust.

decoys.why: Beaches buried in trash would upset turtle lovers, not make them happy and excited.
Photographs cannot wear people away by chemical action; they shock the viewer.
The photos show a disgusting mess; they do not prove anyone right or innocent.
Photos cannot hate people; the people would hate what the photos show.
Photos do not judge the value of people who care about sea turtles.

traps.why: Please is the opposite of appall.
Applaud starts like appall, but it means to clap in approval.
A surprise can be pleasant; appall means a shocked, disgusted feeling.

syn2.tip: Appall has a strong negative feeling. Picture your face going pale at something disgusting.

sc2.stem: The guests expected a tasty meal, but the moldy bread and the hair in the soup were enough to _____ even the least picky eaters at the table.

traps.why: Delight fits a tasty meal, but "but" signals a disgusting one.
Meals feed people, but moldy bread and hair would disgust them.
Applaud looks like appall but means to clap, which makes no sense here.

sc2.tip: "Expected a tasty meal, but" signals a letdown, and "moldy bread" and "hair in the soup" would shock and disgust anyone.

decoys.why: Moldy bread and hair in soup would disgust guests, not make them happy and excited.
The food cannot hate the eaters; the eaters would be disgusted by the food.
Moldy bread cannot wear away eaters by chemical action; it shocks and disgusts them.
The food does not judge the value of the eaters; it disgusts them.
Bad food proves nobody right or innocent; the guests expected a tasty meal.

meaning: make very happy and excited
example: The roller coaster's huge drop exhilarated every rider.
hook: Exhilarate shares a root with hilarious; both come from a Latin word meaning cheerful.

traps.why: Bore is the opposite of exhilarate, which means to excite.
Exhaust looks like exhilarate, but it means to tire out.
A big ride can frighten you, but exhilarate is a happy feeling.

syn1.tip: Picture the huge drop on a roller coaster that leaves every rider thrilled and cheering.

sc1.stem: Sledding down the steepest hill in town never failed to _____ the twins, who shrieked with joy all the way to the bottom.

traps.why: Bored kids don't shriek with joy.
Exhaust looks similar but means to tire out, not to thrill.
Shrieking can mean fear, but these were shrieks of joy.

sc1.tip: The twins "shrieked with joy all the way to the bottom," so the sledding must have filled them with excitement.

decoys.why: The twins shrieked with joy, so the sledding thrilled them rather than disgusted them.
The twins shrieked with joy, not anger, all the way down the hill.
A sled ride cannot scold anyone; the twins were shrieking with joy.
Sledding did not warn or scold the twins; it filled them with joy.
Sledding cannot hate the twins, and the twins clearly loved the ride.
The ride proved nothing; the clue is that the twins shrieked with joy.

traps.why: Sadness is the opposite of the joyful excitement exhilarate means.
Exhilarate shares a root with hilarious, but it means thrill, not make laugh.
Fear is the wrong feeling; exhilarate is joyful excitement.

syn2.tip: Exhilarate is a strong positive word for the joyful rush you feel on a fast ride.

sc2.stem: Long car rides usually bore my little brother, but the first glimpse of the ocean through the window seemed to _____ him, and he bounced in his seat cheering.

traps.why: Soothing calms you down, but he bounced and cheered.
Exhaust looks like exhilarate but means tire out; he was full of energy.
Car rides can make kids sick, but cheering shows joy.

sc2.tip: "Usually bore..., but" signals the opposite of boredom, and "bounced in his seat cheering" shows the ocean thrilled him.

decoys.why: He bounced in his seat cheering, so the ocean delighted him rather than disgusted him.
He was cheering, which shows excitement, not anger.
The ocean view cannot scold him; it made him bounce and cheer.
The ocean did not reject him; seeing it made him cheer happily.
The ocean cannot hate him, and his cheering shows he loved seeing it.
Seeing the ocean proved nothing; the clue is his excited bouncing and cheering.
